This model has become a key aspect of the intervention approach within Indigenous communities and is seen to have particular application in addressing community justice issues. This article examines a suite of community justice initiatives being used in Indigenous communities in Australia with a view to ascertaining how the principles of community engagement are operationalized. The article draws on this information and argues that community engagement is only one aspect of a number of community-oriented justice initiatives currently being applied. These initiatives range from concepts of community as a location, community as an interest group, and the leveraging of community capital so as to tap into and build better and stronger relationships. In so doing, the latter attempts to increase the social infrastructure, resources and capacity of communities. However, despite government attention in this area, there is a lack of a policy and programmatic framework to guide a coherent and apposite approach to issues of community in specific policy settings. The article contributes to the development of a framework that begins the process of differentiating and assessing justice administration interventions. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Water: Changing the Course of the Titanic?
authors: Alario, Margarita V; Freudenburg, William R
abstract: Although some of the most provocative sociological thinking about risks is associated with Anthony Giddens & Ulrich Beck, past assessments have judged the more nuanced views of authors such as Short & Erikson as being sociologically superior, both as theory and as guides to empirical interpretations. The key difference is that, while Giddens & Beck see the risks of "The Risk Society" as transcending all social boundaries, the world we inhabit is one of what we have called Titanic Risks. As was the case for the ill-fated ocean liner, the entire ship may have sunk, but the actual risks were strongly related to victims' positions in society and in space. Still, past assessments have focused on highly specialized, "advanced" technologies, such as those involving nuclear materials; the question is whether similar conclusions would emerge from analyzing older or more basic technologies. To answer that question, we turn to what may be the most fundamental of all human resource needs -- water. International organizations began devoting serious attention to the significance of water, including potential conflicts over access, during the 1980s, leading eventually to the 2003 United Nations Report, Water for People, Water for Life. Natural resources in general, & water in particular, have been the focus of growing significance for the systematic study of environmental risks, & the end of the Cold War has intensified the search for appropriate social scientific models for understanding their relevance for new constellations of world conflict. In this examination, we find that insufficient or degraded water access often serves as a proxy variable for global environmental conflicts linked to poverty & gender inequality. For water as well as weapons, sociological approaches to risk, exemplified by Short & Kai Erikson, prove to be superior to the emphasis on technological mega-risks typified by Giddens & Beck. Far from "transcending" social boundaries, the risks of the 21st century wind up reinforcing & exacerbating them.

title: Legitimacy and Public Administration; Constructing the American Bureaucratic Fields
abstract: Legitimacy claims can only be made and processes of legitimation can only unfold in a specified context. This article uses Pierre Bourdieu's concept of the social field to name this context and to analyze the construction of the bureaucratic or public administrative field in the United States. Field is meant in a triple sense--public administration as a general, institutionalized field in the structure of government; public administration as a professional field; and public administration as an academic field of study. Thus, rather than the bureaucratic field, the relationship of these bureaucratic fields or an "ensemble of fields" is analyzed to consider how each field both bounds its own legitimation struggles and draws from other fields for symbolic resources--what Bourdieu called symbolic capital --to establish its legitimacy and position. The multifield quality of public administration is used to show how the nature of the general bureaucratic field is distinct from other fields insofar as it purports to represent a universal, general interest. This difference is used to theorize a distinction between "general" and "specific" legitimation processes.

title: Industrialization and Environmental Water Pollution in Developing Countries with a Focus on Tehran
abstract: The paper explores as to how far water is responsible for the environmental pollution mainly caused by unplanned or under-planned industrialization specially in the developing societies. Environmental water pollution may be defined as the unfavorable alteration of our surroundings, wholly or largely as a by-product of man's actions, industrial force and process, direct or indirect effects of changes in energy patterns, chemical and physical constitution of organisms etc. These changes may affect man directly or through his supplies of water. Environmental water pollution is concerned with our population too. When societies were small with thin populations and largely pastoral, no attitude usually gave rise to obvious pollution, but with the population increase, and the use of modern technology, the concept of water pollution was emerged, and it has now converted into an environmental crisis. Hence, with the increase of consumption per capita of food, detergents, fuels, chemicals, manufactured products of all kinds etc., more water is used, polluted, and wasted which eventually causes different kinds of pollution, so far as the environment is concerned. The paper explores that every use to which water has been put-including washing, irrigation, flushing away wastes, cooling, making papers etc., has been adding something to water, and creating environmental water pollution. The paper also analyses the major sources of water pollution and the resultant pathological effects. We will see that the developing countries still have a long way to go to solve/treat their water pollution problems as a result of unfair use of industrial development. If not so, generations to come, will face hazardous challenges so far as water use is concerned. Though the industrial water pollution is a new phenomenon, if adequate measures are not taken, developing countries including Iran, will have to pay a heave price for, particularly at the turn of the new century. Education on water use and economy must be put on the agenda by many countries. Also, controlling the industrial plants to minimize their pollution will help have safer ecosystem.

title: Making Decisions about Groundwater: Ecological versus Economic Considerations
abstract: The Ogallala aquifer, the largest known underground reserve of clean water in the world, is being depleted rapidly. Agricultural irrigation in the Great Plains accounts for the overwhelming majority of the water withdrawn from the Ogallala each year. From west Tex to southern SD, vast expanses of previously nonarable & marginal farm land are being planted in irrigated feed grain & forage crops. Recently published estimates of how long current levels of intensive irrigation will remain possible or economically feasible vary considerably. Despite this variability & the lack of precise projections, many wells have run dry in recent years & many more have shown substantial reduction in output. Irrigation with Ogallala water is essentially a mining operation of a scarce finite resource. Within fifty years, & probably much sooner in many areas, this mining will be complete. Identified are some of the central issues, actors, options, & ideological positions involved in the process of making decisions about Ogallala groundwater use. Data & observations are derived from intensive interviews with western Kan irrigators & loan officers; examination of Kan water agency policies & deliberations; & previous research. Primary consideration is given to the contradictory nature of long-term ecological concerns & the short-term profitability interests of capital intensive agriculture.

title: Pollution of River Ganga: An Environmental Concern
abstract: Rivers have been an integral part of human settlements right since the dawn of civilization. Some of the biggest and most populated cities of the world have developed along these riverbanks. The Ganga basin is the largest river basin of India and the Indo - Gangetic plain and it provides water to about 40 per cent of the Indian population. As such it is the backbone for various industrial, domestic and agricultural use of water in most of North India. The Ganga is also India's holiest river and holds a special place in the minds of devout Hindus. However, the water quality of the river Ganga has been deteriorating for a long time. This is mainly due to two reasons. Firstly, the withdrawal of a huge quantity of water for irrigational, industrial and domestic purposes. Due to this, flow of the river is severely reduced, especially in the dry months. Secondly, the discharge of domestic, industrial and agricultural waste into the river basin. Realizing the consequences of this pollution, the Government of India undertook a highly ambitious project to clean the Ganga and to restore its quality. Government was able to control the discharge of industrial pollution with the help of legal Acts. However, the Indian government is not able to control the discharge of domestic waste because it is linked with the ways of living. Hence, the community has to come up with some plans to restore the water-quality and the quantity of water in the river. In this paper, the author has tried to point out a few practices and attitudes which are the casual factors for the decay of water quality of Ganga. The practices are given below: (1)Burning of (human) bodies on the banks of rivers, especially on the Ganges; (2)Immersion of dead-bodies of persons who have premature death due to poisons, snake bites, burns etc.; (3) The practice of washing dirty clothes (in the river) by washer men using phosphate contained detergents; (4) The attitude of masses towards the immersion of clay-idols and bathing in the river of Ganges at certain time. The above-mentioned practices are degrading water-quality and are making the situation so bad that some reports have mentioned about possible lack of potable water in the country in another three decades or so. [Author abstract shortened by Sociological Abstracts].

title: Notes from the Underground: On the Nineteenth-Century Urban Water Economy
abstract: Increasing population density in nineteenth-century cities disturbed the equilibrium between micro-organisms & their human hosts as used water flowed back in the supply channels carrying disease agents. Poverty & filth were believed to be the cause of the resultant cholera epidemics, but they seemed impervious to reform. Only when the causal chain was understood could a feasible program of sanitary reform be advanced. This nevertheless provoked dilemmas of collective action, which were overcome because city areas became socially more homogeneous, & dwellings in the wealthier neighborhoods were connected to a common water supply & sewerage network. By the time the city was saturated with these networks, the remaining poorer areas were compulsorily connected, & water supply & sewerage became public goods.

title: Linguistic Minority Rights in the Danish-German Border Region: Reciprocity and Public Administration Policies
abstract: Language equality is not public policy in Denmark or Germany, and neither country has adopted an official state language constitutionally. Both countries protect minority languages through regional and local statutes on culture and education and have signed relevant international standards on linguistic rights for minorities and protection of regional or minority languages. Neither system is very transparent, nor comprehensive. This has created consternation and dissatisfaction among the national minorities residing in the Danish-German border region resulting in recent tensions in the municipalities in Southern Denmark, whereas the government of Schleswig-Holstein decided in 2015 to address the issue with policy reforms for public administration. This article focuses on linguistic minority rights in the Danish-German border region with specific attention to minority languages in public administration and specifically to the on-going reforms in Schleswig-Holstein.

title: Book reviews -- Beyond Bureaucracy: Essays on the Development and Evolution of Human Organization by Warren Bennis / The Case for Bureaucracy: A Public Administration Polemic by Charles T. Goodsell
abstract: Review.

title: Where the Waters Divide: Governance, Inequality, and First Nations: An Ethnography of the Changing Canadian Water Sector
abstract: This ethnography-an in-depth look at First Nations' reflections & experiences concerning the significant changes in systems, institutions, & practices of drinking water distribution in Ontario elucidates the social spatial inequalities & injustices associated with the recent restructuring & re-regulation of the (drinking) water sector in Canada. Why single out like First Nations in my analysis of public drinking water? Many First Nations communities have been & continue to be the recipients of a disproportionate share of environmental & health risks when compared with their larger, & usually more affluent, upstream or adjacent municipal relative. The purpose of this research is to draw public attention to these inequalities. I argue that the transformation of the drinking water systems, institutions, & practices in Canada has been the subject of intense social struggle for First Nations; a struggle for access to resources, & a struggle for participation in & control over decision-making processes, legislation, & land-use practices that affect the health & welfare of their communities.

title: Subsidies and Agricultural Polution [How Much Do We Have To Pay Farmers to Control Their -- -- -- -- (Manure)?]
authors: Lovejoy, Stephen B; Bouwes, Nicolaas W, Sr
abstract: Reported are preliminary results from an assessment of a water quality project in Ru Wisc. This project was instituted to curb nonpoint source water pollution resulting from the run-off of animal wastes in this predominantly agricultural watershed. Investigated were attitudes about & effects of various levels of cost-sharing assistance, society's "optimal" level of cost-sharing assistance, & the rationales of cooperating farmers for their participation. The existing level of cost-sharing assistance does not seem efficient from a societal view, at least not in terms of greatest benefit for least dollars. In order to establish optimal or at least more efficient levels of cost-sharing assistance (from both an economic & political viewpoint), greater bureaucratic flexibility in levels of cost-sharing assistance as well as more extensive evaluation of the agricultural community's willingness & ability to pay for measures which improve or protect water quality are recommended.

title: Designing Planning for Natural Resources: A Study of Desired and Achieved Planning Outcomes in Federal Water Resources Programs
authors: Bolton, Patricia A; Lord, William B; Chase, James A
abstract: Using the judgments of a purposive sample of 146 Rs who had participated in federal water resources planning at the local (nonnational) level, selected from 12 different planning projects within 5 federal water resources programs, investigated was what participants in the water resources planning arena think the planning process should achieve. Using the 4 outcomes of responsiveness to local problems & concerns, responsiveness to national goals & objectives, conflict resolution, & public understanding, a social judgment technique was used to tap what Rs thought should be the relative importance of each outcome. Rs were asked to assess the level of attainment of each of these planning outcomes for a complete planning effort in which they had participated. The findings are: (1) responsiveness to local problems & concerns is considered the most desirable of the four outcomes, while responsiveness to national goals is given virtually no emphasis at all; & (2) responsiveness to local problems are observed to have been given the most attention in past planning activities, with responsiveness to national goals in second place -- compared to its last place position for desired outcomes. Such differences among the Rs are more strongly correlated with participants' roles in the planning process than with the particular federal program in which participation had occurred. Except when the principal planning focus for a federal water resources program is carefully defined & explicitly stated at the federal level, the local problem-solving objective will likely become the principal planning focus.

title: An Analysis of the Social Impacts of the Availability and Provisions of Water in Rural Kentucky
abstract: Based on information from a comprehensive survey of the 418 Ru water supply systems in Ky, data are compiled on the proportion of the Ru population unserved by public water supplies, & the quality of water in their wells, cisterns, etc. Also, analyzed are the financial & physical characteristics of public water supply systems. Several significant social impacts of the current situation in Ru Ky are revealed. Among these are: the presence of industrial customers in a system raises the residential water rate 20 -- 50%; the development of new water systems in Ky usually means the extension of existing systems rather than water resources development projects, thereby placing increasing pressure on the resource base; water systems which buy water from another system tend to charge their customers more than customers in the "selling" system must pay resulting in periphery systems making up the losses of the central system producing water, & the apparent lack of any economies of scale in the relationship between operating costs & size of population served. Interpretation of these findings is pessimistic in view of the needs for Ru water system development: switching from poorer quality individual systems may only substitute a different set of problems for Ru residents. Institutional modifications may be in order in the arrangements for providing public water service in Ru areas.

title: Water, Power and Gender: Pressing Questions and Overlooked Interests in a Poor and Crowded Delta
abstract: Because of the prominence of water in production (primarily for irrigation) & in domestic use (drinking, washing, cooking), conflict over water & the effects of gender-influenced decisions about water have far-reaching consequences on human well-being, economic growth, & social change. At the same time, social conflicts & social change are shaped & mediated, often in unexpected ways, by the natural conditions in which water occurs. This paper examines some of the issues relating water & gender in the particular social & environmental conditions of Bangladesh. First, extraction of groundwater for irrigation has made many drinking water handpumps run dry. Second, this irrigation extraction has also been associated with the poisoning of at least 20 million people through the release of naturally occurring arsenic into the groundwater. Third, the paper examines some of the ways access to water has been changed by the rise of shrimp aquaculture for export. The literature has tended to focus on the implications of gender analysis for government policy, especially development projects & water resources management, & for women's organization. In this paper, we begin to sketch some questions that arise from a concern to understand the tripartite interaction of gender, water, & power in the broader context of social change.

title: In search of the glass ceiling: gender and recruitment to management in Norway's state bureaucracy
abstract: There are still fewer female than male managers in Norway's state bureaucracy. This article asks if there are organizational barriers which prevent women from entering these positions. Is there really a glass ceiling, or must one look outside the organizational environment to find an explanation? Is it rather the case that the scarcity of female managers is caused by women's own preferences or their life situations outside work? Or do both contribute to the situation? The study shows that female managers are treated just as well as male managers in central parts of the state bureaucracy. Employers give equal shares of respect and attention to both genders. Female managers are encouraged to apply for the same number of jobs as men and are offered an equal number of jobs as men when they apply; in fact, women are offered more jobs than men, when one controls for the number of job applications. This indicates that organizational barriers are not the problem. The study also shows that there are no differences in work orientation between male and female managers. Female managers are just as ambitious as male managers. Nor do female managers find it more difficult than male managers to combine work and family life. So, how can one explain the low number of female managers? The study shows that one reason can be that female managers apply for management jobs less often than their male colleagues. The cause of this seems to be anticipated discrimination rather than lack of ambition or self-confidence.

title: The Sociological Perspective and Policy Analysis
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency's 208 Water Quality Management program is examined from a sociological perspective. The utility of a "sociological imagination" for policy analysts, program evaluators, administrators, & consultants in analyzing the success or failure of public policy is addressed.

title: Obstacles to Effective Water Management in a Rural Development Scheme: The Case of the Mahaweli H System
authors: Jayewardene, Jayantha; Amerasena, Gamaathige; Parlin, Bradley W
abstract: An investigation of the ways in which elements of social organization impacts the implementation of a water delivery system in a Ru resettlement community in Sri Lanka. The questions posed are neither mutually exclusive nor exhaustive, but rather suggest important points of articulation between the social & technical systems that have implications for effective water use. The attitudes & skills that individuals bring to farming & irrigation systems can contribute significantly to its success, failure, & efficiency. Investigated are the comparative skills, resources, & knowledge of irrigation & agriculture of traditional villagers vs the formerly landless villages in the resettlement schemes. Also evaluated are the attitudes of the villagers toward the resettlement scheme & the irrigation bureaucracy. The nature of family life, including gender & age task differentiation & traditional networks of social obligation, can help or hinder project success; the existence of effective labor sharing traditions among farmers, kin, or friendship groups is considered. Explored are the links of contemporary & traditional community organizational structures to the technical system, the stability & effectiveness of the leadership structure, formal & informal organizations of water management (eg, users association or turnout groups), & the nature of the relationship between the farmers groups & the irrigation authority management. The economic subsystem plays a crucial linking role to the water delivery system. Examined are: the credit mechanisms to cover farmer inputs in good & bad crop years, local market development to support crop diversification policies, the economic contribution of handicrafters & household agricultural production of farm women.

title: Community Water Systems: A Typology
authors: Francis, Joe D; Jussaume, Raymond A, Jr
abstract: The phrase "information society" reflects the growing interconnectedness of all segments of society. As mass media, business, & interpersonal communications among all reaches of society have become more numerous, the traditional distinctions between Ru & Ur society have become less meaningful. Coupled with this pervasiveness of information transferral has been the influence of reverse migration trends of the past decade. Consequently, in many spheres of life, Ru & Ur societies are becoming more like one another. Perhaps nowhere else is this melding more obvious than in the demand for community services. These developmental processes are examined through an investigation of one central, critical, pervasive local service -- community water supply (CWS). Factor analysis was used to uncover the main dimensions of attributes that characterize Ru CWS systems, including a typology. Special emphasis is given to understanding how ownership patterns of CWS systems relate to the development, use, & larger service goals (or purposes) of the community. The analysis concludes with a theoretical interpretation of the results in terms of general community infrastructure & the consequences for residents in terms of who pays for, & who benefits from, the creation & modification of CWS services. Specifically, the case of Ru CWS systems & services is used as an example of how Ru society is becoming increasingly interwoven with other aspects of US society in this day & age of extensive communication & information transferral.

title: Towards a General Theory of Resource Use: Constructing Alternate Institutions to Cope with the Future and the Commons
abstract: Our objective is to delineate analytically a more generalized theoretical orientation regarding the management of water & other resources. We make no claim that we are constructing a general theory: our objective is more modest. We are intent on isolating steps that move the theoretical argument forward. Our theorizing is grounded in the research conducted for about a decade by the Douglas on a major social experiment underway in central Texas: the creation & development of the Edwards Aquifer Authority (EAA). A social regime has been constructed in order to manage the use of the aquifer's water usage in the event of a major drought. This particular case highlights basic processes that have been neglected by environmental sociologists & by sociologists more generally. In discussing some of these processes we stay in some instances relatively close to the data at hand, but in other instances the activities of the Aquifer Authority becomes the basis for outlining broader theoretical patterns & processes. Our analysis unfolds in the following manner: First, we briefly outline the growth and development of the Edwards Aquifer Authority in central Texas. Second, we specify our theoretical point of departure, employing as we do Walter Firey's pathbreaking book Man, Mind & Land (1960) as our take-off point for detailing our perspective. Among leading environmental sociologists Firey stands almost alone in privileging the cultural system. Yet he also stresses the interrelationships among the cultural, economic & ecological systems. Third, our analysis modifies & extends his framework in several differing respects. For example, & in contrast to Firey, we articulate an alternative conception of culture & stress the centrality of the political system. Additionally, the activities involving the creation of the Edwards Aquifer Authority suggests several fruitful areas for sociologists to examine (or reexamine as the case may be) including the role of the future; the nature of property; the construction of alternative institutions & organizations; & a reconceptualization of social planning in order to more effectively address the problem of looming water shortages & related, large-scale environmental issues confronting the globe.

title: Spectrum, trajectory and the role of the state in workers' self-management
authors: Upchurch, Martin; Daguerre, Anne; Ozarow, Daniel
abstract: This article examines self-management in the wider context of political economy and the role of the state. Most literature focuses either on labour process analysis or on social movement aspects of the phenomenon. Most importantly, there appears less emphasis on understanding the role of the state in shaping or reshaping practice, or the state is even eschewed as an inevitably conservative and bureaucratic independent agent. In developing our understanding, we utilise documents from Titoist Yugoslavia, and surveys and case study interviews conducted in Argentina and Venezuela. First, we examine self-management in Titoist Yugoslavia in the aftermath of the Tito-Stalin split of 1948. Self-management was a central policy of the Titoist regime as it sought to distance itself from authoritarian and bureaucratic Communism. Indeed, Yugoslavia has been used as a comparator yardstick in recent discussions of other experiments such as those in Chavez's Venezuela. To pursue this comparison, and make more sense of the role of the state and the market, we examine the particularities of the new movements for self-management and cooperative working in the contemporary Latin American arc of protest against neoliberalism, focusing on both Argentina and Venezuela. The national specificities of each of these two countries are different, with the recovered companies having emerged 'from below' in Argentina contrasting with the movement 'from above' as part of Hugo Chavez' Bolivarian Revolution and 'Twenty First Century Socialism' in Venezuela. In our examples, we present a model of spectrum and trajectory from which self-management can be judged within a frame of socialist transformation. We record the contextual factors which shaped the movements, and isolate the state's influence to either promote or contain them. In our conclusion, we analyse factors of continuity and change, and discuss the state's role in relation to these different episodes of workers' self-management. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: THE KEYNESIAN PARADIGM AND PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION
abstract: KEYNESIAN THEORY IN MACROECONOMICS AND PUBLIC FINANCE IN THE UNITED STATES WAS COMPATIBLE WITH A PARALLEL DEVELOPMENT IN THE PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION BRANCH OF POLITICAL SCIENCE THAT AROSE IN THE 1930'S GREAT DEPRESSION.  THE THEORY EMPHASIZED THAT THE INITIATIVE IN ACHIEVING WELFARE GOALS SHOULD BE TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT AGENCIES ACTING TO RESOLVE CONFLICTING INTERESTS.  THE ADMINISTRATORS EXPANDED GOVERNMENT INTO A NEW BUREAUCRATIC STATE BY INITIATING AND TAKING LEADERSHIP IN BRINGING ABOUT SOCIAL CHANGE.

title: Knowledge, Power and Environmental Reform: The Role of Experts and the Lay Public in Building a Sustainable Society
abstract: When the transition to an environmentally sustainable society is considered as a political question, what does it suggest about the capabilities & limitations of modern democratic government? Are environmental problems & reforms so complex & the task so urgent that the public must grant experts a predominant role in decision making? Given the challenges posed by environmental reforms to democratic institutions, the political roles presently played by knowledgeable professionals & everyday citizens in identifying environmental problems & fashioning policies are examined. Reviewed are William Ophuls on the politics of scarcity, Anthony Giddens on expert systems in modern society, & other social scientists on the relationship between government & resource management. A case study is also presented of CA's water scarcity & its recent water management reforms as an example of how expert knowledge, citizen activism, & policy making intersect. Briefly, analysis suggests that in absence of either a crisis that undermines the authority typically granted to those holding specialized, technical knowledge, or a sustained effort to educate & involve citizens in such complex issues, experts act conservatively to protect their (& other elites) privileged position, & the public acquiesces to the expert rather than actively press for sustainable alternatives.

title: Comparing Research-Supported Stakeholder Involvement in the Rhine and Amudarya Basins: Is It to Compare "Apples and Oranges?"
abstract: Stakeholder involvement is considered as one of the prerequisites for adaptive & integrated water resources management. It is closely linked to learning which is in the core of the adaptive management process. Participation is required by international agreements as well as by European environmental directives such as the Water Framework Directive. In order to support participation processes in water management, the EU FP 6 NeWater project (www.newater.info) encourages direct interaction of research & consultancy with stakeholders. Within the project, participatory processes are being supported in European case studies (Rhine basin) as well as beyond Europe (Amudarya basin). The research presented here builds on work within these two case studies & seeks answers to the following questions: what can research induced processes change in the existing water management practice & what are prerequisites for such processes to function properly? We also discuss how far research induced participatory processes help practitioners to engage on their own in the future or if involvement of researchers is rather impeding for future initiatives. We also draw on the question in how far the two participatory interventions are comparable, as they have started out with similar motivations, but have to cope with fundamentally differing background conditions. The research builds on a range of data sources. The authors had a leading role in the case study work & setting up of the respective participatory processes. Empirical data used for this research includes meeting documents & minutes, interviews, evaluation documents as well as observations. In the case studies, research & consultancy worked closely with the respective water associations & supported tasks such as the stakeholder analysis, process design & facilitation as well as evaluation. Both processes recently ended (spring 2008) & were successful in meeting the set process goals.

title: 'Street-level Bureaucracy' Revisited: The Changing Face of Frontline Discretion in Adult Social Care in England
abstract: This reassessment of the continuing significance of Lipsky's (1980) work on 'street-level bureaucracy' for frontline decision making is based on a retrospective review of the author's research on assessment practice in adult social care in England. The studies span the past two decades during which time successive governments have restructured and modernized social services departments. When these were established in 1970, they represented the high watermark of bureau-professionalism - a mode of administration which dominated social welfare at the time Lipsky was writing. The subsequent dismantling of bureau-professionalism calls into question the validity of his findings, and the author draws on her own research to assess conflicting views about the impact of social care reforms on the discretion which social workers exercise as street-level bureaucrats. She concludes that the distinct types of discretion to emerge from her findings, represented in a taxonomy, are shaped by the differing micro environments of frontline practice which, in turn, affect the relative force of managerialism, professionalism and user empowerment in countering the defensive exercise of discretion described by Lipsky. Whilst her analysis affirms the continuing significance of Lipsky's analysis, it also points to the need for some revision to accommodate major shifts in welfare administration since the publication of his work. She highlights the potential relevance of these insights for investigating the next planned transformation of adult social care, personalization, as well as for the implementation literature more widely. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Public Participation in Water Resource Management in South Africa under the New National Water Policy - A Means to Equity and Sustainability? A Case Study of the Inkomati Basin
authors: Sherwill, Tamsyn; Rogers, Kevin; Fig, David
abstract: Public participation is an integral part of South Africa's new water policy and offers the potential to achieve much-needed social and environmental change. The National Water Act (1998) enables the devolution and decentralization of decision-making power to a local, catchment-delineated scale, through the establishment of Catchment Management Agencies. These are to be governed by a board containing both stakeholder representatives and resource management expertise. However, this combination of decentralization and participation does not in itself add up to greater equity and sustainability of resource use. It is also possible that the structure and process of participation enhances existing power imbalances, resulting in decisions that perpetuate past inequities. This issue was examined in a case study of a three-year participatory process held toward the establishment of the country's first Catchment Management Agency in the Inkomati basin. This study was based on both written records and personal observation of this process, and contributions within workshops by a variety of participants and other role-players. Though some successes were noted, particularly in the education of stakeholders regarding the new water law, the overall process appears to have favored the interests of the historically advantaged, and delivered few rewards to marginalized communities. Key factors influencing this outcome were the general use of a 'public meeting' format, little attempt at prior capacity building for disadvantaged participants, and a highly restrictive agenda designed to deliver the specific requirements of government, but which also coincided most strongly with the main concerns of established resource users.

title: Effect of Rural Industrialization on Residential Water Costs in Kentucky
abstract: Based on information from a comprehensive survey of over 400 Ru water supply systems in Ky, data from existing sources & a mail survey are compiled on the proportion of the Ru population unserved by public water supplies, & the quality of water in the systems serving the Ru population. Also, analyzed are the financial & physical characteristics of the public water supply systems. Numerous significant social & environmental impacts are documented. One of the most important for studies of the effects of industrialization on Ru communities is the finding that residential customer water rates are 20% to 50% higher when industrial & commercial customers are also supported. The reasons for this higher rate structure are examined, & the findings are related to similar studies in the literature. Findings support the contentions of the growing number of critics of industrialization as the primary strategy in Ru development.

title: ''Committing the Truth'': Whistle-Blowing, Organizational Dissent, and the Honorable Bureaucrat
abstract: Several studies reported in current management literature address the issue of organizational dissent, or ''whistle blowing.'' Willbern (1984) discusses types or levels of morality for public officials, while Hart (1984) comments on the unique moral obligations of the public administrator, arguing that resignation is an abdication of responsibility.  A 1980 survey of federal employees by the Merit Systems Protection Board categorized organizational members by their reactions to wrongdoing.  Results of Dyer and Dyer's (1984) survey of 1,000 business administration students' reactions to the television series MASH provide some indirect support for the Merit Systems survey's conclusion that the difference between those who blow the whistle and those who do not is that the latter are not willing to jeopardize their careers.  Parmerlee used O'Day's (1974) framework as a guide in studying organizational retaliation against whistle blowers to determine how retaliatory tactics varied with dissenters' characteristics.

title: Performance-Based Contracting in Social Welfare Programs
abstract: The Wisconsin Works (W-2) program changed the administrative structure for social welfare services delivery from county government administration to one that includes performance-based contracting and private sector management of programs. We present a theoretical discussion of government contracting and the implications of alternative contract structures for service provider behavior and performance. We then analyze W-2 contract design and management across four contract periods (1997-2005) as the state transitioned to a performance-based contracting regime. We find that the state made rational changes in the W-2 contract specifications and performance measures that should have improved contract efficiency and effectiveness over time, and service providers responded to these changes in allocating effort toward the achievement of priority performance goals. At the same time, deficiencies in program administration and contract management contributed to some contract and performance failures and setbacks.

title: Attitudes toward Alternative Uses of a Reservoir: A Longitudinal Assessment
authors: Napier, Ted L; Goe, W Richard
abstract: Data were collected in 1980 from 303 adult residents of a reservoir-impacted community situated in the Ru fringe of a large metropolitan area in central Ohio. Rs were asked to evaluate four alternative uses of the project: flood control, water supply, recreation, & fish & wildlife. The data were disaggregated according to Rs' length of residence (+/- 5 years) & analyzed using multivariate statistics. Findings show that residents become significantly more positive toward flood control, water supply, & recreation uses over time. Fish & wildlife conservation uses were perceived very positively by Rs of both groups. Regression findings reveal the vested-interests model to be useful in predicting variance in the four uses evaluated. The best predictive variable is attitude toward recreationists.

title: Agriculture and Production Process: A Comparative Study of Three Villages of Marathwada Region of Maharasthra
abstract: This paper is based on an intensive study of three villages of the Marathwada region of the Maharasthra state of India.. The selected villages differ from each other on the basis of irrigation facility and development of agriculture. The first village is selected amongst the villages having canal irrigation facility where as the second village is selected from the ground water irrigated villages category. The third village is selected amongst the dry villages which completely depend upon the monsoon for its sustenance agriculture. The data collected from the field reflects wide variation in the production process of the village agriculture. The canal irrigated village cultivators are more tempted to go for cash crops like, Sugarcane, Soybean, Wheat & other staple food crops because of assured irrigation facility, where as the ground water irrigated village cultivators are cultivating crops like, vegetables, cotton, Turmeric & other staple food crops. The Ground water is costly & not available so easily. In the Canal and Groundwater irrigated villages, cultivators apply more fertilizers, pesticides, & use modern agricultural implements and depend upon hired labourers in the production process. The third, dry village cultivators are cultivating the crops like, Cotton, Soybean & other staple food crops completely depending upon monsoon. The production process in the dry village reveals that the agriculture still depends upon monsoon & the practice is traditional. The above study reveals that assured irrigation facility has a definite impact on the production process. It has diversified agricultural economy by encouraging farmers to go for cash crops which are having market demand. Productivity of crops have increased many fold & there by helped in increasing net income of the farmers. This scenario is not visible in dry village, as the agriculture is still dependent on vagaries of nature.

title: River Pollution and Local Environmental Action
abstract: Water pollution, namely fresh water pollution, is a severe problem in today's world, one that is associated with water scarcity and constitutes one dimension of the increasingly acknowledged "water crisis". In a time of mounting concentration of population in urbanized areas, urban rivers are under intense pressure, originated by industrial & domestic waste waters, land usage and intrusion on both their beds & margins. The Tinto river, a tributary of Douro - one of the main rivers of the Iberian Peninsula - runs across three cities in the Porto Metropolitan Area, the second largest & most populated urban agglomeration in Portugal. This river has been affected by pollution problems along the last few decades a & still is, despite residents' protests and interventions by political authorities. A local environmental group emerged from this scenario, defining the rehabilitation of the river as their primary objective. Using data from interviews and documental analysis, this paper intends to rebuild the history of the Tinto's degradation, stressing its social causes & the measures adopted to address the issue, as well as the local environmental group's origins & its role in the acknowledgement of & response to the problem.

title: Silent professionalization: EU integration and the professional socialization of public officials in Central and Eastern Europe
authors: Meyer-Sahling, Jan-Hinrik; Lowe, Will; van Stolk, Christian
abstract: This paper applies theories of international socialization to examine the impact of European Union contact on the professional socialization of public officials in Central and Eastern Europe. Based on a survey of officials in seven new member states, the paper finds that daily work on European Union issues is associated with favourable attitudes towards merit-based civil service governance. The distinction between types of European Union contact shows that officials dealing with 'reception'-related European Union activities such as the transposition and implementation of European Union policies develop more meritocratic attitudes. By contrast, 'projection'-related activities that involve personal contact with European Union officials have no effect. The paper concludes that the small but consistent impact of European Union contact on professional socialization promotes the silent professionalization of public administration in Central and Eastern Europe.

title: Spatial Distribution of Population, Water Resources and Sustainability in Sao Paulo State, Brazil
abstract: The subject of this paper is the study of the relationships between demographic dynamics and water questions. The purpose is to verify the existence and facts which effect environmental limits, especially the limits that can result from water shortage, and the implications of these limits over the local sustainability. Limit is usually defined as the utmost point, degree, or extent beyond which something no longer functions, avails. In this paper limit is seen as a turning point from which there is significant change. Overtaking the environmental limits in a region that would lead to a crucial change in the life quality of the population that lives or is related to that region. The paper focuses on water availability and kinds of water use in three regions of Sao Paulo State (Brazil): Metropolitan Region of Sao Paulo, Piracicaba/Capivari/Jundiai River Basin and Pontal do Paranapanema. Water consumption was divided into three categories: urban consumption (basically residential use); industrial consumption and irrigation. The data show the differences of consumption in each region, and through this it was possible to identify, for example, the impact of demographic dynamics or economic activity on the demand for water resources. One conclusion is that, even in a place where there is an important volume of water, water can become a limiting factor to improving quality of life of the population and to economic development in function of inadequate use. Another conclusion is the necessity of a population redistribution policy, that takes into account the availability of natural resources, especially water.

title: Sustainable Development and Municipalities: Getting the Prices Right
abstract: Municipalities can play an important role in promoting sustainable development by pricing services correctly. How we pay for municipal services has an impact on our behaviour: how much water we consume, how much waste we generate, whether we drive to work or take transit, and other economic decisions. How we pay for services and infrastructure also affects the nature, location, and density of development. Correct pricing will improve the efficiency with which resources are used to provide the services that residents and businesses want. Moreover, if cities are interested in pursuing compact development, they need to consider the impact of other financial tools (such as property taxes and development charges) on how cities grow and develop.

title: Development and Health: Improved Water Supply and Childhood Nutrition in the Philippines
abstract: Diarrheal disease is the leading cause of infant & child mortality in the world. Frequent bouts of diarrhea have been linked to a greater incidence of undernutrition in children. Increases in the quantity & quality of water supplies should reduce the incidence of diarrhea & undernutrition by aiding the removal of infectious agents. Data collected over a 5-year period for an experimental group, which was provided access to a municipal water system, & a control group, which was not provided such access, in 2 Philippine cities are assessed to gauge differences in childhood undernutrition & changes in those disparities over time.

title: People's Participation and Water Management in the State of Gujarat
authors: Rao, Hemixa V; Merchant, Amrapali M
abstract: Gujarat state is situated in the Western part of the country. Most half of the populations of this state are badly affected with water scarcity & water crisis because 250 towns & cities & 1800 villages having a very serious problem of drinking water. The demand of water is continuously increased due to over population, urbanization, industrialization & the changes of consumption pattern. Monsoon is very irregular & very uncertain, so there are very huge water crises in the state. We divide the state in the three parts in the geographical context, 1. Central Gujarat, 2. South Gujarat & 3, Saurashtra & Kutch. There is different geographical environment in these three regions it affects on the water resources & water management. Saurashtra & Kutch region is facing permanently scarcity of water & most of the time drought. After independence this state is facing water crisis, almost eight times. There were very huge conflicts for the hesitation on water problems. Water problem is very crucial problem because this is directly affected on economical, social & cultural development of region. The supply is less compare to demand. Where as in South Gujarat region there is a opposite situation. More than 2 crores of the population is badly affected drinking water problem in the state. Government has taken various steps to solve the water problem; still this problem is remaining unsolved. There is huge movement of people's participation for rainy water conservation movements in Saurashtra there are three types of people participation in the movement: 1.Voluntary Organization; 2. Water co-operative society; 3. Water panchayat; 4. Water company. There are many NGOs of the state who have tried to solve the water problem. Some NGOs trustees, institutions, religion institutions, etc, have joined the movement of water revolution. Orpat Charitable Trust, Agakhan Gram Samarthan Programme, Sarathi, Saurashtra Jaldhara Trust, Gujarat Ambuja Foundation, Vivekanand Research & Training Institute etc. are prime institutions of the water revolution through people revolution. We have a brilliant example of the Andhra Pradesh in which Satyasaibaba Charitable Trust have solved the drinking water problem of 700 villages. In the district of Bhavnagar, Amreli, Jamnagar & Junagadh more than 15000 Check dams have been constructed through peoples participation & more than 40,000 Check dams have been constructed in the Saurashtra & Gujarat. In the Jamka water construction model, there are various advantages of people participation for water conservative movement. The cost of construction of check dams is very low, the maintenance cost is zero & we are able to maintain qualitative standard due to people participation movement. Rural unity between different castes has become stronger. Agricultural production, productivity, income have increased so many times. Therefore rural development becomes high. Political destructive problems are reduced. Rural development movement becomes fast. Rural infrastructure becomes speedier.

title: The Third Sleeve; Emerging Labor Newspapers and the Response of the Labor Unions and the State to Workers' Resistance in Vietnam
abstract: This article focuses on how the Vietnamese General Confederation of Labor (VGCL) responds to workers' strikes. A complex, non-monolithic VGCL has developed a "third sleeve," its dynamic pro-labor press, which plays strategic mediating roles among the state, labor unions, and management. The labor newspapers use their forums to champion workers' rights and interests and empower labor unions that negotiate with state bureaucracies and management on the workers' behalf. Simultaneously, the labor press must respond to policies and agendas of the VGCL and the state, which still hold to their power to monitor and control workers' collective action.

title: Greek Society and Risk Assessment for the Year 2000
abstract: As anthropogenic transformations of modern Greek society occur -- ie, regional population imbalances & the resulting phenomenon of hyperurbanization, economic growth, & development -- insufficient consideration for water resources utilization will create shortages. The aim here is to develop a water resources risk assessment framework for the year 2000 that will incorporate: (1) a comprehensive water-resources utilization planning scheme; & (2) an improved water resources management uncertainty framework involving responses for extreme shortages-floods, public participation, & development of public information channels.

title: Barriers to enrollment in drug abuse treatment and suggestions for reducing them: Opinions for drug injecting street outreach clients and other system stakeholders
authors: Appel, Philip W; Ellison, Aletha A; Jansky, Hadley K; Oldak, Rivka
abstract: Alcohol and other drug abuse (AOD) treatment is a major means of HIV/AIDS prevention, yet clients of street outreach programs (SOP) who are injection drug users (IDU), and outreach workers and staff as well, report various obstacles to enrolling clients in AOD programs. This study assessed the barriers to AOD enrollment facing high risk street outreach clients and obtained suggestions for reducing them. Data were obtained from semistructured field interviews with: 1) IDU outreach clients (N = 144) of the six SOPs in New York City (NYC) and northern suburbs supported by the Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS), the single state agency in New York State for AOD prevention and treatment, 2) outreach workers and staff of the six SOPs (N = 55), 3) staff of detox and AOD treatment programs in major modalities treating IDUs (N = 71), and 4) officials and administrators (N = 11) in OASAS, the AIDS Institute of the Department of Health (addresses all aspects of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in New York State), and the agency for public assistance in New York City, the Human Resources Administration (HRA). Principal barriers for street outreach clients included personal-family issues, lack of insurance/Medicaid, ignorance, suspicion, and/or aversion to AOD treatment (methadone maintenance especially), 'hassles' with Medicaid, lack of personal ID, lack of 'slots,' limited access to intake, homelessness, childcare-child custody issues. Further, about 18% had no desire for AOD services, reported no barriers, or were too enmeshed in addiction to enroll. Outreach staff cited prospective client's lack of ID and lack of Medicaid, lack of 'slots,' and stakeholder agency bureaucracy. Treatment staff cited lack of client readiness, 'hassles' posed by welfare reform, AOD programs' own 'red tape,' waiting lists, and near exclusionary preference for the Medicaid-eligible. Finally, agency managers cited client factors, inadequate funding and lack of appropriate programs, treatment program requirements, and societal stigmatization of addicts. Proposed remedies included dropping ID and insurance requirements for admission, major increases in resources, funding the transporting of outreach client treatment candidates to AOD services sites, education and training initiatives, increased inter-agency cooperation, and the need for stakeholder agencies, OASAS especially, to more effectively integrate abstinence-oriented AOD services with harm reduction and the public health aspects of AOD problems. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Factors Influencing Farm Operator Readiness to Implement Animal Waste Treatment Improvements
authors: Molar, Joseph J; Wu, Litchi S
abstract: Farmers face an increasingly critical public as the environmental consequences of many present-day farm practices are measured & recognized, eg, the treatment & disposal of animal waste. New regulations for drinking water & waste treatment are causing significant new costs for animal producers. Animal producer attitudes toward animal waste as a pollution problem & their relative readiness to implement changes in animal waste facilities & land application practices are examined via data obtained from a mail survey of producers of 5 watersheds in 2 northern Ala counties, with a dense population of chicken & beef production, & potential environmental problems associated with many small streams & limestone aquifers. Analysis focuses on the relative levels of problem perception & activation found among the animal producers, endeavoring to profile the personal & situational characteristics associated with problem perception as well as responsiveness to planning & financial assistance from public agencies.

title: The Process of Bureaucratization in the U.S. State Department and the Vesting of Economic Interests, 1886-1905
abstract: The effect of the bureaucratization of the US State Department from 1886 to 1905 on the development of vested interests in economic segments was studied.  Vesting of interests was defined as the extent to which a government agency takes the interests of a private industry or organization into account in policy-making and administration.  Analysis of data showed the interests of financial-industrial core industries became more vested, while those of affiliated and peripheral industries were stable or decreased.  Bureaucratization affected the pattern of vested interests through the institutionalization of particular tasks in routine administration.  In this way, vested interests in the bureaucratic structure became ''frozen''.      Appendices.

title: Studying fiascos: bringing public and foreign policy together
abstract: Mistakes happen. In politics no less than everywhere else. Their causes and consequences are at the heart of what scholars in public policy and foreign policy have always been interested in. Policy decisions in either field tend to attract much greater scholarly attention if they are seen to have gone wrong than if they are considered a success. It is small wonder, then, that many of the best-studied public and foreign policy episodes are precisely those which have been linked to ‘disastrous’ failures or consequences. Prominent examples in public policy include ‘planning disasters’ such as Sydney's Opera House, San Francisco's rapid transit system or the Concorde supersonic passenger jet (Hall 1980 Hall, P. (1980) Great Planning Disasters, London: Weidenfeld and Nicolson.); large-scale policy ‘blunders’ such as the Thatcher government's poll tax initiative and the attempt to introduce identity cards in Britain (Butler et al. 1994 Butler, D., Adonis, A. and Travers, T. (1994) Failure in British Government. The Politics of the Poll Tax, Oxford: Oxford University Press.; King and Crewe 2013 King, A. and Crewe, I. (2013) The Blunders of Our Governments, London: Oneworld.) or the European Union's (EU's) Common Fisheries Policy (Ritchie and Zito 1998 Ritchie, E. and Zito, A. (1998) ‘The common fisheries policy: a European disaster?’, in P. Gray and P. ‘t Hart (eds), Public Policy Disasters in Western Europe, London: Routledge, pp. 157–76.); as well as various ‘crises’ such as the Swedish monetary crisis of 1992 (Baggott 1998 Baggott, R. (1998) ‘The BSE crisis: public health and the risk society’, in P. Gray and P. ‘t Hart (eds), Public Policy Disasters in Western Europe, London: Routledge, pp. 63–80.) or the British bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) crisis in the 1990s (Stern and Sundelius 1998 Stern, E. and Sundelius, B. (1998) ‘In defence of the Swedish Crown: from triumph to tragedy and back?’, in P. Gray and P. ‘t Hart (eds), Public Policy Disasters in Western Europe, London: Routledge, pp. 137–54.). Well-researched cases in foreign policy, in turn, include the British policy of appeasement towards Nazi Germany in 1938 (Stedman 2011 Stedman, A.D. (2011) Alternatives to Appeasement: Neville Chamberlain and Hitler's Germany, London: I.B.Tauris.), the attempted occupation of the Suez Canal zone by Britain, France and Israel in 1956 (Gorst and Johnman 1997Gorst, A. and Johnman, L. (1997) The Suez Crisis, Abingdon: Routledge.), the inability of the United Nations (UN) peacekeeping mission to stop the Srebrenica massacre in 1995 (Brändström and Kuipers 2003 Brändström, A. and Kuipers, S. (2003) ‘From “normal incidents” to political crises: understanding the selective politicization of policy failures’, Government and Opposition 38(3): 279–305. doi: 10.1111/1477-7053.t01-1-00016[CrossRef], [Web of Science ®], [CSA]); as well as a number of cases in United States (US) foreign policy, like the failure to prevent the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941 (Wohlstetter 1962 Wohlstetter, R. (1962) Pearl Harbor: Warning and Decision, Stanford, CA: Stanford University Press.), the Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba in 1961 (Blight and Kornbluh 1998 Blight, J.G. and Kornbluh, P. (1998) Politics of Illusion: The Bay of Pigs Invasion Reexamined, Boulder, CO: Lynne Rienner.), the Vietnam War (Kaiser 2002Kaiser, D. (2002) American Tragedy: Kennedy, Johnson, and the Origins of the Vietnam War, Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.; Tuchman 1984 Tuchman, B.W. (1984) The March of Folly. From Troy to Vietnam, New York: Alfred A. Knopf.), the 1980 Iran hostage rescue mission (Smith 1985 Smith, S. (1985) ‘Policy preferences and bureaucratic position: the case of the American hostage rescue mission’, International Affairs 61(1): 9–25. doi: 10.2307/2619777[CrossRef], [Web of Science ®], [CSA]) or the 2003 Iraq War (Yetiv 2011 Yetiv, S.A. (2011) Explaining Foreign Policy: US Decision-Making in the Gulf Wars, 2nd edn, Baltimore, MD: Johns Hopkins University Press.).In both fields, the predominant concern of research has been with understanding and explaining why policy fiascos have occurred. In public policy, scholars have, for example, focused on competing values and motives of decision-makers, unrealistic policy objectives and expectations, increasing social and technological complexity, uncertainty, implementation failures or various deficiencies in decision-making, such as undue haste, incrementalism, competing bureaucratic interests and inadequate checks and balances (Bovens et al. 1998 Bovens, M., ‘t Hart, P. and Peters, B.G. (1998) ‘Explaining policy disasters in Europe: comparisons and reflections’, in P. Gray and P. ‘t Hart (eds), Public Policy Disasters in Western Europe, London: Routledge, pp. 195–214.; Dunleavy 1995 Dunleavy, P. (1995) ‘Policy disasters: explaining the UK's record’, Public Policy and Administration 10(2): 52–70. doi: 10.1177/095207679501000205[CrossRef]). In foreign policy, different theories have similarly identified numerous sources of fiascos, most notably cognitive biases and misperceptions (Janis 1989J anis, I.L. (1989) Crucial Decisions. Leadership in Policymaking and Crisis Management, New York: The Free Press.; Jervis 1976 Jervis, R. (1976) Perception and Misperception in International Politics, Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press.) or the emotions of individual decision-makers (McDermott 2004 McDermott, R. (2004) ‘The feeling of rationality: the meaning of neuroscientific advances for Political Science’, Perspectives on Politics 2(4): 691–706. doi: 10.1017/S1537592704040459[CrossRef]); socio-psychological dynamics in small decision-making groups (Janis 1982 Janis, I.L. (1982) Groupthink. Psychological Studies of Policy Decisions and Fiascos, Boston, MA: Houghton Mifflin.; ‘t Hart et al. 1997‘t Hart, P., Stern, E. and Sundelius, B. (eds) (1997) Beyond Groupthink. Political Group Dynamics and Foreign Policy-Making, Ann Arbor, MI: University of Michigan Press.[CrossRef]); or bureaucratic politics and an over-reliance on organizational routines (Allison and Zelikow 1999 Allison, G. and Zelikow, P. (1999) Essence of Decision: Explaining the Cuban Missile Crisis, Boston, MA: Little, Brown and Company.). Since decision-makers are expected to learn primarily from their own or others’ past mistakes (Howlett 2012 Howlett, M. (2012) ‘The lessons of failure: learning and blame avoidance in public policy-making’, International Political Science Review 33(5): 539–55. doi: 10.1177/0192512112453603[CrossRef], [Web of Science ®]), many accounts of public and foreign policy fiascos also seek lessons to avoid such mistakes in the future.

title: Voluntary Organizations as New Street-level Bureaucrats: Frontline Struggles of Community Organizations against Bureaucratization in a South Korean Welfare-to-Work Partnership
abstract: In recent years, the role of voluntary organizations in welfare partnership has received considerable critical attention from scholars working in the field. While mainstream debates have valued state-voluntary sector partnership as participatory governance, critical studies have argued that it leads voluntary organizations to serve as a shadow state. The present study, however, contends that partnership does not necessarily entail participatory welfare or the complete subordination of the voluntary sector to the state's bureaucratic system. Rather, as new street-level bureaucrats, voluntary organizations can exercise a degree of autonomy on the frontline despite the bureaucratic constraints engendered by partnership. Through an ethnographic analysis of Korean community organizations engaged as frontline agencies in a welfare-to-work partnership, this study unveils how the former have recreated democratic and inclusive environments in a particular policy setting by organizing non-work activities and transferring administrative authority to recipients. Delineating such street-level practices, this article demonstrates that state-voluntary sector partnerships may be sites of struggle where voluntary organizations continuously strive to actualize participatory governance in diverse and indirect ways.[PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Water Shortage in Ankara, Turkey and Disaster Management Policy
abstract: Disasters emerging as a result of interactive relations between nature and culture also have close connection with development policies. The concept of vulnerability has an important place in this relation. In this relationship, women are among the most vulnerable groups. Disaster management tries to reduce this vulnerability but any disaster management approach must recognize that while women can suffer from a disaster, they also have the capabilities to mitigate a disaster's effects. In this study, water cutting policy and its effects on the women living in Ankara, Turkey during the summer of 2007 are examined. The inquiry proceeds by using some concepts from Actor Network Theory. Due to a drought & water shortage accepted as the effects of global warming, Ankara decided to implement the "water cutoff policy" for three months during that summer. Throughout the policy's implementation, residents had access to fresh water only three days in a week. This situation adversely affected the women, especially those responsible for domestic work. In this paper, these conditions & women's capabilities are examined & a more comprehensive & sustainable water & disaster management policies based on Community Based Disaster Management approach is presented.

title: The Struggle against the Poisoning of Harlan County's Dayhoit: Fighting the Good Fight
abstract: In Feb 1989, state officials reported levels of vinyl chloride, trichloroethylene, PCBs, dichlorethene, lead, barium, & other chemicals in the well water of the community of Dayhoit, in Harlan County, to be considerably above federal EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) standards; this poisoning was caused by the nearby National Electric Coil plant. Residents were informed that while the state did not know the duration of their exposure to these toxics, their health was not likely to be adversely affected. The primary concern of most of the residents of Dayhoit was with the health of their children & themselves. Following their initial meetings with state & local officials, the citizens determined that the explanations to their most compelling questions were not forthcoming. They formed a citizens group whose membership included residents of the community, former workers, & other concerned citizens. The citizens group has had to confront seemingly indifferent county, state & federal governments plus the multinational corporation which owned the electric plant. Over the past two years, they have educated themselves about the deleterious consequences of multisyllabic poisonous chemicals, & discovered their personal fortitude to discern self-defined ends through cooperation, forged from grassroots activity. Proactive initiatives that they have implemented, including health tests & a community survey, are described.

title: Global Governance for Resource Dispute Resolution: Connections between Energy Scarcity, Ecological Conflict, and the Future of International Regimes for Addressing Environmental Crises
abstract: Numerous scholars in the social sciences, international relations, and other areas related to public policy have been discussing the evolving regimes of global governance over the last half-century, particularly as they relate to clearly international or global problems such as global warming & energy supplies. Some go so far as to argue that formal, constitutionally established international institutions are necessary to create binding mechanisms for adjudicating between conflicting parties & to seek justice for under-represented groups, such as indigenous peoples or very small countries. Others, recognizing the complexity of establishing such institutions & the traditional bounds of national sovereignty, suggest developing existing global governance mechanisms through the UN & other international political & economic organizations to implement strategies that are both democratic in principle and effective at solving international crises. In terms of environmental concerns, peak oil, global warming, and trans-boundary water conflicts, for example, all present unique and challenging problems that the societies of the twenty-first century will need to address. Do we have governance mechanisms in place that will prevent these issues from erupting into regional or global conflict? What are the specific mechanisms that are necessary to prepare for potential environmental problems that are unique in comparison to society's past problems? This presentation identifies specific problem areas in international energy and natural resource policies & considers the effectiveness of both existing global governance avenues & alternative models.

title: Governabilidade, Governança e Democracia: Criação de Capacidade Governativa e Relações Executivo-Legislativo no Brasil Pós-Constituinte
abstract: The article first offers some considerations regarding the concepts governability and government as used in the recent literature and, for analytical purposes, suggests the term governing capacity. In a context of economic reforms and democratization, Executive-Legislative relations form one of the key elements of governing capacity. Contesting Brazilian literature on this topic, the article grounds itself in basic policies on the agendas of the Collor and Itamar Franco administrations to argue that if there is a deficit in the implementation of a good share of economic stabilization policies and policies to open up trade, produced within relatively insulated bureaucracies, at the same time the structural reform policies submitted to Congress (social welfare, privatization, administration, taxation) have fallen short not just in the realm of implementation but in the realm of formulation as well. Underscoring the complexity of the policy-making phase, the text cites some causes, such as problems the government encounters in building stable majorities within Congress. Given this difficulty, the Executive must often engage in tough negotiations to get governmental policies approved, and it ends up entering into a pattern of conflict in its interactions with the Legislative branch. As a consequence, government leaders are tempted to favor the relatively insulated arena of bureaucracies over the parliament, with foreseeable consequences for the process of democratization within Brazil. Based on this scenario, the article asks what type of democracy Brazil can or is willing to build

title: `Without Affection or Enthusiasm' Problems of Involvement and Attachment in `Responsive' Public Management
abstract: The paper focuses on the changing ethical template that programmes of `responsive' or `entrepreneurial' managerial reform require of civil servants. Contemporary demands for responsive public management contain two emotional injunctions to public bureaucrats. The first, derived from populist doctrines of political right, requires bureaucrats to be responsive to the needs of their `clients'. In the name of `recognition' and the `politics of care', for example, it is thought vital to inculcate in bureaucratic conduct a sense of `compassion' or close identification with others' feelings. Secondly, in the name of responsiveness to political superiors and the delivery of their policy objectives, bureaucrats are expected to exhibit `ownership' of and identification with particular policies. They are required to be committed champions for and enthusiastic advocates of those policies. Both of these injunctions are deemed to be more in tune with democratic principles and the currents of contemporary ethical culture (`diversity' or `human rights', for example) than what is represented as the unlamented Weberian world of rule-bound hierarchy. The paper seeks to question this assessment.

title: Norm and Boundary of "Invisible" Water Use in the Terrace Paddies
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to clarify the mechanism to help to generate the norm & the boundary of 'invisible' water use in the terrace paddies. In the process of modernization, two different kinds of water have been clearly recognized as property rights. One is 'visible' water, river & pond, & the other is 'invisible' water, groundwater & river-bed water. The difficulty of the institutionalization of invisible water use in Japan has caused unfairness for farmers without water rights & also inefficiency of allocation of water in community. I did field research of a lakeside community in Shiga prefecture in Japan. Most of the farmers in the area have both paddies with water rights & paddies without water rights. Facing the constant shortage of the irrigation water, farmers without water rights invented devices to use invisible water. Irrigators recognize the rights of invisible water use as legitimatized property. Irrigators & non-irrigators have generated the communal norm of invisible water use & share the communal water rights. These interactional practices among the stakeholders with no water rights have made it possible to reconstruct the communal water rights.

title: Back to the nineteenth century: the managerial reform of the French civil service
abstract: The French civil service managerial reform initiated in 2007 was supposed to establish a brand new professional world where civil servants would be called to use new public management (NPM) methodology and tools in order to be more efficient and accountable. The final goal was to 'privatize' civil servants at least partially. Beyond the economic argument in a time of deep fiscal crisis, the rationale of the reform was political and philosophical, to eliminate the specificity of the civil service. The implementation of the reform and a massive reduction in force have produced systematic conflicts with unions, and most managers have rejected measures that had been designed to foster their individual motivation. A central argument of this article is to show that the values of this NPM reform run counter to those of a majority of civil servants and that public management is not politically neutral. Another argument, based on empirical surveys, is to demonstrate that this reform is of a conservative nature, designed to reinforce traditional hierarchies within the State bureaucracy. Finally, the so-called modernity of public management has produced an involution regression toward the social and professional structures of the nineteenth century. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Comparing Attitudes to Recycled Water: The Difference between Generalised and Salient Options
authors: Marks, June S; Martin, Bill; Zadoroznyj, Maria
abstract: Australia has experienced several years of drought resulting in increased activity in developing & implementing alternative water sources for major urban population areas. This paper investigates the hierarchy of acceptability of different water sources & different uses of recycled water, using data generated in a national telephone survey of seven Australian capital cities (n=2504). Following previous surveys, the least acceptable use of recycled water is drinking water sourced from highly treated sewage effluent. As this option is being planned for implementation in at least two cities, through a process known as 'indirect potable reuse', influences on acceptability were explored in depth. Firstly, the issue of salience was investigated through a number of scenarios put to respondents. These results were assessed against a number of demographic & attitudinal variables & then compared to those generated at three Australian sites where householders recycle water for garden watering & toilet flushing.
