The aim was to investigate whether people who are more familiar with safe uses of recycled water, & have developed an 'active trust' in the practice, are more confident in using this source for drinking after it has gone through a higher treatment process.

title: The Process of Bureaucratization in the U.S. State Department and the Vesting of Economic Interests: Toward Clearer Thinking and Better Historyeply
authors: Carstensen, Fred V; Werking, Richard Hume; Roy, William G
abstract: Roy (1981) examined US history in an attempt to locate the simultaneous processes of bureaucratization in the US State Department and the ''vesting'' of economic interest groups.  Instead of analyzing substantive policy, Roy utilized a new statistical compass to locate the shift from ''reactive'' to ''proactive'' conduct.  According to Roy, the standardized routine in itself protected, or vested, the outside economic interest.  Carstensen and Werking contend that Roy's approach is questionable; that his statistics do not support the interpretation he imposes on them; and that the landscape he explores bears little resemblance to the shape of American diplomatic and business history.  In his reply, Roy states that in the process of criticizing his paper, Carstensen and Werking became overinvolved in detail.  Roy claims that Werking and Carstensen have superimposed their agenda for studying the State Department upon his and that the resulting distortions have been further magnified through an intolerant attitude toward quantitative history.

title: Female Dam Migrants' Place in Regional and Urban Development: A Case Study of Keban Dam Female Migrants
abstract: Presents a comparative analysis of high dam development projects, differentiating their visible & invisible impacts & emphasizing women's involvement in them. In particular, migrants' ability to alter visible impacts is stressed: ie, the technical & physical appearances of a resettlement in an urban area & their power to establish new forms of relations, tenure structures, & forms of employment & social organization. A number of international projects are discussed & two Turkish cases are scrutinized. The findings presented are drawn from interviews with Keban Dam female migrants 20 years after their resettlement in an urban area. These findings show that the visible aspects of the project have been taken into account & the invisible ones have been overlooked. Results illustrate that social aspects of the Keban Dam urban resettlement were mainly dealt with by the women or migrants themselves. The transition from invisible experiences of the Keban Dam case to visible changes in relevant policies regarding the Southeastern Anatolia project is traced. The awareness of migrants' power to alter the results through their invisible participation & the necessity of reassessing policies relevant to high dam development & related resettlement projects are discussed.

title: Environmentalism: Urban and Rural Differences Revisited
abstract: A multivariate theoretical model on the individual & social determinants of environmental concern is tested using data collected through telephone interviews with a random sample of 330 Ur & Ru North Carolinians -- separately for Ur & Ru Rs as well as for the entire sample. The specific concerns examined are related to groundwater pollution, nuclear radiation, & soil erosion. It is shown that: formal education is positively related to environmental concern; younger people tend to be more concerned; evidence of sex differences is not conclusive; & income has an important, but inconsistent, relationship to environmental concern. Most research indicates that Ur residents hold stronger environmental attitudes than Ru residents. Political activism & orientation tend to also influence environmental concern. Also analyzed is the importance of different information sources relative to environmental issues -- including mass media, interpersonal sources, & formal organizations. Finally, Rs' willingness to pay for improved environmental quality is assessed, as are preferred government policy alternatives.

title: Public Agencies and Collaborative Management Approaches; Examining Resistance Among Administrative Professionals
authors: Kumar, Sushil; Kant, Shashi; Amburgey, Terry L
abstract: Resistance among administrative professionals to participatory approaches is analyzed by means of a case study involving the implementation of community-based forest management (CBFM) in India. The model consists of two dimensions of attitudinal resistance to change--disapproval of CBFM regime by forest managers (a) at individual level and (b) at organizational level--and four categories of factors influencing resistance: personality traits, organizational factors, external environmental factors, and socialization factors. The model is empirically tested using the perceptions of forest managers working in state Forest Departments of four states in India. The empirical findings are used to suggest strengthening of organization and public administration theories on four aspects and to suggest some specific measures to deal with the attitudinal inertia of public administrators.

title: Performance Management, Caseloads and the Frontline Provision of Social Services
abstract: Caseloads and performance management are important working conditions of workers delivering public social services in street-level organizations. The literature on these working conditions argues that high caseloads and performance management have considerable consequences for workers' performance in terms of the quality of services they provide and the results they realize. This article empirically investigates and compares these consequences, drawing on the results of a quantitative study of frontline workers in 14 local welfare agencies in the Netherlands. These workers are responsible for the delivery of welfare-to-work policies to social assistance recipients. The findings show that high caseloads do, indeed, have a detrimental effect on workers' performance, whereas the impact of performance management is more modest, though confirming some of the findings reported in other studies on performance management. The results also show that by focusing service provision on a proportion of their caseload, workers are able to reduce the negative impact of high caseloads somewhat. Overall, the article finds that the negative impact of high caseloads is more pervasive than that of performance management. The article concludes that the recent focus in the literature on performance management and its consequences for public services should not turn scholars' attention away from the 'traditional' public administration problem of high caseload sizes.

title: Financializing Desalination: Rethinking the Returns of Big Infrastructure
abstract: Against the trend prevalent during the 1990s and 2000s, large-scale infrastructural projects have made a comeback in the water sector. Although sometimes framed as part of a broader sustainable transition, the return of big infrastructure is a much more complicated story in which finance has played a crucial role. In the following article, we explore this encounter between finance and water infrastructure using the case of Britain's first experiment in desalination technologies, the Thames Water Desalination Plant (TWDP). On the surface, the plant appears to be a classic example of the successes of normative industrial ecology, in which sustainability challenges have been met with forward-thinking green innovations. However, the TWDP is utterly dependent on a byzantine financial model, which has shaped Thames Water's investment strategy over the last decade. This article returns to the fundamental question of whether London ever needed a desalination plant in the first place. Deploying an urban political ecology approach, we demonstrate how the plant is simultaneously an iconic illustration of ecological modernization and a fragile example of an infrastructure-heavy solution to the demands of financialization. Understanding the development of the TWDP requires a focus on the scalar interactions between flows of finance, waste, energy and water that are woven through the hydrosocial cycle of London.

title: Social and Environmental Recovery in the Surroundings of Portman Bay, in the South East of the Iberian Peninsula
authors: Banos Paez, Pedro; Banos Gonzalez, Isabel
abstract: For over thirty years, the waste from the mining industry located in the area has been dumped on the Portman bay, such waste originates in the plant where galena, blende & pyrite ores are concentrated. The Portman bay is one of the most important sources of pollution in the whole Mediterranean. Furthermore, the dumping of waste from mining caused the silting of the Portman bay & most of the continental platform facing this bay. After multiple denunciations, protest demonstrations, pressures from several groups, etc., in March 1990, the dumping to the Mediterranean Sea ceased. Immediately following this, the question was raised whether or not to recover the bay & its surroundings. In this communication the prospects for the environmental recovery for the surroundings of the Portman bay are analyzed as well as the standpoints of the different social actors concerning various options under consideration for its recovery.

title: Improving Municipal Governance in China: Yantai's Pathbreaking Experiment in Administrative Reform
abstract: In recent years, a serious effort to remake the Chinese administrative system has accelerated. This article explores the dynamics of reforms aimed at improving the bureaucracy's effectiveness in providing services to the public. To illuminate key features of the process of local-level administrative reform, it examines in detail the pathbreaking Service Promise System experiment carried out in the city of Yantai. This case study shows how useful innovative ideas about reform filter into China and then diffuse across organizational and administrative boundaries. It sheds light on the role played by "entrepreneurial executives" (local bureaucrats) in promoting innovative policies and on the features of the Chinese administrative system that shape how reforms are implemented. Drawing on the New Public Management approach to administration, the Service Promise System represented a serious attempt to make the bureaucracy more customer-oriented and professional. The analysis presented in this article highlights the difficulty of achieving these aims while the Chinese Communist Party remains averse to being bound by clear rules and by public opinion. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: A Case of Weak Architecture: The French Ministry of Health
abstract: This article asks whether the public administration of health in France fits the general description of French state institutions as autonomous, powerful bureaucracies. Existing sources on the French Ministry of Health indicate that three types of processes have shaped its institutional structure, its official mandate and its actual policy influence since its inception in the 1920s. Faced with the rise of private-practice medicine, the Ministry first emerged as a resource-poor institution, and still remains an endemically weak ministerial portfolio by virtue of institutional path dependence. Since the 1980s, it has aligned itself on cognitive influences from other ministries, and has been especially sensitive to the pressure exerted by spending ministries to control health expenditure. Finally, in the light of recent health scandals, the creation of several health agencies has contested its effective mandate over public health issues. As a result, the current Ministry struggles to redefine its role in the competitive landscape of French health policy formulation. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: WATER RESOURCES: VALUED OR VIOLATED - A SOCIOLOGICAL APPROACH TO THE PROBLEM OF WATER POLLUTION
abstract: Over 600 interviews were conducted within 2 watersheds in upstate NY to discover the degree of awareness of water quality problems & to determine the processes leading to support for remedial action. Results showed a high general awareness of water pollution & a high degree of willingness to act to improve the situation. Little difference is noted between the stream & lake watersheds. The populations sampled are unsure of how regulation & control should proceed, but are willing to bear the financial burden of improvement. Both cross tabulations & path analysis techniques are used in the study & path diagrams are presented to model causally the processes associated with both private & public action. Suggestions are made which single out the important obstacles to the improvement of water quality.

title: Advances to the study of international public administration
abstract: As an area of research, specifying crucial conditions under which international public administration (IPA) may enjoy independence from member-state governments has become an increasingly vibrant research area. This collection responds to three as yet unresolved research tasks: (1) systematically comparing IPAs by offering large-N data across cases; (2) taking organization seriously by identifying how the organizational architectures of IPAs affect decision-making processes and subsequently the pursuit of public policy-making; and (3) examining the varied consequences of the autonomization of IPAs, notably for member-state public sector governance and for the integration of transnational regulatory regimes.

title: Chief Joseph Dam Community Impact Report
abstract: In 1973, the Corps of Engineers announced that funds were available to add 11 hydropower units to an existing hydroelectric dam at Bridgeport, Wash. Most nearby communities had a population of about 1,000 people or less. During construction of the original dam & 16 hydropower units in the early 1950's, local communities suffered hardships in not having enough public facilities to handle the influx of construction workers. Local citizens & governmental officials were fearful of the anticipated wave of new construction workers into the area. The study was a planning tool which (1) identified population impact problems for each community within commuting distance, (2) provided guidelines to selected communities to deal with the problems, & (3) identified potential sources of assistance. The study projected total population associated with construction activities. Community public facilities & services within commuting distance were inventoried & population service capacity determined. Evaluation developed current standards for the use of water supply systems, sewage disposal systems, schools, police protection, fire protection, & medical facilities & services. Result provided degree of present use of excess or deficient capacity to provide for increased population. Difficult areas of evaluation were (A) determination of size of public facility or service as standards vary, & (B) allocation of construction related population to several communities. The evaluation provided base conditions with projections of possible impacts. The report has been & is currently used by local planners & government officials in requesting governmental funding for public utilities & schools. Follow-up studies are discussed.

title: The Road to Collective Debt in Rural China: Bureaucracies, Social Institutions, and Public Goods Provision
abstract: Focusing on the episodes of the government's Paved Road to Every Village (PREV) project in an agricultural township in northern China, this article examines two research issues: First, the role of state policies, government bureaucracies, and village cadres in the provision of public goods, especially the unintended consequences that led to huge collective debts and the erosion of the collective basis of governance and second, the role of local institutions and social relations in resource mobilization, problem solving, and response to crises, especially in the aftermath of the PREV project. The episodes provide an occasion to rethink the role of governments in economic development and the lessons learned from, to borrow an expression by James Scott, "seeing like a state." [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Environmental Justice Issues Related to Inadequate Wastewater Treatment in Small Communities in Tennessee
authors: Mookherjee, Harsha N; Riemer, Jeffrey W; George, Dennis B; Wells, M J M; Clark, Y R; Rollins, Sharon; Gilbert, Anne; O'Connell, Ann
abstract: Identifies environmental justice issues related to inadequate wastewater treatment facilities in small TN communities & develops a decision-making process model, including socioeconomic, political, environmental, & physical factors that cause or prolong environmental injustices. Demographic information was gathered from secondary data sources for 22 communities that showed evidence of a combination of public health, water-quality, & aesthetic problems, & on-site visits were made to 12 of them. Here, public health officials, community residents, water treatment plant representatives, & key informants were interviewed, & wastewater problem areas observed. The resulting community profiles -- coupled with evidence of water-quality problems, public health problems, on-site visits, & resident concerns -- allowed for refinement of the elements in the decision-making process model. The developed model shows how other communities can be systematically approached & evaluated as to possible environmental injustices & how each community can have its own unique set of problems & possible solutions.

title: Water Conservation Policy Making in Local Government during Drought
abstract: Focus is on water conservation policy-making processes in 12 Iowa communities during the 1977 drought. The sample includes 3 Ur, 2 metropolitan, & 8 Ru communities. Their water resources vary. Data were gathered by in-depth personal interviews with local policy makers. Water conservation policy makers varied from community to community. Included were mayors, councilmen, personnel of public water works, members of water boards, etc. The following aspects are analyzed & discussed: (1) how the water conservation policies were made at the local government level, (2) whether or not types of water conservation policy-making processes made differences in actual policy decisions made & in their rationales, & (3) whether or not types of policies made resulted in differences in objective & subjective measures of effectiveness, the policy makers' equity evaluations, & the degree of citizen cooperation & reasons for it as perceived by the policy makers.

title: Social Capital and Institutional Performance -- Methodological and Theoretical Discussion on the Water Basin Committees in Metropolitan Sao Paulo, Brazil
abstract: The paper presents an overview of the theoretical debate & the main outcomes of a survey with all members of the five subcommittees that compose the water basin. The background is the institutional transformations that have taken place in the environmental management process in Brazil since the 90's, specially in the field of water management. The focus is on the water basin committees, an institutional engineering that has become one of the references of institutional innovation in the water management process in Brazil that emphasizes the decentralized management by watersheds & community participation in the management & preservation of water resources. The research developed in 2004 in the water basin of Alto Tieta that covers the Metropolitan Region of Sao Paulo is based in the framework of social capital, as a tool to evaluate the institutional development of these democratic spaces. Water basin committees are the appropriate arenas to develop a comparative study of institutional performance & its relations with cooperative practices linked to preservation & spatial & environmental management. The analysis based on the conceptual framework allows to evaluate the level of associativism, trust, reciprocity & cooperation that enables the consolidation of an effective performance.

title: Reflexivity of Risk Society: Urban Water Recycling
abstract: Water scarcity and water pollution are two of the side effects of modern development that, for Beck (1992), produce a 'risk society'. Technological solutions include recycling municipal effluent, which can be treated to a standard suitable for non-potable uses (garden watering and toilet flushing), or to a higher level for potable consumption such as cooking and drinking. Public perceptions are recognised by the water industry as being the key to the success or otherwise of water reuse initiatives. This research approaches the problem of perceptions of water reuse at the community level to consider the experience and views of providers as well as users of this technology. Cross national findings are presented from case studies undertaken in Australia and the USA involving stakeholder interviews with 35 providers and 84 users. Previous research in this field is compared to the current work as well as to subsequent outcomes of proposed recycled water projects. Research findings suggest that the challenge to the water industry goes beyond achieving current best practice in water reuse technology, and must necessarily involve community consultation and participation from the initial planning stages. These findings are discussed in terms of their implications for the reflexivity characteristic of 'high modernity'.

title: Water Quality Management and Public Policy: A Survey of Farmer and Non-Farmer Attitudes
abstract: To determine the PO context for non-point-source pollution policies, a sample of Okla agricultural & environmental leaders were asked to respond to a set of 88 attitudinal items. Previously applied scales measuring traditional agrarianism, environmental, & water quality concerns, as well as more general political & economic attitudes, were included to explore the extent & type of variation between farmers & nonfarmers. Padgitt & Hoyer (1987) found little difference between farmers & nonfarmers with respect to water quality beliefs & concerns in one area of Iowa. Although this has not been a frequent finding, the data in this study support that contention. Also explored are areas of agreement & disagreement as they relate to SC, place of residence, & scale of farming.

title: Belonging, Believing, Behaving; The Religious Character of Public Servants
authors: Freeman, Patricia K; Houston, David J
abstract: How do public servants compare to the general public in their religious affiliation, beliefs, and behaviors? Using data from the 2004 General Social Survey, we compare public servants in government and outside government to the general public through a series of logistic regression models. Although there is little difference in terms of denominational affiliation, public servants have a stronger commitment to, and are more active in, their religious communities. The implications of these findings for public administration are discussed.

title: Innovation in Public Management: Is Public E-Procurement a Wave of the Future? A Theoretical and Exploratory Analysis
abstract: Project management has become an answer to many traditional organizational structuration and performance shortcomings, while gaining currency in business and public sector organizations. Public procurement systems have evolved into public electronic procurement systems with variations and distinctions in the age of globalization and digitalized complexities. This article examines the development of public e-procurement as an innovation in public management in the contexts of project management, public procurement management, and e-governance. It also links practice to theory-through a fourfold theoretical perspective-with contributions to the knowledge in public procurement, governance, and public administration.

title: Machinery of government and standards in public service: teaching new dogs old tricks: Texts reviewed
abstract: For much of the last thirty years the main leitmotif animating Civil Service reform in the UK has been that efficiency and effectiveness in public services can be achieved by adapting management methods and practices derived from commercial enterprise. In the process of making the dreams and schemes of that plural singularity we have come to call `managerialism' operational though, something valuable appears to have been lost, and that something is the Civil Service as a unified `constitutional bureaucracy'. In this article I explore some of the unfortunate governmental and administrative consequences of these managerially minded reforms. In particular, I seek to highlight the continuing relevance of what have been routinely characterized as outmoded and anachronistic machineries of government, and to stress the importance of the increasingly forgotten core business of public administration: the running of a state and of a constitution. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Nurturing Leaders for Government and Opposition: Political Schools in Japan
abstract: This article examines why political schools have emerged in Japan. While the roles of founding fathers, the angst of national decline and the perception of a 'leadership deficit' in Japan have paved their emergence, a fundamental reason for their existence is the failure of Japanese political parties to recruit candidates from broader social backgrounds beyond political dynasties, the bureaucracy and narrow interest groups. The article examines four political schools in Japan including the Matsushita Seikei Juku (MSJ, Matsushita Institute of Government and Management). I argue that while the MSJ has successfully produced many students who have won elections, it has not nurtured visionary leaders who can lead Japan out of its economic and political malaise. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Crisis of Ukrainian Statehood: Political, Legal, Axiological and Geoeconomic Aspects
abstract: The article focuses on the complex political, legal, sociocultural and geopolitical problems generated by the current political crisis in Ukraine. The authors analyze its historical and sociopolitical preconditions as well as its global context. This crisis sheds light on prospects for geopolitical and geoeconomic reconfiguration of the post-Soviet space. The focus is on problems of the Ukrainian state's national consolidation, dysfunctions of the democratic process in Ukraine, efficiency of Ukraine's democratic political institutions, and transformations in the constitutional and legal system and the political regime. The authors analyze in political terms the risks of the failure and possible disintegration of Ukrainian statehood, prospects for re-establishing the state as a crisis management option, postrevolutionary destructive practices, and the growing role of informal institutions in Ukrainian politics. They also consider the growing and qualitatively aggravating rifts in Ukrainian society, which are largely the consequence of the nation building policy conducted within the ethnonational model and based on the mobilization resources of xenophobia. A comparative analysis of the Ukrainian and Russian post-Soviet political systems' transformations is presented. The authors also look at alternatives to the interaction between the oligarchy, the bureaucracy and political personalism in these countries. As a result of this interaction, we have two different consolidation prospects of their political systems.

title: The Public Participation Process in Water Quality Planning
abstract: A case study of the public participation formats developed by the Illinios Environmental Protection Agency for its 208 water quality management programs. Agency planning documents & reports, & minutes of area- & state-wide advisory groups are examined to trace the process whereby water quality planning issues are identified, developed, & resolved. The study of agency documents is supplemented by participant observation at advisory group meetings & by interviews with public participation coordinators & agency personnel. The focus is on the criteria which the agency uses to design public participation agenda & tasks, & on the effectiveness of their implementation.

title: Thinking with Flint: Racial Liberalism and the Roots of an American Water Tragedy
abstract: The lead poisoning of Flint, Michigan's water is popularly framed as a case of "environmental racism" given that Flint's population is mostly black and lower income. In this essay I argue that we see the environmental racism that underlies Flint's water poisoning not as incidental to our political-economic order, nor even as stemming from racist intent, but as inseparable from liberalism, an organizing logic we take for granted in our modern age. I expand on the idea of "racial liberalism" here. While upholding the promise of individual freedoms and equality for all, racial liberalism -- particularly as it was translated into urban renewal and property making in mid-20th-century urban America -- drove dispossession. In Flint racialized property dispossession has been one major factor underlying the city's financial duress, abandonment, and poisoned infrastructure. Yet, through austerity discourse, Flint is disciplined as if it were a financially reckless individual while the structural and historical causes of its duress are masked. Tracing the history of property making and taking in Flint and the effects of austerity urbanism on its water infrastructure, my central argument is that our understanding of Flint's predicament -- the disproportionate poisoning of young African-Americans -- can be deepened if we read it as a case of racial liberalism's illiberal legacies.

title: Migration in a Mexican Border Community in the Context of Economic, Political and Environmental Dislocations
abstract: This paper is based on ethnographic research conducted from 2007 to the present in Sonora, Mexico in a community located 70 km from the international border between Mexico & the U.S. The impact of the global economic crisis as well as environmental crises related to water & climate are evident there. This community is the locus of both in & out-migration. In-migrants come from Sonora or other regions in Mexico, & from the U.S. With the economic crisis, these migrants are settling in the community to try to obtain work in, for example, nearby mines & U.S. assembly plants. Other migrants are returning from the U.S. & settling there; some have never lived there before. Their return migration is precipitated by the economic crisis & strict migration enforcement in the U.S. The community's economy is still dominated by agriculture but growing water scarcity & climate change are altering this production. An exploration of the linkages between in and out-migration, the economic crisis, the changing environment, and agriculture showed that, for example, as wells are going dry, farmland is being sold to in-migrants for new housing construction. The pace of this construction, however, is slowing with the economic crisis.

title: Impact of Globalization on Core Engineering Education in India
abstract: The education system in India continued to be based on the colonial legacy of bureaucratic administration even after fifty years of independence. But, under globalization and liberalization policies of the government, engineering higher education has acquired a new interpretation of increasing credential value, where the degree per se is more important for securing a high-paying job, primarily in the software and information technology sector, than for acquiring specific knowledge and skills. This is reflected in the employment pattern of the graduates with a core engineering background. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Perceptions on Healthy: Water and Sanitation Problems in Nigeria. A Comparative Study of Rural Small Town and Urban Shantytown
abstract: Presents some preliminary findings from an ongoing comparative study of household environmental health problems in urban & rural settings in Nigeria & their impact on human well-being. The importance of safe water supply & sanitation are described in-depth. It is suggested that more emphasis should be laid on local knowledge when conceptualizing a health risk, particularly as new healing methods are defined to promote the living standard of local people. The theoretical frame of the study is based on Mary Douglas's theory concerning risk acceptability in different societies, with emphasis on the sociological formulation of norms, beliefs, patterns, & practices of everyday life within a community. The discussion of culture & risk is based on an ecosocial approach to the reproduction of everyday life. Fieldwork has been conducted in a small town & village in Ile-Ife (Osun State) & in an urban shantytown in Lagos (Lagos State), including 29 focus group discussions, 37 in-depth interviews, & participatory observations of participatory rural appraisal practices.

title: Poverty and Mass Unemployment in Mineral-Rich Botswana
abstract: The economic plight of the poor in Botswana has worsened directly as a result of the mining sector's success.  The process of economic expansion and modernization has created an economic elite made up of: 1.  government bureaucracy, 2.  a military salariat, and 3.  a small number of corporation officials and managers.  Purchasing land and cattle from savings out of relatively high salaries in the mining and public sectors, the elite have joined white farming families as larger scale land and cattle owners.  The distribution of land holdership is skewed greatly in favor of larger holders.  Expansion of cattle raising is related to land access and investment in water supplies, especially boreholes, which require a high capital outlay.  Botswana's growth, development, and stability are endangered by 4 socioeconomic problems: 1.  inequality based on agricultural underdevelopment, 2.  rapid expansion in water demand, 3.  food insecurity heightened by drought and food import dependence, and 4.  increasingly strong links to South Africa.

title: Thatcher, Reagan, Mulroney: in search of a new bureaucracy // Review
Civil Society and Water Governance: A Study of Hiware Bazar Village in India
abstract: Hiware Bazar is a village with 257 households. Popat Pawar became the village headman in 1989 unopposed. He took water conservation work. He transformed Hiwre Bazar from water scare village to surplus one with the active cooperation of all the villagers & it has won many state & national awards. In 1970-80 the water scarcity & land degradation made agriculture redundant. In 1995 Hiwre Bazar was selected as the village that could be developed as the model village. Under this program, about 52 earthen bunds, two percolation tanks, 33 loose stone bunds were constructed. About nine check dams have also been constructed in a series on the downstream nallah. In 2006 the surplus was nearly 50 % of total water available. In the land use the gross cropped area of 821 ha. in 1996-97 has been increased to 1007 ha. in 1998-99 and 1125ha. in 2002-03. Since 2004 the annual water budgeting is discussed through village meeting & implemented. 70 ha forestland has been developed with cooperation of the forest department. 35 lakh trees have been planted in the past 20 years. The paper based on the secondary sources discusses the contribution of civil society in the water conservation & governance.

title: Household Composition and Men's and Women's Physical Well-Being
authors: Blair, Sampson Lee; Morgan, Carolyn S; Hardesty, Constance L; Wenk, DeeAnn
abstract: Previous research has recognized that individual well-being varies across the stages of the family life cycle. Here, using data from the 1988 National Survey of Families & Households, it is shown that women's & men's well-being is differentially affected by various forms of household composition. For both men & women, the presence of resident adult children & dependent parents is associated with decreased well-being, but the detriments are greater for women. Implications of these findings are discussed.

title: Using Administrative Data in California to Evaluate Welfare Reform
abstract: Describes how administrative data have been used in CA to evaluate welfare programs & how it will be used to evaluate CalWORKS, the new welfare program. Several concrete examples are presented, along with a comparative analysis of administrative & survey data.

title: State, Market, and Class in America's Environmental Decade (1970-1980)
abstract: Three questions are addressed: (1) What was the nature of class struggle during the environmental decade? (2) What forms did it take? (3) What forces shaped & limited the forms & outcomes of this struggle? The theoretical component of the analysis is based on Eric Olin Wright's formulations on class boundaries & contradictory class locations; also considered are Nicos Poulantzas's formulations on class boundaries & the mental vs manual labor distinction. Wright's & Poulantzas's formulations are compared & contrasted against key developments in the federal environmental legislation during the 1970s. Empirical data are drawn from the testimony of key witnesses in the 1971 & 1977 US Senate Federal Water Pollution Control Legislation hearings, focusing on the structure of interests & concerns regarding this legislation. The political-economic context of water pollution control legislation is also considered. It is argued that because of the noneconomic emphasis of this legislation, Poulantzas's class analysis is especially valuable because it enables the identification of specific forms of class struggle. In addition, Poulantzas's theory is useful in closely examining the role of the state & the role of the market in shaping & limiting the outcomes of class struggle during the environmental decade. Wright's class analysis is less useful in explaining the formation of water pollution control legislation because of its overemphasis on class struggle at the production level.

title: Indigenous Groups, Private Prawn Farms and Mangrove Ecosystem
abstract: Discusses the Irula (an indigenous group in the Pichavarem mangrove wetlands at the northern end of the Cauvery delta in India), the mangrove ecosystem (on which they rely for subsistence), & two new private prawn farms (which are polluting the ground water & disturbing the ecosystem & the Irula peoples' way of life). As a part of the "Wetlands: Conservation & Management" project with participatory approach in the Pichavaram mangroves, the M. S. Swaminathan Research Foundation (Madras, India) is acting as a facilitator to develop partnership between the state forest department & the dependent communities, including the Irular community. To strengthen the Irulas' livelihood security, the microplan PRA was conducted, & the following problems were identified through the resource mapping method specific to ground water pollution: (1) The villagers are forced to abandon the ring & tube wells located in the settlement & spend 2-3 hours a day transporting drinking water from neighboring settlements. (2) Hundreds of Palymyra trees in the area are gradually dying due to the increase of ground water salinity. These trees are the major source of fuel wood for these people, reducing the pressure on the mangroves for fuel wood. (3) The land available close to their homes is no longer suitable for vegetable gardening. The microplan, which follows the PRA, discusses opportunities & solutions to the problem.

title: Power and Policy Processes in Drinking Water Supply in Karnataka, India
abstract: Susanna Ghosh Mitra looks into the ways power is negotiated and resisted within cities in India in the context of piped drinking water supply. Taking a World Bank-funded water privatization project in Hubli-Dharwar as a case study, she critically examines the regional- and local-level power dynamics underlying urban water management. The study uses the methodology of a discursive approach to policy processes and identifies the specific contexts in which power and politics is operating, together with the related discourses and representations of the environment through which people communicate. By seeing policy as a discourse, analytical attention is turned to the webs of power underlying the practices of different actors in the policy process. Adapted from the source document.

title: French Artistic Institutions during the Third Republic: The Beaux-Arts System [1870-1940]
abstract: The republican liberal state in France created a civil service for the fine-arts based on official aesthetics, which combined a theory of service with an administrative culture. In the same department (Instruction Publique et Beaux-Arts) the development of a unified system of education, encompassing arts, humanities, & sciences, has given birth to a national culture that expresses the spirit of a French bourgeois society. By so doing, the state quickened the pace of the liberalization & the modernization of both institutions & the market, & set up a model for the management, growth, & preservation of a national heritage. Thus, democratization has pervaded a cultural life hitherto dominated by aristocractic values, & the Third Republic has been successful where its two predecessors had failed: its prize is the double legitimization of public authority & national sovereignty as embodied by its institutions.

title: Public infrastructure and private costs: Water supply and time allocation of women in rural Pakistan
abstract: How the quality and quantity of infrastructure affect the time women allocate to their various activities is investigated. How variations in the water infrastructure's quality - at both the household and community levels - relate to differences in time allocated by rural women to market-oriented activities, water collection and leisure is discussed. The case study focuses on Pakistan, where a large proportion of the population lives in poverty and where there exists a significant gender gap in education as well as labor force participation. The results indicate that improvements in Pakistan's public water supply infrastructure, women increase the time that they allocate to income-generating activities.

title: The Theory of Games and Bureaucratic Behavior
authors: Tootell, Geoffrey; Bianchi, Alison; Lloyd, Paulette; Munroe, Paul T
abstract: Applying game theory to bureaucratic settings can raise serious implications for social, economic, & organizational theories. It is proposed that no unitary concept of power can accommodate the distinct differences between noncooperative two-person (Prisoner's Dilemma) games embedded in strong power situations & other power situations in social networks. Game theory (eg, agency theory) is patched onto a productivity model, extending general-sum cooperative games beyond allocation problems & adding another dimension (power) to members' utility schema. Strong power in the productivity model produces negative elements (equilibria) in solutions, suggesting that it is counterproductive.

title: Applied Environmental Ethics
abstract: The Arkansas Land Stewardship Project (ALSP) addresses the important public policy issue of the loss of topsoil & the depletion of underground water in Ark from a sociological perspective. The project is designed to heighten Ark's awareness that soil & water are fundamental components of the earth's biological skin, the biosphere, on which all life depends, & that land management is essentially an ethical proposition. The project is exploring the idea of a land ethic -- a notion of man as responsible steward. A central component of our high technology society, & one that has been largely ignored by social scientists & sociology in particular, is agriculture. This is surprising when one notes that agriculture is the US's largest industry, accounting for almost 25% of the nation's gross national product, & also its largest foreign exchange earner. Few issues are of greater importance to the world than adequate food & knowledge about the components of the agricultural system. The sociological perspective guiding the ALSP & some of the methodology being used are discussed. The ALSP examines current agricultural problems in Ark & the US from a sociohistorical perspective. The utility of looking at agricultural issues as ethical choices as well as technological &/or economic choices is emphasized.

title: The Impact of Size and Number of Administrative Units on Quality of Public Services
authors: Christenson, James A; Sachs, Carolyn E
abstract: A major question for macrosociological theory is the nature of the relationship or organization size &/or structure with organizational performance. This research tests the hypothesized relationships between size & number of administrative units with citizens' perceptions of the quality of various public services for 100 different localities in NC. The method includes the construction of a scale of public services which provides a new mode of investigating & developmentally evaluating the quality of a wide range of common public services. The findings reveal that size of administrative units is strongly & positively related to the perceived quality of public services scale regardless of ecological, economic, or social considerations. A nonsignificant relationship is apparent between the number of administrative units & perceived quality of services.

title: How To Organize the Black Community?: A Power Struggle between White Administrators
abstract: To retain control over the "social problems" of black communities in the mid-1960s, social scientists & welfare administrators, heavily financed by foundations & the federal government, constructed new theories & strategies of community organization, a development which led to inevitable conflict between practitioners of the traditional & the "vanguard" approaches within the welfare establishment. Using documents, tapes of meetings, & interviews, this analysis of a battle between white welfare administrators over jurisdiction, control of resources, appropriate perspective & welfare practice in the black community of Richmond, Calif, in 1964, demonstrates: (1) the negotiated, adaptive character of liberal welfare ideology & practice, (2) the ways in which changing historical conditions & oppositional ideologies are assimilated into the hegemonic system, (3) the process by which the administrator representing the more traditional "integrationist" approach lost power to the administrator representing the vanguard "nationalistic" approach, & (4) how the victorious nationalist approach to community organization, regardless of the intentions of its white designer, led to a form of indirect as opposed to direct rule over black leadership in Richmond.

title: THE LANGUAGE OF PERSUASION IN BUREAUCRACY: 'MODERN' AND 'TRADITIONAL' APPEALS TO ISRAEL CUSTOMS AUTHORITIES
abstract: A report on findings of a study of the natural language of persuasion in one particular setting, that of written communication between a bureaucratic organization & its clients. The data are drawn from a content-analysis of letters addressed by clients to the head office of the Israel Customs authorities. The main dependent variable studied were the strategies of persuasion clients of varying socio-cultural backgrounds used to influence Customs officials to grant their requests. The method developed for the content-analysis of persuasive appeals, as well as findings on the sources of variation in the communication styles of clients, should attract the attention of sociologists & social psychologists alike. While most of the current interest of sociolinguistics is in patterns of speech in face-to-face interaction, rather than in written communication, & in the code used, rather than the content conveyed, we are convinced that it is only a matter of time before sociolinguists join with content-analysts & others in the study of the social & cultural determinants of form & content of all types of language usage. AA.

title: The impacts of state growth management programmes: A comparative analysis
abstract: This paper examines the impact that alternative state planning frameworks have on five dimensions of urban development: density, the spatial extent of urbanized land area, property value, public expenditures on infrastructure and population change. The objectives of the analysis are threefold. First, the background discussion provides a brief overview of urban sprawl as a public policy problem and outlines how state growth management programs attempt to respond to it. Secondly, the empirical analysis examines the effects of growth management in a cross-section of metropolitan counties during the 1982-97 time-period. The five outcome measures are modeled in a simultaneous equations framework in order to test several specific hypotheses about how state land-use policies affect the character of urban growth. Thirdly, the results of the empirical analysis are described within the context of previous research on the effectiveness of growth management. The findings suggest that state growth management programs with strong consistency requirements and enforcement mechanisms hold much promise for reducing urban sprawl, while programs that do not require consistency and/or have weak enforcement mechanisms may inadvertently contribute to it.

title: The Supreme Court and the Myth of Plea Bargaining: A Sociological View of the Brady Decisions
abstract: Addressed is the intersection of law & bureaucracy. Examined is transformation of traditional adjudication by bureaucratic administration. Three US Supreme Court decisions, known informally as "the Brady cases" are examined in some detail. These cases show that the Court constructs a myth of "plea bargaining" to justify existing, bureaucratic criminal justice practice by appealing to democratic imagery & values such as voluntary & knowing defendants who enter a contractual relation with the Court. The argument is discursive. Emphasis is on the organizational & institutional locus of many social problems issues. How documents such as court decisions may be used to analyze organizational & institutional aspects of social problems is pointed up.

title: Organizational Level Correlates of Alienation as Indicated by Absenteeism and Turnover Rates
abstract: Ten hypotheses are examined to explain variation in absenteeism & turnover rates in a sample of 110 NJ factories & 44 Japanese factories. Technological & structural characteristics of these factories are hypothesized to cause employees to withdraw by absence & separation because of alienation from their organizational roles. Advanced technology is found to be either unrelated or negatively related to absenteeism & turnover rates. Bureaucratically structured roles & organization size are found to be either unrelated or negatively related to withdrawal behavior. Some Some organizational characteristics, such as the supervisory ratio & centralization of decision making, are positively correlated with absenteeism & separation rates. In contrast, the administrative differentiation of the organization structure into specialized units, & the social integration inferred to be associated with this, decreases absenteeism & separation rates. Some evidence suggests that efficient operation has an inverse relation with withdrawal behavior. However, "relative exploitation" (ie, wage differentials) are more positively correlated with absenteeism & separation rates than objective measures of low wages.

title: THE CONFLICT BETWEEN THE PROFESSIONAL AND THE BUREAUCRATIC STRUCTURE: A SURVEY OF RESEARCH ISSUES.
abstract: (I) Bureaucracy & profession as ideal-types: The assumption of conflict between bureaucratic & professional structure is based upon ideal-typical formulations of the 2 key concepts, bureaucracy & profession. Examination of the idealtypes indicates that structural incompatibility is established by definition. (II) Bureaucratic & professional elements in organizations: The empirical examination of organizations has provided some support for the argument that bureaucratic & professional directives are incompatible. However, serious questions about the argument have also been raised by the research evidence. It has been found that bureaucratic & professional features often occur jointly, that conflict between bureaucratic & professional directives often is not perceived by participants, that bureaucratic & professional elements often appear to reinforce each other. (III) Explanations of Contradictions: Students of organizations have attempted to salvage the argument regarding structural conflict (1) by referring to peculiar historical features of specific organizations & professions; (2) by relying upon psychological indicators of conflict, eg, anxiety; & (3) by identifying mechanisms of mediation & articulation. The attempts to salvage the original argument are not wholly satisfactory. Thoroughgoing re-formulation of theory in this area is needed.

title: Energy Development and Community Conflict
abstract: Data collected between 1980 & 1982 on the social effects of transferring water from agriculture to electrical power production in two areas of Utah show that the areas differed dramatically in their satisfaction with the processes used for negotiating water sales. Where selling was a unified effort by sellers, there was general satisfaction with the bargaining process, & little desire for alterations for possible future transfers. Where the power company negotiated sales with individual water owners, there was much less satisfaction with the process, & a perceived need for greater controls on future negotiations. More importantly, although both areas experienced intracommunity dissension & conflict as a result of the water sales, the focus of hostilities was different. Where there was satisfaction with the sales process, antagonism existed between residents of the community. These hostilities were personalized & appeared to result from expectations that were perceived by nonsellers to have been violated. Where dissatisfaction with the sales process was observed, antagonism between area residents was absent, & all hostility was directed toward the power company involved. Even though overt hostilities appear to have declined considerably between 1980 & 1982, covert hostilities remain in both communities.

title: Perspectives of Growth and Nongrowth among Public Officials
abstract: Data were gathered by interviews with public officials in 81% (325) of the incorporated places in Ky. Officials of metropolitan core cities were the most growth oriented, while officials of suburbs were the most nongrowth oriented. Among nonmetropolitan cities, officials of large towns were more growth oriented than those of small towns. Per capita city income was related to growth/nongrowth orientation only within suburbs, in which the higher the per capita city income, the more nongrowth oriented were the public officials. Contrary to expectations, population growth had no relationship with growth/nongrowth orientations of public officials. The theories of Molotch (1976) & Logan (1976, 1978) were only partially supported when taking into account cities of all sizes, within nonmetropolitan as well as metropolitan areas. Within both metropolitan & nonmetropolitan cities, officials of larger cities were found to be growth oriented. The theory of the predominance of the growth orientation among public officials, however, was supported only within metropolitan core cities. There was a definite residential suburban tendency toward nongrowth. A spill-in effect of growth advantages from metropolitan core cities to the suburbs, & the lack of such a spill-in in nonmetropolitan cities, is suggested by differences in growth/nongrowth orientations of city officials.

title: Public Attitudes toward Water Quality in Coastal North Carolina
authors: Hoban, Thomas J; Clifford, William B; Godwin, Michael A
abstract: Public attitudes toward water quality in the watershed of the Albemarle-Pamlico Estuarine system of NC are examined, using information collected through in-person interviews with 30 leaders of various interest groups & telephone interviews with a random sample of 800 people from 33 counties. Detailed information is provided on the nature & extent of different groups' awareness of water quality problems & attitudes toward major natural resource issues. A theoretical model is developed & tested that analyzes the factors influencing concern for & awareness of water quality problems. Recommendations are provided for future research & for programs for improving management of water resources.

title: Vulnerability, Adaptation, and Resilience to Flood and Climate Change-Related Risks among Marginal Riverine Communities in Metro Manila
abstract: This study examines the vulnerability, adaptation, & resilience of urban poor households living in Metro Manila. Based on a survey & case studies, the study found that the environmental/ecological vulnerability of the low-lying flood prone areas interacts strongly with the social vulnerability of urban poor households, highlighting the impacts of climate related changes (increased typhoons, intensity of monsoon rains, floods and tidal/storm surges) on this vulnerable population. Most of them belong to low-income households, live in slum/squatter settlements and do not have adequate access to potable water, electricity, health, sewage & sanitation facilities. About two-thirds of them suffered losses (e.g., income, work, health/sickness, household appliances/things, housing damage) from typhoons, floods, and tidal/storm surges but only a small portion of them obtained help from formal institutions & informal support networks. A third of these households appeared more vulnerable & consistently incurred higher losses & intense inconveniences (e.g., water source buried by floods, toilets blocked & overflowed with wastes/large worms to their floors) compared to their neighbors. The study concludes with a set of theoretical implications & policy recommendations regarding urban governance, technology, climate change and sustaining urban life.

title: Community Responses to Chronical Technical Disaster: The Case of the Pigeon River
abstract: Based on 1992/93 fieldwork, community & family reactions to 85 years of pollution of Pigeon River in rural Cocke County, TN, caused by a paper mill in a neighboring state, were investigated using interviews, participant observation, & a review of archives. Focus is on the effects of environmental awareness, family relationships, level of stress, risk perception, community perception, & perception of social support. It is found that continued presence of water resources contamination has delayed economic development in this rural community, socially stigmatized the area, & contributed to a defeated attitude among residents. Local resources to address the problem are limited, but social activism has proven most effective in increasing public awareness.

title: Sine Ira Ac Studio: Emotional Nexi in Weber's Ideal-Typical Conception of Organizations
abstract: An examination of the bureaucratic-functionary, who, according to Max Weber's ideal-typical conception of organizations, is expected to execute required tasks without expressing personal preference or animus; this dehumanized performance enables the organization to operate in a rational, predictable way. It is contended that there is an unintended irony underlying this construction of the bureaucratic role, ie, to the extent that it can be attained, it is possible only by emotionally linking the functionary to the organization. Weber's criteria for affectless performance of duties include three structural conditions that instigate positive emotions: (1) employment security, which generates the emotion of security; (2) status honor & social esteem, which set the official above clients & foster a sense of superiority, pride, & general good feeling; & (3) impersonal dedication to office, which engenders an emotional loyalty to the organizational structure & its rules. Organizational structure also generates the negative emotion of fear of dismissal or being overlooked for promotion. Recent works by Merton, Shils & Janowitz, Crozier, & Kanter are examined for additional instances in which organizations can ensure conformity, performance, & reliability only on the basis of emotional nexi.

title: Accessing Water Channeling Power: Class, Gender, and Caste Inequalities in India's Desert
abstract: An investigation of why social groups have unequal access to natural resources & unequal risk through their participation in state-of-the-art sustainable development, & whether these social-political processes are related to processes of ecological degradation. A case study is presented of one of the world's largest irrigation projects, the Indira Gandhi Canal in India's Thar desert, financed by the World Bank. It is argued that the state's expansion into the desert, & its control over its natural resources, worsens class, caste, & gender relations. The literature on the Third World capitalist-developmental state considers questions of risk, access, & inequality, but fails to understand the role of nature as dynamic, instead reducing & reifying it as site & input for production. Here, it is suggested that water, as well as other natural resources & processes, should not solely be analyzed as inputs, but as critical variables interacting with cultural, political, & economic forces on the local, regional, & global levels. Nature is socially embedded & production relations & village life have ecological-historical & naturalized elements. From this perspective, the state's control over natural resources has its manifold disempowering effects on nonelite communities & their access to, & control over, production on the desert's common lands, pastures, & forests. Typically, the commons were managed by low-caste, poor communities, & the desert's water resources managed by women before the construction of the Indira Gandhi Canal. It is concluded that sustainable development practices do two things best: sustain social inequalities & develop ecological crises.

title: The Urban Origins of Suburban Autonomy
abstract: Drawing heavily on extant newspaper accounts, published histories of individual cities, and official records, Professor Dilworth argues that sewer, water, gas, street lighting, and other infrastructure in New York, Newark, and Jersey City had differing impacts on the propensity of suburban jurisdictions to submit to annexation or to seek municipal incorporation and home rule.  Increased competition and the growing expertise of such companies helped to tame prices for such infrastructure investments, making sewers, sidewalks, water systems and the like affordable to smaller suburban communities.

title: Losing Value Diversity: The Bureaucratization of Hospital Ethics Committees
abstract: Hospital & health care ethics committees represent a growing force within the rapidly changing US health care system. Building from Max Weber's description of bureaucracies, explored here are some of the unacknowledged bureaucratic influences both on & in hospital ethics committees. Negative consequences of such committees uncritically developing (& ultimately overdeveloping) their bureaucratic structures are analyzed, suggesting that they have the unintended consequences of limiting considerations of diverse moral views. In response to such a bureaucratic trend, five questions for addressing the negative consequences of bureaucratic development are outlined.

title: Community and Institutional Impact of a Major Chemical Accident
abstract: Examines a major chemical accident that took place in the southwestern part of England. Known as the "Lowermoor" or "Camelford" case, the accident involved the contamination of the drinking water supply for a substantial portion of North Cornwall. In the late 1980s & early 1990s, the accident & its possible health implications became a matter of considerable controversy, & the case generated litigation, government reports, medical research, & citizen action. Here, an overview of the case is provided, based on extended field observation, a wide range of published & unpublished documents, a group interview, & 40 in-depth interviews with key actors. Central elements of the case are presented, along with information on the social, economic, & political context. Also discussed are some of the accidents main consequences, including its community & institutional impacts.

title: SUCCESSION AND ORGANIZATIONAL INNOVATION: SOME EXPERIMENTAL FINDINGS
abstract: This study was concerned with the effects of various types of bureaucratic succession on managerial innovation in 102 simulated business organizations established in the laboratory. Single outside succession, succession of a manager with an ally, dual subordinate succession, inside succession, & no-succession, were compared & their relative effectiveness in promoting managerial innovation assessed. The main finding was that a single outside succession was aversive to innovation, thereby supporting several field studies that have shown the disruptive effects of succession. Due to an inadequate number of cases, only a preliminary analysis of the other three types of succession could be undertaken.

title: The Social Logic of Professionalism
abstract: With his theory of professionalism as an ideal type different from bureaucracy as well as marked, Freidson has opened a new and important discussion of professionalism. Extracting an essence of decades of inductive empirical research to specify the main characteristics of professions & professionalism, he also turns the research agenda into a direction where deductive clarification is in focus. If the power position & status of a profession is associated with autonomy in the work performance & labour marked monopoly, the basis of these social relations is the sociocultural principle of a good work that reflects theoretical knowledge and self-discipline through the maintenance of occupational & ethical standards. The logic or rationale of professionalism is first and foremost associated with this occupationally determined control of the work performance, which contrasts the ways in which a bureaucracy or marked organizes & controls work. However, Freidson does not really fulfil the ambition to explicate professional expertise as closely associated with both micro and macro levels of society. Another limitation in his approach is a rather narrow & traditional focus on labour marked and occupational policy issues (division of work, specialisation, etc.) at the cost of the more profound discussion of how professionalism is associated with the very notion of modernity. A third problem is about Freidson's somewhat loose distinction between the three ideal types, which leaves it very open how we must proceed methodologically from theoretical to empirical studies of professionalism. My paper sketches an attempt to tackle these shortcomings in Freidson's position on the basis of a sociological approach, which is anchored in Merleau-Ponty's social phenomenology and includes closely related concepts from Bourdieu & others to clarify in what sense the ethical character of spontaneous social interplay is set aside in the modern work life through political and economical power.

title: Politics of Nature and Citizenship: How to Use Water As a Source of Energy and Carbon Trade or Eco-tourism and Sustainability?
abstract: This paper examines the case of a conflict over the development of hydroelectric facilities on ADGkizdere Valley's rivers in Rize, Turkey in order to document how the nature is constructed vis-a-vis the country's hegemonic citizenship regime, & to identify the counter-hegemonic voices of alternate green citizenships. This is achieved by comparing the discourses of nature & citizenship employed by various actors in this conflict, including proponents of the development of hydroelectric facilities and opponent's--- members of the Ikizdere Organization & others. The analysis of narratives over nature construction & protection reveal the fact that opponents, while addressing the issues and their concerns (such as, hydro-electric development are seen to be a threat to the sensitive eco-system & environment as well as cultural, social & economic structures of the region), constructed the counter-hegemonic sustainable citizenship. This counter-hegemonic sustainable citizenship insists on an eco-tourism-based development model for the region. Thus, this article argues that opponents not only have advanced significant challenges to the neo-liberal capitalist hegemonic citizenship regime, which treats nature as a set of resources for exploitation in the course of "development," & water as commodity, but also have fostered a hybridized conception of green citizenship, that is, counter-hegemonic sustainable citizenship.

title: Village Irrigation in Laos: Traditional Patterns of Common Property Resource Management
abstract: Rural society in Laos has been characterized by relatively independent villages & subsistence agricultural production, even as late as the mid-1980s. In such a situation, farming households are highly dependent on the local natural resource base & affected by the vagaries of weather. Village social institutions provide some mechanisms for protecting a family against calamities due to poor harvests or illness, & in certain situations also facilitate the management of common property resources for the well-being of the village residents. Here, the means by which villages manage water for paddy rice irrigation are described, & related to selected models of common property management. Traditional Lao irrigation institutions demonstrate that the assurance problem model of collective behavior is applicable to common property management, & that individuals' willingness to contribute to community irrigation systems must be understood in the context of household interdependence in Lao villages. Examples of poorly managed irrigation systems illustrate the limits of village institutions in shaping individual behavior.

title: The State on a 'Hydraulic Mission': The Political Ecology of Large Dams in Maharashtra (India)
abstract: This paper will discuss the cause & genesis of these mega hydraulic structures in the state of Maharashtra from the year 1921. Its political ambition of control & distribution of water resources and river basin development for a large scale cash crop production and industrial development, has consistently created a separate propertied class of "water-elites" on the one hand & a "drought affected" & a "dam affected" population on the other & a seemingly unbridgeable political fault line between the two. There are varieties of movements centered on large dams in Maharashtra, which focus on questions of "rehabilitation" as well as "equal distribution of dammed water", who are striving to develop solidarity between the "dam affected" & the "drought affected" population & mobilizing them as a political force against the state. They have achieved success in many of the cases. In this paper, I will discuss the above details from the perspective of "political Ecology", which will contextualize the metaphorical category of "large Dams" & "water" to the "local/regional histories, environment & social relations" & address the issue of "equity" & "justice" in distribution of ecological resources.

title: Technology Assessment, the Environment Movement, and Natural Resource Bureaucracies
abstract: Examined is the interaction between social movements & government agencies. A simple "model" views government agencies as involved with both social movement organizations & those who oppose movement goals (countermovement organizations). Using the environmental movement in the US as an example, traced is the relationship between movement organizations & government agencies through several stages of movement evolution. These stages include premovement conditions, in which supposedly regulatory agencies are closely linked to industrial interests; the early movement, in which movement organizations attempt to disrupt this linkage; the cohesive movement, in which both movement & countermovement interests compete for agency attention & response; the mature movement, in which interests may attempt to create new agencies, or drastically alter the mission of existing agencies; & the final stages of the movement, in which a new bureaucratic layer is created to mediate between conflicting agencies, with a potential loss of autonomy for both movement & countermovement interests. The impact of these changes on the technology assessment process is explored.

title: Making Sociology Work in Employment Settings Outside Academe: Perspectives of a Government Administrator
abstract: The dwindling number of available academic slots for new PhDs in sociology has stimulated an interest in the nature of employment for sociologists in nonacademic settings. The following questions are addressed: (1) What are key points of difference between academic & nonacademic roles of sociologists? (2) What are the factors producing job satisfaction & dissatisfaction for nonacademic sociologists? (3) How can the sociological viewpoint be put to work in nonacademic settings? (4) How might the graduate training of sociologists be modified to equip them to perform more effectively in nonacademic roles? (5) What are useful steps in jobhunting for the sociologist seeking nonacademic employment? Focusing on the question of how the sociological viewpoint can be implemented in nontraditional settings, particular work experiences as a research administrator concerned with issues of women's educational equity in the context of an agency committed to the support of educational research & development are detailed. Sociologists in nonacademic positions tend to have many-sided roles that involve them with actors having different discipline perspectives, values, & work styles from those who served as role models during graduate school days. Role conflict & identity problems may occur. If graduate training is to prepare for broader possibilities than those of the academic world, it should be revamped to provide greater emphasis on skills in effective presentation of the sociological viewpoint to nonsociologists & in relating that viewpoint to those of other disciplines in seeking solutions to identified problems. In these ways, the discipline of sociology may improve the likelihood of its being a major contributing force to social research & policy for the 1980s.

title: Managing Water Usage in Texas: Reconstituting Socio-Cultural Theorizing about the Environment into a More Generalized Framework
abstract: Extensive social research conducted on the formation & development of the Edwards Aquifer Authority in central Texas grounds our effort to construct a more encompassing theoretical perspective for managing water resources (or environmental issues more generally). In our analysis we stitch together key elements of theorizing by three major scholars who have addressed the environment: Ulrich Beck, Walter Firey, & Elinor Ostrom. After sketching out the basic conceptual contributions of these scholars, we suggest how their conceptual advances may fit together into a broader socio-cultural framework for interpreting the environment or, more specifically, resource use. We are especially concerned with Beck's emphasis on the future, with Firey's three pillars -- the economic system, the ecological system, & the ethnographic system -- and his emphasis on the nonexistence of any well-defined optimum, & with Ostrom's stress on the commons & on institutions. We link their ideas together with our own attention to social planning & the building of alternative organizational (institutional) arrangements.

title: Aesthetic of Resistance in the Social Protest: The Expressive Resources in the Defense of Water
abstract: As part of a line of inquiry within the studies on Collective Action and the Sociology of the Bodies & Emotions, this paper suggests an approach from the perspective of qualitative methodology, which thinks about the expressive sphere of collective action along with the analysis of expressive resources in the politics of resistance of the social protest. In this paper we will work specifically around the identification, selection & description of different expressive resources & images produced by the constituted groups of people that work for the Defense of Water in Argentina. Around the recovery of visual data about the protest for the Defense of Water between 2005 & 2009, we will select a micro-cycle of this conflict in the city to investigate about the framing processes and requirements / expectations at play. The expressivity forms are able to turn, thus, into ways of retaking the action when including actors in their relation with the background, at the same time they allow an access to the inside of experiences of life, expressed along with the selection & creation of new expressive resources -as an actualization of collective actors' sights/perceptions/practices within the conflict. This process involves also a reading of diverse characteristics: on the one hand interrogations about the expressivity of accounts of social actors' experiences of life -- not restricted only words & verbal accounts as the only ways of telling. On the other hand, a reading of the capturing techniques as an estrategy of data collecting that makes possible the re-construction of situations & interactions. In this sense, to recognize & understand the possibilities of the various ways in which aesthetics means hegemonic resistance, in various expressions of challenge & contestation, represent the central work issue from which we will able to approach the expressivity of the studies on collective action & social protest.

title: Decentralisation's Effects on Public Investment: Evidence and Policy Lessons from Bolivia and Colombia
abstract: This paper examines decentralisation in Bolivia and Colombia to explore its effects on the uses and spatial distribution of public investment, as well as government responsiveness to local needs. In both countries, investment shifted from infrastructure to social services and human capital formation. Resources were rebalanced in favour of poorer districts. In Bolivia, decentralisation made government more responsive by redirecting public investment to areas of greatest need. In Colombia, municipalities increased investment significant1y while running costs fell. Six important lessons emerge from the comparison. For decentralisation to work well: (i) local democracy must he transparent, fair and competitive; (ii) local governments must face hard budget constraints; (iii) central government must be scaled back; (iv) significant tax-raising powers must be devolved; and (v) decentralisation is composed of distinct, separable components, the sequencing of which is important. Finally, (vi) what decentralisation achieves, and whether it is advisable, hinges on how central government behaved pre-reform. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Public/Private Dynamics in a Global Frame: Narratives of Water Management in the UK and the Netherlands
abstract: Globalization viewed as the continuation of modernization is nonlinear in one important respect. The modernizers expected an expansion of the state; the globalizers a contraction.
