Both agree, however, on one trend, convergence on a similar public/private mix, overriding national differences. Postmodern critiques of modernity have suggested that the public/private divide itself is an artifact of the narrative. But a comparative narrative analysis of modernizing and globalizing accounts, conducted in the Netherlands and the UK for different historical periods, suggests that the reconstruction of the divide is a feature of the dynamics of societies in general. Globality disrupts any linear view of public/private development while it intensifies the differences in and range of national responses. In the 19th century the Dutch and British shared a view of progress even as they maintained distinctive accounts of the public/private divide in water management. In the late-20th-century, national differences in water management persist even as each country subscribes to a global sustainable future. But there is no single direction towards the globalization of the water industry and the relations of public and private spheres are constantly redefined through dynamic exchanges between the nation-state, business interests and civil society. Water defined as a public good has a protean quality that challenges nation-state definitions of the public/private divide and visibly represents the collective interest embedded in the new global society.

title: Sociological Analysis of Irrigation Water Management -- A Perspective and Approach to Assist Sociologists and Decision-Makers
authors: Freeman, David M; Lowdermilk, Max K
abstract: Irrigation water is of sociological interest because people must organize collectively to secure it, transport it, divide it into usable shares, enforce rules for its application, pay for it, & dispose of unused portions. The kinds of social organization, the patterns of power, decision making, & conflict people create & maintain for the social control of water intimately affects the productivity of its use. When water moves efficiently from rivers, through a network of canals, to plant root zones, it is because people have effectively organized a decision system capable of enforcing technically sound rules for pursuing the collective interest. Defects in the delivery & application of irrigation water are typically associated with deficiencies in social organization. Defined are the roles of sociological research in irrigation water management. The bundle of highly diverse technologies is analytically broken down through the use of social organizational & collective goods theory. Constituent technologies of irrigation water management can be usefully divided into six mutually exclusive categories. Each major category implies a different research thrust on the part of sociologists.

title: Extrinsic and Intrinsic Services in Public Administration
abstract: Public administration is hardly a function that provides the grounds for a cohesive political movement. The personnel who perform this function are an aggregate of planners, experts, technicians, & "bureaucrats" who work for myriad national, state, & local agencies. Some are organized into professional associations, others are protected by civil service, some by no organization whatsoever. One unifying bond among those involved in this function is their shared commitment to the ideal of public service. The first vestiges of this commitment appeared in the publications of reform liberals such as F. J. Goodnow & W. Wilson. They argued that efficiently organized, scientifically administered agencies could serve the public. By this they meant that state bureaucracies could deliver a battery of extrinsic services to the American public -- services that would enhance, but not alter traditional American culture & institutions. Early pragmatists, disturbed with a series of problems in American society, proposed that the authority of state administrative agencies be expanded to include the provision of intrinsic services to the public -- psychological growth of the self, improvement of traditional institutional goals, & cultural enrichment. There are utopian aspects to the latter definition of service, & public administrators have found it difficult to deliver intrinsic services to the public.

title: Cultivating Hot Peppers and Water Crisis in India's Desert
abstract: An analysis of the politics of groundwater extraction & use in a Ru region of India's Rajasthan desert. The most common agricultural crops produced are locally consumed food grains, cereals, pulses, & oil seeds. The local cash crop, chili peppers, however, is the newly emergent product; it consumes many times more water than all the locally consumed crops combined, at a time when water levels are falling. It is hypothesized that access to & appropriation of natural resources (in this case, water) result in the production of cash crops, on the one hand, & transform the relations of production to suit the emergent needs of capitalist farming, on the other. A theoretical question is posed: whether groundwater depletion is affected/influenced by caste, class, & access to political power. Taking a historical perspective, first examined are local & regional ecological problems: the degradation of the water catchment & body system by the mining industry; the deforestation of the Aravali mountains & watershed by the state forestry department; & the intensive extraction of Ru water resources for Ur/industrial consumption. The recent Ru drought is seen as a result of the local struggle over access & control of a historically common property resource, water. The impact of the water crisis is described: poor-peasant farming & animal husbandry are disappearing, & women are experiencing an increased workload in supplying water for the household; the configuration of the local economy & culture is being transformed; young men are being forced to migrate elsewhere for wage-labor; women (with their infants) are taking up wage-labor work with "famine relief" projects; & men are taking jobs are wage-laborers with local mines & the cash-crop chili farms. The local water crisis is ecological, economic, & cultural. These findings are based on ethnographic, oral historical, & comparative historical research, with particular emphasis on interviews with poor peasants, rich farmers, social workers, & state officials.

title: Social Control of Environmental Crimes as an Ideological Phenomenon
abstract: Social Control of Environmental Crimes as an Ideological Phenomenon. The paper deals with the social control of water pollution and pollution crimes in Finland during the period of 1960-2000. According to statistics, elimination of environmental offences has been common within the courts of justices, among prosecutors but especially among the environmental authorities. It is the social control that gives crimes, deviance & social harms their special shapes (Cohen 1985, 6). Therefore the ideological aspects, i.e. beliefs & practices based on certain social relationships that have got dominant position in social control but that also produce paradoxical consequences, are examined through the ethoses of moral regulation of water pollution, through the justifications concerning control work & strategies & through the mechanisms of defining lawbreakings as deviance. The data consist of court documents concerning crime cases, articles of the Water Economy journal & interviews with the environmental authorities. The analysis is based on discourse analysis. The environmental authorities' trust in big companies' self-regulation & technology as a solver of pollution problems have exposed social control to weaknesses, such as decrease of the relevance of authority control, increasing asymmetry in regard to access to relevant information and misuse of trust relationships.

title: Influence of Tourism and Internet on Oasian Communities in Southeast Morocco: Towards Adaptation or Extinction
abstract: Nomad communities in Southeast Morocco answered to decolonization and the birth of new countries, by changing gradually their ancestral way-of-life for sedentarization. Nowadays, they constitute micro-societies next to the oasis in order to ensure the access to the most vital & scarce resource: water. Their organisation is fundamentally based on the construction & maintenance of the infrastructures that pick up water (khettaras) & the management of its distribution. In the last decades, with the improvement of communications, the isolation is broken & these communities witness the huge arrival of tourists. In the present work, the social changes that consequently affect these populations are analyzed, with their largely unpredictable consequences. Tourism activities begun in this region with the first Paris-Dakar in 1978; then, thanks to the extension of the road network in the 1990s, it passed from small to large-scale tourism. Such massive tourism flow carried out with it the associated installations: telephone and, above all, Internet. This paper aims also to analyze the consequences: on the one hand, young men immigrate massively to the countries of origin of those rich tourists, which is made easier by the contacts they make on the Internet; on the other, the local economy is developed around tourism, without taking into account the environmental & social sustainability. Traditional structures are shaking & social cohesion disappears. Finally, an analysis is carried out to assess/determine if these Oasian societies will be able to adapt themselves & survive, maintaining their roots and environment, or if they are doomed to extinction.

title: An Economic Interpretation of the Urban Political Machine: Chicago Model
abstract: Investigated are the distributional effects of local public policies in Chicago, Ill. The goal was to discover whether any pattern of policy bias was evident in Chicago -- or if bureaucratically defined "decision rules" were the primary determinant of policy outcomes. The data include Census of Government figures on municipal spending & employment (by which Chicago's expenditure pattern is analyzed comparatively with other US cities), agency reports on service distribution & internal procedures, & narrative accounts of some typical cases of policy decision making. A number of inferences are drawn: (1) that much analysis of Ur policy distribution has been overly drawn to public services as the focal point of local policy effects, when in fact dispersal of jobs, avoidance of public "bads" & the like may be just as important, (2) that in Chicago the variability of policy effect appears to result from the local needs of & decision-making character of the city's fifty-ward Democratic Party organization, & (3) that the longevity of the party may be attributed to its ability to manage public resources via a decentralized, variable distribution of public goods.

title: Police Administration: Policy and Operations in the Wake of Hurricane Katrina
abstract: The aftermath of hurricane Katrina gave rise to unprecedented problems & challenges for the men & women of the New Orleans Police Department. Officers were forced to contend with issues never before seen in the city of New Orleans. This paper will strive to uncover policy issues relevant to the New Orleans police that were in place before, during, & after the storm's wrath. The relevant policy issues will be framed in accord with the history of the city, residential characteristics, & political environment. In addition, any changes that have taken place within the operational policy of the New Orleans police as a result of the storm's devastation will be discussed.

title: Water planning:: From what Time Perspective?
authors: Segrave, AJ (Andrew; van der Zouwen, MW (Mariëlle; van Vierssen, W (Wim
abstract: Integrative planning for water technology and infrastructure depends on various social, behavioral and environmental factors. Since water is a common-pool resource, water planning commonly involves addressing the views of diverse groups of people on multiple levels. Inter-group differences, especially if they go unrecognized, can be problematic for planning processes. Research into the Time Perspectives of people fulfilling different roles in the water sector worldwide revealed fascinating differences in how people perceive the Foreseeable Future. The aim was to characterize the heterogeneity so that it might be explicitly accounted for in planning. One-on-one interviews were held with 309 managers, practical workers, and scientists in the Netherlands, Ghana, Brazil, and Japan. Each interviewee's Time Perspective was characterized using a multi-measure method. The most noteworthy conclusions concern differences in the temporal extent of the goals and events that motivate people. Scientists are motivated by objects that lie furthest into the future followed by managers and then practical workers (Group medians: 8.4, 3.5, 1.7 yrs). Across national cultures, the time horizons of the Japanese and Brazilian interviewees are longest. These conclusions are important because the time horizons considered in planning influence what problems are perceived, what questions are asked, and what solutions are sought.

title: Biofuels, Climate Change, and Local Environmental Vulnerabilities
abstract: In response to U.S. Federal & state level policy initiatives, ethanol production has expanded rapidly especially across the country's Midwest region. Based on in-depth interviews in the Midwest state of Iowa -- the national leader in ethanol production -- this paper examines the specific environmental vulnerabilities that the intensification of corn production for ethanol has created in the state. The paper then assesses responses by key political, economic, & environmental actors to these local vulnerabilities. I find that that while much of the discourse at the national & state level concerning ethanol & the environment has focused on climate change, debate & action over ethanol's impact on local environmental vulnerabilities, such as water quality, is largely absent. I conclude that productionist agricultural interests continue then to shape the political economy of place, while debate over climate change overshadows the risks that "large-scale energy plantations" (Mol, 2007) pose to local environment sustainabilities.

title: Agriculture and Rural Development in India
abstract: About 75% of India's poor are in rural areas & a large proportion of them depend on agriculture for employment & a major source of livelihood. According to the latest census, about 235 million people ( 58 % of the labour force ) were employed in the agricultural sector in India in 2001 most of them in low productivity activities. Large numbers of workers are tied to agriculture in almost all states. The share of agriculture in GDP is shrinking form about 35% in 1980-81 to 23 % in 2001-02. And the opportunities for employment in the rural non form sector are limited. This empirical research is based on a theoretically sound & intuitively plausible framework. The analytical frame work of this study considers a static optimization model under uncertainty. The theoretical model of Fader (1980) has been used in this study to formulate hypothesis for empirical test. The data on which the present study in bases , are farm level cross-section data, collected by a primary survey in sum villages in Utter Pradesh in India, 2003-2004. In this paper following major parts which are related to the agriculture in Rural India will be discussed (A) Performance of agriculture in rural development, (B) Food grain policy, (C) Fertilizer policy, (D) Power supply to agriculture, & (E) Water resource & irrigation.

title: Local Women's Policy Machineries in the Region of Madrid, Spain
abstract: Explores women's policy machineries at the local level in the region of Madrid, Spain. Using the literature on women's interests & citizens' representation, the process of establishment of local women's departments is examined, describing the main features of these institutions (budget, staff, & relations with other state units). The impact of local women's bureaucracies in the policy area of gender equality is tentatively assessed.

title: ORGANIZATIONAL ASPECTS OF IRRIGATION SYSTEMS
abstract: The paper is a preliminary descriptive statement of an on-going research project dealing with organizational attempts of consolidating selected public & private irrigation companies in 5 western states. Anticipated water shortages in the West & related shifts in national & regional trends (such as increasing population, increasing urbanization & industrialization) create new & different demands for water to be supplied to communities. This implies that new alternatives of organizational structure must be found to increase the effectiveness of water distribution. A model of water resources management is discussed around the 2 major environments, ie, external & internal. Specific variables of the model are discussed in 3 dimensions: (1) Inputs, such as the natural resources, population characteristics, normative resources, economic viability, political networks, & technology. (2) 'System' with 3 component parts, personnel, facilities, procedures. (3) Output (& feedback mechanisms) serving as important indices for measuring the extent to which available resources are effectively handled. The final part of the paper delineates measures of effectiveness of irrigation companies & such indicators of intra- & inter-organizational effectiveness as output, satisfaction with the organization, relationships between organizations. Organizational-effectiveness would then imply the extent to which an irrigation system achieves its objectives without incapacitating its means & resources, & without placing undue strain on its members.

title: New Public Management Reforms in France and Britain: Towards a Redefinition of the Professional Autonomy of General Practitioners (GPs)?
abstract: Based on the study of key health policies over the last twenty years, this paper analyses the impact of New Public Management-inspired reforms on the professional status of GPs in France & Britain. Although the international comparative framework identifies common trends, it also highlights the contrasting impact of New Public Management reforms on GPs in the two countries. Pre-existing modes of governance regulating relationships between the state, the medical profession & the users/insurance companies tend either to weaken or to strengthen the process of reform implementation. Finally, the paper suggests that New Public Management reforms have an impact on the status of GPs & on their professional practice. While they have led to a relative weakening of medical autonomy in both countries, this has been partly compensated -- especially in the British case -- by salary increases & increased status relative to other sections of the medical profession. However, the changing framework has also contributed to bringing the position of GPs closer to that of other healthcare sector professionals as far as organisational structures & remuneration are concerned. Our study provides an illustration of how the professional status of a traditionally devalued segment of the medical profession -- i.e. general practice -- is being redefined.

title: Legal System and Economic Governance: The Institutionalization of Cartels and Trade Associations in 1931-1945 Japan
abstract: Critiques the economic & Marxist views & then articulates a Weberian-institutional view on the legal system. Through an analysis of the economic legislation that promoted the development of mandatory cartels & trade associations in Japan during the Great Depression & WWII, a legalcentric theory of economic governance is offered. It is argued that the characteristics of the legal system have a huge impact on the how the state defines property rights & governance structures, & many cross-national differences in economic governance can be attributed to the differences among the legal systems. In contrast to the Western legal system, which emphasizes individual rights, the Japanese legal system, influenced by the Asian legal tradition, focuses on duty & penalty. Different from the common law tradition in which the court is the center of legislation, the Japanese legal system, having followed the continental tradition since the Meiji Restoration, gave more juristic power to the executive branch office of the state. When the Japanese faced the challenges of the Great Depression & WWII, these institutional legacies, together with the new reception of German economic law -- a major revision of the principles in civil & business laws -- enabled that state to pass economic legislation that gave the state bureaucracy much more power to maintain industrial order & mobilize the nation into war by constraining property rights of private companies & supporting the state-led governance structures.

title: Coupling in Networks
authors: Sim, Francis M; Spence, Larry D; Takei, Yoshimitsu
abstract: Recent literature on bureaucracy has imparted the notion of "loose coupling" to repair defects in received conceptions of organizations, but the idea remains vague. Identified are the principal mechanisms of variation in coupling & formal models of concepts & processes. Examples are analyzed from usage in control, communication, & causation.

title: Water in Our World: A Study of Aesthetic Preference
abstract: Individual preference for different outdoor water-related scenery is examined. Six hypotheses were derived from the literature. Independent variables included: socioeconomic status, age, sex, residential patterns, & outdoor recreational activity. The dependent variable, scenic preference, was measured by the respondents order of preference of color photographs of scenes & impressions on semantic differential scales of adjective opposites. A stratified, random cluster provided a sample of 237 adult Wyo residents. Age was found to be the best determinant of scenic preference. The reasons for choosing scenes revealed the importance of color combinations & the affective dimension of the attitudinal component. Consistent with previous research, scenes demonstrating human modification received lower preference ratings, especially among the youth, than those which appeared to be unmolested, colorful, & accentuated by moving water.

title: Private Regulation of the Public Sector: A Neglected Facet of Contemporary Governance
abstract: The centrality of regulation among the tools deployed by governments is well established in the social science literature. Regulation of public sector bodies by non-state organisations is an important but neglected aspect of contemporary governance arrangements. Some private regulators derive both authority and power from a legal mandate for their activities. Statutory powers are exercised by private regulators where they are delegated or contracted out. Contractual powers take collective (for example self-regulatory) and individuated forms. But a further important group of private regulators, operating both nationally and internationally, lack a legal mandate and yet have the capacity to exercise considerable power in constraining governments and public agencies. In a number of cases private regulators operate more complete regulatory regimes (in the sense of controlling standard setting, monitoring and enforcement elements) than is true of public regulators. While private regulators may enhance the scrutiny given to public bodies (and thus enhance regimes of control and accountability) their existence suggests a need to identify the conditions under which such private power is legitimately held and used. One such condition is the existence of appropriate mechanisms for controlling or checking power. Such controls may take the classic form of public oversight, but may equally be identified in the checks exercised by participation in communities or markets.

title: Old and New Organizational Cages: What about Autonomy?
abstract: The issue of autonomy has become increasingly important in the discourse on the shift from a bureaucratic organizational order to a post-bureaucratic one. In fact, this discourse tends to emphasize some values like freedom, creativity & auto-realisation of members of organizations. The first part of the paper addresses these issues from a conceptual perspective on the basis of the metaphor of the glass cage. This metaphor stresses some aspects of the present organizational forms, in particular regarding the contingency (the glass can be chipped, cracked, broken off) & the ambivalence (the glass cage is fragile & resistant; transparent and opaque; it involves more freedom but new constraints as well). After discussing the issue of the organizational autonomy in this framework, the paper reports over research work which is based on a case-study regarding Italian Local Health Agencies. In particular, it will focus on a specific pilot programme which was launched by the Local Health Agencies in a north-east Region of Italy (Friuli-Venezia Giulia) in order to develop innovative practices and institutional change in dealing with health policies and services. The aim of the case study is to investigate the meanings and implications of New Public Management wherever local and situated organizational cultures seek to promote conditions of autonomy. Deriving from this analysis some conclusions on changing organizational cages, New Public Management & autonomy are being developed.

title: Municipal Reform and Participation in Medium-Sized Cities in Chile
abstract: An examination of how local government in different medium-size cities in Chile has been affected by reform enacted by the present military government, with focus on their organization, legal status, staff, budget, the social programs & services they administrate, & the behavior of the actors involved in decision-making processes both inside & outside the municipal institution. The reform of the political & administrative systems of town councils in Chile stands among the most important attempts at administrative decentralization of the state carried out in Latin America during the last decade. It has meant updating the local administration & increasing its technical capabilities & efficiency. Nevertheless, this reform has created a local government whose main feature is the lack of democratic representation for the citizens. This remains as one of the greatest challenges of the transition to democracy in Chile.

title: The Interests of Bureaucrats: Implications of the Asian Experience for Recent Theories of Development
authors: Kraus, Richard C; Maxwell, William E; Vanneman, Reeve D
abstract: Neither modernization studies nor the newer world system approach to development have treated bureaucrats as an autonomous group which pursues its own interests in competition & collusion with other social groups. An examination of bureaucrats & higher education politics in Thailand, India, & China over the past three decades reveals a notably similar vision of group interest, despite great differences in historical origin & in the success with which these interests have been pursued. The comparative success of Thailand's bureaucrats & failure of China's can be illuminated in part by considering differences in relationship to the world system, although this is by no means a sufficient explanation. Bureaucrats choose allies in conjunction with possibilities presented by the world system, as well as by such internal factors as the strength of rival social groups & the continuity of bureaucratic organization. Theories of development are currently in considerable flux; the world system contribution would gain analytical power by adopting a more realistic perception of bureaucrats.

title: Berlin's Urban Waterfronts: Places of Opportunity, Spaces of Conflict
abstract: "Berlin has more bridges than Venice!" Although this is a frequently heard tourist slogan in the German capital, Berlin's urban waterfronts do not yet live up to their true potential. This paper will focus on key inner-city waterfront areas located right along the Berlin wall's former Death Zone, particularly the lower end of the Spandauer Schiffahrtskanal between the Northern & the Humboldt harbors, right next to Berlin's new Central Station and just north of the new Federal Government quarter. Despite numerous plans & concepts, development is still lagging along this extensive stretch of waterfront right in the heart of the city. This contribution will trace the area's history & compare its potentials to alternative waterfront locations in Berlin, notably the so-called Mediaspree development along the southern part of the Spree river. The paper will also analyze the city's official framework plans for its various urban waterfronts, including the Spree, Humboldt harbor & the canal, as well as the private initiatives complementing them. The paper will provide both a general & a location-specific assessment of the complex challenges, prospective user conflicts & trade-offs which public and private sector actors face in the overall process of waterfront regeneration in prime locations, paying particular attention to large-scale redevelopment initiatives involving urban mega-projects.

title: Making the Technological Transition - Citizens' Encounters with Digital Pension Services
abstract: We examine in this article the impact of digitization on the provision of public services by studying how citizens experience the use of web portals in their pension planning. Based on focus groups and user test material, we elucidate five critical phases that each operate as an obstacle for citizens' further engagement in the digital self-service process: interest, access, comprehension, reflection and support. We argue that these phases and the obstacles they entail illustrate a transition away from a situation in which control and agency over the quality of public services is embedded in a dyadic relationship between citizens and frontline personnel, and to a situation characterized by more complex relations between citizens, the front line, and the digital infrastructure. We argue that this transition implies that citizens are required to possess a new type of competence that contains both financial and digital skills. Citizens who are unable to develop or acquire such competence are likely to be disadvantaged by the services. Lastly, we argue that these developments pose significant challenges for public administrations to ensure the overall quality of the public services.

title: Studying the State from the Ground Up: Ethnography of a World Bank Irrigation Project in India's Desert
abstract: A discussion of epistemological & methodological differences between development institutions & rural poor peasants (their clients) in understanding social & ecological problems resulting from large-scale technological projects. Ethnographic data collected during a 1-year study in India's Thar desert along one of the world's largest canal & irrigation projects revealed peasant causal explanations quite distinct from ones constructed by the World Bank, the Indian government, & scholars. Data also showed that hegemonic development discourse is itself a development project, with historical, cultural, & ideological meanings & realities produced to make the project's institutional practices & growth appear rational & necessary. Deeply divergent interpretations of why a severe waterlogging crisis exists along a sustainable development project are analyzed, noting how technical correctives to environmental problems were developed & managed by the Indian state & the World Bank in ways that strengthened centralized state control over natural, capital, & labor resources, & disempowered the poor majority, weakened local resource-management institutions, & degraded ecological resources. It is concluded that studying state-society-nature relations at the grass-roots level most clearly reveals the structural contradictions of capitalist-directed development, & its most devastating ecological & social effects.

title: A False Dilemma: Between the Bureaucrat and the Professional -- A Sociological Analysis of the Role of Judges
abstract: The possibility of using a model of the professions is analyzed in terms of the role & structural approach applied to judges in Yugoslavia. The model in its classical form notes the inherent conflict between the attributes of professionalism & the bureaucratic characteristics of a judge's role. Data were gathered by mailed multiple-choice questionnaires. Factor analysis of the scale of professionalism, initially constructed on the premises of the classical model, revealed the existence of 13 latent structures. Judges exhibit the attributes of both "the model professional" & "the model bureaucrat." There is an intrinsic link between these characteristics, rooted in the structural configuration of the role. The role structure of judges is the natural environment for exercising professional tasks within the realm of specific ideological attributes of the profession & values of the bureaucrat. The sociologist must carefully weigh the differential utility of the models "professional" & "bureaucrat" in the study of the legal occupational structure. Furthermore, sociological theory should be freed from theoretical & methodological biases built upon old-fashioned & abstract notions of professional & bureaucratic ideology.

title: PROFESSIONAL-BUREAUCRATIC CONFLICT AND DEVIATION FROM ORGANIZATIONAL PROCEDURES
abstract: Studies of professionals employed by bureaucratic organizations have typically emphasized the problems posed for the professional when professional norms & organizational norms conflict. Loss of creativity & innovation, loss of autonomy, weakening of professional standards, & job dissatisfaction are usually posited as the negative consequences of professional-bureaucratic conflict. This anti-organizational, professional orientation tends to overlook the possible dysfunctions of conflict for the organization. This paper reports the results of a study which was designed to quantitatively examine the negative consequences of professional-bureaucratic conflict for organizations that employ professionals. Specifically, the following hypothesis was tested: the more conflict a professional experiences when he wants to provide services to clients, the more likely the professional will be to deviate from organizational rules, regulations, & procedures to assist clients. The hypothesis was tested among social service caseworkers employed by a large, metropolitan public social services (welfare) department which provided financial & social casework services to approximately one million clients. A mail questionaire was sent to 1,190 randomly selected caseworkers in December, 1968. Usable responses were returned by 45.0% of the 1,052 caseworkers who actually received the F. Deviation from organizational rules was measured by asking caseworkers whether they had ever used each of 5 procedures to help clients even though these actions contravened standard organizational operating procedures (eg, ignoring missing documents, ignoring client financial resources). Professionalbureaucratic conflict was operationalized by giving caseworkers a list of 9 possible organizational barriers & asking them how often they sense departmental opposition toward their barriers. The results showed a definite relationship between the experience of conflict & deviation from departmental rules: the more conflict a caseworker reported, the more likely he was to acknowledge using each of the deviation techniques, & the more likely he was to have used several of them.

title: Perceptions of Organizational Structure: A British, Japanese, and Swedish Comparison
authors: Azumi, Koya; Hickson, David; Horvath, Dezso; McMillan, Charles
abstract: Country or culture has no effect upon organizational structure, as seen from the results of applying the Aston schedule in factories matched for size, products, & status in Britain, Japan, & Sweden. The perceptions by members of the same structures as seen through the Hall-Bonjean bureaucracy scales, however, do show considerable differences by country & rank of the R. The Japanese perceive their organizations to be far more bureaucratic than do the British & the Swedish. The degree of bureaucracy is seen to rise in the three countries as one descends the organizational ladder. One's rank, however, is less powerful a predictor of structure than country except in the case of hierarchy of authority. The cross-national differences in the subjective cognition of the objectively similar stimuli are discussed along with "control graph," morale, & other data obtained in the same study.

title: Social Action for Reluctant Citizens: Confronting a Siltation Problem at Lake Red Rock
abstract: Over the past twenty years, heavy siltation of Lake Red Rock in south-central Iowa has reduced its storage capacity by 50%, diminishing the quality of the lake & its recreational appeal & increasing the potential for serious flooding. A group of private citizens & public officials, in cooperation with the Soil Conservation Service, are seeking to develop local social action strategies to plan, implement, & fund solutions to these problems. Information for developing such strategies was collected via mail & telephone survey from landowners & operators, agribusiness managers, & elected officials & leaders of civic organizations within the watershed. Initial findings indicate that the benefits of reduced siltation will acrue primarily to recreation businesses, nearby communities, & lake users. To preserve the viability of the lake & to enhance local economic development, farmers within the watershed must change cultivation & tillage practices & adopt soil conservation measures. However, since they will obtain no direct benefit from the reduced siltation of the lake, they have little interest in making changes & adopting practices that will reduce their profits. The challenge of the social action strategy, therefore, is to suggest ways to involve landowners & operators in change & to involve & encourage those who will benefit from these changes to help fund the cost incurred by farmers.

title: Bureaucracy, Health, and Social Services: The Case of the Elderly
abstract: The development of industrial Ur society has been accompanied by increasing use of bureaucratic mechanisms for meeting human needs which are no longer adequately met by traditional institutions. This trend continues in spite of considerable theoretical & empirical evidence that bureaucratic organizational forms are not fully suitable for such purposes. Several dimensions of the issue are examined in terms of: (1) the individual-society relationship & societal emphasis upon performance norms, (2) the characteristics of bureaucratic structures & their impact upon the personality of their functionaries, (3) the impersonality of bureaucratic norms & behavior in rule-oriented interaction with clients, & (4) the modes of client behavior intended to influence bureaucratic decisions in favor of the client. These characteristics are evaluated with respect to the needs of clients in the bureaucratic service delivery nexus. Some alternative approaches are reviewed & needed areas of research & policy implications are outlined.

title: Barriers to Shift to Efficient Farming Methods: A Case Study of SRI Cultivation Method from Southern India
abstract: Traditional rice cultivation involves wasteful flood irrigation. Systematic Rice Intensification (SRI) requires occasional watering of fields thus saving precious water resources. However, not many are shifting to this method. In this study based on Mid Godavari Basin & Krishna River Command Area, we focus on barriers other than that of financial or technological. Our primary findings hint that the approach of the State to promote (SRI) in water scarcity regions is major impediment.

title: Socio-Cultural and Economic Position of Rural Women: A Comparative Study of Two South Indian Villages
abstract: Investigates the status & sociocultural & economic position of women in 2 villages -- one irrigated (Chelgal) & another nonirrigated (Cheppial) -- in the Telangana region of Andhra Pradesh in south India. Data were collected via observation, group discussion, interview schedule, census reports, mass media books, & village & revenue records. It is concluded that irrigation has helped women in terms of more opportunity for work, better wages, regular payment, fixed timings, better working conditions, less bondage, & more freedom to choose the type of work. It has increased production, raised the status, style, & living standards of women, & freed them from the bondage of work. Their value system has changed in favor of modernization, positive attitudes to work culture, & active participation in decision making at home & in trade unions.

title: Bureaucratie, ou la republique pretre. Marx, Balzac and the Bureaucratic Revolution
abstract: The development of Karl Marx's reflections on the problem of bureaucracy are analyzed over three periods: (1) up to 1844, when he completed his economic & philosophical training, & wrote, among other things, his critique of the Hegelian theory of the right of the state; (2) 1845-1852, dominated toward the end by the coup of Louis Bonaparte; & (3) post-1852, influenced by the Paris Commune. Marx often referred to the problem of bureaucracy, its importance in capitalist/bourgeois society, & the dangers it represented for the development of new social & political relations after the proletarian revolution. Although he did not use the term bureaucracy in a consistent or systematic way, he seems to have developed his theory mostly in relation to French events, from the Great Revolution, to the coup d'etat of Louis Bonaparte, in 1851, & the Paris Commune, in 1871, which led him to write the essays, "The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte" (1852), & "The Civil Wars in France" (1871). It is suggested that Marx relied heavily on his French contemporaries, not only the recognized political thinkers, eg, C. H. de Saint Simon or Alexis de Tocqueville, but also Honore de Balzac & his caustic analysis of the French bureaucratic phenomenon.

title: Education and the Culture of Administrative Rationalization: A Cross-National Analysis, 1985-1995
authors: Drori, Gili S; Jang, Yong Suk; Meyer, John W
abstract: The paper uses cross-national & longitudinal data to assess the state of administrative rationality worldwide during the 1980s & 1990s. We also investigate the factors -- economic, political, & cultural; national & international -- that contribute to the worldwide change toward greater administrative rationality. Defining an administrative arrangement as a more rational, ordered, predictable, & less corrupt system of management (in either state, public, or private sectors), we find an overall expansion of such Weberian notions of administrative arrangements in countries worldwide. The greater rates of change toward a more rational & predictable national administration during the 1985-1995 period occur in developing countries & in some previously communist countries. We attribute this trend to globalization. From our causal empirical models we conclude that whereas the common expectation is that social complexity is the core factor in such changes in the national administrative culture, the main effects are neither economic nor political in nature but rather cultural. The main effects are of expanded education & science sectors & meaning, cultural forces stemming from the nature of the modern world polity. In general, therefore, cross-national changes toward greater administrative rationality are tied to the ideological commitment to social rationalization: on the one hand, to global trends toward cross-national standardization of national practices (from production functions to education programs to information gathering), & on the other hand, an intense adherence to the dominant global model of governance -- the liberal world polity -- according to which rational bueaucracy is the preferable & more beneficial mode of system management & control.

title: AWARENESS OF WATER CONSUMPTION BY SOCIO-ECONOMIC STATUS
abstract: Abstract not submitted.

title: Public Policy Councils in Brazil: Limits and Possibilities
authors: Pessanha, Lavinia; Campagnac, Vanessa; Matos, Denise Ferreira de
abstract: Public policy councils are new deliberative instances legally based on the Brazilian 1988 Federal Constitution. Characterized as arenas for non-conventional social & political participation, in which the public administration is shared between the State & the society, through legally instituted governmental & civil representations. The article presents a quantitative panorama of the Brazilian city councils of sectoral policies, after information found on the 2001 Survey of Basic Municipal Information (MUNIC), carried through by the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE). The MUNIC 2001 edition researched the country's 5,560 cities & investigated city councils of 13 public policies sectors, generating the most updated & complete database on the subject. The article analyzes the city councils in relation to their formal existence, their effective activity, the balance between social & governmental representation, & the existence of a special fund in each sector; it also presents the councils' spatial distribution in Brazil. Additionally, it synthesizes the literature's main conclusions regarding the councils' qualitative limits & possibilities in being participative instances in which the State & the society may walk towards democracy. The authors also wonder about the social organization capacity of the cities, regarding the effectiveness of these arenas.

title: The Black Urban Regime, the Union Bureaucracy and the Working Class: The Case of New Orleans
abstract: How do black urban regimes simultaneously maintain a black working-class electoral base, while carrying out policies detrimental to their most loyal supporters? The New Orleans, LA, Marc Morial administration (1994-1998) is used as a case study to determine how black urban regimes successfully impose anti-working-class policies. Three contentious public policy issues during the Morial administration affecting the wage levels, political organization, & social wage of working-class New Orleanians, primarily the black working class, are studied: (1) defeat of living wage referendum, (2) defeat of city worker unionization drive, & (3) downsizing of public housing. Interviews, participant observation, & archival research are used to gather data on these three political conflicts. It is found that critical to the implementation of these anti-working-class policies, & the survival of the contradictory black urban regimes, is the role played by the union bureaucracy, co-opted community activists & university "partners." The influence of business interests is important, but the black urban regime's other partners are also essential in the successful implementation of these polices. Nonetheless, political conflict generated by these issues are generating an indigenous, working-class political alternative to the hegemony of the post-civil rights black political leadership. Further, findings give support to the Reed (1997) thesis that progress for African Americans comes when black working-class forces break through the hegemony of those that speak for the "black community." Findings question McAdam's (1982) thesis that sees black insurgency declining when radical forces challenge race spokespersons.

title: The Study of Sociology on People States Inhibitors in Caspian Sea
abstract: The Caspian Sea is the largest inland body of water in the world and its coastlines are shared by Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Russia, and Turkmenistan. This Sea is a highly productive water body, the reasons of which are intensive solar radiation & wealthy biogenic flow (till 300km3/year).The total fish biomass constitutes about 2900 thousand tons marine & fluvial ichthyofauna has species and subspecies including 25 commercial & sturgeon Fisheries occupy a prominent place in the economy of southern part of Caspian Sea. The main benefits which can be derived from fishery development & associated growth can be categorized under six different heads, a) nutrition & food supply b) income, c) employment, d) infrastructure e) rescue, f) defenses services. Public interest & government activity may be concentrated on other industries there by limiting the resources available for fisheries development. Then a new fact, such as increasing need for protein food stuffs, or the profitable exploitation of resources by foreign fleets may change the climate resulting in diversion of finance & man power to fisheries development. The various aspects of fisheries development of this local are discussed in the light of at the above resource characteristics & conditions. Key words: world, sociology, Caspian Sea.

title: Organizational and Occupational Professionalism: The Challenge of New Public Management
abstract: The paper considers the contrast between two different forms of professionalism in knowledge-based work: organizational & occupational professionalism. Organizational professionalism is a discourse of control used increasingly by managers in organizations. It incorporates rational-legal forms of authority, standardized procedures, hierarchical organization, managerialism, accountability & externalized forms of regulation. Occupational professionalism is a discourse constructed within professional groups which involves the occupational control of work & is based on practitioner trust by both clients & employers. It is operationalized by practitioners & controlled by professional institutes & associations. The paper will argue that these two different forms of professionalism are currently in competition at both state & international levels where both forms are operating simultaneously in knowledge-based occupational & professional work. New forms of public management & consumer cultures in health, welfare & education, will be used to illustrate current challenges to, & opportunities for, professional workers.

title: Flood Control and Reclamation Project: Curse or Blessing to the Rural Spanish-Speaking People of the Middle Rio Grande and Gallinas Valleys in New Mexico and West Texas
abstract: From the 1900s to the 1940s, the Federal Bureau of Reclamation built numerous conservation, flood control, & irrigation projects in the southwestern US that now produce much of the nation's food supply. However, since WWII, many of these projects have undergone such rapid industrialization & urbanization that available water supplies are threatened. The impact on the original landowners of two such federal projects in the Middle Rio Grande Valley in NM & western Tex & one abortive private project in the Gallinas River Valley in NM are analyzed. These projects reduced numerous Mexican-American & Spanish-American farmers from independent landowners to migrant farm workers, tenant farmers, & Ur immigrants.

title: Information Transfer Strategies for Promoting Soil and Water Conservation
authors: Hoban, Thomas J; Korsching, Peter F
abstract: Readily available & accurate information is critical in the adoption & diffusion process of soil & water conservation technology. Several strategies are presented for enhancing the adoption & diffusion process through the facilitation of information transfer about soil & water conservation problems, which were developed from an information needs assessment of nearly 700 farmers in southwestern Iowa. The process for transferring conservation information is divided into five main steps: (1) infrastructure & organizational development, (2) information needs assessment, (3) market selection & segmentation, (4) promotional communication, & (5) interpersonal farmer referral networks. These strategies are shown to be theoretically grounded in several areas, including the Knowledge-Attitude-Practice model & a Supply-Side Perspective on Innovation Diffusion. The strategies are presently being implemented as part of a quasi-experimental research project designed to evaluate the effectiveness of voluntary soil conservation efforts.

title: Australian Femocracy, Economic Rationalism. "Incorporating" Women's Differences and the Republicanism Debate
abstract: Australia's unique brand of feminism -- femocracy (women appointed to government bureaucracies to enhance the status of women) -- is based on political proclivities for "representative bureaucracy," fairness, & pragmatism. Explored here is how these enabling conditions have become obstacles to women's political engagements. Representative bureaucracy conceives that the various state organs have an obligation to serve different interest groups. When women belong to more than one such special group (eg, rural or Aboriginal women), their needs are ignored by policy-making apparatuses. Programs for these women are subsumed with those of men in the same interest group category, marginalizing women's specific requirements. Over the last decade economic rationalism has increasingly contended with equity or "fair go" rhetorics, forcing femocrats to reconceptualize some programs & abandon those that do not produce women as self-supporting workers. Pragmatism has meant that feminists were not paralyzed by abstract debates concerning the inherently patriarchal or capitalist nature of the state. Australian feminism, however, lacks the breadth of vision to constructively enter the republicanism debate with an agenda addressed both to the needs of women vis-a-vis men & to the constitution of women's diversity within an emerging nationalist umbrella of multiculturalism.

title: Aspects of Interpersonal Relations in Iran (a Case Study)
abstract: When an Iranian decides that his dossier is advancing rapidly, that he is escaping from the current administrative circuit & its slowness, he persues his dossier, ie, he personally solicits the intervention of each official involved & carries his dossier from office to office. Often in cases of complicated procedure, the slowness of the normal circuit renders the affair impractical; but as soon as one has dealings with the administration, even for a simple procedure, one seeks the intervention of anyone one might happen to know to obtain favored treatment. To this systematic use of personal relations is added the habit of establishing, by a series of courtesy visits, a personal tie with the functionary in charge of the dossier. These two complementary habits are at the same time the consequence & determinant principle of work organization of administrative personnel. Examined were 200 dossiers in summer 1976 in an administrative bureau concerned with fundamental operations permitting the extension of urbanization works in an Iranian city. Studied were: (1) calculation of the time spent on each of of seven stages for each dossier, & (2) the reasons for time inequalities perceived for the different stages of a dossier as well as for the dossiers themselves. Concluded were the existence of great administrative slowness & the game of personal relations as motivating factors. The slowness is explained by the mediocrity of salaries, amplified & compensated for by involvement in personal relations. Rendering a service to an acquaintance is an investment (direct or indirect) for the functionary -- profitable supplementary work actively engaged in. Thus, privileged clients can rapidly advance their cause while the ordinary dossiers are proportionally retarded. In the mind of the bureaucrat, the real work is no longer the work itself, but the maintenance of old acquaintances & the acquisition of new ones. Tr by A. Rubins.

title: Barriers to Local Participation in Techno-Environmental Decision Making: Contradictions between Residents' and Scientists' Assessments of Groundwater Contamination
abstract: Decisions relating to environmental problems must often incorporate technical knowledge that is beyond the reach of laypersons. This follow-up study reports on evaluations by residents of a rural MI community of an innovative university-based technical assistance program that was designed to provide them with accurate & comprehensive information about local groundwater contamination. Resident interviews suggest that while the intervention provided accurate assessments of their well water problems, it did not successfully communicate scientists' concerns about the quality of the local aquifer as a secure long-term community-level drinking water source. Program shortcomings in assisting residents to assess & remedy local water problems are attributed to limited financial resources & narrow institutional definitions of the intervention, which completely excluded residents' contextual understandings of their water resources from the formal assessment process. A range of alternative stakeholder intervention processes that might promote more genuinely democratic local decision making are evaluated.

title: BUREAUCRACY AND THE POOR: A STUDY OF THE WELFARE RECIPIENT IN PUBLIC HOUSING
abstract: The central purpose was to examine the welfare recipient in public housing as an example of the dependence of socio-economically deprived groups upon bureaucratic structure. The study tested the contention that bureaucratic structure is a medium through which advantaged groups maintain their socio-economic position vis-a-vis the poor. A 5% sample was drawn consisting of 456 F tenants from the 25 public housing projects located in a large northeastern city. The F head of each household was interviewed by a racially matched staff of trained interviewers. Results suggested that the relationship of the welfare recipient to the public housing authority is not unlike that between disadvantaged groups & client-centered bureaucracy generally. Public housing tenants receiving welfare assistance were less knowledgeable about bureaucratic power-structure & less likely to obtain adequate housing-related services than other tenants. Welfare status generates an independent effect on the relationship between the tenant & bureaucracy which cannot be explained solely on the basis of differences in race, project income, or education.

title: Growth Patterns of Governmental Activities in Small Political Systems (Swiss Cantons)
abstract: Starting with general hypotheses about the relationship between system size & structural characteristics, a comparative analysis of public expenditures in the twenty-five Swiss cantons (1930-1975) confirms that (controlling for SE factors) population size has an impact on the growth pattern & present state of governmental activities. The following tendencies are found among the smaller cantons: (1) relatively one-sided government organization as far as function is concerned, with a preference for activities that demand less institutionalization & organization, (2) a greater influence of exogenous, & a lower influence of endogenous factors, on the expansion & allocation of governmental activities, & (3) greater irregularities & unforeseen situations regarding amounts & growth rates of different sources of income & spheres of public expenditures. These & other findings lead to a discussion of the extent to which size has to be taken as a causal factor for the development of modern political systems (on the national level as well) & the extent to which it is an intervening variable which conditions the influence of SE development on governmental development.

title: Commoditization of Rural Water Supply System for Irrigation and the Social Formation of the Peasant Society: A Case Study of Indian Rural Society
abstract: Presents a case study of a small river-based canal in a village in Tamil Nadu, India, focusing on the policy issues of participatory management of the water-users. Water for irrigation in the village was, in the past, seen as a public good, requiring construction of reciprocal ties & participation in the water management & delivery system. Over time, water was transformed from a public good/commodity into a private good/commodity, with consequent deconstruction & reconstruction of the traditional participatory system. In this case, the greater the commoditization of inputs in the peasant activities in rural society, the greater the deconstruction of traditions. Thus it is imperative for policies to look into this inevitable social formation at the village level for better understanding agrarian society & alternative models of rural development.

title: Less Safe--The Dismantling of Public Information Systems After 9/11
abstract: Since the terrorist attacks of 9/11, there has been a tightening of public access. In response to perceived security threats, government agencies have taken information down from web sites, curtailed or restricted access to electronic sources of information, broadened the interpretation of Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) exemptions, created or augmented new categories of restricted information, and prohibited public access for critical infrastructure information. These policy responses have been based on the perceived security threat and an inhospitable attitude toward open government on the part of the Bush administration. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Process of Democratizing Power in the Environmental Conflict of Pascua-Lama
abstract: Chile constitutes a strongly centralised country with a long mining tradition. Its open market economy has stimulated foreign investment as a main development strategy, generating a proliferation of extractive projects with a high socio-environmental impact. In many cases, these projects face the rejection of the local population that has been officially excluded from the decision making process. This paper focuses in the Pascua-Lama conflict, in the border between Chile & Argentina. A gold mining project going to be placed in their water sources generated an opposition movement in the affected community. The environmental evaluation process, undertaken by technicians and approved by governmental politicians, impeded information and decision access to the community, promoting alternative ways of achieving it. The contact with national NGOs & groups involved in other environmental conflicts enhanced sharing related knowledge and spreading their demands at the national & international level. The internationalization strategy implied community empowerment & acquirement of political opportunities. However, the knowledge & power attainment does not mean a direct & real access to decision making. In fact, despite the high international impact of Pascua-Lama, until now its opposition movement has not been successful. This makes us reflect on the possibilities of different strategies of power democratization in environmental conflicts.

title: Friend or Foe? Assessing Bureaucracy's Role in the Implementation of Social Policy
authors: Sacks, Michael Alan; Lacey, Rodney O
abstract: Organizational research needs to advance scientific understanding of bureaucracy if it is to be used effectively to foster social policy. Assumptions inherent in linear models have been a key constraint in research on organizational structure. A configurational approach is theoretically more appropriate; thus, Boolean-based qualitative comparative analysis (Ragin, 1987) is used to overcome the linear model limitations. Data from the National Organizations Study are used to illustrate trends among the bureaucratic components of a representative sample of US organizations. It is shown that, of the 64 logically possible configurations of bureaucratic components, 19 are currently not in existence among these organizations. Logically minimized sufficiency equations show that a limited set of configurations is sufficient to cause improved performance. Implications of these findings social for policy & future research are outlined.

title: The Loomis Social System Framework: Application to Irrigation System Research
authors: Layton, James J; Lowdermilk, Max K
abstract: Irrigation system research performed to help solve specific problems occurring within the geographic area served by that irrigation system should be both interdisciplinary in nature & problem oriented in focus. These two requirements demand that the research process itself be constructed in a manner that will yield as a first step a systematic means by which realistic appraisals of the situation can be attained. One method of organizing the sociological component to appraise the situation in concert with other disciplines is the utilization of the Loomis social system framework. A description of how the Loomis framework has been constructed into a working format to be applied to a problem identification study comprises the focus here. The format which has been constructed is then placed into the arena of on-farm water management where dimensions of the problem are extracted & where a description of how the format may be used in a Pakistani irrigation system is presented. The purpose is to show how the Loomis framework can be used as a means to identify problems of irrigation farming systems.

title: Watering the Grass Roots: Federal-Local Interdependence in the Solution of Water-Related Problems
abstract: The purpose is to examine political barriers (sources of activity) to mobilization for the solution of general & water pollution problems at the local level. Political barriers are classified as: (1) veto efforts by politically unsocialized strata, (2) the 'free rider' effect operative in the delivery of public services, & (3) nondecision-making. Data are presented from six small communities in Del, & pertain to community leaders' (80% interviewed) & community residents' (13.5% response to mailed questionnaire) perceptions of the nature of local water-related problems; community residents' confidence in local political structures for the solution of these problems; & community residents' attachments, SES, & political values. Leaders & residents perceive water-related problems differently, with residents more likely to perceive general water & water pollution problems for which no ameliorative actions have been taken. Residents also lack confidence in traditional political institutions for initiating solutions to these problems. Further, those that claim that noninstitutionalized types of political action are more effective for influencing decision-making are as well integrated into the community as others, are of higher SES, & have relatively high political efficacy. Given these conditions, nondecision-making is the likely explanation for inactivity on water-related problems in these small communities. Given the present pollution control strategy, the grass roots are likely to remain without control, & water pollution uncontrolled.

title: Government and Sustainability in Mexico City
abstract: Mexico City has 20 million inhabitants. It is located in the central zone of Mexico's river basin, which is considered an environmental unit of great value for both the country and at global scale. Particularly, the South zone of Mexico City is maintaining around two percent of the world-wide biological diversity. However, there is a strong urban pressure on this zone since the city's poor and rich population are demanding land for housing. The main objective of this paper is to show the actions that the government of Mexico City is carrying out to avoid changes in the use of the ground, from rural to urban, particularly in areas protected by urban-environmental laws. In order to fulfill this objective, we will present the institutional frame and some of the instruments used by the local government. In addition, the social conditions that determine the difficulties or enable the application and fulfillment of the environmental normativity will be presented. The way in which the democratic process, initiated in 1997 with the first elections for local administration, has opened new forms for intervention of the authorities, a strict application of the existing legal frame (in contrast with the non transparent traditional procedures of urban administration) and a greater participation of the organized population will be emphasized.

title: The Effect of Gender on Career Activities and Attitudes of Political Executives and High-Level Bureaucrats in the United States, Canada, and Great Britain
abstract: Gender differences among M & F political executives & high-level bureaucrats in the US, Canada, & the UK were examined. Controls for cohort & status were introduced by a matched sample design. Overall, Rs were more similar than different in their occupational roles, responsibilities, & attitudes. But there was a pattern of persistent differences, especially in career motivations. Gender differences in roles & responsibilities were compared with cohort differences. Ms' perceptions of their activities were similar to the perceptions of more experienced cohorts.

title: Hierarchy, Mobility, and Domination: A Network Theory of Bureaucracy
abstract: The prevailing view that bureaucratic domination rests on legitimacy is challenged by offering a network theory relating domination & obedience to mobility. Earlier network-exchange experimental research demonstrating that mobility in a hierarchy produces domination is extended to larger structures, & related to the work of Max Weber. Bureaucracies are seen as the result of historically successful attempts to design social networks that reduce chronically disruptive & tenuous bargaining relationships among minimally differentiated power holders. The theory considers unit mobility structures as the parts out of which complex hierarchies of domination are constructed. This view of bureaucratic development being rooted more in network structures than ideas about legitimacy contradicts the formal Weber. There is, however, a substantive Weber who recognized that separation of office holders from the means of administration was a necessary condition for the centralization of domination. As separation is also a necessary condition of hierarchy/mobility, this is used as a point of departure to uncover a second theory of bureaucracy in Weber consistent with that discussed here.

title: Women, Water and Migration: Vulnerable Territories in Development Projects
authors: Jardim, Gabriel de Sena; D'Avila Neto, Maria Inacia
abstract: Although its close contact with water, women are not contemplated as protagonists of development. Their conditions of vulnerability are reinforced by roles carried traditionally, preventing their mobility. Almost always associated with climate change & the scarcity of vital natural resources, female migrations have increased in several regions of the planet, which is also observed in Brazil. This paper aims to discuss this phenomenon, in relation to women, on environmental issues, & in particular, management of resources such as water & its significance in everyday life and cultural imagery. This research is justified on the study of the vulnerability of local & global projects, in face of the feminization of migration, as well as the importance of gender mainstreaming water policies for development ("Gender & Water", UNDP, 2006). This work is inserted in the contemporary debate of women on struggle for recognition, discussed by social justice theoreticians (Fraser, 2001; Honneth, 2003), feminism (D'avila Neto, 2004, 2005; Butler, 2007; Braidotti, 2000, 2004), cultural studies (Said, 2007; Hall, 2003), Post-Colonialism (Gilroy, 2001; Santos, 2006) & subaltern studies (Spivak, 2007).

title: Legislative Framework and Implementation Challenges in Wetland Conservation in South Africa: Case Study Focus on the Isimangaliso Wetland Park
abstract: Water scarcity is a critical sustainability challenge in South Africa -- water being one of the country's most limiting natural resources. In this context, one of the major concerns facing the South African water sector is the degradation & loss of wetland resources. Between 40 & 60% of South Africa's wetlands have been lost, mainly due to infrastructure & urban development & mining (DWAF, 2006). These losses bring to the fore conflicts between economic & social development & natural resource conservation in South Africa. Although legislation protecting South Africa's water resources is widely regarded as amongst the most progressive in the world[challenges in the implementation of policy frameworks are significant. This paper will centre on a critical assessment of the traditional policy paradigm for wetland conservation in South Africa. The hypothesis that traditional government policy paradigms remain reactive, piecemeal & tactical will be explored. The question will be addressed specifically with regard to the limitations of a legal regulation towards natural resource conservation, in the context of pressing social development needs. The case study focus will be on the iSimangaliso Wetland Park, in northern KwaZulu Natal. The iSimangaliso Wetland Park was listed in 1999 as South Africa's first UNESCO World Heritage Site. Although iSimangaliso is a protected area, the catchment extends beyond the boundaries of the Park. Economic and social development priorities for the region mean that impacts from forestry, mining & farming have a significant cumulative impact on the catchment. The paper questions to what extent a purely legislative framework for wetland conservation is effective in a wider context of pressing economic & social development priorities, where concerns around economic growth take precedence over those of sustainability.

title: PERCEPTION OF ALTERNATIVES AND ATTRIBUTION OF RESPONSIBILITY FOR A WATER POLLUTION PROBLEM
abstract: Both legal philosophy & attribution theory suggest that if a person had no alternative courses of action open to him then he is less personally responsible for the outcomes of his behavior. Data based on over 400 interviews with a random sample of Denver, Colo water users suggests that a direct linear relationship between attribution of alternatives & attribution of responsibility to various social roles for a water pollution problem is quite weak although not negligible. This does not imply that alternatives plays no part in the attribution of responsibility to social roles. Further analysis revealed that attribution of alternatives was generally a necessary, but not sufficient condition for attribution of responsibility. There were great differences across roles with over 90% of the sample attributing responsibility to either state & local officials or to top management at the company involved & only about 10% feeling that the individual or low level management was responsible. It also appears that perception of alternatives mediates between attribution of responsibility & other variables in the study. Finally we can very tentatively suggest that there are differential causes of perception of alternatives for various roles.

title: State-Centric Child Protection Discourse
abstract: It is argued that the child protection discourse instituted in most Anglo-American jurisdictions in the mid-1980s has very little to do with the rights or interests of children, & a good deal more to do with the reshaping of state strategies of political management. These strategies have a colonizing thrust with respect to the domestic population, & are located within a general disestablishment of liberal & social democratic citizenship discourse. It is proposed that child protection discourse is homologous in many respects to nineteenth-century colonial discourses of protecting native women against the cruel or brutish traditions & men of their culture, & that in both instances, the conferral of victim status on children or women reproduces the very power that ensures they need to be protected against that power. The displacement by the state of protocitizenship claims on behalf of children within child abuse discourse is described, along with their conversion to claims on behalf of the state's surveillance & controlling powers with regard to potential perpetrators in the child protection discourse. While the former is a civil discourse with some potential for the development of democratic process in respect of adult domination over children, the latter is a state-centric discourse sequested within the domain of what Fraser terms the "juridical-administrative-therapeutic state apparatus.".

title: Educational Change in Estonia. The Interplay Between Politicians and Policy Communities
abstract: This is a first report of a project that studies to what extent the activities of bureaucracies of the public sector change by means of directives from politicians. Do the services offered to citizens change, when the political regime changes from an authoritarian socialist system to a democratic liberal one? The main issue is policy of education at state level. It looks at the activities of policy communities during the 90's, & their interaction with politicians in the field of education. It points to tensions between policy communities & politicians. The policy communities are quite permanent with reference to participants, ideological cleavages & ways of influencing policy, while politicians are working in short-time terms. They therefore have difficulties to navigate policy proposals through the process of democratic decision-making. This results in a lack of clear policy guidance from the state level, which leaves street-level bureaucrats a great deal of discretion. A change in implementation approach is also noted. A bottom-up approach was used to introduce educational change, during the last years of soviet rule & the first decade of independence. This involved street-level bureaucrats, that is, teachers & principals, in the reform work. This was later changed to a top-down approach, where reforms are designed at higher levels of bureaucracy & later communicated to the street-level.

title: Community Responses to Toxic Hazards: Acceptance vs. Resistance of Injection Wells in Two Texas Communities
abstract: The goal of this research is to understand what makes some communities able to coordinate their members & mobilize resources in response to a toxic hazard in their midst, whereas others remain relatively passive in their acceptance of potential risk to health and property. These latter communities endure the physical consequences of the toxic hazard as well as the added affronts of feeling marginalized & powerless. This project is a qualitative study of two Texas communities impacted by toxic hazards associated with waste water injection wells. One site is dealing with the effects of the new presence of a waste water injection well & the other has mobilized to resist the location of similar threats in their community. Data was gathered through in-depth interviews using a snowball approach to identify respondents. Interviews, field notes and study of related news stories & legal documents began in February of 2009 & are ongoing in May 2010. Interviews have been transcribed, coded & analyzed using qualitative analysis software. Emerging themes indicate that bridging social capital (Putnam 2000) & the degree to which the local economy is diversified are two principal factors in how actively a community resists toxic hazards.

title: Methods for Assessing the Transformation of Human Needs Satisfactors Associated with Natural Resources. The Case of the Peri-Urban Community of Tultepec, Mexico
