abstract: This paper focuses on the methods utilised to assess the change in the perception, use & knowledge of natural resources, particularly water, in a community located in the peri-urban interface of Mexico City. The purpose of this research is to analyse the relationship between water uses & the construction & transformation of some satisfactors of human needs (goods, relationships, activities, capabilities, institutions) & therefore, people's well-being, which is defined as the coverage & realisation of several of those human needs. The case study refers to the transformation in the quality of life of inhabitants of San Pedro Tultepec, a peri-urban village between the Metropolitan Zones of Mexico City & Toluca. In this place, people's livelihoods were traditionally based on lacustrine resources that disappeared during the course of the second half of the 20th Century, due to the desiccation & pollution of local wetlands caused by the construction of a supplying water system for Mexico City & local industrial developments. Then, livelihoods radically changed to a combination of furniture production & trade, & industrial work. The paper focuses specifically on the methods for registering & measuring the relationship between well-being & environmental degradation, such as focus groups, genealogical survey & spatial attributes mapping survey.

title: Public Participation and the Fostering of Societal Learning in Watershed Management in Brazil
abstract: The paper analyses the institutional transformations that have taken place in the environmental management process in Brazil since the 90s, emphasizing the enlargement of democratic spaces & popular participation in the field of water management. The focus is on the water basin committees, an innovative institutional engineering in the water management process in Brazil since 1997. The new watershed law presents a framing of the issue of watershed protection, recognizing the prime importance of a management system, extending the protection instruments proposed & opening the possibility of developing widespread agreement among stakeholders for the actions that are needed. Water basin committees are the appropriate arenas to develop a comparative study of institutional performance & its relations with cooperative practices linked to preservation, spatial and environmental management. The text presents an overview of the theoretical debate & the main outcomes of several researches developed in Brazil on social participation in watershed management, using as reference multi-stakeholders platforms (MSPs) as mode of involving civil society in decision-making on resource management. The main arguments of this study are to show how these MSPs can make a difference & their potential to bring about creative experiences of social learning in the context of sustainability.

title: RATIONAL AND LEGAL AUTHORITY WITHIN HIERARCHICAL AND AUTONOMOUS BUREAUCRATIC STRUCTURES
abstract: An attempt to ascertain the independent & interactional effects of autonomy-hierarchy, rational, & legal authority, on the dependent variables of job satisfaction & productivity. A weighting procedure for the independent variables was devised for each of the dependent variables resulting in the following hypotheses: Individuals exposed to the autonomy group structure have the same productivity as individuals exposed to the hierarchical group structure. Null hypothesis accepted if p= >.80. Individuals exposed to superordinates who possess low legal authority have the same productivity as individuals exposed to superordinates who possess high legal authority. Null hypothesis accepted if p= >.80. Individuals exposed to superordinates who possess superior knowledge express greater job satisfaction than individuals exposed to superordinates who possess inferior knowledge. Individuals exposed to superordinates who possess low legal authority express greater job satisfaction than individuals exposed to superordinates who possess high legal authority. Hypotheses were also formulated for both dependent variables & each independent variable with the remaining 2 independent variables held constant. 5 groups of 3 subjects for each tested variable were used. Summarily, the main findings indicate that the independent variable of superior rational authority was significant in explaining variation of 'employee' productivity. The independent variable of autonomy-hierarchy was significant in explaining 'employee' job satisfaction, though contrary to the hypothesis, subjects exposed to the hierarchical group structure expressed the greatest satisfaction. Though productivity & job satisfaction were not expected nor hypothesized to co-vary, trends in the data suggest that given a technically competent supervisor, individuals exposed to an autonomy group structure & a supervisor with high legal authority, as well as a hierarchical group structure & a supervisor with low legal authority, have high productivity as well as moderate job satisfaction. In brief, the hypotheses regarding productivity were confirmed while those regarding job satisfaction were not found to be significant.

title: BUREAUCRATIC RATIONALITY AND SOCIAL CLEAVAGE: INTER-FIRM VARIATION IN RATES OF MINORITY GROUP INCORPORATION
authors: Eidson, Bettye K; Rossi, Peter H
abstract: The purpose was to account for variation in the rates at which a sample of major private urban firms were incorporating Negroes. Interviews with personnel officers in 15 cities were conducted during the Spring of 1968. In each city, the 10 firms with the largest number of employees were selected along with a 20% sample of the next 90 largest firms, yielding Completed interviews were obtained for 447 firms. Negro representation was reported for 3 stages (% Negro among recent applicants, among the recently hired & among the currently employed) by 3 skill levels, generating 9 separate Negro incorporation rates for each firm. 2 linear regression models were rotated over each of the 9 rates. The 1st model contained information on market characteristics of the firm, administrative characteristics, attitudes of the firm's personnel officer toward minority group members, & information on the firm's city location. The 2nd model was identical to the 1st except that the % of the firm's current LF that was Negro, at each skill level, was added to the equation. This modified equation was used to predict variation in rates at which Negroes were applying & were being hired, at skilled & at unskilled levels in the firm. The original model was found to be more useful in accounting for variation in Negro skilled & unskilled incorporation rates than in accounting for variation in rates of Negro assimilation at the professional & white-collar level. At bluecollar levels, factors such as industry growth rates, recruitment channels used to obtain workers, firm size, city-level unemployment rates, etc, appeared to predict fairly well (R2 = .30, average) rates of Negro incorporation, at each state of the employment process. At the professional & white-collar level, the best predictor of the rates at which Negroes were applying to major private firms was the proportion Negro among the firm's current professional & white-collar employees. Holding constant the same factors as in the first equation & adding only information about the 'current' Negro employment distribution increased the amount of explained variance by about 50%. The rate at which Negroes were being hired for professional & white-collar jobs also was best predicted by the 'current' distribution of Negroes among the firm's professional & whitecollar employees-an improvement of about 75% over the original equation.

title: Public Participation in Environmental Protection Proceedings: Tempering Bureaucracy with Democracy
authors: Schwartz, Richard D; Ksander, Margret M
abstract: An examination of the fundamental social problem of tempering bureaucracy with democracy, specifically with reference to toxic waste problems. Scholarly work in both law (Frug, 1985) & social science (Page, 1985; Wolin, 1981; Crozier, 1964) argues that bureaucracy, as a phenomenon in contemporary society, poses a threat to participatory democracy. Toxic waste management is an area in which such a threat represents an increasingly critical issue for administrative agencies charged with environmental protection, as well as for local communities & concerned citizens. Data generated in an ongoing study in a related environmental problem area (wastewater treatment) are drawn on to examine a possible method for opening bureaucratic decision making to the influence of citizens & groups representing diverse interests in the community. After examining the present pattern as framed by existing governmental regulations, a revised model of public participation is proposed for possible use in dealing with toxic waste problems. This proposal is a serious attempt to implement what Cambell described as "methods for the experimenting society.".

title: Interorganizational Structure and the Survival of State Agencies: Embeddedness and Autonomy in State Organization
abstract: Addressing Weber's problem of state bureaucratic autonomy, it is argued that organizational autonomy must be explained as an interorganizational phenomenon, rather than as an intrinsic property of organizations. Implications of this argument for understanding differential rates of survival among CA state agencies, 1850-1975, are developed. Interorganizational ties & monopoly status protect agencies from death & restructuring. Connections to nonstate political organizations have nonlinear effects on organizational survival, suggesting that social organization of the polity & society can serve both as a base of support & a liability for state activities & organizations. Structural embeddedness enhances organizational survival at lower levels, but may be detrimental at higher levels by creating environmental complexity & imposing organizational inertia, which may lead to failure at both the organizational & network levels.

title: Obstacles to the Democracy at Work in the Public Sector: Sociotechnics of Debureaucratization
abstract: The ineffectiveness of the public sector is a major problem for both socialist & nonsocialist countries throughout the world. A variety of solutions to this problem are considered. The development of alternatives to bureaucracy appears to be necessary both because of the complexity of modern economies & as a means of improving the self-images of public employees. Autonomization & self-management offer a path to such an alternative, which can be achieved through cultivation of awareness of alternative organizational forms; mobilization of forces within the public sector; & learning from innovative organizational experience of other organizations. Collective bargaining on a cooperative rather than antagonistic basis, & directed toward transformation of the work environment, rather than toward economic goals, is recommended.

title: SOME NOTES ON THE POSSIBILITIES OF POLITICAL INTERVENTION OF ITALIAN BUREAUCRACY
abstract: An attempt to analyze the possibilities Italian bureaucracy has of acquiring political power. The most important factors that influence the relationship between bureaucracy & politics are: The characteristics of the political system & those of bureaucracy, especially such elements as the facilities available to bureaucracy, the social & professional characteristics of its personnel, their orientations, etc. A description is given of some features of the Italian political system, pointing out the numerous --power vacuums' existing at the highest decision-making levels. The Italian bureaucracy's history shows that it has never known a period of strong political power. The present features of the bureaucratic structure are then examined, considering the facilities available to it (found to be very inadequate). The main characteristics of the personnel are outlined: Me to LMc, southern background, prevalently legal education, economic motivations for joining the civil service. Among the mechanisms which the structure employs for the socialization of its personnel, considered especially are recruitment & career patterns. They are found to be seriously inadequate, as is the case in the evaluation of the bureaucrats themselves. All these factors must lead to a far from aggressive orientation on the part of the personnel: indeed, their attitudes show defensiveness & resignation. It is concluded that the Italian bureaucracy is not a dominating factor in political life. However, the weakness of the political system in general is such that even a weak bureaucratic structure can exercise some power: it is mainly negative power (power to stop more than power to initiate). In this sense Italian bureaucracy can be considered as a veto group. Modified AA.

title: The Contribution of Bureaucracy to Diagnostic Uncertainty: An Idiographic Account
abstract: A patient's experience of serious illness naturally includes feelings of anxiety about his/her fate. Such feelings can be exacerbated by the inability or failure of specialist physicians to inform the patient of the name & nature of the condition or disease from which he/she is suffering. While diagnostic uncertainty is an intrinsic feature of scientific medicine, it is typically reinforced by the bureaucratic features of hospital organization & routines. Drawing partly on personal experience as a hospital patient who received an uncertain diagnosis of a gastrointestinal condition & a mistaken diagnosis of a musculoskeletal condition, it is suggested that the characteristic features of bureaucracy -- its complex division of labor, hierarchical authority structure, procedural rationality, & impersonality -- amplify diagnostic uncertainty.

title: Accounts and "New Public Management": The Case of Universities
abstract: L'evaluation de l'activite des universitaires connait en France de grands changements, generalement surtout rapportes a l'utilisation de divers indicateurs, dont l'analyse critique a ete abondamment documentee. On voudrait dans la presente communication montrer un aspect jusqu'ici peu etudie de cette nouvelle evaluation: une mise en recit de l'activite passee, et meme future qui, en fait, argumente l'activite scientifique des individus et des equipes selon des regles qui retrouvent les plus anciennes regles de la fiction. En particulier, la dierese prime sur la diegese, dans la mesure ou l'attente esthetique du lecteur, puis de l'auditeur, est la premiere demande que le texte doit combler. On proposera d'analyser ce phenomene dans ses manifestations ecrites, mais aussi dans sa scenographie et sa dramaturgie a l'oral. On retrouvera ainsi les regles venerables d'unite de temps, d'action et d'intrigue, les notions de "mission", "d'entreprise" et de "heros". On reperera aussi la mise en scene du narrateur legitime. On mettra cette analyse de la mise en recit dans la perspective theorique de "la connaissance des evenements futurs", analysee par Alfred Schutz Cette analyse reposera sur une observation participante de ces processus, dans laquelle nous assumons un role d'observateur implique, sur lequel nous reviendrons brievement. Nous montrerons ainsi que la "fiction" est au cAur du Nouveau Management Public, que les regles du recit sont celles d'un pacte communicationnel qui unit dans une meme foi les lecteurs-auditeurs-critiques et les auteurs-narrateurs-personnages. Ce pacte repose sur ce qu'on pourrait appeler un "grand secret", dont le devoilement par l'observateur implique fait scandale.

title: Organizational Structure and Dynamics as a Link to Social Equality in the Case of Arson Control
abstract: A case study on organizational process, examining how formal bureaucratic structure & informal subcultures direct the performance & effectiveness of government agencies in serving urban populations. Organizational sociologists have focused on how organizations carry out goals, largely as a measure of how closely organizational dynamics fit the ideal-typical bureaucratic arrangement, & have left the links between process & outcomes largely to political scientists. The links between public organizational & social outcomes have been addressed by researchers concerned primarily with issues of legal process & crime control, & not necessarily with organizational or political theory in general. Here, theories of organizational & legal process are brought together, & an attempt is made to reach some conclusions about the political goals of state agencies themselves. It is argued that state organizational processes translate, in a political sense, into what Claus Offe has called "selection mechanisms." Selection mechanisms determine social class outcomes by constraining forms of government intervention.

title: Government Downloading and the "Third Sector": The New Public Administration of the Canadian Post-Welfare State
authors: Shields, John M; Evans, B Mitchell
abstract: The neoliberal assault on the Keynesian welfare state & the demand that government be "reinvented" have come to focus increased attention on the so-called "third sector," because of (1) the moves by neoliberal governments to downloading former public responsibilities onto the market, nonprofit organizations, & individuals; (2) their desire to forge new partnership relationships with nonstate actors (eg, voluntary bodies) to develop alternative service delivery options; & (3) the neoliberal assertion that intrusive government has worked to undermine voluntary citizen participation, charitable giving, & self-help. The question of the place of the third sector in a reformed public administrative structure is of central importance to governance itself. The neoliberal impulse to revive voluntarism & a more participatory civic culture, &, in the process, transfer many social support functions to the nongovernment voluntaristic sector, speaks to its desire to disinvest responsibilities for various citizenship rights in the social & economic spheres, &, in the process, transform the state's role in society. Moreover, in the government's shift to develop a more contractually based relationship with nonprofit/voluntary organizations, the political economy of the third sector itself is being significantly altered. Explored here is the link between the role neoliberalism sees the third sector playing in its attempt to reinvent government & the implications this holds for public administration practice & governance. The roles of alternative service delivery, partnerships, & contract government as they relate to the new public administration of the postwelfare state are examined.

title: Is Participation Possible in a Bureaucracy? A Case Study within the Swedish Armed Forces Focusing on the Work That Preceded the 1996 Resolution of Defence
abstract: This thesis is about the conflict between participation and bureaucracy. This conflict is illustrated by a case study within the Swedish Armed Forces under the activity that preceded the 1996 Resolution on Defence. More closely it focuses on the decision-making process that led to the Swedish Armed Forces reports that were handed over to the Government in March 1996. In this decision-making process the Supreme Commander tried different ways to create participation among all the high-ranking officers, from a regional level to the Headquarters, to make them participate in the process. The thesis answers the question if it is possible to create participation in a bureaucratic organisation such as the Swedish Armed Forces, and the conclusion that I draw is that participation is hard to establish. First there is a conflict within the bureaucratic form itself, since a bureaucracy implies a diversification of assignments and responsibilities in different functions and at different levels in a hierarchy. Every level has its own task to fulfill, and this states how reality is to be understood. In the Swedish Armed Forces the bureaucratic structure is reinforced by the fact that the officer is promoted to a higher rank after his or her military training. Both the bureaucratic structure and the military training will lead to a differentiation between individuals, and they will be placed in different skills and status levels within the organisation. Besides this, individuals will gather information mostly from their own level, which will further fortify the difference between the levels. Furthermore there are also individual factors connected to the bureaucratic structure that have shown to complicate participation. For example individuals choose not to participate because they lack the necessary competence for the task, they do not have time, they have not been consulted, or they consider the task one to be solved at a higher level. So even if the military decision-making model encourages and advocates participation, it is difficult to break the bureaucratic design. Leaders often show inability to go from a bureaucratic leadership style to a democratic one. At the same time subordinates support their leaders when they act as a traditional leader.

title: THE BASIC SOCIAL CONFLICT IN SOCIALISM AND ITS SOURCE
abstract: According to the classic Marxist views, classes & class conflicts are a product of DofL in society. Thus the communist revolution strives to abolish social action based upon the DofL. All proletarian revolutions up to the present have been successful so far only in the political sphere. Social revolution, ie the abolishment of the class structure, still goes on. All socialist societies are divided into 2 antagonistic parts according to their respective attitude towards this fundamental goal of the revolution, ie the abolishment of the DofL. This conflict is represented by the juxtaposition of bureaucracy, whose status & privileged position depends upon divided labor, & of the We, which remains in a class position until it is the only class engaged in productive labor. Peter Jambrek.

title: THE ROLE OF BUREAUCRACY IN CONTEMPORARY SOCIAL CONFLICTS
abstract: The basic goal of socialism is the abolition of exploitation. This process, however, paradoxically implies the existence of bureaucracy, which on the one hand is not identical with the We, & on the other hand claims to represent the class interests of workers. Several functions of bureaucracy in contemporary Yugoslav society are noted: (1) In the role of a representative of social structure as a whole, bureaucracy is continuously involved in conflicts with all parts of the social structure. In these cases the bureaucracy mostly cooperates with the We. (2) It is a special class or group within those segments of society which produce surplus value necessary for its existence, & which thus demand its abolishment. (3) Finally, bureaucracy acquires the role of a mediator in all conflicts, including those in which it is an interested party. Peter Jambrek.

title: Private Sector Participation and Performance of Urban Water Utilities in China
abstract: In the early 1990s, China began opening its urban water sector to nonstate capital to meet increasing urban water demand. By 2007, more than 30% of large and medium urban water utilities had attracted private sector participation (PSP), of which two thirds have a majority of nonstate shareholders. To understand the factors that drive PSP in urban water supply and to answer the key policy question of how PSP has affected water utility performance, we assemble and analyze a unique data set consisting of 208 urban water utilities servicing more than 300 million urban residents from 1998 to 2007. We find that a utility's profitability and liability level and a host city's road infrastructure in the prior year play important roles in driving private investors both to enter and to withdraw from the sector. It is further found that PSP utilities, and mainly those with majority nonstate shareholders, have made substantial cost savings through employment downsizing and cutting managerial expenses, which leads to a remarkable profit increase. Other estimates, although statistically insignificant, show that PSP increases a utility's investment and efficiency, and PSP cities have lower total and domestic water supply but more domestic water users.

title: FUNCTIONS AND DYSFUNCTIONS OF BUREAUCRACY IN TRANSITIONAL SOCIETIES
abstract: Bureaucracy as a form of organization has been regarded as a universal characteristic of societies undergoing a rapid process of modernization. This assumption has been extended to South American nations characterized as 'underdeveloped societies' where bureaucratic principles of organization marked by rationality are considered to be functional to the general process of development. Analyzing some of the characteristics of South American nations, it is concluded that the term underdeveloped, used to characterize these nations. is both nartial & misleading_ Partial in the sense that it is mainly based on economic considerations & misleading in the sense that it assumes the applications of certain principles & the elaboration of certain policies, elaborated elsewhere, & defined as necessary to attain the state of development. Within this context bureaucracy is regarded as functional to the process of development. In view of the stated limitations, the concept of 'transitional societies' is formulated to characterize South American nations. The concept 'transitional' implies mainly a process of transformation from a condition of structural dualism (elite-mass) to a condition of societal integration. Such a process implies conflict of interests. On the one hand, members of the elite try to maintain the situation as it is, &, on the other, members of the mass try to change the structure of society. Within the context of such a conflict, bureaucracy, or more appropriately, bureaucratic principles of organization, are used by the elite in order to attain more power & keep other segments of the population away from the power structure. 'Rational modern bureaucracy,' therefore, becomes an instrument of, & for, the status quo; & a tool to increase the separation between the priveleged sector of the society & the deprived sector of it. Consequently, bureaucratic principles of organization as conceived & defined by M. Weber & empirically manifested in the political structure of the US, are considered dysfunctional to the process of societal integration, basic for South American nations. AA.

title: Special Treatment: Information Technology and the Constitution and Government of Fragmented Populations
abstract: Traditional approaches to social stratification have emphasised the salience of class, gender and ethnicity in differentially structuring and shaping the life chances and meaning making of individuals. Importantly, class, ethnicity and gender also define groups or collectivities. In contrast to these forms of stratification, this paper examines patterns of stratification based on bureaucratic or administrative forms of classification to which information technologies have contributed and enhanced. For example, information technologies have greatly assisted the identification and differential government of 'risk groups'. Governments single out particular groups of unemployed individuals for more personalised, intense and interventionist programs, while banks differentially target products to their customer base to maximise profits. Although the former is often intended to reduce social inequalities, the latter reinforces and heightens it. Based on a comparative, historical study of the use of information technologies in the Australian and British welfare state and banking sectors, this paper theoretically examines the emergence of increasingly differentiated and targeted forms of acting upon individuals and the way this in turn differentially structures individual life-chances and capacity for action. In presenting a theoretical account of these developments, the paper will draw upon and contribute to the Foucault-inspired 'governmentality' approach, Actor Network Theory and Weber's account of bureaucracy.

title: Citizen Participation vs Bureaucratic Power
abstract: In the framework of a democratic & participatory constitution, economic systems follow an opening path, attempting to adapt to changing necessities in an increasingly global society. The opening path in democratic systems is protected in a principle triangle: transparency, information, & civic participation. The aim here is to deepen the citizen participation principle that is fed, to a large extent, by the development of information & transparency principles. The diversity of the processes by which people are channeled into citizen participation is the key, so that, in the society of the third millenium, "the functionary secret," ie, the element that Max Weber noted as characteristic of bureaucratic domination systems, disappears little by little.

title: PROFESSIONAL AUTONOMY AND BUREAUCRATIC ORGANIZATION
abstract: Autonomy is regarded as an important dimension of professionalism. A number of investigators claim that bureaucratic organization limits professional autonomy. This study was undertaken to determine empirically the validity of this claim. The relationship between bureaucratic structure & degree of professional autonomy within the client-professional relationship was examined by systematically comparing the perceived autonomy of professionals in 3 types of bureaucratic settings, nonbureaucratic, moderately bureaucratic, & highly bureaucratic. A total of 1,628 questionaires was mailed to professionals who worked in the 3 setting types in a large, highly urbanized area (Los Angeles County). Returns were received from 40% (230 of 580) of those in the nonbureaucratic group, 53% (276 of 520) in the moderately bureaucratic setting, & 34%0 (178 of 528) in the highly bureaucratic group. A Likert-type autonomy scale was developed from the responses to the multiple-choice questions included in the questionaire. The scale was then empirically divided into 3 degrees of autonomy-high, medium, & low. When degree of bureaucracy was related to degree of autonomy & statistical analyses (chi-square) were made, the data revealed that those professionals associated with the moderately bureaucratic setting are most likely and those in the highly bureaucratic setting are least likely to perceive themselves as autonomous. These findings do not support the contention that bureaucracy is necessarily detrimental to professional autonomy.

title: Why Are Bureaucrats Slow Adopters? The Case of Water Management in the Gezira Scheme
abstract: The slowness of bureaucratic structures to respond favorably to innovation is studied, using the example of the Gezira Scheme irrigation project in the Sudan. The farmers have, over the years, developed three major innovations in irrigation practice; technically, however, the improved practices are being carried out illegally because they are at variance with officially prescribed procedure. Nevertheless, they have made a major contribution to the diversification & intensification of cropping patterns over the last fifteen years. While it is conceded that a large-scale agricultural project such as this must be run from the top, organizational mechanisms should be designed to allow for eventual feedback to the center of experience gained at field level. Such mechanisms are vital as part of any monitoring & research function, in order that innovations be recognized early & fed swiftly into the policy-making & planning process. Modified HA.

title: The Picture as a Weapon in the Conflict of Elites. On Public and Private Resistance of the Bourgeoisie against the Spanish-Catholic Government in the Netherlands during the Sixteenth Century, as Articulated in the Oeuvre of Pieter Bruegel (1524-1569)
abstract: During the Dutch revolution, as Philip II based his absolutistic, modern, bureaucratic rule on traditional claims of legitimacy, his subjects & parts of the apparatus in their demand for a return to traditional, feudalistic forms of government argued with a modern concept of authority, based on contractual rules. When studying this process, documentary materials, eg, pamphlets, caricatures & prints, graphics, & painting, are of great importance. In the struggle of the Dutch, one can discern a moderate center-party for the Burgundian state under humanistic-Erasmian influence. While the separatists' anonymous pamphlets did not target the king, but his "evil advisers," the royalist's pamphlets accused the former of crimes against the Catholic church. Pieter Bruegel's graphics & paintings are distinctly critical toward society & the system, supporting the center-party. He blaims the conflicting elites & even the king. This is quite remarkable, as in spite of overall censorship on picture-production & in contrast to anonymous pamphleteers, the artist was identifiable by his style.

title: COPING WITH BUREAUCRACY: THE ISRAELI CASE
abstract: Results are presented of a national survey of attitudes of the Israeli public toward government & public bureaucracy. It is suggested that the problem of developing competence in dealing with bureaucracy is important in both modern & developing societies. Special focus is given to 2 forms of alienation from bureaucracy-feelings of incapability of achieving one's aims through the bureaucratic apparatus, & discontentment, or dissatisfaction with the functioning of bureaucracy-& to the consequences of such alienation for attitudes & behavior with respect to bureaucracy. A major goal is to identify those groups in Israeli society which have relatively greater difficulty in dealing with bureaucracy. The main findings are as follows: (1) Ls groups both had relatively less contact with bureaucracy & felt less capable of dealing with it; at the same time, they were less critical than Hs R's of its functioning. (2) Education & actual experience with Israeli bureaucracy are the 2 most central variables in shaping R's' orientations. (3) Findings on the consequences of alienation from bureaucracy did not all conform to expectations, though they made sense. Those critical of bureaucracy were led to action, rather than to apathy. The dominant mode of action was use of a combination of bureaucratic channels of complaint & personal connections. (4) Apparently, bureaucratic & non-bureaucratic means of obtaining desired goals are institutionalized side by side. As in other developing countries, Israeli bureaucracy operates as a 'mixed' system.

title: Power, Democracy and Ideology in the Reform of Educational Policy in England -- The Role of Producer and Consumer Governors
abstract: GB's 1986 (No. 2) Education Act & 1988 Education Reform Act have given more powers & responsibilities to primary & secondary school governing bodies, increasing their concerns beyond exercising popular democratic control over state schools to running their financial & other administration. The 1986 Act also endeavoured to reduce the numbers of governors who represent the producers of education (notably political appointees from local education authorities), & to increase consumer representation by allowing more parent & business/community governors. Some proponents of the legislation see it as a way of legitimating an otherwise largely centralizing form of educational change by appearing to introduce more parent, community, & employer control & direction. Here, the notion of producer & consumer governors & the extent of their power are critically examined. It is suggested that governors themselves are not aware that their power is limited by the degree of central control of education.

title: Determinants, Expenditures and Performance of Common Public Services
authors: Christenson, James A; Taylor, Gregory S
abstract: Studied is the relationship between expenditures (inputs) for selected public services & both quantitative & qualitative output measures of these services. The economic expenditure determinant literature has used public service expenditures as the dependent variable & various demographic & SE locality conditions as independent variables in most studies of public services. Extending this line of investigation, the degree to which the situation/locality in which the service is produced, variations in service expenditures, &/or quantitative service performance measures influence citizens' perceptions of service quality are assessed. Data come from the Bureau of the Census, state agencies, & a statewide survey of county residents in NC. Findings indicate the per capita expenditures for each of the five different public services (law enforcement, libraries, parks, health & education) are not powerful predictors of either quantitative performance or perceived service quality when adjustments are made for demographic & SE location factors. However, quantitative service performance measures do seem to have a modest relationship with service quality measures. Overall, the situation in which the service is produced seems to be more important than either the level of expenditures or quantitative measures of service performance in predicting peoples' perception of service quality. Peoples' perceptions of service quality may be misleading in that they seem to be more a product of the locality situation than an attribute of a service itself.

title: Legitimacy and Integration in Complex Organizations
authors: Mitchell, David F; Knox, William E
abstract: The integration of complex organizations is hypothesized to be dependent on the legitimacy of their societal functions. The mechanism linking legitimacy & integration is identified, described, & termed the process of positional legitimation. Data from teachers in a public school system show that participants in less legitimated subunits of the system are less likely to approve its structure, personnel, & activities than participants in more legitimated subunits, & to devalue their own activities to a greater degree than particpants in more legitimated subunits. It is suggested that the process of positional legitimation, involving a "flow" of legitimacy from the carrying society, to the organization, & then to positions, is crucial for maintaining the integration & effectiveness of formal structures, at least in societies in which bureaucracy as a form of organization is highly institutionalized & in which societal demands are satisfied by the activities of complex, formal structures.

title: Authoritarian Hospitalization
abstract: Totalitarian, authoritarian practices in Brazilian psychiatric institutions are examined, based on research of practices in two public hospitals. Two functions in public hospitals are considered: (1) the public hospital as a public service, with career lines & systems of promotions & transfers that permeate the types of therapies offered to clients, & (2) professional expertise, among which are two types of psychiatric orientations -- the organic interpretation of mental illness, & the psychoanalytically based approach. The interactions of these functions vary according to hospital timetables throughout the day & year. At times, authoritarian practices are used, & bureaucratic personnel prevail over young professionals; in other periods, decisions are reached by collective discussions & group dynamics, which give patients a larger role in determining their own leave. There is continuing conflict, however, & the liberal practices are not allowed to prevail. Totalitarian & liberal practices coexist according to: (A) combinations of private & public clinical practice in the country, (B) types of professional training received by psychiatrists, based on their ages & the extent of their careers, & (3) the role of hospitals as public institutions. The resolution of the conflicts between totalitarian & liberal practices is never attained, since the dilemma emerges at varying times in different public hospitals. Effects of the relative dominance of each of these practices & sources of power on patient turnover are examined. Forms of entering and leaving institutions vary according to types of authority & the conflicting practices in each hospital's internal milieu.

title: Disenchantment, Meaning and Religion - The Postmodern Condition
abstract: This paper considers Max Weber's thesis that the impact in the West of the dominance of instrumental forms of rationality and their articulation to specific institutionalized forms (bureaucracies), caused a process of cultural disenchantment and onset of collective meaninglessness. The paper evaluates empirical evidence that postmodernity represents a form of re-enchantment of the cultural world, and can be seen as a resistance to the highly rationalized forms of body and soul in late modernity.

title: The Effect of Hyperbureaucratization on the Organization and Its Members
abstract: A case study of a large public university is used to examine whether efficiency increases with structural change. A new top executive was hired who created many new offices, which added more levels to the hierarchy, & resulted in more centralized decision making. The impact of these changes on organizational efficiency & the power of individual members is analyzed, based on interviews conducted with 75+ middle managers, their assistants, & other staff, supplemented by formal organizational documents.

title: Bureaucracy and Risk during Organizational Decline
abstract: One of the implied promises of workplace bureaucracy is that formalized systems of control tend to mandate fair & ethical treatment of workers. Such assurances take on added importance during organizational reversals that result in large-scale layoffs. In this paper, I examine issues related to layoff practices at Pendulum Inc, a volatile high-tech company that underwent two episodes of severe decline within a 5-year period. In the interval between the two layoff periods, Pendulum implemented a number of bureaucratic reforms that should, in principle, have increased the chances that layoff decisions were based on fair, equitable criteria. Analyses of qualitative & event-history data concerning skilled blue-collar workers, however, offer only limited support for the thesis that greater bureaucratization increased the fairness of layoffs. The implications of these findings & suggestions for future research will be discussed.

title: With Weber against State and Market: A Theory of Social Control in World Society
abstract: Develops a theoretical framework on the basis of the sociology of Max Weber that accounts for historical developments of international social control, specifically the formation of international police organizations since the beginning of the 20th century. Weberian processes of bureaucratization & the place of the modern bureaucracy relative to the influences from political & economic factors are discussed, arguing that the formation of international networks of police institutions cannot be understood in terms of political or economic processes. State-centered & neo-Marxist sociological perspectives are challenged, maintaining that the formation of international police organizations was made historically possible when state-sanctioned police institutions were sufficiently detached from their political contexts to function independently as expert bureaucracies & were motivated by a professionally defined interest in the fight against international crime. Advocated are sociological perspectives on social control that are not reductionist in terms of political conditions & economic developments, but instead bring out the specific, social, & sociological significance of control mechanisms.

title: CREATING ACCOUNTABLE PUBLIC BUREAUCRACIES
abstract: Municipal public bureaucracies have gained a high degree of autonomy in their internal operations. The extension of civil service coverage, professionalization, & well organized employee associations have contributed to this trend. Clients as well as social policy critics have become concerned with the power vested in these agencies & the quality of services provided. 4 strategies (legal aid, community control, confrontations, & citizen-initiated complaint procedures) that clients employ to challenge the power of these agencies are reviewed & their structural weaknesses are assessed.

title: Leadership in Civil Society Organizations
abstract: The purpose of our paper is twofold: on one hand, to explore the relationship among authority & leadership in civil society organizations (CSO). On the other hand, to analyze the relationship between decision-making rules & leadership forms. We use some insights about leadership in private enterprises & public administration organizations formulated by organizational theory to analyze a different kind of associations: CSO relying mainly on solidarity & on norms criteria & characterized by voluntary relations. Drawing on a perspective emphasizing the relational character of leadership, we part from organizational theory two main distinctions in order to inquire on the type of leadership which best suits the fulfilment of functions assuring membership commitment; among others, cohesion enhancement, motivation maintenance & consensus building. The first distinction is formulated at an individual level, among "soft" & "hard" leadership, the soft type implying a slight directive form, & the "hard" one, a great control on the organization members. The second distinction refers to an organizational level proposing three leadership categories: centralized, dispersed, rotational. We will analyze information gathered in questionnaires applied to 9 civil society Mexican organizations.

title: Ecuadorian Promotores Learn to "Facilitate" Rather than to "Direct"
authors: Aubel, Judi; Hanson, Bill; Cevallos, Napoleon; Morales, Homero
abstract: An innovative training program for Ecuadorian promotores (administrators) responsible for the dissemination of water sanitation & hygiene methods is discussed. Sponsored by the Ecuadorian Instit of Sanitary Works, the workshop focused on teaching the integration of local beliefs in structuring the content of hygiene education efforts, & the employment of informal collective activities in analyzing & solving water & sanitation problems. The techniques of this participatory strategy (in which facilitation is favored over more traditional top-down strategies) are divided into five steps, from the perspective of promotores: entry into the community; collection & analysis of information from the community; identification of program priorities; implementation of a community program; & evaluation of the program. These stages, & the manner in which associated techniques were presented in training, are considered in turn. 7 References. A. Levine

title: Ming and Ch'ing China as a Patrimonial Bureaucracy
abstract: Of Max Weber's three "pure types of legitimate domination," sociologists have paid more attention to the bureaucratic & charismatic than to the traditional type. The issue addressed here is the adequacy of Weber's analysis of patrimonialism -- one subtype of traditional domination -- in the case of China during the Ming & Ch'ing dynasties (1368-1912). Recent studies of traditional China are used to assess Weber's analysis of patrimonialism in the Chinese bureaucracy, under three headings: (1) the beliefs in legitimacy that sustained patrimonial authority; (2) the organization that enabled patrimonialism to function; & (3) the recurrent issues that characterized the struggle for power in China's patrimonial bureaucracy. It is concluded that the main limitation of Weber's hypotheses is not that they are empirically incorrect, but that, as formulated, they are too vague in their scope conditions. Future research in the historical sociology of patrimonial domination needs to specify the conditions under which each of Weber's hypotheses holds.

title: Sociology in the Administrative State: Profession or Discipline?
authors: Vidich, Arthur J; Lyman, Stanford M; Goldfarb, Jeffrey C
abstract: Issues & problems facing contemporary American society are viewed in terms of their effects on sociology as both a profession & a discipline. The economic & intellectual crises in the discipline & the profession reflect the present accommodation that much of American sociology has made with the administrative state. Past professional practices as well as dominant positivistic & policy science claims have reached the point of exhaustion. Defined is a set of potential problems for future sociological research on modern society.

title: SOLUTIONS OF PROBLEMS IN INDUSTRY, A UTOPIA?
abstract: The aim of this report is to present a critical synthesis of an anthropological approach to solving certain problems in the industrial or bureaucratic setting. After a summary description of the method of 'solving' problems in an organizational setting, used & tested by a team of specialists in the social sciences, a critique of 2 cases in point is presented. The first deals essentially with the analysis of the reactions of high executives, while the second leans more toward the reactions of the participants themselves. Tr by H. Lachs.

title: Controversy of Health Studies: Risk Acceptance in Communities Affected by Hazardous Waste
abstract: Analyses of health risks & epidemiological studies performed by state & federal agencies relative to hazardous waste erode the trust that communities place in these agencies rather than resolve the conflicts between bureaucracy & community. Here, the process of the social perception of risk is qualitatively analyzed, focusing on the effects of community trust & risk acceptability. The conceptualization of risk by bureaucracy, which is based on economic costs & benefits, & that of the community, which is based on social rationality, are compared. Several case studies are presented that describe the historical responses by bureaucracies to social concerns in recipient communities of health studies.

title: The Effects of Bureaucratic Structure on Job Satisfaction and Organizational Commitment
abstract: In light of recent challenges to the traditional Western bureaucratic form presented by technological advances, changing markets, & international competition, a reevaluation of its advantages & disadvantages for creating hospitable work environments was undertaken. The effects of several dimensions of bureaucracy on the job satisfaction & organizational commitment of 523 NC employees are explored through logistic regression, using hierarchical models that include both organizational & job level variables. Findings indicate that establishment size, formality, & complexity interact to influence employee attitudes independent of, as well as through, job characteristics. In particular, although formality in relations increases commitment, its effect on satisfaction is conditional on the complexity of the firm. In addition, establishment size & centralization of work process decisions decrease satisfaction, but have no significant effect on commitment.

title: Bribing as a Rational Strategy of the Rich: On the Interdependence Between Corruption and Income Inequality
abstract: This paper aims at a deeper understanding of the mechanisms, which are at the base of the positive correlation between personal income inequality & corrupt practices of state agencies. For this purpose, the author develops a game theoretic rational choice model of the interaction between civil society & the state bureaucracy. The paper argues that high income inequality increases the percentage of the population, which is rich enough to pay bribes to state functionaries. Those who are able to buy illegal state services may in turn have economic advantages. Thus bribing is a rational strategy of the rich, which however increases the already existing income inequality. The proposed game theoretical model quantifies & formalizes the mentioned hypotheses. By assuming rational choice behavior of the bribers & the recipients, the author is able to draw conclusions about the dynamics & the evolutionary stability of corruption & income inequality. These conclusions are finally used for a preliminary empirical test of the model with data from World Bank & Transparency International.

title: Economy behind Ecology: Shifts in the Bases of Environmental Policies and Adjustments in the Role of the State. A Viewpoint from Some Evolutions of French State Strategies in the Environmental Field in the Early Nineties
abstract: Explores processes that participate in the integration of environment-based requirements into the administrative realm. In the French case, such a matter is worth examining because the treatment of environmental problems by the state in the early 1990s seems to have undergone some changes in the referential system that guides public actors of this policy field. Stakes on which environmental policies are built actually call for a more thorough insight, for they express intersections of interests that may transform apparent motives. In fact, economic considerations have gained increasing weight in the ecological decision-making processes &, consequently, have tended to alter enforcement of public strategies. Issues raised by such an evolution are considered in terms of: (1) translations that affect environmental concerns in the public sphere of activity (extension of stakes & displacements of interests); (2) increasing confidence in an economic apparatus so as to integrate environmental objectives; & (3) handling of environmental problems as an incentive to reorganize the role of the state & the resulting trend toward an economic-administrative management of ecological requirements. These trends indicate shifts that tend to reshape state strategies regarding environmental matters & eventually reveal a need for a framework that could account for the influence of economic logic in this policy field.

title: Inside the Fortress: Femocrats and the Australian State
abstract: Based on 32 taped interviews, & using a snowball sample, oral history methodology is used to report on the experience of the "femocrats," a cohort of feminists who entered state & federal bureaucracies in Australia after 1972 to influence policies concerning women. Their decision to enter government as self-proclaimed feminists has been controversial. Do the gains -- state funding & widespread acceptance for services such as child care, women's health centers, & women's shelters -- outweigh the risks of containment & cooptation? How have feminist initiatives been shaped by alliances with mainstream political parties? What has been the experience of women at senior levels of an Anglo-male bureaucracy? How have femocrats managed their relationship to the women's movement, women of color, & working class women? Exploration of these issues focuses on three themes: (1) the accountability of femocrats to the women's movement; (2) their experience of gender in the bureaucracy; & (3) achievements of the femocratic experiment, & the major obstacles to change.

title: Postcards of Exclusion and Places Off the Map: The Legal Dimension of Conflicts Over Public Spaces in the Case of Donostia-San SebastiaN, Basque Country
abstract: This paper discusses the legal dimension of public spaces in tourist cities, taking the Basque city of Donostia-San Sebastian as a case. Empirical evidence was gathered through qualitative methods, such as observation & analyses of newspaper reports, documents and tourist materials. In Donostia some places are selected to become attractions, whereas others are kept outside the tourist market. The process raises a duality between the tourist enclave and the rest of the city that results in two patterns of exclusion concerning public spaces. The first is metaphorically named "postcards of exclusion." Within the tourist zone, non-profitable presences, actions & discourses are subjected to a series of mechanisms of control in order to favour the ones encouraged by the tourism industry. The second is called "places off the map." Not only private entrepreneurs, but also agencies of the state bureaucracy address relevant financial & non-financial resources to promote public uses in places situated within the tourist enclave, while other places remain neglected. As a closer analysis of some exemplary situations of conflict found in Donostia reveals, in order to understand how those patterns of exclusion successfully work in everyday life it is necessary to unpack the property arrangements governing public spaces.

title: Awareness of Social Scientific Research Information in State Government Agencies
abstract: Data from a nationwide mail survey are used to investigate awareness of social-scientific information among state correctional agency headquarters staff (N = 319). Findings indicate that respondents are respectful of social science, & believe that greater use of it should be made in their agencies. Although they feel themselves to be quite aware of social science research, this knowledge is gained primarily from nonscholarly sources. Research staff differ from nonresearch staff in their patterns of awareness & use, but levels of use by both subgroups are low. Greater awareness & use of social-scientific research results may require that scholars actively disseminate their findings through the sources of information that are routinely utilized in state government agencies.

title: Analysing the Relationship between Urban Livelihoods and Water Infrastructure in Three Settlements in Cusco, Peru
abstract: This paper explores the role played by water infrastructure in urban livelihoods. It is based on a study of three settlements in Cusco, Peru, and shows that different modes of organising infrastructure co-exist within the same city, despite national policy prescriptions for urban water provision. Further, unequal access of households to these services exists within the same settlements and amplifies household vulnerability which, in turn, feeds back to undermine local, autonomous governance of water. This paper draws on the work of van Vliet et al. and Marvin and Graham to develop a framework that considers infrastructure organisation alongside household livelihoods in order to analyse the features of governance and vulnerability that affect urban livelihoods by privileging some groups and bypassing others. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Legitimacy v. Legality: Case Study of Contemporary China
abstract: State claims legitimacy for effective domination, but the belief in it is from the society. In Weber's point of view, legality is the source of legitimacy in modern state. These two terms would have the same meaning within the context of the modern state. While modern states are increasingly crystallized into certain forms, a higher level of rationality, the development process is still important. It implies two meanings. First, the forms that the state takes on have developed alongside the development of the society. The constant interaction of the two make it possible that one derive its meaning from the other. Second, such state forms have been consistently practiced over the society & are ultimately habitually accepted. When these structures, eg, legal system & bureaucracy, are transplanted from one state to another for modernization purposes, as in the case of China, these structures may lose its original meaning without the appropriate societal base. Legality can be alienated from legitimacy in this case in a modern state domination. Based on fieldwork, I am going to make a case study of Chinese rural society, where state structures of legal order & bureaucracy are established but the society is still largely a traditional one. State power claims its legitimacy by legality but through an interpretation in accordance with traditional values & operated through the agent of local authorities in the rural areas of China. At the same time, state power loses its formality that is the essence of modern state structures.

title: NON-BUREAUCRATIC ADAPTATIONS OF COMPLEX ORGANIZATIONS IN NATURAL DISASTERS
abstract: Data gathered by The Ohio State U Disaster Research Center in studying complex organizations suggest that the bureaucratic model is inadequate to explain organizational adaptation to stress. The informal structure does not take over from the formal structure in such situations. There is, instead, a variety of patterned responses in adapting to the stress. The paper illustrates these general points, sets forth a typology of possible patterned variations in bureaucratic adaptations, & indicates some internal & external factors to the organization which influence the direction & kind of adaptation followed.

title: Organizational Access to Research Settings: Entering Secondary Schools
abstract: Using preliminary evidence, it is suggested that fieldworkers seeking to enter formal bureaucracies can better understand access problems & more easily resolve them by referring to the organizational logic of the setting. Adopting an organizational perspective to analyze access issues, a comparison is made of public vs private religious schools, showing how access problems & the strategies to overcome them vary according to the schools' organizational features. The research was developed in four steps: (1) examination of the organizational literature on institutionalized organizations to highlight the structural problems of gaining entry to public schools for research purposes; (2) adoption of an organizational perspective to identify strategies for overcoming problems of access to public school; (3) comparison of the access to private religious vs public schools to demonstrate that problems & solutions vary; & (4) demonstration of the usefulness of organizational access by showing that researchers' ability to gain entry is enhanced by a preliminary understanding of the organizational characteristics of a formal setting. Illustrative examples are provided from research in public & private religious schools in a large midwestern city.

title: Streamlining People Processing in Service Industries by a Systems Approach: A Case Study of the Public Services on Employment in the Netherlands
authors: Oeij, Peter R A; Vissers, Adrian M C
abstract: Applies the principles of sociotechnical systems typically used in manufacturing industries to people-processing service industries. A theoretical statement is made on how the public services on employment in the Netherlands can be reorganized. Despite the need to overcome several institutional obstacles, it is concluded that sociotechnics offers promising opportunities for streamlining people-processing.

title: An Educational Model Applied to South African Transformation
abstract: South Africa faces a critical need for well-trained, ethical public policy practitioners who are able to listen to the people's needs, network, & deliver sustainable programs for transformation and development. The Public Policy Partnership (PPP) is established to create the critical mass of committed policy-makers & change agents that South Africa urgently needs. It gives South African university students, who want to make serious commitment to the public good, training & hands-on experience needed to become skilled, critical agents of South Africa's ongoing transformation. Students are funded to complete undergraduate & graduate school ending with a Masters Degree in Public Policy from South African Universities. Upon completion of the MA Degree, they go into government for a minimum of four years. This paper will analyze the history, characteristics, demographics, & potential impact of this program on South Africa. The focus will be: 1) to analyze the effectiveness & sustainability of this educational program as a significant reform to improve the workings of South African government; 2) to serve as a model to expand accessibility of previously marginalized persons; & 3) to posit program sustainability since PPP has become a wholly independent institution since July 2003.

title: School to Work Transitions as Status Processes
abstract: School-to-work transitions constitute a distinct set of situations where inequality becomes manifest due to different status characteristics. This paper reports on the transitions to the labour market of Swedish university graduates. It analyzes whether or not graduates with child care responsibilities are more likely to be employed in the public sector, which is known to apply a more transparent form of employment compared to the private sector. According to Status Construction Theory (Ridgeway, 2006) we expect that diffuse status characteristics (such as gender, graduates family background & current family situation) will be less operative in the public sector & more operative in the private sector. The salience of more specific status characteristics, like credentials, will reduce the influence of more diffuse status characteristics within the public sector. The study population consists of university graduates born between 1974 & 1976. Data are derived from national registers. Implications of results will be discussed. In particular, we argue that the bureaucratization and resulting credentialization of the public sector has potential benefits for the cause of equality.

title: SCHOOL BUREAUCRACY AS A RESPONSE TO PARENTS' DEMANDS
abstract: This study examines propositions regarding the influence of environmental demands upon the structure of organizations. Following Rushing's work, it is proposed that schools will make greater use of formal controls when confronted with a high level of demand from parents, both because formal controls help deflect demands, & because formal controls help insure that minimum performance levels are attained. Survey data from administrators, teachers, & parents in 18 urban public elementary schools are analyzed. While the study design contains important limitations, the associations found among the variables examined generally support the propositions. Further steps for testing the propositions are also suggested.

title: Academia in the Face of Electronic Leviathan
authors: Sobral, Fernanda A. da F.; Barra, Marcello C
abstract: The concept of electronic Leviathan was created in the scope of the research process on an artifact of electronic government: the Brazilian Public Key Infrastructure ("ICP-Brasil," or PKI-Brazil). The main data source were interviews with participants in the process of building the PKI-Brazil: politicians of the executive branch of the federal government; civil servants; a representative of financial institutions (Brazilian Federation of Banks -- Febraban); an entrepreneur; a representative of attorneys (Order of Attorneys of Brazil -- OAB); scientists; & representatives of the information technology industry. This work also carried out research in the archives of PKI-Brazil & analyzed its regulations, the Brazilian president's speeches at the time, and the legislation on e-government. Evidences showed the technical-political role of bureaucracy & the political role of the university: bureaucracy has had more impact on the technological knowledge directly employed in the PKI-Brazil than the university. The political role of the latter is evident through its criticism of the process through the press as being authoritarian, which, therefore, contributed to increase the number of representatives of society in the executive committee. Finally, these findings allow us to interpret some trends & to make a reflection on the future of the academia.

title: Mandarins, Retainers, Transients and Functionaries
abstract: In many countries, military officers, supported by civil servants, have seized power through coups. In these bureaucratic polities, appointed officer holders are, in fact, the ruling groups. Even in countries where elected politicians or hereditary rulers dominate a polity, public officials often exercise a great deal of power. Both mandarins & retainers existed in premodern times, but since the mid-nineteenth century, mandarin bureaucracies have increased in the Western world, normally replacing retainer bureaucracies. The potential of both retainers & mandarins for exercising great political power is explored here, focusing on Third World parliamentary regimes & new world presidentialist regimes. It is shown that, in the latter, retainers still hold most public offices -- the major exception being the US, where functionaries & transients largely replaced them during the nineteenth century. Bureaucratic structures help explain the exceptional stability of the US presidential regime in contrast to all others that have adopted this constitutional design.

title: Classes and Bureaucratic Domination: A Note on Weber's Sociology of the State
abstract: The relations between classes & bureaucratic domination according to M. Weber's sociological approach are considered. Classes are relevant to the sociology of the state to the extent that they influence that particular type of domination which has found typical expression in the bureaucratic administration of the modern state. The classes that are relevant in this perspective are the propertied entrepreneurial classes. However, capitalist influence may be controlled if there exists a strong & effective parliament based on universal suffrage.

title: THE IRRELEVANCE OF LOCAL POLITICS: CHANGING PATTERNS OF REPRESENTATION
abstract: An exploration of Max Weber's proposition that the unimpeded trend of social differentiation & the concentration of the means of administration can lead to a form of 'bureacratic despotism.' Using the structure & process of state & municipal politics as concrete sites for exploring these problematic issues, the paper examines the relations between the legislative & executive sectors of government & attempts to develop a research agenda for the study of changing patterns of bureacratic control. While not presenting any new empirical findings, an attempt is made to focus the existing literature on the development of new forms of political representation & control at the local level.

title: When Journals Challenge Their Ratings: The Politics of Classification in Social Sciences and Humanities
abstract: In a growing number of countries, public administrations & agencies seek to systematically evaluate the scientific outputs of their universities & research institutions, The impact factor (IF), fashioned by the Institute for Scientific Information, was for a long time the gold standard for the ranking of scientific productions according to their forms of publication. Nevertheless, even when used, IF was less accepted & integrated into social sciences & humanities practices. It is currently being superseded by ad hoc tools such as peer-reviewed journals lists & ratings. Journals were usually not consulted during the rating processes: they remained mute objects, manipulated & compared by expert panels & administrations. In June 2008, a group of British journals a specialized in history of science, technology and medicine & dominant in their field a published a joint declaration entitled "Journals under Threat" to ask for their withdrawal from the European Reference Index for Humanities (ERIH). From this moment on, journals began to publicly act as competent actors to provide judgments on the hierarchies made, forecasting the performative dimension of ratings on the organization of research, especially funding & publications strategies. The balance of power between scientific communities & research management institutions thus went through the very design of academic journal lists & ratings.

title: Institutions, Property Taxation and Local Government Finance in China
authors: Tang, Bo-sin; Wong, Siu-wai; Liu, Sing-cheong
abstract: China's rapid urbanisation has prompted its government to explore new sustainable sources of public revenue to finance the continued demand for urban infrastructure and services. Property tax advocates have sought to take advantage of the real estate booms that have occurred since economic liberalisation by actively campaigning for a real property levy as an appropriate policy choice. Against this background, this study evaluates the prospect of implementing market-value-based property tax reforms in mainland China. Based on the new institutional economics perspective, it posits property tax as an institutional arrangement which requires complementary mechanisms in land registration, property appraisal, tax administration, social security and dispute resolution. Property tax reforms would not only necessitate technical changes, but would also have extensive social, political and legal repercussions for Chinese society.

title: Bureaucracy Reconsidered
abstract: Three propositions about bureaucratic organizations are established: (1) change in bureaucratic structures is endemic, (2) rates of structural change increase with organizational hierarchy, & (3) the presence of substructure & structural change in subunits promotes stability in more inclusive units of organization. These results tend to discredit Weberian & classical organizational theories emphasizing permanence & stability of bureaucratic structures & may sustain alternative models of organizations.

title: Analysis of Decision Making in Public Administration [Applied to a Social Security Office and Its Clients]
abstract: It is to be expected that, in the near future, social security offices will enlist computerized systems to support decision making. These systems contain human knowledge culled almost exclusively from experts, eg, welfare workers. There is doubt, however, about the quality of this abstracted knowledge, since some people who have a right to welfare benefits do not request them. An investigation was undertaken in a social research setting in which clients would be inclined to keep their financial problems to themselves -- a social security office. In particular, it was found that status inconsistency (defined as an imbalance between income & other factors, eg, sex, education, had much to do with clients not requesting welfare benefits. This finding could be used to improve the knowledge base of an expert system designed to support the welfare worker's decision making.

title: ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE AND GOAL SUCCESSION: A COMPARATIVE STUDY OF THE NAACP AND CORE
abstract: This paper is an exploration of why, during the middle 1960's, the NAACP & CORE responded so differently to the separatist trends popularly classed under the concept, 'Black Power.' Though their tactics differed, originally both organizations had identical goals-full participation of American Negroes in an integrated society. While CORE's ideology & goals changed radically, those of the NAACP remained remarkably stable, with the leadership of the latter reaffirming its original position. The hypothesis was that this contrast was a function of the different organizational structures. The NAACP is a centralized national voluntary organization, with basic policy-making in the hands of a strong, bureaucratized staff. CORE, on the other hand, was essentially a federation of autonomous groups, with a national office lacking in power & possessed of what can best be described as an 'incipient' bureaucracy. Data were obtained from articles in the New York Times, 1960-1968, from the archival records of the 2 organizations, & from confidential interviews with officials intimately involved with the affairs of the 2 organizations during the period under consideration. The conclusions substantiate the hypothesis only in part. CORE's structure did indeed facilitate rapid change, while the elaborate centralized structure of the NAACP served as a brake. Yet, a second variable, the very different constituencies of the 2 organizations, appears to be almost as important in accounting for this as the structural differences.

title: New Public Management and the Interplay between Professional and Organisational Controls: The Case of Governing Medical Performance
abstract: New public management is a specific type of public sector reform & has a number of distinct characteristics. The focus of control moves from the macro level of the welfare state to the micro level of the delivery of public services. The corresponding mechanisms of control are therefore closer to the practice of professionals & potentially pose considerable challenges to traditional professionalism. At the same time, empirical studies point to the adaptability of professionalism & highlight the emergence of new forms of professionalism that combine different forms of professional & organisational control. The present paper contributes to these strands of the literature by analysing the interplay between professional & organisational forms of control & how they combine to form new types of hybrid controls. More specifically the paper suggests that to fully capture such hybrid forms of control it is necessary: first, to disentangle the notions of professional & organisational control; & second to examine more closely how different forms of control interact with each other. The paper uses recent changes to the governing of medical performance across a number of European countries as a case study.

title: THE ADAPTATION OF PROFESSIONALS AND BUREAUCRATIC STRUCTURES
abstract: Observers have noted that professionals resist the constraints which accompany bureaucratically structured organizations such as fixed rules, extensive administrative reports, hierarchy of offices & authority identified with organizational positions rather than individual competence. Several modes of adaptation of professionals & organizations are proposed. These include a structural separation of role figures whose authority is vested in positions from those whose competence is requisite for decision-making, an expanded emphasis on horizontal communications as well as mutual influence in vertical interaction & a greater dependence on normative compliance to organizational goals & procedures by both the professionals & their supervisors. Some implications of the increasing professionalization of the work force for future organizational forms are also discussed.

title: Economic Openness, Political Capacity, and Poverty Alleviation: India and Chile in Comparative Perspective
abstract: The impact of greater openness to world economic forces, such as trade and investment, on a country's poverty rate has been much analyzed in the literature in recent years. However, the inconsistent use of a wide range of indicators that define income, inequality, perceived poverty, & aggregate growth has made it impossible to find sustained patterns of relationships between global economic forces & national poverty alleviation rates. It would be too simplistic to argue that since countries do not open their borders at the same rate & undertake the required policy reforms to the same degree, the outcome rates in poverty alleviation would vary. What is missing in the above conundrum is the omission of a string of variables that may prove to be pivotal in explaining a significant part of the cross-country variations in poverty alleviation rates. This paper will examine the role of domestic political institutional dynamics as a major intervening force in deciphering the variations in country-level poverty rates. In particular, the paper will investigate the intervening effects of "political participation," "administrative capacity of the governing apparatus," & "state spending in the civilian-public and military sectors."
