A powerful segment of the literature maintains that the intervening effects of these variables may explain the outcome inconsistencies found in the cross-national studies of globalization & economic growth or poverty (Bardhan, 2004; Birdsall, 2004; Graham, 2004; Ravallion, 2006, Robeyns, 2005; Sachs, 2002). With regard to the issue of operationalization, first, using aggregate cross-national data (1990-2006), the paper will present regression analyses that indicate global, Asian, and Latin American trends in the impact of global economic openness on changes in country-level poverty rates in recent years. Subsequently, it will examine the intervening impact of specific political variables as indicated above. In the final analysis, the paper will supplement the cross-national analyses with an investigation of Chile & India. Through these two case studies, the paper will investigate how the variables of "political participation," "administrative capacity," & "state spending patterns" have crystallized & have affected the relationships between global economic openness & poverty alleviation in Chile (in Latin America) & India (in South Asia). A deeper understanding of these two cases would probably be helpful in generating a sense of how political variables may indeed work in mediating the potential effects of greater economic openness on poverty alleviation worldwide.

title: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission: A Case of Administrative Reorganization?
abstract: The trade in commodity futures contracts is a multibillion-dollar industry with the potential for exerting substantial influence on American agriculture. Yet little is known about the continuity & changes in the administrative agencies designed to regulate commodity futures contract trading. Recent changes in the organizational mechanism for regulating commodity futures contract trading for America's major agricultural commodities are examined. The purpose is to consider the circumstances surrounding the change in the means of regulating the commodity futures industry. The analysis sheds light on the topic of public agency reorganization. After reviewing the literature from which tentative explanations for the establishment of independent regulatory commissions may be derived, a brief historical account of the regulation of commodity futures trading is presented. Reasons which may explain the creation of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) are examined. Judging from the sources of support for various forms of a revitalized agency to regulate commodity futures trading, an assessment is made, drawing from Congressional hearings & GAO reports, of whether unjustly treated interest groups, Mc reformers, the Congress, or some combination of these forces was responsible for the creation of the CFTC. The correspondence between establishment of the CFTC & Edelman's discussion of symbolic acts & political quiescence is also considered. Policy dilemmas for the regulation of agricultural markets are noted.

title: Improved health outcomes in urban slums through infrastructure upgrading
authors: Butala, Neel M; VanRooyen, Michael J; Patel, Ronak Bhailal
abstract: sThe world is rapidly urbanizing with over half the population now living in urban areas. As the urban population grows, so does the proportion of these persons living in slums where conditions are deplorable. These conditions concentrate health hazards leading to higher rates of morbidity and mortality. This growing problem creates a unique challenge for policymakers and public health practitioners. While the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) aim to address these conditions and standards for water and sanitation as well as pertinent health outcomes, little evidence on interventions exists to guide policymakers. Upgrades in slum household water and sanitation systems have not yet been rigorously evaluated to demonstrate whether there is a direct link to improved health outcomes. This study aims to show that slum upgrading as carried out in Ahmedabad, India, led to a significant decline in waterborne illness incidence. We employ a quasi-experimental regression model using health insurance claims (for 2001-2008) as a proxy for passive surveillance of disease incidence. We found that slum upgrading reduced a claimant's likelihood of claiming for waterborne illness from 32% to 14% and from 25% to 10% excluding mosquito-related illnesses. This study shows that upgrades in slum household infrastructure can lead to improved health outcomes and help achieve the MDGs. It also provides guidance on how upgrading in this context using microfinance and a public-private partnership can provide an avenue to affect positive change. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Structural Implications of System Size and Growth: Cross National Evidence
abstract: An empirical exploration of the nonproportional growth model of social change. The central thesis is that system size & growth have a significant impact on the level & pattern of change in administrative fabric. By administrative fabric is meant the occupational activities that facilitate: (1) communication among the components of a system, (2) management & coordination of these components, & (3) expert evaluation of the information relevant to that management. The cross-sectional & longitudinal evidence is mixed: data drawn from a sample of 46 nonagriculturally based nations generally follow the expected pattern, while data from a sample of 22 agriculturally centered nations do not support the hypothesis. The major finding is that system growth exerts a significant effect on changes in administrative fabric. Moreover, it is noteworthy that even after considering alternative explanations such as the level of technology, level of complexity, & level of economic productivity, the relative contribution of system growth remains substantial.

title: Take Off or Take Over? The Westernization of East German Higher Education
abstract: After a short period of attempts toward autonomous reforms, east German higher educational establishments were completely westernized. The reunified German state bureaucracy simply incorporated the eastern part into the western system of higher education. On the one hand, mostly in the West, the winners of that kind of unification praise the whole operation as a glorious liberation in the domains of science & education, whereas on the other hand, the losers represented by a major part of fired academics in the East criticize that integration from above. Empirical data are presented to demonstrate that the westernization of east German higher education is paradoxical. This is interpreted in a broader theoretical framework using the concept of internal cultural colonialization, which has not only a negative connotation, but also opens new paths of development.

title: Deconstructing Vocabularies of Learning and Change: A Methodological Challenge
abstract: Dialectical irony functions as an act of emancipation & counter-discourse on managerial change in the Finnish public sector (Filander 2003). My aim is to identify the counter-discursive resources used by professionals in their fight against New Public Management. The meaning of the responsibility & collective identity in which professionals have earlier positioned themselves is changing into something profoundly different. I have analysed discourses of change through particularly selected key interviews that I call special cases or deviant cases. Discourses of truth linked with the development work promoting New Public Management were deconstructed with the help of irony. Examining such deviant cases is particularly necessary in a situation in which alternative perspectives have lost their legitimacy & in which counter-narratives can no longer be conveyed in their own terms.

title: New Federal Mandates and the Educational System's Delivery Services
authors: Carpenter, Robert L; Robson, Donald L
abstract: Presented are the rationale, design & methodology, results & discussion of a three-part statewide survey of special education teachers, special education directors, & parents of handicapped children on their knowledge of, & expectations for Public Law 94-142. Data were collected during the early implementation phase of the law, a time in which the response of the special education bureaucracy to a federal mandate could most clearly be observed. Directors reported themselves to be relatively knowledgeable about key elements of the law, heavily dependent on the State Education Agency (SEA) for such information, & only mildly positive about changes in services as a result of the law. Teachers reported themselves much less knowledgeable than directors about most elements of the law, dependent on their directors for that information, & even less positive about significant changes in service delivery. Parents, with significant individual exceptions, reported themselves to be the least knowledgeable about the law, dependent on their child's teacher &/or their local parent group for information, & significantly more positive than either teachers or directors about changes that would result from the law's implementation.

title: Interest Intermediation in the Norwegian Administration
abstract: Patterns of interest intermediation are outlined using data on 1,000 nationally organized interest groups, 1,000 administrative committees of the national administration, & 6,000 representatives (participants) in the committee system of Norway. Findings are used to evaluate the appropriateness of corporatism in explaining interest group behavior in Norway.

title: Women's Political and Economic Incorporation and the Professionalization of U.S. Abortion Activism
abstract: Outlines the extent to which women in a northeastern US metropolitan area have built paid, professional careers & large, women-dominated bureaucratic organizations out of their activism on both sides of the abortion conflict. Women abortion activists in the Albany, NY, area have also infiltrated formerly male-dominated organizations & frequently work as equals with men in all-volunteer, coed groups. These findings suggest that abortion activism represents more to women activists than simply a symbolic expression of their conflicted attitudes toward motherhood. This evidence of the professionalization & bureaucratization of women's activism around a "women's issue" also suggests the direction in which women's political & economic incorporation is heading today. Ironically, this trend may render women activists both too powerful & yet still weak -- too powerful, in that these women are demolishing radical feminists' dreams of women transforming society by leveling bureaucratic & professional hierarchies; too weak, in that even powerful women are still ghettoized in "women's" political & economic sectors.

title: Stable Patterns within a Network of Urban Bureaucracies: Domains or Positions?
abstract: Based on the communication between all 64 municipal offices in the city of Nuremberg, the regularized pattern of work-related daily interactions among municipal offices is described as the persistent pattern of interorganizational cooperation in a mandated setting. The underlying dimensions of structural differentiation -- integration & sectoral differentiation -- are identified by means of multidimensional scaling. Sectoral differentiation, however, does not explain the existence of zones of dense interaction, ie, domains of municipal authorities. The conditions under which sectoral differentiation corresponds to an overlap of functions are analyzed using social network analysis. The interaction between structural differentiation & functional specialization is investigated. Positional analysis reveals that offices which do not interact in an administrative domain occupy unique positions in the overall network. Separated & self-contained fields of problem solving within the persistent pattern of work related cooperation can therefore be ascertained. Two fields: "people processing" & "object processing" result from several interacting agencies; other problems are solved by single offices alone. As these different fields of problem solving do not interact, the administrative system, when confronted with a problem that does not fit into the established framework, must handle it either by defining it as a nonproblem, or by dividing it into parts which are then solved separately. Problems are therefore defined by their solutions. The relevance of these structural properties is also described in terms of their interrelationship in a multilevel community network.

title: Perceptions of Financial Management in Australian Local Government -- A Preliminary View
abstract: Results of a financial management survey conducted as part of the international Fiscal Austerity & Urban Innovation Project show that Australian local government is in the first stages of a period of financial stringency. The evaluation of this situation by principal officers identifies the cause as the withdrawal of federal & state grants at a time when there are rising service demands & inflationary pressures. Measures deemed appropriate to cope with this situation largely involve better management of existing services & the raising of further revenue from own sources. More draconian measures are not envisaged at this stage. Elected members regard officers as having a great influence on budgetary decisions, though mayors perceive themselves to have considerable influence. Officer influence is greater with routine allocations, & more innovatory policies give greater weight to elected members. Should the financial crisis deepen, there are indications of possible strains in the future, with divisions among members about priorities. Many favor a retreat to traditional environmental services, while others prefer maintaining human services. There is also likely to be a shift in policy-making power from officials to elected members as more radical decisions have to be made about financial allocations.

title: Bureaucracy as Belief, Rationalization as Repair: Max Weber in a Post-Functionalist Age
abstract: Max Weber's discussion of bureaucracy is generally descriptive of organized social structure within a rational-legal society, yet elsewhere he cautions against precisely this kind of analysis. Several factors -- ie, his counsel against reification, emphasis on subjective ideas standing behind social action, characterization of society as subjective orientation to legitimacy, discussion of organization & social relationships as probabilities of behavior in accordance with subjective belief in their existence, & tendency to describe the wide range of world views within the vocabularies of those who subscribe to them -- mitigate against viewing his description of bureaucratic standardization as Weber's own worldview, much less as his sociology. Rather, the discussion can be understood as a description of bureaucracy from within the bureaucratic setting & as a set of ideas subjectively held to as a basis of legitimacy -- ideas whose truth value are largely irrelevant for Weberian analysis. This qualification of bureaucracy as a mentality supplements the more widely acknowledged ideal-type qualification & provides a basis for increased Weberian insight. Such insight dovetails with postfunctionalist sociological theory, explains the origins & consequences of functionalist theory, & provides new understandings of recent findings in empirically based research. Moreover, it helps to focus current research away from bureaucracy as an existent entity & toward a phenomenon Weber identifies as the central process of Western civilization: the rationalization (bureaucratization) of human behavior.

title: SOCIOLOGY, BUREAUCRACY AND TRAINING: THE RISE OF THE SOCIOCRAT
abstract: An examination of the relationship between the sociological profession, its bureaucratic structure & the training of future sociological bureaucrats or sociocrats. The sociological profession through its main institutional setting, the U has been analyzed as a bureaucracy; first, through an examination of the nature of labor in the discipline; second, through the application of K. Mannheim's distinction between functional & substantial rationality. An argument is presented for the non-neutrality of research tools, in this case those most associated with quantitative research. These tools are seen essentially as aspects of the increased bureaucratization of sociological research. Learning & the transmission of knowledge are related to this emerging 'sociocracy' by means of an examination & critique of one recent proposal (Campbell, 1970). 3 recommendations are made: (1) the sociologist's role must be redefined in more humanistic terms; (2) sociology dept's might choose to affiliate with the humanities instead of the social sciences; (3) the cybercultural consequences of research technology must be taken into account both before & after the introduction of new tools.

title: The Halved Participation: Tools, Techniques and Processes of Social Participation in the "Environmental Issue"
abstract: In the last years, as a result of the emergence of the "environmental issue," the organisms of public administration have been promoting multiple instances of dialogue addressed to obtain a certain amount of citizen involvement in the environmental problematic & the resolution of socio-ecologic conflicts. In this text, we'll analyse the restricted role of these instances of intervention as a way of social & political participation, as they are activated mainly to intervene over the consequences even though they have scarce or no capacity of influence in the causes that originate them. The analysis of the mechanisms of participation needs to reflect on the typology of the tools & techniques used in relation to the level of participation achieved (information, consult, co-decision, self-management) & in relation to its fields of intervention. It is also pertinent to think about the consensus obtained & its functionality in the buffering & control of socio-environmental conflicts. Finally, some considerations derived from the process of institutionalisation of social participation & characterised by a clear structural isomorphism (public-private) are provided which, while it manages to obstruct the developmental consensus, it also legitimates the initial unequal relationship between the stakeholders & the social groups placing, moreover, the social value & private interest rates at the same level.

title: Bureaucracy and Public Opinion of the Police: An Application of Weber's Theory of Bureaucracy to a Small Southeastern Police Department
abstract: Even after the heroism shown during the terrorist attacks of nine-eleven (2001), many police officers are still regarded negatively by the American public. I expect the strict adherence to policy & procedure required by modern-day police bureaucracy may contribute to a detachment of the public from police officers. In this paper I apply Weber's theory of bureaucracy to a small southeastern police department, in a college town with a population of about 60,000 people. The research methods used in this study are content analysis of the police department's policy & procedure manual, ethnographic interview of the chief of police, & observation during my internship with the police department. I use this data to gauge the extent to which policies, procedures, & structures are adhered to in the department & determine whether these policies, procedures, & structures follow the pattern of dehumanization that Weber feels occurs in a bureaucracy. The police department studied is a nationally accredited police agency. The accreditation makes this study more relevant since the accreditation has the same requirements & structure nationally.

title: Bureaucratic Hyper-Reality and Homeless Agencies' Case Plans, Tracking the Self-Sufficient Client
abstract: An analysis of the ideological structure of agencies serving homeless people in Maricopa County, Ariz, based on a year of attending meetings, interviewing staff & directors, & reading official funding documents for 20 agencies. These sources generated narrative texts that embody the assumptions of Western rationality & postmodern bureaucratic "hyperreality." Agency staff represent a mix of philosophies & backgrounds, from 1960s progressive to right-wing Christian crusaders. Their ideological orientation impacts how the bureaucratic reality is translated through their work. Some challenge & transform the agencies; these individuals represent the conflicts inherent in working for immediate relief from homelessness in a socioeconomic context that guarantees permanent homelessness for a portion of the population. Additional data from clients reveal their feelings of frustration, dehumanization, & rejection. Several examples of work that has been empowering are provided in contrast to the limitations of bureaucratic hyperreality.

title: OCCUPATIONAL SPECIALISTS, SOCIAL STRESS AND NORMATIVE ELASTICITY IN A MORAL BUREAUCRACY
authors: Offutt, J James; Koval, John P
abstract: This paper proposes to focus on one major bureaucracy, the Catholic Church, characterized by a growing erosion of organizational norms, & to examine the relationship between normative & social power in that organization as a means of controlling the behavior for 6 types of task-specific priests whose activities differ according to task specialization, structural relation to authority, & social context, among other variables. 2 broad types of religious function (task specialization) are typically recognized within the normative organization of the Catholic Church, 'general practitioners' & 'specialists.' Another important distinguishing characteristic of the work that priests do-either as 'generalists' or 'specialists'-is the different ways in which such work is structurally related to the parent organization. Furthermore, the very existence of task specialization for the Catholic Clergy indicates service to different 'clients' & thus, activity within different social contexts. Paralleling Gross, 3 types of work stress are considered: (1) stress of organizational careersstress produced by problems of relating work status to the other statuses of the individual; (2) task stress-stress imposed by the difficulties of performing satisfactorily the task one is asked to perform; & (3) organization structure stress'stress resulting from the demands & needs of working together to obtain an end, such as having to listen to what others have to say, being willing to accept orders...' The data for this paper came from a national study of Catholic priests, completed in March of 1971, for the National Federation of Priests' Councils. The incidents & type of stress reported by men in task specializations vary markedly from group to group. General practitioners, parish priests, have on the average, the the least amount of normative elasticity of all task groups. The logic of the present conceptualization leads us to expect a relationship between stress & elasticity for specific issues common to the life space of task specialists. It is concluded that it is more likely that normative elasticity is more a means of reducing stress than of producing it. Normative elasticity seems to cope with differential stresses in one or more of their environments.

title: Making Workers Owners: Beyond Bureaucratic Control
abstract: Nationwide data are consolidated on three different organizational devices currently being used to transform US workers from being the employees to being the owners of US businesses. These devices include: (1) outright divestitures of entire plants to their employees; (2) creation of employee stock ownership trusts in thousands of US corporations; & (3) the spread of franchising, leasing, & other forms of labor subcontracting in labor-intensive sectors of the US economy. It is argued that these three phenomena have similar causes, & that, together, they constitute a widespread & significant set of changes in the US economy & polity. Since these changes are occurring not at the workers' initiative, but at that of their employers, serious questions arise as to whose interests they really serve, & what actual advantages they offer to the employees who are their ostensible beneficiaries. These questions are examined with regard to each of these devices in turn, & an attempt is made to identify strategies that give these new forms of worker ownership the best chance of becoming more that mere shams.

title: MODERNIZATION AND QUASI-BUREAUCRATIZATION IN BLACK AFRICA
Living Dangerously: Discourses and Dimensions of Poverty in the Third World
abstract: Explores the alternative meanings of poverty in a variety of discourses. Poverty & its various social constructions have grown exponentially. Unlike in the postindustrial revolution context, when it was a concern of national states, in the second half of the 20th century, poverty has been globalized. The acceptance of a taken-for-granted notion of poverty transported to various parts of the globe was facilitated in part by the growing field of development literature as well as the bureaucratization of poverty alleviation globally. Social science was complicit in this process, taking part with development experts in a common crusade against poverty. With increasing questioning of the hegemony of Western development paradigms, Western discourses of poverty are being challenged. As counterhegemonic discourses gain ground, poverty risks being normalized. An alternative conceptualization of poverty is proposed, taking a middle ground between the Western hegemonic discourse & the nativist counterdiscourse.

title: Organizational Control in Secondary Schools
abstract: A comparison & test of two prominent & contradictory views of organizational control in schools: (1) holds that schools lack appropriate levels of teacher accountability & are too decentralized, & (2) holds that schools lack appropriate levels of teacher input & are too centralized. Data come from the nationally representative 1988 Schools & Staffing Survey (N = 25,985 teachers & 6,183 school administrators). Results indicate that, in most schools, teachers have substantially less influence than principals over a range of decisions & policies. Moreover, increased teacher influence is far more important for the working environment within schools than is increased administrative influence. In particular, results draw attention to the importance of faculty influence over the often overlooked social & behavioral domain within schools. Faculty infrequently have substantial control over behavioral & tracking decisions, but it is faculty control over these issues that exhibits the strongest relationship to a positive school working environment.

title: The Absent-Minded Professors, or How Universities Forgot to Imagine: The Globalisation of Managerialism and the Management of Globalisation in Higher Education
abstract: This paper argues that, during the late 20th & early 21st centuries, universities have been captured by neo-liberal regimes of truth. We suggest that this may inhibit the 'research imagination' within universities and, consequently, their role in the democratisation of knowledge. We consider the role of capital in the globalisation of higher education, & the resulting global circulation of people & knowledge. We then examine how what we have termed the 'neo-liberal colonisation' of higher education has been achieved, ending with a discussion of the implication of these processes for the idea of the research imagination in universities.

title: Convergences and Hybridation of Educational Policies around "Post-Bureaucratic Models of Regulation"
abstract: The paper will be focused on some results of European funded research (REGULEDUCnetwork ; 2001-2004) The object of this research was to understand & compare the evolution of modes of regulation of education systems in five countries & to grasp some of their effects on the processes producing the social inequalities encountered in (secondary) school within the relevant local school spaces. The countries concerned are Great Britain (England), Belgium (the Francophone Community of Belgium), France, Hungary & Portugal. Six school spaces have been observed within the urban agglomerations of Budapest, Charleroi, Lille, Lisbon, London & Creteil (Paris region). The modes of regulation of the education system are closely linked to the whole range of mechanisms of orientation, coordination, control & balancing of the system. Thus we are dealing with one activity of 'governance' of the system (Dale, 1997). But regulation has many sources & does not derive solely from the controlling activity of political or institutional authorities of the system. Autonomous regulations exist as well (Reynaud, 1989). The goal of the project was to understand how different modes of regulation (political regulation, market regulation, autonomous regulations by local actors) evolve & combine in six local spaces, & how they affect the schools' logics of action. Indirectly we want to see how these changes can contribute to reconstructing local processes producing inequalities. The paper will present some part of the theoretical background of the project & will be focused on the comparison of the evolution of institutional & political regulation of education in the five countries. Our thesis is the following. Partially convergent policies (the increasing autonomy of schools, the search for a balancing point between centralization/decentralization, the rise in external evaluation, the accent put on 'free choice' of school, the will to diversify school offer, the erosion of teacher autonomy) construct, in varying degrees & with different temporal rhythms, variants of a 'post-bureaucratic' regulation regime, which seek to go beyond the 'bureaucratic-professional model' still dominant today, by accentuating either the traits of an 'evaluative State', or those of the 'quasi-market' model. However beyond the influence of these 'transnational models', path dependencies also exist & we assist at the same time to hybridization of these models with institutional, political or ideological constraints specific to each country. This paper draws upon the comparison of five national reports, based on national & international literature.

title: Transforming water infrastructure by linking water management and urban renewal in Rotterdam
authors: de Graaf, Rutger; van der Brugge, Rutger
abstract: Urban water systems have to deal with the impacts of climate change. In response, urban water managers in the city of Rotterdam developed a new water management strategy combining the renewal of water infrastructure with neighborhood revitalization projects. A key factor was the recognition that additional water retention in existing urban areas could only be realized if these projects were linked to urban renewal programs. Moreover, it was acknowledged that through new water retention infrastructure the quality of the social environment of deteriorated neighborhoods could be restored. The results from this historical analysis show that this turn in thinking initiated a successful water policy innovation in Rotterdam, in which the urban water policy is used to solve other urban problems as well by improving the quality of the public amenity. This paper presents key factors that contributed to this process and provides recommendations to further advance the transformation of urban water management infrastructure and the link with spatial planning. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Recent Changes in the Scientific Knowledge Production and Dissemination Regime in Brazil
abstract: The hereby proposed paper addresses the transformation of the production & dissemination regime of scientific knowledge in Brazil, during the period comprised between the political opening of the 1980s until the redefinition of the national policy of science & technology in the year 2000. The research was oriented by the concept of regimes of production & dissemination of scientific knowledge that conceive science both as an institution (that means, a champ with its own rules & needs of legitimation) and as a practical activity (that means, encompassing patterns of research accomplishment, broadcasting of the results & formation of new researchers). Therefore, it articulates two viewpoints: (1) the analysis of the legal-institutional change & the legal organization of science in the country; (2) the study referred to alterations of concrete scientific practices. The main aim is to show how changes in the legal framework of science influence scientific practices of the Brazilian scientific elites. The paper will present the results of an empirical research based on (1) the analysis of the Brazilian scientific & technology laws policies; (2) interviews with laboratory directors, members of scientific bureaucracy (directors of innovation agencies, coordinators of funding agencies, etc.); (3) a survey applied to 211 scientists working with nano & biotechnology in the most important Brazilian laboratory (National Light Laboratory Sincrotron). The foremost conclusion is that Brazilian scientific elites both articulate the change of the legal framework to promote the university-enterprise links & support scientific practices that preserve the relative autonomy of science.

title: CITIZENS AS BROKERS: COOPTATION IN AN URBAN SETTING
abstract: Although Selznick laid important groundwork for it in TVA AND THE GRASS ROOTS, the systematic analysis of governmental bureaucracy's relations with client publics has not proceeded very far. One particular area needs much research-the rise of 'brokerage structures' that mediate demands of clients with bureaucratic planning. These brokerage structures are quite varied ranging from private interest groups, to local 'mayor-appointed' boards, to new federally-required structures. But within the present urban context, they have all taken on several characteristics in common: (1) highly involved in 'bureaucratic politics'; (2) concerned with one issue or type of issue; (3) composed of citizens not directly elected by the people (or if elected, it is under questionable procedures for assuring 'representativeness') who nevertheless must claim to represent clients' interests; & (4) forced into the role of broker of client demands with administrative bureaucracies & government. A basic theoretical framework is laid out for understanding the brokerage process as an outgrowth of the development of organizational character in brokerage structures, & the environmental constraints placed upon these structures. Implications will be drawn for problems of integrating bureaucratic planning with citizen demands in the urban setting.

title: Bureaucracy and Formal Democracy in Professional Associations
abstract: The structure of authority associated with bureaucracy would seem to challenge democracy within large voluntary associations. Ironically, according to this cross-sectional study of 83 national professional associations in medicine, the structure of authority within bureaucracy increases democratic procedures when members subscribe to a democratic or egalitarian ideology. Bureaucracy concentrates authority in relatively high offices, differentiated vertically, & expands the prerogatives of elected officials. The democratic procedures that result from the concentration of authority are conditional on internal & external demand for rational organization, stimulated by the size of the organization & its ties to other organizations & contingent on an egalitarian ideology among its membership. Democratic procedures do not appear to result from facets of bureaucracy such as specification of offices & of administrative rules, functional specialization, & strategies for recruitment & promotion. To understand the development of voluntary associations, further research should be longitudinal & guided by theories of social conflict that interpret the democratic rule construction as a mechanism for assuring substantive democracy in the face of bureaucratization.

title: Reading the Board Quality Report: Who Knows How?
authors: Campbell, Marie L; Green, Carolyn J
abstract: This textual analysis argues that different readings of a "quality" report by people located differently in relation to its construction & use, & captured in ethnographic data as the report was being presented to the Board of Governors of a Canadian health region, identify a moment in the transition to a new mode of accountability, one fully based on texts & action in texts. The paper draws on institutional ethnography's social ontology, where institutional action is understood to be framed & regulated textually & this analysis focuses on how the report is active in constituting the region's health care operations as of accountably adequate quality. Writing up the actual (in this case, how long people waited for surgical admissions and treatment) is framed & regulated in specific ways, constructing texts for actions designed to participate in the institutional discourses of the New Public Management. The paper maps one such action-text-action sequence in which the everyday world of health care is made actionable, in & as texts & shows how this mode of action supersedes & can overlook what actually happens, as action orientates to the textual version of "quality".

title: Educational Change and Science Fiction: A Subversive Approach
abstract: An attempt to show the utility of science fiction (SF) materials within the bureaucratic educational system. The developmental argument draws on five themes: (1) liberal education (ideationally expanding) is on the decline, (2) bureaucratic education (ideationally delimiting) is pervasive, (3) bureaucratic education produces bureaucratic man, who is not a whole man, (4) activist challenge to bureaucratic structures is most easily recognized & halted by institutions of the state, a subversive approach is suggested &, (5) SF is one source which can provide, with metathemes of "as if" & "what if," the basis for alternative ideational systems without actively attacking the educational bureaucracy. Liberal education is conciousness expanding; it allows for self-discovery. Bureaucratic education is conciousness delimiting; it exposes the individual to the world of bureaucratic ideas. It is about the business of conciousness formation not conciousness raising. Bureaucratic thought is not fully social thought & bureaucratic man not whole man. Following G. H. Mead's model of social interaction, bureaucratic systems are unidirectional, nonreciprocal, & seek to treat the person as "me" while systematically eroding the 'I'. The goal of bureaucratic systems is to replace individual thought with bureaucratic thought, under the guise of rationalism & efficiency. The activist mood of the 1960s was eradicated by the state (the nonreaction to Watergate & the nuclear incident at Three Mile Island are examples). The metathemes contained in SF are "as if" & "what if." Both approaches are consistant with the assumptions of symbolic interactionism. SF has the capacity to extend present societal trends "as if" they were to proceed to their logical conclusion. It also serves a utopian function asking the question "what if" this were true, what would happen then? SF can be one source of material that challenges bureaucratic systems & thought without directly attacking the bureaucracies in which we are all embedded. George Orwell's 1984 is a case in point.

title: Professionals in Bureaucracy: Role Conflict among Social Workers in Social Service Agencies
abstract: Utilizing a role strain perspective, the literature is reviewed in an attempt to determine the sources of role conflict for social workers who operate within formal service organizations. A theoretical model which focuses on the dynamics of adjustments to role conflict was presented as a method for investigating the conditions under which conflicts arise & some of the psychological consequences of these role conflicts. Future research conducted from this perspective could provide agency directors with better information for designing mechanisms to manage the dysfunctional consequences of role conflict.

title: Bureaucratic Legitimacy and the Drug Menace: Notes on the Marijuana Tax Act
abstract: A recurring controversy in the area of deviance & social control is the relative influence of moralistic, organizational, & structural processes in the passage of the Marijuana Tax Act of 1937. Recent papers by Galliher et al attack the moral entrepreneur argument of Becker & the bureaucratic dilemma position of Dickson as methodologically ill-founded & theoretically misleading. According to their examination of the data, structural pressures (in the form of racial & economic conflict) alone account for the legislation. In contrast to this position, data presented here suggest that, while all three factors appear to be operating in the activities leading to the Marijuana Tax Act, the organizational processes stressed by Dickson are more crucial than Galliher has acknowledged. Conscious efforts to shift organizational goals in a turbulent bureaucratic environment led to manipulation of agency statistics & a highly selective public relations campaign aimed at key decisionmakers & support groups. In contrast to Galliher & Walker, it is suggested that the Marijuana Tax Act was more than merely symbolic, & that due to its control over beliefs about drugs, the bureau's moral crusading was critical for its passage.

title: Transport policy and public involvement
abstract: This paper examines the possibility of establishing a public space of deliberation concerning transport policy. It deals with the question of whether it is possible to envisage instances of concertation that deflect conflict. Based mostly on French experience with public inquiries on transport infrastructure, it discusses the relevance and applicability of the sociology of collective action, as well as theories of deliberative democracy. The paper's main argument is that concertation does not occur in a vacuum but is instead structured by power relations. It is, therefore, first and foremost an opportunity to express dissatisfaction and frustration. At the same time, public debate represents--perhaps for the same reason--an opportunity to criticize forms of social domination. It thus may give rise to citizen mobilization rather than help contain it, as is often naively expected by its promoters within the public policy administration. Conflict is thus always the actual subject of public debate. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: "Administrative Discretion" within the U.S. Wetlands Protection Program: The Organization of Social Regulation
abstract: "Administrative discretion," or unformalized decision making, constitutes a crucial component within federal regulatory agencies' implementation of often nebulous, & sometimes quite contradictory, statutory mandates. Because of historical circumstance & political compromise, the Clean Water Act (CWA) Section 404 wetlands permit program is implemented by the US Army Corps of Engineers, but under the oversight of the Environmental Protection Agency. Here, primary & secondary historical sources, agency enforcement data, & legislative & case law are drawn on to put into relief the primary forms & dynamics of administrative discretion within this division of regulatory labor. The CWA Section 404 program provides particularly good empirical terrain with which to examine administrative discretion within regulatory law because these two agencies have repeatedly developed statutory interpretations & administrative policies with conflicting programmatic consequences. The history of the Section 404 permit program illustrates both that the legal & organizational parameters of administrative discretion have been historically contingent variables within regulatory law, & highlights the role of this dimension of regulatory law in determination of practical & analytical boundaries between the federal regulatory agencies' "public interest" goals & private property rights.

title: Autonomy and Professionalism: Study of Indian Work Organization
abstract: Explores implications of organizational milieu for level of professionalism among Indian executives, drawing on interview & other empirical data from 126 top executives in public & private work organizations in southern India. Following Weberian classification, work organizations are categorized as bureaucratic & patrimonial based on structural features. Findings indicate that Indian work organizations represent a blend of both types, minimizing disadvantages of extreme bureaucratization & chaotic arbitration of purely patrimonial structures. Contrary to general belief, Indian executives are found to exhibit a reasonably high degree of professionalism in their approach & management of work organizations, in spite of the conservative scale of professionalism. Further, the general assumption pertaining to negative association between degree of bureaucratization & level of professionalism in work organizations appears unfounded, at least in the Indian context; executives operating in highly bureaucratic work structures tend to exhibit a relatively higher degree of professionalism. As such, Mertonian dysfunctions of bureaucratization need to be reexamined in the context of Indian work organizations. Results are attributed to general socioeconomic & cultural milieus in which organizations operate.

title: Precarization and Risk Transitions. Rethinking the Boundaries of Work in the Life Story and in the Everyday Life
abstract: The paper aims to analyze the critical transitions intersecting the work careers & the methodological implications concerning the study of risk biographies. This approach is motivated by the awareness that in today's social contexts, marked by the growth of work & social precariousness, an analysis of work trajectories cannot be confined to contractual & economic aspects, but should take into account a variety of fields & spheres of life that are articulated in different ways. From a methodological perspective, the attention goes to the narrative approach, which allows to study both biographical transitions in the life stories, related to specific & "critical" moments in the lives of the people, and the everyday transitions, where transit refers to the passage between different areas of life (paid & unpaid work, free time, etc.). The research is based particularly on fifty narrative interviews, conducted with men & women working in the Italian public administration, which represents one of the new paradigmatic sectors of the present configuration of precariousness. The use of the narrative approach highlighted the subjective aspects related to life & to the meanings attributed by people to their own experiences of biographical transitions between work & non-work.

title: Moral and Market Entrepreneurs: Aspirations, Values and Ambition amongst Transnational Employees
abstract: This paper examines what is distinctive about global professionals in different sectors: international NGOs, UN agencies and multinational corporations. These are the moral & market entrepreneurs of globalization. It analyses the practices and strategies developed by professionals in order to face the challenges associated with transnational working. The analysis draws on survey data & interviews with transnational professionals working in global organisations to address these themes. This in turn facilitates evaluation of what the "globalizing of minds" entails for these employees, both personally & professionally. Moreover, in order to bridge the gap between individual orientations & the institutional landscape, I will analyse the strategies by which corporate & not-for-profit organisations standardise practices across different sites, countries & regions. This, in turn, may involve analysis of processes of professionalisation & bureaucratization, to examine whether these detract from NGO workers' motivations & passions to "make a difference in society" & corporate employees' more individualistic ambitions. This paper thereby addresses intersections between cultural & economic rationalities for transnational professionals, since their values & aspirations are invariably informed by organisational incentives & hierarchies.

title: Urban Governance and Inequalities: A Comparative Political Economy Analysis of Mass-Transit in Two Towns in the South: Gurgaon (India) and October City (Egypt)
abstract: Urban areas in developing countries are characterized by inequalities of incomes, livelihoods, citizenship rights, communal rights, access to public services & amenities, & moral rights (Sen 2000). Driven by an urge to understand how systems of capital accumulation & resource distribution affect our lives in cities, this research focuses on issues of inequalities of access to mass-transit in two urban settings in the South, Gurgaon in India & 6th of October in Egypt. These two cities have their genesis in the era of centralized national planning during the late 1960s & early 1970s in both countries, when the states of Egypt & India sought to manage their over-populated cities of Greater Cairo & Delhi by dispersing their respective economic activities & populations into the surrounding areas. While the failure of this strategy is well documented in the literature, & while the relative success or failure of these cities to achieve their initial objectives is heavily debated, the same could not be said about a thorough sociological understanding of life within these cities. October City, envisioned as a future growth pole, is now developing into a location for hybrid economic activities where industries, media, IT & financial services, private educational institutions operate along side high-income residential complexes. Gurgaon city, established as an industrial satellite, is now becoming an alternative location for IT business offices & high-income residential property. Field visits & surveys of print media revealed that mass transport constitutes one of the major problems in both urban settings. Little work is done to analyze the systems of providing mass transit services or understand the institutional structures & norms that underlie them. This research is an attempt to fill this gap. It focuses on processes of provision of private mass transit services & aims to analyze the 'urban regime(s)' that regulate these processes. It argues that the roles of central states are redefined with regards to the provision of mass-transit in both urban settings; that private mass-transit operators are setting the parameters for this redefinition through their interactions among themselves & with existing local government institutions. These institutions are undergoing strategic changes to cope & survive within these parameters. In the final analysis this research purports to express how 'statehood' is being redefined in both spatial & scalar terms. This research will compare the structures of local government in both urban settings, the policies & laws that regulate public & private mass-transit, the forms & modes of mass-transit that operate in both locations & the institutions that ensue. It will rely on extensive reviews of literature including published academic work, government documents & print media as well as ethnographies of the provision & access to mass-transit in both research locations. Findings from interviews, observations & literature reviews will be combined to formulate a methodological & analytical framework for the study of urban mass-transit in two urban settings in Egypt & India.

title: The Effect of Bureaucratic Structure on Individual Contributions to a Public Good
abstract: It is proposed that individuals placed in the context of an ideal-typical bureaucracy (as described by Max Weber) become oriented toward collective outcomes & contribute more to a public good than do those placed in a nonbureaucratic setting. In an experiment with a 3 X 2 factoral design, with the factors being position (worker, supervisor, manager) & organizational structure (bureaucratic vs nonbureaucratic), 135 Ss were randomly assigned to 6 treatments, with gender being a block variable (at least 10 males & 10 females are in each treatment). The dependent variable, individual contributions to the publc good, is measured by the number of tokens contributed by the individual to a group fund. An analysis of variance finds no significant difference between the mean contributions of each treatment group, concluding that bureaucratic structure has no effect on individual contributions to a public good.

title: The Limits of Instrumental Rationality: Enculturating Innovation
abstract: The fact that some large US-based firms cannot generate new products as quickly & as successfully as their international competitors is often blamed on bureaucratic structure. It is argued here that bureaucratic structure per se does not impede innovation; rather, it is the ideology of instrumental rationality -- Max Weber's original but often overlooked basis for the modern organization -- that is anathema to innovation. Data on 40 cases of new products in 15 large bureaucratic firms are utilized to argue that instrumental rationality fosters ways of thinking & acting that, while perhaps improving efficiency & control, suppress the skills & abilities necessary for innovation. Three cultivated capacities of instrumental rationality are identified -- incrementalism, closed system thinking, & abstraction -- & it is demonstrated how they disrupt the day-to-day practice of innovation. It is concluded that reformulating theories of innovation within this cultural perspective resolves empirical ambiguities & explains problems with innovation more straightforwardly; suggestions for additional conceptual & practical development are offered.

title: Public Policy on Modernization from a Phenomenological Perspective
abstract: Public policies regarding modernization are either comprehensive or intensive. Comprehensive policies attempt to affect both the material base (development), the social aspects, & the cultural dimension (egalitarian justice). Intensive policies focus on development only. The implementation of these policies has led to a high degree of centralization with an organizational tension between functional specialization & territorial coordination, & between territorial administrators & local political spokespersons. These dilemmas imply deficiencies in the process of setting priorities. They also assume the superiority of the perspective of national views on modernization over local needs assessments. The unrest that results is recognized as a consequence of the policy but it is hoped that a new situation will be created before any radical outburst. Analyzed are the cultural beliefs underlying these policies in terms of a behavioral model or a motivational model. The first stresses performance & assumes a commonality of interpretation. The second reifies the need to achieve. Both models have two types according to a focus on the material base or the social order. Both models have shortcomings that their adherents cannot see. The blindness is to idiographic, ecological, & historical reality. Alternative organizational approaches are suggested.

title: Secrets of Powerlessness. The Moral Feelings of Bureaucratic Actors
abstract: Uses current theories of social action to examine moral aspects of the work activities of bureaucratic actors in a public assistance administration, & points out the importance of feelings of powerlessness, suspicion, or shame concerning the service relation. Explored is how to restitute this dimension of what the actors do, & with which methodological implications. The empirical investigations recently imported in French sociological developments from Anglo-Saxon constructivism, interactionism, & ethnomethodology attempt to address this dimension, but the extent to which they are still compatible with more established approaches is questioned.

title: With the help of one's neighbors: Externalities in the production of nutrition in Peru
authors: Alderman, Harold; Hentschel, Jesko; Sabates, Ricardo
abstract: Both public and private resources contribute to the nutritional status of children. In addition, the investments made by one household may contribute to the health of other households in the neighborhood through improvements in the sanitation environment and through increases in shared knowledge. This paper measures the externalities of investments in nutrition by indicating the impact of the education of women in Peruvian neighborhoods on the nutrition of children in other households, after controlling for the education and income of those households. We find that in rural areas this shared knowledge has a significant impact on nutrition, with the coefficient of an increase in the average education of women in the neighborhood being appreciable larger than the coefficient of education in isolation.  In addition, we indicate the impact of the water and sanitation environment in the neighborhood, again controlling for the household's own access to sanitation and water. In both urban and rural areas, we observe externalities from investments in such household level infrastructure with the evidence particularly strong for sanitation made by neighboring households. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Classification of Drinking Water between Public Administration and Rural Communities in South Kordofan, Sudan: Travelling Models and Technologies
abstract: This article discusses different technologies used to classify water as potable or non-potable in South Kordofan, Sudan. The case of a water pump in the village Abol is presented to show how different actors dealt with the uncertain situation, when changes in the water coming from the pump caused doubt about its potability. Officials in South Kordofan's public administration system attempted to follow the model procedures for such a case, but failed to produce a relevant link between their results and Abol's community of water users. The water users reacted in different ways to the situation, due to their different belief systems and their unequal practical options. The article employs the terminology of 'travelling models' as developed by Richard Rottenburg (Rottenburg 2005; 2009) in analysing this heterogeneity in the face of a joint problem. Adapted from the source document.

title: ELITE REVOLUTIONS
abstract: This paper conceptualizes a unique type of political revolution-based on a secondary, historical study of the Meiji Restoration (1868) in Japan & the Ataturk Revolution (1919-23) in Turkey. In such an elite revolution, the revolutionary leaders are themselves members of the ruling stratum, holding Hs & office in the old regime. Moreover, revolutionary conflict & change are contained primarily within elite institutions & do not involve mass participation. The paper compares the social bases, processes, & results of an elite revolution with the attributes of a coup d'etat & a 'mass' revolution led by elites recruited outside the power structure of the old regime. Study of this unusual type of revolutionary action provides certain insights into more general problems of revolutionary change: (1) Contrary to the social theories of Weber, Michels, & others, this study finds that under certain conditions, bureaucrats may become revolutionaries. It hypothesizes 3 conditions that are necessary, & perhaps sufficient, to generate revolutionaries from within the ranks of state bureaucrats. (2) Study of the tactics used by elite revolutionaries indicates organizational methods which permit a revolutionary take-over of power & the initiation of fundamental social change while minimizing the amount of violence, terror, & social upheaval involved. (3) Analysis of the change generated by elite revolution indicates some of the costs of limited mass involvement in revolutionary change. Parallels are drawn between the elitist nature of revolution by state bureaucrats & the elitist tendencies of other types of 20th century revolution.

title: The War of Bureaucracy with Society
abstract: An examination of the warfare between bureaucracy & society, between the new culture & the old culture, in which two-way social action is being transformed into one-way bureaucratic action with a corresponding change in the old prescriptions of social norms. The method of transformation of these social norms is by means of an intellectual warfare in which the foundations of concept formation needed for two-way social action are destroyed in individuals & replaced by one-way bureaucratic commands. One-way Aristotelian logic & habit formation in the individual are utilized in this warfare to reduce social consensus to bureaucratic command, with a corresponding regression of whole man to bureaucratic man. Social man & bureaucratic man are one in whole man & a splitting of whole man into two warring perspectives is destructive to the intellectual foundations of thought needed for survival by both man & society.

title: Muddy Waters: The Political Construction of Deliberative River Basin Governance in Brazil
authors: Abers, Rebecca Neaera; Keck, Margaret E
abstract: Over the last two decades, numerous international conferences and organizations have espoused managing water as an economic good, involving participatory forums in systems of decentralized management at the river-basin level. In the 1990s, Brazil adopted such a model. More than a simple transfer of power from the national to the local level or from bureaucratic to deliberative decision-making, however, this process requires multi-directional power transfers among a variety of policy arenas and actors and among national, state, municipal and river-basin institutions, as well as a complex--and ongoing--negotiation over the meanings of both water pricing and participation. Focusing on the politics of reform legislation in the state of Sao Paulo and nationally, the article examines how political-institutional features of federalism and executive-legislative relations constrained the passage of reform legislation, and how pro-reform actors attempted to surmount such institutional limitations with networking strategies and by fostering incremental changes in practices on the ground. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Campbell, Robert M & Leslie A Pal. The Real Worlds Of Canadian Politics: Cases In Process And Policy // Review
authors: Campbell, Robert M; Pal, Leslie A; Williams, Cynthia

title: The exploratory analysis of trade-offs in strategic planning: Lessons from Regional Infrastructure Foresight
authors: Störmer, E; Truffer, B; Dominguez, D; Gujer, W; Herlyn, A; Hiessl, H; Kastenholz, H; Klinke, A; Markard, J; Maurer, M; Ruef, A
abstract: The sustainable transformation of infrastructure sectors represents a challenge of prime importance worldwide. Due to long life times of infrastructures, strategic decision making has to explicitly consider uncertainties in context conditions, value considerations and available technological alternatives. However currently, strategic infrastructure planning is often carried out in a very narrow perspective. The present paper argues that foresight informed strategic planning allows addressing trade-offs related to context uncertainties, value conflicts, and sustainability deficits in a structured way. The paper introduces a specific procedural proposal, the Regional Infrastructure Foresight method, and illustrates its potential virtues through an application to urban water management planning in a Swiss region (Kiesental).

title: Climategate, Public Opinion, and the Loss of Trust
authors: Leiserowitz, Anthony A; Maibach, Edward W; Roser-Renouf, Connie; Smith, Nicholas; Dawson, Erica
abstract: Nationally representative surveys conducted in 2008 and 2010 found significant declines in Americans' climate change beliefs, risk perceptions, and trust in scientists. Drawing upon the Social Amplification of Risk Framework, this analysis empirically examines the impact of "climategate" -- an international scandal resulting from the unauthorized release of emails between climate scientists in England and United States. The results demonstrate that "climategate" had a significant effect on public beliefs in global warming and trust in scientists. The loss of trust in scientists, however, was primarily among individuals with a strongly individualistic worldview or politically conservative ideology. Nonetheless, Americans overall continued to trust scientists more than other sources of information about global warming. Several other explanations for the declines in public understanding are also explored, including the poor state of the economy, a new administration and Congress, diminishing media attention, and abnormal winter weather. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The United Mine Workers of America vs Michel's Iron Law of Oligarchy
abstract: Examined are the structural & ideological changes within the 250,000-member UMWA between 1968 & 1980, from the perspectives of: (1) theories of bureaucracy, especially those of R. Michels, & (2) theories of class conflict. Specifically, the ability of the "iron law of oligarchy" to explain these developments within one organization is tested. Supplementary, & in many respects alternative, explanations offered by stressing class conflict in the Appalachian coal fields are explored.

title: On the Decline of Japanese Bureaucrats' Prestige
abstract: For long Japan's bureaucrats occupied the centre stage of policymaking, but now there is some evidence to suggest that their power is in retreat. The bureaucrats, once almost the sole actors when it came to policymaking, are now almost disappearing in obscurity. Their prestige has declined for several reasons: first, they have lost confidence and respect of ordinary citizens in Japan as a result of the discovery of their misconduct and corrupt practices and second, for a series of their misguided policies. Referring to the results of the survey research conducted in 1999, this paper shows how the policymaking role perceptions and attitudes are in a transitional phase with regard to the power relationship between bureaucrats and politicians.

title: Organizational Capacity for Monitoring Delivery Systems: Some Sociological Clues.
abstract: Sociol'ts have historically been concerned with the possibility of rationality in soc units. The capacity of a formal org such as a gov'al agency to monitor & evaluate its performance is therefore of great sociol'al interest. The relation between org'al structure & delivery is one between means & ends of action. This paper attempts to delineate certain org'al characteristics which appear to be more or less influential in determining whether org's will in fact concentrate on means -- ends linkages. It is suggested that 3 types of soc factors provide clues concerning the possibility & extent of delivery system evaluation. These factors are grouped in terms of technology, power, & ideology. The writer tries to show how each of these kinds of forces was influential in an empirical setting involving the implementation of a programming-by-objectives system in the State of Pa. Specific org'al characteristics are related to the ability of org's to evaluate their means in terms of stated goals. The implications of the findings for practical application, esp in the public sector, are explored. AA.

title: Modernization and Organizational Culture: The Challenges of Globalization in Public Administration in Venezuela
abstract: Presents preliminary results of a case study on a modernization project in public organizations in Venezuela. How modernization has been developed & shared in artifacts, values, & assumptions is measured by using Schein's organizational culture definition. Culture is the clue to creating internal integration & to share assumptions & values to bring about a sense of direction & competencies in surviving to globalization strategy. The findings point out that most of the modernization's dimensions in public organizations -- eg, commitment, participation, leadership, competitiveness, productivity, quality processes, technology -- are threatened by organizational culture itself, because modernization issues are driven by cultural forces in which assumptions about reality, time, truth, & human nature are different from those that claimed modernization. Only artifacts have been taken: technology, structures, & buildings. To be successful, the modernization agenda in public organizations should be redefined including how its dimensions are culturally measured. These findings are important to introduce alternative public management models, which include those critical issues, to promote change processes.

title: Economic Development and Political Interests
abstract: Views the bureaupolitical setting of economic development, focusing on public & private sector partnerships in Europe with reference to experience in the US, presents a typology of partnerships, & reviews innovative approaches to economic development with particular reference to crossborder partnerships. The interests of public agencies & the private sector are set within the bureaupolitical framework & are seen as the source of both cooperation & conflict within the economic development process. Bureaucratic politics has both functional & dysfunctional effects on partnerships. Partnerships represent the integration of conflict & the potential for alliances between agencies with differing longer-term objectives & interests. Alliances are not always designed to cater for community interests, even where a "shared vision" is the desired stated objective.

title: New Middle Classes in Periphery
abstract: The composition, culture, & social functions of new middle classes in the Western periphery are discussed based on research in southern Italy in 1988/89. Two different segments of new middle classes are identified: bureaucratic public employees & new professional strata from both the public & private service sectors. These groups have different political attitudes, values, & interests that make them the carriers of different strategies for modernization & for southern Italy's integration into the Italian social, political, & economic system. Some general hypothesis about new social conflicts within the middle classes in contemporary societies are offered.

title: Drowning in Inequalities: Swimming and Social Justice
authors: Hastings, Donald W; Zahran, Sammy; Cable, Sherry
abstract: Social injustice is suffered by lower status groups when drowning is a health concern, much of the impoverished population lacks swimming skills, & no policies counter the principle of social exclusivity, restricting access to swimming programs. Drowning deaths are few in Europe, North America, South America, & Oceania, with higher levels of economic & social development, sizeable middle & upper classes, & a well-developed swimming infrastructure. Conversely, African & Asian countries have lower levels of economic & social development & less developed swimming infrastructures. We hypothesize that countries with well-developed swimming infrastructures & less social exclusivity have fewer numbers of deaths by drowning. We examine this hypothesis using deaths by drowning by county, age, sex, race, selected population & household data, & percentages on sport participation by county for the US. Any difference in numbers of drowning deaths by county would constitute conservative support for the social justice argument.

title: The Development of Indicators in New Zealand
abstract: A first wave of social indicator activity in New Zealand in the late 1970s & early 1980s faltered, but the current wave (put in place from 1999) appears well institutionalised (in terms of quality & acceptability). In some part, this success is a consequence of the contemporary approach in public administration which emphasises output goal setting followed by monitoring to assess progress, which has resulted in an apparent 'indicator-ilisation' of much social policy work both in central government & outside. The paper describes this wider process & seeks to account for its diffusion throughout many spheres of policy work in New Zealand.

title: Engagement, Gentrification, and the Neoliberal Hijacking of History
abstract: Drawing primarily on fieldwork in Greece, Italy, and Thailand, I examine the use of historic conservation to justify gentrification. This commoditization of history expands into urban design a classification that serves the goals of neoliberal modernity. By thus refocusing the classic anthropological concern with taxonomy on the analysis of the bureaucratic production of everyday experience and knowledge, I explore a new global habitus in which dominant interpretations of history spatially reinforce current ideologies. Historic conservation often provides an excuse for intervention into urban life. In a revision of high modernism's focus on science, logic, and efficiency, this trend invokes "the past." But which past? The concept of "heritage" is grounded in culturally specific ideologies of kinship, residence, and property, but the universalization of the nation-state as a collectivity of similar subunits has given those concepts globally hegemonic power. In consequence, phenomena that governments treat as "merely" cultural or symbolic are not taken seriously as sources of poverty and subjection. By juxtaposing historic conservation and gentrification with a critique of the public management of knowledge, I thus sketch a critical trajectory for anthropological engagement in "the politics of mereness" by asking who defines what matters in residents' lives. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Reviews -- The Changing Organisation and Management of Local Government (Government Beyond the Centre Series) by Steve Leach, John Stewart, and Kieron Walsh
abstract: Review.

title: Environmental behavior in Bangkok, Thailand: A portrait of attitudes, values, and behavior
authors: Daniere, Amrita G; Takahashi, Lois M
abstract: A detailed portrait of attitudes and behavior regarding environmental practices, health, and community participation among slum households in Bangkok, Thailand, is developed.  A case study of Bangkok provides the background information for an assessment of environmental attitudes and behavior and suggests their importance to the improvement of planning processes and outcomes regarding water, sanitation, and solid waste disposal.  Such attitudes and behavior affect a household's capacity and willingness to participate in environmental projects or initiatives and thus they have important policy implications in terms of the design and implementation of environmental management strategies.  In particular, an attempt is made to test the linkages between specific cultural values, socioeconomic characteristics, and environmental practices, such as participation in community projects or initiatives, water treatment, waste disposal behavior, and health practices.

title: Daniel Hoan and the Golden Age of Socialist Government in Milwaukee
abstract: This article examines Mayor Daniel Webster Hoan's socialist administration of Milwaukee from 1916-1940. The analysis delves into Hoan's challenges and victories -- especially in the early years of his administration -- and examines whether the citizens of Milwaukee actually embraced socialism. To answer that question, this article draws extensively from primary sources, including newspaper articles and archived documents, as well as several secondary sources. The evidence shows that Hoan's long tenure as mayor came in spite of, not because of, his socialism. Indeed, Hoan's popularity was due in part to his willingness to break from the Socialist Party platform when it was politically necessary. Ultimately, the people of Milwaukee embraced a popular reformer rather than the ideology he represented. [web URL: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ajes.12136/abstract]

title: What Happens When the Producer Cooperative Grows? Developmental Qualities of a Non-Bureaucratic Structure
abstract: In the transition from an industrial to an information economy, entrepreneurial activity is flourishing. As the transition becomes institutionalized, however, there is a tendency toward bureaucratization. Formalized control & hierarchical relationships tend to stifle the entrepreneurial spirit. Questioned is whether this stifling organizational process will occur during the current transition. More than any previous social economy, the information society is based on knowledge, & those who have access to & know how to use knowledge for entrepreneurial development will have power. Power is typically manifested in organizational forms characterized by hierarchy &, eventually, bureaucratic inertia. It is suggested that the worker cooperative is an organizational form that can maintain itself without hierarchy & bureaucracy. In recent years, worker cooperatives have grown in number, & compared to companies in similar markets, they are 50% more profitable. They may be an alternative to hierarchical, bureaucratic organizations that stifle entrepreneurship.

title: Bureaucracy and the Mexican American Elderly: Policy and Programming Issues
abstract: Using the National Survey of Hispanic Elderly People, 1988, examined are the support system of Mexican American elderly, & their interaction with formal service providers. Highlighted are large-scale poverty, poor health, & a lack of reliance on the family for assistance with finances & limitations. Further, while respondents (Rs) indicated a desire for more formal social services, utilization rates of formal services remained low. It is demonstrated that these Rs are confronted with a variety of barriers to formal assistance, eg, Supplemental Security Income (SSI), including a lack of knowledge about availability, accessibility, & eligibility for services. Results indicate that the family is unable to provide substantial support to many older Mexican Americans. Through an application of Weber's analysis of bureaucracy, the data reveal that some older Mexican Americans find it difficult to interact with modern bureaucracies. The most frequently cited reasons for their nonreceipt of SSI include a lack of knowledge of service & feelings of discomfort in the bureaucracy. Moreover, several Rs indicated that the street-level bureaucrats (social workers) had mistreated them or made them feel uncomfortable. There is a pervasive need for intensive planning & programming efforts -- eg, service packages to address dimensions of problems, efforts to assist the Mexican-American community to help the older generation, & the need for cultural sensitivity training among providers.

title: Careers of Individuals in a Bureaucracy
abstract: Max Weber's rational bureaucratic model has been extensively criticized as unrealistic; organizations do not work that rationally. Jeffrey Pfeffer has shown convincingly that power is important to organizational relationships; when bureaucratic methods are not feasible, the powerful make the decisions. However, Pfeffer has also shown that the powerful sometimes legitimize & consolidate their power by creating rule systems, ie, by bureaucratizing. Power must be used only when established rules & patterns are not effective; during periods of stability, bureaucratic order may prevail.
