Corporate & government entities are unique in that their deviant behavior may be caused by systemic patterns in their organizations, rather than by individual malfeasance. Moreover, once deviant behavior has occurred, they are well positioned to evade responsibility. Managers may often refuse responsibility by hiding behind organizational structures, or by adopting the view that they were merely following orders. The process of deviance is usually initiated by a particular action taken by managerial elites, which is then institutionalized in the organizational culture. Contributions explore deviant behavior in several case studies, including antitrust cases, aircraft brake hazards, the Ford Pinto production process, the Nazi Holocaust, the My Lai massacre, the Challenger disaster, the Rodney King beating, Rely tampons, & asbestos exposure. In these cases, the way in which organizational patterns produced the deviant behavior, & led the parties involved to evade responsibility, is discussed. The book contains 15 Chpts with Notes in IV PARTS. D. Ryfe

title: Terror in the Sahara: the implications of US imperialism for North & West Africa
abstract: Whichever way one looks at it, the Sahara has now become an extremely dangerous place. If one             believes all that has been said and written on events in the Sahara by US and other (notably             Algerian) military intelligence and associated government agencies and the media since early 2003,             then the Sahara-Sahel region of Africa has become a front line in the 'War on Terror'. If that is the             case, the inability of the security forces to apprehend the key terrorists, notably the GSPC             (Groupe Salafiste pour la Prédication et le Combat) under the leadership of their supposed emir             Abderrezak Lamari (aka Amari Saifi but generally known as El Para after his stint as a parachutist             in the Algerian army), would suggest that the current US administration and its military, which now             has special forces and 'contractors' fanned out across the region and whose intelligence and             operational services have the region under more or less total satellite, air and ground surveillance,             is remarkably inept - something which should no longer surprise us in the light of their debacles in             Afghanistan and Iraq. If, on the other hand, and as now seems increasingly likely, the Sahara has             been made the arena of an elaborate intelligence deception, then the danger to the local             populations and the security threat presented by the seemingly inevitable 'blowback' from this             operation to other regions, notably West Africa, North Africa and Europe itself, is probably even             greater. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: BUREAUCRACY AND POLITICAL DEVELOPMENT IN EASTERN EUROPE
abstract: A discussion of bur'tic theory re the Eastern European case, with emphasis upon the impact of bur'cy as a soc process on pol'al systems. Pol'al doctrines, admin'ive patterns, & the character of pol'al elites in the area are described. It is concluded that classic bur'tic theory is inadequate as a framework for the analysis of East European pol'al development for 2 reasons: (1) the theory is only partial - concerned with isolating only certain factors - pol'al power & ideology are ignored; & (2) like other polities, the totalitarian regimes of Eastern Europe are systems, & are thus subject to fluctuations caused by unpredictable external events. (See SA 0715-B3371). D. W. Ball.

title: MAX WEBER: SOCIOLOGICAL WRITINGS
abstract: Published as Vol 60 of The German Library (Volkmar Sander, general editor), this book offers translations of 31 essays introducing the sociological thought of Max Weber -- widely considered to have supplanted Marxism as the most influential social thought of the postmodern era -- to a new generation of students & scholars. The book's IV PARTS are organized around four subject areas that were central to Weber. All the major Weberian themes are here, including: the extent to which Western history can be viewed as the development of ever-increasing forms of rationality, the role of charismatic leaders, how religious ideas influence the formation of economic structures & attitudes, the nature of ideal types, & the structure of bureaucratic authority. An introduction by the editor, Wolf Heydebrand, precedes the IV (unnumbered) PARTS, which contain 31 Chpts. SOCIAL ACTION AND SOCIAL RELATIONSHIPS - offers (1) The Concept of Social Action; (2) The Types of Social Action; (3) The Concept of Social Relationship; (4) The Concept of Legitimate Order; (5) The Bases of Legitimacy of an Order; (6) The Concept of Conflict; (7) Types of Solidary Social Relationships; (8) Open and Closed Relationships; (9) Power, Authority, and Imperative Control; & (10) A. M. Henderson & Talcott Parsons (Trs) -- Political and Religious Corporate Groups. DOMINATION AND STRATIFICATION - contains (11) Legitimacy and the Types of Authority; (12) Charismatic Authority; (13) The Routinization of Charisma; (14) Martin Black (Tr) -- Collegiality and the Division of Powers; (15) Martin Black with Lance W. Garner (Trs) -- Bureaucratic Authority; (16) Martin Black (Tr) -- The Distribution of Power within the Political Community: Classes, Status Groups, Political Parties; & (17) Hans H. Gerth & C. Wright Mills (Trs) -- The Chinese Literati. RATIONALIZATION IN ECONOMY, RELIGION, AND LAW - includes (18) The Origins of Modern Capitalism; (19) Frank H. Knight (Tr) -- The Evolution of the Capitalistic Spirit; (20) Hans H. Gerth & Don Martindale (Trs) -- The Dualism of In-Group and Out-Group Morality; (21) Judaism, Christianity, and the Socioeconomic Order; (22) Ephraim Fischoff (Tr) -- The Attitude of the Other World Religions (Islam, Buddhism, Christianity) to the Social and Economic Order; (23) Rationality and Formalism in Law; (24) Formal and Substantive Rationalization of Law; & (25) Edward A. Shils & Max Rheinstein (Trs) -- The Formal Qualities of Modern Law. SOCIOLOGY AND SCIENCE - presents (26) Definition of Sociology; (27) A. M. Henderson & Talcott Parsons (Trs) -- The Methodological Foundations of Sociology; (28) "Objectivity" in Social Science; (29) The Tension between Science and Policy-Making; (30) Edward A. Shils & Henry A. Finch (Trs) -- Ideal-Type Constructs; & (31) Hans A. Gerth & C. Wright Mills (Trs) -- Science as a Vocation. References are encompassed in Chpt Notes. W. Howard

title: Getting the Salt Out: Innovative Solar Technologies for Rural Clean Water
abstract: Uzbekistan easily gets 300 days of sunshine a year, and is a natural choice for development of solar technologies and their implementation. Central Asia is working together to solve critical water problems including contamination and dry wells. This chapter addresses the need to find solutions for rural populations living in the shadow of the Aral Sea disaster, with poor quality drinking water and limited infrastructure. With assistance from generous government funding, the Institute for Solar Energy is developing new point-based solar desalinization and pumping technologies. Preliminary designs are promising and government support for raw materials mining and wafer production are growing. Domestic R&D and production ensures cost-effective dissemination options. The Institute houses both research and project management for all solar technologies and expects to field test prototypes within 2-3 years. Solar energy is a growing sector in the economy of Uzbekistan. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Rhetoric and policy realities in developing countries: Community councils in Jamaica, 1972-1980
abstract: The relationship between rhetoric and policy in developing countries is examined using a case study drawn from the administration of Michael Manley in Jamaica in the 1970s.  Particular attention is paid to problem definition, policy formulation, and implementation processes.  The policy relating to community councils was based on socialistic political and economic arguments.  Despite minor successes, most of the objectives associated with the community councils policy were not realized.  This failure was due to the Manley government's inability to transcend electoral and economic (national and international) realities and to convince a majority of the public and opposition of the validity of its rhetorical constructions.  Parallels to 3 other developing countries are briefly explored.

title: The Disenchangment of Logically Formal Legal Rationality: Or Max Weber's Sociology in the Genealogy of the Contemporary Mode of Western Legal Thought
abstract: The first section surveys the Western jurisprudence of Weber's time, stressing the contrast between mainstream & critical legal thinking. The next section discusses Weber's sociology of law & his ambivalent support of legal formalism, which required a discarding of the social current's critique. The third section considers Weber's views of legal formalism in relation to his theory of domination, whereby modernity's Iron Cage is fortified by bureaucrats bound by that form of legal reasoning. The fourth section contends that Weber's position contradicts the irrationalist & decisionist elements in his own theory of modernity. Section 5 interprets the contemporary type of legal thought as a segment of the narrative of disenchantment evoked by Weber's theory of history, & draws on Weberian features to build a singular contemporary ideal mode of jurisprudence. The conclusion aligns Weber with modern critical legal scholars. K. Coddon

title: News and notes
abstract: The Social Science Computing Association Internet listserv of Web sites on several subjects, including anthropology, economics, political science and public administration, is presented.

title: EUROPEAN SOCIAL CLASS: STABILITY AND CHANGE
abstract: A collection of essays re European soc stratification, in 12 essays, an Ed's' Introduction, & Foreward by Bruce Mazlish, including: (1) 'Class Divisions in England, 1540-1640,' by Lawrence Stone; (2) 'Entrepreneurial Activities of the Swedish Aristocracy,' by Goran Ohlin; (3) 'The Myth of the Middle Class in Tudor England,' by J. H. Hexter; (4) 'The Composition of the New Bureaucratic Elite in Prussia,' by Hans Rosenberg; (5) E. G. Barber (SA 2022); (6) 'Social Mobility Among the Servant Class of 18th Century England,' by J. Jean Hecht; (7) 'Elite' and `Nobility' in the Second Half of the 18th Century in France;' (8) 'The Revolutionary and Napoleonic Era: How Much of a Watershed?' by Franklin L. Ford; (9) 'The Business Interests of the Gentry in the Parliament of 1841-47,' by William O. Aydelotte; (10) 'The Place of Businessmen in the 19th Century French Class Structure,' by David Landes; (11) 'Social Class of Cambridge University Alumni of the 18th & 19th Centuries,' by Hester Jenkins & D. Caradog Jones & (12) B. Barber (SA 4729). D. Cooperman.

title: A NEW NEW ORLEANS? UNDERSTANDING THE ROLE OF HISTORY AND THE STATE-LOCAL RELATIONSHIP IN THE RECOVERY PROCESS
authors: Burns, Peter F; Thomas, Matthew O
abstract: Two years after Hurricane Katrina struck New Orleans, the city still struggles to rebuild and recover. In this article, we examine how deeply rooted historical patterns of state-local conflict reasserted themselves even after the terrible destruction of Katrina and the redemptive promise of a new beginning. We also explain how state government, some city leaders, and most New Orleanians took advantage of the opportunities presented by Hurricane Katrina to change certain aspects of governance in New Orleans. This research highlights the importance of the state-local relationship in understanding urban affairs and the critical nature of historical patterns and their persistence. State-local conflicts over finances, control of local politics, and cultural differences have plagued New Orleans for decades, and they continue to do so in the post-Katrina era. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Fetishizing the Modern City: The Phantasmagoria of Urban Technological Networks
abstract: Water & water networks are used as an emblematic example to excavate the shifting meanings of modern urban technological networks. Indeed, as water becomes commodified & fetishized, nature itself becomes reinvented in its urban form (aesthetic, moral, cultural codings of hygiene, purity, cleanliness, etc) & severed from the grey, "muddy," kaleidoscopic meanings & uses of water as a mere use value. Burying the flow of water via subterranean & often distant pinpointed technological mediations (dams, purification plants, pumping stations) facilitates & contributes to masking the social relations through which the metabolic urbanization of water takes place, & facilitates the severing of the intimate bond between use value, exchange value, & social power. It is argued that during early modernity, dams, water towers, sewage systems, & the like were celebrated as glorious icons, celebrating the modern promise of progress. During 20th-century high modernity, the symbolic & material shrines of progress started to lose their mobilizing powers & began to disappear from the cityscape. Water towers, dams, & plants became mere engineering constructs, often abandoned & dilapidated, while the water flows disappeared underground & in house. Thus, urban networks became "urban fetishes" during early modernity, "compulsively" admired & marvelled at, materially & culturally supporting & enacting an ideology of progress. The subsequent failure of this "ideology of progress" is paralleled by their underground disappearance during high modernity, while the abandonment of their "urban dowry" announced a recasting of modernity in new ways. It is concluded that the dystopian underbelly of the city that at times springs up in the form of accumulated waste, dirty water, pollution, or social disintegration produces a sharp contrast when set against the increasingly managed clarity of the urban environment. 4 Figures, 68 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Organizing America
abstract: Grapples with how the US economic system came to revolve around large privately held corporations that are minimally state regulated. While the industrial revolution played a role, it was insufficient alone to produce corporate capitalism; it does not stress the weakness of government & the capacity of diverse economic elites with organizational interests to rework the legal structure in a manner that favored the accumulation of private capital for large-scale national markets, which in turn allowed the emergence of large corporations. Strong private organizations can manipulate a weak state to their liking. Unlike Europe, the US had no national church & the federal state was kept small, weak, & divided. Also, various legal impediments to this economic development had to be removed, eg, limited liability. In addition to a weak state & a diverse economic elite that developed modern bureaucracy, the role of capital & labor in creating this economic system are elaborated. Attention then turns to the critical part that railroads played in the surge of giant organizations in the late-19th-century US. It is asserted that US corporate capitalism & the US society of big organizations was a path-dependent process with some historical accidents that was not inevitable until the end of the 19th century when the path firmed. 26 References. J. Zendejas

title: BUREAUCRATIC CULTURE AND ESCALATING WORLD PROBLEMS ADVANCING THE SOCIOLOGICAL IMAGINATION
abstract: On this fiftieth anniversary of the publication of Mills's "The Sociological Imagination," the "bureaucratic ethos" that he described has continued to escalate. The 11 authors of this book carry further and systematically develop Mills's broad vision of the scientific method as they analyze escalating bureaucratic barriers that prevent us from solving our many pressing social, environmental, & economic problems.

title: Sites of entitlement: claim, negotiation and struggle in Mumbai
abstract: This paper develops a conception of "sites of entitlement" as a basis for better understanding how infrastructure and services are perceived and experienced in informal settlements. While legal and policy frameworks are often viewed as the source of entitlements to infrastructure and services, the complexity of provision, access and negotiation in informal settlements demands a conception of entitlement that exceeds those domains. Based on ethnographic research on sanitation and water in informal settlements in Mumbai, we focus on the ways in which people's everyday experiences, interactions and practices constitute sites of entitlement. These sites are unevenly produced, contested, often in flux and ambivalent, sometimes made through collective struggle and at other times through quiet individual practice, and always constituted by social relations. Sites of entitlement emerge in close relation to moral economies, and are characterized by often profound and - for research, policy and practice - challenging levels of spatial and temporal variation. We argue that sites of entitlement are vital for thinking through the possibilities of realizing the universal right to sanitation and water.

title: Medical Licensing Board Characteristics and Physician Discipline: An Empirical Analysis
authors: Law, Marc T; Hansen, Zeynep K
abstract: This article investigates the relationship between the characteristics of medical licensing boards and the frequency with which boards discipline physicians. Specifically, we take advantage of variation in the structure of medical licensing boards between 1993 and 2003 to determine the effect of organizational and budgetary independence, public oversight, and resource constraints on rates of physician discipline. We find that larger licensing boards, boards with more staff, and boards that are organizationally independent from state government discipline doctors more frequently. Public oversight and political control over board budgets do not appear to influence the extent to which medical licensing boards discipline doctors. These findings are broadly consistent with theories of regulatory behavior that emphasize the importance of bureaucratic autonomy for effective regulatory enforcement. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The hidden regulation of carbon markets/Die versteckte Regulierung des Marktes für CO2-Emissionen
abstract: This article tracks the creation and maintenance of markets for emission rights and the role that law-creation plays within this process. From a recent example of a market creation -- the European Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS) -- , insights will be gained about the intrinsic and fundamental connections between market creation and bureaucratization. This process unfolds in a paradoxical way: The free-market hypothesis is, in fact, creating a demand for regulation, administration, and control. Law creation that is informed by the free-market hypothesis (the Law and Economics School in general, the EU Directive as a specific case), separates the "inside of the market" from the "outside of the market." This, firstly, causes a need for extra-administration at the "outside of the market" in order to resolve the uncertainty that emanates from the self-imposed requirement of leaving "the market itself" unregulated. And it, secondly, exposes the "rational actor" to an open and uncertain situation, which then leads to private regulative and administrative attempts at the "inside of the market."

title: Se questo è un lavoro. Meccanismi estrattivi e pratiche di resistenza nell'economia fondamentale / If this is a job. Extraction mechanisms and practices of resistance in the foundational economy
authors: Barbera, Filippa; Dagnes, Joselle; Salento, Angelo
abstract: The article introduces the concept of foundational economy - i.e. the activities providing the economic infrastructure of social reproduction – and analyzes it focusing on the transformation of work in the foundational sectors (e.g. food production and distribution; water and energy supply; waste management; education; health and social care; public transports). In recent decades a neoliberal approach, based on value maximization and financial accumulation, has spread in the foundational activities which should be driven by the idea of collective well-being. This profound transformation consistently affects workers as well as consumers. In fact, the pursuit of extra profits takes places also through the suppression of unprofitable services, the lowering of quality standards and the reduction of fixed costs related to the labour force. In this scenario, however, we also observe a number of innovative experiences opposing the value extraction process in the foundational activities. These practices propose alternative forms of production, organization, and distribution, aiming to place the role of labour and the workers at the heart of the economy.

title: Becoming a Slum: From Municipal Colony to Illegal Settlement in Liberalization-Era Mumbai; [1]
abstract: This article argues that the transformation of a Mumbai neighborhood from municipal housing colony into illegal slum has been facilitated by the politically mediated deterioration and criminalization of its water infrastructure in the context of liberalization-era policy shifts. These policy shifts hinge upon a conceptual binary that posits the unplanned, illegal and informal 'slum' as the self-evident conceptual counterpoint to a planned, formal, 'world-class' city. The story of Shivajinagar-Bainganwadi problematizes this assumption by evidencing the deeply political and highly unstable nature of this binary -- and thus insists upon an account of the shifting political and economic stakes imbued in these categories. The case of Shivajinagar-Bainganwadi reveals that the neighborhood's emergence as an illegal slum has been mediated by the liberalization-era politics that have come to infuse the neighborhood's water pipes -- dynamics that have produced the illegality/informality of the neighborhood as a discursive effect.[PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Conflict and legitimacy: explaining tensions in Swedish hunting policy at the local level
abstract: This article reveals the existence of a so-called "ghost policy" (informal tradition and/or obsolete policy rules) that resists new official policy concerning the management of natural resources in Sweden. These ghost policies are often ignored in the Swedish policy making process inhibiting, therefore, viable and legitimate solutions to the profound negative consequences that costly local conflicts of interest have on democracy. These conflicts of interest expose and represent a classic and current problem intrinsic to the communitarian policy process in Sweden. That is, since the Swedish policy process has a blind spot, it focuses on the views of experts and interest organisations and, subsequently, overlooks the perceptions of those stakeholders (in this case local game hunters) affected by policy. This undermines the policy's goals since they are alien to local tradition. Furthermore, not just the existence and ubiquity of ghost policies, but even social facts such as the physical size and membership of an organisation influence conflicts of interest. This implies that there is still room for collaborations with locals as well as social engineering in the policy process. In order then for the Swedish policy process to gain more legitimacy from stakeholders involved with natural resource management the government must review and change its present processes of policy making. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Meeting the Decent Homes Standard: London Housing Associations' Asset Management Strategies
abstract: The English government's 10-year flagship Decent Homes programme ended in 2010. The purpose of this article is to examine the asset management strategies that a sample of London housing associations took to meet the Decent Homes Standard. Drawing on the concept of institutional logics, the article outlines the social housing sector's conflicting regulatory context, whereby organisations were statutorily obliged to improve housing standards, without being able to raise rents as a way to fund improvements. Depending on whether the housing association adopts a market-orientated or traditional, task-orientated approach to asset management, the associations sampled have either disposed of non-decent stock to generate cash flows or else retained the stock, undertaking minimal repairs to meet the government's target deadline. The article concludes that not only has this national performance target triggered different organisational responses, it has also led to longer-term unintended consequences for existing and future tenants. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Bureaucratic Structures for Coordination and Control
authors: Marsden, Peter V; Cook, Cynthia R; Kalleberg, Arne L
abstract: Examines the organizational structures of establishments in the 1991 National Organizations Study, drawing on theories developed since the 1960. The principle postulate advanced by these theories is that organizations employ structural arrangements to achieve coordination & control over their activities. Further, coordination & control are assumed to be more difficult to achieve as the size of the organization increases. It is found that measures of coordination & control techniques eg, structural complexity, formalization, decentralization, & administrative intensity, are associated in ways that the literature proposes. Significant differences between large & small organizations in terms of organizational structure are found. Further, for-profit companies tend to be less formalized & more decentralized than nonprofit & public sector establishments. Thus, the dominant trend in organizational theory to stress the external, institutional sources of structural forms is confirmed. 5 Tables, 2 Figures. D. M. Smith

title: The Problem of Democracy in the European Union
abstract: The lack of democracy in the European Union (EU) has traditionally been examined as an institutional problem, but it is argued here to be a manifestation of the widespread disagreement about what constitutes the essential character of the EU. To make this point, the historical particularity of the EU is taken into account, the EU's governmental structures are discussed, & the conditions for democracy in the EU are compared to those in a sovereign state. The new instruments that the Maastricht Treaty sets up to work against the democratic deficit -- most notably, the concepts of subsidiarity, regionality, & EU citizenship -- are also examined & found wanting. M. Maguire

title: ORGANIZING MODERNITY: NEW WEBERIAN PERSPECTIVES ON WORK, ORGANIZATION AND SOCIETY
authors: Ray, Larry J. Ed]; Reed, Michael
abstract: This collection of essays by Australian & European scholars of international repute provides a reevaluation of the significance of Max Weber's work for the current debate over the organizational & institutional dynamics of modernity. Here, Weber's accounts of modernity & bureaucracy are reexamined in relation to the strategic social structures that dominated the development of modern society, with analyses devoted to specific contemporary issues such as the dismantling of communism, corporatism, Fordism, & traditionalism in both Western & Eastern societies. The contributions attempt to minimize the import of orthodox readings of Weber & emphasize global modernity's potential for both disarticulating rational structures & more deeply colonizing daily life. The book is particularly relevant not only to Weber specialists, but also to undergraduates & postgraduates in sociology & organizational studies. The book is presented in 7 Chpts with an Introduction & a Conclusion. Larry J. Ray & Michael Reed -- Weber, Organizations and Modernity: An Introduction. (1) David Chalcraft -- Bringing the Text Back In: On Ways of Reading the Iron Cage Metaphor in the Two Editions of The Protestant Ethic. (2) Stewart R. Clegg -- Max Weber and Contemporary Sociology of Organizations. (3) John Eldridge -- Work and Authority: Some Weberian Perspectives. (4) Martin Albrow -- Accounting for Organizational Feeling. (5) Bryan S. Turner -- Max Weber on Individualism, Bureaucracy and Despotism: Political Authoritarianism and Contemporary Politics. (6) Keith Tribe -- Commerce, Science and the Modern University. (7) Larry J. Ray & Michael Reed -- Max Weber and the Dilemmas of Modernity. Larry J. Ray & Michael Reed -- Conclusion: Autonomy, Pluralism and Modernity. References accompany each essay. 4 Figures. W. Howard

title: Bureaucracy as an Issue in Third World Management: An African Case Study
abstract: The need to reorient study of public sector management in the Third World from an ideal-typical bias emphasizing assumed optimal performance to evaluation of actual performance is discussed, with focus on the case of Liberia. The Liberian bureaucracy originated, in part, from attempts of an Americo-Liberian elite to control Liberian society through incorporation or administrative employment. Subordination was extended into the hinterland through material enhancement & development of an idiosyncratic bureaucratic ideology emphasizing a civilizing mission. The Liberian bureaucracy is characterized by a low level of boundary definition & rule structure. The Liberian bureaucracy is discussed as a failure from the perspective of the ideal-typical case, but as successful in achieving the organization's goals. 18 References. D. Generoli

title: UNDER THE IVI TREE: SOCIETY AND ECONOMIC GROWTH IN RURAL FIJI
abstract: A Vol in 3 Parts & 21 Chpts, presenting: I-PROLEGOMENA, (1) The Fijian Way of Life: A Romance, analyzing Fijian soc org, based on the assumption of functionalism & lack of stress. (2) A View of Fiji and the Sigatoka Region, summarizing Fijian geography & statistics & placing the fieldwork region of Sigatoka in perspective. (3) The Village and Social Structure, analytically describes village org & kinship structure, including affinal linkages & alliances. II-ENTERPRISE EMERGENT, (4) The Nadroga Banana Venture, detailing bur'tic control of Fijians producing bananas for the export market. (5) Bureaucracy Guides Enterprise, accounting official development schemes initiating by various levels of gov. (6) Fijian Corporate Organizations, describes Fijian cteation & management of productive & commercial group enterprises. (7) Sugar: Company Paternalism, considers the detailed control of the sugar industry & the lives of the farmers by the Colonial Sugar Refining Co. (8) Experiments of the Fijian Farmer, deals with peasants operating independently for cash purposes within the market econ & Fijian soc structure. (9) Market Middlemen, discusses Fijian competition with Indians to purchase & market Ru produce in the towns after completion of a road into farm areas. (10) Conservatism or Change?, shows that Fijians have not been conservative but have responded to stimuli to cultural & econ change on many fronts. (11) The Preference for Leisure, asserts that the myth of Fijian laziness does not explain the slow rate of change. (12) The Ambiguity of Communalism, shows that the frequently used term, communalism, hides the realities of interaction between individual & soc structure. (13) The Role of Ceremonialism, gives major attention to the analysis of ceremony & concludes that it may even on occasion motivate expansion & production. (14) Belief and the Spirit of Enterprise, explores interaction between belief & enterprise & indicates that the Protestant ethic is less signif than the personal history of the entrepreneur & his position as having minority values diff from those of the soc group. (15) The Supply of Labor, analyzes the manner in which labor is called forth & organized. (16) The Manipulation of Land, demonstrates that land use traditionally derives from soc structure & pol'al org & allows for manipulation & flexibility. (17) Capital and the Supply of Credit, cites lack of capital in the Ru sector as a major bottleneck to mobilizing credit. (18) Fijian Bureaucracy, analyzes the structure & operation of Fijian admin. (19) Social Services and the Church, examines the financing & cost of educ & the Church, including description of some semi-traditional methods of raising cash capital. (20) Communication, investigates the signif of verbal & physical message transport & transmission for econ viability & adjustment. III-CONCLUSION, (21) Under the Ivi Tree, examines the main factors explaining econ growth & the lack of it primarily as an interaction of instit's & the presence of absence of key instit's & org's. The 2 main themes are the nature of stress & tension in an organized system & the effects of paternalistic gov. Modified AA.

title: Postcode Lottery for Europe's Undocumented Children
abstract: This article explores the competing policy imperatives within and between tiers of government and policy makers' perceptions of the relative "deservingness" of undocumented children, which contribute to an uneven geography of entitlements to public services across the European Union. While scholars have contrasted the formal exclusion of undocumented migrants with their informal inclusion, the article explores the tension between formal exclusion and formal inclusion: where the state, through granting legal entitlements to services, contradicts the logic of its own enforcement paradigm. The analysis presents the findings of a comprehensive mapping of entitlements to health care and education for undocumented children across the European Union's 28 member states and draws on interviews with policy makers across 14 member states to explore the justification for entitlements granted at national and substate levels. It finds that competing policy imperatives are most acute in relation to children where the logic of immigration control faces competing social and humanitarian imperatives within the national administration and in regional and municipal tiers of government. That tension reflects the social construction of undocumented children as both "illegal" and vulnerable, negative perceptions among policy makers of the deservingness of undocumented migrants countered, to a degree, by positive perceptions of the deservingness of children.

title: Is Greed America's New Creed?
abstract: Business and Society Review polled several business and academic leaders regarding the prevalence of greed in today's business world and the adequacy of ethics teaching in US business schools.  Among the respondents were: 1.  W.  Michael Hoffman, director of the Center for Business Ethics at Bentley College, and Robert E.  Frederick, the center's assistant director, who suggest that responses to malfeasance in the system should include legislation, regulation, and consensus on an underlying ethics system, 2.  A.  L.  Gitlow, retired dean of the College of Business and Public Administration at New York University, who contends that, despite the persistent notion that business is inherently less ethical than other pursuits, other fields are motivated equally by profits, and 3.  Carlton E.  Spitzer, a Washington-based public affairs consultant, who advocates a national renaissance to recapture and integrate basic values into all business, finance, government, and institutional activities, beginning in the elementary schools.

title: Shirking the State: Globalization and Public Administration "Reform"
abstract: Shirking the State: Globalization and Public Administration "Reform" by John Shields and B. Mitchell Evans is reviewed.

title: Divergent Paths: Civil Service Employment Relations in Australia and Canada
abstract: At the end of 1983, the government in Australia issued a discussion paper that addressed 3 areas in which public administration could be made more efficient.  This paper became the basis of the Public Service Reform Act of 1984, which amends Section 22 of the Public Service Act.  The law now requires departments and prescribed statutory authorities to develop and maintain industrial democracy action plans.  The content of these plans gives rank and file employees the opportunity for involvement in problem resolution and work improvement.  To reinforce the change process, the Public Service Board is placing a strong emphasis on training, both in terms of management education and in the internalization of the value of industrial democracy.  There are other indicators of government support of the Australian federal civil service as well.  Aspects of the general philosophy underlying the Australian model may find some useful applications as the public-sector systems in Canada continue to evolve.

title: THE COMMISSION FOR RACIAL EQUALITY: BRITISH BUREAUCRACY AND THE MULTIETHNIC SOCIETY
abstract: A Vol in the Social Policy and Social Theory Series (David Marsland, series editior) investigates the policies & practices of the British Commission for Racial Equality (CRE), an organization issuing from the 1976 Race Relations Act. It is suggested that the CRE has functioned as a kind of race lobby that has produced an inaccurate portrait of the UK as a society riddled with racism. This mischaracterization is traced to provisions in the original 1976 Race Relations Act, which assume that (1) minorities have special needs, (2) these needs must be met according to the statistical makeup of these groups, & (3) the state ought to have the power to enforce statistical equality regardless of other rights involved. Armed with these assumptions, the CRE has proven successful in putting forward its view. In the process, it has exercised its considerable legal powers to curtail the freedoms of association, contract, & speech. This situation is discussed in the context of US race relations. The official British approach to race relations ought to be rethought according to four basic questions: What conceptions of human rights ought to underlie race relations? Should a race relations bureaucracy be developed between the state & society? Should it be assumed that minority groups lack sufficient resources to help themselves? Should the US experience be ignored? An Introduction precedes 13 Chpt with Notes. 61 References. D. Ryfe

title: Producing Disunity: The Constraints and Incitements of Welfare Work
abstract: A 17-month ethnography of a welfare office & two welfare rights groups during 1989/90 in MI explores the blocks to solidarity & alliance between welfare workers & welfare recipients despite common life experiences & similar class positions. For women, both roles are devalued. Bureaucratic control of welfare workers limits their ability to help welfare recipients, & they are forced to use neoliberal ideology in selecting the poor considered worthy of assistance. The poor women who are rejected view the workers as the source of the problem & label them as arbitrary & unfair. The disunity & hostility in worker-recipient relations echoes the current ethos of welfare in the US. L. A. Hoffman

title: Leadership and Bureaucracy in the Late CIO
abstract: After the death of its leader in 1952, a leadership struggle ensued in the Congress of Industrial Organizations.  The history of the power struggle is discussed.

title: AMERICA AS A MASS SOCIETY
abstract: An anthology in 4 Parts with a Preface & a Prologue, discussing the massive growth of Corp's, Ur centers, gov bur's, & mass COMM's, mass society (MS) as a freeing or restrictive agent, its instit'al correlates, & the implications that is holds for the community & the individual. PART I THE THEORY OF MASS SOCIETY, presents: Philip Selznick, Institutional Vulnerability in Mass Society, examining instit's capable of self-maintenance, & defining MS re creative & culture-sustaining elites, participation & org, & diagnostic symptoms of mass behavior; & Edward Shils, The Theory of Mass Society, outlining the structure of MS's. II THE CENTRAL INSTITUTIONS OF AMERICAN SOCIETY, presents: Henry Bamford Parkes, The Growth of Industrialism, describing indust'ism from the Civil War & corresponding changes in sci, business & corporate structure, immigration, Ru & Ur living, SC org, etc; National Resources Committee, The Structure of Controls, indicating the non-market controls influencing econ activity; C. Wright Mills, The Power Elite, discussing the instit'al bases of power & the coordination of elites; Gabriel Kolko, The American 'Income Revolution', examining the radical redistribution of income in the US in the past 20 yrs. Thurman Arnold, The Society of the Corporation, examines corporate structure in the US. W. Lloyd Warner, The Corporation, the Community, and the Emergent Process, notes the changes & relationships between the Corp & the community; Anselm Strauss, The Course of American Urbanization, outlines the characteristics of US urbanization; Lewis Mumford, The Tentacular Bureaucracy, discusses urbanization & bur'tion. Joseph Bensman & Bernard Rosenberg, Mass Media and Mass Culture, compares the COMM's of folk & feudal societies with that of the MS & describes the democratization of taste. III THE TRANSFORMATION OF COMMUNITY, presents: ArtGallaherJr., Urbanizing Influences on Plainville, which studies the impact of Ur culture on Plainville, the community studied by Carl Withers in 1939; Alicja Iwanska (SA A8351); Samuel Pr attitude (SA 4702); Harvey Swados, The Miners: Men Without Work, Daniel Seligman, The New Masses, discusses the trend toward greater SC homogeneity in the US; Arthur J. Kover, The Academic Community and the Professors' Audiences, indicates the changes in the academic environment as going from personally small to dense, & from socially reacting to demanding, & its effects on US Coll & U teachers; Maurice Stein (SA A1276) & David Riesman (SA 6492); A. C. Spectorsky, Exurbia, describes the exUr community of Fairfield County, Conn; Scott Greer, Individual Participation in the Mass Society, & William J. Goode (SA 4344); Alexander Alland Jr., The Semantics of Revivalism, analyzes the functions of Ur Negro revival cults; Gerald N. Grob, Organized Labor in an Industrial Age, reviews the emergence of trade unionism out of 19th cent indust'ism; Will Herberg, Religion and Culture in Present-day America, indicates the role played by religious belonging in contemporary US life; & Daniel Miller & Guy Swanson (SA A0767). IV THE CONVERGENCE OF MASS AND COMMUNITY, presents: Paul Goodman, The Calling of American Youth, discusses youth & modern society; David F. Aberle & Kaspar D. Naegle, Middle-Class Father's Occupational Role and Attitudes Toward Children, considers the relationship between the occup'al role of the Mc M & his concerns with the socialization of children; Leopold Bellak, Personality Structure in a Changing World, investigates changes in character structure as responses to increased mobility of SE, technological, & geographical frames of reference for identification; Philip Olson & Carlton Daley, The Education of the 'Individual', discusses the Sch system & child development; Dorothy Lee, What Kind of Freedom? analyzes US conceptions of time, space, & freedom; Joseph Bensman & Arthur Vidich, Business Cycles, Class and Personality, attempts to relate major tenets of econ analysis with soc-psychol'al & pol'al aspects of class; Daniel Miller & Guy Swanson (SA A0767); John R. Seeley, R. Alexander Sim, & E. A. Loosely (SA 4282); William H. Whyte Jr., The Wives of Management, Edward Ziegler, Payment by Status, examines executive & sub-executive status payment; Ellentine M. Mullaney, Status Symbols and the Timecard Employee, & Ely Chinoy, The Tradition of Opportunity and the Aspirations of Automobile Workers, explores the concept of opportunity held by a group of automobile workers in a midwestern city; Louis Schneider & Sanford Dornbusch (SA A0694); Morton Hunt, The Age of Love, examines the themes of love & sex in the modern era; Donald Horton & R. Richard Wohl, Mass Communication and ParaSocial Interaction: Observations on Intimacy at a Distance, analyzes the relationship between spectator & MM performance; & Erich Fromm, The Marketing Orientation, analyzes a type of personality orientation as an analogue of the contemporary abstract & impersonal market. G. Jacobs.

title: Building a Fragmented State: Land Governance and Conflict in South Sudan
abstract: Land governance reforms are part of donor-sponsored liberal peacebuilding projects which have state-building as one of their core elements. After the end of the civil war with Sudan (1983-2005), South Sudan undertook a process of institution-building and policy-making supported by international donors to create a decentralised system based on local 'communities' and their 'traditional authorities'. Communal customary rights to land have been legalised to reduce rural people's economic vulnerability and satisfy one of the major grievances that led to war. In fact, the land reform encouraged the overlapping between the spheres of local state administration and the ethnic community ruled by traditional authorities. To date this has appeared to strengthen ethnic affiliation as a means to access resources and enrich government officers' repertoires for claiming control over the territory on behalf of the 'community', thereby increasing competition in a context marked by the militarisation of ethnic identity.

title: EDUCATION AND SOCIAL AWAKENING IN IRAN, 1850-1960
abstract: In analyzing the trend of modern educ in Iran, the educ'al changes in the last 100 yrs are related to the soc & pol'al events of that period, & a long-range view of educ'al needs for the future is presented. Chpt (1) Education in Ancient and Medieval Iranian Society, describes socialization & educ in ancient times & the educ'al ideas of prominent medieval Persian scholars. (2) Education for Bureaucracy and Civil Service, relates the development of higher educ to the gov's pressing needs for personnel. (3) Vocational Education and Technical Change, traces the development of vocational & technical educ. (4) Education for Citizenship and Literacy, describes the efforts of Ur communities to bring about public elementary Sch educ. (5) Secondary Education and the Dilemma of Youth, indicates how secondary educ 'arose out of 2 needs: the demand for higher educ'al instit's for better qualified candidates & the shortage of elementary Sch teachers.' (6) Physical Education for Group Affiliation, discusses physical educ as an outgrowth of nat'l program of physical fitness. (7) Teachers as the Agents of Change, views the modern Iranian teacher as an agent of change in helping 'develop in the child att's, beliefs & patterns of behavior that [often] directly conflict with those of his parents.' (8) Socio-Political Education, views the development of pol'al parties & the press in the present cent as 'most strongly ... [reflecting] the soc & pol'al awareness & educ of the people.' (9) Missionary Education in Iran, describes the efforts of foreign religious & econ missions to promote educ in Iran. (10) The Role of Education in the Reconstruction of Iran, evaluates the past cent of Iranian educ as marked by 'discontinuity & disharmony'. Modified AA.

title: 'White knuckle care work': violence, gender and new public management in the voluntary sector
abstract: Drawing on comparative data from Canada and Scotland, this article explores reasons why violence is tolerated in non-profit care settings. This article provides insights into how the predominantly female (paid) workers' orientations to work, the desire to care and the intrinsic rewards from working in a non-profit context interact with the organization of work and managerially constructed workplace norms and cultures to offset the tensions in an environment characterized by scarce resources and poor working conditions. This article also outlines how the same environment of scarce resources causes strains in management's efforts to establish these cultures. Working with highly excluded service users, workers find themselves working at the edge of their endurance, beginning to participate in various forms of resistance, suggesting that even among the most highly committed, 'white knuckle care' may be unsustainable.

title: No-Collar Labour in America's 'New Economy'
abstract: Looks at the emergence of "Casual Fridays" in the workplace as part of a new managerial ethos that claims to empower workers, undo rigid bureaucratic constraints, & eliminate workplace hierarchies. Americans were again encouraged to find their identities in work rather than in leisure time or consumption. Diminishing boundaries between work & leisure are exemplified by New York's "Silicon Alley," where workplace environments include communal spaces, game rooms, gyms, & other amenities. It is maintained that these environments are the ultimate physical embodiment of the "flexibility" discourse that has recently dominated corporate culture. The decline in steady full-time jobs between 1973 & 1993 & the rise in free agents, or independent contractors, are explored. It is contended that the "liberated" artists/writers who work on one side of the professional divide are counterbalanced by low-wage contingent employees who are exploited by cost-cutting managers. The conflicts created by placing principles of public interest or creative expression above the pursuit of material security in a labor environment dominated by neoliberal business models are discussed. J. Lindroth

title: Beyond the Abolition of Dual Administration: The Challenges to NGO Governance in 21st Century China
authors: Yang, Yongjiao; Wilkinson, Mick; Zhang, Xiongxiong
abstract: The abolition of dual administration of non-governmental organizations (NGOs) in China is an inexorable and essential trend toward a genuine civil society. This article seeks to examine the challenges that come with the abolition of the dual administration and to explore how to address them during this transitional period. It considers the state dominated NGO governance in China and its transformation since the 1990s and argues that the decisive role the government plays in NGOs' development, which is criticized by many scholars, is the outcome of Chinese history, political culture and the needs of NGOs. It gives account of the challenges for NGO governance and development following the abolition of dual administration. Suggestions for new approaches to NGO development are discussed from the perspectives of a value-based partnership between NGOs and the government, the importance of securing public trust, the development of legal systems and finally, the role of NGO network organizations.

title: People Qualification and Administrative Procedures
abstract: This article deals with forms of bureaucratic control of administrative personnel & public finances in China, at a time when, at the beginning of the Song Dynasty (960-1279), a centralized state emerged, dominated by government officials. It focuses on the relationship of procedures, a consequence of the formalization of information that circulated between the base units -- prefecture & sub-prefecture -- & the center. The formalization of evaluations of men & goods caused a durable hypertrophy of control systems: for the government officials, data processing became an essential part of their work & this reality of paper shuffling became as important as the facts themselves. E. Sanchez

title: The US influence in shaping Iraq's sectarian media
abstract: After the Anglo-American invasion, the US neo-conservative administration established the Iraqi Governing Council in July 2003, which included 25 members selected for their ethnic and religious origins; it was the most obvious sign of the US political separatist strategy. As a result of the new political reality, the Iraqi media was divided into ethno-sectarian lines, resulting from previous policies followed by the US administration. This article argues that the US media policy prior and after the US invasion of Iraq played a part in enhancing and encouraging the sectarian divisions in the Iraqi society. This was mainly done by sending biased media messages through the state-run Iraqi Media Network (IMN) and other US-aligned channels and allowing militant voices from different Iraqi sides to wage wars of words without interfering. In fact, the only time US officials interfered is when they were criticized by Iraqi media outlets. This study cites different US government reports, accounts from media practitioners who worked for IMN and other journalists that monitored the Iraqi media. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: MODERN ORGANIZATIONS
abstract: A text in the Foundations of Modern Sociology Series under the editorship of Alex Inkeles - in 10 Chpts: (1) Rationality and Happiness: The Organizational Dilemma, (2) The Organizational Goal: Master or Servant?, (3) The Classical Approach, (4) From Human Relations to the Structuralists, (5) Bureaucracies: Structure and Legitimization, (6) Organizational Control and Leadership, (7) Organizational Control and Other Correlates, (8) Administrative and Professional Authority, (9) Modern Organization and the Client, & (10) Organization and the Social Environment, Selected References & an Index. L. P. Chall.

title: THE BUREAUCRACY AND POLITICAL DEVELOPMENT IN VIET NAM
abstract: A discussion of the Viet Namese case within the context of an information energy conversion model, where it is postulated that change is a function of the amount of information available to a society & the way in which such information is converted into energy. Viet Nam is seen as a low energy society, ie econ'ly unadvanced, with little prospects of other than a slow increment in energy, ie, not likely to change rapidly. (See SA 0715-133371). D. W. Ball.

title: The future of the national forests
abstract: The current crisis in the federal government's management of national forests reflects a faulty set of fundamental principles.  The whole national forest system is coming open for reexamination, and some of the main alternatives include privatization of forest lands, transfer of lands to state or local governments, major reorganization of the federal forest system, and other basic departures from current arrangements.

title: THE BUREAUCRATIC PHENOMENON
abstract: An analysis of bur'cy involving the association of 2 distinct approaches: the theory of decision-making in large org's & the cultural analysis of soc patterns of action, in IV Parts & 11 Chpts, with an Author's Introduction. Part I THE CASE OF THE CLERICAL AGENCY, includes: (1) The Over-all Organization and the Employees' Individual Adjustments to Their Tasks, dealing with: (A) the goals of the Parisian Clerical Agency & its general characteristics; (B) the various personnel categories; (C) work & productivity org; (D) employee satisfaction re the 'work load' & general att's about work; & (E) the importance of SS. (2) Interpersonal and Intergroup Relationships and the Problem of Routine, analyzes: (a) soc participation & integration of employees; (b) authority relationships; (c) supervisory problems; & (d) over-all routine pattern. II THE INDUSTRIAL MONOPOLY, includes: (3) The Social System at the Shop Level: The Plant Subculture and the Formal Authority System, analyzing. dominant elements in the indust'al plant soc system re the 'subculture' which develops around the major org'al 'givens' & the nature of the adjustment to formal authority which parallels it. (4) The Social System at the Shop Level: The Relationships between Groups and the Adjustment Patterns of Groups, investigates complex group relationships, & adjustment patterns of various groups. (5) Power Relationships at the Management Level, presents an analysis of HR at the management level, & indicates some sources of bur'tic strain. III BUREAUCRACY AS AN ORGAN- IZATIONAL SYSTEM, offers: (6) Power and Uncertainty, discussing power problems re the analysis of the 2 case studies, esp the indust'al monopoly. (7) The Bureaucratic System of Organization, extrapolates an analysis of burley as 'a general system or org.' IV BUREAUCRACY AS A CULTURAL PHE- NOMENON: THE FRENCH CASE, includes: (8) The French Bureaucratic System of Organization, dealing with the French bur'tic org re: (i) the nature of interpersonal & intergroup relationships; (ii) the character of authority relationships, & the fear of face-to-face relationships; (iii) the paradoxical weakness of the power of the upper echelons of the bur'tic structure; (iv) a development of 'other comparable models for the diff dysfunctions & rigidities that can develop in diff cultural environments.' (9) The Importance of Bureaucratic Patterns of Action in the French Social System, compares the earlier model of bur'tic org with the educ'al, indust'al relations, the politico-admin'ive, & colonial systems. (10) The Bourgeois Entrepreneur and Bureaucracy, discusses the interdependence of rigidity & change processes, soc stratification, & 'the patterns of the soc game that govern it,' comparing entrepreneurial & bourgeois behavior patterns. (11) The Bureaucratic Phenomenon and the 'French Model' as Part of the Over-All Development of Industrial Society, presents this analysis as useful for understanding the growth of 'modern rationality' & those factors conducive to its evolution. Modified AA.

title: WEBER: A SHORT INTRODUCTION
abstract: The author provides a historical account of Max Weber's life & the impact this had on his work before turning to a discussion on some of the major themes -- Methodology, Weber's the socio-historical process, the Protestant Ethic & the Spirit of Capitalism, Sociology of Religion, political power & legitimacy, & bureaucracy & the State -- in his research. Bibliog.

title: A STRATEGY FOR RESEARCH ON SOCIAL POLICY
authors: Bonilla, Frank; MICHELENA, JOSE A. SILVA
abstract: Vol I of THE POLITICS OF CHANGE IN VENEZUELA, representing the 1st of 3 reports on alternative strategies for Venezuela's development based on res by the Centro de Estudios del Desarrollo (Center for Development Studies) of the Central U of Venezuela in collaboration with the Center for Internat'l Studies of the Massachusetts Instit of Technology. The book is arranged in IV Parts & 12 Chpt's by various authors, preceded by a Foreword by Max F. Millikan & Luis Lander, Ed's Acknowledgments & Introduction & followed by a Postface. 'Introduction'-outlines res design & environment. I-THE DIAGNOSIS AND RESEARCH APPROACHES-presents: (1) Jorge Ahumada, 'Hypotheses for Diagnosing Social Changes: The Venezuelan Case,' which is an earlier version of SA 0715/ B4179. (2) Frank Bonilla & Jose A. Silva Michelena, 'An Integrated Analytical Scheme for Conven, Venelite, and Venutopia I,' discusses some large-scale implications of survey data from 3 separate studies dealt with in the book: the 'Conven Study,' the 'Venelite Project,' & the 'Venutopia I' computer experiment described in detail in (12). II-THE CONVEN SAMPLES- contains: (3) Jose A. Silva Michelena, 'Nationalism in Venezuela,' which defines patterns of nat'lism in Latin America & analyzes the various aspects of Venezuelan pol as indicated by the 'Conven' data. (4) Jose A. Silva Aichelena, 'The Venezuelan Bureaucrat,' deals with the role of bur'cy in nat'l development & the problems of Venezuelan bur'cy. (5) John R. ,Vlathiason, 'The Venezuelan Campesino: Perspectives on Change,' examines the position of the peasant in Venezuela in the context of ED & presents data from the Ru group survey samples of the 'Conven' study. III-VENELITE-offers: (6) Frank Bonilla, 'A List-Processing Approach to Qualitative Data Analysis,' which summarizes the principal features of the coding scheme that was developed for qualitative interviews with Venezuelan leaders in the 'Venelite' study. (7) Frank Bonilla, 'The National Perspectives of Venezuelan Elites,' discusses the action patterns & styles of the Venezuelan power elite, based on computer analysis of coded summaries of interviews with members of the elite. A basic diff in orientation toward change is found between cultural & noncultural leaders. (8) Gabriela de Bronfenmajer, 'Elite Evaluation of Role Performance,' gives first impressions & implications of the data on role evaluations obtained in the 'Venelite' interviews & notes the general estrangement between the cultural & other spheres of leadership in Venezuela. (9) Allan Kessler, 'The Internal Structure of Elites,' approaches the data of the 'Venelite' project from the point of view that good COMM is essential to the coordination across many spheres of soc policy aiming at soc change. IV--ALTERNATIVE FORMS OF SYNTHE- SIS-comprises: (10) Walter H. Slote, 'Case Analysis of a Revolutionary,' which presents a detailed psychol'al & sociol'al case history & analysis of a graduate student in soc psychol at the U Central, Venezuela, in an effort to determine the factors which lead to revolutionary pol'al & soc beliefs among yo-mg Venezuelans. (11) Daniel Lerner, 'Conflict and Consensus in Guayana,' focuses on hyp's articulated in Chpt (1) & elaborated in Chpt (2), & deals with Guayana's efforts to become a 'model industr town' & the fact that Guayana is populated mainly by recent migrants who have come to seek industr employment. (12) Jose A. Silva Michelena, 'Venutopia I: An Experimental Model of a National Polity,' describes in detail a computer model of the Venezuelan pol'al system, based on a method of numerical exp'tion; the procedures & problems of this method are discussed & the need for additional exp's is pointed out. Frank Bonilla & Jose A. Silva Michelena, 'Postface,' presents a summary of the Venezuelan situation & the problems examined in the book. It is concluded that COMM between soc sci'ts & policy-makers is made difficult by the fact that soc sci'ts are by training reluctant to speak or give judgments in the absence of certain kinds of information. Computer-aided data processing represents a major breakthrough by which soc sci'ts are now able to assist policy-makers in implementing soc change on the basis of empirical data. 12 Appendices attached to individual Chpt's. A joint Name & Subject Index. M. Maxfield.

title: SOCIOLOGY IN HOSPITAL CARE
abstract: A text which attempts to help hospital personnel to understand 'how staff are organized, what roles they play, & how they interact with one another & with patients in representative general hosp's' in 9 Chpt's, with an Introduction by E. L. Brown, & a Preface. (1) What This Book Is About: Hospitals and the People in Them-explains the perspective afforded by sociol & explores the need for sociol'al work in hosp's. (2) Culture and the Shape of Expectations and Facilities for Health-emphasizes the role cultural concepts play in the health field, reviews concepts of 'disease' that prevail in diff societies, & examines the way in which our cultural assumptions influence change in health practices. (3) Social Structure and the Network of Hospital Relationships-discusses the ways in which the structural soc reality influences the actions of people in hosp's, considers the sick role in terms of the larger society, & explores how patients can be helped to cooperate with practitioners of the healing arts.' (4) Observation: An Old Art and a New Skill-presents a brief course in sharpening observation. (5) Leadership and the Nursebrings together 'some of the diff approaches to leadership, emphasizing what the nurse can profitably consider for use as she functions in this important aspect of her changing role.' (6) Patients and Communication, by J. K. Skipperdiscusses barriers to COMM & the area of expressive COMM. (7) Problems of Work in a Bureaucracy-discusses the difficulties of the hospital admin'or, & those of volunteer workers Emphasis is placed on what hospital personnel can do to manage the problems generated by the bur'tic form. (8) Problems of the Professions in the Healing Arts-looks into some of the dilemmas of the nurse- 'ambivalence of patients, ambiguity of authority, struggles over rank between emerging professions,' etc. (9) Problems the Individual Faces in the Healing Arts-explores questions like 'How much should a patient be told? When do you tell the truth to a patient & to his fam? &, What can you say to a patient who knows he is dying?' A Joint name & subject Index. M. Duke.

title: GENDER AND BUREAUCRACY
abstract: A collection of 9 (unnumbered) essays, published as a Sociological Review Monograph, & presented in IV (unnumbered) PARTS, explores historical & contemporary debates concerning gender & bureaucracy. THEORETICAL INTRODUCTION - offers Anne Witz & Mike Savage -- The Gender of Organizations -- examines reasons why organization theory & feminist theory have begun to engage in dialogue, & argues that traditional conceptions of bureaucracy, including the Weberian one, have become outmoded with the development of new organizational structures. HISTORIES - contains Meta Zimmeck -- Marry in Haste, Repent at Leisure: Women, Bureaucracy and the Post Office, 1870-1920 -- demonstrates the way in which the development of modern organizations defined women as subordinate workers via an examination of the introduction of women into the US Post Office work force from 1870 to the present; Rosemary Crompton & Nicola Le Feuvre -- Gender and Bureaucracy: Women in Finance in Britain and France -- focuses on the use of women's labor in the finance sector to determine if those who have successfully pursued careers within banking have done so by becoming "surrogate" men; & Mike Savage -- Women's Expertise, Men's Authority: Gendered Organization and the Contemporary Middle Class -- draws on research on contemporary GB to rethink some of the implications of the increased numbers of middle-class women entering the work force, arguing that organizational hierarchies are central to understanding the processes of middle-class formation. STRATEGIES - offers Susan Halford -- Feminist Change in a Patriarchal Organization: The Experience of Women's Initiatives in Local Government and Implications for Feminist Perspectives on State Institutions -- argues that feminist perspectives that conceive the state as a functional tool in the service of patriarchal interests compromise understanding of local government, women's initiatives, & the relation between gender & the state in Western society; & Sophie Watson -- Femocratic Feminisms -- offers a comparison of British & Australian interventions in the politics of state, focusing on issues of power, discursive struggle, & the concept of "femocracy." THEORIES - presents Lisa Adkins -- Sexual Work and the Employment of Women in the Service Industries -- explores the factors that structure & modulate sexual relations in the labor market, showing that gendered employment relations contribute to the production of obligatory heterosexuality for women. Celia Davies -- Gender. History and Management Style in Nursing: Towards a Theoretical Synthesis -- offers an analysis of gender talk in nursing to show how it structures organizational relationships & affects issues of management style; & Karen Ramsay & Martin Parker -- Gender, Bureaucracy and Organizational Culture -- presents a critical assessment of Max Weber's treatment of bureaucracy, discusses the gendered nature of organizational culture, & argues that feminism needs to find nonbureaucratic ways of organizing. References are provided for each Chpt. 4 Tables, 4 Figures, 1 Appendix.

title: BUREAUCRACY AND MODERNIZATION: THE RUSSIAN AND SOVIET CASE
abstract: A discussion of the historical development of Russian pol'al bur'cy, particularly from the time of the Czars onward - esp as it may serve as a model for the newly developing nations. Historically, Russia has been characterized by autocratic rule, with few restraints; the burley began as an extension of the Prince's household, but Peter the Great separated the concepts of the ruler & the state. Even in Czarist Russia, the bur'cy took the leading role in the promotion of econ development; however, the Bolsheviks came to power promising a purge of the bur'cy. The new 'loyal' post-revolutionary burley assumed the task of aiding the process of modernization. This task proceeded via dictatorial & totalitarian means until the death of J. Stalin. Since then, admin'ive structures & practices have begun to be adjusted to the more mature & developed contemporary industrial economy; much more than Stalin, N. Krushchev has utilized the party bur'cy as a socially integrative force. However, it should not be assumed that totalitarian dictatorship & complex industrial society are fundamentally incompatible, esp since the Soviet pattern of econ development presents an attractive model for the newly developing nations; yet, it should be remembered that industrialization in Russia had begun long prior to the Bolsheviks' ascension to power. A frequent dilemma is that of the Soviet bur'crat who is faced with greater & greater production demands from his superiors, without the capacity to satisfy them; such pressures make the periodic admin'ive scandals endemic to the system. (See SA 0715-133371). D. W. Ball.

title: Tracing the Growth of Alienation: Enculturation, Socialization, and Schooling in a Democracy
abstract: Employs E. Erikson's (1950) theory of human development & the objective & subjective dimensions of alienation to trace tensions between decisions about education in a democratic society & how the system actually works, drawing on two case studies comprising regulation data & interviews with 1,459 students & 749 teachers in Jewish & Arab schools in Israel. It is found that the bureaucratic regulatory structure was an alienating setting in both contexts designed to discourage participation. Further, the regulations are taken to challenge students in such a way as to foster trust, industry, & role identity, thus cultivating obedience & passivity, rather than autonomy or initiative. This process is interpreted as fitting naturally in a larger social system that favors passive, obedient workers & citizens. Students are found to ignore the regulations by constructing a world of mutual involvement & intimacy. On the basis of these findings, it is argued that any serious examination of alienation in modern society must consider the preparation for adult life embedded in the structures of the educational system. D. M. Smith

title: Usurpers or Pioneers? European Commission Bureaucrats and the Question of 'European Consciousness'
abstract: Explores the image & self-image of European Community (EC) bureaucrats & their relevance for debates about European consciousness, drawing on ethnographic observations & case studies of EC initiatives to promote the European idea. To create European consciousness, EC officials have taken the lead in the integration process, particularly in their use of media technologies & cultural symbols. Their stress on sociocultural aspects of integration, eg, efforts to invent European traditions, use information & public relations to disseminate these traditions, & create European statistics & measurements, demonstrates the technocratic goal of functionalist strategies. Anthropologists should focus on conceptions of consciousness & how they are embraced by particular groups or individuals rather than assuming monolithic definitions of the term. Thus, anthropologists are encouraged to approach consciousness as a social fact rather than an individual attribute. 56 References. D. M. Smith

title: City, Region, and In Between: New York City's Water Supply and the Insights of Regional History
abstract: Urban historians have greatly expanded their geographical purview in recent years, incorporating suburbs and hinterlands into their analysis of social and environmental change. Urban environmental historians and suburban historians have played a critical role in the regionalization of urban history over the last decade. This case study of the development of New York City's water supply reveals the benefits of taking a regional approach to urban history. From the New York Public Library to Central Park's Great Lawn to neighborhood parks, the New York City landscape bears the traces of the continuous development of the city's water network. Expansion of the water system in rural hinterlands enabled municipal officials to put urban reservoirs to new uses, creating some of the city's most beloved public spaces. The rehabilitation of urban infrastructure underscores the intimate linkages between rural development and the urban built environment. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright holder.]

title: Sanitary services and decision making in Houston, 1876-1945
abstract: In the late 19th century and early 20th century, city leaders in Houston had responded promptly to perceived community needs for a safe and plentiful water supply, an effective sewer system and practical solid waste disposal facilities, although services were not always delivered equitably.  By the 1940s, however, Houston's environmental infrastructure faltered, deficient in scale and kind to keep pace with the city's rapid expansion.

title: Bureaucratic Erasure: Identity, Resistance and Violence -- Aborigines and a Discourse of Autonomy in a North Queensland Town
abstract: Explores the nature of identity as a process integral to contemporary bureaucratic orders & political power of modern states in the context of events that occurred in 1990 in the town of Mossman, Northern Queensland, Australia. It is observed that for whites in Mossman, local Aborigines represent the alienating & destructive potentiality of state & bureaucratic power. At a local town meeting convened in Mar 1990 in response to recent governmental changes in the area, it is shown that whites tended to frame personal agency & identity in opposition to the state bureaucratic regime, while Aborigines capitalized on perceived victimhood to assert rhetorical power. It is noted that, paradoxically, Aborigines enter the state & achieve power in it as citizens by virtue of their victim status. Thus, central to the disembodied abstraction of the bureaucratic order is the construction of Aborigines as a category against which to measure the progress of dominant realities & to express resistance. It is concluded that Aborigines are threatened with reimprisonment in identity categories that make them the focus of contradictions they may be powerless to overcome. 17 References. D. M. Smith

title: The Figures behind Facts: Photo-eliciting Infrastructural Consequences in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania
authors: Thunqvist, Eva-Lotta; Ilskog, Elisabeth; Mvungi, Abu
abstract: Access to affordable infrastructure services is necessary for sustainable development and poverty eradication, and provides major benefits in the area of health, literacy, and equity. In this study, the qualitative method of participant-driven photo-eliciting (PDPE) was used to investigate the access of infrastructural services for female-headed household groups in the informal settlement of Vingunguti in Dar es Salaam. Almost all the informants called water scarcity a critical issue that heavily affected their livelihood due to limited services and poor quality. There was a vast seasonal variation in the quality and quantity of water: The rainy season led to flooding in the area, and the water was prone to contamination by waste and sewage from pit latrines and the sewage dam; the dry season, on the other hand, was characterized by shortage of water. In the discussion that followed, the informants blamed the outbreak of various diseases in the settlement on the limited quantity of water, and its contamination. Photo-eliciting also tended to feature more informed participants by encouraging the informants to talk more exhaustively than while answering interview questions. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities on the Use of Languages in Relations with the Public Administration, and on the Supervision and Enforcement of Linguistic Requirements
abstract: Linguistic rights and their implications for societal cohesion and state stability, have been recognized as a core component in the conflict prevention work of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe High Commissioner on National Minorities (OSCE HCNM). Linguistic and associated rights proved a challenge in many OSCE Participating States, and the HCNM repeatedly advised the relevant authorities on how to secure a fair balance between the promotion of the state language and the protection of linguistic minority rights. This article overviews the advice which the successive HCNMs have throughout the years put forward on two key areas touching upon the linguistic rights of national minorities - namely, the use of languages in relations with the public administration, and the supervision and enforcement of linguistic requirements - and analyses how this advice aligns with the recommendations put forward by other international actors and institutions working on minority rights and minority issues.

title: Book reviews -- The Changing Organisation and Management of Local Government by S. Leach, J. Stewart and K. Walsh
abstract: Review.

title: Subverting Social Policy on the Front Line: Agencies of Resistance in the Delivery of Services
abstract: An understanding of policy implementation issues in many of the core fields of social policy requires attention to the mode of service delivery that is characteristic of those fields: face-to-face interaction between frontline service staff and service users. A focus on implementation as interaction between these groups reveals the significance of 'agency' to the analysis of why and how certain social policy outcomes occur - and in particular why outcomes may sometimes be different from those anticipated by formal policy objectives. This article considers how the agency of workers and users shapes the processes of mediation, negotiation and adaptation that occur in different service delivery contexts, and identifies ways in which resistance to intended policy outcomes, and to the practices expected to deliver them, is formed and expressed. Drawing on a wide range of empirical research material, the article shows how agencies of resistance produce outcomes that are uncertain, fragile and contested, and whose effect can be the subversion of formal policy intentions. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Court Culture and State Science
abstract: This article aims to propose a hypothesis regarding the links between knowledge & power in the 14th century, during an epoch when the beginnings of western political science, the rapid development of state administrations based on intellectual competences, & the emergence of humanism can be observed. In order to understand the relationships between these developments, their common birth place at the royal court must be studied. At the courts of the 14th century, intellectual groups faced each other such as lawyers, philosophers, humanists, & astrologers, each attempting to impose a legitimate concept to the state science. Their rivalry was not only theoretical: these men that theorized power were also adept at administrative practices; consequently, the discourse of each social group is set in its place within the curial system. Overall, these conflicts are at the origin of state science: from the point of view of the prince the different discourses & competences must be integrated into the practice of power.
