The whole field of knowledge is therefore reorganized according to its relationship with power, whose curialization represents a decisive step in western history. Adapted from the source document.

title: Ecology in Public Health
abstract: After the turn of the l9th-20th century even in Hungary more & more emphasis has been laid on the connection between the natural or built environment & the health situation. Health experts started to deal with the questions of canalization, water-supply, disposal of sewage, etc. Improving the infrastructure became partly a health issue. Between the two world wars significant progress has been made: the state got more concerned & involved that resulted on one hand, in the implementation of professional solutions & on the other hand, appropriate financial resources for such developments. 1 Table, 1 Figure, 69 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Exploring women's employment in tourism under state socialism: Experiences of tourism work in socialist Romania
authors: Dumbraveanu, Daniela; Light, Duncan; Young, Craig; Chapman, Anya
abstract: Recent academic debate into women's experiences of tourism employment has emphasised the extremely heterogeneous nature of such work and the need for sensitivity to local political, economic, social and cultural contexts. This article focuses on one such context which has received little attention - state socialism - and we explore women's experiences of tourism work in socialist Romania. Such work had characteristics in common with non-socialist contexts, but in other ways took a form which was distinctive to the socialist state. It was characterised by extensive training, good pay and opportunities for promotion (at least to middle management level). The socialist state also devised unique solutions to the problem of the seasonality of tourism work. However, women also faced extensive surveillance by the state's security services and faced harsh penalties for under-performance.

title: Reforming the staffing process in the European Union institutions: moving the sacred cow out of the road
abstract: Since the 1960s, the EU institutions have relied on a system of open competitions (or concours ) for hiring staff, with only incremental changes. That system is now undergoing a major reform that is currently in the implementation phase. A policy analysis approach explains how the leadership of the European Personnel Selection Office (EPSO) overcame resistance to change. Analysis from a public management and political sociology perspective sheds light on the challenges EPSO faces in the implementation and evaluation of the reform.Points for practitionersOne strength of the EU staffing model is the active role of EU staff in selecting their peers through the use of Selection Boards. The new system maintains staff involvement while professionalizing the Selection Boards. The reform was responsive to complaints by managers and heads of EU institutions with a slow, complex, and antiquated system, and it is they, as key clients, who will ultimately evaluate the effectiveness of the reform in enabling them to hire top-quality staff more quickly.

title: Functions and Spatial Structures of Local Utility Systems
abstract: Common to public infrastructure systems is that they supply populated areas with basic services largely by means of networks (power, heating, water, telecommunications) and dispose of what is no longer needed (sewage, waste). Another commonality is high path-dependency. They differ, however, in technical and operational boundary conditions. The functions and spatial structures of supply and disposal systems are currently undergoing major changes. This raises the question what general interest services local authorities really have to provide in future.

title: The Visibility of Social Systems
abstract: Examines the development of social systems, drawing on the Foucauldian notions of "visibility" & "gaze" to explore the privileging the visualization of perception wherein the labor of divisions allows greater control over the social & material world by way of enhanced clarity, transparency, & visual certainty from a distance. Discussion opens with a consideration of the 16th-century emergence of the hospital system & medical examination & the manner in which early schools, via weekly examinations, became an apparatus for similar surveillance. Jeremy Bentham's architectural concept of the Panopticon, Foucault's gaze writ large, is then evoked, maintaining that it exemplified the role of surveillance in the construction & maintenance of visibility. After delineating Foucault's three ways in which the examination promotes visibility while linking the latter to knowledge & power, some space is given to Hoskin & Macve's (1986) history of accounting as developing from the technology of the examination, which showed accounting's power to generate a specific form of knowledge that subjects individuals to a "fixed & determinate visibility." This is seen to be an example of the development of "knowledge-power" via professionalization; professions are groups tasked with creating & maintaining the appropriate "visibility" of social agents through techniques like the examination. Goldstein's (1984) four criteria of a profession are cited, along with Frug's (1984) analysis linking professionalism to bureaucratic legitimation, which utilizes Derrida's idea of interaction. The process of making bureaucratic structures clear & legible results in an intertwining of objectivity & subjectivity that undermines the "transparent or obvious features of bureaucratic logic," which makes either hard to see for the lack of division between the two; thus, a fiction of objectivity is created. Weinstein & Weinstein (1984) address the possibility that this fiction is vision based in an analysis of the visual constitution of society centered on the Foucauldian gaze, which objectifies the social world. This objectifying gaze, ie, disciplined vision, has diffused into unexpected institutions, asserted to be a defining characteristic of modern society; the example of I. A. Richards's professionalization of Anglo American literary criticism illustrates. Two key functions of the analysis of knowledge-power & the labor of division in social systems are noted in closing. 16 References. J. Zendejas

title: THE SELF-DEFEATING ORGANIZATION: A CRITIQUE OF BUREAUCRACY
abstract: A critical analysis of bureaucracy as an organizational form, in 9 Chpts with an Introduction by the author. The book views bureaucracy as more & more historically obsolete due to its conflict with the modern reality, shaped by sophisticated technology, the growing educational level of the LF, the need for organizational flexibility, & the demand for work humanization. The Introduction explains how the book originated, ie, based on personal experience as an organizational instructor of workers' productive co-ops in eastern Europe in the late 1940s. (1) A Socio-Organizational Challenge for the West -- reviews the problematic situations in which Western developed societies are involved. Although moral cohesion is much needed, the traditional spiritual institutions cannot meet the actual demand; the reform of social organization, including the workplace, is needed. (2) Vulnerable Structures -- discusses how much structuralization is actually needed in the organizational micro- as well as macrostructures. Overstructuralization demotivates people & leads to the malutilization of the human potential; minimalization & flexibility of structures are advocated. (3) Organizational Opening to New Technologies -- reviews the adaptational problems people face in implementing modern technology, especially computer systems. The informational revolution is quite often misunderstood; the social aspects of human engineering need more attention. (4) A Perspective on Work Cooperation -- see SA 31:5/83N4267. (5) The Swedish Case -- reviews the general findings on participation & sociotechnical solutions in Swedish plants, presenting examples of successful sociotechnical change. (6) Professional Ethics and Bureaucracy: The Case of Sociologists -- examines the employment problems of social scientists, particularly sociologists, in both the West & the East, based on personal experience, ie, in Poland until 1968 & since then, employed in Canada & other countries. The point is made that even in a democratic academic setting, there is a danger of bureaucratization spoiling the professional ethics of sociologists. (7) Obsolescence of Bureaucracy -- reviews the contradictory forces inside bureaucratic structures. Mediocre people gain power over innovators by dominating the organizational controls & using them for their own benefit. Such "victory" is actually self-defeating, however, because any structure unable to innovate will not long survive. It is suggested that suicidal tendencies in Western civilized nations are correlated with the overgrowth of bureaucracy. (8) The Discontents of Mass Society -- reviews problems occurring in modern Western societies as a result of the leisure orientation promoted by the mass media & advertising. This orientation contradicts the traditional work ethic, on which Western business is still based. The organizational dilemmas of modern business must be considered from a joint work/leisure perspective. (9) Towards "Mature" Systems? -- see SA 32:1/84N7241 & 25:2/77I4616.

title: Dignity as (Self-)Determination: Hopi Sovereignty in the Face of US Dispossessions
abstract: In 2013, the Arizona Snowbowl Ski Resort began spraying artificial snow made from reclaimed wastewater on Arizona's highest peak, a place the Hopi people call Nuvatukya'ovi, "Snow-on-top-of-it." As one of the Hopis' most sacred places, the home of the katsinam and the southwestern boundary marker of their aboriginal territory, the Hopi have fought for decades to stop development of the ski resort, which today sits on US Forest Service land. Viewing the history of this dispute through the lens of Atuahene's notion of a "dignity taking," this article argues that despite never having been relocated, the indignities that the Hopi have suffered by US dispossessions of much of their aboriginal territory are the product of a series of bureaucratic sleights of hand that only bear the mark of legality if one ignores history and denies the enduring right to self-determination and sovereignty that Hopi have continuously claimed with regard to the totality of their aboriginal land.

title: Culture and Justice
abstract: Invoking Zygmunt Bauman's acute exposition of a left-critical hesitation between intellectuals as saviours and intellectuals as oppressors, this essay argues that while Bauman reveals this hesitation as crucial and symptomatic, nevertheless he leaves it unresolved. The essay shows how the human nature/ culture distinction (which is also a continuity) is, in fact, constitutive of human culture as such; moreover, the essay argues that this constitutive distinction reproduces itself within culture in terms of reciprocal hierarchies of social division -- intellectual/non-intellectual, shamanistic/folk, aristocratic/popular. This pattern of vertical reciprocity is precisely what the purely horizontal axis of capitalist-bureaucratic liberalism excludes, collapsing the hierarchical axis of political culture into the horizontal false-binary of 'left' versus 'right'. In this way the essay argues that the crux of an authentic resistance to capitalist-bureaucratic liberalism will involve not a triumph of the 'left' over the 'right' , but the retrieval of the dynamic paradox of the vertical axis of the hierarchical communion of guiding excellence fused with popular spontaneity. The hierarchical yet dynamically educative interplay between innovators and those being constantly innovated is the organic root of human culture and the means of the authentic practice of human justice.

title: Do state growth management regulations reduce sprawl?
abstract: Thirteen states in the United States have adopted state growth management legislation that aims to preserve environmentally sensitive areas, improve the quality of urban areas, and reduce urban sprawl. Although there is a considerable amount of literature describing such policies, there is very little that examines the effectiveness of such policies. The author researched the efficacy of state growth management laws in controlling urban sprawl by examining the change in urban densities in 49 states over a 15-year period. He found that growth-managed states generally experienced a lesser density decline than states without growth management. However, regression analysis revealed that state growth management programs did not have a statistically significant effect in checking sprawl. The author concludes with several suggestions for modifying state regulations to curb sprawl more effectively. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: CHINESE CIVILIZATION AND BUREAUCRACY
abstract: A collection of essays composed over a 30-yr period concerned with certain major themes in Chinese history in III Parts, 16 Chpts, a Preface by John K. Fairbank & Arthur F. Wright, & an Introduction by Arthur F. Wright. I-INSTITUTIONS- presents: (1) Significant Aspects of Chinese Society-which identifies enduring influences on Chinese development; (2) China as a Permanently Bureaucratic Society-explores conservative factors such as an agrarian economy, a powerful mandarinate, secret police atmosphere, & principles of collective responsibility; (3) Chinese Feudalism-asks & answers the question, Does Chinese feudalism contain the seeds of capitalism? (4) The Birth of Capitalism in China-asks why, despite favorable conditions, this phenomenon failed to arise before exposure to the West? Or, did it?; (5) Fairs in China-attempts to distinguish fairs from markets, although no diff'iation exists in the Chinese language; (6) Chinese Towns-examines the Chinese town, which had no Ur class comparable to the Western bourgeoisie; (7) Marco Polo in the Capital of China-recreates the forces which shaped the Chinese empire just before the Venetian's visit & the sights which greeted his eyes; (8) Evolution of Landownership in Fourth-and Fifth-Century China-indicates that when the formation of large estates threatened the free peasant to servitude voices were raised for the revival of the Ching-T'ien land reform, & (9) Landownership in China from the Fourth to the Fourtheenth Century-maintains that equal distribution of land was a fiction, & all attempts at reform were ineffective. Free peasants were in fact no more than tenant farmers for the large estates. II-HISTORY-examines: (10) History as a Guide to Bureaucratic Practice-which states that 3 factors have prevented the development of Western historiography in China: (a) fragmentation by dynasty; (b) dependent status of historians; & (c) the traditional art of using quoted passages; (11) Tradition and Revolution in China-opposes the concept of China as a sleeping dragon, exploding in the 20th cent after 3,000 dormant yrs. III- TOUGHT-presents: (12) Two Songs by Ts'ao Ts'ao; (13) Political Philosophy and Social Crisis at the End of the Han Dynastywhich studies the impoverishment & refeudalization of society, the eruption of the barbarians, & a profound religious feeling that had never before existed; (14) Nihilistic Revolt or Mystical Escapism-examines the currents of Chinese thought during the 3rd cent AD; (15) The First Chinese Materialist-discusses the Chinese bur'cy's attack on Buddhism as antisoc, unproductive, & parasitical. The career of Fan Chen, author of the materialist tract Shen-mieh lun, is traced; & (16) A Forerunner of Wang An-shih-analyzes the philosophy of the pol'al reformer Li Kon. Chronology: China from 500 BC-1949. A name & subject Index. M. Duke.

title: YESTERDAY S RULERS, THE MAKING OF THE BRITISH COLONIAL SERVICE
abstract: A Vol in 8 Chpts, a Foreword by Sir John Macpherson, & an Introduction by Margery Perham, describing the growth of the British Colonial Service from before WWI until after WWII. (1) Before 1914-defines the geographical limits of the study-the British 'Colonial Empire' to the exclusion of India & the 'White Dominions'-& traces the operations of the unreformed colonial service. (2) Years of Construction-describes the reforming efforts in the 1920's by Major Sir Ralph Furse, the man chiefly responsible for the selection of the colonial officials. (3) Brief Limelight-presents his proposals to the Fisher Commission of 1929, which were accepted. (4) The Public Schools-gives a description of these English private Sch's which Furse chose as the best recruiting ground for future officials. (5) Oxford-gives an account of the Tropical Admin'ive Services (renamed Colonial Admin'ive Services in 1933) which Furse organized in Oxford & Cambridge U's, esp the former. (6) For a New Age-outlines the efforts centering in the Devonshire Committee to prepare the British Colonial Service for the changed conditions after WWII. (7) A New Service-describes the re-organized Colonial Service, still recruited on Furse's recommendations from Oxford & Cambridge, with London U added. (8) Retrospect-offers the author's conclusion. Disagreeing with the claim of the last British governor of Cyprus that Britain left behind 'the conception of an impartial & dedicated public service,' he says: 'The colonial service has left behind not dedicated & impartial admin'ors-these are British concepts & therefore inappropriate-but capable ones. That is the enduring monument to the colonial service.' I. Langnas.

title: Thinking about think tanks in health care: a call for a new research agenda
authors: Shaw, Sara E; Russell, Jill; Greenhalgh, Trisha; Korica, Maja
abstract: Little sociological attention has been given to the role of think tanks in health policy and planning. Existing work in political science and public administration tends to define and categorise think tanks and situate them as a disinterested source of policy expertise. Despite the increasingly visible presence of think tanks in the world of health care, such work has done little to reveal how they operate, by whom and to what ends. Our article seeks to redress this firstly by examining why they have remained relatively hidden in academic analyses and secondly by advocating an interpretive approach that incorporates think tanks within the wider landscape of health policy and planning. In contrast to most existing literature, an interpretive approach acknowledges that much of the messy business of healthcare policy and planning remains hidden from view and that much can be gleaned by examining the range of organisations, actors, coalitions, everyday activities, artefacts and interactions that make up the think tank stage and that work together to shape health policy and planning. Given the paucity of research in this area, we urge the medical sociology community to open the field to further academic scrutiny.   [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Impressions of North Korea
abstract: The tribunal also heard from a bevy of experts who brought forth well-documented details of US aggression against the DPRK. Professor Oh Il-Son of Kim Il-sung University clarified the details of US economic warfare over the past 50 years. Although forbidden by the Armistice Agreement of 1953, the US has nonetheless imposed an economic blockade that has crippled the North's economy. Other countries, especially Japan, have been persuaded to join the effort to isolate and impoverish the DPRK. Although the agreements of 1953 and 1974 banned economic sanctions, even international law has not stopped the US from constraining DPRK trade, financial transactions and almost all areas of its economy. Beginning with the Trading with the Enemy Act and Export Administration Act of 1950 through the Foreign Assistance Act of 1975 and the Export Banking Act of 1988 (forbidding loans to North Korea), the US has continually sought to break the North Korean system. Altogether more than 100,000 articles have been banned by the US from being exported to North Korea. Airplanes, trucks, computers, semi-conductors are all included in the ban as are cosmetics, face powder and bicycles. Although the Clinton administration took steps to lift the sanctions, Bush & Co. have sternly reinforced them. Today, finance, trade, fixed investments, transportation and postage--all branches of the economy--are subject to US restrictions. The direct cumulative effects of US economic warfare were estimated to be in the hundreds of billions of dollars. Indirectly, when one factors in the continual US military threats and the necessary defense expenditures of the DPRK, the US has bullied a small country into economic crisis--and then mobilized the international mass media to blame the victim. Whether or not the leadership of the DPRK has made mistakes in economic management, the cumulative effects of more than half a century of US economic warfare have been devastating.Sadly, few Americans understand the pain our government inflicts upon Korean people--that it has done so since 1945--and that it continues to threaten the people of the DPRK with genocide. Since the armistice of 1953, US aggression has continued unabated. From 1976 to 1993, "Operation Team Spirit" threatened invasion and nuclear war on the DPRK. According to the DPRK, every day US planes capable of dropping nuclear weapons approach the 38th parallel and, at the last minute, veer off. For people in the DPRK, the possibility of a US nuclear attack has thus been a daily reality for decades. In the 1980s and 1990s, North Korea reports that there were more than 7900 provocative acts per year, and the US admits to daily high-altitude surveillance flights over North Korea. Over the years since the armistice, at least ten US planes, including an EC 121 spy plane, have been shot down by the DPRK. In March 2003, the US deployed a dozen B-52 bombers and an equal number of B-1's to the US Pacific territory of Guam, within range of the DPRK.The long history of US nuclear threats against the DPRK is an ominous sign of what may happen in the future. Beginning with General [Douglas MacArthur]'s resolve during the war to detonate nuclear weapons along the Chinese border to create a zone of death, through Eisenhower's decision to use nuclear weapons in 1953, 7 the US has been poised to devastate the DPRK. "Honest John" nuclear artillery was brought to South Korea in 1957 and when the neutron bomb was developed, it was deployed in Korea. In the early 1990s, Operation Team Spirit was suspended, but other nuclear war exercises occurred. Today, the US has a "don't ask don't tell" policy as to whether it has nuclear weapons in South Korea. To be sure, dozens--some say hundreds--of nuclear weapons are on US ships and planes within range of the DPRK.

title: Governance in gridlock in the Russian health system; the case of Sverdlovsk oblast
abstract: Epidemiological, demographic and environmental crises, transition to a new political regime and exceptionally severe economic crises were powerful stimuli to health sector reform in Russia. The Russian Federation responded by introducing medical insurance whilst decentralising public administration. Yet despite intense contextual pressures to do so and a new policy climate, Russian hospitals found it difficult to reprofile services and reallocate their resources. A case study analysing governance structures in Sverdlovsk oblast reveals that medical insurance created incentives to reduce costs by reducing bed-days, but if hospitals did so they would lose money under the formulae through which decentralised local government still allocated around three-quarters of hospital income. If instead hospitals tried to increase budgetary income by increasing numbers of bed-days, the insurance system would penalise them. This specific form of policy mess can be called 'governance in gridlock'. The juxtaposition of two overlapping but incompatible sets of governance structures practically immobilised official hospital management systems. It is as one-sided to blame residues of the Soviet system for this gridlock as it is to blame the medical insurance system. Gridlock resulted from the interaction of the two, a problem to which all health system reform is potentially vulnerable.  [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: THE IMPACT OF UNEMPLOYMENT ON WELFARE EXPENDITURES
abstract: A STUDY WAS CONDUCTED, BASED ON ECONOMETRIC ANALYSES, TO DETERMINE THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE UNEMPLOYMENT LEVEL AND NUMBER OF PEOPLE RECEIVING AID TO FAMILIES WITH DEPENDENT CHILDREN.  SOME PREVIOUS STUDIES SHOW THAT A NEGATIVE CORRELATION EXISTS, BUT THERE ARE CIRCUMSTANCES WHICH INDICATE THAT THIS IS NOT THE CASE.  THE WELFARE SYSTEM IS MODELED BY 2 EQUATIONS.  THE FIRST SHOWS DEMAND IN TERMS OF ACTUAL AND POTENTIAL WELFARE RECIPIENTS.  THE SECOND DEPICTS THE ADMINISTRATION, INCLUDING BUDGETARY ADJUSTMENTS FOR DEMAND AND ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS.  THE RESULTS OF THE STUDY SHOW THAT THERE IS A DEFINITE INCREASE IN THE NUMBER OF WELFARE RECIPIENTS AS THE UNEMPLOYMENT LEVEL INCREASES.  GOVERNMENT POLICYMAKERS SHOULD BE AWARE OF THIS RELATIONSHIP AS THEY ADJUST PRICE/WAGE FACTORS TO CONTROL INFLATION.  THE TYPICAL EFFECT OF INCREASED UNEMPLOYMENT IS AN EXPANSION IN THE WELFARE BUDGET.  GRAPHS.  TABLES.  FORMULAS.

title: Administrative and Policy Issues in Reimbursement for Nursing Home Capital Investment
authors: Boerstler, Heidi; Carlough, Tom; Schlenker, Robert E
abstract: The ways in which capital costs are reimbursed by state Medicaid programs can have adverse consequences for patient care.  An innovative system known as fair-rental reimbursement uses replacement cost to determine the nursing home's capital value, which is then used as the basis for payment of a fee for capital, called an imputed fair-rental amount.  The 2 base methods under the fair-rental approach for applying the rate selected by the state to the rate base for determining the rental payment are the gross-rental approach and the net-rental approach.  Overall, these 2 systems are more similar than different.  The analysis suggests that fair-rental systems may be superior to traditional cost-based reimbursement in promoting and controlling industry stability, while at the same time providing an adequate return to investors without incurring long-term increases in the costs of administering programs.

title: MASS SOCIETY, PLURALISM, AND BUREAUCRACY: EXPLICATION, ASSESSMENT, AND COMMENTARY
abstract: Three major social theories -- mass society, pluralism, & bureaucracy -- are often employed to interpret & explain modern societies. Although frequently invoked, the theories themselves are poorly understood. This book seeks to clarify the background, context, & major arguments of the theories, assess the claims & validity of each, provide expert commentary, & suggest avenues for further work in each area. Drawing on work in the humanities, history, sociology, economic history, & political science, Hamilton is able to provide readers with a clear, concise, & accurate overview of the adequacy of these theories as well as their empirical validity. A systematic empirical assessment of the major tenets & abundant shortcomings of mass society theory does not support its validity. More support is found for pluralism, although a more realistic & partitive reading of the theory is suggested. Finally, while the image of an all-pervasive & growing bureaucracy seems to overwhelm society, it is argued that the theory seriously misrepresents the character of modern life. Each theory is assessed using an integrated approach, &, for each, suggestions are proffered for which elements of the theory should be retained, reworked, or discarded altogether. Bibliog, 1 Appendix. Adapted from the source document.

title: Is China's e-governance sustainable? Testing Solow IT productivity paradox in China's context
abstract: The role of technology in economic development and productivity change has always been an important issue, and it is also a debated topic that whether the ICT (information and communication technology) succeeded in promoting the productivity or not, thus proposing a famous notion of "Solow paradox". If the ICT could drive the productivity, we could state that the e-governance management of Chinese government is sustainable. By using the SBM and super SBM method, this article measures the regional efficiency and productivity in China, and then conducts an empirical investigation to examine whether the Solow paradox applies in China or not. We found that in recent two decades, the regional disparity of productivity has been widening accompanied with the bigger wealth gap between the east and the central, west regions. ICT may contribute to the widen discrepancy of productivity in part, and the west region has outperformed the central region in both catch up effect and frontier shift, which means that the productivity gap between central and west region has been narrowed. The empirical results also show that the ICT has a negative impact on the regional productivity in China, while for the east region, the negative impact can be basically ignored, while the central and the west region are negatively affected. This result may indicate that with a higher development level, the current period negative impact of ICT on productivity will be lessened and maybe converted to positive impact in the future.

title: COMPLEX ORGANIZATIONS: A SOCIOLOGICAL READER
abstract: A reader defining org's a la Parsons as 'soc units which are predominantly oriented to the attainment of specific goals' - in 7 Chpts with Ed's comments for each. (1) TOWARD A THEORY OF ORGANIZATION -reprints Max Weber on `The Three Types of Legitimate Rule', Chester I. Barnard on `Organizations as Systems of Cooperation', Philip Selznick on `Foundations of the Theory of Organization', T. Parsons (See SA 3096), Robert K. Merton (See SA 6037), J. G. March & H. A. Simon (See SA 6963), A. W. Gouldner (See SA 3351), &, Terence K. Hopkins on `Bureaucratic Authority: The Convergence of Weber and Barnard' wherein the concepts of authority, legitimation, org'al status, etc, of both authors are seen to be closer than previously perceived, which results in a new base for a general theory of bur'tic authority. (2) ORGANIZATIONAL THEORY APPLIED -reprints William F. Whyte on `Human Relations -A Progress Report', Reinhard Bendix & Lloyd H. Fisher on `The Perspectives of Elton Mayo', G. C. Homans on `Some Corrections to 'The Perspectives of Elton Mayo", & the Ed (See SA 8350). (3) ORGANIZATIONAL GOALS -presents D. L. Sills (See SA 8845), B. R. Clark (See SA 3359), D. R. Cressey (See SA 6294), &, J. D. Thompson & W. J. McEwen (See SA 5556). (4) ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE- reprints G. M. Sykes (See SA 3469), M. Janowitz (See SA 6961), Melville Dalton on `Conflict Between Staff and Line Managerial Officers', Harold L. Wilensky on `The Trade Union as a Bureaucracy', Alfred H. Stanton & Morris S. Schwartz on `The Mental Hospital and the Patient', Howard S. Becker on `The Teacher in the Authority System of the Public School', &, H. Becker `Four Types of Religious Organizations'. (5) ORGANIZATION AND SOCIETY- presents Seymour M. Lipset on `Bureaucracy and Social Reform', S. N. Eisenstadt on `Bureaucracy, Bureaucratization, and Debureaucratization', Morris Janowitz, Deil Wright & William Delany on `Public Administration and the Public', R. Dubin (See SA 6871), Peter H. Rossi on `The Organizational Structure of an American Community' finds that business corporations & voluntary assn's are the 2 major local branches of nat org's & their interactions determine to a large extent the policy of the community's pol'al bodies. Business leaders seem more interested in their own pol'al, soc, & prestige needs than being concerned with the kind of image their corporation creates in the eyes of their clients, workers, etc. Erving Goffman's `The Characteristics of Total Institutions' presents a description & analysis of 'a soc hybrid [org] : part residential community & part formal org'. (6) ORGANIZATIONAL CHANGE -presents Peter M. Blau on `The Dynamics of Bureaucracy', Philip Selznick on `Critical Decisions in Organizational Development', Bernard Levenson in 'Bureaucratic Succession' shows that the flow of personnel, the ways in which people leave an org, & the channels & media by which new employees are recruited, invariably exert an influence on the soc structure of the org. Richard H. McCleery describes `Policy Change in Prison Management', & Allen H. Barton & Bo Anderson in `Change in an Organizational System: Formalization of a Qualitative Study', analyze the McCleery study methodologically & construct a bridge between the qualitative & quantitative methods, & show how one would go about conducting the same study using quantitative methods, & finally formalizing McCleery's theory through mathematical models. (7) METHODS FOR THE STUDY OF ORGANIZATION - presents Paul F. Lazarsfeld & Herbert Menzel in `On the Relation between Individual and Collective Properties', define analytic, relational, comparative, contextual, etc, properties of `collectives' & `members' thus helping to differentiate & determine the nature of various types of propositions dealt with in org'al analysis. James S. Coleman discusses 'Rational Analysis: The Study of Social Organizations with Survey Methods'. Robert S. Weiss & Eugene Jacobson (See SA 2461), Morris Zelditch, Jr & Terence K. Hopkins in `Laboratory Experiments with Organizations' discuss how the properties of org's prevent their being constructed in the laboratory, & detail the ways in which various types of exp's are relevant to org'al theory; & Arthur L. Stinchcombe writes `On the Use of Matrix Algebra in the Analysis of Formal Organization'. A separate name & subject index.

title: PATTERNS OF INDUSTRIAL BUREAUCRACY
abstract: An analytical treatment of industrial bureaucracy, integrated with an empirical study of a work plant in its community setting. Bureaucratization, rather than an undifferentiated process, is found to be composed of 3 distinct tendencies: (1) the 'mock-bureaucratic' pattern, formal rules, neither enforced nor obeyed; (2) the 'representative bureaucratic' pattern, rules enforced and obeyed; and, (3) 'punishment-centered' bureaucracy, in which efforts at enforcement are made by management, and persistent resistance among workers is encountered. Sources of data included interviews (partially non-directive), observations and documentary material. The book is divided into 4 parts. I describes the plant, its community setting and the 'indulgency pattern' in supervisory relations. II is concerned with the succession of new local management and its effects. III deals with organization, worker's beliefs, and motivation of management and workers. IV analyzes the bureaucratic patterns in terms of the data from this plant. An appendix describes field work procedures. E. Scott.

title: BUREAUCRATS AND POLITICAL DEVELOPMENT: A PARADOXICAL VIEW
abstract: The existence & self-interest of gov'al bur's affects other pol'al structures. In transitional societies the burcy's growth & power contrasts with the relative weakness of the non-bur' tic pol'al instit's. In these developing nations bur'tic growth has occurred within a context of other pol'al structures which have not evinced similar change. '...too rapid expansion of the bur'cy when the pol'al system lags behind tends to inhibit the development of effective pol.' The bur'cy vitiates nascent pol'al parties through the merit system's reduction or elimination of potential spoils. Without this traditional source of rewards, parties can appeal only to a narrow base of committed ideologies. Additionally, a centralized bur'cy reduces the opportunity for the politicizing functions of participation at the local level. What interest groups & assoc's there are, exist via bur'tic rather than popular initiative. Capital is exploited through corruption-ridden regulation, esp since most bur'crats are under-paid. Often legislation merely ratifies bur'ly determined policy, rather than initiating it. Further bur's have exploited the judicial process as a result of their superior knowledge to give spurious legality to their actions. Even the executive branch finds itself subject to the bur'cy in an inversion of the classic relationship. US foreign policy has often shortsightedly aided in the growth of these bur's in transitional societies with the above resultant effects, inimical to actual long range goals. (See SA 0715-B3371). D. W. Ball.

title: Citizenship and Modernity in Soweto
abstract: Under apartheid in South Africa, the Soweto population was denied or restricted from modern urban technologies in the separate development path. Since 1995, their responses to the introduction of new technologies have been enigmatic & contradictory. To understand these responses, the Cultural Studies Research Program at Vista U, described here, was tasked with exploring the relationship between citizens & local government in Soweto. Their research reveals that the citizens & local bureaucrats appear to have different understandings of responsibility, responsiveness, & the new social formation. The research hypothesis that technocratic forms of government may be compatible with mass democracy & popular sovereignty is discussed in the context of the local government's delivery of services & their confiscation of possessions when services are not paid for. M. Pflum

title: THE POLITICAL FORMS OF MODERN SOCIETY: BUREAUCRACY, DEMOCRACY, TOTALITARIANISM
abstract: A translation & republication of works that span the career of political theorist Claude Lefort (previously published in Elements d'une critique de la bureaucratie [Elements of a Critique of Bureaucracy], Geneva: Librairie Droz, 1971; Les Formes de l'histoire: essais d'anthropologie politique [The Forms of History: Essays in Political Anthropology], Paris: Editions Gallimard, 1978; & L'Invention democratique: les limites de la domination totalitaire [Democratic Invention: The Limits of Totalitarian Domination], Paris: Librairie Artheme Fayard, 1981), in III PARTS & 10 Chpts, with a Preface & Introduction by the editor, John B. Thompson. PART I - PROBLEMS OF POLITICS AND BUREAUCRACY - describes (1) The Contradiction of Trotsky -- (translated by Alan Sheridan) criticizes the Trotskyist view of Stalinism & the Soviet bureaucracy, arguing that the bureaucracy was a central part of the new system of exploitation that emerged in the USSR; (2) Totalitarianism without Stalin -- (translated by Alan Sheridan) argues that Stalinism was a phase in the rise of totalitarianism, defined as a form of society; the Soviet bureaucracy is seen as a new SC defined by its relation to the state rather than its position in the economy. The denunciations & reforms of the Twentieth Congress of the Communist Party were merely attempts to make totalitarianism more acceptable to Soviet citizens; (3) What Is Bureaucracy? -- critically analyzes the concepts of bureaucracy that can be derived from Karl Marx & Max Weber, focusing on the social nature & dynamic character of modern bureaucracy. Events that foreshadowed & facilitated the growth of Soviet bureaucracy are pointed out; & (4) Novelty and the Appeal of Repetition -- discusses experiences contributing to Lefort's critique of bureaucracy, eg, his critique of Marx's work, & his own experiences in the leftist group, "Socialism ou Barbarie." PART II - HISTORY, IDEOLOGY AND THE SOCIAL IMAGINARY - includes (5) Marx: From One Vision of History to Another -- (translated by Terry Karten & previously published in Social Research, 1978, 56, 615-666) contrasts Marx's discontinuous & continuous visions of history, & their relation to his theory of the emergence of capitalism; & (6) Outline of the Genesis of Ideology in Modern Societies -- attempts to reconceptualize ideology, based in part on the sense of ideology in Marx's works, & to demonstrate its value in analysis of modern societies. PART III - DEMOCRACY AND TOTALITARIANISM - presents (7) Politics and Human Rights -- (translated by Alan Sheridan) treats Marx's critique of the "rights of man," concluding that the struggle for human rights is a "generative principle" of democratic society & a democratic impluse within totalitarianism; (8) The Logic of Totalitarianism -- (translated by Alan Sheridan) examines the logic & nature of totalitarianism, finding that leftists failed to understand it due to their lack of conception of political (vs economic) society; (9) The Image of the Body and Totalitarianism -- (translated by Alan Sheridan) first presented as a lecture to a group of psychoanalysts, gives an account of the system of representation characteristic of totalitarianism; & (10) Pushing Back the Limits of the Possible -- offers a pessimistic evaluation of Solidarity's prospects in Poland, seeing the uprising as contradicting the logic of the totalitarian system from within. A Bibliog of 26 items.

title: THE ORGANIZATIONAL SOCIETY
abstract: A Vol in 9 Chpts with a Preface, utilizing pol'al, sociol'al, & psychol'al theory to analyze individual accommodations to largescale org's. (1) Big Organizations: Definitions and Dysfunctionsintroduces the concept of the org, the influence of soc values & bur'tic structure upon org'al members, & notes the org'al imposition of soc'ization through authority systems, rational procedures, & limited objectives. (2) The Bureaucratic Model-defines the characteristics of large org's: large size; specialization hierarchy; status anxiety; oligarchy; co-option (the org'al elite's selection of their successors); efficiency; & rationality all constituting an ideal typical model of bur'cy. (3) Toward the Organizational Society-traces historically in the US, the development of bur'cy as a major form of org, assessing trends, beginning in 1875, including the separation of ownership from manag, increasing size & concentration in business & industry, the decline of competition, the development of a pol'al economy, & the emergence of an 'employee' society. (4) The Social Basis of Organizational Personality-discusses the process of secondary org'al soc'ization utilizing H. S. Sullivan's interpersonal theory of psychiatry. (5) The Psychology of Big Organizationsconceptualizes the bur'tic model as a 'structured field' with diff'iated systems of authority, status, & small groups, providing stimuli evoking the individual's deference to authority. (6) Patterns of Accommodation: Upward-Mobiles-analyzes the 'upward-mobile' as a bur'tic type whose values include the capacity to identify with the org enabling a form of accommodationadjustment through the acquisition of power. Superiors are viewed as threats to his own mode of conduct; subordinates are regarded in a detached fashion, faciliting a universalistic type of decision-making eclipsing individual needs through meeting org'al ones. (7) Patterns of Accommodation: Indifferents-characterizes this type as those who have accommodated their environment through withdrawal & redirection of interests to offthe-job satisfactions. (8) Patterns of Accommodation: Ambivalents-analyzes this type as one unsuited to the bur'tic situation by dint of the distortion of interpersonal relations through fear & rejection of authority & systems of status, a 'tenderminded' view of HR precluding an upward-mobile orientation, a desire for creativity, an inability to accept org'al goals, & a corresponding lack of identification with the small work group. (9) The Social Dysfunctions of Organization-includes the antinomy between org'al logic & individual growth & creativity, stressing the abandonment of notions about efficiency in favor of a permissive work environment. Name & subject Indexes. G. Jacobs.

title: The Outdated Concept of Apartheid
abstract: South Africa is moving toward an unprecedented political crisis.  Black South Africans are beginning to challenge and resist the authority of the white government.  Education has been brought to a standstill, and the civil administration in many black townships has dissolved.  South Africa is being restructured -- away from apartheid and discrimination and toward a new society involving greater social freedom, economic opportunity, and political power for all South Africans.  The most important impetus for this restructuring process is the dynamics of the country's economic development.  Newly established and voteless black urban communities are gaining economic power.  In light of this growing power, the Nationalist government has responded with ''reforms'' of its traditional apartheid policy, but the reforms have not been able to undo the damage of decades of apartheid.  Apartheid cannot be reformed; the only acceptable solution is to eliminate it.

title: Reinventing, restructuring, and the big band theory of organizational change
abstract: Even though the management literature is replete with articles about "empowering employees," "satisfying customers," "working smarter, not harder," "decentralization," and other forward-looking management practices, the reality is that most contemporary organizations look more like the bureaucracies that Max Weber first described nearly a century ago.  It was during that era - the turn of the 20th century - that the last "big" (in the sense of Kuhn's paradigm shift) organizational change took place, as professionally managed and rationally structured bureaucracies replaced family firms.  A number of observers of the contemporary organizational landscape think that business is at another crossroads, and that if the US is to retain its preeminent place in the world economy and the family of nations in the 21st century, a transformation of organizational and managerial practices comparable to the managerial revolution of the early part of the 20th century will have to happen.

title: URBAN SOCIETY
authors: Gist, Noel P; Fava, Sylvia F
abstract: A revised Ed of a text previously co-authored by N. P. Gist & the late L. A. Halbert. Over 75% of the text consists of new or rewritten material. Historical cross-cultural, metropolitan, & soc change aspects of Ur development are given increased attention. 1960 census data for the US & other countries are incorporated. There are 25 Chpt's, in 5 Parts. Part I - THE GROWTH OF CITIES - presents (1) The Origin and Development of Cities, a new Chpt, describing pre-Ur settlement patterns & ancient cities re 3 signif factors (environment, technology, & soc org). (2) Conditions of City Growth in Historic Times, traces the continuing roles of the 3 factors in Ur development, before & after the industrial revolution. (3) The Urbanization of the US, describes Ur concepts in the US census, & trends in Ur growth over time, & by state & region. (4) Contemporary World Urbanization, classifies nations into a 3-part typology of levels of urbanization & presents a comparative analysis of metropolitan development. (5) Classes and Type of Cities, covers functional & ideal typologies. Part II - URBAN ECOLOGY - has been revised to focus on recent theory in human ecology & the effects on public policy stemming from the movement of pop & business enterprises into subUr areas. Chpt (6) The Ecological Approach, describes the elements in the ecological system, processes, & the resulting spatial patterns. (7) Ecological Segregation, & (8) Ecological Change,' Invasion and Succession, compare ethnic, occup'al, & religious segregation & desegregation in the US & other countries, emphasizing the increasing importance of racial segregation in US metropolitan areas. (9) Urban and Suburban Residential Areas, deals with the characteristics & change in slums, suburbs, & Ru/Ur fringe in US SMA's, comparing them with residential patterns in other countries. (10) The Ecology of Urban Institutions, covers transportation & ecological change, the old & new spatial distribution of business, industry, & cultural & recreational instit's in the US & abroad. (11) The Metropolitan Region and Urban Dominance, describes the rise of the metropolitan region & presents case studies applying various measures of metropolitan influence. Part III - THE ORGANIZATION OF URBAN LIFE - opens with (12) Urbanization: Process and Impact, which has been rewritten to stress the importance of the world's rapid Ur transformation. (13) Urban Status Systems, presents various conceptual approaches to Ur stratification & case studies of the changes under way in systems of Ur status & SM. (14) The Urban World of Work, describes Ur status & mobility re occup'al specialization, esp re the effects on the position of women & minority groups. (15) Bureaucratic Organization and Power, indicates why such org is pervasive in Ur life & the particular problems involved in analyzing Ur power structure. (16) Urban Family Life in Transition, illustrates with case studies the multiplicity of fam patterns in the city, noting the general effects of urbanism on the fam in developed & underdeveloped countries. (17) Voluntary Associations and Neighborhood Interaction, describes the overall relationship between urbanization & voluntary assoc's, in addition to the factors related to differential participation in assoc's among urbanites. (18) Leisure and City Life, is a new Chpt, reflecting the increased prominence of recreation in an age of growing affluence. Part IV - SOCIAL-PSYCHOLOGICAL ASPECTS OF URBAN LIFE - opens with Chpt (19) Personal Organization and Disorganization in the City. The theoretical constructs of Ur personality are described, followed by summaries of empirical studies of folk-Ur & Ru/Ur personality diff's, & statistical data on Ru/Ur contrasts in crime, DEL'cy & other soc problems. (20) Adjustments of Migrants to Cities, is a new Chpt contrasting the Ur impact on migrants in industrialized & non-industrialized nations. (21) Intergroup Relations in the City, describes the integrative & divisive influences of Ur residence on racial, religious, ethnic, & cultural minorities. (22) Communication, Public Opinion and the Community, examines the impact of MM on Ur consensus. (23) The Image of the City, is a new Chpt, re the emotional response to the city. The city is analyzed as a symbol, with historical, literary, & professional, soc sci illustrations. The prevalence of an anti-Ur bias in US life is examined. Part V - SOCIAL ASPECTS OF HOUSING AND DEVELOPMENT - includes (24) Urban Housing, & (25) Planning, encompassing statistics & case studies on the physical magnitude & soc consequences of Ur residential deterioration in diff countries, with description of specific programs for improvement. Tables, charts, maps, photographs, index. S. F. Fava.

title: Organized Bodies: Gender, Sexuality and Embodiment in Contemporary Organizations
authors: Witz, Anne; Halford, Susan; Savage, Mike
abstract: The nature & implications of the gendered aspects of institutional organization were examined in an interview survey of 90 men & women from all levels of the organizational hierarchy in a hospital ward, local government office, & bank branch. Although the modern ideal-type bureaucracy is often depicted as rational & gender-neutral, recent critiques of bureaucratic organizations have revealed the persistent patriarchal nature of many supposedly gender-neutral organizational structures. The results suggest that organizations are regulated by heterosexualized discourses that define appropriate relationships & power structures. At the local government office & bank, these heterosexualized discourses presented a complimentary perception of male (M) & female (F) genders, & were endorsed by M & F employees. In the hospital ward, however, the sexualized discourses of M doctors in power positions were rejected by F nurses while high-ranking F staff used familial-type discourses that empowered women, rather than sexual-type discourses that confirmed M superiority. It is concluded that the embodied & gendered structure of bureaucratic organizations are determined by three overlapping dimensions: spatial (physical proximity, personal space, hierarchical structure); verbal (language & discourse); & physical (the sexual politics of body presentation). 23 References. T. Sevier

title: MULTIVALENT MAN
abstract: A study of personal & soc implications of cultural contradictions in IV Parts & 23 Chpts. I-MANY VALUES, MANY MINDS- presents: (1) On Conforming and on Being One's Self-which discusses ways in which cultural models influence man, primarily 'societal, group, personal, & self models.' The diff values of the subcultures are not really choices, because they are automatically internalized by members. (2) On the Importance of Looking and Seeing-states that C&P understood dynamically must replace static concepts like `rational man'; a sociol based upon the 'study of spontaneous human problem solving as observed clinically' can now evolve. (3) Culture's Many Facesdemonstrates how culture, a model for emulation, provides modes of action for individuals in terms of a quaternary continua: conventions, folkways, practices, & att's. (4) Morality in Society and in Groups-discusses the relationship between the 2 broadest levels of cultural expression, conventions & folkways. Conventions 'define instit's-as-they-should-be, but folkways & mores define ass oc's-as-they-have-to-be in an operating in-group sense.' (5) How Individuals Live with Culturestates that the innermost levels of cultural expression are the practices of the person, man-as-he-appears & the att's of the self, mas-as-he-is. (6) Multivalence: Pros and Cons-suggests that while multivalence enables individuals to function in many roles, an exaggerated or inept version of it resembles a schizoid personality. (7) Individual Conflict and Integration-asks questions keeping in mind that people must learn to live with their actual multivalence rather than a fancied monovalence: (i) What influences other than culture also help shape the `ego?' (ii) Do the bases of individual integration change during life? (iii) What are the relations of soc categorization & of multiple contrasting group identities to individual stability? (iv) What about role conflicts in the individual? II-GROUP MAN-presents: (8) Groups in Process-which defines groups as 'aggregates of 2 or more people who have occasion to associate or at least to identify themselves with one another once or repeatedly.' (9) Types of Groups-shows that a rough set of types would include 'intimate pair-groups & primary, quasi-primary, & secondary groups.' (10) How Groups and Their Members Vary-analyzes groups in terms of character of interests or identification, size, character of interpersonal interaction, character of group org, & character of intergroup interaction. (11) People Grow Up Within Groups-examines patterns of a child's earliest associations in connection with continuous & discontinuous aspects of soc replacement. (12) Prototypes of People, Groups, and Society-examines child-mother, son-mother, daughter-mother, child-father, son-father, & daughter-father as prototypes of forms & roles. (13) Bridges from Self to Community-describes how prototypical figures which draw the child into the community are formed from parents, siblings, substitutes, etc. III- SOCIETY'S FABRIC OF VALUES-describes: (14) Tissues of Orthodoxy and of Legitimacy-which states that soc `system' is an oversimplification. Society is an infinitely overlapping patchwork of barrier-bound status-giving in-groups. The 4 status ladders are (a) enterprisers, (b) bur'crats, (c) technicians, & (d) power or fame. (15) Enterprisers and Bureaucrats-describes how their value interpretations help to weave the soc fabric. Enterprisers tend to use org's, bur'crats to be used by them. (16) Technicians and Creators-discusses values & modes of these soc ladders. (17) Four Melting Pots Within One-sketches the interrelations of the white (Protestant, Catholic, Jewish) & colored in terms of relative opportunities & viewpoints, noting the pressures for & against ethnoid stratification. (18) Enterprise, Marginality, and Social Change-describes marginality, which may reverse adaptive tendency of persons or groups, as the major factor behind innovation. (19) Pathways to Marginality-discusses 9 causes of marginality. IV-THE INDIVIDUAL CONFRONTS SO- CIETY-includes: (20) On Learning More About Society-which demonstrates how soc studies are often distorted by reductionism, narrow problem solving, sociologizing, & disguised evaluation. (21) Conformity and Nonconformity: A Case-presents suggestions for clinical study of freedom in academia. (22) The Challenge of the 'Clinic'-suggests that the `Clinical study' of soc phenomena, akin to psychiatric study of real individual problems, be used as means of widening sociol's grasp. Difficulties & illustrious past users of the method are noted. (23) Cultures and Personalities in the Human Struggle-details obstacles to sociol's extension of the sphere of truly individual action. Joint author & subiect Index. M. Duke.

title: Les politiques de l'eau en Europe (Water Policy in Europe)
abstract: "Les politiques de l'eau en Europe (Water Policy in Europe)" edited by Bernard Barraque is reviewed.

title: Political contexts and maternal health policy: Insights from a comparison of south Indian states
abstract: Nearly 300,000 women die from pregnancy-related complications each year. One-fifth of these deaths occur in India. Maternal survival rose on India's national policy agenda in the mid-2000s, but responsibility for health policy and implementation in the federal system is largely devolved to the state level where priority for the issue and maternal health outcomes vary. This study investigates sources of variation in maternal health policy and implementation sub-nationally in India. The study is guided by four analytical categories drawn from policy process literature: constitutional, governing and social structures; political contexts; actors and ideas. The experiences of two south Indian states -- Tamil Nadu a leader and Karnataka a relatively slow mover -- are examined. Process-tracing, a case study methodology that helps to identify roles of complex historical events in causal processes, was employed to investigate the research question in each state. The study is informed by interviews with public health policy experts and service delivery professionals, observation of implementation sites and archival document analysis. Historical legacies -- Tamil Nadu's non-Brahmin social movement and Karnataka's developmental disparities combined with decentralization -- shape the states' political contexts, affecting variation in maternal health policy and implementation. Competition to advance consistent political priorities across regimes in Tamil Nadu offers fertile ground for policy entrepreneurship and strong public health system administration facilitates progress. Inconsistent political priorities and relatively weak public health system administration frustrate progress in Karnataka. These variations offer insights to the ways in which sub-national political and administrative contexts shape health policy and implementation. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: THE IMPACTS OF STATE GROWTH MANAGEMENT PROGRAMS ON URBAN SPRAWL IN THE 1990S
abstract: The urban landscape in the United States has been characterized by sprawl for decades. Despite arguments in favor of sprawl or its component attributes, it is widely believed that sprawl leads to many contemporary United States urban and environmental problems. Since 1961, 15 states in the United States have adopted state growth management programs (SGMPs) with various goals, including curtailing sprawl. This article, among a few previous studies, examines the effectiveness of SGMPs on containing sprawl. We create sprawl indices for 294 metropolitan areas in 1990 and 2000, measuring two major dimensions of sprawl: density and land-use mixture. Our examination of SGMPs involves not only a dummy variable indicating whether a SGPM exists or not, but a score system measuring the degree of state involvement in local growth management and three variables measuring three major attributes of SGMPs. With the refined measurements for both sprawl and SGMPs, we examine the impacts of SGMPs on the sprawl measures in the 1990s of the selected metropolitan areas in the United States. Our statistical results show that SGMPs effectively promoted compact development in terms of population density and land-use mixture. However, the statistical results do not support the claim that SGMPs with a higher degree of state involvement in local growth management, on average, worked better at curtailing sprawl than those with a lower-degree involvement in the 1990s. This article suggests that state governments in the United States should more fully exercise their responsibilities to control urban sprawl rather than just leave this issue to local devices. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: La Guerra de Agua: Notions of Morality, Respectability, and Community in a Madrid Neighborhood
abstract: This article is part of a larger work in progress that tells the story of Orcasitas--fifteen hundred shacks built by immigrants during the 1950s on the southern outskirts of central Madrid. Without any electricity, running water, paved roads, or health or education centers, this section of the city was for many years the embodiment of urban alienation. Yet, Orcasitas is also a success story of a shantytown that has turned into a residential neighborhood through the efforts of its inhabitants. For more than twenty years, the dwellers of Orcasitas struggled, against the backdrop of a weakening dictatorship and then within a new democracy, to obtain proper infrastructure, health and education facilities, and apartments to replace their shacks. This article looks at one aspect of this process: the struggle to obtain running water and sanitation services and the way this struggle shaped and was shaped by the inhabitants perceptions of morality, respectability, and community life. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: AKP's Housing Policy: TOKI as the Loyalty Generator
abstract: Two general elections were held in Turkey in 2015 within only 5 months. The AKP, the party which has governed Turkey since 2002, promised nothing else but economic stability to the voters. In this article, I demonstrate in what way the housing policy of the AKP shapes lower class families' dependence from the financial system and the government party. I argue that the TOKI (Mass Housing Administration), the leading actor in AKP's housing policy, functions as a (political) loyalty generator in the name of the AKP.

title: Justice Through Bureaucracy: The Ukrainian Model
abstract: This paper examines legal proceedings in the court of first instance for civil cases in Ukraine. Using ethnographic methodology, it demonstrates that a large part of a court judgement is predetermined by the institutional infrastructure and by practices established more widely in Ukrainian society. By observing case hearings and interviewing litigants and judges, the paper reveals that an unbridgeable gap separates a legal case, as constructed through documentary files, from the reality of life. This affects the very meaning of 'evidence' and the way that judicial decisions are made. The paper also illustrates the benefits of viewing a lower-level civil courtroom as a microcosm of a society, demonstrating that it provides rich insights into different layers of that society. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Open skies, closed markets: Future games in the negotiation of international air transport
abstract: How can we explain an international agreement that appears to run counter to the declared objectives of one of the key players? This article examines the US-EU Open Skies agreement signed in 2007 and asks why Europeans accepted the agreement after having rejected a comparable version three years earlier. Theoretical approaches that explain time inconsistency in international negotiations tend to focus on reasons why states can be constrained to accept suboptimal solutions. In multi-level bargaining, principal-agent and bureaucratization theories focus on loss of control and constructivists suggest that governments can become trapped in rhetoric. This article shows that paradoxical agreements can be voluntary and explains them by showing the rationale behind multi-games that include ambiguity about the future. In particular, increasing the flexibility of the agreement allowed negotiators to escape present-day constituent pressures by remaining ambiguous and betting on shifting coalitions. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: A Duration Model for the Estimation of the Contracting Out of Urban Water Management in Southern Spain
abstract: Research that tries to explain the decisions of local government in the contracting out of certain services frequently disregards the temporal dimension. In this article, the authors take time into account in the analysis, proposing a duration model as an alternative to discrete choice models. The objective is to analyze the explanatory factors in the contracting out of municipal services. This methodology is applied to the water services of 744 municipalities in southern Spain during the period from 1985 to 2006. From the results, the authors conclude that complexity in the environment, economies of scale, financial restrictions, and stability of the local government are determinants in the decision.

title: Paid Emotional Care: Organizational Forms That Encourage Nurturance
abstract: A study of paid care work argues that, contrary to the ideology of separate spheres, market relations & bureaucracy do not have to sabotage emotional caregiving. Although low salaries, a desire for profits, & overblown bureaucracies sometimes diminish the ability of paid care workers to provide good care, organizational structures can be arranged in ways that encourage the provision of nurturing & compassionate care. Three organizational characteristics that enhance emotional care are limiting profit making/cost cutting; minimizing hierarchy/rigidity; & emphasizing nurturing/interpersonal skills rather than scientific knowledge. Emotional care work is analyzed in two nursing homes in which a focus on profit making & bureaucratic procedures undermines emotional care; as well as a hospital & an institution for persons with severe mental retardation that display both a work culture & bureaucratic procedures that encourage nurturance. The critical need for workers to have some degree of autonomy from supervisors & administrators is discussed, along with the clinical model of nursing that fosters emotional caregiving by bureaucratizing it. 1 Table. J. Lindroth

title: Models for Understanding Collective Intelligence on Wikipedia
abstract: Through examining established and evolving conceptions of intelligence across natural and social science and applying them to Wikipedia, this article argues that the world's largest encyclopedia and broadest implementation of the wiki is an online instance of collective intelligence (CI), as it fits key models for this concept. Further, by relying on sociotechnical ensembles of human intelligence, programmed bots, social bureaucracy, and software protocols, a more humanistic CI, as proposed by Levy, is realized in a virtual knowledge space that embodies information as both product and process while empowering its community to explore the cultural possibilities of its collectivism.

title: "A trade union oriented war on the slums": Harold Gibbons, Earnest Calloway, and the St Louis Teamsters in the 1960s
abstract: Bussell reiterates the story of Harold Gibbons and the end of a 1960's rent strike by public housing tenants in St. Louis Missouri. The settlement of the strike was accompanied by the formation of the St. Louis Civic Alliance for Housing, a business, labor, and community partnership that included a prominent managerial role for the Teamsters and provided for direct tenant participation in the administration of public housing as well as transitioning Gibbons from a pariah to a statesman.

title: The legacy of Popular Unity: Chile 1973-2003; The Chilean road to socialism
abstract: What lessons can be learned from Chile's 'Road to Socialism', 1970-73? In contrast to the predominant focus on the undermining of the government by opposition forces (the US administration, domestic and foreign capitalists, the Chilean military and right-wing movements), this short comment highlights the importance of social property and mass mobilisation to the UP programme. It points to the large-scale land redistribution that took place, also the changes in industrial control. The conclusion stresses that the legacy of the UP government should be one of social mobilisation and the possibilities for rapid changes in social relations.

title: Diversity and inclusion in local governance: An Australian study of seniors' participation
authors: Petriwskyj, Andrea; Warburton, Jeni; Everingham, Jo-Anne; Cuthill, Michael
abstract: The importance of hearing older people's voices within local governance processes is well recognised; however, the increasing diversity among older people makes this complex. Questions around inclusion and exclusion, representation and representativeness create challenges for the ways in which diverse older people are engaged. This paper uses the results from a qualitative study conducted in Australia to address the key research question: how does diversity impact on older people's perceptions and experiences of barriers to participation in local governance? Results indicate that diversity impacts not simply on what barriers are reported by seniors, but on how those barriers are experienced. Patterns among the barriers reported and their relationship with diversity reflect questions around representation and inclusion. Thus despite broad acceptance of the notion that understanding diversity is integral to inclusion, challenges remain for older people's engagement with local governance processes. A deeper understanding of diversity and how it relates to inclusion are required. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: MAX WEBER: RELIGION AND SOCIETY
abstract: A recapitalution, in Italian, of the major works of Max Weber on religion & civilization, with some attempts at interpretation, in III Parts & 22 Chpt's, preceded by an Introduction. 'Introduzione Generale' (General Introduction)-gives a brief sketch of Max Weber's life & Germany after 1870 & notes that the book concentrates on 3 great res works: CON- FUCIANISM AND TAOISM, HINDUISM AND BUDDHISM, & THE JUDAISM OF ANTIQUITY. I-IL PROTESTANTESIMO ASCETICO E 'LO SPIRITO DEL CAPITALISMO' (Ascetic Protestantism and the 'Spirit of Capitalism')-contains: (1) Premessa all 'Etica Protestante' (The Premise of the 'Protestant Ethic')-which deals with Weber's motive for this study, the study's limits, & Weber's methodology. (2) Lo Spirito del Capitalismo (The Spirit of Capitalism)-places this work in the context of other theories (eg, those of K. Marx, B. Franklin, & T. Parsons) & quotes from M. Weber's writings on the subject. (3) Lutero (Luther)-examines M. Weber's concept of occup & his interpretation of Martin Luther's role. (4) Calvino (Calvin)-summarizes Weber's ideas on Calvin & Calvinism. (5) Riforma, Rivoluzione e Sviluppo Capitalistico in Inghilterra (Reform, Revolution and Capitalist Development in England)-delineates Weber's conception of the relationship between Puritanism & capitalism in English history. (6) Il 'Calvinismo (Calvinism)-describes the 'Calvinism' of M. Weber & its influence upon Weber's work, ECONOMY AND SOCIETY. (7) Etica Protestante e 'Spirito del Capitalismo' (The Protestant Ethic and the 'Spirit of Capitalism')-deals with Weber's attention to the theories of Richard Baxter & the anti-capitalist elements contained therein. (8) Etica Protestante total/sum Capitalismo, Ieri e Oggi (Protestant Ethic and Capitalism, Yesterday and Today)-examines Puritan Life, sci & technology, capital formation, the methodism of the industr revolution, & the Puritan heredity of capitalism in the light of Weber's work. (9) Religione e Carattere Nazionale (Religion and National Character)-presents a synopsis of Max Weber's conclusions re the influence of Puritanism on British nat'l character. (10) Le Sette Protestantd total/sum lo Spirito del Capitalismo (The Protestant Sects and the Spirit of Capitalism)- analyzes Weber's essay on the 'Protestant Sects and the Spirit of Capitalism' in the COLLECTED ESSAYS ON THE SOCIOLOGY OF RELIGION. II-LE GRANDI RICERCHE COM- PARATE (The Great Comparative Studies)-presents: (11) L'Etica Economics delle Religioni Mondiali (The Economic Ethic of the World Religions)-which recapitulates Weber's ideas on world religions, the relationship between soc structure & religion, the glorification of suffering in Christianity, & the role of religion in authority & soc structure. (12) Confucianesimo e Taoismo (Confucianism and Taoism)-summarizes Weber's ideas on Confucianism & Taoism & their influence on Chinese society. (13) II Rifiuto Religioso del Mondo e le Sue Direzioni (The Religious Refutation of the World and Its Directions)-presents the basic principles of Weber on asceticism & mysticism & the religious influence on the econ & pol'al sphere of society. (14) India (India)-discusses & sums up M. Weber's study on Hinduism & Buddhism & the econ & soc tradition which arose from these religions. (15) Antico Mondo Ebraico (The Ancient Hebraic World)-focuses on Weber's essay on Ancient Judaism & the influence of Hebrew values on the West. (16) Le Chiese e Is Chiesa (The Churches and the Church)-is concerned with Weber's conception of Jesus Christ, the instit'ization of charisma in Christianity, & the role of the Church & the Churches in soc order & soc change. (17) Riepilogo Selettivo total/sum Critico (A Selective and Critical Recapitulation)-sums up some major strands of Weber's thinking as previously analyzed in detail. III-GLI ULTIMI STUDL CONCLUSIONI (The Last Studies. Conclusions)-offers: (18) Riesame delle Origini del Capitalismo (Re-Examination of the Origins of Capitalism)-which searches Weber's ideas for an understanding of soc change & modern capitalism under reference to contemporary history & Weber's essay 'The Origin of Modern Capitalism.' (19) II Razionalismo Occidentale (Western Rationalism)-considers Weber's view of capitalism as an aspect of the rationalization of Western society. (20) II Futuro della Societa Capitalistica (The Future of Capitalist Society)-examines Weber's ideas on bur'cy & charisma in modern societies. (21) La Politica Come Vocazione (Politics as Vocation)-briefly discusses M. Weber's pol'al sociol under reference to his lectures in Munich in 1919 on 'Politics as Vocation.' (22) Conclusions (Conclusions)-notes the large general scale of M. Weber's theories & views their development under reference to such other large-scale general theories as Marxism & socialism. Their validity for contemporary history, the evolution of a bur'tic machinery, technology, power & leadership in modern times is affirmed. Weber's main aim was the defense of human freedom. An Index of Names & a Bibliog. M. Maxfield.

title: Society at Risk in a Society of Organizations
abstract: A historical survey traces the absorption of US society in the nineteenth century into large-scale organizations. It is suggested that wage dependency & the externalization of business costs were two important factors leading to the growth of organizations. The way in which the bureaucratic form of organizations eventually permeated all aspects of society is described. In that it tied workers through wage dependency to a lifestyle marked by minimization of risk & high consumption, this organizational society has eroded every effort at resistance. Finally, it is argued that the democratic culture that built this society is endangered by this trend. 1 Figure. D. M. Smith

title: Nothing Fails Like Success: The Evaluation-Research Industry and Labor Market Policy
abstract: Active labor market programs (ALMP) use direct government action to: 1.  create a demand for labor, 2.  increase the supply and quality of labor, and 3.  encourage labor mobility.  Relevant ALMP issues include: 1.  the relative importance of training, 2.  funding and administration, 3.  worksharing, and 4.  elimination of guest and/or aged workers.  Evaluation research is often narrow and limited, and frequently produces misleading results.  A recent careful and comprehensive evaluation of the Job Corps shows that evaluations could be accurate.  However, they may still be unhelpful in garnering support for programs.  Sweden and Germany prefer action over evaluation.  Sweden's programs are especially interesting, since its unemployment rate has been less than 4% for 20 years.  Although many differences limit the transferability of Swedish programs, the US can expand in this direction.  Factors which encourage this view are that: 1.  support for ALMP is not limited to the political left, 2.  relevant administrative talent is already available, and 3.  demographic trends are favorable.

title: Class Relations in Brazil's New Neoliberal Phase
abstract: While maintaining the neoliberal capitalist model, the Lula administration has ushered it into a new phase. With respect to the bloc in power, national and international financial capital today shares its hegemony with the important domestic industrial and agrarian bourgeoisie. However, with respect to the working class, there have been two changes. First, the new unionist elite that has been moving toward a micro-corporativism since the mid-1990s has established an alliance with the domestic bourgeoisie against financial capital. Second, the poor and unorganized laborers, who have been serving as a support class for neoliberal politics since the Collor and Cardoso administrations, today are more linked to the government and are a passive base for the rise of "Lulismo," a political phenomenon separate from the Partido dos Trabalhadores.

title: The Wisdom of Whores. Bureaucrats, Brothels, and the Business of AIDS
abstract: Santow reviews The Wisdom of Whores: Bureaucrats, Brothels, and the Business of AIDS by Elizabeth Pisani.

title: Alternative Sources of Energy: Indigenous Renewable Resources
abstract: This paper sees in indigenous biomass and other natural resources such as sun and wind and water, especially in Third World countries (most of which lie in the torrid or semi-torrid zones and a vast majority of whose populations live in rural areas), a potential alternative to non-renewable sources of energy such as oil and nuclear power. Biomass can be transformed into various forms of energy: solids (firewood and charcoal), liquids (alcohol and oil), gases (methane and hydrogen), and electricity. They are at once renewable and non-polluting, viable and inexpensive, decentralized and labour-intensive. The paper also surveys the efforts being made in Third World countries to make use of these energy-producing resources. But it adds that care will have to be taken, using appropriate social measures, to ensure that, unlike oil and nuclear energy, biomass energy is not only decentralized (which it has to be by its nature) but also equitably shared (which mere decentralization does not guarantee) by all sections of the rural population.

title: Equality and Income Security in Market Economies: What's Wrong with Insurance?
