abstract: This article critically assesses the marketization of income security, and identifies links between equality, self-reliance and welfare reform. Marketization in emergent economies is distinguished by a strong separation between the use of insurance for the mainstream economy and relief for the poor. The impact of this model on the shaping of working lives and on market rigidity is discussed through a review of implications in the areas of subsistence, integrity interests and employment transitions. The broad faith in insurance solutions is argued to derive from a highly abstract approach to welfare reform and to result in a lack of attention to uneven and unstable markets, and to self-government as a motive to work. Evidence of this emerges from a comparison of insurance in its more ideal form (in Chile) with modified models (Brazil and Korea). In the last two cases a developmental orientation has aided in the provision of broad-based security. Other factors that appear to enhance the importance of direct assistance are also discussed, including aspects of state administration and labour services that limit work opportunity and individual autonomy in uneven economies. The segregated dual approach to income security is argued to be broadly deficient, but not because insurance is inherently wrong. Countries as diverse as Barbados and Denmark show that more cohesive economies are a better foundation for integrating insurance with general welfare and for income security and individual enterprise broadly conceived. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: From Embodied to Disembodied Professionalism? Discussing the Implications of Medico-Managerial Management in Welfare Service Work
abstract: Welfare service work is traditionally understood to comprise embodied, situational and social practices of care that are central to a worker's professional self-image. Over the past few decades, public management reforms have called for reassessment of welfare service workers' professional accountability through practices of medico-managerial service management. These practices promote the production of transparency and accountability in welfare service work through checking-based trust and disembodied professional practices. This article argues that the changes in the nature of trust toward welfare service professionals have implications for care work cultures and workers' professional agency that has traditionally built on the idea of the embodied, situational and social practice of welfare service work. Drawing on an interview study with Finnish welfare service workers (n = 25), the article analyses frontline workers' descriptions of medico-managerial management in the social and healthcare sector. The results point to the significance of embodied practices of care in creation of client trust and for workers' professional self-images. The conclusion is that while disembodied professionalism offers opportunities for workers' self-management and evaluation of accountability and transparency of service processes, it may disregard the importance of embodied practices for the workers' professional self-images and client relations.[PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: LABOR AND TRADE UNIONISM: AN INTERDISCIPLINARY READER
abstract: A Vol 'designed as a contribution to a rapprochement between the econ & sociol'al views of labor problems & trade unions,' with 24 selections chosen because of (i) their distinct contribution to labor & industrial relations, primarily by economists & sociol'sts, (ii) their theoretical & not descriptive points of view, (iii) their recent publication in scholarly journals. The Vol is in IX Sections each with a brief introductory summary of its contents by the Ed's. I - THE THEORY OF THE UNION - reprints M. W. Reder 'The Theory of Union Wage Policy, ' & E. H. Phelps Brown on 'Wage Policy and Wage Differences.' U- LABOR MARKETS-presents Robert J. Lampman on 'New Facts and Interpretations in Labor Market Analysis.' Simon Rottenberg 'On Choice in Labor Markets' (See SA 5738) & Robert J. Lampman concludes with 'Comments: On Choice of Labor Markets.' III - TRADE UNION HISTORY - presents Irving Bernstein on 'Union Growth and Structural Cycles,' & John T. Dunlop on 'Structural Changes in the American Labor Movement and Industrial Relations System.' IV - THE UNION MONOPOLY ISSUE - contains a reprint by Edward S. Mason on 'Labor Monopoly and All That.' V - UNIONS: WAGES AND INFLATION -presents James R. Schlesinger on 'Market Structure, Union Power and Inflation,' M. Bronfenbrenner on 'The Incidence of Collective Bargaining Once More.' J. R. Hicks on 'Economic Foundations of Wage Policy.' & H. M. Douty on 'Post-War Wage Bargaining in the United States.' VI-DEMOCRACY AND BUREAUCRACY IN TRADE UNION GOVERNMENT - contains selections by John R. Coleman on 'The Compulsive Pressures of Democracy in Unionism,' (See SA 4293) & S. M. Lipset on 'The Political Process in Trade Unions: A Theoretical Statement' (a revised version of SA 2869). VII-THE INTERNAL POLITICAL LIFE OF TRADE UNIONS - presents selections by Daniel Bell on 'The Racket-Ridden Longshoremen: A Functional Analysis of Crime,' Leonard I. Pearlin & Henry E. Richards detail the theatre's 'Equity: A Study of Union Democracy,' & George Strauss on 'Control by the Membership in Building Trades Unions' (See SA 4500). VIII- FACTORS SHAPING OCCUPATIONAL BEHAVIOR -presents R. W. Revans on 'Industrial Morale and Size of Unit' (See SA 4531), K. G. J. C. Knowles on "Strike- Proneness' and Its Determinants' (See SA 897, 1667). Robert H. Guest on 'Work Careers and Aspirations of Automobile Workers' (See SA 725), & Bernard Goldstein on 'Some Aspects of the Nature of Unionism Among Salaried Professionals in Industry' (See SA 1798). IX - THE SOCIAL ENVIRONMENT OF WORK ATTITUDES - contains reprints by Robert Blauner on 'Work Satisfaction and Industrial Trends in Modern Society.' Donald F. Roy on 'Work Satisfaction and Social Reward in Quota Achievement: An Analysis of Piecework Incentive' (See SA 175), & William A. Faunce on 'Automation and the Automobile Worker' (See SA 6310). No index.

title: THE SOVIET BUREAUCRATIC ELITE: A CASE STUDY OF THE UKRAINIAN APPARATUS
abstract: A study of the Ukrainian (Ukr) apparatus re an analysis of the background characteristics, career patterns, & turnover rate of officials in the Soviet bur'cy, in 10 Chpts. (1) Identifying the Decision Makers, discusses the means by which the Soviet elite may be identified & studied, & states that the governing apparatus of the Ukr Soviet Republic provides abundant material for case study, though results of the examination cannot be generalized without qualification to the entire ruling group of the USSR. (2) The Elite as a Social Group, discusses personal status & soc relationships as stemming primarily from position within bur'tic structures. The soviet system furnishes categories indicative of the importance of the particular official within the apparatus; the stratification of positions within the apparatus & the nationality & soc backgrounds of officials are discussed. Mobility opportunities are analyzed. (3) Training for Rule, deals with Party educ & training programs, & the effects of this educ'al opportunity on the officials. (4) Bosses of the Apparatus, presents descriptions of various members of the Party elite, & their functions for the Party. It is seen that `line generalists' have greatest access to the most important apparatus positions. (5) Supervising the Economy, states that, next to pol'al control, the supervision of econ affairs is the major concern of the Soviet regime. The role of the Ukr apparatus in econ matters is analyzed re agri. (6) Mechanisms of Control, discusses the role of staff agencies in assuring the efficient functioning of Party machinery. Staff agencies are characterized by continuity of personnel, esp at lower apparatus levels. (7) Indoctrination Specialists, indicates the importance of Party propaganda `sections' & of various propaganda `secretaries' & officials. Evidence indicates that indoctrination officials are a group characterized by a high degree of internal solidarity & special interest. (8) The Apparatus in Crisis: Expansion, examines the adaptation of the Ukr apparatus to a stress situation engendered by pop & territorial increase & econ & soc difficulties. (9) The Apparatus in Crisis: War, discusses the adaptation of the Ukr gov'al apparatus to a crisis situation caused by the German invasion of 1941. (10) A New Oligarchy?, states that 'the att's & experience of the Ukr elite members ...enable them to fit more smoothly into the present oligarchic system than can many prominent officials from other segments of the apparatus in the USSR. Officials with experience in the Ukr can also use it as a working model for operating as an oligarchy on an all-Union scale. ...the increasing importance of the Ukr apparatus elite means a strengthening of oligarchic control of the USSR.' D. Cooperman.

title: Adaptive climate change governance for urban resilience
abstract: Climate change poses new challenges to cities and new flexible forms of governance are required that are able to take into account the uncertainty and abruptness of changes. The purpose of this paper is to discuss adaptive climate change governance for urban resilience. This paper identifies and reviews three traditions of literature on the idea of transitions and transformations, and assesses to what extent the transitions encompass elements of adaptive governance. This paper uses the open source Urban Transitions Project database to assess how urban experiments take into account principles of adaptive governance. The results show that: the experiments give no explicit information of ecological knowledge; the leadership of cities is primarily from local authorities; and evidence of partnerships and anticipatory or planned adaptation is limited or absent. The analysis shows that neither technological, political nor ecological solutions alone are sufficient to further our understanding of the analytical aspects of transition thinking in urban climate governance. In conclusion, the paper argues that the future research agenda for urban climate governance needs to explore further the links between the three traditions in order to better identify contradictions, complementarities or compatibilities, and what this means in practice for creating and assessing urban experiments.

title: Moving beyond BAC in DUI : Identifying Who Is at Risk of Recidivating
authors: Dugosh, Karen L; Festinger, David S
abstract: Driving under the influence (DUI) is one of the nation's top risks to public safety. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) (2010), approximately one third of all traffic fatalities in the United States are alcohol related. Furthermore, almost 20% of fatally injured drivers test positive for illicit substances, and when one considers only those cases where the fatally injured driver was tested for illicit substances, this proportion rises to approximately one third. Importantly, these statistics only reflect traffic accidents that resulted in a fatality. Although the majority of first-time offenders arrested for driving while impaired do not go on to repeat the offense, it is estimated that between 20% and 35% will become recidivist DUI offenders (e.g., Cornish and Marlowe, 2003; Schell, Chan, and Morral, 2006; Timken, 2002). In fact, impaired drivers who are involved in fatal car crashes are four times more likely to have a prior DUI conviction than nonimpaired drivers (NHTSA, 2012), and approximately 40% of fatally injured drunk drivers have a history of repeat DUI offenses (Lapham, Skipper, Hunt, and Chang, 2000). These alarming statistics highlight the need to identify first-time DUI offenders who may be at risk for becoming recidivist offenders. Although there has been a significant amount of research conducted to identify predictors of DUI recidivism (see Nochajski and Stasiewicz, 2006, for a review), the field has made fewer strides in identifying practical methods to determine who is at risk of recidivating in a way that is clinically useful to stakeholders and decision makers.

title: Governmentality and the politics of CSR
abstract: In this article we argue that an analytics of governmentality has an important contribution to make to the study of governmental approaches to corporate social responsibility (CSR). Looking at developments within the EU, we see government emerging as an enabling and empowering facilitator that a) promotes a strategic understanding of CSR as a lever for economic competitiveness and growth and b) disregards regulatory measures in favour of liberal and indirect means of steering. We argue that the analytical vocabulary of governmentality makes it possible to address and problematize the indirect modes of power and governing that are prevalent in governmental approaches to CSR in general and in neoliberal modes of CSR governance in particular. Using EU and member states policy developments as an empirical backdrop, we provide a conceptual exploration of the prospects of applying governmentality to the study of the changing roles of government in CSR. We position our contribution within the critical literature on CSR as a political phenomenon. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: THE DYNAMICS OF BUREAUCRACY
abstract: An empirical study (based on observation interviewing, & analysis of documents) of bur'tic org, with emphasis on the formal & informal mechanisms of control, adaptation, & change, & with a view toward conceptual refinement & theoretical generalization about structure & process in org's, in IV Parts & 15 Chpts. Chpt (1) The Empirical Study of Bureaucratic Structure and Function - discusses the functional approach to the study of structure & change in soc org. Part I - THE DEPARTMENTAL STRUCTURE IN A STATE EM- PLOYMENT AGENCY - contains (2) - Rules and Their Interpretation - analyzing the modification of the rules of employment interviewing that occurs as they are interpreted & applied on various levels of the bur'tic hierarchy & in particular situations; including a replication after 10 yrs. (3) Statistical Records of Performance - conceptualizes the use of statistical performance records as mechanisms of control & shows how the dysfunctional consequences of this innovation lead to new patterns of conduct superseding old ones, rather than to the re-establishment of an equilibrium. (4) Competition and Productivity - represents a comparative analysis of the structure & productivity of a competitive & a non-competitive Dept'al section, & demonstrates the existence & nature of structural effects as well as the dysfunctional consequences of competition for productivity & work satisfaction; & discusses the implications of these findings for the study of group structure. (5) 'Sine Ira Et Studio' - takes issue with the impersonality hypothesis of bur'tic theory by showing how racial & ethnic bias influences bur'tic decisions; shows also how, in turn, the specific bur'tic mechanism of statistical record keeping constrains officials to act impartially. Conclusions are qualified & refined in light of subsequent findings regarding discrimination, & point to the significance of the power & market structure of the surrounding community for bur'tic operations as well as their functional analysis. (6) Conflict With Clients - presents an 'analysis of practices that developed in response to strains in the relations to clients & their effects on bur'tic operations' & deals with the soc cost of resolving conflict & the development of anti-client norms. II - THE DEPART- MENTAL STRUCTURE IN THE FEDERAL ENFORCEMENT AGENCY - contains (7) Consultation Among Colleagues - discussing the pattern of consultation among agents as a response to legal regulations & operating rules, analyzing the functions of consultations in disguise, & introducing the concept of soc exchange. (8) The Network of Interpersonal Relations - discusses basic elements of a theory of group structure by way of analyzing the processes of interaction among co-workers, with a detailed discussion of the interrelation between SS & the processes of differentiation & integration. (9) Social Cohesion and Law Enforcement - is concerned with the soc mechanisms that enhance soc cohesion among agents & co-workers, which, in turn, contributes to effective law enforcement. The findings support the hypothesis that 'congenial informal relations between co-workers, & not completely detached ones, are a prerequisite for efficient bur'tic operations'. A theoretical note on the concept of particularism is included. (10) Unofficial Norms - analyzes the emergence of unofficial norms & their enforcement, & discusses the significance of norms as an integral element of the emergent soc structure of the dept'al group; & a discussion of studies of informal status & conformity. (11) The Exercise of Authority - discusses the concepts of authority & informal leadership, & shows how review of performance & supervisory control can be used to expand the scope of legitimate authority by transforming power relations into authority relations through the creation of soc obligations. III - THE PERMANENCE OF CHANGE - contains (12) Bureaucracy and Social Change - which 'is concerned with att's of officials toward change, esp with the hypothesis that bur'tic conditions [may] engender favorable att's toward change, & not necessarily resistance to change'. The concept of `succession of goals,' which refers to the development of new objectives subsequent to the attainment of original objectives, & which results from the soc, econ, & psychol'al interests & commitments of the members of the bur'tic org - is introduced. (13) The Dynamics of Bureaucratic Structure - reviews the relation between emergent org'al needs & structural change & places the discussion into a broader theoretical perspective on the adjustive development & change of soc structures. The paradox created by the co-existence of democratic & bur'tic instit's in society is discussed & it is suggested that the development of democratic methods for governing bur'ies. IV - METHODOLOGICAL EPI- LOGUE - contains (14) Fieldwork in Bureaucracy - deals with problems of study design & fieldwork, with the chronology of the study here reported, with the problem of entry into an org, & with the methodological & professional-ethical problems associated with the role of the field O. (15) The Process of Conceptual Refinement - represents a discussion of 4 'case histories of conceptual clarification': (a) Consultation - derived from the general principle that 'informal relations influence the performance of duties' & leading to the analysis of status differentiation among agents as well as to the concept of soc exchange; (b) Supervisory Authority - as based on the use of soc obligations, &, again, related to exchange processes; (c) Statistical Records of Performance - which at first were interpreted merely as a source of information about the performance of officials, & only in the course of fieldwork was the full significance of quantitative evaluation procedures for bur'tic operations realized; & (d) Organization of Analysis in terms of a Functional Framework - which served as a general guide throughout, but also led to the reconceptualization of functions & dysfunctions in terms of the concept of emergent need, & to the conception of 'dynamic processes of change in org's.' The Vol concludes with a discussion of the historical role of the case study & its contributions & limitations, & points to a 'new phase in the sociol'al investigation of formal org's' focussing on the 'principles that differentiate formal structures on the basis of systematic comparisons of org's'. R. V. Heydebrand.

title: La institucionalización del análisis de políticas públicas en España: Un campo científico dual/The Institutionalization of Policy Analysis in Spain: A Dual Scientific Field
abstract: Este artículo se centra en la institucionalización del análisis de las políticas públicas (app) en España entre 1975 y 2010 desde una perspectiva histórico-bibliométrica. Este análisis se basa en una muestra de 209 artículos (de un total de 3 098) publicados en cinco revistas científicas españolas de referencia en el ámbito de la sociología y la ciencia política. Este estudio explica como el app se institucionalizó en el ámbito de las ciencias sociales a partir de mediados de los años ochenta. Este proceso de difusión no ha sido homogéneo en términos de repartición geográfica, temas de estudio, métodos de análisis y teorías utilizadas. La conclusión insiste sobre el carácter dual de esta dinámica de institucionalización: por un lado, sigue existiendo un tipo de análisis de políticas públicas muy localista en España; por el otro, un conjunto de autores participa activamente en los debates internacionales.

title: From Government to Governance: Implications for Social Work Administration
authors: Frahm, Kathryn A; Martin, Lawrence L
abstract: The way in which our society governs itself has undergone a quiet revolution over the last two decades. Society is in the midst of a paradigm shift from what is known as a "government" paradigm to what is being called a "governance" paradigm. This article seeks to inform social work administrators about the importance of the shift. First, some background is provided on the "dueling paradigms" of the 1980s and 1990s, from which the governance paradigm emerged. Next, the major characteristics of the governance paradigm are identified and contrasted with the older, more established government paradigm. The implications of the governance paradigm for social work administration are then discussed. Finally, the article concludes with some thoughts about changes in the educational preparation of social work administrators required by the ascendance of the governance paradigm. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Ich versuch hier auch immer so dieses Amtliche irgendwie noch 'n bisschen zu überspielen Emotions- und Gefühlsarbeit in der öffentlichen Verwaltung als Ausdruck von Staatlichkeit im Wandel
abstract: In an increasingly pluralized society the public administration and its traditional inherent values like rationality, objectivity and impersonality have lost part of their legitimacy. Most citizens no longer accept an authoritarian manner or an approach in which they are subjected to bureaucratic rules and regulations. The new emphasis on customer and service orientation, which emerged in the public administration with the New Public Management reform of the last three decades, reflects the rising importance of new sources of legitimacy like proximity to citizens and procedural justice. However, empirically based research rarely addresses the issue of how this shift of sources of legitimacy affects the daily work of civil servants. This article describes, drawing on qualitative data, how emotional labor is becoming an important resource for the interaction of state and citizens. Moreover, we will show how the forms of emotional labor vary according to the interpretations of statehood and the professional identities of the civil servants.[PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Tissue Banks: Drafting New Rules for Grafting
abstract: In a case in Virginia in 1985, 56 patients received organ transplants and tissue grafts from a donor infected HIV.  Although there is no indication that the agencies involved were in any way remiss, the case focused attention on the fact that tissue banks have been heretofore unregulated.  The case prompted a surprisingly swift response from the government.  A working group was quickly formed, and a memorandum outlining the group's findings was submitted by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner to the Department of Health and Human Services.  The report included recommendations that: 1.  the Public Health Service prepare national standards for donor screening, testing, reporting, and record keeping, 2.  tissue banks and transplant programs be required to comply with these standards through voluntary compliance, contract, or regulation, and 3.  the FDA assert jurisdiction over currently unregulated tissue banks and tissue-processing facilities so that federal oversight would be provided for all biological products.

title: BUREAUCRACY AGAINST DEMOCRACY AND SOCIALISM
authors: Glassman, Ronald M; Swatos, William H, Jr; Rosen, Paul L
abstract: Oriented in part to Max Weber's analysis of bureaucracy, this collection of essays, No. 65 in the Contributions to Sociology series (Don Martindale, series editor), attempts to assess the current state of bureaucratic administration in both capitalism & socialism, & to consider solutions to the problems posed by bureaucracy, in III PARTS & 14 Chpts with Epilogue & editors' Introduction. PART I - THE PROBLEM - includes (1) Wolfgang Schluchter -- From Government over Persons to the Administration of Things: Marx and Engels on Bureaucracy -- examines texts of Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels, & V. I. Lenin to demonstrate their concern with the elimination of bureaucracy in favor of a primitive democracy embodying the principles of self-government; (2) Ernest Kilker -- Max Weber and the Possibilities for Socialism -- see SA 33:5/85Q1131; (3) Wolfgang J. Mommsen -- Max Weber and the Crisis of Liberal Democracy -- argues that for Weber, the adaptation of liberal principles to the conditions of industrial society required a critical understanding of the restraints placed by bureaucracy on the free initiative of the individual personality; & (4) Ronald M. Glassman -- Conflicts between Legal and Bureaucratic Systems of Authority -- discusses the evolution of systems of authority based on rational efficiency, on the one hand, & adherence to law, on the other, delineates the areas in which they frequently conflict, & poses the question of whether bureaucratic authority must eventually undermine legal authority. PART II - AUTHORITARIAN TENDENCIES - contains (5) Kathi Vallone Friedman -- Social Rights in the Welfare State: The Contrast between Adjudication and Administration in the United States -- develops a distinction between social rights & gratuitous benefits, describes the growing power of the welfare state in administering benefits, & argues that the weaker legitimation of the welfare state will make necessary the creation of a welfare society based on social rights & the free exchange of talents; (6) Paul L. Rosen -- The Patient at Peril: Hospital Bureaucracy and Medical Records; (7) Robert Jackall -- The Moral Ethos of Bureaucracy -- see SA 33:5/85Q1532; (8) Kenneth O'Reilly -- Bureaucracy and Civil Liberties: The FBI Story; & (9) William M. Jones -- Bureaucracy and Rationalization in the Soviet Police. PART III - SOLUTIONS IN SERVICE TO DEMOCRACY - includes (10) Ira Glasser -- Power versus Liberty in the Welfare State: A Bill of Rights for Social Service Beneficiaries; (11) Ralph Nader, Mark Green, & Joel Seligman -- "Constitutionalizing" Corporations: An Employee Bill of Rights; (12) Robert A. Dahl -- Industrial Democracy in the Era of Corporate Leviathan -- argues for a concept of self-government opposed to both private & state ownership of economic enterprises; (13) Donald C. Rowat -- Why Democracies Need a Legislative Ombudsman; & (14) Lisa K. Armour -- Quality Circles: Implications for American Management. Epilogue -- William H. Swatos, Jr. -- Bureaucracy and Its Discontents. 2 Tables, 85 References.

title: Are Some Citizens More Equal than Others? Evidence from a Field Experiment
authors: Grohs, Stephan; Adam, Christian; Knill, Christoph
abstract: The equal treatment of all citizens is one of the fundamental principles of good administrative practice. Nevertheless, there are growing numbers of media and scientific reports on unequal treatment by public administrations. This article examines the unequal treatment of citizens by gender and ethnic origin by means of a survey-based field experiment in German local government. With the help of two vignettes and randomized assignment of names, responses to fake citizen requests by local governments are analyzed for speed, quality, and service orientation. The results show very limited discrimination effects. While there is no evidence for general ethnic discrimination, a more differentiated analysis indicates patterns of ethnic discrimination conditioned by gender.Grohs, Adam, and Knill Podcast Episode

title: BUREAUCRACY AND RACE: NATIVE ADMINISTRATION IN SOUTH AFRICA
abstract: This 53rd Vol in the series Perspectives on Southern Africa explores the relation between racial domination & bureacratic growth in South Africa, drawing on a history of the Dept of Native Affairs in the 1940s & 1950s. It is demonstrated that apartheid was not implemented through military means, but through the everyday work of civil administration. During the segregationist liberal era, the department had to negotiate conflicts between farmers, miners, & industrialists for cheap African labor & its role as a moderating influence on the economy. Doing so required the development of an official ideology that claimed that extensive state interventions into the economy conflicted with the rationality of the free market. This free market ideology accommodated a variety of voices in native administration in the 1930s & 1940s. By steering clear of extensive involvement in the proletarianization & distribution of cheap African labor, the department avoided a large role in state formation in the 1950s, & succeeded in ameliorating the harshest implications of racial supremacy. In the 1950s, native administration was reorganized to take a more active role in native relocation & labor allocation, policies that eroded the paternalist sensibilities that characterized the earlier segregation era. Four analytic points are culled from this history: (1) paternalism was eroded in native administration over time, to be replaced by greater bureaucratic modernization & rationalization; (2) divisions between liberal & proapartheid administrators were negotiated at the level of civil administration, but not at the policy level; (3) myriad bureaucratic tools opened considerable space between coercion & compliance, resistance & consent, for both the administrators of apartheid & the blacks at whom it was directed; & (4) bureaucracy & race were therefore deeply entwined in the apartheid era. A Preface, Introduction, & Conclusion frame the book's 8 Chpts with Notes, organized in II PARTS. 540 References. D. M. Smith

title: Opening Government: Designing Open Innovation Processes to Collaborate With External Problem Solvers
abstract: Open government initiatives in the U.S. government focus on three main aspects: transparency, participation, and collaboration. Especially the collaboration mandate is relatively unexplored in the literature. In practice, government organizations recognize the need to include external problem solvers into their internal innovation creation processes. This is partly derived from a sense of urgency to improve the efficiency and quality of government service delivery. Another formal driver is the America Competes Act that instructs agencies to search for opportunities to meaningfully promote excellence in technology, education, and science. Government agencies are responding to these requirements by using open innovation (OI) approaches to invite citizens to crowdsource and peer produce solutions to public management problems. These distributed innovation processes occur at all levels of the U.S. government and it is important to understand what design elements are used to create innovative public management ideas. This article systematically reviews existing government crowdsourcing and peer production initiatives and shows that after agencies have defined their public management problem, they go through four different phases of the OI process: (1) idea generation through crowdsourcing, (2) incubation of submitted ideas with peer voting and collaborative improvements of favorite solutions, (3) validation with a proof of concept of implementation possibilities, and (4) reveal of the selected solution and the (internal) implementation of the winning idea. Participation and engagement are incentivized both with monetary and nonmonetary rewards, which lead to tangible solutions as well as intangible innovation outcomes, such as increased public awareness.

title: Does location matter? Measuring environmental perceptions of creeks in two San Antonio watersheds
authors: Brody, Samuel D; Highfield, Wes; Alston, Letitia
abstract: In the past, researchers in the field of environmental psychology have explained environmental perceptions primarily through socioeconomic and demographic factors. However, knowledge of and support for protecting specific natural features of the landscape should also be influenced by one's location, setting, and proximity to such features. This article focuses on residents'familiarity with and concern for two creeks passing through San Antonio, TX. Using Geographic Information Systems analytical techniques, we expand on previous studies by introducing driving distance from the creeks to identify the effects of this location-based variable on environmental perceptions. Specifically, we test the degree to which the actual driving distance respondents live from two creeks affects respondents' knowledge and perceptions of the water bodies. We show that when controlling for socioeconomic and geographic contextual variables, the residential distance variable remains a significant factor in explaining both familiarity with the creeks and views on the level of water pollution in them. Based on the results, we discuss the implications of incorporating proximity factors in watershed planning and policy.

title: Scaling-up antiretroviral treatment in Southern African countries with human resource shortage: How will health systems adapt?
authors: Damme, Wim Van; Kober, Katharina; Kegels, Guy
abstract: Scaling-up antiretroviral treatment (ART) to socially meaningful levels in low-income countries with a high AIDS burden is constrained by (1) the continuously growing caseload of people to be maintained on long-term ART; (2) evident problems of shortage and skewed distribution in the health workforce; and (3) the heavy workload inherent to presently used ART delivery models. If we want to imagine how health systems can react to such challenges, we need to understand better what needs to be done regarding the different types of functions ART requires, and how these can be distributed through the care supply system, knowing that different functions rely on different rationales (professional, bureaucratic, social) for which the human input need not necessarily be found in formal healthcare supply systems. Given the present realities of an increasingly pluralistic healthcare supply and highly eclectic demand, we advance three main generic requirements for ART interventions to be successful: trustworthiness, affordability and exclusiveness - and their constituting elements. We then apply this analytic model to the baseline situation (no fundamental changes) and different scenarios. In Scenario A there are no fundamental changes, but ART gets priority status and increased resources. In Scenario B the ART scale-up strengthens the overall health system: we detail a B1 technocratic variant scenario, with profoundly re-engineered ART service production, including significant task shifting, away from classical delivery models and aimed at maximum standardisation and control of all operations; while in the B2 community-based variant scenario the typology of ART functions is maximally exploited to distribute the tasks over a human potential pool that is as wide as possible, including patients and possible communities. The latter two scenarios would entail a high degree of de-medicalisation of ART. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Corporate Philanthropists Give Up on the "Free Lunch"
abstract: People the world over are examining the value and uses of charity, philanthropy, and volunteerism.  In the US, however, the current readjustment of world markets, currency, and trade balance and the rise of the international-multinational firm, have retarded corporate giving.  The lean corporate structure has become a goal.  The lack of continuity and training in corporate contributions management has led to a less than consistent record of giving.  Some firms have emphasized the link between charitable donations and the special product and corporate marketing interests of the firm.  The new entrepreneur looks at charitable giving in creative and unconventional ways.  The Japanese now are realizing that they need to be perceived by the US people as more charitable, returning part of what their businesses make through sales to the US market.  The Reagan Administration's attempt to promote private-sector solutions to public problems was not sufficiently far reaching to have a major impact.

title: Modernist Infrastructure and the Vital Systems Security of Water: Singapore's Pluripotent Climate Futures
abstract: Singapore climate change adaptation planning for water infrastructure is assessed against the concept of "vital security systems." Cast against the historicity of water planning and postcolonial urbanism, water supply, coastal protection, and flood control are understood in terms of vigilance, emergency, prediction, and control. It is argued that climate adaptation planning relies on a naturalistic understanding of predictable, linear transformations in base climatic variables and thus fails to take into consideration the "pluripotency" of climate futures -- that is, the inherent unpredictability of nonlinear transformations that arise in the conjunction of human and nonhuman systems. [web URL: http://publicculture.dukejournals.org/content/28/2_79/415.abstract]

title: CORRUPT EXCHANGES: ACTORS, RESOURCES, AND MECHANISMS OF POLITICAL CORRUPTION
abstract: In offering a new model for studying & understanding political corruption, & with focus on the Italian case, this Vol looks at the resources that fuel corruption & examines corruption in politics -- particularly the corruption that surfaces among business, or career, politicians. Also addressed are the role that political parties play in corrupt political transactions, & the corruption that emerges as a result of the high cost of politics. Bureaucratic corruption & corruption of the judiciary are discussed, along with corruption among actors on the political fringes, covert power, & the hidden agenda of corruption. The role that organized crime plays in political corruption is examined. The book concludes by looking at Italy's "crisis of the regime": ie, the collapse of the country's political system as a result of the political protection accorded organized crime. The book concludes that democracies throughout the world must make attempts at substantial self-reformation. If corruption is allowed to continue in its current state, the democratic political system will rapidly begin to degenerate. This text contains 39 Chpts in IX PARTS. References. K. A. Larsen

title: Good Governance, State Capacity, and the Millennium Development Goals
abstract: International development agencies argue that "good governance" is crucial to attaining the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), but there are many ways to define and measure good governance. The paper begins by examining the World Bank's minimal state conception of governance and then proposes an alternative approach based on strengthening state capacity. The paper tests this framework by developing a provisional Millennium Governance Index (MGI) for 126 countries. In comparative empirical analysis, the MGI has noticeably higher statistical correlations than the World Bank's governance indicators on six out of seven MDGs even after controlling for per capita income levels. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Infrastructure in the Air: The Office of Education and the Development of Public Broadcasting in the United States, 1934-1944
abstract: This paper examines the origins of the institutional organization and advocacy strategies that later culminated in American public broadcasting. Previous to the Communications Act of 1934, which privatized American broadcasting, educational radio lacked standards for best practices and functioned in a decentralized and localized form. After the Act, the Office of Education (OOE) took interest in radio as a medium to expand federal initiatives related to educational 'public forums,' town-hall style meetings centered around community debate. Noting the lack of noncommercial channels in which to broadcast forums to a larger audience, the OOE began to collaborate with the National Association of Educational Broadcasters (NAEB) to lobby the FCC, while producing civic programming with commercial broadcasters. Instead of fighting the regulation, the OOE and NAEB founded an advocacy approach centered on creating an alternate broadcasting infrastructure as a way to address regulatory precedents. In this process, early forms of production, distribution, and infrastructure later associated with public broadcasting were devised out of a hybrid of commercial broadcasting aesthetics and federal educational bureaucracy. Contrary to the received view, discussion of the origins of American public broadcasting must be framed as advocacy to change the national system through strategies of research, collaboration, and governmental incorporation instead of resistance. Adapted from the source document.

title: Book review: Transboundary Water Politics in the Developing World
abstract: Mirumachi, Naho Transboundary Water Politics in the Developing World. London: Routledge/Earthscan, 2015; 202 pp.: 9780415812955, £85.00 (hbk).

title: The Manufacture of Popular Perceptions of Scarcity: Dams and Water-Related Narratives in Gujarat, India
abstract: This paper critically examines some narratives of water scarcity in Kutch, western India. It argues that images of dwindling rainfall & increasing drought largely serve to legitimize the controversial Sardar Sarovar dam & manufacture dominant perceptions concerning scarcity. This manufacture has naturalized scarcity in the region & largely benefits powerful actors such as politicians, industrialists, & large farmers. But the needs of the poor in water-limited areas are neglected. By exploring the various connotations of scarcity, the paper argues that scarcity is both a biophysical phenomenon as well as a powerful discursive construct. By distinguishing between the "real" & "manufactured" aspects of water scarcity, the paper attempts to enhance understandings of environmental change at the local level. 2 Tables, 3 Figures, 51 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Professionalisation of the public service in South Africa: A reflection on past and future challenges within the context of a public governance and leadership paradigm
abstract: The essence of a healthy state demands the establishment and maintenance of a professional public service. From this perception, questions such as appropriate structure and competent and responsive incumbents of such structures often arise. This article explores the need to ensure that senior public officials, in particular, meet the requirements of professionalism. The challenge is predominant within the management and leadership cadres of the public sector, which should ensure that the state is indeed meeting its strategic developmental goals and objectives, and that such effect is filtered down to all the spheres of government. This article explores and critically reflects on the post-1994 history of training and development of a new and emerging cadre of senior public officials in South Africa – and the contextual factors that impacted on this challenge. It focuses on the evaluation of institutional arrangements for the delivery of education and training programmes for this purpose, and provides reasons for the general sense that these institutions and programmes have failed to produce a professional senior public service. The pursuit of a Public Governance and Leadership model in favour of deficient Public Administration and Management models is proposed. In addition, the author explains why there needs to be holistic plans in place to ensure professionalisation of the senior public service and proposes requirements for a significant improvement in competent, ethical and performancedirected leadership qualities – that would ultimately lead to improved service delivery to the South African public.

title: The Anxious and Ambivalent Partisan: The Effect of Incidental Anxiety on Partisan Motivated Recall and Ambivalence
abstract: Affective Intelligence Theory (AIT) asserts that anxiety reduces the effect of party identification on candidate preferences (Marcus, Neuman, and MacKuen 2000), but recent studies have raised doubts about this causal claim. Rather than functioning as a moderator of party identification, perhaps anxiety has a direct effect on preferences, or perhaps the relationship is reversed and preferences drive emotions (Ladd and Lenz 2008). Alternatively, Marcus et al.'s measure of anxiety may simply be capturing partisan ambivalence, so the posited relationship is spurious (Lavine, Johnston, and Steenbergen 2012). This paper addresses each of these questions by examining the effect of experimentally induced emotions on the types of considerations that came to mind when a national sample of adult Americans was asked what they liked and disliked about Barack Obama. By directly manipulating anxiety, this experiment avoids the causal ambiguity plaguing this debate and ascertains the true nature of the relationship between anxiety and ambivalence. Consistent with AIT, anxiety led respondents to recall more contemporary considerations, whereas enthusiasm brought to mind more long-standing considerations. Because the political context at the time of the study (fall 2013) was a very tumultuous time for the Obama administration, the increased accessibility of contemporary considerations led Democratic participants to experience more ambivalence in the anxiety condition. This effect was concentrated among those Democrats who were exposed to the most newspaper coverage. [web URL: http://poq.oxfordjournals.org/content/80/2/460.abstract]

title: PUBLIC BUREAUCRACY AND JUDICIARY IN PAKISTAN
abstract: A lengthy discussion of the relationship between the judicial & admin'ive sectors of the Pakistani public service. At the time of partitioning, the Pakistani bur'cy lacked an adequate pool of talent because of the lack of Muslims with colonial admin'ive training & experience in the old Indian public service. The few officials imbued with the traditional bur'tic orientation were unable to transmit these norms to the new members of the bur'cy; at the same time, such an orientation (rationality, impersonality, etc) provoked hostility within the society at large, at least to some extent because of its symbolic links with the colonial past. By way of contrast, the judiciary was popularly viewed as a symbol of liberty & independence, a picture it has tended to reinforce through its legal restraints upon the bur'cy via writ jurisdiction; however, recent events have tended to weaken this power. (See SA 0715-B3371). D. W. Ball.

title: Transition experiments in Amsterdam: Conceptual and empirical analysis of two transition experiments in the WATERgraafsmeer program
authors: Porter, Nadia; Claassen, Maarten; Timmermans, Jos
abstract: In the wake of a rapidly changing world, cities need to cope with global threats and opportunities, and changing societal demands regarding living standards in cities. These are urgent issues for mega cities in the global South, and are becoming increasingly relevant for the more consolidated cities in the North. In the Watergraafsmeer area, a low-lying urban polder area in the eastern part of Amsterdam, water issues are a salient problem and are perceived as persistent by citizens, businesses, and the municipal and water management authorities alike. Therefore, under the flag of the WATERgraafsmeer (WGM) program, municipal and water management authorities and local partners adopted transition management as a governance approach to change. In transition management, experimenting is a vital activity. The present research analyzed the WGM program and the Eenhoorn redevelopment project in the Watergraafsmeer as transition experiments. The research used recently developed management guidelines for transition experiments as an evaluative framework for the systematic analysis of project documentation and written communication. The analysis shows that the WGM program functions well as a transition experiment, and that the limited transition potential of the Eenhoorn project is strengthened by its incorporation in the WGM program. Furthermore, we conclude that the management guidelines for transition experiments do not incorporate interaction processes between projects and program, and do not pay attention to technology and engineering.

title: 'Working Together?': The Salvation Army and the Job Network
abstract: This article explores the changing relationship between government and The Salvation Army, as manifested in the development and implementation of employment policy in Australia between 1998 and 2007. This exploration focuses on the introduction of market discourse throughout the contracting process, in particular how this discourse seeks to reconstruct service users as 'consumers', and the Salvation Army's response to this. By studying the ways in which this religiously and socially motivated non-profit organization sought to mediate neo-liberal discourses of competition and consumerism, we seek to shed light on the processes and pressures affecting faith-based and other non-profit organizations that increasingly find themselves acting as agents of government policy under the principles of New Public Management (NPM).

title: THE EXECUTIVE: AUTOCRAT, BUREAUCRAT, DEMOCRAT
abstract: A description of the essential characteristics of the executive's (EX's) role, emphasizing the fact that the EX's selfimage is the most important factor in his role, with an author's Preface, in 8 Chpts. Chpt (1) The Blurred Executive Image, traces the transition from personal rule to group rule, with its resulting confusion & ambiguity. (2) The Executive Duality, suggests the conflict between the desire for & impermanence of resolution, a duality which administration must recognize & cope with in order to function properly. (3) Executive Calisthenics, traces the `composite of emotional opposites' caused by the simultaneous recognition of authority & assumption of authority. The effective EX perceives his role realistically, as being a composite one. (4) How Executives Develop, describes 3 basic approaches: (A) the autocratic (B) the bur'tic, & (C) the democratic. (5) The Autocrat, analyzes a 'basic behavior pattern that is rich with tradition,' ie, that of a man who is masterful & competent, who controls & manipulates forces about him, & on whom everyone relies. (6) The Bureaucrat, characterizes the man who copes with responsibility by means of procedures & org's. Relationships are highly formalized. Such an approach tends to produce petrification. (7) The Democrat, discusses 'the sharing orientation'. While incorporating some elements of autocracy & bur'cy, democracy is able to bring 'the EX's instruments of power & order within Neurocrat and the Flexible Executive, studies the role of personal anxiety & neuroses in the performance of the EX, & contrasts him with the flexible, healthy EX. An Index. A. Chapman.

title: Hard Choices or No Choices: Assessing Program Review
abstract: A book review of Hard Choices or No Choices: Assessing Program Review, edited by Amelita Armit and Jacques Bourgault, is presented.

title: Under New Public Management: Institutional Ethnographies of Changing Front-Line Work
abstract: Hallett reviews Under New Public Management: Institutional Ethnographies of Changing Front-Line Work edited by Alison I Griffith and Dorothy E Smith.

title: The global construction of development models: the US, Japan and the East Asian miracle
abstract: During the heyday of the 'Washington Consensus' in the 1980s and 1990s, the Japanese government became an increasingly vocal critic of its market-liberalizing prescriptions. Drawing on documents produced by the Japanese development bureaucracy, this paper analyses the origins of the Washington-Tokyo controversy, and suggests that it provides new insights into the nature of models of economic development. Such models are based on post hoc social constructs--interpretations of past events forged in part by development experts, but also by states, which can play a major role in selecting, interpreting and packaging development facts. Washington's 'Anglo-Saxon' model and Tokyo's 'East Asian' model were based on distinct interpretations of development facts, but were not as far apart as they seemed on the surface. We conclude that although development models may draw on local materials, they are also very much global products, constructed in the context of transnational networks and organizational fields.

title: Second Generation Reform in Latin America: Reforming the Public Sector in Uruguay and Mexico
abstract: Uruguay & Mexico have both passed laws aiming to professionalise the public sector bureaucracy according to what might be considered 'second generation' reform principles. They did so under what might initially have seemed to be politically unpropitious circumstances. The reforms might have been vetoed by interests that feared that they would lose out from the changes, but were not. They might have been blocked by conditions of minority presidentialism, but were not. This article seeks to explain the successful passing of this reform legislation. Framing issues played a significant role in reducing opposition. Notably important was the way in which the reforms were presented, & specifically the ability of their proponents to avoid presenting them as market-friendly reforms. The political context also provided the reformers with arguments that in the end proved persuasive. Adapted from the source document.

title: Are We Really on the Same Page? An Empirical Examination of Value Congruence Between Public Sector and Nonprofit Sector Managers
authors: Miller-stevens, Katrina; Taylor, Jennifer A; Morris, John C
abstract: Much attention has recently been paid to comparative work in the public and private sectors looking at work values, motivations, and the impact of government reform movements in organizations. Several studies have compared the public and private sectors in the dimension of values; but none have questioned the popular assumption that nonprofit and public managers share the same or a similar set of values or the value expectations they have for each other. This paper reports on the results of an empirical survey of public and nonprofit managers that compares their individual democratic, ethical, and professional values. In brief, the results lend strong support to the assumption that nonprofit employees share the same value set as their public sector counterparts; but their value sets do have statistically significant differences in the perceived level of importance of altruism, generosity, and individualism.

title: Limits of the Game of Masks: Class, Ethno-religious Identities, and the Rise of Salafi-Jihadism in Northern Nigeria
abstract: The intermediary bourgeois (our ruling elite) cannot claim political leadership openly on the grounds that he is, or wants to be, an exporter, shareholder, rentier or rich bureaucrat. He has to take over as a Muslim or Christian. He has to take over as an Ibo, Hausa, Idoma or Efik.... The manipulation of religion in Nigeria today is essentially a means of creating the context for this fancy dress ball, for this charade of disguises. This game of masks. (Yusuf Bala Usman 1979: 88-89)

title: Mussolini, charisma and decision-making
abstract: Mussolini's authority was established on the basis of a complex system of rivalries that existed between different agencies (political, personal, party, senior administration, traditional and parallel bureaucracies, business, etc.) which brought the competition into a political market. In this market, the Duce and the Fascist Party - each with their own respective infrastructures - controlled access to resources and exchange mechanisms that determined the quality of the actors. Mussolini was perfectly aware of this, and he managed it by favouring the most faithful and loyal of groups. At the same time, he had to be vigilant not to dilute his charismatic authority by becoming merely the organisation's leader: such work required the continuous intensification of his myth. All these operations inevitably led to a process of deregulation that upset the decision-making process.Keywords: Mussolini, Fascism, decision-making, government, authority, Charisma

title: Corporate CEOs, 1890-2015: Titans, Bureaucrats, and Saviors
authors: Mizruchi, Mark S; Marshall, Linroy J, II
abstract: Corporate chief executive officers (CEOs) have occupied important positions of power in developed societies since the nineteenth century. In this article, we describe how the nature and extent of this power has changed over time in the United States: from the corporate titans of the early twentieth century, to the bureaucratic organization men of the mid-twentieth century, to a new generation of dynamic, charismatic corporate leaders today. We discuss how the shareholder value movement in the 1980s transformed the role of the CEO and how, paradoxically, as the CEOs' compensation increased, their autonomy declined, potentially reducing their ability to focus on the long-term concerns of their firms or the larger society. We review the literature on CEO compensation, tenure, and discretionary actions, including philanthropic contributions, research and development expenditures, and political action. We conclude with a discussion of the social responsibility of contemporary corporate leaders, while pointing to the need for studies with which we can compare the views of today's CEOs with those of earlier decades.

title: Urban Spaces and Experiences of qigong
abstract: Investigates the practice of qigong, traditional breathing & health exercises, among the Chinese urban populations, drawing on ethnographic fieldwork conducted in Beijing (People's Republic of China) in the early 1990s. A common complaint among city inhabitants is that the city has become more chaotic & dangerous. Qigong is practiced in urban parks as an antidote to this chaos, which represent a refuge from urban turmoil. Qigong associations are formed by groups along a continuum from officially bureaucratic organizations to popular revitalist movements headed by charismatic masters. The bureaucracy has attempted to harness the power of qigong by creating boundaries of legitimate scientific enterprise, while appropriating it for use in officially mediated public space. However, the bureaucracy is being challenged in this regard by the rise of charismatic masters who see in the practice a lucrative enterprise. Thus, qigong is representative of the ambivalent nature of public space in the postreform era, where an ever-watchful state remains eager to harness the popularity of new urban forms & wrest them away from the control of entrepreneurial individuals. D. M. Smith

title: THE ORGANIZATION OF SOCIETY,
abstract: A sociol text with the concepts of soc org & org'al change as themes, & utilizing a multilineal evolutionary frame of reference for the analysis of soc org, in IV parts & 22 Chpts, with an Author's Preface & Index. I-THE CONCEPTUAL TOOLS OF SOCIOLOGY, contains: (1) What is Sociology? (2) A Definition of Social Organization, (3) Some Sources of Variation Among Social Organization, (4) Some Important Types of Organizations, & (5) Organizational Change. II-THE URBANIZATION AND INDUSTRIALIZATION OF SOCIETIES, includes: (6) The Social Organization of the Pre-Urban Society, (7) The Social Organization of Agrarian Societies, (8) Organizational Change: Industrialization, (9) The Social Organization of the Mass-Industrial Society, & (10) The Social Organization of the Welfare-Bureaucratic Society. III-OR- GANIZATIONAL INTEGRATION AND CHANGE IN AMERICAN SOCIETY, offers: (11) An Introduction to American Society, (12) Social Classes in American Society, (13) Class Differences in American Society, (14) Religion in American Society, (15) Race and Nationality, (16) The Consequences of Segmentation, (17) Some Sources of Integration, & (18) The Family as Integrative Influence. IV-THE CENTRALIZATION OF INFLUENCE AND THE EMERGENCE OF THE TOTAL SO- CIETY, presents: (19) The Centralization of Influence in Contemporary Societies, (20) Socialisms, (21) Totalitarianism, & (22) The Changing Shape of American Society. D. Cooperman.

title: MEN WHO MANAGE: FUSIONS OF FEELING AND THEORY IN ADMINISTRATION
abstract: A study of 'compromises among key individuals & groups in rational org's, & the human strictures on compromise,' in 11 Chpt's, with an Author's preface. Data was drawn from 4 industrial firms in the Central US, & 1 department store in the same region. Methodology relied on formal & informal interviews, & participant-observation. The field of study concentrated on 'concessive exchanges among & between vertical & horizontal groups,' generalizing on compromise between 2 types of managers: the systematizers & routinizers, & the adapters & reorganizers. Chpt (1) serves as an Introduction commenting on the companies studied, related literature, & a list of problem areas to be examined in later Chpts: (i) pressures for economy of operation, (ii) `cooperation' of officially powerless experts with their admin'ive superiors, (iii) local meaning found by union & management in the high level work agreements to which they are subject, (iv) uncertainty about the route to a place in middle & upper manag, & (v) the task of recognizing & rewarding differential contributions. A residuum & accompaniment of these org'al problems are (vi) the psychol'al & moral conflicts of the individual executive who must balance the spirit & letter of the firm & the claims of subordinates & associates. Chpt (2) Managers on Paper - describes the formal structure of Mil, 1 of 2 firms observed through participation, & 3 theories of industrial org: StraightLine org, Functional Org, & Staff-Line Org, with tables. Chpt (3) Power Struggles in the Line - charts the schisms between nominal & exercised authority in struggles for dominance between managers of production & maintenance branches, & between the entire Milo unit & its Office. Official vs Unofficial Authority, Operation vs Maintenance, & Cliques as Fountainheads of Action, are analyzed in detail. Intrinsic factors contributing to the rise of cliques are seen as: (i) DofL, (ii) variations in identification with the firm, (iii) changes in the industrial community, & (iv) compulsion of growth. Cliques fall into 3 groups: vertical (V), horizational(H), & random. V symbiotic, V parasitic, H aggressive & H defensive cliques are particularized. Still studying Milo, Chpt (4) details Relations Between Staff & Line - discussing the Informal Staff Practices Conflicts Over Methods & Authority, & analyzes disharmonies in terms of diff's in: educ, age, professional consciousness, & external soc diff's. The diverse expectations & job prospects of Staff & Line, reflected in soc & functional diff's, are considered. Chpt (5) Local Meanings of High Level Labor Agreements - deals with union- management relations, under nat'l labor contracts, in all 3 firms in terms of The Labor Contract consequent behavior in local plants. This behavior is seen as a series of internal & plant-community compromises involving minority groups, & is characterized by: resistance to contract, worker initiative, managerial expediency, & econ & production pressures. Chpt (6) The Managerial Career Ladder - treats problems of entry & climb through the hierarchy, limited to a study of Milo. Res methods utilized formal interviews with high officers, official statements in supervisory manuals & handbooks, unofficial statements from initiates, a check of the accumulated data against open plant files. Informal, rather than formal factors are shown to have more significance in successful upward mobility, through a scrutiny of: occup'al data (age, yrs of service, educ), unofficial choice of candidates for open positions, demotions, sinecures competence for office, salary variations, & unofficial Requirements for Success (including Masonic membership, ancestry or ethnic composition, club membership, & pol'al affiliation). Chpt 7 - The Interlocking of Official and Unofficial Reward - considers the problem of unofficially rewarding implicit contributions to the org, as distinct from the need to prevent misuse of the firm's materials & services. The unofficial use of company resources as inducements, rewards, & perquisites & the link between ineptly used tacity reward & pilfering rights, is explored in relation to managerial motivation, the question of theft, & unofficial incentives. (8) The Interconnections of Formal and Informal Action - presents the historical background of the problem of fusing open & covert phases of org, & considers formal & informal as terms & as aspects of org, before examining the interplay of formal & informal. The org is seen as a shifting set of disruptive yet contained phases of action. Some steps & mechanisms that connect the formal & informal & enable them to maintain ongoing action are: official meetings, ordered unofficial action, granted departures from formal methods, the transitional role, & prefigured justifications. (9) The Manager Between Formal & Informal - develops the effects of compromise on individuals in terms of: the clash of individual vs org, the paradox of coerced freedom (ie, the freedom to choose alternative means, official or not, to gain ends, to devise new means, or to appear to conform if necessary), & the issues of ambiguity. 'The individual manager is caught in a scheme of rational, emotional, soc, & ethical claims' which cause some inner conflict. 'Competence in mastering confusion is achieved through a vague reworking of perspectives that stem from critical interpersonal involvements. Org's are systems of formal roles that direct & shape role occupants. The org forces role occupants to assert, but compromise, their innately human purposes.' Chpt (10) Conclusions - presents the larger meanings gleaned from the study: (i) all firms were typical, (ii) conflict is therefore typical also, & can have some positive aspects, notably: creativity, development, & innovation, (iii) a bur'tic theory surveys the att's current in the US & suggests the combination of autocracy, oligarchy, & democracy as necessary to the structure & operation of an org. The bur'tic firm is termed an extension of the community. Conformity as a means, & conditions promoting conformity, are considered, in relation to the individual vis a vis society, as largely an urge toward consistency in the recurring issue of the impersonal org vs the personalizing individual. An `Appendix on Method,' bibliog, & separate author & subject indexes. J. Atkins.

title: The Making of the Chinese Industrial Workplace: State, Revolution, and Labor Management
abstract: Lee reviews The Making of the Chinese Industrial Workplace: State, Revolution, and Labor Management by Mark W. Frazier.

title: 'Cold spots' of Urban Infrastructure: 'Shrinking' Processes in Eastern Germany and the Modern Infrastructural Ideal
abstract: This article explores the unfamiliar, but increasingly prevalent problem of overcapacity in urban infrastructure systems in regions subject to dramatic socio-economic restructuring. Taking the case of water supply and wastewater disposal systems in Eastern Germany as an example, it examines firstly how infrastructure overcapacities have emerged since reunification in 1990 as a result both of sharply declining water consumption in the wake of 'shrinking' processes and of infrastructure expansion. Secondly, the article analyses what impact chronic overcapacity is having on the governance of water infrastructure systems. This empirical analysis is framed conceptually in terms of the current debate on the changing relationship between infrastructures and the localities they serve. It assesses specifically how far and in what ways the phenomenon of overcapacity in technical networks resonates with the 'splintering urbanism' thesis developed by Stephen Graham and Simon Marvin. It argues that the serious technical and economic problems posed by overcapacity are intensifying spatial disparities in service quality and price, and--more fundamentally--are challenging the supply-driven 'modern infrastructural ideal' of universal and equitable water services.

title: Intrahousehold Disparities in Women and Men's Experiences of Water Insecurity and Emotional Distress in Urban Bolivia
abstract: This study is one of the first to examine the links connecting water insecurity, gender, and emotional distress. The article presents quantitative and qualitative analyses of interview data collected from randomly selected pairs of male and female household heads (n =48) living under the same household-level conditions of water insecurity. The results provide partial confirmation of past findings that women are more likely than men to be burdened with everyday water responsibilities. However, there were no significant differences between men's and women's experiences in household water emergencies (i.e., water shortages and last-ditch attempts to buy water) and reports on some measures of emotional distress (i.e., worry, annoyance, and anger with family members). The results suggest that intrahousehold gender disparities may be mitigated in times of severe water scarcity. The discussion raises questions about the comparability of men's and women's expressions of emotional distress. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: A brief review of radiolarian research
abstract: The biosiliceous Shells of radiolarian Zooplankton are common fossils since the Cambrian. With several hundred species living in all ocean regions and at all water depths, their fossils provide a richly detailed record of Phanerozoic oceans and biological evolution for study. Radiolarians have been employed with great success in studies of climate change (e. g. CLIMAP), in biostratigraphic dating of both Cenozoic deep-sea Sediments and more ancient sedimentary rocks, often in metamorphosed tectonic terranes, and in studies of evolutionary processes, including speciation and factors Controlling macroevolutionary change in entire faunas. More recently radiolarians have been employed to understand productivity change in the oceans, using the ratio of surface to deep-water species as an organic carbon export indicator. Radiolarian research, while successful, is still limited by poor knowledge of the biology of the group, and by incomplete taxonomy, even at the most basic level of species descriptions.

title: Some Observations on Bureaucratic Capitalism: Knowledge about What and Why?
abstract: The failure of contemporary sociology to acknowledge the role played by large organizations in bureaucratic capitalism & the need to hold such organizations accountable for their actions are addressed. Consequently, an approach informed by Max Weber's (1978 edition) focus on hierarchy & labor division & by US pragmatism that seeks to redirect sociological inquiry to analyze large corporations' participation in bureaucratic capitalism is presented. The nature of hierarchical power relationships & large organizations' influence on modern markets is emphasized, arguing that organizational structures are not reducible to human agency because such organizations possess distinct economic & political resources & normative orders. Implications of the vitality of the "corporate-bureaucracy" apparatus are considered. The development of universal moral standards by which to hold multinational corporations morally & socially accountable is strongly advocated. 83 References. J. W. Parker

title: MAX WEBER ON CAPITALISM, BUREAUCRACY AND RELIGION: A SELECTION OF TEXTS
abstract: This is a selection of available translations of Max Weber's works, with an Introduction by the editor, a list of the writings of Max Weber, & a note on the sources. Texts presented are concerned with Weber's historical explanations, rather than with his methodology or classification of social structures, in the conviction that his historical analyses form his most important work. (1) The Uniqueness of Western Civilisation. (2) The Failure of Capitalism in the Ancient World. (3) The Confucianist Bureaucracy and the Germs of Capitalism in China: The City and the Guild. (4) Hindu Religion, Caste and Bureaucratic Despotism as Factors of Economic Stagnation: The Caste and the Tribe. (5) The Nature of Modern Capitalism. (6) Protestantism and the Spirit of Capitalism. (7) Religion and Other Factors in the Development of Modern Capitalism. (8) The Distinctive Features of European Cities and the Rise of the West. (9) The State and Business Enterprise. (10) The End of Capitalism?

title: A tax for water
abstract: The World Bank proposed recently that a water tariff be levied.  The rate would be steeply progressive.  With the rate of water consumption rising, the need for water management has grown.  The major aspects to managing water supplies are: 1.  the overriding need to recycle water wherever possible, 2.  the complexity of a water tariff capable of inducing the user to husband this vital resource, and 3.  the urgency of cooperative water management.   Cooperative water management will involve not only recycling and purification, but also flood control and navigation, irrigation and drainage, watershed management, and electric power production.  Joint water management is all the more important because water is highly unevenly distributed over seasons, regions, and years.  Water cannot be a free resource any longer.  We must all become as water conscious as we are oil conscious.

title: BUREAUCRACY AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
abstract: A discussion of factors increasing the effectiveness of the gov'al bur'cy's role in aiding in development of mixed economies. 'The most important responsibility of the bur'cy in a developing country - in addition to that of strengthening the preconditions of development - is that of supplying a long-run & broad time horizon & an expanding set of developmental objectives to be realized through input transformation in both the private & public sectors.' There is a discrepancy in that the role of the bur'cy in developing societies is not matched by its strength; this can be vitiated by a modernization in skills & outlook of the bur'cy, & by funneling achievement motivation into econ developmental channels. (See SA 0715-B3371). D. W. Ball.

title: Trust and Welfare State Reform: The Example of the NHS
abstract: This article discusses the impact of New Public Management on public trust in welfare state institutions, using the example of NHS reform. Discussion of trust in public institutions across political science, psychology and sociology indicates that it is based on both rational/objective considerations (competence and capacity to deliver the service) and affectual/subjective factors (shared values, belief that the trustee shares the trustor's interests). The New Public Management foregrounds individual responsibility and incentives for both suppliers and users of services, in the NHS example in quasi-markets, management by target and patient choice. These accord with an individualized market rational-actor model rather than with affective considerations. Analysis of attitude survey data on the NHS confirms that rational/objective and affectual/subjective factors contribute to public trust in this field. However, a comparison between perceptions in England, where the internal market has been vigorously pursued, and Scotland, where the purchaser/provider split was discarded after devolution, indicate that the market does not offer a royal road to perceptions of superior quality in the objective factors. Conversely, the more market-centred system can make progress in relation to the more subjective affectual factors. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Conceptions of Decision Quality and Effectiveness in Decision Processes According to Administrative Officers and Investigators Making Decisions for Others in Three Swedish Public Authorities
abstract: This study investigated conceptions of decision quality and efficiency held by administrative officers from three Swedish public authorities (the Tax Board, the Social Insurance Agency, and the Police Authority) with respect to decisions made for other people. Research on conceptions of decision quality held by decision makers making decisions for themselves shows that decision outcome is emphasized. In contrast, the participants emphasized aspects relating to the communication step in the decision process as relevant for decision quality. This relates to the accountability aspect of decision making. Differences among the three organizations indicate the importance of domain-specific aspects.

title: (De)politicizing good governance: the World Bank Institute, the OECD and the politics of governance indicators
abstract: Since the early 1990s there has been a surge in international efforts to calculate the comparative performance of states in terms of various characteristics of governance. In this article we show how numerical objectification of social phenomena can function to depoliticize potentially political issues. As a case of example we examine the evolving field of measuring good governance through analyzing the documentation of the World Bank Institutes established Worldwide Governance Indicators and its recent contender, the OECD project "Government at a Glance", which argues to provide an alternative to the existing rankings. Although we observe certain methodological discontinuities in measurement practices of the OECD, these have hardly been serious enough to activate its potential in repoliticisizing the issue of "good governance". Moreover, the work of OECD further strengthens and legitimates the epistemic expert authority of global index producers.

title: MANAGING EXISTENCE IN NAPLES: MORALITY, ACTION AND STRUCTURE
abstract: A Vol from the series, Cambridge Studies in Social & Cultural Anthropology, investigates how working-class people in everyday life negotiate the terms of morality & bureaucratic rule of the market & civic society in Naples, Italy, drawing on ethnographic data collected in three neighborhoods, 1984-1986. It is generally found that people's purposive actions were consistently inflected by their application of nonmaterial aspects of existence, eg, superstition & subalternity. People drew not only on resources such as time, information, identity, & contacts, but also on more complex symbolic, moral, & spiritual constructs, eg, the relation between body & soul, & between the living & the dead. It is suggested that this material-nonmaterial interaction allows ordinary people to negotiate choices in their lives & construct a sense of fulfillment & self-worth.
