The prevalence of small reservoirs is due to their role as 'anchoring devices'; they embed a narrative of 'having great potential' but in ways that intersect multiple interests and development discourses. The gap between intention and practice that characterizes small reservoirs marks a stable interpretation of their nature and outcomes in the face of conflicting evidence. Understanding the interactions between discourse, policy formulation, and implementation that sustain development projects departs from a linear vision of development. It paves the way toward improved agricultural water management. Adapted from the source document.

title: Communalism and the Clientele Bureaucracy: Research into the Relations between the Administration and the Administered in the Netherlands
abstract: Public administration as a subject of research has achieved popularity in the Netherlands only during the past 10-15 years. The Public Administration Dept of the Free U has taken up a clearly recognizable position. It has propagated 3 theories: the 'communalistic' doctrine of democracy (local democracy would be crucial to the democratic quality of public administration), the theory of 'clientele bureaucracy,' & the theory of strong local government. Research based on these theoretical premises has revealed a considerable amount of information about relations between local government services & their individual clients. Free U studies considered 5 government tasks: the implementation of the Public Assistance Law, tax levying, the allocation of housing, the issue of passports, & street maintenance. The results are surprising to anyone who is only interested in the hard facts. These facts raise doubts about the correctness of the diagnosis as well as about the suitability of the cure for the putative illness. In particular, the axiomatic acceptance of the communalistic & clientele approaches causes a strongly biased perspective. The hard facts do not show that the degree of public orientation shown by service departments & officials has much to do with the (dis)satisfaction of the citizenry with the government & its agencies. Nor do they present conclusive evidence to the proposition that Dutch governmental services show unhealthy, Weberian characteristics. AA.

title: Water Services in Mexico: Are they a Public Priority?
authors: Cisneros, Blanca Jimenez; Torregrosa Armentia, Maria Luisa
abstract: Mexico is among the most important economies in the world, but as far as its water services coverage and the quality of these services are concerned, its achievement is not as outstanding. Along with the income inequity, water services differ notably between the urban and the rural population. This paper analyses the reasons for this situation. After assessing the relationship between Mexico's Gross Domestic Product, water availability, legal framework, institutional capacity and available technology, the paper concludes that poor water services in Mexico are due to a lack of political will rather than to the other considered variables. Therefore, to improve the situation, it is important to engage the government in the development of public policies and long-term programmes towards universal access to safe water and sanitation (including treatment and disposal). The necessary socio-political engagement will depend on achieving wide social involvement in the preparation of local and regional integrated water management programmes. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Spirit's Wish: Possession Trance and Female Power among the Punu of Congo-Brazzaville
abstract: Among the rural Punu of Congo-Brazzaville, possession trance is an essential part of the mainly female celebrations dedicated to the bayisi or water spirits. It is a privileged medium through which these spirits reveal their wishes and conditions their willingness to assure the community's well-being. On the human side, in order to be possessed an 'opening of the mind' is requested and needs to be activated through collective song-dance performances that recall the flowing motions of the spirits' water world and convey the longing for this maternal universe. As a critique of the predominant use of the term 'agency' in reference to autonomy and resistance, this paper adheres to a context-based view that relies on the way the actors experience the phenomenon. In line with the Punu reality this paper considers receptivity, in its ambivalent link to suffering, as the main source of the power these possessions grant to women. Adapted from the source document.

title: Calm waters or tsunamis?: the impact of renovation currents on the professionalization of federal representatives (1999-2003)
authors: Silva Junior, Jose Alexandre da; Figueiredo Filho, Dalson Britto
abstract: What effects have renovation currents had on the professionalization of federal representatives? Starting from the assumption that organizations need time and a favorable environment for their institutionalization, this article tests the hypothesis that the internal organization of the House of Representatives adopts institutional criteria that block the entrance of outsiders. Empirically, we believe that those who occupy commanding positions (party leadership, executive board, commission presidency) are more professionalized than ordinary representatives. In methodological terms, we use descriptive statistics, factorial analysis of major components and means tests to estimate the degree to which professionalization varies from group to group. Our results suggest that those who occupy major leadership positions present a degree of professionalization that is significantly higher than that of ordinary representatives. Adapted from the source document.

title: Scarcity-Induced Domestic Conflict: Examining the Interactive Effects of Environmental Scarcity and "Ethnic" Population Pressures
abstract: This study argues that environmental scarcity is more likely to result in civil conflict in countries that experience "ethnic" population pressures (i.e. where the size of the largest minority group is close to parity with the majority group). I refer to this argument as the "parity-threat" approach to the study of scarcity-induced domestic conflict. I empirically test my argument by analysing time-series cross-section data for the period 1979-2000 using four alternative environmental indicators: (1) ecological footprint, (2) biocapacity, (3) scarcity of ecological reserves and (4) water scarcity. The results demonstrate that environmental scarcity increases the probability of civil conflict when conditioned by "ethnic" population pressures. Adapted from the source document.

title: Democracy and child health in developing countries
abstract: The rise of democracy across the world brought with it expectations that governments would be more attentive and responsive to the welfare of the people, creating better services and better health. Indeed, a considerable body of scholarship finds that democracy has significant, direct effects on multiple measures of well-being, particularly life expectancy and infant mortality. Despite several recent critiques, the paramount theme is that democracy is good for health. This study contributes to this literature by assessing the relationship between democracy and child diarrhea and malnutrition across 52 developing countries. Using a multilevel modeling strategy, the analysis examines the country-level effects of democracy and development on child health, while simultaneously taking into account wealth, education, and other household characteristics at the individual level. Contrary to much previous scholarship, democracy does not exhibit a significant association with diarrhea or malnutrition. Instead, gross domestic product (GDP) per capita and improved sanitation and water have substantial effects on child health at the country level. At the individual level, household wealth and maternal education have the largest health-enhancing impact on child diarrhea and malnutrition. Furthermore, the size and strength of the relationship between wealth and health does not vary by political regime. These results demonstrate the enduring importance of socioeconomic status regardless of political context, and they support a small but growing literature that calls the democracy-health link into question.

title: Behavior in Water Supply and Sanitation
abstract: Health planners often conceptualize improved public health infrastructures, eg, the provision of water & sanitary facilities, as keys to improved public health results. These improvements alone, however, rarely result in the anticipated health improvements. Changes in hygiene behavior, ie, in how people utilize their existing resources along with improved infrastructure, are critical to achieving sustained improvements in public health conditions. This behavioral/human component tends either to be considered last in the planning process, or thought to happen once infrastructure improvements are in place. It is argued that such components need to be planned for & utilized in the overall planning of infrastructure improvements intended to change public health conditions of the periurban & rural poor. 27 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Evaluating Training Effectiveness: Focus on the Training of Public Enterprise Managers
abstract: Evaluation of training effectiveness is generally accepted as important in measuring levels or changes in individual, unit, & organizational performance. A comparison of the experience of selected developed & developing countries, however, shows that there has been relative neglect, on the part of the latter, to use more rigorous & reliable evaluation instruments, techniques, & methodologies in measuring the effectiveness of the training of public enterprise managers. There is need to strengthen the capability of training institutions in evaluating training effectiveness. 5 Tables. HA.

title: Challenges Facing Families of Sexually Abusive Youth: What Prevents Service Engagement?
abstract: Although it is becoming increasingly important to integrate families of sexually abusive youth in treatment, there are many families who resist engagement. Little is known about why families are not more involved and what factors prevent service engagement. In collaboration with a state sex offender management board, this qualitative study analyzed the perspectives of approved treatment providers (N = 19) on factors that deter family engagement. Findings revealed engagement is determined by detailed contexts and circumstances such as stress, preparedness, and subjective barriers. Pragmatic recommendations are offered to procure and sustain family engagement in treatment.

title: Role Transition and the Interaction of Relational and Social Identity: New Nursing Roles in the English NHS
authors: Currie, Graeme; Finn, Rachael; Martin, Graham
abstract: Our study provides an analysis of role transition, examining how macro-level influences and micro-level practice interact in framing role transition, with a focus upon professional identity. Empirically, we examine the case of nurses in the English NHS, for whom government 'modernization' policy has opened up a new occupational position in the delivery of genetics services within a professional bureaucracy. We track the experiences of the nurses through their recruitment to, enactment of, and progress on from, the new genetics role over two years. Our qualitative interview-based study encompasses six comparative cases. Analysis draws upon two linked literatures -- role and identity, and sociology of professions -- to examine the tension between the identity expected by the profession and the role expected by government policy-makers. While policy encourages reconfiguration of roles and relationships to support the new, less-bounded role, concerns aligned to professional identity mean that inter-professional competition between doctors and nurses, and intra-professional competition within nursing itself, constrain the enactment of the new role. Through our empirical study, we develop literature on role transition through its application to a professionalized context, and sociology of professions literature, within which issues of identity are relatively neglected. Our study demonstrates that the emphasis of identity within a professional bureaucracy lies at the collective level. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: Neoextractivismo, megaprojects and conflict in Guatemala and Nicaragua
abstract: The article is an analysis of the new phase of the extractive economic model in Guatemala and Nicaragua, countries that consider the construction of inter-oceanic corridors for linking the Pacific with the Atlantic, in order to compete eventually with the Panama Canal. The thesis is that new corridors in addition to increase trade and revitalize the maquiladora industry would stimulate new foreign capital investment in these countries, mainly in the fields of mining, production of hydro and wind power, and biofuels. These projects constitute the forefront of agricultural and mining neoextractivism, and the use of strategic resources such as water and wind for generating electrical power, where the multinational capital has much interest. Adapted from the source document.

title: "For a Social Anthropology of Administration in Africa II" Methodological Comments on an Article by Jean-Pierre Olivier de Sardan
abstract: The hypotheses put forth by J.-P. Olivier de Sardan in his analysis of African administrations must take into account the last forty years of research on government administrations. While an exhaustive review of such work is not necessary, this account would add to the hypotheses advanced. The latter would thus be reformulated according to a process of validation/invalidation constituted through reasoned knowledge, & with reference to fieldwork completed in both sub-Saharan & North Africa. This article is a methodological discussion about the relationships between fieldwork & theory & the movement from specificity to general propositions. Adapted from the source document.

title: Formation of Public Administration in Slovakia after November 1989 and the Movement for Local Self-Government
abstract: The privatization of all areas of life in Czechoslovakia was a vital part of establishing a new democratic state & reviving civil society after the political turmoil of Nov 1989. One specific result of this change was the separation of public administration from local & territorial self-government. This goal involved the resurrection of a dual-track model of public administration developed under the Austro-Hungarian monarchy & passed on to the new nation of Czechslovakia. In Slovakia, the result of the dual-track system was many battles between: the state & civil society, the government bureaucracy & representative democracy, & the central government & local/regional authorities. Local governments were subordinated to central authorities not only in the interbellum republic, but also in the independent Slovak state during WWII & in postwar communist Czechoslovakia. Since 1990, in contrast, the state has actively fostered the revival of local self-government in Slovakia as part of the building of a new democratic state. However, problems are emerging in the form of a power conflict between the government of the Slovak Republic & the Assoc of Towns & Communities of Slovakia. 12 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: "Greeting Tablets" in Early China: Some Traits of the Communicative Etiquette of Officialdom in Light of Newly Excavated Inscriptions
abstract: Since the 1930s, Chinese archaeologists have discovered a number of inscribed wooden tablets from the early Han to the Western Jin, which were identified as "greeting tablets" of two types, ci and ye. As attested in transmitted accounts, these tablets played an important role in the communicative etiquette of early imperial and early medieval officialdom; during a meeting ceremony, they were presented by the guest to the host. The present article offers a systematic survey of the available corpus of excavated greeting tablets and explores their wider socio-cultural implications. As a component of the communicative etiquette of the bureaucracy, greeting tablets were instrumental in the adaptation of elements of aristocratic culture to the needs of mass officialdom-a new social stratum that in terms of cultural background differed fundamentally from the hereditary aristocracy of the pre-imperial era but occupied a comparable position as a social and political elite. Adapted from the source document.

title: Consequences of Decentralization: Environmental Impact Assessment and Water Pollution Control in Indonesia
abstract: After having been one of the most centralized states in the world for more than thirty years, in 2001 Indonesia introduced a sweeping program of decentralization with important consequences for the management of the industrial sector. This article explores whether the decentralization process has led to substantial changes in Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) and enforcement of water pollution law. Its main findings are that the general division of authority in both fields has become less fragmented and that differences between districts have increased, but, in practice, not so much has changed as one would have expected. For EIA, 'horizontal' disputes between sectoral agencies have been supplanted by 'vertical' disputes between different levels of government. Monitoring and sanctioning of industrial water pollution have mainly continued within the scheme of the provincial program started under Soeharto's centralized regime, with still few initiatives at the district level. If any, such initiatives are usually driven by public complaints. On the other hand, there are indications that in the longer run the institutional changes may have more significant effects on EIA and enforcement practice. For EIA, these seem to be negative; for enforcement of water pollution regulation this depends much on the situation within a district or a province. Adapted from the source document.

title: Electronic Governance: Locals and Cosmopolitans "In and As" a Virtual Academic Community
authors: Mulkey, Lynn M; Dougan, William L; Steelman, Lala Carr
abstract: This investigation revisits Robert Merton's concepts of "locals" & "cosmopolitans" with respect to academic organizations. It explores the normative structure of electronic governance by analyzing the discourse of a virtual bulletin board. Data from a sample of faculty at a large state university are analyzed to conduct a semi-ethnographic exploratory analysis of the professional role structure & organizational consequences of a virtual academic community. A traditional organizational model used for understanding the public administration of higher education is one of bifurcated governance. In the context of this model, faculty & administration may have separate & conflicting interests. To negotiate & articulate competing interests, members of each constituency organize a formal forum of civil dialogue to initiate & resolve disputes (e.g., faculty meetings; unionized groups such as the American Association of University Professors). Two diverse professional role orientations emerge for airing concerns -- locals & cosmopolitans. Formal interactions seem to be a mainstay & vehicle for cosmopolitan interests; locals, who rely more typically on informal discourse, have not found ample outlets for communication. The advent of e-bulletin boards has made possible a virtual community distinguished by norms for both formal & informal discourse, allowing for the clear identification of local & cosmopolitan interests & their competing agenda. The virtual context of discourse was expected to blur the distinctions between locals & cosmopolitans; because of the medium, institutional & local goals become aligned & apparent as opposed to discrepant & inaccessible. But in fact, electronic governance that seems to encourage coalition in the approach to solving tasks makes the demarcation more pronounced, whereupon conflict ensues & the localism & cosmopolitanism professional role structure persists. Tables, Figures, References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Structural Origins of Territorial Stigma: Water and Racial Politics in Metropolitan Detroit, 1950s-2010s
abstract: This article develops the concept of territorial stigma by analyzing how it can be cultivated at the level of political institutions across administrative divides. I consider the case of Detroit's regional water department, which until 2016 was owned and operated by the city and served over 120 suburban regional municipalities. I start by examining the cooperative city-suburban water system expansion in the 1950s and then analyze the rise of Detroit's first black-led administration in 1974, after which the water authority became a key regional institution that provided an opportunity for white suburban leaders to organize against the city. I find that suburban leaders advanced their immediate goal of mitigating rate hikes by declaring the city to be greedy and inept, instead of acknowledging structural conditions that increased operational costs. This had the effect of reproducing racialized stereotypes at the political level, which had enduring effects. The argument builds on the existing literature on territorial stigma by (1) identifying state institutions as sites for the propagation of stigma and (2) considering stigmatized places in relation to their non-stigmatized neighbors. The analysis integrates material-structural and cultural-symbolic factors in order to understand the perpetuation of regional urban inequalities.

title: Making Sense of the Walkerton Crisis
authors: Mullen, Jane; Vladi, Natalie; Mills, Albert J
abstract: Drawing on analysis of the Walkerton (Ontario) contaminated water crisis of 2000, this paper explores the viability of Weick's sensemaking approach to organizational crises. The paper begins by showing how a sensemaking approach is a useful heuristic for revealing the complexity of organizational disasters that often rely on simplistic blaming of individuals. It goes on to explore the limitations of a sensemaking account that downplays the role of power and individual responsibility. The paper concludes by suggesting further theoretical developments of sensemaking to include Foucauldian notions of discourse and Sartrian notions of existential responsibility. Adapted from the source document.

title: A review essay: Recent literature on leading and managing change in public service organizations
abstract: Downes reviews "Banishing Bureaucracy:  The Five Strategies for Reinventing Government" by David Osborne and Peter Plastrik, "Catalytic Leadership:  Strategies for an Interconnected World" by Jeffrey S.  Luke, and "Changing by Design:  A Practical Approach to Leading Innovation in Nonprofit Organizations" by Douglas E.  Eadie.

title: Reforming Regional Governance in East Central Europe: Europeanization or Domestic Politics as Usual?
abstract: In recent years, a number of East Central European (ECE) governments have undertaken to radically alter the territorial structures of their public administration. Some have suggested that this development represents the growing Europeanization of ECE politics, in particular the role of the European Union. This article questions that view by examining the crucial role of domestic party politics in the enactment and implementation of regional governance reform. It does so through a close comparison of Poland, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Spatializing states: Toward an ethnography of neoliberal governmentality
abstract: In this exploratory article, Ferguson and Gupta ask how states come to be understood as entities with particular spatial characteristics, and how changing relations between practices of government and national territories may be challenging long-established modes of state spatiality. In the first part of this article, they seek to identify two principles that are key to state spatialization: verticality (the state is "above" society) and encompassment (the state "encompasses" its localities). They use ethnographic evidence from a maternal health project in India to illustrate our argument that perceptions of verticality and encompassment are produced through routine bureaucratic practices. In the second part, they develop a concept of transnational governmentality as a way of grasping how new practices of government and new forms of "grassroots" politics may call into question the principles of verticality and encompassment that have long helped to legitimate and naturalize states' authority over "the local."

title: Refah Party and the City Administration of Istanbul: Liberal Islam, Localism and Hybridity
abstract: Examines Istanbul city administration activities since the 1994 victory of the Islamist Refah Party to illustrate the multifaceted identity of political Islam, which confronts Turkish modernism & secularism by participating in parliamentary politics. Analyses of the transformation of the Camlica restaurant-coffeehouse & Cemal Resit Ray Concert Hall & limits imposed on alcohol consumption in public spaces show how political Islam uses political power to shape, control, & change urban life. It is argued that the discursive strategy reflected in these actions is not Islamization, but a form of localism that adds local influences (eg, values, customs, & art forms) to a public space dominated by Westernized modernization. The emergence of discourse of localism is traced, showing how it became independent of the political intent of its creators & has been institutionalized in certain practices, images, decorations, & cultural programs at these sites. It is concluded that localism creates a hybrid & culturally heterogeneous atmosphere that includes & celebrates representations of Islam, the West, & the Ottoman Empire; modernity & tradition; & rural & urban. 19 References. T. Arnold

title: Ruling Authority and the Bureaucracy in the New Russia [Reports from Two Surveys]
abstract: English translation (C) 2008 M. E. Sharpe, Inc., from the Russian text (C) 2006 the authors. "Vlast' i biurokratiia v novoi Rossii," Sotsiologicheskie issledovaniia, 2006, no. 3, pp. 3-4..

title: Satisfaction in Work and Formalism as Bureaucratic Phenomena: An Analysis of Attitudes in Chile
abstract: An attempt is made to find a satisfactory explanation for certain attitudes & behavior in a bureaucratic organization. Factors involved are of three types: sociological, value-oriented, & organizational. Satisfaction with work is seen as an indicator of efficiency, although the meaning of "efficient" may vary. The major hypothesis examined here is that the professionals working in the Ministry of Housing in Chile are satisfied with their jobs. Justification for this proposition, apart from the evidence accumulated from other studies of several different cultures, is that despite the general negative attitude in Chile toward public service occupations, the labor market is so restricted that Coll graduates must be satisfied with the first position available. Focus is on the degree of formalism found among these professionals. Formalism is defined as the tendency to adhere strictly to the letter of the law, which was not found to be true in this particular case. The implications of satisfaction & formalism on administrative efficiency are discussed. The image of the Chilean public employee that emerges is one of a bureaucratic official apparently well-adjusted, & more modern than traditional. 5 Tables, 1 Graph, Appendix. J. Shiffer.

title: MARX ON STATE ADMINISTRATION
abstract: An investigation of K. Marx's analysis of bur'tic admin. Marx distinguished 3 features of the bur'tic relationship: the law of hierarchy, activity conducted according to instit'al reason, & the perception of citizens as divided into 2 categories: activeadmin, & all others-passive. The law of hierarchy meant for Marx that the same personal & instit'al channels have both executive & controlling duties. Performance is also evaluated according to its compliance with rules & not its effectiveness. Diff strata within the hierarchy are isolated & task & competence are strictly divided between them. Instit'al reason means that the rule becomes an autonomic goal. In Weberian terms org is characterized by its formal rationality. In the case of the bur'ization of the administration the gap between the principles of the administration & the real needs of the situation widens; bur'cy also becomes a state within the state in time. A sketch is presented of the Marxist critique of the Hegelian idea of law & admin. J. Gross.

title: On holism and individualism
abstract: When ideologies collapsed, having been reduced to miserable mouth pieces of official state bureaucracies, it seemed natural to expect the coming, if not the triumph, of sociological analysis. In fact, while ideology pointed to the final, at times mythical, goal, sociology would limit itself to the critical examination of the process. Unfortunately, sociologists missed the great chance. Instead of sociology, the day was won by the individual methodologists. Society was then conceived as a pure abstraction, that is to say as the unintentional product of individual behaviors. In other words, in the name of freedom as individual arbitrary and unpredictable behavior society was conceived as a pure fictio mentis. The present day economic depression has tragically demystified such illusion. Structural, olistic causes are determining both government and individual decisions. It is true that society is not conceivable without individuals but, at the same time, individuals cannot live in a social vacuum. Not solimde, but togetherness is perhaps the essential, structural feature defining the human presence in the world. Adapted from the source document.

title: The final frontier: The UK's new coalition government turns the English National Health Service over to the global health care market
abstract: The authors describe the incremental approach to the marketisation of the English National Health Service (NHS) since the introduction of an 'internal market' in 1990 until the 2010 White Paper, 'Equity and Excellence: Liberating the NHS', and the subsequent Health and Social Care Bill published in January 2011. The introduction of a competitive market for a universal, tax-financed health system requires fundamental changes in regulation in order that market bureaucracy can be substituted for direct management. The components of reform are insufficiently captured by the framework of hierarchies and networks in new public management theories of decentralisation. Adapted from the source document.

title: SOME SOCIOLOGICAL OBSERVATIONS ON THE RESPONSE OF ISRAELI ORGANIZATIONS TO NEW IMMIGRANTS
abstract: Contacts between Israeli officials & newly-arrived immigrants from traditional societies are less bur'tic than might have been predicted. Case studies of relationships between bus-drivers & passengers, nurses & patients, etc, suggest that the official often departs from his formally prescribed role to teach the client how to perform in the client role or to influence him in other ways. These official-client relationships are analyzed in terms of (1) a theory of role impingement in which bur'tic roles are become intertwined with officially irrelevant roles & (2) a theory of socialization in which officials serve as socializing agents for their clients. AA.

title: OpenStreetMap, Collaborative Map Editing for Development and Disaster Response
authors: Chapman, Kate; Engelsted, Katrina; Iliffe, Mark
abstract: Chapman, Engelsted and Iliffe's contribution looks at Mapping. Mapping works similar to Wikipedia; everyone anywhere can edit and expand on mapping material. The community has been growing steadily since and potential uses also increase. In natural disaster or crisis areas, open editing of maps can assist in more rapid reaction capabilities, thus becoming useful for governments and assistance organisations. The authors look at the Philippines and Indonesia as past application areas. In Ramani Tandali, the project's uses include assisting providers in finding clean water and improving sanitary conditions. According to the authors, the greatest challenge lies in handling participants' diverse experiences, as different cultural backgrounds can lead to differing interpretations. The OpenStreetMap concept, having previously been applied by governments in their sovereign interpretation, thus becomes an approach that wants to act from below. Adapted from the source document

title: Policy Making by the Lower Federal Courts and the Bureaucracy: The Genesis of a National AIDS Policy
abstract: An investigation of how & why judicial-bureaucratic interaction contributed to the development of a national, antidiscrimination AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome) policy in education. The incremental development of the policy is traced via a review of actual court decisions & bureaucratic regulations & recommendations. Analysis confirms that the lower federal courts & bureaucrats are important but overlooked policymakers, illustrating that the courts can both fulfill their traditional roles of examiners of administrative procedures & defenders of individual rights while also crafting complex social policy. Modified HA

title: Restructuring citizenship in Bolivia: El Plan de Todos
abstract: Current international development policies promote both free markets and democratic states through privatization and decentralization programs. Building on T.H. Marshall's concept of citizenship, this article examines how these programs have affected the rights associated with citizenship in Bolivia since 1993 when the administration of President Gonzalo Sänchez de Lozada introduced a broad set of economic and political reforms. His administration sold state firms that had accounted for 50% of government revenues at the same time as it adopted a new constitution that recognized the multicultural and pluri-ethnic nature of Bolivian society. His administration also began decentralization programs in government, health and education that transferred 20% of national revenues, as well as the responsibility for providing services, to municipal governments. I show how current development practice has strengthened a neoliberal citizenship regime in which civil rights associated with ownership of private property, and political rights associated with formal democracy and representation, have been promoted at the expense of social rights associated with access to health, education and welfare.

title: THE HORIZONTAL DIMENSION IN BUREAUCRACY
abstract: The literature on bur'cy has concerned itself predominantly with superior-subordinate relationships (the vertical dimension). Relations between those not linked by the bond of authority are generally discussed only in the special form of staffline relationships, in which the staff gives advice on special problems & frictions are due to personal rivalries & ambitions, informal group formation etc. In this study of middle management behavior in 3 comparable companies, the quantitative importance & routine occurrence of horizontal relationships was established through a modified form of R. F. Bales' Interaction Process Analysis. A questionnaire focusing not on personal satisfaction with work but on the individual's stand on various policy problems revealed that R's occupying similar positions (eg, Sales Manager) in diff companies held similar views & were thus in conflict with the same opponents. (On other issues they might be in alliance.) This similarity of views across companies was interpreted to indicate that the nature of the problems faced by the incumbent of a given job, which in turn reflect genuine reality problems & dilemmas facing the org, determined these interdepartmental conflicts. Intraorg'al conflicts are not exclusively due to `company politics' unique to each one of them. Analysis of the history of the departments indicated that the resolution of these conflicts was also in accord with the nature of reality pressures: departments whose subgoal involved concern with what happened to be the more pressing aspect of a problem were likely to win. This was confirmed by the similarity in diff companies with which departments were ranked according to their power & influence. Conflicts are thus based on real dilemmas, inevitable & to a certain extent functional. AA.

title: Max Weber and the Sociology of Crises
abstract: Weber's political thought stems from the post-Bismarckian crisis of German society. It aims at building up a heuristic framework, but it is also an implicit proposal of a political strategy for a confused bourgeoisie. Two basic concepts are placed in the forefront: the bureaucracy (& the bureaucrat), & the political leader. They both rely on two unstated theoretical premises: (1) neo-classical economics--the logic of marginalism is traced in Weber's theory of action & in the economic concepts of his "Economy and Society," & (2) the influence of Nietzsche's philosophy--the latter expressing the new bourgeois approach to ideological legitimization, propounding reconciliation to reality as it is, tragic as it might be, because no real change is possible. Three major points are noted: (A) There is an analogy between the "death of God" theology & the "disenchantment" with historical reality which lies at the core of Weber's comprehensive sociology. (B) Nietzsche's concept of tragedy exhibits startling structural similarities to Weber's notion that capitalism is a historical necessity. (C) Nietzsche's doctrine of "will to power" is readily understood in terms of bureaucratic power in modern industrial societies. They are epitomized by the ideal type of bureaucracy which is the leading category of Weber's political thought. Bureaucracy (& its individual expressions, ie, political & bureaucratic officials) is the model of social & sociopsychological organization which fully developed capitalism needs. The bureaucrat is the universal, abstract individual who enters history as a byproduct of capitalist society. Modified HA.

title: Wellbeing by Eating Well
abstract: The article describes the availability of food in the traditional food system in a village in Andhra Pradesh before the advent of borewell. The borewell era has seen disappearance of water both underground and over ground and the article describes its impact on the food system. People have now become from net producers of food to net purchasers of food from the PDS and the market. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: Water rights and watershed management in Mexico. The Sonora river case
authors: Pablos, Nicolas Pineda; Vaquez, Jose Luis Moreno; Adams, Alejandro Salazar; Ley, America Nallely Lutz
abstract: This article analyzes the role of water rights in watershed management. The watershed is seen as a common pool resource where State intervention and the register of water rights might be used to constrain water tapping and avoid overexploitation. For this purpose, it reviews the ideas of watershed management and revises the Mexican legal framework for water rights. Then, it analyses a database of water rights in the Sonora River. At the end, findings are presented such as the disagreement between the principles devised by the legal framework and the practical implementation of water rights and that those are not used to undertake watershed management. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Politization of the French Administration
abstract: In the French admin, functionaries have rather extensive possibilities for participation in pol'al life. Although methods of recruitment are "objective" due to their competitive nature, a certain politization can be noted re the development of careers; however, this politization does not take place in only one direction. In admin'ive action, & notably in the distribution of financial aid to local collectivities, considerations of a pol'al nature play a certain role, but one must not exaggerate the importance of the phenomenon. AA Tr by A. Potter.

title: Nigerian selections
abstract: While there have been some positive results from the last eight years of Nigeria's "democratic" government, they weigh little against the scarcity of electricity, lack of an adequate water supply, unemployment, universities on strike, destruction of industrial production, & predominance of cheap consumer goods imported from China. Public transport, health, housing, & education have deteriorated, & crime is rampant. The consequent violence is beyond the ineffective efforts of police & military. That the ruling People's Democratic presidential candidate won by 70% in the Apr 2007 polls is not surprising in light of the fraud & violent disruption of the voting. It is believed, however, that the people's patience may soon reach an end. If president-elect Yar'Adua does not begin to resolve these horrific problems & rapidly earn legitimacy from the people, which he desires & will certainly try to do, the people will once more lose faith & elect another brutal leader, to their further detriment. Yar'Adua's tasks are outlined & the hopes for his success considered. Adapted from the source document.

title: WATER MANAGEMENT
abstract: The role of water management has always been an important one for the Netherlands. A history of water management is given, begining with the 12th cent & leading up to the contemporary water needs & the canalization of the Riju river to be completed in 1970. Problems of filtering out salt, of evaporation, providing drinking water reservoirs, & consolidating water management under central control are discussed. Of particular importance in water manag are the Zuiderzee, The Ijsselmeer, & the fresh water works at Andijk. It Is noted that the ingenious system of water manag devised by the Dutch is quite unique in the world. The Netherlands is probably the only country where over 6 million people live in an area that is kept dry artifically & that would simply be wiped off the map, if the pop were ever to leave the country, or if a prolonged strike were to break out. Water management is a matter of survival. 8 Figures. M. Maxfield.

title: THE EXTERNAL BUREAUCRACY IN UNITED STATES FOREIGN AFFAIRS
abstract: An effort to lay a foundation for more fruitful analysis of the behavior of outside experts (external bur'crats). 21 propositions are developed that may be applicable to the behavior of all external bur'crats, whether affiliated with private or public bur'cies. The paper is based on an earlier study of the participation of external bur'crats in the civilian foreign affairs agencies of the US gov. This study utilized data drawn from congressional files, other documentary material, & interview with some 60 external bur'- crats & gov'al officials who had worked with them. The external bur'crats included in this study served as individual consultants, members of public advisory committees, nongov'- al members of delegations to internat'l conferences, & those furnishing a variety of contract services (including res, instruction, evaluations of gov'al operations & the conduct of operations for the gov). The functions of external bur'crats are discussed under 4 headings: (1) they transfer information from the environment to the bur'cy & vice versa, (2) there is a similar 2-directional flow of perspectives about relationships between elements of information & about the significance of particular items of information, (3) external bur'crats provide manpower to the bur'cy, helping it at peak periods & providing skills not available within the bur'cy, & (4) external bur'crats can convey an image of nongov'al participation in the bur'cy. External bur'crats also carry an image of gov'al participation into their nongov'al relationships that enables them to speak with greater authority on public issues. There is a discussion of 4 kinds of interorg'al relations in which external bur'crats are involved. In the first 2 they are utilized to facilitate cooperation between the executive branch of gov & (2) kinds of external org's: congress & private business. In the 3rd they help the executive branch to coordinate separate departmental viewpoints into an overall nat'l policy. The 4th occurs when they are used to obtain coordination between activities of private org's. It is concluded that the scope of the 21 propositions suggests that external bur'crats may be an adaptive mechanism in societies which have large org's playing important roles, helping to integrate these org's into the total/sum society. AA.

title: Autonomization of Organizational Units in a Planned Economy
abstract: Discussed is one form of pathology of organization that occurs in different institutions, namely that of autonomization of organizational units & other forms of organized action. The field of research is limited to the activity of intellectual workers in the economic, financial, & state administration in Poland. Thus, the topic is included within the thematic sphere of theory of bureaucracy. Autonomization is an abnormality that appears in the following theoretically defined variant forms: (1) displacement of the main goal of the institution to a side or another main goal; (2) change of the method of activity; & (3) dislocation of an established balance between the basic & internal functions in an organized unit. Presenting the typical symptoms of autonomization, an attempt is made to find their causes through cognitive-individualistic, cultural, organizational, & economic analysis. Modified AA.

title: Nomenclature [A Historian's Notes]
abstract: A review of Russian & Soviet history demonstrates that a similar pattern has often been repeated: reforms create a new ruling class that then becomes entrenched & exploits the rest of the population. This process was clearly operating in the aftermath of the 1917 October revolution, when the czarist aristocracy was replaced by Communist party officials. This new "nomenclatura" eventually acquired enormous power & privilege, & became increasingly ossified, especially in the massive bureaucracies of Josef Stalin & Leonid Brezhnev. The roots of the nomenclatura are traced to Peter the Great's 1722 Table of Ranks, which established a formal hierarchy of bureaucrats. In Western European countries with similarly bureaucratic power structures, advancement depends on merit. Because this has never been the case in Russia, the ruling class has often been replaced but never successfully reformed. Perestroika (restructuring) is in danger of repeating this historical pattern if reformers simply usurp conservative communists to become another new ruling class. 29 References. K. Pizer

title: Seeing the Person First: Living with Moderate-Stage Dementia
abstract: Rose (88 years old) lives at home with George (97 years old), her husband of fifty-five years. She is in the middle of her journey through Alzheimer's. The days of fixing meals, going shopping, and planting a garden are gone. As George takes over many daily tasks, their life steadily closes in, with less activity, less conversation, and fewer plans for the future. On a typical day, Rose wakes up mid-morning and enters the bathroom to get ready, often spending an hour or two with the water running and the door shut. She looks at the towel and soap and water with no clear understanding of how to put the steps together. Finally, George knocks on the door and asks what she is doing in there. As people move into the middle stages of dementia there is increasing tendency to see only losses and frailties instead of strengths and remaining abilities. To keep seeing the person as creative, resourceful, and whole requires a major reframing of people's thought processes. Adapted from the source document.

title: THE INDEPENDENCE OF THE OFFICE OF JUSTICE OF LAW
abstract: A major problem for any pol'al class that achieves dominance is how to assure the loyalty of the bur'cy & the judicial instit. This is discussed in the context of recent Italian history. It is noted that the independence of the judicial branch of gov is only then achieved when the new pol'al class feels sufficiently certain that its functionaries & judges are loyal. The new Upper Council of the judiciary, prescribed by the Constitution of Italy since 1948, has had its first timid application since 1958 & has operated less timidly only since 1967. Now the time has come for a true independence of the judiciary in Italy. The composition of Parliament & the division of power in Italy are examined under reference to G. Maranini's STORIA DEL POTERE IN ITALIA, 1848-1967 (History of Power in Italy, 1848-1967), Vallecchi, 1968. It is asserted that the burley is Italy's real source of power, while the Parliament is only 'the voice of the country.' The Italian judiciary is compared with that of England. The concern in Italy has mostly been with the external independence of the Italian gov, less with the problem of internal independence or autonomy, & not at all with the educ of the new judge. Constitutional guarantees are meaningless where no judge exists who is knowledgeable of the functions the judiciary must fulfill in a legal state & yet preserves his independence, & who is ready to carry them out internally as well as externally. The new Upper Council of the judiciary can help, but detailed res should be undertaken as to the soc, geographical, & cultural background, from which the judges in Italy are recruited. M. Maxfield.

title: Meeting Women's Needs and Priorities for Water and Sanitation in Cities
abstract: Since women in developing countries are generally responsible for the provision of the family's water & sanitation, they are disproportionately affected by poor water infrastructure. Lack of access to clean water often underlies conditions of poverty & sickness in women & children, & consumes time that could be better spent in economic pursuits. These problems continue because social & cultural constraints limit women's participation in the planning & execution of water supply & sanitation projects, causing such projects to operate at less than optimal efficiency. It is recommended that to make these projects successful, women should have a major role in their design & implementation. Training suggestions are offered. 1 Table. M. Pflum

title: Ladies' Water Aerobics Swim Group
abstract: Over the course of the past year (2012-2013), the author has been swimming at his local YMCA (Y). Every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday he observed a group of between 10-12 women participating in an aerobics swim group. It gradually dawned on him that this was a recreational, activity support group. What impressed him was the way the women interacted with one another; they were always talking, laughing and clearly enjoying one another's company. In June of this year, the author decided to approach one of the members of the group and see if she would be willing to share some of her experiences of attending the group. This resulted in her speaking and e-mailing all of the women, who in turn e-mailed and spoke to the author about their reasons for participating in and the benefits they derived from the group. The paper incorporates the narratives of the women regarding the reasons for joining and also the numerous, physical, psychological, emotional, mental health, and social benefits of the group. The author also provides the reader with a number of theoretical concepts from groupwork literature, which further reinforce the numerous benefits of the Ladies' Aerobic Swim Group. Adapted from the source document.

title: Water supply and sewerage system: comparative study of management models in Santa Catarina
abstract: This article is a comparative analysis of management water supply and sewerage system of municipalities of Indaial and Itapema (Santa Catarina). The context was described as a synthesis of the diagnosis on the water situation at the global and national regulatory frame work of water supply and sewerage system in Brazil and Santa Catarina. Among the features are compared: the historical, socioeconomic, environmental policies, and especially the political context and the results of two selected cases. The general data were based on information available in public documents, academic studies, official web pages, in order to standardize the parameters. The period compared accompanies the beginning of the discussion of the problem, ie, from 2003 until 2009. The experiences of two cities analyzed led to the conclusion that the models of management are important decisions that influence the outcome of policies. Adapted from the source document.

title: New Modes of Governance in Activation Policies
abstract: This editorial aims to introduce the first of a set of two special issues on New modes of governance in activation policies. Design/methodology/approach - The article explores the concept of governance, distinguishing a broad and more narrow use of the concept. Then, it argues that issues of governance should be an integral part of studies of welfare state transformations. Not in the last instance, because governance reforms do have an impact on the content of social policies and social services such as activation. The article continues by discussing three models of the provision of social services. Findings - The article states that the development of the modes of governance in activation in various countries reveals that a mix of service provision models is being used. Adapted from the source document.

title: Small town in mass society revisited
abstract: A small New York town's thesis of macro forces--urbanization, industrialization, bureaucratization--permanently reduce the autonomy of small communities.  "Small Town in Mass Society" probable origin in populist ideology undermines its testability in social sciences.

title: Differences in Managers' Attitudes Toward Mexican and Non-Mexican Americans in Organizational Authority Relations
authors: Whitehead, Carlton J; King, Albert S
abstract: A study of att's & expectations managers have re Mexican Amer employees. These aspects were investigated: whether managers expect Mexican Amer's to respond to authority similarly to other employees, whether managers evaluate Mexican Amer's diff'ly from other employees, what components of managers' att's, expectations &/or perceptions need to be changed to alter managerial authority relations & improve the role & status of Mexican Amer's in org's, etc. The sample consisted of 601 industr managers, 301 responding to questions concerning only Mexican Amer's & 300 others responding to parallel questions containing no reference to Mexican Amer's. Managers represented 5 hierarchical levels & 175 org's. Geographical location was found not to influence managers' att's. Managers generally held higher norms than perceptions, leading them to lower their evaluations of both Mexican Amer & non-Mexican Amer employees' behavior. This suggests that levels of evaluation largely depend upon the degree to which managers perceive their norms as being met. Managers both expect & perceive more favorable behavior from non-Mexican Amer's than Mexican Amer's in authority relations. Mexican Amer's are expected & perceived to be more dependent than other employees. They are subjected to diff supervisory techniques & standards of performance than other employees & are both expected & perceived to show less initiative in authority relations than other employees. Managers also expressed higher levels of dissatisfaction with Mexican Amer's than with other employees. The implications of these findings are briefly explored. 5 Tables. M. Maxfield.

title: America's Paradox
abstract: A review essay on books by (1) Michael C. Dawson, Behind the Mule: Race and Class in African-American Politics (NJ: Princeton U Press, 1994); (2) Paula D. McClain & Joseph Stewart, Jr., "Can We All Get Along?": Racial and Ethnic Minorities in American Politics (Boulder, CO: Westview, 1995); & (3) Joe E. Feagin & Hernan Vera, White Racism: The Basics (New York: Routledge, 1995). It is suggested that US society is rife with contradictions between rhetorical freedom & actual racial oppression. Dawson confronts readers with abundant empirical data about African Americans & develops a black utility heuristic to explain the appeal of a figure like Louis Farrakhan. However, Dawson sees the likelihood that unifying black political movements will fade as class division in the black community widens. McCain & Stewart contend that, while the black position will improve, fragmentation of black orientation, beliefs, & political behavior will occur. Feagin & Vera concentrate on causes of racism rather than effects, emphasizing human wastage as a result of racism but ignoring its underlying logic. M. Pflum

title: The Institution of Bureaucracy: Administration, Pluralism, Democracy
abstract: A review essay on a book by Paul du Gay [Ed], The Values of Bureaucracy (Oxford: Oxford U Press, 2005).

title: BUREAUCRACY, POLITICAL POWER AND PROGRAMMING
abstract: Attention is focused on the general problem of administration in the modern world. Presented are concrete propositions re Italian bur, largely with reference to the conclusions of the Commission for Reform of administration which has just completed its work. The discussion centered around res on the balance between the independence of admin, an indispensable guarantee of its impartiality, & its coordination with pol'al power. The directors of admin, of whom we demand a greater & greater competence & technique, are in effect expected not only to intervene in the econ & soc domain, but also to participate directly in the decision & application of measures which arise from a precise pol'al choice. A third element is also involved: the influence which can be exercised on administration by private citizens or organized groups, at a time when the always growing complexity of the problems of admin make more difficult the control of gov, Parliament, & PO. Tr from IPSA by E. Weiman.

title: Vulgar Ethics for Public Administration
abstract: Following philosophical debate on whether morality can be taught via educational systems, some guidelines for the ethical preparation of those entering public administration are outlined, arguing that ethics may be, paradoxically, both the easiest & the most difficult aspect of public administration to teach. The possibilities of teaching a "vulgar ethics" are discussed, & specific guidelines for teachers are offered. 61 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Viability of small-scale arsenic-contaminated-water purification technologies for sustainable development in Pakistan
abstract: Drinking arsenic-contaminated water leads to a series of health problems that has limited development for the largely poor rural people of Pakistan who are unable to afford bottled water, centralized treatment plants or expensive water filter systems. This paper reviews the available appropriate technologies for the removal of arsenic from drinking water to assist in just sustainable development in Pakistan. Several technologies were found to be both technically and economically viable, supporting the large-scale deployment of these small-scale, appropriate technologies. The economic viability determined in this study was based on both first costs and operating costs. The cost of implementing such technologies for an individual Pakistani family is made acceptable with the use of local materials, which the family may already own. For example, systems using sand and iron nails in the filters, and that are placed in plastic buckets that are already in common use in the villages, drive down the overall costs of the technology and put it in the reach of even the most destitute. This study found that complications from the variability of local supplies result in the need to identify the locally most appropriate solution from both a technical and economic standpoint. This review article should be helpful for any practitioner in determining the locally optimal solution for the removal of arsenic from drinking water in Pakistan. . [Copyright John Wiley and Sons, Ltd.]

title: Socialism and Bureaucratic Collectivism in Developing Countries
abstract: Bureaucratic collectivism is a social formation in which the principal opposing classes are workers & bureaucrats. This mode can be contrasted both to capitalism & to ancient, Asiatic, & feudal modes. It is often defined by its supporters as socialism; however, this definition involves identifying socialism in subjective terms, rather than objectively, as society without class opposition. Bureaucratic collectivism has nothing in common with socialism. It is genuinely progressive in the countries where it occurs, but only in contrast to the previously dominant Asiatic mode of production, not in comparison to capitalism. It is not valid to assert that any progressive development is automatically socialism. W. H. Stoddard.

title: Bureaucracy, Patronage Politics and Educational Spending in Brazilian States: The Case of the Education Department of Bahia
abstract: This article analyzes institutions & processes yet understudied in the state level of government: the role of public bureaucracies in the formulation of social policies, as well as the connections between social spending & party & electoral dynamics. The analysis concentrates on a program of school construction & reform implemented in the state of Bahia from 1999 to 2002. To assess the extent in which the State Education Department relied on party-political criteria to allocate investments, we develop a logistic regression model. We also rely on a series of interviews with qualified informants to unveil the internal dynamics of the Education Department. Our conclusion reveals that the results of the expansion program for the secondary & fundamental schooling were shaped by the conflict between technical & political staff, which in turn promoted the coexistence of distinct rationalities within the education bureaucracy. Adapted from the source document.

title: RESISTANCE AND OBSTACLES TO DEVELOPMENT: THE OTHER FACE OF A "THEORY"
abstract: THERE IS A WIDE CONSENSUS ON THE EXISTENCE OF RESISTANCE & OBSTACLES TO CHANGE & DEVELOPMENT. MANY SCHOLARS HAVE ATTEMPTED TO ADVANCE A THEORY FOR THEIR EXPLANATION. ALTHOUGH THE REALITY OF DENIAL & REJECTION THAT OCCUR ALONG WITH ANY PROCESS OF INDUCED CHANGE (IE DEVELOPMENT) IS NOT QUESTIONED, IT IS CONSIDERED MORE FRUITFUL TO ASSESS THE REASONS WHY THESE REACTIONS ARE SYSTEMATICALLY LABELLED AS OBSTACLES & RESISTANCE DOOMED TO BE OVERCOME, SUBDUED, OR BY-PASSED. INDUCED CHANGE IS A PROVOCATION & THAT PROVOCATION GIVES RISE TO A RANGE OF RESPONSES AMONG WHICH DENIAL OR INDIFFERENCE NORMALLY FIGURE. IDEOLOGICAL BIAS OCCURS WHEN THESE DENIALS OR THAT INDIFFERENCE EXPRESSING AN OTHER WILL ARE DETERMINED AS OBSTACLES & RESISTANCE. THE LANGUAGE OF SCIENCE MATCHES A REACTION TO EACH ACTION WHILE THE LANGUAGE OF OUTRAGED DESIRE TRANSLATES IT INTO AN OBSTACLE. ANALYZING 4 CONTEMPORANEOUS TEXTS SELECTED FOR WHAT THEY REVEAL IN WHAT THEY TRY TO CONCEAL OR FOR THEIR CONCEITED FRANKNESS DEMONSTRATES THAT THE SO-CALLED THEORY OF OBSTACLES & RESISTANCE TO DEVELOPMENT DOES NOT MERIT SCIENTIFIC STATUS, HOWEVER ITS SUCCESS & DURABILITY ARE ESSENTIALLY DUE TO ITS IDEOLOGICAL BACKGROUND & TO WHAT IT PERMITS TO BE ACHIEVED UNDER THE LABEL OF SCIENCE. IN TOO MANY CASES, THIS THEORY LEADS TO CULTURAL OR ECONOMIC DOMINATION. UNDER ITS COOLEST ASPECTS THE 'THEORY' IS NEVER TOTALLY DEVOID OF MORALIZING INTENTIONS: RESISTANCE & OBSTACLES ARE EVIL & HARMFUL. YET NO QUESTIONS ABOUT THE LEGITIMACY OF THE GOALS & MEANS OF INDUCED CHANGE ARE ASKED. WITH A MORE SOPHISTICATED APPROACH THE 'THEORY' REVEALS MORE: THAT EFFORT COMES BEFORE LEISURE, THAT SUFFERING IS MORE NATURAL TO MAN THAN PLEASURE, & THAT DESIRE MUST BE REPRESSED. WITH THE HOBBYISTS OF INDUCED CHANGE, THE 'THEORY' DEGENERATES TO A ROUGH FUNCTIONALISM: ANYTHING CAN BE JUSTIFIED BY ANYTHING GIVEN THAT ONE HAS ADOPTED A SUFFICIENT LEVEL OF ABSTRACTION OR CONFUSION. THE 'THEORY' SHOWS THAT ITS CONTRADICTIONS & LACK OF RIGOR WOULD DEFINITELY DISCREDIT IT IF OUR KNOWLEDGE OF THE SOCIAL REALITY WAS NOT SO CRIPPLED & REIFYING AS IT IS. WE MIGHT JUST BE CREATING A NEW KIND OF TOTALITARISM. MODIFIED AA.

title: Globalization and Postcolonial States/Comments/Reply
authors: Gupta, Akhil; Sharma, Aradhana; Agrawal, Arun; Benei, Veronique; et al
abstract: The experiences of two programs aimed at poor rural women in India suggest that postcolonial contexts might give us reason to reconsider commonly accepted characterizations of neoliberal states. An anthropological approach to the state differs from that of other disciplines by according centrality to the meanings of the everyday practices of bureaucracies and their relation to representations of the state. Such a perspective is strengthened when it integrates those meanings with political economic, social structural, and institutional approaches. Although the two programs examined here originated in different time periods (one before and the other after neoliberal "reforms") and embodied very different ideologies and goals (the earlier one being a welfare program that provided tangible services and assets and the later one an empowerment program aimed at helping rural women to become autonomous rather than dependent clients of the state waiting for the redistribution of resources), they were surprisingly alike in some of their daily practices. In a postcolonial context with high rates of poverty and a neoliberal economy with high rates of growth, what we witness is not the end of welfare and its replacement with workfare but the simultaneous expansion of both kinds of programs. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Glass Cages and Glass Palaces: Images of Organization in Image-Conscious Times
abstract: Max Weber's metaphor of 'the iron cage' has provided an abiding image of organizations during the high noon of modernity. But these organizations -- rigid, rational & bureaucratic -- may no longer be sustainable in our times. Instead of a preoccupation with efficient production & rational administration, management today is increasingly turning to the consumer as the measure of all things, a consumer who seeks not merely the useful & the functional, but the magical, the fantastic, & the alluring. Management of organizations thus finds itself increasingly preoccupied with the orchestration of collective fantasies & the venting of collective emotions through the power of image, in what Ritzer has named the cathedrals of consumption, such as shopping malls, tourist attractions, & holiday resorts. The core thesis of this paper is that decline of Weber's iron cage of rationality has exposed us neither to the freedom of a garden of earthly delights nor to the desolation of the law of the jungle. Instead, I propose that the new experiences of work & consumption allow for greater ambivalence & nuance, for which I offer the twin metaphors of glass cages & glass palaces. As a material that generates, distorts & disseminates images, glass seems uniquely able to evoke both the glitter & the fragility of organizations in late modernity. The metaphor of the glass cage suggests certain constraints, discontents, & consolations quite distinct from those we encounter at the high noon of modernity. Shared features of the glass cage of work & the glass cage of consumption are an emphasis on display, an invisibility of constraints, a powerful illusion of choice, a glamorization of image, & an ironic question mark over whether freedom lies inside or outside the glass. Above all, there is an ambiguity about whether the glass is a medium of entrapment or a beautifying frame. 39 References. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright 2005.]

title: Vanishing Farmers: Taiwan's Early Environmental Protests Revisited
abstract: Forms of modern, mass-based environmental activism have emerged with different sizes and shapes. On both sides of the Atlantic, environmental movements of the 1960s arose in response to environmental hazards disturbing the landscapes of affluent societies. As a late industrializer, Taiwan's first wave of environmental actions began as an inter-sectoral struggle over the access and control of natural resources in the early 1970s. Aided by the developmental state, industrial capital seized water resources and took arable land away from smallholding farmers to build industrial parks and factories. Without proper regulations in place, unregulated liquid toxins were dumped in the surrounding irrigation systems, the emission of harmful fumes resulted in crop failure, and groundwater and fishing harbors were badly contaminated. Understandably, farmers and fishers continuously protested against such industrial practices and demanded proper compensations. Yet the intervention of intellectuals and middle classes, armed with an American-styled, class-interest-free version of environmentalism, changed the landscape of the environmental struggle. The early 1980s heralded the birth of an environmental movement wary of public health and food safety, yet devoid of genuine concerns about the economic survival of the disadvantaged. Previous struggles prompted by agricultural livelihoods had been forgotten and unequal distribution of natural resources unaddressed, and in the next ten to fifteen years, this movement bulldozed the opportunity to simultaneously pursue ecological and economic justice. Adapted from the source document.

title: Public-Private Partnerships in Water: A South African Perspective on the Global Debate
abstract: Despite widespread consensus on the importance of meeting the basic human rights of all people for safe water & adequate sanitation, the debate on the role of the private sector is loud, & at times destructive. In South Africa the gross inequalities inherited with the end of apartheid in 1994 drive the strategies of the Department of Water Affairs & Forestry (DWAF). Government policy has deliberately avoided adopting a particular stance on privatization, preferring to focus on the goal rather than the instrument. Nevertheless it has been recognized that a strong public sector is needed. Experience is showing that there are roles for a wide variety of public, private & civil society partners. South Africa could not have achieved what it has since 1994, were it not for a well developed private sector capacity. However, criticism of private sector operation has been noisy. Protest against 'commoditization' & pricing of water has been particularly vociferous. In the attempt to enter into dialogue with the critics, the importance of consensus in society has been highlighted. South Africa's inequalities are mirrored on a global scale & its experience is thus relevant to the global water policy debate. The involvement of the private sector should not be forced through global agreements such as GATS or loan conditionality, & international finance should put the poor first. 5 References. [Copyright 2003 John Wiley and Sons, Ltd.]

title: Veins of Concrete, Cities of Flow: Reasserting the Centrality of Circulation in Foucault's Analytics of Government
abstract: The 'governmentality' lectures that Michel Foucault gave at the College de France considered the question of urban circulation and how its fluxes and flows have been problematised in different historico-political contexts. To establish the critical parameters of this question, Foucault's understanding of the 'urban problem' will first be addressed and how this relates to governmentality. Subsequently, his analytics of government will be outlined in respect to the wider literature on urban circulation and applied to the flow of water in Singapore, examining how water has shifted from being primarily a locus of sovereignty, discipline and more recently, security. It will be argued that the urban problem and the concomitant question of circulation have been disassociated from more general renderings of governmentality.

title: "Save the Life"
abstract: The decline of the judicial profession within Chinese institutions, since the 14th century, is due to the progress of autocracy. Divided into more or less marginal categories, the lawyers have preserved their solidarity thanks to a rich professional literature. Maxims dating back to the 13th century require lawyers to use their knowledge to "save the life" of the accused. This deontology has justified an occult exercise of the law of reprieve encroaching on the prerogative of the emperor. By doing this, the lawyers presented their discipline not as a simple bureaucratic know-how, but as a science of interpretation of the governing laws of the State. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucratic socialism in reform mode: the changing politics of Cuba's post-Fidel era
abstract: Standard wisdom explains Cuba's current transformation as one of economic change but political immobility. However, Cuban politics have also undergone a major change since the handing over of power from Fidel to Raúl Castro - even if the rhetoric used has been one of continuity. This article traces this process by looking at four areas: the depersonalisation and re-institutionalisation of the political structures; the diversification of the public sphere, particularly through the use of digital media; the liberalisation of travel and migration, with its transformative impact on state-citizen relations; and the turn to a moderate foreign policy, as highlighted by the rapprochement with the USA, with its implications for legitimising the underpinnings of Cuban socialism. Although the shift has been well below the threshold of a transition to multiparty democracy, Cuba has evolved from the charismatic model of the past to what can be understood as bureaucratic socialism in reform mode.

title: From the ‘right to the city’ to the right to the planet
abstract: The debate on emancipatory socio-spatial change can be by no means only a matter of ‘right to the city’ − not even within the framework of the Lefebvrian concept of ‘the urban’ (l’urbain), whose scope is wider than is usual. I believe this implies meeting the challenges of reflecting deeper and with more sophistication on how to practically overcome the following aspects of reality: 1) the state apparatus and statism (be it properly capitalist or ‘socialist’) as well as the institution called ‘political party’ and all hierarchical, bureaucratic and vertical modes of collective organisation; 2) the technological matrix and the spatiality inherited from capitalism; 3) the capitalist ideology of ‘economic development’ (somewhat shared, albeit in a distinct and recontextualised way, by typical Marxism with its economism and productivism), full of economistic, Eurocentric, teleological and rationalist presuppositions. At the end of the day, what is at stake is the right to the planet, which requires rethinking a number of issues regarding spatial organisation (pointing out the necessary, radical economic-spatial deconcentration and territorial decentralisation, but without degenerating into parochial localism and self-insulating economic processes), the social division of labour, exploitation and alienation (in the context of which the trends of deterioration and regression such as labour precarisation and ‘hyperprecarisation’ should be highlighted), ethnocentrism (in this regard its renewed facets relating to xenophobia, nationalism and racism must be vehemently denounced), the various types of oppression (class, gender, etc.) and heteronomy in general - all this ultimately examined and judged on the basis of autonomy in the strong sense as the crucial parameter of analysis and evaluation.

title: Does Authoritarianism Breed Corruption? Reconsidering the Relationship Between Authoritarian Governance and Corrupt Exchanges in Bureaucracies
abstract: This article advocates for ethnographic and historical study of the political roots of corruption. Focusing on informal economies of Belarusian universities, it reexamines two theoretical propositions about corruption in autocracies. The first proposition is that authoritarianism breeds bureaucratic corruption; the second is that autocrats grant disloyal subjects corruption opportunities in exchange for political compliance. Using qualitative data, the author finds that autocracies can generate favorable as well as unfavorable preconditions for bureaucratic corruption. The author argues that lenient autocratic governance, characterized by organizational decoupling, creates favorable conditions for bureaucratic corruption. In contrast, consolidated autocracy, defined by rigid organizational controls, is unfavorable to such corruption. The author also concludes that in autocracies, disloyal populations may be cut off from rather than granted opportunities for bureaucratic corruption. These findings suggest that the relationship between autocratic governance and corruption is more complex than current studies are able to reveal due to their methodological limitations. Adapted from the source document.

title: Trakya-İstanbul geriliminde hidro-sosyal döngüler
abstract: The article focuses on the effects of Istanbul's urbanization on Thrace region of Turkey. Thus, it explores regional and city-based hydrological cycles with specific interest in production of drinking water and its relations to social processes in sustaining these hydrological cycles. The analysis, here, concentrates on three fundamental features of the conflicting hydro-social cycles of Istanbul metropolitan area and Thrace sub-region. These are production of drinking water, the production of Ergene River basin's pollution and the institutional conflicts over the regional planning of Thrace. By examining these three elements, I argue that hydro-social cycles of Thrace region are peripherialized at the expanse of producing Istanbul metropolitan area.

title: Patronage and Administrative Structure at the Brooklyn Navy Yard in the 1850s
abstract: An explanation of the formal structure of naval administration at the Brooklyn (NY) Navy Yard in the 1850s, as outlined by congressional mandate, drawing on an 1853 report by the Senate Committee on Naval Affairs. Alternative mechanisms, rising out of US political culture, undermined the formal with an informal system that accomplished similar goals, but yielded additional benefits. Controversies & factions within the Navy lessened as patronage worked its way into the evolving naval bureaucracy, & used the formal structure in ways not foreseen by its designers. As a result, the informal structure served a civilian political authority more powerfully than its original master (the Navy Dept), subverting what seemed on paper to be an effective command & control apparatus. Recent work in the field of organization theory that might explain why the formal structure was unable to resist the informal structure is briefly examined. 2 Figures, 55 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Why Did Universities Start Patenting? Institution-Building and the Road to the Bayh-Dole Act
abstract: This paper draws on institutional theory to explain the rise of university patenting in the USA.
