However, the second, the particular industrial economic ideology defining the correct role of the state in industry and industry in a state, is at least as important, if under-researched. In order to do empirically advance the argument the paper merges a cognitive-based constructivist argument with a neo-developmental state structuralist one, to present a new understanding of the role of the state in the Irish miracle that explains not only its success and failures but its internal dissonances, such as the continuous discrimination of the local, Irish-owned, industry in favor of foreign-owned MNCs. The paper illustrates how a particular industrial economic ideology has been formed and crystallized in Ireland. Focusing on the IT industry and using a multimethod research strategy, it traces the influence and evolution of this ideology at five critical decision points over a fifty-year period. Adapted from the source document.

title: TECHNOCRACY AND THE ETHIC OF SOCIAL WORK
abstract: Social work has compromised its humanitarian ethic by embracing technology to meet the demands of professionalism & bur'cy. From the soc sci"s it has borrowed a conservative body of theory on the nature of man & his relationship to the state, & a philosophy which denies the reality of ethical phenomena. The success of the technocratic logic has resulted in the erosion of the sources of legitization of the state & expanded rs her than reduced human conflict over commodities. In earlier times, poverty was a result of scarce goods; today it is a symptom of injustice, & affluence itself has become a soc problem related to alienation. AA.

title: It's All in How You Keep Score: Making Computer-Aided Decisions More Objective
abstract: Advantages of utilizing computer-aided multicriteria decision-making (MCDM) packages in public administration to compute policy outcomes are that more alternatives & goals can be incorporated in a complex matrix & outcomes can be computed utilizing simple scoring schemes for estimating soft data. Here, the differences in impact on MCDM outcomes of an ascending value scale, a Likert-type scale, & a descending value scale are demonstrated, employing the part-whole %s program to determine whether going to trial is better than plea bargaining. An alternative descending value scale approach is recommended to make outcomes more objective & realistic. 4 Tables, 1 Figure, 15 References. V. Wagener

title: International Non-State Actors and Social Development Policy
abstract: This article focuses on two broad groups of actors, international non-governmental organizations (INGOs) & international consultancy companies (ICCs), & situates them within wider trends in aid & development policies. In the context of a neo-liberal policy agenda, many leading INGOs reorganized so that they became closer to emerging ICCs, as consulting, outsourcing & subcontracting became key features of aid & development policy. Throughout the 1990s, in the context of declining ODA & increasing spending on emergencies, trends towards concentration & oligopolization among private development actors grew apace, fuelling short-termism, projectization, & intense competition within the aid market. The article discusses a new aid & development regime, which is focused on coordinated poverty reduction. It suggests that, notwithstanding its progressive elements, the regime will provide added impetus to existing tendencies towards concentration, oligopolization, mergers & consortia among non-state actors, given that it is being implemented within the core principles of the new public management. 2 Tables, 58 References. [Copyright 2003 Sage Publications Ltd.]

title: The failure of foresight in crisis management: A secondary analysis of the Mari disaster
abstract: Foresight the ability to plan and think systematically about future scenarios in order to inform decision-making in the present has been applied extensively by corporations and governments alike in crisis management. Foresight can be complicated because dispersed groups have diverse, non-overlapping pieces of information that affects an organization's ability to detect, mitigate, and recover from failures. This paper explores the failure of foresight in crisis management by drawing on data on events that preceded and followed the Mari disaster in a naval base in Cyprus in July 2011, where a large explosion killed 13 people and injured 62 others, while completely destroying the major power plant of the island. The paper examines how foresight into crisis management decisions was compromised because of a conscious effort by high ranking decision-makers to minimize emergent danger and avoid responsibility for the crisis, in joint with red tape, bureaucracy, and poor coordination and information flows. The paper explores the notion of operational and political responsibility of individual decision-makers and discusses an alternative approach to foresight in crisis management, one that is built on multiple layers of decision-making. [Copyright Elsevier Inc.]

title: The 'Skill Bureaucracy' and Interorganizational Control: The Case of the Data Processing Unit
abstract: Conflicts between bureaucratic organizations & professional occupational groups within such organizations have received considerable attention. One such professional group is the personnel of the electronic data processing departments in United States local government bureaus. The orientations & behaviors of such personnel are assessed through interview, questionnaire, & observational data on larger United States municipalities & counties, covering nearly 500 local governments. Such departments are examples of 'skill bureaucracy'-units which provide services to clients, have a relative monopoly over both skill provision & technical expertise, & have an external, professionalized reference group. Such units have a distinctive perspective regarding their own role responsibilities, anchored in the standards of their professional group, rather than those of their superordinates or clients. This skill bureaucracy is autonomous in its operations & remarkably expansionist. 4 Tables. Modified HA.

title: Modernization and Sex Roles: The Status of Women in the Thai Bureaucracy
authors: Springer, J Fred; Gable, Richard W
abstract: Thai women have traditionally been active in the economy & enjoy a social equality unusual for Asian women. To examine F roles in a modernizing bureaucracy, data were gathered through 414 in-depth interviews with officials of the Rice Production Project, 50% from Bangkok offices & 50% from field locations. F participation in the project was 17.7% -- many times higher than in similar programs in Indonesia, South Korea, & the Philippines. Despite comparable educational credentials, however, F Thai civil servants were found to have lower rank, lower pay, & less supervisory responsibility than Ms, & tended to be clustered in clerical occupations. They were also less likely to be married or have children, suggesting that they needed to make sacrifices in family life to compete with Ms. F Rs, however, expressed greater job satisfaction than did the Ms. 7 Tables. C. Waters.

title: Orissa's highland clearances: The reality gap in R & R
abstract: There is clearly an institutionalized attitude of neglect towards the displaced people. For example, no record of the number of people displaced is maintained. Such attitudes prevent the bureaucratic mindset from understanding the enormity of what is involved when tribal people, stripped of their land, are forcibly dumped to unlivable places euphemistically called resettlement colonies. Often it is this lack of understanding that gives rise to strong resistance to projects. In addition, the disjunction between policy and practice is almost total. The aim of all resettlement policies is developmental, to see that the living standards of affected people improve, but this seldom happens. Most often, impoverishment is the lot of those forced to relocate. The respect for human rights of tribal people requires that stringent steps be taken to avoid displacement, that no further displacement takes place until those previously displaced are properly resettled, that the process of consultation be real, not a ritual, and that only those officials be put in charge of resettlement who are properly trained and have an understanding of tribal life and culture.

title: Perspectives on the Luhmann School of Management Structures and Policy
abstract: Niklas Luhmann's scientific career began with publication on the theory & practice of management structures & policy; aspects of his general theory of social systems use insights gained from decision theory, management theory, & personal management experience. In this light, his critique of Max Weber's (1946) bureaucratic model is reviewed. Special attention is given to how Luhmann's early works laid the foundation for his approach to social systems in general & to politics & management more specifically. Also discussed is the autopoiesis of the welfare state & the consequences in terms of the ability of its managers to adapt & implement policies. 10 References. M. Meeks

title: The Influence of Bureaucratic Factors on Welfare Policy Implementation
authors: Gryski, Gerard S; Usher, Charles L
abstract: It is argued that previous welfare policy research has suffered from its neglect of bureaucratic factors, as well as a tendency to exclude policy-making arenas above & below the state level. Using several measures of organizational structure, administrative professionalism, & within-state need, they attempt to relate these variables to within-state variations in welfare policy implementation. While certain SE conditions are found to be significant determinants of this variation, of greater importance are characteristics of state welfare bureaucracies such as the degree of administrative centralization & the level of professionalism of administrative staff. Research suggests the need for further refinement of conceptualizations of the policy process & its components, & indicates the potential significance of bureaucratic factors in explaining policy implementation. 4 Tables. HA.

title: The Public Role of Women: Initial Results of an Investigation of the Italian Bureaucracy
authors: Curcio, A M; Occhionero, M Ferrari; Maniscalco, M L; Memoli, R; Salatiello, G
abstract: Women constitute 43.5% of the 1.5 million ministerial employees of the Italian government. A random sample of F ministry employees (N = 2,000) completed a 31-item questionnaire focused on: (1) professional goals; (2) motivation in the choice of profession; (3) generational mobility; (4) job satisfaction; (5) interaction of family & professional commitments; & (6) use of leisure time. The findings show generally later entry than men into the public administration field, & earlier anticipated withdrawal (age 40-44). Later entry is partially explained by the fact that 57% of the Rs had held one or more jobs in other fields before entry. Job satisfaction is not high; 62% desire to change careers, & 52% find their work "uninteresting." Conclusions should not be considered reliable until a more representative study is completed. S. Karganovic.

title: Panacea or Pandora's Box? The Program Manager Reform
abstract: Based on a case study of the acquisition of major weapon systems in the Dept of Defense, a reform initiative is examined from the standpoint of its relevance & effect on the governmental operations with which it is concerned. The investigation demonstrates two factors that hamper meaningful reform: the complexity of government bureaucracies & the general lack of knowledge concerning their operations. 3 Tables, 3 Figures, 22 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Migration of Bureaucracy: Contracting and the Regulation of Labour in the Telecommunications Industry
abstract: This is a study of the reconfiguration of bureaucracy, based on a case study of subcontracting within BT plc, the UK's largest telecommunications firm. The 1990s witnessed significant quantitative & qualitative changes in the utilization & management of subcontracting. The expansion in the use of subcontractors in this period was paralleled by reforms to the processes of negotiating, administrating & monitoring contracts. This article traces these developments & analyses their implications. The continuing process of reform saw a significant redrawing of the boundaries of responsibility between the patron firm & its supplier, as discrete elements of the production process were transferred to the remit of subcontractors. This migration of responsibility was, however, predicated upon the exportation of bureaucracy, from the patron to the supplier; the relocation of the bureaucratic mechanisms appropriate to the management of the widening range of tasks. The movement towards an increased reliance on external sources of labour could ostensibly bring greater exposure to market imperatives, but it is argued that, contrary to the theme of dismantling hierarchical employment structures, these reforms represented the reconfiguration of the bureaucratic organization of production. 35 References. [Copyright 2002 Sage Publications Ltd.]

title: Bureaucracy vs Community? The Origins of Bureaucratic Procedure in the Upper Canadian School System
authors: Gidney, R D; Lawr, D A
abstract: The growth of bureaucracy has generally been regarded as a phenomenon initiated & directed by government & central authorities. Analyzed here is how the bureaucratization of the Ontario educational system during the mid-nineteenth century stemmed in large part from the demands of the local voters, parents, school trustees, teachers, & superintendents who used, worked in, & paid for the schools. Relying on such sources as the department of Education files of correspondence from these local people, it is shown that bureaucratic forms developed because the clients & personnel of the schools needed & asked for efficient, fair, & publicly-established regulations & procedures. Conflicts over issues such as the location of the schoolhouse, the financial base of the schools, the range of the curriculum, the nature of religious instruction, & the role of local officials produced a recurring demand for bureaucratic modes of procedure. It is concluded that, to some extent, there is a need to reassess the common explanations of the origins of bureaucratization. AA.

title: On Bureaucratic Collectivism
abstract: A review essay on a book edited by Ernest E. Haberkern & Arthur Lipow, Neither Capitalism nor Socialism (Humanities Press, Atlantic Highlands, 1996). Utilizing a revolutionary socialist approach, this collection of essays examines the development of bureaucratic collectivism in Stalinist Russia. It is contended that bureaucratic collectivism necessitated the complete participation of the working class in constructing a new social order; moreover, the theory emphasized the importance of maintaining the inextricable relationship between socialism & democracy. The emergence & downfall of Stalinist bureaucratic collectivism is discussed; Haberkern & Lipow's contention that corporate capitalism was superseded by bureaucratic collectivism is questioned. It is concluded that bureaucratic collectivism, regardless of form, remains linked to the decline of capitalism; in addition, bureaucratic collectivism demonstrates that some form of collectivization is prerequisite for social advancement. J. W. Parker

title: Clientelism and Political Control in Rural Argentina
abstract: Scholarship on clientelism frequently addresses political clientelism using strong ideological presuppositions and/or neglecting its subjective dimension. In this article I explore political clientelism in a rural community of the province of Formosa, Argentina from the peasants' point of view. The results suggest that peasants consider the clientelist relation as one that recognizes their personal needs, while the bureaucracy of the state does not. Thus, they perceive clientelist ties as legitimate, criticizing only the fact that the provision of resources by patrons takes place only during elections. Adapted from the source document.

title: License for the New Barbarism
abstract: Desai views on the Sep 11 event, which US government seized the event as the closest thing to license containment of Communism and the defense of democracy and human rights, the war against terrorism veils the pursuit of the US real goals. He also talks about a more violent world that links to everyday structural and normalized forms of oppression and subordination, which are more closely policed by violence.

title: FROM VOLUNTARISM TO BUREAUCRACY IN AMERICAN EDUCATION
abstract: 4 models for the org of public educ conflicted in the US during the 1st half of the 19th cent. They are termed paternalistic voluntarism, corporate voluntarism, democratic localism, & incipient bur'cy. Debate between the proponents of the models revolved around 4 structural questions: scale, control, professionalism, & finance. However, underlying the controversy over details was a conflict among soc values, & an analysis of org'al models thus provides direct insight into the key value conflicts within 19th cent society. The 4 models are compared, & it is demonstrated that the intensity of the debate over org reflected the key role that instit's such as Sch's had come to play as mediators between soc change & soc values. In their arguments over the details of org, 19th cent Amer's revealed most clearly their aspirations &, as well, their anxieties concerning the society which they would build & bequeath. It is suggested that Amer's made org uniquely their own nat'l problem precisely because they lacked fixed traditions & the security of ancient forms. The mediating position of org re 3 broad areas of importance is sketched: soc change, changes in soc structure & demographic characteristics, & org'al change itself. Paternalistic voluntarism was the form of org characteristic of educ in the pre-industr, mercantile city. Corporate voluntarism & democratic localism characterized Ru areas & were proposed for Ur places precisely at times of transition between mercantile & industr stages of development. Incipient bur'cy spread with incipient industr'ization. Some evidence indicates that the poor & We's threatened by industr'ization supported democratic localism in moments of technological transition. However, an attempt by the Me to secure advantage for their children, as technological change heightened the importance of formal educ, assured the success & acceptance of universal, elaborate, graded Sch systems. Modified HA.

title: Colonial Conspiracies
abstract: Using records from the Lima office of the Spanish Inquisition, this article explores the cultural politics of Spanish colonialism in the Andes. Spain's imperial enterprise was rooted in the construction of new social beings at the core of modernity: (1) the racialized triad--Indian, Spaniard, and black; and (2) bureaucratized beings created in tandem with institutions of state. Conspiracies and confusions were the result as inquisitors, officers in the most modern bureaucracy of the time, intertwined stereotypes of Jews, Indians, African slaves, and women as part of an etiology of blame. Seventeenth-century Peru provides a glaring example of how fears could coalesce, develop, and ultimately balloon into absurd conspiracy theories, made all the more dangerous by an ideology of reason and the support of an institution of state. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Problem of Rationality in Organizational Structures
abstract: Argues that Max Weber's arguments on the high rationality of organizations based on ideal-type bureaucracy have become obsolete in the modern world. Sheer size of modern organizations & the heterogeneity of their environment do not allow for successful application of routine knowledges & practices produced & reproduced by classical, ie, Weberian, bureaucracies. It is argued that hierarchical structures, behavior regulation according to fixed prescriptions, strict subordination, & narrow specialization are the ballast of modern society. The whole mechanism of bureaucratic management is seen as nonrational. 26 References. J. Klimov

title: DECISION-MAKING IN A MENTAL HOSPITAL: REAL, PERCEIVED, AND IDEAL
authors: Lefton, Mark; Dinitz, Simon; Pasamanick, Benjamin
abstract: An attempt to examine the decision-making (DM) process in a small, institute type of psychiatric hospital in terms of the diff's in real, perceived, & ideal influence patterns of 53 mental health specialists. It was hypothesized that these DM patterns would reflect the influence of a dual criteria system with respect to the org & functioning of the hosp. These criteria are: (1) the traditional med bur'cy & (2), the currently emphasized `team' or equalitarian approach regarding the care & treatment of patients. Under investigation were the nature & implications of this org'al dualism for both the involvement of staff members in the ongoing DM process & their evaluations of this process. AA, & faulty classification. H. Adapted from the source document.

title: Administrative Deviance and the Ideology of "Injustice"
abstract: A theoretical exploration of deviant behavior theories with special reference to R. K. Merton's theory of bureaucratic structures & the concepts of "anomie" & "deviance." According to Merton, bureaucratic inefficiency derives from ritualism & ultraconformism to the rules & methods to the point where sight is lost of the purpose. Merton's viewpoint is contrasted with that of M. Weber. It is suggested that a mere examination of the bureaucratic personality does not suffice; rather, the entire bureaucratic structure must be examined. While Merton's view has promoted a behaviorist view that has enlarged the conceptual horizon of the problem, he has not researched the central problem of the structural & functional attributes of the bureaucratic organization. North American sociologists such as P. Blau, M. L. Kohn, C. Perrow, & others who have explored this problem are discussed. It is concluded that American theories are based on a liberal ideology that has become liberalist & has been condensed into an "ideology of injustice." 1 Table. S. Whittle.

title: Job Satisfaction Among Long-Term Care Staff: Bureaucracy Isn't Always Bad
abstract: The study investigated the influence of role conflict, workload, centralization, and formalization on job satisfaction of long-term care staff. Regression analysis revealed that role conflict, workload, centralization, and formalization together contributed 40.0% variance in job satisfaction. Role conflict and workload decrease job satisfaction while centralization and formalization increase it. Adapted from the source document.

title: On Bauman's Interpretation of Weber
abstract: This article provides a re-assessment of Bauman's interpretation of Weber. It refers to this end to Du Gay's critique, which came out in the late 1980s and called into question the accuracy of Bauman's interpretation of Weber as contained in Modernity and the Holocaust. Du Gay objects of Bauman that Weber's ideal type of modern bureaucratic organizations is not incompatible with ethical considerations, and Bauman has therefore misrepresented Weber. The article dwells on and evaluates this objection also in the light of this work, and other and more recent works by Bauman. Bauman has consistently praised Weber for his ability to understand the modern condition, and Bauman considers him as a sociologist of the modern age, but also as an academic outsider. Weber could therefore understand better than other scholars that 'lighter' (rather than 'heavy') modalities of the capitalist order are conceivable. 'Lighter capitalism' is however a trait of Bauman's conception of post modernity (which this article briefly considers), rather than of modernity. Weber has also grasped, according to Bauman, the inconclusiveness of the rationalization process and called attention to a future, which is different from that prefigured by the modernity project. Bauman is accordingly not entirely consistent in considering Weber a sociologist of modernity. It has also been argued here that the scope of Du Gay's critique of Bauman's interpretation of Weber should be extended, as there are for Weber several aspects of modern society that are not compatible with instrumental rationality. In particular, Weber has dwelt on value-rational aspects of modernity -- such as the persistence of the values of solidarity and honour in the market, in the workers' unions, and in the bourgeoisie as a status group -- which Bauman has neglected to consider.

title: THE ROLE OF BUREAUCRACY IN TRANSITION
abstract: An examination of 2 instances of modern pol'al transition which involved drastic changes not only in the gov structure but also in the very bases of public power: the changeover from Imperial Germany to the Weimar Republic, & the transformation of the Weimar Republic into the Third Reich. Focus is on one segment of the gov'al structure (the bur'cy), & on one section of that (the Foreign Office), & mainly on the changes which Nazi Germany brought about within the bur'cy & the response of the bur'cy to the changes effected or attempted. IPSA.

title: Legal Challenges Facing Lesbian and Gay Youth
abstract: Legal constraints on minors can be especially problematic for lesbian and gay youth, who frequently lack support from their families and from school authorities, and whose circumstances are often misunderstood or disregarded by authorities throughout the juvenile system. Legal mechanisms exist or can be crafted to meet the needs of lesbian and gay youth who have been rejected by their families of origin. School, welfare, and juvenile justice administrators must become sensitive to the personal, economic, and societal pressures faced by lesbian and gay youth, and must tailor bureaucratic responses to the youth's particular needs. Finally, it is imperative that adults in the lesbian and gay communities take responsibility for protecting the interests of younger members of the community.For a complete reprint of this article contact Haworth Press by telephone (1-800-HAWORTH) of EMail (getinfo@haworthpressinc.com). Article copyright The Haworth Press, Inc.

title: Producing Evaluations in a Large Bureaucracy
authors: House, Ernest R; Haug, Carolyn; Norris, Nigel
abstract: The development of evaluation issues & processes is empirically examined in one branch of the National Science Foundation (NSF). The study, which involved 3 years of intermittent participant observation & 44 interviews with NSF office personnel, program directors, & evaluation contractors, indicates that evaluations are heavily influenced by the way the work is organized & produced, as well as by the usual considerations that shape evaluations elsewhere. Two primary issues are identified as critical to the successful establishment of an evaluation office: (1) the evolution of an evaluation culture within the organization, & (2) the management of a semi-internal/external evaluation production process. 19 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: LARGE-SCALE RESERVOIR CONSTRUCTION AND POLITICAL CENTRALIZATION: A Case Study from Ancient Korea
abstract: The relationship between centralized political authority and the construction of large-scale irrigation systems has been a major research topic in both anthropology and archaeology for many decades. One of the objects of this research has been to determine whether large-scale irrigation works were a cause or a result of political centralization. Some scholars (e.g., Wittfogel) have argued that construction of such projects played a critical role in the emergence of centralized, bureaucratic social structures. Others believe that large-scale irrigation works were constructed only after a centralized government emerged, and that before this, local people managed relatively small-scale cooperative irrigation works without intervention of a centralized political authority. This paper argues that large-scale reservoirs were constructed only after and because of the appearance of centralized political organization, in this case, the Silla Kingdom in ancient Korea. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: THE INTERNAL PROBLEMS OF A BUREAUCRACY
abstract: In the modern world bur'cy has become a characteristic instit. It greatly determines the character of almost every contemporary instit. Bur'cy is a system of org, admire & of discipline & control. Bur'tic administration is efficient, predictable, impersonal & fast. Not bur'cy, of which several adumbrations have appeared in the past, but the bureaucratization of society, is specific to our times. Russia today affords a highly developed case in point. The USSR is run by competing, struggling & intertwining bur's, each fighting for dominion over the others. However, the phenomenon can exist in any large-scale soc system with or without private property, & in a basically dictatorial or basically democratic climate. Bur'cy is a technical means of administration whose ends are given by these in control. Despite many efforts to hold the bur'tic machinery in check & provide independent bases for policy making, bur'tic growth continues - as our society expands in size & complexity, the bureaucrat assumes more & more important functions. To the official himself, the bur'cy is a whole way of life which makes sharp demands & imposes rigid standards. The official has to repress certain prebur'tic sentiments & he will invariably be forced to reject or neglect non-occup'al roles that are more continuous with his self than with his profession. Certain conflicts are generated by the fulfillment of bur'tic roles. Given an atmosphere of compulsive sociability to subordinates as well as to equals & superiors of impersonality towards associates as well as clients, & a general sense of isolation, the bureaucrat searches for identification in a variety of forms. One official may seek out others in defiance of rules, & thereby make attachments that have no org'al sanction. Less frequently noted is the process of dis-identification the same sense of isolation that leads one bureaucrat out of the organization to seek his `self' may lead another to over-identify with the org. Structurally determined powerlessness leads to other pathologies which foster such phenomena as white collar sabotage, the myth of incompetence, downward identification & authoritarianism. AA.

title: Contraction Way to Harmonic Execution
abstract: As a method of administrative law enforcement which is made use by administrative subjects, administrative contract enrich the mode of administrative law enforcement. Furthermore, administrative contract make administrative law enforcement suaver & more humanism, & it is very helpful in Building a harmonious society. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: POWER CLIQUES IN BUREAUCRATIC SOCIETY (NOTE)
abstract: The coordination of separate org's in the same or diff instit'al orders are dealt with via personal, non-instit'al connectionssie, inter-instit power cliques. The process by which such cliques operate, & their consequences for individuals, org's, & segments of a society or community are specified, as is the relationship between informal cliques & formal org's. J. Bensman.

title: The myth of the golden years: One older woman's perspective
abstract: Adjusting to old age requires more than coming to terms with eventual physical decline. It also demands accepting the permanent loss of loved ones. This autobiographical account describes both positive and negative experiences during the seventh decade of life. My coping skills have been enhanced by previous employment as a mental health professional. As an older woman, I have been forced to become my own social worker, acting on my own behalf with medical and other bureaucracies. And, as a retired social worker, I have the ability to evaluate the skills and limitations of those care providers who have been called upon to assist me in coping with the problems of old age.For a complete reprint of this article contact Haworth Press by telephone (1-800-HAWORTH) or EMAIL (getinfo@haworthpressinc.com). Article copyright The Haworth Press, Inc.

title: Rule Orientation and Bureaucratic Reform
authors: Foster, John L; Jones, Judson H
abstract: Scholars, popular writers, & the general public often assume that large organizations produce the petty bureaucrat syndrome. Academic literature pertaining to the bureaucratic rule orientation phenomena is reviewed, & a number of hypotheses drawn from that material are tested. The data base is the Atlanta Model Cities program; interviews covering 70 subjects were conducted in 1970 within 23 participating organizations. Organizational structure is found to have a negligible relationship with bureaucrats' attitudes, contrary to expectations. Career orientation appears to provide the best explanation of rule orientation. 4 Tables. Modified HA.

title: REVISITING CONFUCIAN BUREAUCRACY: ROOTS OF THE KOREAN GOVERNMENT'S CULTURE AND COMPETITIVENESS
authors: Im, Tobin; Campbell, Jesse W; Cha, Seyeong
abstract: This paper looks at Korea's Chosun dynasty bureaucracy and the Neo-Confucian principles that formed the basis of its governing philosophy. We argue that Korea's traditional bureaucracy had a number of modern characteristics, including a system of formal and informal checks on the powers of the sovereign and a decision-making system that encouraged deliberation among highly qualified civil servants. On the basis of this exposition, we also argue that there are strong links between the traditional bureaucracy and its current, modern form. We firstly show how the institutionalization of a strong state during the period of rapid development was as much a return to traditional governing principles as it was a revolution and, secondly, how contemporary organizational culture is shaped by Korea's Confucian heritage. In the final section, we argue that the distinctive characteristics of the Korean bureaucracy have played an important role in limiting the success of a number of Western-oriented reform efforts. [Copyright John Wiley and Sons, Ltd.]

title: Negotiating the Superfund: Are Environmental Protection Agency regional officials willing to bargain with states?
abstract: Negotiation and bargaining are important activities in the implementation of intergovernmental public policies. Given the design of environmental policy, intergovernmental negotiations are an essential part of the interaction of environmental program managers. This study examines the willingness of Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) regional officials to bargain with their state counterparts in the national Superfund program. A model of working relationships is developed to analyze the negotiating behavior of regional EPA officials. The findings of this study indicate that both strategic (trust, involvement) and structural (relations with EPA headquarters, state program capacity, and state political context) factors are associated with whether or not regional officials are willing to negotiate with state-level administrators. The implications of these findings for the national Superfund program, the larger context of intergovernmental management, and larger themes in public administration are discussed in the conclusion of this paper. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Politics, Power, and Pathologies of International Organizations
abstract: International relations scholars have vigorous theories to explain why international organizations (IOs) are created, but they have paid little attention to IO behavior & whether IOs actually do what their creators intend. This blind spot flows logically from the economic theories of organization that have dominated the study of international institutions & regimes. To recover the agency & autonomy of IOs, we offer a constructivist approach. Building on Max Weber's well-known analysis of bureaucracy, we argue that IOs are much more powerful than even neoliberals have argued, & that the same characteristics of bureaucracy that make IOs powerful can also make them prone to dysfunctional behavior. IOs are powerful because, like all bureaucracies, they make rules, &, in so doing, they create social knowledge. IOs deploy this knowledge in ways that define shared international tasks, create new categories of actors, form new interests for actors, & transfer new models of political organization around the world. However, the same normative valuation on impersonal rules that defines bureaucracies & makes them powerful in modern life can also make them unresponsive to their environments, obsessed with their own rules at the expense of primary missions, & ultimately produce inefficient & self-defeating behavior. Sociological & constructivist approaches thus allow us to expand the research agenda beyond IO creation & to ask important questions about the consequences of global bureaucratization & the effects of IOs in world politics. 1 Figure, 65 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Use of Reorganization as a Management Tool
abstract: An analysis of Norwegian public administration based on organizational theory is presented, focusing on the extent of political control possible in a bureaucratic administration. Factors affecting the capacity of leadership to politically utilize this organization are first reviewed, eg: clear identification of objectives, understanding interactions between organizational form & political content, & ability to avoid prior mistakes. Although significant changes have occurred in the formal organizational structure of various departments since 1945, no consistent political design or motives for the changes can be identified. Using reorganization as a means of political control is discussed; problems in its use include conflicting objectives, limited opportunities for proposal implementation, & the growing influence & autonomy of the civil service workers. Increased use of reorganization tactics for political control is anticipated for the future. 23 References. Modified HA.

title: BUREAUCRACY AND THE IMPLEMENTATION OF ECONOMIC PLANS IN INDIA
abstract: Econ'ts of developing & developed countries alike have devoted their attention in the past primarily to the formulation aspect of planning to the detriment of the implementation aspect. The problems posed by implementation are far less glamorous than those of devising & manipulating sophisticated programming models, but advances in this bottle-neck area may be far more useful for ED than those achieved in programming techniques. This study looks at the admin'ive implications of plan implementation, the mechanics of bur'cy, bur'cy as an instrument of development policy, functional proliferation & regional coordination. It is to be hoped that the various Admin'ive Reforms Commissions set up in the States & at the center will come up with more than the customary generalizations on present inefficiency, red-tape & corruption & will have improvements to suggest that go beyond the perpetuation & instit'ization of their own work & the setting-up of more investigatory bodies, coordinating agencies & working groups. IPSA.

title: Advancing Administrative Supports for Research Development
authors: Briar-Lawson, Katherine; Korr, Wynne 'Sandra'; White, Barbara; Vroom, Phyllis; Aabora, James; Middleton, Jane; Shank, Barbara; Schatz, Mona
abstract: Research administrative supports must parallel & reinforce faculty initiatives in research grant procurement. This article features several types of developments that draw on presentations at the National Association of Deans & Directors of Schools of Social Work meetings. Key changes in social work programs are addressed, including the growing research portfolio, the growing number of centers & institutes, & National Institutes of Health funding. Mission-driven strategies are seen as essential to building effective research cultures & diverse research funding. Key developmental steps in building more robust research climates & cultures are cited in brief case scenarios. The article describes several features of research infrastructures & administrative supports that range from associate dean for research to research administrators. Adapted from the source document.

title: Individualization and Equality: Women's Careers and Organizational Form
authors: Wickham, James; Collins, Grainne; Greco, Lidia; Browne, Josephine
abstract: Some feminist writings have claimed that 'bureaucracy' is inherently 'patriarchal'. This article challenges this argument by comparing the experience of women in Ireland in a state sector organization and in a cluster of software firms. While the bureaucratic state company has been reformed to incorporate equal opportunities, in the individualized or 'marketized' software companies women's progress is at the whim of individual managers and motherhood and a career are largely incompatible. If bureaucratic organizations can be reformed in this way, it cannot be claimed that there is any inherent link between bureaucracy and patriarchy. Instead organizations can be either bureaucratic or marketized, and either patriarchal or woman-friendly. These are two separate dimensions which change independently of each other. On this basis the article suggests that the contemporary 'remasculinization' of management occurs because earlier reforms in bureaucratic organizations are now being eroded. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright 2008.]

title: Personality and Bureaucratic Structure
abstract: An attempt is made to ascertain the connections existing between bureaucratic structure & the personalities of those belonging to it. The hypothesis is that the process of secondary socialization, which is made in the organization in order to create personalities more suitable to its purposes, involves an adaptation of the employee's personality & a taking up of values which reflect in the attitudes & in the political guidances which are expressed outside the apparatus. The data were obtained from questionnaires administered to a proportionally stratified sample equal to 30% of the population of the universe examined. The stratification has been formed on the basis of the % incidence, of the whole universe, of M & F population & of 5 groups of hierarchic qualifications. Elements at top hierarchic levels were not included, as they present basic features very different from those of the personnel. The stay in the organization constitutes a determining element of the conformism to the current values of the apparatus. In other words, the administration, structured in a rigidly authoritative manner, in the end determines particular character manners which, in their turn, generate a specific conception of the world & certain social orientations in those who find themselves regimented in the same. The private bureaucratic official is inclined to have a vision of the world substantially conservative in that he tends to consider any form of innovation, any weakening of the established power as dangerous for the state & for the society. 1 Graph. AA.

title: Street-Level Bureaucracy, Social Work and the (Exaggerated) Death of Discretion
abstract: Lipsky's classic study of 'street-level bureaucracy' (1980) provided a perceptive analysis of front line practice in public organizations that has continuing relevance to recent literature, which has debated whether discretion continues to operate in social work or whether it has been curtailed. Having considered contributions to the debate on the continuation and curtailment of professional discretion in social work, it becomes clear that there are significant differences between these two positions, differences which focus on beliefs about manager' desire for, and ability to secure, control and workers' ability to resist control and seek discretion. However, after examining these issues further, through an examination of key aspects of Lipsky's work and Howe's (1991) critique of that work, a unifying strand is identified in the curtailment and continuation perspectives. Both perspectives have a tendency to treat professional discretion as a phenomenon that is either present or absent and rest on a background assumption, particularly in the curtailment literature, that professional discretion is self-evidently a 'good thing'. An alternative argument is advanced, based on two propositions: first, that the proliferation of rules and regulations should not automatically be equated with greater control over professional discretion; paradoxically, more rules may create more discretion. Second, discretion in itself is neither 'good' nor 'bad'. In some circumstances it may be an important professional attribute, in others it may be a cloak for political decision-makers to hide behind or it may be an opportunity for professional abuse of power. If this alternative argument is soundly based, future analysis of and research into professional discretion rooted in 'all-or-nothing' formulations are unlikely to advance understanding much beyond the impasse in the existing literature. Rather, the alternative argument suggests that discretion should be regarded as a series of gradations of freedom to make decisions and, therefore, the degree of freedom professionals have at specific conjunctures should be evaluated on a situation-by-situation basis.

title: Institutionalization and change in cultural policy: CONACULTA and cultural policy in Mexico (1988-2006)
abstract: This paper analyses the process of institutionalization of Mexican cultural policy and its evolution after the political alternation of 2000. It demonstrates that since its institutionalization with the creation of the National Council for Culture and Arts in 1988, the objectives, definitions and bureaucratic organization of the cultural policy have not known important changes in the period studied (1988-2006). The inertia observed in Mexican cultural policy can be explained by the institutional structures' constraints inherited from the Partido de la Revolucion Institucional (The Party of the Institutionalized Revolution) and by the actors' resistance to change. Adapted from the source document.

title: Political Organizations and Commedia Dell'Arte
abstract: Employs the dramatistic metaphor of commedia dell'arte to interpret developments in a set of interlocking public administrative organizations in Sweden. More specifically, the performances given by state & municipal politicians studied in several projects are analyzed, drawing on this special kind of theater. The symbolic acting, the public performances, & the ambiguous connection between ideas & realities of various sorts that are evident all made the theater metaphor appear relevant to an analysis of politics in society at large & in organizations within it. Of the different forms of theater, commedia dell'arte renders itself best to the exploration & interpretation of contemporary organizations within the public sector, imprinted as they are with the stamp of modern democratic politics, which bespeaks force but is highly contradictory. 44 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Social Foundations of the Bureaucratic Order
abstract: This article views the bureaucratic form of organization as both an agent & an expression of key modern social innovations that are most clearly manifested in the non-inclusive terms by which individuals are involved in organizations. Modern human involvement in organizations epitomizes & institutionally embeds the crucial yet often overlooked cultural orientation of modernity whereby humans undertake action along well-specified & delimited paths thanks to their capacity to isolate & suspend other personal or social considerations. The organizational involvement of humans qua role agents rather than qua persons helps unleash formal organizing from being tied to the indolence of the human body & the languish process of personal or psychological reorientation. Thanks to the loosening of these ties, the bureaucratic organization is rendered able to address the shifting contingencies underlying modern life by reshuffling & re-assembling the roles & role patterns by which it is made. The historically unique adaptive capacity of bureaucracy remains, though hidden behind the ubiquitous presence of routines & standard operating procedures that are mistakenly exchanged for the essence of the bureaucratic form. 78 References. [Copyright 2004 Sage Publications Ltd.]

title: Industrial Democracy and the State of Theory in the Sociology of Organization
abstract: Sociol'ts who occupied themselves with the sociol'al problems of industr democracy could be categorized as either structuralists (emphasizing the relation between function & form, eg, T. Parsons, & A. Etzioni), interactionalists (focusing on att's & COMM, eg, C. Argyris, R. Likert), or relationalists (who find a synthesis between structuralism & interactionalism, eg, J. G. March, H. A. Simon, P. Blau, & G. Homans). On the basis of relationalism a systems theoretical paradigm of an industr org can be developed. From this model a system of hyp's on the relation between flexibility, autonomy & the probability of success of democratization in an org is proposed. AA.

title: Social networks and labour market outcomes in a meritocracy
abstract: This paper examines the significance of personal contacts in job searches, in the context of Singapore's meritocratic system. I show that in certain sectors. such as the state bureaucracy, social networking brings no distinct advantages as appointments are made exclusively on the basis of the academic credentials of the candidates. Thus. personal contacts are not always useful. especially in labour markets that rely heavily on the signalling role of academic credentials to match persons to jobs and allocate rewards. In contrast. personal contacts are more useful among less qualified job searchers in the private sector. [Copyright Elsevier B.V.]

title: Partialism, Executive Control, and the Deportation of Permanent Residents from Australia
abstract: Many migration policies in Western democracies can be categorised as what Matthew J. Gibney calls a 'partialist' approach to migration. Drawing from communitarian, conservative, and constitutionalist realist political theories, a partialist approach prioritises the interests and values of citizens and the community over the needs of non-citizens. Stepping outside the normative debate, this paper examines the political implications of a partialist approach to migration policies. The paper argues that it is possible for such policies to be inconsistent with liberal democratic processes of government. Specifically, there is a risk that partialist ideas can be used to justify policies that set aside legal and administrative checks and balances in favour of executive control over migration policies. This is evident in the Australian policy of deportation of long-term permanent residents on character grounds. The paper argues that partialist ideas have been used to justify a high level of executive control over deportations. Executive control is achieved in three ways: broad powers of ministerial discretion; a mechanical bureaucracy, and the use of immigration detention. The cumulative effect means that deportation policy is implemented without the checks and balances fundamental to ensuring limits to executive power. Adapted from the source document.

title: Documenting Disputes: Law and Bureaucracy in Organizational Disputing
abstract: In an examination of how legal & bureaucratic concerns are interrelated in organizational dispute processing, observational data on dispute emergence in a Work Incentive Program & administrative hearings intended to adjudicate the disputes are analyzed to show how staff-client disagreements evolved as they were considered in different intra- & interorganizational dispute resolution settings. Of special concern is how staff members' routine, organizationally mandated, record-keeping practices anticipated the possible escalation of staff-client disagreements into formal disputes by providing staff members with documentary resources for justifying their actions to legal adjudicators. The staff's prospective orientation is contrasted with the shorter-term & relational orientation of most clients, which left them poorly prepared for the argumentative demands of legal adjudication, even when they were represented by legal counsel. Implications for reforming dispute processing in public bureaucracies are discussed. 1 Table, 11 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: A Basic Model Explaining Terrorist Group Organizational Structure
abstract: Terrorist groups strive to balance efficiency with their need for security. This article examines the factors that affect a group's choice of organizational structure. I classify 254 groups from the Global Terrorism Database into one of four basic structures: market, all-channel, hub-spoke, or bureaucracy. The results of a multinomial logistic regression reveal that as secret organizations, terrorist groups are not just driven by achieving efficiencies in their organization but rather by protecting against infiltration and threats. Internal factors such as target selection, operational pace, ideology, and stated goals shape a group's structure. External environmental factors such as political rights, civil liberties, polity durability, and state wealth also help shape a group's structure. Adapted from the source document.

title: Where Silenced Voices Speak Out: The Hidden Power of Informal Communication Networks
abstract: Explores how the masculine bias in patriarchal organizational reality marginalizes women & how women, when silenced, attempt to gain voice, using data on silencing episodes from interviews with 5 female employees & participant observation at a CA for-profit educational institution. Patriarchal bureaucracies foster social isolation of employees, monopolize information, & create bureaucratic dependency that employees can counter by building social relations & informal communication networks. Because of the feeling of helplessness when silenced by a male superior, these women turned to their informal communication networks for support, more information, & empowerment. Some information channels were deemed exclusive; they were not seen as instruments for change, but there was an overall perceived benefit in tapping into these networks. Examples of interaction where not remaining silent would have been inappropriate or ineffective are given. 40 References. M. Pflum

title: Subverting the Assembly-Line: Childbirth in a Free-Standing Birth Centre
abstract: Across the world, concern is being expressed about the rising rates of birth interventions. As a result, there is growing interest in alternative organisational models of maternity care. Most of the research to date on these models has examined clinical outcomes. This paper, discussing key findings from an ethnographic study of a free-standing birth centre in the UK, explores organisational dimensions to care. It suggests that the advantages of scale have been under-recognised by policy makers to date. The birth centre displays organisational characteristics that contrast with the dominant Fordist/Taylorist model of large maternity units. These characteristics allow for greater temporal flexibility in labour care & tend to privilege relational, 'being' care over task-orientated, 'doing' care. In addition, features of a bureaucracy are much less in evidence, enabling entrepreneurial activity to flourish. There may be lessons here for other heath services as well as maternity services in optimising the advantages of small-scale provision. Tables, References. [Copyright 2005 Elsevier Ltd.]

title: Dualing with gender: teachers' work, careers and leadership in physical education
abstract: The discursive practices of physical education reflect not only the expectations and constraints of discourses in the wider society, educational organizations and bureaucracies, but also the pervasive influences of working with and within sport. Within physical education, and specifically in the lives, work and careers of physical education teachers, in what ways are gender dualisms breaking down and in what ways are powerful gendered discourses still influential? This paper will outline results from research on teachers' work, careers and leadership in physical education, with a particular focus on gendered patterns. A mixed methods research design was used with 556 female and male participants in the quantitative phase and 17 participants in the qualitative phase. Some of the results challenged gender dualistic ways of thinking about physical education teachers' work, careers and leadership while other results indicated ways in which powerful dominant discourses still shape gendered patterns. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Multiple Faces of the Ideology of Intervention: A Story of Administrators' Fantasies and Implementors' Anxieties
abstract: The effects of state development programs are studied, with a focus on the Integrated Rural Development Program in the Atlantic zone of Costa Rica. The role of state bureaucrats in fostering modes of social control is emphasized; it is suggested that bureaucrats use ideologies of intervention to resolve practical administrative problems, & that community justice is an attempt by villagers to respond to efforts by state authorities to regulate their lives. It is argued that labels are used by bureaucrats both to explain complex situations & as a means of social control, & that this model is transformed by state workers as a protective device against political opposition. 21 References. B. Persky

title: Improving Social Work Education in Vietnam Through International Cooperation: The 'Social Work Education Enhancement Program'
authors: Hines, Alice; Cohen, Edward; Nguyễn, Hoa Thi; Drabble, Laurie; Han, Meekyung; Sen, Soma; Trâàn, Tuâán Dình
abstract: This paper describes an initiative to improve social work education in Vietnam through a three-year international collaborative, including US Aid for International Development, San José State University, eight universities in Vietnam, Vietnam's government ministries, and Cisco Systems, Inc. The social work profession was officially recognized by the Vietnamese government in 2010. Despite the rapid expansion of social work education programs, there are significant limitations in the universities' ability to provide social work education. The goal of the Social Work Education Enhancement Program (SWEEP) is to strengthen the capacity of Vietnam's undergraduate social work programs to deliver quality education and prepare trained, job-ready social workers. The SWEEP project aims to improve the administration of social work education, the professional capacity of faculty, social work curriculum, and networking technology to enable centers for excellence in learning and scholarship. To ensure that the SWEEP team targeted training and technical assistance activities that were culturally congruent, a comprehensive needs assessment and frequent mid-course evaluations were conducted, showing many shared and unique contextual issues facing universities. The collaborative process of developing social work education which fits the local context can be replicated in other countries that are in the early stages of social work development.

title: Markets, Bureaucracies, and Clans
abstract: Evaluating organizations according to an efficiency criterion would make it possible to predict the form organizations will take under certain conditions. Organization theory has not developed such a criterion because it has lacked a conceptual scheme capable of describing organizational efficiency in sufficiently microscopic terms. The transactions-cost approach provides such a framework because it allows the identification of the conditions that give rise to the costs of mediating exchanges between individuals: goal incongruence & performance ambiguity. Different combinations of these causes distinguish three basic mechanisms of mediation or control: markets, which are efficient when performance ambiguity is low & goal incongruence is high; bureaucracies, which are efficient when both goal incongruence & performance ambiguity are moderately high; & clans, which are efficient when goal incongruence is low & performance ambiguity is high. 2 Tables. HA.

title: Tasks in Changing the Organization from Within (COFW)
abstract: After an introduction of the basic components of changing an organization from within (COFW), an attempt is made to provide for the potential change catalyst in the human services organization more specific guidelines for action than are found in previously published material in this field. These guidelines are in the form of tasks-analytical & interactional. The analytical tasks discussed are: (1) goal determination (what the change will be); (2) resistance assessment (who & what may be potential obstacles to this change); & (3) strategy selection (which guidelines or strategies may be utilized to achieve the change goal. Of the many interactional tasks in an organizational change project, two major ones are presented & explored: developing the action system, & meeting with the administrators for decision making. HA.

title: The Political Economy of Federal Government Paperwork
authors: Bennett, James T; Johnson, Manuel H
abstract: Despite all the paperwork generated by the federal bureaucracy, little has been done to reduce its burden on individuals & private businesses. Since the late 1880s, a host of agencies, boards, bureaus, committees, commissions, departments, & task forces have undertaken appraisals, analyses, hearings, investigations, & studies that have resulted in directives, executive orders, legislation, recommendations, & reports to control federal paperwork. All to no avail. By almost any method of measurement, the dimensions of the paperwork created by the federal bureaucracy are enormous. In 1972, the federal government reported that 5,566 repetitive-use forms were being employed which generated more than 400 million responses from the private sector & required more than 145 million man-hours to complete. Because of the costs & the potential for abuse of the information collected through the paperwork process, some method must be instituted to reduce bureaucratic appetites for paper. Among such measures are a "tax" on bureau budgets which reduces funds available for such purposes as travel when a bureau increases paperwork, & continued monitoring & public exposure of the volume of paperwork generated on an agency-by-agency basis. It would be helpful, for instance, if every government form were to be required to display, in prominent type, the cost to the taxpayers of printing all copies of that form. Modified AA.

title: Sociologists in Public Administration
abstract: The author of this article presents the work responsibilities of sociologists in public administration. This is not an easy task because sociologists only seldom can be found working in the field under the job title of sociologist. In addition to a short historical introduction, the author gives an overview of the professional duties that sociologists tend to undertake in public administration. The author contends that the positions sociologists hold in public administration differ greatly. The author supports making sociology studies to more work-oriented in order to make the characteristics of public administration more familiar to students & to make better use of expert potential. Adapted from the source document.

title: INTERCULTURAL COMMUNICATION: A GUIDE TO MEN OF ACTION
authors: Hall, Edward T; Whyte, William F
abstract: An examination of the process of intercultural communication reveals how anthropol'al knowledge can help the business & gov administrator. Culture affects communication in determining the timing of events, discussion places, physical distance, tone of voice, amount & type of physical contact & intensity of emotion. Cultural influences without relation to honesty may occasion an agreeable rather than a factual response. The businessman's 5 temporal concepts are: appointment time, discussion time, acquaintance time, visiting time & time schedules. Latin American custom demonstrates a diff interpretation of both punctuality & appointment scheduling. Discussion in US culture is a means to an end, while elsewhere a soc element is interpolated. Acquaintance time, how long you must know a man before doing business, traditionally calls for 3 visits in Central America. The time schedule concept, key to US work patterns & informal communication process, touches off fundamental conflicts. Place restrictions on the discussion of business & politics are unwritten laws. Differing ideas on speaking distance give Latin Americans the impression that Americans are cold. Beyond a collection of customs, a society's communications pattern is part of its z culture pattern, with class channelling & limiting communication. Adjustment goes both ways when cultures interact, the problem being to induce changes skillfully. While complete conformity to other cultures is suspect as insincere, Americans can learn to observe unwritten communications patterns & adjust to time, distance & emotional orientations. For org'al effectiveness, res is needed on schemes of observation & testing to enable personnel selection on criteria of personality & culture. J. Field.

title: The Quarters of Bologna: Elements for the Analysis of a Case of Communal Decentralization
abstract: The main stages of the development of decentralization in Bologna are reconstructed & documented. (1) Introduzione (Introduction). The movement toward local autonomy stems from the inefficiency of public administration & the desire of citizens to participate in government to fulfill their own political & social demands. (2) I motivi e il contesto generale dell'esperienza bolognese (The Motives and the General Context of the Experience in Bologna). The internal political struggles preceding the official governmental provisions establishing various decentralizing politico-administrative offices are detailed. (3) Le tappe fondamentali del decentramento (The Fundamental Stages of Decentralization). The evolution & internal dynamics of decentralization are delineated more specifically. The most important stages, with regard to either internal development, or to determining factors of a more general nature, are the following: (A) Gli anni della gestazione (1955-1960) (The Years of Gestation), (B) Gli anni della fondazione (1960-1963) (The Years of Foundation), (C) Gli anni dell'avvio dell'esperienza (1964-1967) (The Years of the Beginning of the Experience), (D) Gli anni dell'impatto con la realta (per i quartieri) e dell'incertezza (per i partiti) (1967-1970) (The Years of the Impact with Reality [for the Quarters] and of Indecision [for the Parties]), & (E) Gli anni recenti (1970-1974) (The Recent Years). 6 Appendices, Bibliography, Index of Illustrations, Tables, Charts. A. Rubins.

title: The Principle of Proportionality and Its Implementation in Lithuanian Administrative Law
abstract: This article deals with the role of the principle of proportionality in the system of Lithuanian administrative law. The aim of this article is to observe the implementations of the principle of proportionality in Lithuanian administrative law and the application of this principle in Lithuanian courts. This paper offers an examination of the nature of the principle of proportionality in administrative law, a review of the representation of this principle in Lithuanian legislation, and in particular makes an observation of the role of this principle in the judicial review of Lithuanian courts - specifically, the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Lithuania and the Supreme Administrative Court of Lithuania. The article reviews the recent practice of these courts. The article consists of two main parts: a review of relevant legislation and a review of the implementation of this principle in Lithuanian courts. In connection with the place and importance of the principle of proportionality in Lithuanian administrative law, this article distinguishes two fields for the implementation of this principle: (1) the application of the principle of proportionality when the subject of public administration makes the decision on a private person and (2) an assessment of the legitimacy of the decision made by the subject of public administration in the judicial process on the basis of this principle. Adapted from the source document.

title: Constructing a new political spectacle: tactics of Chen Shui-bian's 2000 and 2004 Inaugural Speeches
abstract: This article explores how the Taiwan President Chen Shui-bian uses political language rhetoric as a powerful tool to defuse dangerously tense relations with China, repair relations with the US government and gain public support in the country. I focus on Chen's inaugural speeches delivered on 20 May 2000 and 2004, which present the rationale for his new administration and his socio-political ideologies, and I review his political spectacle for Taiwan. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Police Bureaucracies, Their Incentives, and the War on Drugs
authors: Benson, Bruce L; Rasmussen, David W; Sollars, David L
abstract: After 1984 local law enforcement agencies in the US substantially increased arrests for drug offenses relative to arrests for property & violent crimes. Here, it is explored why this reallocation of police resources occurred, focusing on alternative public interest & bureaucratic self-interest explanations. In a case study, the Comprehensive Crime Act of 1984 is shown to have altered the incentives of police agencies in FL by allowing them to keep the proceeds of assets forfeited as a result of drug enforcement activities. Empirical evidence is presented which shows that police agencies can increase their discretionary budgets through the asset forfeiture process. 1 Table, 1 Figure, 71 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Legal protections against criminal background checks in Europe
abstract: This article discusses whether there is an increasing demand for criminal background checks in continental Europe. It also presents the legislative framework regulating criminal background checks in Europe where a requirement of 'proof of a clean criminal record' in public administration often co-exists with a situation where no specific laws regulate the rights of private employers to ask for such proof. Finally, the article suggests some legal protections for ex-offenders against the increasing use of criminal records in the job market and suggests that a law may be necessary to regulate the right of private employers to conduct criminal background checks. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Dissidents, disloyal citizens and partisans of emancipation: Feminist citizenship in Yugoslavia and post-Yugoslav spaces
abstract: This paper aims to offer an alternative reading of the history of feminism in Yugoslavia and its successor states, relying on the concept of citizenship. Assuming that one could differentiate between three different citizenship regimes -- the first framed by the socialist self-management state, the second by the nation-building processes and violent disintegration of the former state, and the last one by post-socialist, post-conflict transitional circumstances -- the paper explores their impact on an uneven development of gender regimes and feminist activism. Seen as the model instance of activist citizenship, feminist activism is presented through three different phases in order to show how they, as well as the frameworks of their interpretation, change, changing also the meaning of feminism as a political force.

title: The Role of Bureaucracy in Soviet Patterned Societies and in Their Transformation. The First Attempt at the Problem
abstract: A literature review shows that stratification models cannot adequately account for the origin, development, & function of bureaucracy in the former USSR. In countries failing to distinguish state from society or economy from politics, there are many possibilities for strategic action by the bureaucracy that do not exist in Western democracies. To some extent, the Soviet bureaucracy was shaped by the bureaucratic experience of Czarist Russia, which also lacked the notion of a civil society. After the Bolshevik revolution, bureaucracy was strengthened by the ambiguous policies toward the new economic policy, the rise of the Communist party apparatus, the availability of prerevolutionary specialists in executive positions, insufficient executive power in the villages, & the emergence of an underground economy. The highest-ranking party officials enjoyed enormous privileges, while lower-ranking members enjoyed power incommensurate with their ostensibly low income. Those with access to key goods & services formed the nouveau riche, deriving special income through bribery in an economy plagued by perpetual shortages. Instability resulted because the nouveau riche depended on the arbitrariness of the political elite while lacking the dynamism to accumulate productive capital. Since the movement away from communism in 1991, new possibilities have arisen to misuse power & strategic resources, leading to a dangerous political situation. 25 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Crops, cattle, and capital: Agrarian political ecology in Canyons de Chelly and del Muerto
abstract: Andrews examines the differential impacts of a number of factors on Navajo farming and ranching, including government-sponsored resource-management programs in and adjacent to New Mexico's Canyon de Chelly and Canyon del Muerto.  In part, these programs reflected both general US federal-Indian policies and regional political economic interests.

title: Action research in nursing homes
abstract: This article concerns the experiences gained from the action research project, Quality in Elder Care, involving social dimensions of quality in public elder care. The aim of the project was to improve the professional skills and engagement of the care workers and to improve the life quality and participation of the residents. Furthermore, the idea was that the project could strengthen a public and professional discourse about more democratic and inclusive alternatives (for staff as well as residents) to the currently growing bureaucracy and expansion of top-down control systems in elder care. The project was inspired by critical utopian action research with future workshops as an important methodological tool. The project followed the core characteristics of action research to be "a shared commitment to democratic social change". The article discusses how the project contributed to changes in care quality in a joint effort between care workers, residents at the nursing home, and researchers. It concludes that the project led to empowerment of the residents and staff and played an important role in the development of democratic knowledge building about better quality and ethics in elder care.

title: CRITERIA FOR RECRUITMENT AND SUCCESS IN THE JAPANESE BUREAUCRACY 1868-19 TRADITIONAL AND MODERN CRITERIA IN BUREAUCRATIC DEVELOPMENT
abstract: It is often assumed that bur'cies in developing societies must possess the chief characteristics of M. Weber's legalrational model if they are to be successful in carrying out rapid pol'al, econ & soc change. Japan presents an excellent case study since, after 1868, a new nat'l civil bur'cy recruited ostensibly from a traditionally-oriented society carried out widespread reforms with great success & speed. The validity of the assumption is tested by examination of the criteria for eligibility, recruitment & success in the civil bur'cy in the period 1868-1900. Analysis was carried out by examination of the soc, econ & educ'al backgrounds of a selected random sample of upper civil servants. The analysis indicates that eligibility was based on birth in the traditional pol'al elite, but that recruitment & success were based on the possession of 2 achievement-oriented criteria: (1) participation in nontraditional pol'al activities, (2) possession of some Western educ &/or knowledge. Several conclusions may be drawn: (a) the presence of ascriptive criteria need not hinder & may help, by bestowing prestige & status, in the formation of an effective bur'cy at early stages of development, & (b) civil bur'cies in developing societies appear to require to some degree some of the characteristics of the legalrational type to be effective. AA.

title: THE USSR-FROM CHARISMATIC SECT TO BUREAUCRATIC SOCIETY
abstract: To what societal type does the Communist world belong? Western models (slavery, feudalism & capitalism) are not applicable. The Communist institutional type differs from the Western by (1) a statist or nationalized economy, (2) a bur'tic ruling class, & (3) a system of authority based on charisma, not legal-rational rules. The result is bur'tic despotism or totalitarian society. Following Max Weber's insights, 2 kinds of bur'cy are distinguished: charismatic & legal-rational. Bolshevism is analyzed as a charismatic movement which, through institutionalization, results in a charismatic bur'tic society. The Communist bur'cy is a ruling class, administering a state property system. In that institutional setting, industrialization serves not so much to raise the standard of living (as under capitalism) but primarily to maintain & extend Communist power & guarantee its charismatic claims to superiority & salvation. Though a common historical form, existing in Incan Peru, Pharaonic Egypt & classical China, charismatic bur'tic despotism is outside the Western tradition of pluralistic societies based on private property. Western bur'cies are not totalitarian; they neither raise total moral claims nor constitute a ruling class but remain sources of countervailing power in a pluralistic, not monolithic, society. It is in the distinction between charismatic bur'cies (inherently totalitarian institutionally & ideologically) & legal-rational bur'cies (merely functional, admin'ive & hence, democratically controllable) that hope lies for a deeper understanding of the problems of the contemporary world. AA.

title: Rapid Needs Appraisal in the modern NHS: potential and dilemmas
authors: Balogh, Ruth; Whitelaw, Sandy; Thompson, Jane
abstract: This paper reports on our experience of undertaking a Rapid Appraisal of Health and Social Needs (RNA) in West Cumbria, UK. RNA aims to identify community-defined problems and to collect intelligence for action rather than simply for documentation. The broad nature of the study is summarised and we reflect critically on methodological and structural issues that arose. A number of inter-related themes were significant: the limitations of a 'rapid' approach; within an action frame, the implications that arose from focusing on locality capacity-building; the ability that commissioning organisations had in this public health domain; and the way in which such organisations tend to construct 'needs'. These themes then are located in problematic contexts. Primarily, we were working with a fledgling NHS organisation, arguably set unrealistically high expectations to deliver innovative public health functions.
