A 608 item classified annotated bibliography is presented, organized as follows: I-Bibliographies & Anthologies (16); II-General Studies: 1-Theory of Burley (88), 2-Theory of Org (54), 3-Public administration as related to Burley (22), 4-Problems of Control of Burley & its Soc Setting (65); III-Bur'cy & Society: 1-Major Historical Types of Bur'cies & Conditions of their Development (53), 2-Major Modern & Contemporary Types of Bur'cies & Conditions of their Development (49); IV-Major Types of Bur'tic Org's & Processes of Bur'tization in Select Types of Org's: 1-The Civil Service (49), 2-Special Gov Agencies (9), 3-Econ & Industrial Bur'cies (36), 4-Public Corporations & Nationalized Industries (15), 5-Municipal Gov (8), 6-Pol'al Parties (15), 7-Trade Unions (20), 8-Army & Military Org's (19), 9-Professions (18), 10-Hosp's (5), 11-Voluntary Org's (5), 12-Educ'al & Cultural Org's (19); V-The Bur'crat: Types of Bur'tic Roles (32). J. Neyer.

title: Whither Bureaucratic Influence?: A Cautionary Note
abstract: The diminishing bureaucratic influence theory of Francis Rourke (see abstract in this section of SOPODA 14:1) is critiqued, based on a review of the literature on bureaucracy. It is argued that, although Rourke identifies real trends in evaluations of bureaucratic advice & discretion, the diminishing influence theory is contradicted by current research. It is argued that a contingency theory of bureaucratic influence needs to be developed to explain current trends. 51 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Organizations and Society
abstract: Questions are raised re whether a sci'fic concept of "org" or a sci'fic "sociol of org" are possible & what the scope & function of res into org's should be. Org studies, esp in the US, are summarized with special focus on the contributions of the sf & the actionalist Sch's of thought. In terms of the latter, A. Touraine, SOCIOLOGIE DE L'ACTION (Sociology of Action, Paris, France: 1965), is discussed. Some other approaches, eg, through the existentialism of Jean-Paul Sartre & the phenomenological orientation of Jean Lojkine, are noted. It is found that a pertinent sociol'al theory of org's can only be developed within the framework of a theory of society as a whole. The org'al phenomenon is one aspect of soc reality & must be seen in its dialectical relationship with it. Modified HA.

title: The Rationalizing Logics of Public School Reform: How Cultural Institutions Matter for Classroom Instruction
abstract: The research herein uses a mixed methods approach to examine how organizational phenomena at the macro level of analysis translate into phenomena at the micro level. Specifically, the research attempts to explain how cultural institutions may translate into individual attitudes and actions, such as public school teachers' decisions about using instructional practices prescribed by reform. The findings suggest that public school teachers rationalize their instructional practices by drawing on the logics of three core cultural institutions: bureaucracy, democracy, and markets. When the logics of these institutions are violated, teachers reduce their reported use of prescribed instructional practices. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright holder.]

title: Contribution to the Definition of "Socialist" Bureaucracy
abstract: Professional politicians in socialism & "socialist bureaucrats" are argued to be quite different -- the first a necessary stratum, & the second a continuing danger. Both groups, along with the Wc, have their roots in the DofL, & can only be abolished through its abolition, which will be possible only when there is an integrated system of workers' self-management. Professional politicians have the right to govern or manage only those SE affairs that have been assigned to them by the Wc, or those that the agencies & institutions of workers' self-management are unable to govern. When this stratum interferes with workers' self-management, it becomes a bureaucracy, & changes from the servant of the Wc to its master. Modified HA

title: An Involuntary Ethnography of a Stay in the Hospital: Being Sick in a Sick Place
authors: Miller, Robert K, Jr; Wadsworth, Angela L
abstract: The author describes the events which happened in a hospital after suffering a massive cerebellar stroke on a minor highway while alone in his car. It is concluded that the hospital was a "sick place" and that the hyper-bureaucratization of medical care has victimized all participants, patients and staff alike. Several concerns of the post-Parsonian model of sociological literature are discussed, including full disclosure of information to patients, are found to be of somewhat marginal importance. Adapted from the source document.

title: Professional identities: policy and practice in business and bureaucracy
abstract: Demetriou reviews Professional identities: policy and practice in business and bureaucracy edited by Shirley Ardener and Fiona Moore.

title: Participatory Practices in Organizations
abstract: The literature on participatory practices in organizations has been less coherent and more limited to subspecialties than the literature on bureaucracy in organizations-despite a number of celebrated studies of participation in 20th century American sociology. Due to the practical nature of participatory reforms and the ambiguity of participation as a concept, attempts to review participatory knowledge have a tendency to focus on refining definitions and clarifying frameworks within subfields. This article instead provides a broad thematic overview of three different types of research on participation in organizations, all critical to an understanding of today's dramatic expansion of participatory practices across a variety of organizations. Classic research studied participation as dynamic and central to organizational legitimacy. Institutional design research has focused on participation as a stand-alone governance reform with promising empowerment potential, but mixed results in domains such as health care, environmental politics, and urban planning. Finally, recent research seeks to place participatory practices in the context of shifting relationships between authority, voice, and inequality in the contemporary era. The article concludes with suggestions for building on all three categories of research by exploring what is old and new in the 21st century's changing participatory landscape.

title: Total Quality Management: Antiunion Trojan Horse or Management Albatross?
abstract: Examines a cooperative union-management approach toward total quality management (TQM) by recourse to a case study from the auto components manufacturing sector in GB. In contrast to much critical thinking, under certain conditions, TQM need not undermine trade unions. Indeed, a more moderate trade union stance toward TQM, in some circumstances, may prove to be a more effective form of resistance than a militant one. Insights are offered as to how TQM reinforces existing power relations, hierarchical structures, organizational bureaucracy, & inequality, rather than transforming them, as TQM pundits contend. The argument, however, is not that TQM simply enhances management control in a unilinear fashion. This is because TQM not only poses dangers for trade unions, but also presents management with dilemmas & contradictions. TQM is understood, therefore, to be part of the continuing & complex effort by management to balance control & consent among employees, the dynamics & outcomes of which are uncertain. 73 References. Adapted from the source doument.

title: TOWARD A THEORY OF ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOR
abstract: Org'al analysis has recently shifted emphasis from structured rationality to individual behavior, due mainly to sociol'al influence. Psychol'al formulations are here focussed on the relations of total org'al situation & the individual. The theory emphasizes `locals' interested in adapting to the org. 3 types are postulated: (1) the upward-mobiles-to whom org is satisfactory: (2) the indifferents-to whom dissatisfaction is insufficient to provoke withdrawal; (3) the ambivalents-who react to unsatisfactory org'al situation by rebellion or withdrawal. Org is viewed as a system of structured SR's (explicit authority, status, & role). The psychiatric viewpoint of H. S. Sullivan suggests that accommodation to org is prompted by a wish for anxiety-reduction. Learning theory is invoked to explain the individual's tendency to conform to authoritative commands. The distinctive features of bur'cy (explicitness, specificity, authoritativeness, control of major reward resources) increase the likelihood of conformity. 3 hyp's are advanced: (a) the more structured the stimuli, the more predictable & constant the response; (b) behavior is more predictable & constant in complex org's than in voluntary associations; & (c) individual patterns of accommodation to org's vary with att's to authority & with SES. Finally, the upward-mobiles are seen as those who accept the legitimacy & rationality of the org, the indifferents as those who seek satisfactions outside of org, & the ambivalents as those who accept org'al values but are unable to conform with them. B. Beck.

title: Beyond "Incrementalism," Organizational Theory and Public Policy
abstract: A closer analysis of bureaucratic organizations' role in the public policy process may aid in resolving the debate between advocates of incremental policy models & advocates of rational/synoptic policy models. Based on the assumption that responsibility for formulating & implementing public policy has shifted increasingly to bureaucratic organizations, it is argued that organizational theory suggests a place for both rational & incremental decision making in organizations. Two modes of policy making, diachronic & synchronic, conform generally to the rational & incremental models. In bureaucratically dominated policy areas, the crucial task for students of public policy is to predict shifts between these modes. Several factors which may account for such shifts are defined. Modified HA.

title: Arranging public support to unfold collaborative modes of governance in rural areas
authors: Wellbrock, Wiebke; Roep, Dirk; Mahon, Marie; Kairyte, Emilija; Nienaber, Birte; Dominguez Garcia, Maria Dolores; Kriszan, Michael; Farrell, Maura
abstract: Raising collective agency is key to successful place-based development approaches. Existing policy arrangements have, however, been criticised, suggesting a need to effectuate more collaborative modes of governance. This paper shall contribute to a better understanding of how public support can best be arranged to raise collective agency for a more collaborative mode of governance in rural areas. The paper elaborates on findings of empirical investigations conducted within the EU FP7 project DERREG. It will be shown that differences in effectuating more collaborative modes of governance can partly be ascribed to different political dynamics, economic and demographic situations as well as the presence of a shared sense of place. To raise collective agency effectively requires a joint reconsideration and restructuring of the division of roles and tasks, including those of public administration. This can be supported by facilitating joint reflexivity among development actors and giving room for collaborative leadership and operational flexibility within policy arrangements. [Copyright Elsevier Ltd.]

title: Manuel, Recovering the Sense of the Democratic Movement Through Living Solidarity in Dialogic Literary Gatherings
authors: Pulido-Rodríguez, Miguel A; Amador, Jelen; Rodrigo, Eva Alonso
abstract: Manuel's biography shows a valuable process of re-enchantment and belief in the possibility of social change. Manuel was strongly disenchanted with the bureaucratization established in Spain during the transition from the Franco regime to democracy in the mid-70s. He recovered his enchantment with democratic movements through contact with the social and educational movement of adult education in La Verneda (Barcelona) and especially through his participation in the Dialogic Literary Gatherings held in the school for adults. In Manuel's words, the gathering was the best expression of democracy in the school; it was the democratic experience that he had always imagined. In this outstanding space, he could listen to his friends, who, just like him, had lowly academic backgrounds, and share in the reading of the best universal classic literature. For Manuel, this gathering held the germ of a great debate on social, cultural, and democratic transformation.

title: Symbolic Representation in Police Traffic Stops
abstract: Bureaucratic representation is the idea that nonelected officials can address the interests of citizens as effectively as elected officials can. It has an active component and a passive component. The passive component is the concept that citizens are affected in a different way cognitively by a bureaucratic actor who resembles them than by one who does not. The chief difficulty in addressing the question of a symbolic effect has been a reliance on aggregate data. This study uses as its data supplemental surveys to the National Crime Victimization Survey called the Police-Public Contact Survey. A difference was found in how African American and White citizens react to police officers. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The EU Accession and Strengthening of Institutions in East Central Europe: The Case of Poland
abstract: In Eastern/Central Europe, the progress of democratization has been slower than originally anticipated; this is particularly true for Poland. Here, the weaknesses of the Polish institutional order are outlined, & the growing public dissatisfaction with public institutions & officials is explored, along with the attendant growth of nationalist & populist sentiments. Implications for the integration of Poland into the European Union (EU) are considered, & mechanisms by which Poland & other Eastern/Central European candidate countries can improve their administrative capacity & efficiency so as to increase the success of the integration process are outlined. K. Hyatt Stewart

title: Manipulated Science in a Manipulated Society
abstract: The premise here is that a certain correspondence exists between the nature of the state--in capitalistic societies & under bureaucratic socialism--& the institutions & tenor of science & technology within a given society. A "domino theory" is offered for this situation, & the question asked is whether science & political technologies should perpetuate this theory for society without taking into account economic organization & political ideologies, or whether within a new social order, politics can achieve a harmony between man & nature--& on that ground, acquire a science & a technology that have their differences. Discussed in detail are such related subjects as the external pragmatism of the politics of science, the unity of science & technology, the internal structure of the sociology of science, the manipulation of science in Great Britain, the "machinery" of governmental reports, the domains of man & nature, scientific planning & human freedom, a scientific "factory" or a scientific community, & the disenchantment of science. On the last subject, a general feeling of pessimism is expressed by liberal members of the scientific community. J. Shiffer.

title: A Cognitive Mask? Camouflaging Dilemmas in Street-Level Policy Implementation to Safeguard Older People from Abuse
abstract: National policy to safeguard older people from abuse in England and Wales gives social services the lead role in co-ordinating local multi-agency adult safeguarding procedures. With the exception of Lipsky's (1980) work on street-level bureaucracy, relatively little research attention has considered the day-to-day reality of social workers charged with implementing public policy. This article reports findings of multi-method research carried out in a social services department in Wales to identify the constraints and realities social workers faced when implementing policy to protect older people from abuse. Data sources were thirty-three social workers and managers and local adult safeguarding documentation and statistics. Methods included semi-structured interviews, focus groups, observed meetings, and documentary and statistical analysis of adult protection activity. The research found the dilemmas social workers grappled with were inherent in the structure of their work, as Lipsky had proposed. Dilemmas included known poor practice and quality in some care services, resource shortfalls and delays in investigating alleged elder abuse. The paper concludes by developing the metaphor of a 'cognitive mask' to describe how social workers manage the dissonance arising from dilemmas inherent in the context of their work to safeguard elders and it suggests how this 'mask' can be removed. Adapted from the source document.

title: New Technologies of Administration in Area of Social Assistance and Social Services for the Population
abstract: The article represents the new management tools in social assistance & social service delivery that are promoted by the Institute for Urban Economics since several recent years. These tools include cash consumer subsidies, social vouchers, competitive procurement of social services & contracting, outcome-based social assistance programs, performance measurement tools as well as administrative tools. Tables, References. Adapted from the source document.

title: General Systems Theory and Criminal Justice
authors: Bernard, Thomas J; Paoline, Eugene A, III; Pare, Paul-Philippe
abstract: Criminal justice agencies are organized sequentially -- "output" from one agency is "input" to the next -- but most scholars argue that criminal justice is not a system in a theoretical sense. In this article, it is argued that general systems theory (GST) reveals important insights into criminal justice structures & functions. Specifically, it is argued that the criminal justice system processes "cases" rather than people, & that the common goal of criminal justice processing is to "close cases so that they stay closed." It also is argued that processing capacity progressively declines, in that at each system point the subsequent agency cannot input as many cases as the previous agency can output. Each agency therefore experiences "backward pressure" to close cases in order to reduce input to the next agency. Overall, this article highlights that criminal justice agents & agencies are best understood as operating in the context of the larger whole, thus it is concluded that criminal justice is a system in the sense of general systems theory. 33 References. [Copyright 2005 Elsevier Ltd.]

title: The Transnational Capitalist Class and Contemporary Architecture in Globalizing Cities
abstract: The focus of this article is on the role of the transnational capitalist class (TCC) in and around architecture in the production and marketing of iconic buildings and spaces, in global or world cities. The TCC is conceptualized in terms of four fractions: (1) Those who own and/or and control the major transnational corporations and their local affiliates (corporate fraction). In architecture these are the major architectural, architecture-engineering and architecture-developer-real estate firms. In comparison with the major global consumer goods, energy and financial corporations the revenues of the biggest firms in the architecture industry are quite small. However, their importance for the built environment and their cultural importance, especially in cities, far outweighs their relative lack of financial and corporate muscle. (2) Globalizing politicians and bureaucrats (state fraction). These are the politicians and bureaucrats at all levels of administrative power and responsibility who actually decide what gets built where, and how changes to the built environment are regulated. (3) Globalizing professionals (technical fraction). The members of this fraction range from the leading technicians centrally involved in the structural features of new building to those responsible for the education of students and the public in architecture. (4) Merchants and media (consumerist fraction). These are the people who are responsible for the marketing of architecture in all its manifestations. (There is obviously some overlap between the membership of these fractions.). My conclusion is that many global and aspiring global cities have looked to iconic architecture as a prime strategy of urban intervention, often in the context of rehabilitation of depressed areas. The attempt to identify the agents most responsible for this transformation, namely the TCC, and to explain how they operate, suggests that deliberately iconic architecture is becoming a global phenomenon, specifically a central urban manifestation of the culture-ideology of consumerism.[PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Liberal Protestants and Urban Renewal
abstract: This article examines the liberal Protestant encounter with the urban renewal programs that remade U.S. cities after World War II. Suburbanization had punishing consequences for cities and threatened the already tenuous presence of liberal Protestants there. The concept of renewal -- in both its religious and secular dimensions --promised a solution to these problems. Many renewalists, those clergy and laypeople who viewed deteriorating urban neighborhoods as an opportunity to restore Church unity, initially embraced urban renewal as a secular corollary to their work. But the interaction among ecclesial organizations, government, and inner city parishioners over its implementation exacerbated tensions within liberal Protestantism. Many who initially supported urban renewal came to conclude that its results did not match their own objectives. By supporting challenges to redevelopment from African Americans, Latinos, and other urban residents, renewalists criticized the Church for what they believed to be complicity in the degradation of Christian culture and the urban environment. This history demonstrates the mutual influence of culture and organizational structure within liberal Protestantism and the impact of those changes on secular society. Renewalists grappling with urban renewal programs interpreted both theological and secular concepts through their own experiences with city populations, Church bodies, government, and redevelopment agencies. Their subsequent actions prompted mainline denominational leaders to support, for a time, at least, ministries geared more towards to indigenous community development. Such ministries reflected a more pluralist conception of society and the Church's role in it. Eventually, renewalists' opponents turned this pluralist conception on its head, decentralizing the church bureaucracies that had funded their ministries. An analogous process took place in the urban renewal programs themselves, underscoring the ways in which religious and urban histories intersect.

title: A Methodological Note on Bureaucratic Modernization: Prevalent Attitudes of the Turkish Civil Servants
abstract: Studies of bureaucratic modernization in transitional societies typically seek to determine how closely the civil service, in particular, approximates the Weberian legal-rational bureaucratic model, & conclude that the study of bureaucracy in a non-Western setting reveals the limitations of bureaucratic theory. It is suggested that the way this ideal type has been utilized is misleading. In transitional contexts, it is necessary to use multiple ideal types to empirically compare different organizations &/or their members. A case study of the Turkish civil service, based on mail questionnaire data from 345 civil servants working in 12 central ministries, indicates that this approach yields meaningful findings. It is possible to uncover the relative strengths of bureaucratic attitudes & to account for their mixture in terms of intra- &/or extraorganizational variables. The persistence of traditional elements & the superimposition of modern elements on them can be accounted for. In addition, it can be determined how functional the emerging organizational pattern is for the tasks confronting it. 6 Tables, 1 Appendix, 98 References. Modified HA.

title: States of imagination
abstract: Neoliberals detest the state and aim to downsize it or even make it wither away. And defending it certainly raises problems. Many people disenchanted by formal politics no longer look to the state, despairing of its associations with bureaucracy, hierarchy, corruption, secrecy and lies. Others view it as an outdated institution, a left-over legacy of nineteenth-century nation-building and twentieth-century power politics that has little relevance to those seeking to create new responses to contemporary challenges. However, a politics of the state still matters. And how people imagine the state, how they feel about it, will shape the kinds of politics that are possible. Popular disenchantment with the state reflects the experiences of the kind of state they currently have to live with, at least in Britain -- a state that has been commodified, marketised and managerialised, and seems to ignore the human relationships at stake in its encounters with citizens. Adapted from the source document.

title: Boards of Inquiry, the Siberian Administration and Taxation on Aboriginal Russians in the 18th Century
abstract: Based on the administrative & judicial sources of the Russian State Archive of Ancient Acts in Moscow, this paper analyses several aspects of activity of the extraordinary commissions in Siberia, which is a major contribution to the strengthening of the monarchical power & the imperial control on the country's peripheral provinces during the 18th century. The essential mission of these commissions is to pursue the abuses inside the local administration. Finally, through an analysis of the successes & failures of their investigations, various facets of the reality of the Siberian administration, its social universe, the management practices & its relationships with the native people, just after the conquest of Siberia, will be described. In particular, a great effort is provided by the commissions in order to eradicate the fur trade smuggling developed in the border area between Russia & China to the detriment of the interests of the State. During the years of 1760, these commissions contribute to the realization of the Yasak tax reform which gives a new dimension to the Russian Monarchy's colonial policy. This reform resulted in the improvement of the administrative & financial structures & mechanisms for a better integration of the Siberian territory & people into the Empire. Adapted from the source document.

title: Unblinking: Citizens and Subjects in the Age of Video Surveillance
abstract: A discussion of audio and video surveillance. The author explores a number of questions including "do rules against audio and video surveillance disempower citizens by making government officials" and "can privacy be used to protect government bureaucracies and corporations from oversight." The author also examines the harm associated with surveillance. Adapted from the source document.

title: Public Administration-A Professional Field for Social Scientists? Results of an Empirical Study
abstract: Following a preliminary analysis of the attitudes formally required of civil servants, the type & scope of the activities of social scientists in public administrative offices were studied. Social scientists (number of cases = 510) were found working in 401 administrative offices. Of these, 135 sociologists, 59 political scientists, & 78 economists were given a questionnaire. Sociologists were more often active in planning, social casework, & family policy; political scientists dealt with public relations & adult education. Most functioned more as specialists than as generalists. In their studies, 26% had concentrated on methods of empirical social science research, 29% on sociology, 12% on social & economic policy, 11% on pedagogy & psychology, & 8% on law. As preparation for public service, 41% of sociologists suggested an interdisciplinary curriculum including sociology, economics, & political science; 18% suggested law studies, 13% specialization in a single discipline, & 10% planning. 4 Tables. S. Whittle.

title: Government and Local Public Management in the Decentralization Scenario
abstract: The change toward a new decentralized model of public management for Latin America needs to start by giving municipal councils the necessary power to implement development policies within its sociospatial base. Further, within a democratic society the construction of local decentralized governments requires the active participation of the population. Within this framework, the different types of organization of local governments across Latin America are reviewed & their development potential assessed. Finally, models of public management are discussed in relation to local instances of power, proposing a democratic planning strategy for decentralization. 52 References. R. Jaramillo

title: Feminist Organizations: Harvest of the New Women's Movement
abstract: Readers might understandably be overwhelmed by an edited volume of this length. In the case of Feminist Organizations, this is exactly the editors' intention. Ferree and Martin rightly argue that scholars interested in organization theory and practice have all but ignored nearly thirty years of feminist experimentation with organization structure. Paying homage to Robert Michel's "Iron Law of Oligarchy," many organization theorists in the social sciences and management have focused on questions of efficiency and control assuming the inevitability and utility of hierarchy in public and private bureaucracies (5).For a complete reprint of this article contact Haworth Press by telephone (1-800-HAWORTH) or EMail (getinfo@haworthpressinc.com) Article copyright The Haworth Press, Inc.

title: Almost a Conclusion
abstract: In concluding remarks on this journal issue (see related abstracts in SA 44:4), topics needing further study in Italian public administration (PA) research are outlined. Because PA is composed of both local & central administrations, as well as by public-owned busiesses, research should concentrate more on the different features & challenges of organizational innovations in service delivery at each level. Empirical investigation & categorization of PA's specific actions should incorporate contextualized information linked to the action-defining normative structures, especially the kind of social or organizational actors at both the regional & national levels. Research must also focus on the impact of current political trends & the implications of decisions of elected officials for local PA. Adapted from the source document.

title: THE IDEOLOGY OF PARTICIPATION IN THE 'BUREAUCRATIC PHENOMENON' OF MR. CROZIER
abstract: A critical analysis of LE PHENOMENE BUREAUCRATIQUE (The Bureaucratic Phenomenon, Paris, France: no yr, Seuil), by Michel Crozier, which reviews the central themes of the book. For Crozier the absence of participation as well as the lack of adaptation to change are the consequences of the bur'tic system, & inversely the reinforcement of the bur'tic system is itself a consequence of the absence of participation & of the lack of adaptation. These phenomena are vicious circles from which 2 means of escape are suggested: (I) participation, which leads to a diminishment in rigidity, easier adaptation to change, & a lessening of the dysfunctional influence of the bur'tic system; & (ii) give & take between participation & innovation. Crozier's thesis is criticized on the grounds of the ideological, non-sci'fic character he attributes to participation. The steps of his arguments are retraced, & numerous lacunae are underscored. Participation is adjudged to be nothing more than a means of staving off the eventual collapse of capitalism. M. Duke.

title: The European Union Policy towards Universities As Regards Creating Knowledge-Based Economy
abstract: The purpose of the submitted text is to demonstrate the involvement of the European Union in the reconstruction process of the European knowledge-based economy, as well as the EU policy towards universities in the construction process of the European knowledge-based economy, as well as elucidate the following four theses. As regards the EU policy towards European universities concerning the creation of knowledge based economy, the European Commission undertakes actions in order to influence the external conditions of operating universities, including the character of relations between universities & EU member countries, but also the internal conditions in terms of modernizing universities. The involvement of the European Union includes not only problems which are formally within the responsibilities of this body but -- indirectly -- also matters which remain beyond the range thereof (higher level education is within the competence of the national governments of the EU member countries), although officially it implements the so-called "open coordination rule.' Both the content & the language of the European Commission documents concerning universities & related to implementing the Lisbon strategy & creating the knowledge based economy has clearly been influenced by other parallel processes which took place at the turn of the Millennium, namely the dominance of the neo-liberal ideas, progressive globalization & the New Public Management (NPM). The rhetoric & argumentation of the EU documentation is frequently dramatically different from the language used by university representatives. Examples of such linguistic & formal discrepancies can be observed in the case of the stance taken by the European University Association in reference to a number of crucial documents issued by the European Commission. Adapted from the source document.

title: Inequality in Poverty: Bulgarian Sociologists on Class and Stratification
abstract: The paper analyzes the variety of discourses on social inequalities in postcommunist Bulgaria. The focus is on academic discourse, but political and everyday interpretations are presented as well. Politicians generally avoid talking about social differences and prefer instead the dichotomy of "elite" versus "the people," whose interests the politicians vow to protect. In popular consciousness, the main division is between "the rich" (mafia, politicians, ex-nomenklatura) and "the honest poor." In sociology, three main research trajectories have emerged: from class-based to status-based stratification; from one-dimensional to multidimensional stratification; and from a Marxist class model to a social network model. Perhaps the most important characteristic of Bulgarian society is its high level of poverty, according both to income indicators and self-perception. In this context of a pervasive sense of poverty, status differences lose their significance. This in turn prevents the establishment of group or class solidarity, as everyone feels she or he is competing with all others. Starting in 2013, a new trend can be observed: of social protests organized by those who say they feel powerless and manipulated by corrupt elites. As they try to initiate new types of economic negotiations with the government, sociologists have a responsibility both to study this new movement and to push the problems it raises into public debate.

title: Public Responsibility in a Context of Change
abstract: Under New Public Management reforms, traditional public accountability system is facing a new set of challenges. After reviewing the main features of this system in a representative democracy, the article examines the effects on public accountability of initiatives such as introducing greater degree of autonomy for public managers, & the regular employment of non-government organizations for public services provision. 46 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: A National Center of Telework
abstract: The origins of the idea to create the Centro nationale "Telelavoro, reti, soggetti" (Telework, Networks, Subjects) in Italy are traced, & the organizations & communities collaborating in its foundation are presented. The center's program presented at the U of Bologna in May 1998 is outlined, & efforts to legislatively promote telework in the sphere of Italian public administration are reviewed, noting the limitations of some laws promulgated to date. The center's objectives are listed: (1) promotion & support of empirical research on the social, economic, cultural, & psychological aspects of telework; (2) organization of interpretative & educational seminars & conferences; (3) an international collaboration, within & outside the European Union, in studies devoted to the various practical facets of telework; (4) sponsorship of graduate & postgraduate research on the topic; & (5) development of courses targeting the necessary skills for telework, including its legal & technical aspects. Z. Dubiel

title: People's Power and the Updating of the Cuban Economic Model
abstract: Cuba enters the twenty-first century with a system of social relations in a profound process of change. This presents a clear challenge to the socialist project. It is absolutely necessary to improve governmental and administrative management, so as to both enlarge and streamline activities connected to state property, eliminating the current deficiencies, inadequacies, and lack of coordination. But this public sector also is decisive for organizing and channeling the participation of non-state forms of property in the system of social relations of production, and it must do this in a manner consistent with socialist interests. We must improve the socialist character of the Cuban state in an from the economic sphere. This is linked, however, to a continued strengthening of the state in its capacity to direct social - and particularly economic - activity.

title: Tales of Satisfaction and Disillusionment: Second-Generation "Return" Migration to Greece and Cyprus
authors: King, Russell; Christou, Anastasia; Goodson, Ivor; Teerling, Janine
abstract: We examine the comparative “return” experiences of second-generation Greek-Americans and British-born Greek Cypriots who have relocated to their respective parental homelands of Greece and Cyprus. Sixty individuals, born in the United States or the United Kingdom yet now living in Greece or Cyprus, were interviewed and detailed life narratives recorded. We find both similarities and differences between the two groups. While the broad narrative themes “explaining” their returns are similar—a search for a “place to belong” in the ancestral homeland linked to what is, or was, perceived to be a more relaxed and genuine way of life—the post-return outcomes vary. In Greece there is disappointment, even profound disillusionment, whereas in Cyprus the return is generally viewed with satisfaction. For Greek-Americans, negative experiences include difficulty in accessing employment, frustration with bureaucracy and a culture of corruption, struggles with the chaos and stress of life in Athens, and pessimism about the future for their children in Greece. As a result, some Greek-Americans contemplate a second return, back to the United States. For the returnee British Cypriots, these problems are far less evident; they generally rationalize their relocation to Cyprus as the “right decision,” both for themselves and for their children. Greek-Americans tend to withdraw into a social circle of their own kind, whereas British-born returnee Cypriots adopt a more cosmopolitan or “third-space” cultural identity related, arguably, to the small scale and intimate spaces of social Second-Generation “Return” Migration to Greece and Cyprus exchange in an island setting, and to the colonial and postcolonial history of Cyprus and its diaspora.

title: A multi-scale approach to coping with climate change and other collective action problems
abstract: Climate change is a complex problem and still relatively new on the international agenda. Waiting for effective climate policies to be established at the global level is unreasonable and wastes valuable time. It would be better to adopt a multi-scale approach starting at the local level, maximizing benefits at varying levels and encouraging experimentation and learning from diverse policies. Conventional wisdom tells us that there are only two options for dealing with resource management: either privatization or management by the state. This view is hindering progress. Successfully addressing climate change in the long run requires substantial changes at multiple levels in the day-to-day activities of individuals, families, firms, communities, and governments especially those in the more developed world. Adapted from the source document.

title: Policy Makers, Practitioners, Citizens: Perceptions of the Violence against Women Act of 1994
abstract: The Violence Against Women Act of 1994 (VAWA) is the most comprehensive legislation to date to address violence against women in the United States. Three theoretical perspectives, derived from Foucault, Habermas, & MacKinnon, were used to examine the legislation. These perspectives were the basis of questions that were asked of VAWA policy makers, local practitioners, citizens, & survivors & perpetrators of intimate violence. The results highlight divergent perceptions between these groups. The research implies that public administrators may need to redefine & communicate the problem to more effectively formulate policy because the state is limited in its response to social problems. 3 Tables, 1 Appendix, 50 References. [Copyright 2002 Sage Publications, Inc.]

title: Nonprofit Human-Service Organizations, Social Rights, and Advocacy in a Neoliberal Welfare State
abstract: The hallmark of the welfare state is the extension of social rights to the most vulnerable, a cause historically championed by nonprofit human-service organizations. With the rise of neoliberalism, these rights are threatened. This article attempts to show how the institutional, economic, and political environment of the nonprofit human-service sector is reshaped by a neoliberal ideology that celebrates market fundamentalism. The ideology institutionalizes such rules and practices as new public management, devolution, and privatization of services. Those elements shift the political discourse about the rights of the most vulnerable from the national to the local level. By turning vulnerable citizens into consumers, the ideology also reduces the national visibility of their needs. Most importantly, neoliberalism dampens the sector's motivation to challenge the state and greatly curtails its historical mission to advocate and mobilize for social rights. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Architecture of Risk And Power: A Review Article of Magnus Hornqvist, The Organised Nature of Power: On Productive and Repressive Interventions Based on Consideration of Risk
abstract: In The Organised Nature of Power, Magnus Hornqvist initially synthesizes Foucauldian and Marxian conceptions of power in order to highlight the connection between everyday exercises of power and power relations embedded in social structure and the state. He then proceeds to demonstrate how risk has become the coordinating mechanism in the organization of power Risk is a common language and technology across institutions, linking exercises and structures of state power in ways that have both productive and repressive consequences. The architecture of risk and power is empirically investigated in the context of public employment, prison and customs bureaucracies in Sweden. The investigation is based on readings of policy documents, official forms, risk assessment technologies, surveillance infrastructures and case reports used in these bureaucracies. Hornqvist demonstrates how power is embedded in norms of risk management beyond the law, the multifaceted and variable uses of risk in processes of empowerment and subjection across different state bureaucracies, and the fact that we are still in disciplinary societies more than societies of control. Hornqvist's work is interrogated to indicate some limitations and directions for future research. Adapted from the source document.

title: Issues and Challenges on Public Policy at the Local Level. Interview with Tonatiuh Guillen
abstract: Tonatiuh Guillen, current president of El Colegio de la Frontera Norte (Colef), is a must for public policy at the local level benchmark. Doctor in Social Sciences with a major in sociology from El Colegio de Mexico, in previous years served as director of the Research Department of Public Administration and director of the journal Colef Northern Border. He has been professor at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, the Autonomous University of Coahuila and the Universidad Autonoma de Chiapas, besides visiting professor at other national and international institutions. His research interests focus on the study of regional policy, modernization of local government, federalism and decentralization. He is the author and coordinator of 15 books and more than 60 book chapters and articles in academic journals.

title: Restructuring Municipal Government: Labor-Management Relations and Worker Mental Health
authors: McDonough, Peggy; Worts, Diana; Fox, Bonnie; Dmitrienko, Klaudia
abstract: This study is a mixed-method investigation of the association between labor-management relations and employees' mental health in a municipal sector undergoing New Public Management-style restructuring. Analysis of the survey data (N = 902) demonstrates a relatively strong and persistent relationship between management practices and employee psychological health. Interviews with a subsample of 54 workers reveal that management's excessive control, incompetence, and unresponsiveness, combined with minimal rewards for workers' efforts, left staff feeling devalued. Our findings suggest that workers' mental health was harmed by the undermining of their sense of self-worth and the loss of avenues to improve their working conditions. Adapted from the source document.

title: Black Voter Dilution, American Exceptionalism, and Racial Gerrymandering
abstract: Racial gerrymandering in the U.S. state of South Carolina offers a case study to take a unique look at political control, power management, and government communication from the critical perspective of hidden reward structures. These reward structures result from strategic messaging by which an elite's perspectives deliver to them power by marginalizing others and their perspectives. More specifically, we interrogate one dominant narrative advanced in the United States--American Exceptionalism--by highlighting the irony of how South Carolina elected officials use the 1965 Voting Rights Act to assure a Black Democratic member of the House of Representatives, but simultaneously by gerrymandering elected officials actually reduce the likelihood of a second Democratic representative of any race/ethnicity. Using the paradox of the positive as a critical political public relations framework, we highlight the ways that American Exceptionalism is used to impose control, a control that favors one voting perspective to the marginalization of others in U.S. Southern politics.

title: Citizen Input in the Budget Process: When Does It Matter Most?
abstract: Citizen participation in public budgeting processes has been widely advocated by both theorists and practitioners of public administration. Yet there is less agreement on when the public should be brought into the process and how the timing of citizen inclusion affects the outcomes of public agencies. Using survey data about citizen involvement practices utilized by the state departments of transportation (DOTs) across the country, the authors construct citizen input indices for different stages of the budget process and examine the impact of participation on the overall organizational effectiveness. The study results show that citizen participation in the budget process has greatest positive effect on organizational performance at both the early and ending stages of the budget process, namely, the stages of information sharing and program assessment. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright holder.]

title: ADMINISTATIVE EFFICIENCY IN DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
abstract: On the basis of observations & definitions of bur'tic systems, the hypothesis is discussed that im many area there is a marked discrepancy between the needs of a nation & the efficiency of its admin. While defining the terms `development' & 'modernism,' it is stated that in the recent literature of soc sci these terms are used to refer to 'an incredible mixture of instit's & behaviors at the econ, pol'al, soc & psychol'al level.' 2 subjects are examined: (1) An outline for improving the efficiency of public administration in developing countries; (2) suggestions for admin'ive actions which can accelerate the admin'ive efficiency in various situations. The problems of diff Asian & African nations are considered, & the resources available to them as well as their admin'ive obstacles are analyzed. A country's potential capacity to produce that kind of efficient public administration which is required by its problems is found to be an important factor. Examples are presented. Specific pol'al measures for 2 types of development problems, (a) those connected with nat'l integration & identity & (b) those pertaining to the needs for new goods & services &their distribution, are suggested. Finally, the suggestions of Milton J. Esmanin, 'The Politics of Development Administration,' COMPARATIVE ADMINISTRATION GROUP OCCASIONAL PAPERS, are examined in detail. M. Maxfield.

title: Management, Ethics and the Reform of Quebec Public Administration: Reflections from Three Women Deputy Ministers
abstract: This text presents some reflections about management, ethics & the reform of Quebec public administration. They have been collected from three women who have been deputy Ministers between 1992 & 2002. Their discourse reveals their openness to a renewed management that is more communicative & more respectful of employees than the more classical one. Their management style is characterized by a great consistency between discourse, values & action, as well as by a great trust into the reform, notably into the "service turn" philosophy. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Good Governance and Effective Public Administration in Africa
abstract: This paper is an attempt to respond to the question of whether Africa will be able to meet the NEPAD 2050 vision successfully. In addressing this question, a descriptive approach with a broad focus on the AU and NEPAD is undertaken. The case of South Africa is briefly considered to augment this discussion on the applicability of country-specific AU and NEPAD principles of democracy and good governance. While it is found that the AU and NEPAD initiatives have brought about initial achievements since their inception, a great deal of strengthening of these institutions is required. This discussion has also highlighted the fact that the upholding of AU and NEPAD norms and standards (through the Africa Peer Review Mechanism [APRM]) is declining in the continent, including in South Africa. The article concludes that in the twenty-first century, Africa needs to consolidate the role of civil society in order to effect good governance principles. Adapted from the source document.

title: Nature of Public Administration: Reflections in the Indian Context
abstract: The nature & scope of public administration in India are discussed, with attention to the contributions of Jawaharlal Nehru. Focus is on: (1) public administration's relationship with political science, economics, sociology, social anthropology, & management; (2) the role of bureaucracy in public administration & the myth of the neutrality of civil servants; (3) the need for public servants to address themselves to fulfillment of the basic needs of the people; (4) the emergence of the new discipline of policy sciences; (5) over- & underresearched areas in public administration; (6) methodological problems in the study of public administration, & solutions; & (7) the appropriate relationship between the study of public administration & politicians & bureaucrats. 7 References. D. Generoli

title: 'IMPERIALISM' IN BUREAUCRACY
abstract: Whatever the purposes of the admin'ive politician, his first necessity is to maintain power for his agency. Power is organized around constituency, around jurisdiction. Admin'ive politicians seek, therefore, those jurisdictional assignments most favorable to agency power. Hence, the conflicts over the allocation of jurisdiction or bur'tic 'imperialism.' Not all admin'ive politicians move their agencies with the same f into efforts to claim jurisdiction. Accordingly, in empirical analysis, the problem is to look for clues to their strategies in 3 main considerations: (1) the disposition of members of the agencies to take on or to avoid particular kinds of missions; (2) the occasions for allocation decisions, & (3) the modes which the pol'al system provides for resolution of conflicts. On the normative side, the regiocentric bias of admin'ive theory tends to stigmatize bur'tic imperialism as 'irrational' or 'pathological.' However, the process may actually enhance admin'ive rationality by clarifying constituency preferences & disrupting stale or archaic bur'cies through the emergence of competitors. IPSA.

title: Filipino Public Opinion, Presidential Leadership and the US-Led War in Iraq
authors: Dayag-Laylo, Carijane C; Pedro Laylo, Jr.; Vladymir Joseph Licudine
abstract: The Philippines, long considered an ally of the United States in Muslim-dominated South East Asia, feared being at the losing end of a US-led war in Iraq. At the height of the US-Iraq war, there was fear of increased terrorist attacks in the country and a worsening of the economy. The majority of Filipinos wanted the government to take a neutral stance in the fight against Iraq. Despite this, President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo declared her support for the US-led coalition. As a consequence, her ratings suffered. The national administration made every effort to address issues related to the war, such as price increases, oil supply, the fear of terrorist attacks and the plight of Filipinos working in the danger zones. These efforts were crucial in assuring the public that, despite the government's support for the war, the country would continue to experience security and stability. With the quick end to the war, public anxiety declined, government efforts to keep the country secure and stable were recognized and the President's ratings improved. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: What's Wrong with Patronage?
abstract: Patronage is treated as a discrete phenomenon through which political, bureaucratic, and wider social behaviour may be analysed and explained. As such, it is commonly seen as an obstacle to (or as a stopgap for) effective administration; as a feature that is in some respects compatible with (and may aid) democracy; and as behaviour that is quite simply different from practice within Weberian bureaucracies. I wish to point this debate along a slightly different path. I suggest that a more nuanced approach (and one closer to everyday experience) is yielded when patronage is recognized as an aspect of social relationships. Viewed in this light, there is more than enough material in the existing literature to reveal a link between patronage, formal organizations and democracy. I then go on to discuss briefly why relationships modulate such that certain aspects are brought to the fore; and to consider the implications of this explanation for existing views on patronage and the genesis of organizations and democratic patterns. Adapted from the source document.

title: Technological Innovation and Futures of Work Organization: A Choice of Social Design Principles
abstract: The choice of social design principles for work organization & the implications of alternative design principles in choices concerning new technology are examined to determine the suitability of the traditional bureaucratic framework to new technology. Using the example of an innovative technology implemented in a telephone company in an industrialized Western country in the late 1970s, it is shown that a new automated system was not meeting its goals of speed & efficiency due to problems at both the employee & customer levels that were created primarily by imposing the bureaucratic system on the new technology. An effective solution would be to replace the bureaucracy with "participative organizational redesign," which requires a democratization of work (decentralizing decision making to involve all concerned), learning & skill development opportunities, increased interpersonal interaction, & challenging work. This would enable workers to understand, critique, & direct the work organization so that it satisfies human, organizational, & technical requirements. 2 Tables, 27 References. Modified HA.

title: Administrative Culture and Metaphor Change
abstract: It is argued that culture is a dynamic entity & contested territory. In organization, cultural changes affect employee behavior. The culture of citizen-agency relations in American public administration today, marked by shifts in the metaphor from customer to owner, is discussed, using the example of the Phoenix Water Conservation Office. 12 References. M. Pflum

title: Environmental Disasters and Disastrous Policies: An Overview from India
abstract: Though disasters have been important recurring events in South Asia, the policy framework for addressing the issues arising from disaster has been weak. Taking an alternative perspective on the definition of disaster itself, this article attempts to address the cause of the increasing numbers of disasters in India. I posit that the nation-state still understands disasters as a natural phenomenon, rather than as an intersection between conditions of vulnerability and actual hazards. This is to be observed in the disaster policies adopted. Hence, this article emphasizes the inclusion of 'vulnerability' as paramount. Adapted from the source document.

title: Women in Public Administration in the Federal Republic of Germany
abstract: Only 11% of all civil servants in the more prestigious central government service of West Germany are women. Interviews conducted in 1985 with 24 top women administrators in 7 Federal ministries & 2 state authorities, supported by data from a 1981/82 survey of 80 women & 24 men in public service, show that women in the upper ranks are slightly older & less often married than their male counterparts. Because they are relatively disadvantaged in their educational backgrounds, they lack the access & training prerequisites for promotions to the top grades. Family commitments are the greatest factor hindering their advancement, as the women continue to bear family & housework responsibilities. They feel pressured to adapt to the labor structures determined by men, but operate with cooperative leadership styles. A small minority of the women reported that discrimination against women does not exist, but most had experienced various forms of gender discrimination. It is observed that women in the higher West German public service ranks have not yet reached the critical mass necessary to overcome their disadvantages in the system. 4 Tables, 4 References. M. Pflum

title: Governing Gaza: Bureaucracy, Authority, and the Work of Rule, 1917-1967
abstract: Kelly reviews Governing Gaza: Bureaucracy, Authority, and the Work of Rule, 1917-1967 by Ilana Feldman.

title: Bureaucracy and Organization: Research on Public Bureaucracies in Italy
abstract: Using questionnaire data from 2 1987 studies (of 180 bureaucrats in various offices of Italian state administration, conducted by the Regional Office of Lazio; & of 89 local-level bureaucrats, conducted by the Lazio School of Public Administration), the functionality of bureaucratic organizations is examined. It is discovered that the lack of interaction between local, regional, & state levels has engendered a large "underground" bureaucracy, one that operates against the normal rules. While these underground organizations are allowed to function, their existence is not officially acknowledged. 16 Tables, 17 References. L. Baker

title: ON CHARACTERISTICS OF PROFESSIONAL ORGANIZATIONS
abstract: A comment on SA 1020/E1151. Issue is taken with the statement by Bucher & Stelling that 'Approaches to formal ~, org's dominated by Weberian concepts of bur'cy simply did not fit org's dominated by professionals.' This is rejected because 'Those who invoke Weber, only to dismiss him, are in dialectical danger.' M. Weber's concepts, bur'cy, charisma, etc, should not be applied literally. Bucher & Stelling contend that the professional is really quite autonomous. But a distinction should be made between the autonomy of the individual within his sphere of competence, & his voice in instit'al decisions re the instit's soc role & goals in the larger spheres of community, state or humanity. Any role involves the granting of autonomy in some areas at the price of accepting control in others. When Med professionals challenge the vested interests that perpetuate discriminatory treatment based on ability to pay, they discover the rigid bounds of instit'al permissiveness. Standards of deviance that protect senescent instit's exist for the professionals in US society. The fact that they are not easily perceived &/or effectively challenged is not a measure of their rationality or flexibility. M. Maxfield.

title: Controlling Political Corruption in Italy: What Did Not Work, What Can Be Done
abstract: Explores the control of political corruption in Italy, focusing on reasons why most of the control mechanisms did not work, allowing for the development of "tangentopoli." Why bottom-up controls from citizens or electors did not function in Italy are discussed in terms of the pervasive occupation of the administration & the civil society by political parties, as well as "secret" agreements between political parties to avoid scandals. Two types of institutional control -- administrative & judiciary -- are analyzed, & characteristics of the public administration that hampered internal controls, eg, informal control of parties over the bureaucrats through clientelism & complicity in corruption, are addressed. The peculiar characteristics of a magistracy that enjoyed a high degree of formal autonomy from political power, but was pushed toward politics for varying reasons, eg, complicity in corruption & the need to substitute for the weak policy-making capacity of political parties, are examined. Reform bills to deal with the control of political corruption are considered. Adapted from the source document.

title: Wives, widows, and workers: Corazon Aquino, Imelda Marcos, and the Filipina 'other'
abstract: Niu examines media attention to two famous and infamous Filipinas, Imelda Marcos and Corazon Aquino. She also discusses women migrants from the Philippines and the work of the NGO international group called GABRIELA.

title: Modernization and Sex Roles: The Status of Women in the Thai Bureaucracy
authors: Springer, J Fred; Gable, Richard W
abstract: Thai women have traditionally been active in the economy & enjoy a social equality unusual for Asian women. To examine F roles in a modernizing bureaucracy, data were gathered through 414 in-depth interviews with officials of the Rice Production Project, 50% from Bangkok offices & 50% from field locations. F participation in the project was 17.7% -- many times higher than in similar programs in Indonesia, South Korea, & the Philippines. Despite comparable educational credentials, however, F Thai civil servants were found to have lower rank, lower pay, & less supervisory responsibility than Ms, & tended to be clustered in clerical occupations. They were also less likely to be married or have children, suggesting that they needed to make sacrifices in family life to compete with Ms. F Rs, however, expressed greater job satisfaction than did the Ms. 7 Tables. C. Waters.

title: THE STRUGGLE FOR THE RECOGNITION OF HUMAN RIGHTS IN MOZAMBIQUE: ADVANCES AND SETBACKS
abstract: This article deals with the issue whether human rights are still an effective language for promoting social change. In this article, the author begins with a brief analysis on the main developments in the human rights field all over the world, later focusing on the trajectory of the human rights movement in Mozambique, in order to identify the movement's impacts on the legal and institutional level and on governance. The author concludes that while the human rights movement in Mozambique has made several advances, especially in legal and institutional spheres, the main challenge it faces today in the country is in the area of governance. The challenge lies in how to apply the human rights language contained in the spirit of the laws approved and the institutions created to the day-to-day activities of all levels of public administration, from top to bottom. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Standardization of Race and Ethnicity in Biomedical Science Editorials and UK Biobanks
authors: Smart, Andrew; Tutton, Richard; Martin, Paul; Ellison, George T H; Ashcroft, Richard
abstract: As the search for human genetic variation has become a priority for biomedical science, debates have resurfaced about the use of race and ethnicity as scientific classifications. In this paper we consider the relationship between race, ethnicity and genetics, using insights from science and technology studies (STS) about processes of classification and standardization. We examine how leading biomedical science journals attempted to standardize the classifications of race and ethnicity, and analyse how a sample of UK genetic scientists used the concepts in their research. Our content analysis of 11 editorials and related guidelines reveals variations in the guidance on offer, and it appears that there has been a shift from defining the concepts to prescribing methodological processes for classification. In qualitative interviews with 17 scientists, the majority reported that they had adopted socio-political classification schemes from state bureaucracy (for example, the UK Census) for practical reasons, although some scientists used alternative classifications that they justified on apparently methodological grounds. The different responses evident in the editorials and interviews can be understood as reflecting the balance of flexibility and stability that motivate standardization processes. We argue that, although a genetic concept of race and ethnicity is unlikely to wholly supplant a socio-political one, the adoption of census classifications into biomedical research is an alignment of state bureaucracy and science that could have significant consequences. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright 2008.]

title: Legitimacy and Public Administration: Constructing the American Bureaucratic Fields
abstract: Legitimacy claims can only be made and processes of legitimation can only unfold in a specified context. This article uses Pierre Bourdieu's concept of the social field to name this context and to analyze the construction of the bureaucratic or public administrative field in the United States. Field is meant in a triple sense--public administration as a general, institutionalized field in the structure of government; public administration as a professional field; and public administration as an academic field of study. Thus, rather than the bureaucratic field, the relationship of these bureaucratic fields or an 'ensemble of fields' is analyzed to consider how each field both bounds its own legitimation struggles and draws from other fields for symbolic resources--what Bourdieu called symbolic capital --to establish its legitimacy and position. The multifield quality of public administration is used to show how the nature of the general bureaucratic field is distinct from other fields insofar as it purports to represent a universal, general interest. This difference is used to theorize a distinction between 'general' and 'specific' legitimation processes. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright holder.]

title: 'Policies in Motion', Urban Management and State Restructuring: The Trans-Local Expansion of Business Improvement Districts
abstract: This article examines the ways in which business improvement districts are being introduced into UK cities. In advancing this analysis, the focus here is on the means through which one or two Manhattan business improvement districts have been constructed as 'models' of urban management, taken out of their particular local/regional and national contexts and introduced into a diverse set of local political economic contexts in UK cities and towns. Examining the way business improvement districts have become a policy in motion, the article sketches out the emergence of entrepreneurial urban governance arrangements in the UK as part of the state's changing spatiality in the industrialized economies of Western Europe and North America. I argue that these changes make UK cities and towns increasingly receptive to the business improvement district model of downtown management. Seeking to move beyond the sometimes rather one-sided representations of policies that find themselves on the move, the article seeks to connect the 'exporting' and 'importing' zones of policy transfer, arguing for an open and permeable conceptualization of these places. It draws on work in Manhattan, New York to unpack the nature of the political-economic relations that business improvement districts were part of, before moving on to examine the dynamics of policy transfer and the early days of the introduction of this downtown 'model' into UK cities. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Apparent Actions: The Problem of the Politicization of the Process of Staffing the Senior Positions in the Polish Civil Service
abstract: The civil service is one of the most important elements of governmental administration & has a great influence on the way a state performs its tasks. In the 90's, it could be argued that Central-Eastern European Countries did not take sufficient care in reforming the public administration sector & creating the civil service, with the consequent problem of the politicization of public administration. The first parliamentary act in Poland concerning the civil service was passed only in 1996. Since that time the organizational principles for the civil service were changed three times. Currently in force is the 2008 Act on Civil Service. The civil service was intended to make public administration more professional, objective & independent of particular political interest. The professional civil servants should be politically neutral. Their position should be stable regardless of the changes of the ruling coalitions. However, in Poland political parties tend to restrict public administration autonomy & subordinate it to their interests. The aim of my paper is to analyze the staffing politics concerning senior posts in the civil service & to define the extent to which the actual practices has been in compliance with the formally defined principles. The situation in this field is presented from 1989, the post-Solidarity governance, until 2009, the present Donald Tusk government. In addition, the changes introduced by the Acts on Civil Service from 1996, 1998, 2006, & 2008 will be discussed as well as their influence of the praxis. It is argued that the ways in which the legal principles concerning staffing senior civil service posts have been enacted throughout the years can be seen as classic example of apparent actions considered by Jan Lutynski. Adapted from the source document.

title: Metropolitan and Fiscal Policy: The Record of 40 Years
abstract: In Introduction, Leland S. Burns (U of California, Los Angeles) discusses the importance of assessing progress for the business of public management & prefaces four essays presented at the 1984 meetings of the Assoc of Collegiate Schools of Planning. In The State of Fiscal Policy, Jesse Burkhead (Syracuse U, NY) notes that the issues dealt with by Harvey Perloff (see Burns, Leland S., & Friedman, John [Eds], The Art of Planning: Selected Essays of Harvey S. Perloff, NY: Plenum Press, 1985) forty years ago are still pertinent today, & little progress has been made. The federal budget is weaker as an instrument of stabilizing policy, though federal budget procedure & budget policy are in a transition period. Problems in intergovernmental fiscal relations in the public sector, outlined by Perloff, are far from resolution, & those advocating a responsible & responsive public sector have been disappointed by fiscal developments since 1973. In Policies for Revitalizing Central Cities, Charles L. Leven (Instit for Ur & Regional Studies, Washington U, St. Louis, Mo) explores the rebuilding of central cities relative to Perloff's conception of the tertiary sector in society, & notes that central cities are finding new roles. The nonbasic sector is expanding without complementary growth in the basic sector, & there is a return of jobs without a return of people. In Regional Policy: A Jaundiced View, Anthony H. Pascal (Rand Corp, 1700 Main St, Santa Monica, Calif) claims regions lack both economic coherence & political power. Politicians cannot make effective regional policy, & the alternative, neoclassical regional policy, would fail politically. In Discussion: The Future of Policy, David Dowall (U of California, Berkeley) cites new trends that make many traditional planning principles obsolete. Because of the pace & unknown effects of change, accurate prediction is difficult. A task for the future is to develop plans for cities & regions, & a social policy that can respond to change. 10 References. K. Carande

title: The politics of managerial reform in UK local government: a study of control, conflict and resistance 1880s to present
abstract: The article examines the political origins and impact of recent managerial reform (the shift from the professional bureaucracy model of public administration to the new public management [NPM]) in UK local government. Two key drivers of managerial reform are identified: central-local relations and labour management. The former are historically complex due, partly, to the Victorian expediential justification of local government, and the tenuous constitutional status of local government in the British polity. These factors necessitate and permit central control with models of public administration a key mechanism for achieving this. In addition, as 70% of overall sector costs are made up of centrally funded labour costs, the centre's attempts to control labour management (pay and performance) is a second key driver of managerial reform. And models of public administration, again, are a major mechanism for achieving central control. The analysis is rooted in a brief historical examination of developments from the 1880s, and a longitudinal case study examining more recent developments to illustrate the general case made. Empirical findings show councillor, union and worker resistance to managerial reform. They also show job loss, work intensification, job insecurity and demoralisation of staff. Another key finding is that NPM is not new, but a regression to the Victorian era. Adapted from the source document.

title: Gender and peacekeeping: The United Nations transitional administration in East Timor
abstract: The United Nations establish the United Nations Transitional Administration in East Timor (UNTAET) after a month when East Timorese overwhelmingly voted for independence under United Nations sponsorship. Its mandate went beyond providing security, to first administering the new nation and then to assisting in the building of a government and an economy almost from scratch for a small country with a population of less than a million. The UNTAET was unique in that the regulation delineating the authority of the transitional administration clearly stated that "all persons undertaking public duties or holding public office in East Timor shall observe internationally recognized human rights standards."

title: COSMOPOLITANS AND LOCALS: TOWARD AN ANALYSIS OF LATENT SOCIAL ROLES-II
abstract: A more refined analysis of findings reported in Part I (See SA 8835). The possibility of various types of cosmopolitans (COSMO's) & locals was investigated by factor analysis of the original Guttman scales. Using centroid extraction & Quartimax rotation, 6 orthogonal & unidimensional factors were produced. 4 of these factors are seen as types of locals: (1) the dedicated - true believers in the ideology of the org, (2) the true bureaucrat - loyal to the org per se, rather than the values, (3) the homeguard unspecialized workers, loyal for personal reasons, & (4) the elders - committed by virtue of advanced age & immobility. The remaining 2 types are seen as COSMO's: the outsiders - no commitment to org, mere affiliation, & the empire builders - committed to departments rather than to the org. COSMO's & locals are found to have diff influence, participation, rule tropism, & informal SR's. It is suggested that characterizations of modern org have overemphasized the distinctive nature of manag, without seeing distinctions within manag, specifically, by overemphasizing its commitment to efficiency. The latent COSMO & local roles are seen as the product of the org's need to obtain personnel who are at the same time competent & committed to the org. B. Beck.

title: Administrative Ambitions and Realities within the Reform Discourse of the 1990s. The Discursive Order of Reform Communication
abstract: In regard to the discourse of administrative reform in the 1990s, many social scientists specializing in public administration, indicated their jurisdiction was being threatened by economic experts. The present study refrains from recreating the associated images of public administrations as contaminated by aspirations of an external reform discourse, but instead analyzes this discourse to identify systematic characteristics of reform communication. The recurrent distinction between ambitions & realities in public administration is revealed to be the central organizing element. Analyzing published reform communication, including criticism of reform, the discourse is shown to operationalize the distinction between administrative ambitions & realities in establishing discursive order & defending it against deconstruction. As a result, reform communication within the discourse of the 1990s has become uncoupled from administrative communication, & opportunities for social scientists to build up expertise on current matters of administrative reform have been systematically neglected. In turn, it is suggested, sociological communication should be more thoroughly decoupled from reform communication. 176 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The 'return to community': Challenges to human service professionals
