title: Change in the Benefits Agency: Empowering the Exhausted Worker?
abstract: Using case study data from an investigation of "quality" initiatives & working practices in three offices in a district of the Benefits Agency in England, the contradictory role of new public management on employees is examined. Decentralized management, performance-related pay, teamwork philosophies, & promotion of a customer culture reflect a move away from a traditional civil service bureaucratic form of organization. However, the implementation of change in local settings has brought about variations in local management approaches, work organization, & staff perceptions. The consequences of these are explored, & whether the Benefits Agency's attempts to empower staff have been thwarted by a progressive intensification of workloads is considered. By illustrating the importance of variations in local settings, analysis warns of the dangers of evaluating institutional & employment change in the public sector as if it were the result of a coherent & consistent neoliberal restructuring strategy. Moreover, reasons why some change initiatives have been unsuccessful are examined. A recent shift in emphasis in the Benefits Agency that presages a move away from service quality to economy is identified, & some initial conclusions about the future impact on employment in this sector are drawn. 31 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Group Rights as Instruments of Public Policy in the Development of Viable Democratic Systems
abstract: Despite recent pessimism among experts concerning the viability of democratic systems in Third World countries, it is suggested that some authoritarian leaders, faced with the need for popular support, may now be casting around for new & successful strategies toward democracy. The Malaysian experience, based on cooperation of Malay, Chinese, & Indian communal groups, is viewed as a model. It has been successful because it has maintained a balance between popular demands & resources. While the demand for personal material rewards has been slowed, governments could concentrate on economic growth. Two mechanisms are being tested in Malaysia to maintain this system: (1) a constitutional contract which sets out the terms of intercommunal relations & guarantees the minimal interest of each communal group, granting special group privileges or rights to correct disparities from the past, & (2) a directorate of political leaders, representing all component communal groups, designed to deradicalize democratic processes by preventing popular confrontations along communal lines. At present, the traditional social hierarchies still have some authority & can serve as political intermediaries. In the future, some new & imaginative initiatives are needed, however, to keep the directorate viable. Another strategy would involve the building of a loyal intermediary leadership group capable of mobilizing the masses & establishing a well-disciplined party organization. However, this would foster a one-party state. It is worth attempting to learn whether a democratic system based on communal groups can survive. S. Whittle.

title: Book Review: The Challenge of Crime in a Free Society. Report of the President's Commission on Law Enforcement and Administration of Justice
abstract: The Challenge of Crime in a Free Society. Report of the President's Commission on Law Enforcement and Administration of Justice. U.S. Government Printing Office, 1967. Price $4.10 ( Aust.). xi + 340 pp.

title: The World of Interest-Group Advocacy: An 'Insider's' View
abstract: Offers a perspective based on a 45-year career in social welfare on both the "inside" & "outside" of advocacy efforts, highlighting insights gained as a bureaucrat on the inside of a public agency. The motivations that drive individual advocates -- eg, altruism, political gain -- are explored, & the connection between the inside bureaucrat, the organization, & outside advocates is examined. The different roles of inside & outside advocates in the policy-making process are compared. Issues of advocate accountability & conflicts of interests are also addressed. K. Hyatt Stewart

title: Maladministration: Cause or Result of Underdevelopment? The Algerian Example
abstract: That Algerian public administration functions badly is an opinion shared by Algerian politicians & the population at large. Causes of poor public administration in the Third World are analyzed. Two principal explanations for this phenomenon -- one stressing historical deficiencies perpetuated by external influences, & one blaming cultural origins & internal conditioning -- are not entirely satisfactory; a compromise explanation is proposed. The official Algerian position appears to be based on the first explanation, but administrative practice appears to support the second. Presented are questions relating to Algerian administrative practice that should be examined in the near future. HA Tr & Modified by I. Irwin-Zarecka.

title: IS THE PUBLIC SCHOOL OBSOLETE?
abstract: The 2 main problems of educ are noted as: (1) inadequate public support, & (2) excessive bur'tic timidity & defeatism. The following remedies are proposed: Reverse the pattern of spending half as much for the educ of slum children as for that of subUr children; reduce class sizes & increase the cumulative total of money spent for the educ of one slum child from less than $5,000 to about $25,000. It is stated that such a considerable investment in educ would repay itself by raising taxable income & cutting expenditures for welfare, unemployment, police & other slum symptoms & increasing the GNP. Instead of sprinkling money around in various scattered projects, foundations should try to raise Sch expenditures in one slum area to begin with & attempt to assess the impact of the extra money before going further. It is asserted that funds are often given out of the wrong motives & for the wrong objectives. The roots of this problem may lie in the US system of public control as well as in the incompetence of the educ'al bur'cy. Private control is suggested for the Sch's which serve slum children. Citywide public Sch's should be created to provide slum children with a real choice about the kind of Sch they can attend. Private initiative could be developed by providing tuition grants to children who opted out of the public-controlled Sch's to place them into private Sch's. A U might be given a contract to run a model Sch system in the slums; a group of teachers might incorporate itself to manage a Sch on contract from a citywide board. The basic aim of such measures is to decentralize power & responsibility & to liberate Sch's from the 'dead hand of central admin.' If there is the possibility that the public Sch's can not survive in open competition with private ones, then, it is noted, 'perhaps they should not survive.' M. Maxfield.

title: The Strange History And Problematic Future Of The Australian Census
abstract: When looking back into the first century of Australian history following white settlement we often rely on the records of musters, listings and censuses to provide information on individuals and communities. The first census of New South Wales in 1828 was little more than a directory of names of settlers and settlements, but both professional historians and genealogists regard it as invaluable. As the scientific principles of censuses were developed over the course of the nineteenth century the information collected became ever more important for social scientists and economists. In the twentieth century, professional historians in the UK and USA opened wholly new perspectives on society by looking to the census for records of common families who were not recorded in the newspapers or diaries of the time, and the community structures in which they lived. Unfortunately such innovations have not been possible in Australia. The individual records of most colonial and all Commonwealth censuses are not to be found in the libraries or archives. The destruction of original census records in Australia has been the result of misadventure and government policies reflecting great fear about the impact of popular privacy concerns on public compliance with the census operations. This paper explores the history behind the anomalous practice of destroying census records in Australia, and poses questions about the role of the census in the writing of histories of Australian people and Australian communities. Adapted from the source document.

title: In search for an optimal level of decentralization in Romania
abstract: Starting with year 1990 and until the present, the Romanian administrative system was subjected to continuous reform measures, which had as main objective to increase administrative efficiency and flexibility, recording a substantial increase of the autonomy and competences of the local public administration. The important place that public administration occupies in our constitutional system derives from the consecration of the principle of separation and balance of powers, emphasizing both the defining traits of the state of law, and the type of democratic regime, the pluralism of the Romanian society and local autonomy. Adapted from the source document.

title: Towards a New Professional Focus for Political Science and Public Administration in Arab Universities: A Theoretical Study
abstract: The objective of this paper is to show how policy analysis as a new field in social sciences can help to rescue the fields of political science and public administration in Arab universities from their ongoing crisis. The crisis is embodied in the absence of a professional focus in the two fields. To achieve that objective the paper is divided into main sections discussing the present status of political science and public administration in the Arab world, the development of policy perspective in social sciences, the development of policy analysis as a profession in government, and the reason for the underdeveloped status of policy analysis in Arab universities, and concludes by proposing a multidisciplinary curriculum focusing on government policy to transform the departments of political science and public administration in Arab universities and realize the goal of professionalism. Adapted from the source document.

title: Promoting Home Ownership in a Social-Rented City: Policies, Practices and Pitfalls
abstract: Amsterdam's housing market is dominated by the social-rented sector. It comprises 56% of the total housing stock, while home ownership constitutes only 19%, lower than anywhere else in the Netherlands, & among the lowest in the world. Central government policy is currently seeking to increase the share of home ownership in the Netherlands from 53% (2001) to 65% in 2010. This paper will summarize recent national & local (Amsterdam) housing policy developments, focusing on the recent practice of selling social housing in Amsterdam. Unlike the Right to Buy scheme in GB, the Netherlands employs an 'offer to buy' strategy. Sales, however, have been disappointing so far. Two factors were found to be crucial in this regard: (1) the sluggish change in 'policy mentality' & bureaucracy & (2) the high prices in the home ownership market. By way of conclusion, the paper reflects on the desirability of shifting the tenure structure from tenancy to ownership & on the risks that an (over-) emphasis on home ownership may bring. 1 Table, 18 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Men of the sugarcane fields and their hospitals: the architecture of health under the Estado Novo
abstract: The article explores the emergence of an architectural heritage in the realm of healthcare assistance for workers in the sugarcane agro-industry in Brazil following enactment of the law known as the Estatuto da Lavoura Canavieira (1941), under the auspices of the Instituto do Acucar e do Alcool and as part of Estado Novo policies (1937-1945). The institute proposed solutions biased on surveys conducted at sugarcane mills in cane-producing states and on the medical and hospital system adopted by the institute's enlightened bureaucracy in the 1940s, which took the U.S. system as its model. Special focus is given to the central hospitals in Pernambuco and especially in Alagoas, which opposed institute guidelines. Adapted from the source document.

title: Critical Notes toward a Theory of State Bureaucracy
abstract: Two principal objectives are presented: (1) to examine critically the epistemological bases & biases which underlie the various studies of the administrative apparatus of the state, & (2) to study the relationship between scientific (scholarly) knowledge of bureaucracy & political & technocratic practices. Two types of problems are adduced: (A) how the analytical unity of bureaucracy is defined, & (B) political issues of interest to the researcher. The literature on the subject at present has failed to establish a level of analysis which would make it possible to conceptualize the interrelationship between global social processes & the dynamics of state bureaucracy. The substantive & historical importance of bureaucracy is discussed in terms of its roles within capitalist societies & illustrated with Latin American examples. S. Karganovic.

title: American Welfare Strategies: Three Programs under the Social Security Act
abstract: In the US, a single piece of legislation, the Social Security Act, is the major vehicle through which the cash assistance to citizens is provided. This act contains many subprograms which differ in concept, administration & programmatic implication. Three programs are here examined in a sociohistorical, sociocultural context: social security, unemployment compensation, & public assistance. The roots of these programs are analyzed, their current operations outlined, & the policy problems currently confronting them are detailed. The ways in which the programs relate to the political mythology of the society is seen as important. Because of the continual conflicts arising out of the administration of public assistance, three special cases involving that program are mentioned: the Jenner Amendment, 'suitable homes,' & Title XX. Modified HA.

title: Book reviews -- Property, Bureaucracy and Culture: Middle-Class Formation in Contemporary Britain by M. Savage, J. Barlow, P. Dickens and T. Fielding
abstract: Review.

title: Contextual Beliefs in a Nigerian Quasi-Judicial Public Hearing
abstract: This study examines the contextual beliefs held by interactants in the 2008 quasi-judicial public hearing on the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja Administration in Nigeria, using Odebunmi's (2006) model of context. The data for the study includes forty video recordings of the 2008 quasi-judicial public hearing on the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja Administration in Nigeria. The findings indicate that the shared contextual beliefs in the public hearing are based on shared knowledge of the public hearing aims and procedure, legal codes regarding landed property, government involvement and knowledge of Abuja metropolis.

title: Empowering Communities in the Peri-Urban Areas of Colombo
abstract: This paper describes the work of community-based self-help groups, the community development councils (CDCs), initiated by the Colombo Municipal Council in the late 1970s. Although, initially, the CDCs were exclusively urban-based, the creation of a new layer of local government in the mid-1980s, the provincial councils, allowed them to exist & operate across administrative boundaries in the peri-urban interface. This paper describes in detail the organization & functioning principles of the CDCs, & how the links to higher levels of the city administrative structure such as district, municipality, & province have enabled communities to act in relation to the tensions typical of peri-urban settlements in transition from "rural" to "urban" characteristics. 1 Table, 2 Figures. Adapted from the source document.

title: Building the post-colonial state: Villagization and resource management in Zimbabwe
abstract: Munro discusses three issues concerning Zimbabwe:  the problem of constructing state authority in the countryside, the state's resource management and villagization strategies, and the structural-political constraints.  The villagization strategy in Zimbabwe represents in part an attempt to secure state authority in rural society.

title: Financially and Socially Weak Citizens and Their Encounter with the Legal System
abstract: Between the legislation for & the implementation of laws, much can occur, often resulting in a significant change in goals-or `goal warp'. Programs to help the poor in the US often provide little real help to those who need it. Part of the problem lies in that the `top' of the system has no real notion of what is going on at the `base'. A common misconception is the belief that the poor are not willing to work & to better their condition. Much research is needed to determine what the needs of the socially weak citizen are, & how those needs could best be met. The situation is complicated by the fact that administrators do not always correctly understand the goal message, again leading to goal warp. It may be possible to avoid some of these mistakes by reviewing past programs & determining why some were successful & others were not. Further improvements might be made by soliciting client input into the process, although the exact nature of that input must still be more closely delineated. Various criteria might be used to evaluate such programs, such as feasibility, net achievement, duration, coordination, satisfaction of the client, & others. P. Tiersma.

title: Local Government Growth and Retrenchment in Portugal: Politicization, Neo-Liberalism and New Forms of Governance
abstract: This article deals with the effects of neoliberal ideology on Portuguese local government & the meaning of the new urban governance. The author examines various factors responsible for the increase in local government expenditure since 1974, such as new & greater responsibilities, demographic growth, & changes in social structure & in resource distribution. While noting differences in policy enactment between locations differing in political party & socioeconomic orientations, he describes how local governments react to mounting pressure for improved public services. Local leaders respond like nations experiencing retrenchment & a clawing-back of state actions. Privatization, contracting out, & decentralization are implemented in order to squeeze more services out of restricted local budgets. Innovative delivery mechanisms are adopted to meet the fast-growing local requirements for more funding of local services. 1 Table, 46 References. E. Sanchez

title: Toward an Alternative to the Classic Police Organizational Arrangements: A Democratic Model
abstract: The structural model utilized in organizing Amer police dept's is the classical, normative org'al theory that was first articulated by M. Weber. Scholars criticize this classical theory because: (1) it is culture bound, (2) it mandates att's toward employees & clients that are inconsistent with the humanistic democratic values of the US, (3) it creates immature personality traits in employees, & (4) it is not sufficient to develop an org that can cope with environmental changes, therefore causing org's to eventually become dysfunctional & obsolete. Police bur'cies have 3 signif problems that appear to support the critics' claims: (a) the poor state of police & community relations, (b) the poor morale among police employees, & (c) the inadequacy of COMM & control in law enforcement agencies. One approach to overcoming these problems entails establishing a flexible, participatory, sci-based org'al structure for police operations. The basic model should consist of 3 primary sections: (A) General Services Section, (B) Coordination & Information Section, & (C) Specialized Services Section. The General Services Section would be made up of teams of 15 to 25 officers of equal rank. Each team would be assigned to a specific community, & would share the responsibility with the community for identifying & handling the police problems in their area. The Coordination & Information Section would be staffed by evaluation, org, training, & information processing specialists who would be responsible for identifying homogeneous communities, assigning teams, providing housekeeping activities & information to the entire org, evaluating the comparing teams, & coordinating multiteam efforts. The Specialized Services Section should house the operational specialists, such as investigators, juvenile specialists, & conflict manag officers, who would work for the team members. The adoption of this model would eliminate much of the rigidity & isolation from the community of the traditional police org'al structure. It will permit policy flexibility so that police dept's can make their operations relevant to their communities while at the same time, it provides checks to ensure non-discriminatory, quality policing to all citizens. Implementation of the proposals should be accompanied with a well-developed program of evaluation. Modified AA.

title: Bureaucratic State, Rural Powers and Development in Africa: The Emergence of Peasants' Power
abstract: The article refers to new phenomena generated by international disorder in the closed structure of the state: The emergence of local (communal) powers that some authors refer to as the "rebellion of the social." In fact, rural organizations which have for long been structured by the state & closed within the confines of bureaucratic hierarchy have found a new landscape in the new "world system" characterized by deregulation & liberalisation. They appear as rebellions categories to the englobing propensities of the state thereby trying to construct its own identity in a language that belongs to reception of western culture. However, this emancipation must take into account penpheral constraints, mainly the heterogeneity of situations & peripheral rationalities generated by organizational diversity of the rural (community) & the articulation between different geotemporal scales; in such a way that the interventions of the state & international donors takes into account the various time scopes that enable adaptation of objectives, the modes of organization, methods & financial resources to time constraints. Adapted from the source document.

title: 'SYMBOLIC BUREAUCRACY': A CASE STUDY OF A SOCIAL WELFARE AGENCY
abstract: A discussion of certain ideas about bur'cy presented by M. Weber & qualified & expanded upon by P. M. Blau (BUREAU- CRACY IN MODERN SOCIETY, see SA 5565). Based upon the information gathered in a yr-long participant observation study of 'The Single Men's Unit' of a public welfare dept from Feb 1959 to Feb 1960, during which time he was employed as a 'soc caseworker,' the author has introduced the notion of 'symbolic bur'cy.' The discussion, which is centered around this concept, seriously questions whether Blau's 'unofficial change' & 'adjustive development' will suffice to save Weber's construction of an 'ideal type,' where it is assumed that the org best approximating the central conditions of an ideal bur'cy will function with the greatest efficiency. It seems more likely that the introduction of the concept of unofficial change, if it serves to rescue Weber's 'ideal type,' succeeds in doing so only at the serious risk of losing bur'cv. Modified HA.

title: The past and future of minimum income benefits in Euskadi
abstract: This article summarizes the evolution of the regulations and policies of minimum income benefits in the war on poverty in Euskadi. The influence of the model used in some European countries is reflected in some of these actions which will soon become structural changes and will be integrated into the basic Public Administration budgets. In addition, the lines of action of the various platforms in the war on poverty and social exclusion in the region are analyzed in relation to the Autonomous Government's minimum income benefits and the importance given to institutional policy by them, even though the modeling and management of them is critiqued. Adapted from the source document.

title: Italy: Between bureaucratic power and democratic legitimacy
abstract: For more than a year, Italy has had a stable Center-Right government with a large political majority and the inclusion in the governing coalition of the party once nostalgic for fascism, which had resulted in its ostracism by the republican regime from 1946 to 1994. In order to understand these radically new development de la Grange retraces the crisis of the old Italian regime of parties and of the constitutional predicament.

title: Personnel reform in Chinese hospitals: policy interdependence and the challenge of coherent incrementalism
abstract: Health care in China is plagued with problems, including barriers to access, maldistribution of resources, inefficiencies and uneven quality. The management of human resources in the health care system has a significant effect on what happens in the clinic and the ward. The management of staff appointments and the remuneration system are two critical areas that remain problematic although they have received government attention. We argue that new approaches to policy development and implementation are needed to achieve a high-performance health care system. In particular, we suggest a new focus on the challenges of policy interdependence across sectors and among levels of administration. We highlight the need for a clear vision for health care, which would provide direction for the entire reform process, and also for a restructuring of the system of accountability. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Street-Level Bureaucracy and the Analysis of Urban Reform
abstract: This theoretically-oriented paper reviews & summarizes behavioral characteristics common to the roles of "Street-level Bur'crats:" policemen, welfare workers, teachers, & other public employees who: (1) regularly interact with clients; (2) exercise wide discretion in job performance; & (3) can have relatively signif impacts on clients' welfare. The implications of the analysis are then extended by assessing recent reform proposals in Ur pol to the analysis of these bur'tic behaviors. AA.

title: Bureaucracy as a Moral Issue
authors: Sjoberg, Gideon; Vaughan, Ted R; Williams, Norma
abstract: The reasons for bureaucracy's current status as a major moral problem are explored through two of its moral consequences: the use of secrecy to abuse & enhance power; & the emergence of "triage," defined as "the sacrifice of the socially weakest sector of society." The hierarchy of authority & the stress on secrecy in bureaucratic organizations have produced "system loyalty," or action based on loyalty to authorities & the system, which potentially endangers human dignity. The emphasis on efficiency & rationality have led to the utilitarian expectation that the poor bear most of the moral costs. Current Western interest in the SE rights of the disadvantaged has laid the foundation for a moral standard for the evaluation of bureaucratic personnel & structures. The elements of a moral system must: view human beings as "reflective agents"; recognize the relationship between agents & organizations, including the tensions between them; have a notion of rational action to overcome the problems of the means-end relationship; & require the actor to transcend his perspective to see that of others. 44 References. D. Graves.

title: And Ever the Twain Shall Meet: The Holiness Missionary Movement and the Birth of World Pentecostalism, 1870-1920
abstract: Pentecostalism first appeared as a global movement, built with both modern & antimodern materials provided by the American holiness missionary movement. On the anti-modern side, radical holiness spirituality & theology infused the worldviews of its advocates with supernaturalism, primitivism, & an apocalyptic eschatology. It resisted modern trends toward systematization, bureaucratization, & centralized control. Furthermore, radical holiness minimized the significance of modern categories of nation, ethnicity, race, & civilization. On the other side, radical holiness depended on the modern disintegration of traditional religious deference, used modern techniques for promoting audience-driven or democratized patterns of authority, & effectively equipped its 158 Religion & American Culture followers for the pragmatic methodologies of modernity by skillfully making use of transportation networks, fund-raising techniques, & mass media to reach large audiences. American holiness missionaries carried these characteristics overseas, where non-American advocates adapted them to their particular circumstances. Both American & non-American adherents promoted radical holiness in ways that confounded reigning categories of identity, power relations, & conceptions of East & West. Radical holiness granted religious authority to Chinese men, Indian girls, spirit-filled Zulus, working-class Chileans, female evangelists, & African-American leaders, as well as white American males, without consciously mobilizing its followers along lines of national, ethnic, gendered, racial, or class identity. It demanded that its followers leave "heathenism," but it did so without utilizing the imperialist era discourse of civilization that upheld western cultural superiority & non-western cultural inferiority. In terms of its national or racial characteristics, then, early leaders from diverse backgrounds used tools from the American holiness movement to bring a non-American movement, world Pentecostalism, into existence. Adapted from the source document.

title: Processos de governo no presidencialismo brasileiro: a estrutura de coordenação política da Presidência
abstract: The government policy making process, or decision making process, under Brazilian presidentialism includes beyond the legislative arena, the participation of actors and structures from Executive branch, that work in the advisory and articulation of the government. Based on this understanding, the paper aims to explore an analytical approach that emphasize the Executive branch and its internal dynamics of work, mainly evaluating the differences and continuities that can arise from one administration to another in order to understand how the presidents design their staff to exercise the government. Therefore, this article will emphasize the arrangement of political coordination of the presidency. This study considers that in the coalitional presidentialism the chief of the Executive is, from an institutional point of view, the leading actor (the pivotal role) both to build and to incite the work of the coalition, and also in the policy making process that occur in the Legislative branch, that is why the relationship with Congress should be investigated from an Executive approach. Considering this purpose, maybe, will be possible to begin a reflection about the role of the president in general, and the presidency in particular, to the work of the Brazilian presidentialism.

title: The Police -- Autonomous Actor or Instrument of Rule?
abstract: To shed light on the role of bureaucracy in power structures & its supposed neutrality, the political function of the police in the Federal Republic of Germany is examined as an example of a bureaucratic institution that is key to the state monopoly on the use of force. Focus is on the relationship among the police, law, & politics in protest policing, a multifunctional police action reflecting the ambiguities of this role. Drawing on interviews with 16 leading police officers & analysis of police journals, the perspectives of the police, their knowledge of the availability of resources & how to use them, & the influence exerted by politicians are assessed. It is shown how, in controlling protesters, police interact directly in the political process, &, while they see themselves as a neutral enforcement agent whose actions are controlled by law, they also seek to maximize their scope of action to serve their own goals. It is concluded that police actions will always be subject to political pressures &, with their autonomy, difficult to defend. 27 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Lying the Truth: Practices of Confession and Recognition
abstract: Italy's 1998 Immigration Law 40 includes Article 18, which allows foreign "victims of human trafficking" the right to temporary residence permits on the condition that they participate in a rehabilitation program. The first step of this program, the act of denuncia, is to file criminal charges against exploiters at the police station. However, the resulting testimony cannot be understood through the victim/agent trope of the bureaucratic state, which uses these categories to make the other understandable through a process of what I call "confessional recognition." In this article, I show how, despite the proliferation of biometric technologies to identify foreign others and so control migration flows at borders, confessional practices continue to play a central role in deciding who is admitted legally. Moreover, I illustrate how the question of redemption and expiation is not only a crucial issue for Catholic groups involved in aid programs for foreigners but is also central to Italian state integration policies, thus revealing how juridical norms are deeply influenced by the vocabulary of religious morality and vice versa. [web URL: http://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/683272]

title: Rio de Janeiro and the divided state: Analysing the political discourse on favelas
abstract: This article analyses the discourse on favelas produced by Brazilian society and consumed in the political field of local administration. The ideological conception of favelas (slums) determines the creation of public policies that reinforce the prejudicial notion of favelas. This work employs critical discourse analysis (CDA) to analyse several texts extracted from mass-media stories and press releases of the Rio government. It shows that the state of praxis reproduces the understanding of slums as a phenomenon detached from the rest of society. This alienated vision impacts on different utterances blaming the poor (analysis 1); perpetuating poverty (analysis 2); and reinforcing exclusion (analysis 3).

title: A Garbage Can Model of Organizational Choice
authors: Cohen, Michael D.,; March, James G.,; Olsen, Johan P
abstract: Org'ed anarchies are org's characterized by problematic preferences, unclear technology, & fluid participation. Recent studies of U's, a familiar form of org'ed anarchy, suggest that such org's can be viewed for some purposes as collections of choices looking for problems, issues & feelings looking for decision situations in which they might be aired, solutions looking for issues to which they might be an answer, & decision makers looking for work. These ideas are translated into an explicit computer simulation model of a garbage can decision process. The general implications of such a model are described in terms of 5 major measures on the process. Possible applications of the model to more narrow predictions are illustrated by an examination of the model's predictions with respect to the effect of adversity on U decision making. The garbage can process is shown to be one in which problems, solutions, & participants move from one choice opportunity to another in such a way that the nature of the choice, the time it takes, & the problems it solves all depend on a relatively complicated intermeshing of elements. These include the mix of choices available at any one time, the mix of problems that have access to the org, the mix of solutions looking for problems, & the outside demands on the decision makers. Although the garbage can process does not resolve problems well, it does enable choices to be made & problems resolved, even when the org is plagued with goal ambiguity & conflict, with poorly understood problems that wander in & out of the system, & a variable environment. Modified HA.

title: Relational Municipality: Social Efficacy
abstract: Changes in the conceptualization of the state & its role in society -- from a laissez-faire model, to a service-provider welfare state, to a management-oriented relational state -- are analyzed in terms of their consequences for public management or administration. The requirements for modernizing local public administration are discussed, focusing on models designed to increase efficacy in the public sector, & avoiding mere adoption of private management models. The experience of the municipality of Alcobendas (near Madrid, Spain) is discussed as an example of a relational municipality, whose goal is social efficiency. 4 Figures. Adapted from the source document.

title: College and University Department Structures
abstract: Some comments & thoughts on the control & power models of U admin's are presented, based on news items from the Sep, 1972 through May, 1973 issues of Faculty Memo distributed by the Central Admin of the U of Wisconsin System. 3 main models are found: the leadership model (chairman running the dept); the org model (bur'tic committee system); & the group model (dept faculty as the primary control agent & decision-making group for the dept). The distribution of power & assignment of functions in each is described as is the complexity of internal structures, the sources of disruption, & the safeguards to insure adjustability in crisis (without compromising the model) in each of the 3 control types. Other aspects dealt with include: the relationship of the dept to the entire U; the committee structure; the committee functions; & the name of the chairman's role. A particular dept that has achieved stability might combine in its structure elements from all 3 models as outlined. The diff's to look for in a comparative study of dept's would be diff's in combinations of structural & functional elements. In a developmental perspective, the history of a dept might be written as a record of the compromises in the principles that characterize the roles & the structural models. M. Maxfield.

title: Bureaucracy in Great Britain in the 1980s
abstract: The growth of bureaucracy in the UK in the 1980s is generally seen as undesirable. Concern is directed to the increase in administrative personnel relative to other personnel, to increased concern for formal rather than substantive rationality, & to skepticism about the claimed technical superiority of bureaucratic decision making. The hypothesis is advanced that the growth of bureaucracy in the UK is due to the promotion of bureaucracy by a dominant elite that is concerned with being able to rationalize its decisions as consequences of bureaucratic organization. Social control is increasingly shifting from self-regulation to institutional development. Staff selection takes place through examinations favoring graduates of elite schools. Bureaucracy functions in ways congenial to the preferences of managerial ideology. The symbolism of rational efficiency can be used to create an appearance disguising the reality of subjectively based decisions. Elites accept the necessity of bureaucracy & are able to strengthen their control of organizations through supporting it. To some degree, this tendency reflects more widespread social trends. Three possible results are: successful management, bureaucratic collapse, or, most probably, the perpetuation of existing systems with all their inadequacies & tensions. W. H. Stoddard.

title: Physicians' perceptions of autonomy across practice types: Is autonomy in solo practice a myth?
abstract: Physicians in the United States are now less likely to practice in smaller, more traditional, solo practices, and more likely to practice in larger group practices. Though older theory predicts conflict between bureaucracy and professional autonomy, studies have shown that professions in general, and physicians in particular, have adapted to organizational constraints. However, much work remains in clarifying the nature of this relationship and how exactly physicians have adapted to various organizational settings. To this end, the present study examines physicians' autonomy experiences in different decision types between organization sizes. Specifically, I ask: In what kinds of decisions do doctors perceive autonomous control? How does this vary by organizational size? Using stacked 'spell' data constructed from the Community Tracking Study (CTS) Physician Survey (1996-2005) (n = 16,519) I examine how physicians' perceptions of autonomy vary between solo/two physician practices, small group practices with three to ten physicians, and large practices with ten or more physicians, in two kinds of decisions: logistic-based and knowledge-based decisions. Capitalizing on the longitudinal nature of the data I estimate how changes in practice size are associated with perceptions of autonomy, accounting for previous reports of autonomy. I also test whether managed care involvement, practice ownership, and salaried employment help explain part of this relationship. I find that while physicians practicing in larger group practices reported lower levels of autonomy in logistic-based decisions, physicians in solo/two physician practices reported lower levels of autonomy in knowledge-based decisions. Managed care involvement and ownership explain some, but not all, of the associations. These findings suggest that professional adaptation to various organizational settings can lead to varying levels of perceived autonomy across different kinds of decisions. [Copyright Elsevier Ltd.]

title: ‘A dead letter of the statute book’: the strange bureaucratic life of the Bihar Food Economy and Guest Control Order, 1950–1954
abstract: In the years following India’s independence, food shortages threatened to destabilize the country. In response, the Indian Ministry of Food in 1950 introduced the Food Economy and Guest Control Order. This statute was designed to check waste by limiting the number of guests permitted at social gatherings and regulating the types of food items served. The Guest Control Order quickly became a flashpoint between the bureaucrats in Delhi who conceived of the austerity measures and their counterparts in state capitals tasked with implementing the policy. This article examines the correspondence between the Ministry of Food and the Bihar Supply and Price Control Department regarding the Guest Control Order for insight into early debates about the appropriate role of the state in the economy. The exchange reveals the conflicting priorities – e.g. national objectives versus local exigencies, social cohesion versus enforceability – that characterized state policy in the early years of independent India. In these debates, assumptions about Indian culture, in general, and food practices, in particular – e.g. what is good for citizens to eat, how these foods ought to be eaten – became contested in the lawmaking process and emerged as central to the process of early nation-making.

title: Administrative Responsibility: Public Policy and the Wilsonian Legacy
abstract: For Woodrow Wilson & other early twentieth century public administrators, the issue concerning administrative responsibility was lack of operating techniques rather than the ethical-moral vacuousness that is of concern now. Until notions of ethical responsibility extend beyond a mere mechanical adherence to the explicit letter of the law, the study of public administration must continue to reflect the Wilsonian emphasis on operating techniques. The "ethics of civility" are based on a common-sense, day-to-day relevance of political efficacy without reference to moral tenets. A redefinition of administrative responsibility is needed, based more on individual integrity. However, the notion of administrative responsibility is much too important to be left to each individual to define. It must combine the elements of both the collective disparate design & the individual morality. In conjunction with an explicitly avowed ethics of consciousness, a new openness of administrative responsibility would be gained. An ethics of consciousness may provide an authentic public responsibility. B. Hubinger.

title: Collective bargaining and reforms to hospital healthcare provision: A comparison of the UK, Italy and France
authors: Galetto, Manuela; Marginson, Paul; Spieser, Catherine
abstract: Reforms inspired by the 'new public management' approach have changed the provision of hospital healthcare and challenged established arrangements for governing the workforce. We identify four main reform processes in three countries, and examine their impact on collective bargaining and administrative and statutory mechanisms of workforce governance. Although the extent and nature of reforms play a role in the changes to workforce governance, political choices and the interests and responses of organized employers and trade unions intervene to shape outcomes.

title: Freedom in a Bonded Society: The Administrative Mind and the 'Lower Classes' in Colonial New South Wales
abstract: The culture of the administration in New South Wales, Australia, in the early 19th century is examined, emphasizing administrative attitudes toward the lower classes. The administrative system designed to manage convict labor also came to be used in the management of free labor. Like convicts, free laborers worked for rations as well as wages. Additionally, freedom was regulated under the bureaucracy of the administration. This regulation was largely based on moral precepts, in particular the negative connotations associated with idleness. The functioning of the government store is also discussed. The store's role as a provider was based on benevolence & its role as a market was unstable. Anecdotes illustrating these points are presented. It is concluded that both the administration & the store were characterized by the highly personal nature of the power nexus. J. Ferrari

title: A Subtle Governance: 'Soft' Medical Leadership in English Primary Care
authors: Sheaff, R; Rogers, A; Pickard, S; Marshall, M; Campbell, S; Sibbald, B; Halliwell, S; Roland, M
abstract: In many countries, governments are recruiting the medical profession into a more active, transparent regulation of clinical practice. Consequently, the medical profession adapts the ways it regulates itself & its relationship to health system managers changes. This paper uses empirical research in English Primary Care Groups (PCGs) & Primary Care Trusts (PCTs) to assess the value of Courpasson's concept of soft bureaucracy as a conceptualization of these changes. Clinical governance in PCGs & PCTs displays important parallels with governance in soft bureaucracies, but the concept of soft bureaucracy requires modification to make it more applicable to general practice. In English primary care, governance over rank-&-file doctors is exercised by local professional leaders rather than general managers, harnessing their colleagues' perception of threats to professional autonomy & self-regulation rather than fears of competition as the means of 'soft coercion.'. 56 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: British Administration and the Chiefs' Tyranny in Early Colonial Kenya; A Case Study of the First Generation of Chiefs from Kiambu District, 1895--1920
abstract: This article argues that the chiefs' tyranny in early colonial Kenya had its roots in the British administrative style since the Government needed strong-handed local leaders to enforce its unpopular laws and regulations. That was why the chiefs got away with their tyranny because the Government condoned it to a certain extent. They also got away with it because of the alien nature of their positions, their duties and their people inadvertently condoning it. The first generation of chiefs from Kiambu district is used as a case study to illustrate what was happening in the colony during the period under study.

title: Twisting the Law
abstract: Provided is an analysis of the evolution of the policy of affirmative action, from the Civil Rights Act of 1964 through the Bakke & Weber decisions. The emphasis is on the policy of affirmative action as formulated, developed, & applied & interpreted from the point of view of the Dept of Health, Education, & Welfare & the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Concluded is that affirmative action is a total bureaucratic distortion of the original legislative act & subsequent court decisions. A detailed point-by-point comparison of legislative acts & court decisions, with the restatement of these in bureaucratic directives & policy statements, is provided. It is suggested that the distortion is a product of modern liberal ideology. AA.

title: Correctional Officer Job Burnout: A Path Model
authors: WHITEHEAD, JOHN T; LINDQUIST, CHARLES A
abstract: A path model of job burnout among correctional officers from a southern state is examined. The analysis shows that direct contact with inmates is not distressing; however, administrative practices are bothersome to officers. The findings may be interpreted as supporting the recently advanced double-bind theory of correctional officer stress (Cheek and Miller, 1983)--which ascribes officer distress to administrative practices--and/or being consistent with street-level bureaucracy theory (Lipsky, 1980), which attributes worker distress to managerial control strategies. Implications for intervention are discussed.

title: Multicounty Cooperation: Possible but not Inevitable
abstract: This discussion synthesizes information from a recent field res project in multi-county cooperation, previous field res on intergov'al relations, & middle-range sociol'al change strategies. It is proposed that not all counties can achieve their goals independently. Unfortunately, too few counties seem to be cooperating with others in order to achieve collectively what is not possible alone. The change agent could help solve this problem. But he, too, must recognize various limitations such as inadequate internal resources, & a strong emphasis on local autonomy. 3 patterns of soc interaction are analyzed as a source of 4 recommendations for change agent action. They are COMM among leaders, COMM between leaders & electorate, & the instit'ization of repetitive interaction. 1 Table. Modified HA.

title: Corruption as a Result of Social Disorganization
abstract: The multiple & complex causes of corruption at all levels of Mexican society & how causes concatenate are analyzed. The concept of corruption, rooted in conflict between individual & social interests, & the concepts of democracy & power are discussed. Mexico's 6-year-only model of political power fuels the accumulation of personal wealth by politicians during that regime, along with the knowledge that their predecessors & successors acted & will act in the same manner, personal anxiety about future employment, & perverse egoism. Problems with public administration, eg, absence of real social participation & lack of planning & administrative training, are also causes of corruption. Corruption operates in social disorganization where it is ethically tolerated & where power relations are based on inequality & despotism. 21 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Whither the Developmental State in South Korea? Balancing Welfare and Neoliberalism
abstract: Scholars of political economy have been debating the role of the Korean state in the economic development of the country, as the characteristics of a developmental state, a neoliberal state and/or a welfare state have appeared simultaneously in the various governments' policies since the 1990s. This paper argues that although the nature, degree and extent of government intervention has varied from administration to administration, the basic stance of a developmental state has been retained while neoliberal and welfare policies have been used concurrently to further economic and social development. This coexistence of contradictory approaches reflecting alternative market economic systems was the product of a combination of government policies that has for the past 20 years provided the Korean government with the ability to deploy flexible policy mixes in response to changes in the political and economic environment and to maximise the outcomes of developmental policies.

title: BUREAUCRACY AND POLYARCHY AS PREDICTORS OF PERFORMANCE: A CROSS-NATIONAL EXAMINATION
authors: Russett, Bruce M; Monsen, R Joseph
abstract: POLITICAL LEADERS, LIKE OTHER ENTREPRENEURS, MAY FIND THEIR OWN INTERESTS IN ACCORD WITH OR CONFLICTING WITH THOSE OF THE GROUPS FOR WHICH THEY MAKE DECISIONS. POLYARCHIC GROUPS, IN WHICH THE POLITICAL LEADER'S CONTROL IS MORE READILY CONTESTED, CAN BE EXPECTED ON THEORETICAL GROUNDS, TO BE MORE RESPONSIVE TO CONSTITUENT DEMANDS FOR SUCH GOALS AS PEACE, EQUALITY, & MODERATE GROWTH AS OPPOSED TO STAGNATION OR RAPID GROWTH. BUREAUCRATIC ORGANIZATIONS CAN BE EXPECTED TO BE MORE RESPONSIVE WHEN SMALLER & MORE RECENTLY FORMED. SEVERAL OPERATIONALIZATIONS OF THESE VARIABLES ARE TESTED FOR A WIDE RANGE OF CONTEMPORARY NATIONAL GOVERNMENTS. USING THE MOST SIGNIFICANT VARIABLES, POLYARCHY HAS NO EFFECT ON PEACE OR EQUALITY BUT PRODUCES MORE MEASURED ECONOMIC GROWTH. LARGER BUREAUCRACIES PRODUCE LARGER DEGREES OF INCOME EQUALITY &, IN NONPOLYARCHIES, GREATER ECONOMIC GROWTH. HOWEVER, POLYARCHIES SHOW CONSIDERABLY MORE WAR, WHEN LARGE, THAN SMALL POLYARCHIES OR ANY NONPOLYARCHIES. DEMOCRATIC NATIONAL GOVERNMENTS MAY HAVE PASSED THE POINT OF DIMINISHING RETURNS FROM SCALE INCREASES. 4 TABLES. MODIFIED AUTHOR'S SUMMARY.

title: The Role of Bureaucracy in Policy Development and Implementation in India
abstract: The role of bureaucracy in India is not only dominant in the implementation of public policies, but it is also pervasive in policy formation.  An analysis of the role of bureaucracy in the processes of public policy is given.

title: At the limits of spatial governmentality: A message from the tip of Africa
abstract: Urban studies scholars drawing on Foucault's analysis of governmentality have investigated how urban social orders are increasingly more concerned with the management of space rather than on the discipline of offenders or the punishment of offences (Merry, 2001). This paper examines the 'rationality' and efficacy of spatial governmentality in post-apartheid Cape Town, and shows how the city has increasingly become a 'fortress city' (Davis, 1990), much like cities such as Los Angeles, Sao Paolo and Rio de Janeiro. These 'global cities' are increasingly characterised by privatised security systems in middle class suburbs, shopping malls and gated communities (Caldeira, 1999). These spatial forms of governmentality draw on sophisticated security systems comprising razor wire and electrified walls, burglar alarms and safe rooms, as well as vicious guard dogs, neighbourhood watches, private security companies, and automated surveillance cameras. On the other side of the race and class divide are urban ghettoes characterised by growing poverty and everyday violence. These socio-spatial inequalities continue to be reproduced despite urban planning initiatives aimed at desegregating the apartheid city. Although the media and the middle classes highlight the dangers of crime and violence, they tend to ignore the structures of inequality that fuel the growth of crime syndicates and violent drug economies that are reproducing these urban governance crises. Given the diminished resources of the neo-liberal state, the policing of middle class residential and business districts is increasingly being 'outsourced' to private security companies. In working class neighbourhoods of Cape Town such as Manenberg, the state has attempted to re-establish governance by resorting to new forms of spatial governmentality. The paper draws attention to the limits of these attempts to assert state control through the management of space. Spatial governance in places like Manenberg will continue to be relatively ineffectual given existing levels of social inequality and racial polarization. Such processes are reproduced by massive unemployment and racialised poverty resulting from socio-spatial legacies of apartheid and Cape Town's shift from a manufacturing to a tourist, IT and financial services economy. Although this paper focuses on attempts at re-establishing governance in a crime and gangster-ridden working class neighbourhood of Cape Town, it addresses these issues in relation to city-wide shifts to new forms of spatial governmentality after apartheid.

title: Participatory Budgeting in Europe: Potentials and Challenges
authors: Sintomer, Yves; Herzberg, Carsten; Röcke, Anja
abstract: The 'transfer' of participatory budgeting from Brazil to Europe has been a highly differentiated process. In Porto Alegre, this innovative methodology enabled democratization and social justice to be articulated. In Europe, participatory budgeting relies on multiple procedures, and it is therefore necessary to give a clear methodological definition of it so that cases can be coherently compared and ideal-types constructed to understand the variety of concrete experiments. The six ideal-types we propose (Porto Alegre adapted for Europe; representation of organized interests; community funds at the local and city level; the public/private negotiating table; consultation on public finances; proximity participation) show striking differences that are highly influenced by existing participatory traditions. It is, above all, with the models Porto Alegre adapted for Europe and community funds that an 'empowered participatory governance' can develop and that a fourth power beyond the three classical ones, is developing--that of the citizenry when it directly (or through delegates) assumes a decision-making power. However, other models have their strengths, too, for example with regard to the reform of public administration which is a critical aspect in the search for 'another possible world'. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Impact of Presidential Speeches on the Bureaucracy
abstract: Objective. Scholars have long held that presidents use various tools to control the federal bureaucracy. Yet, despite their importance to presidents in achieving their policy goals in Congress, few scholars have examined the impact of presidential speeches on bureaucratic activity. This article analyzes the impact of both positive and negative policy signals on civil rights policy in the bureaucracy. Method. I test this hypothesis using speeches coded from the Public Papers of the Presidents and their impact on criminal cases filed by the Civil Rights Division over time. Given heteroskedasticity in the dependent variable, log-linear time-series methods are appropriate. Results. The president's positive speeches increase the number of criminal civil rights cases filed in U.S. District Court. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 also has had a significant, positive impact on bureaucratic activity. Conclusions. In part because bureaucrats have discretion to resist presidential preferences that oppose an agency's core task, negative signals do not affect the implementation of civil rights policy. Yet, positive presidential speeches are available to presidents who may wish to influence the bureaucracy. Adapted from the source document.

title: A case of mistaken identity: The social welfare professions and New Public Management
abstract: Social welfare professions have been highly exposed to the corrosive effects of New Public Management (NPM) on professional identity and influence. In this article, I argue that ambivalence from within the social welfare professions, and in society more generally, towards professional recognition of these occupations enables NPM to enact an agenda of de-professionalization. Further, gendered assumptions about professional identity, and particularly about the caring professions in which there is a high concentration of women workers, are pivotal to the destabilization of the professional social welfare workforce. I draw on examples from the Queensland Department of Child Safety workforce reforms to illustrate how NPM discourse intersects with, and is enabled by, well-established ambivalence towards professional recognition within and outside the social welfare professions. I suggest that a gender analysis can deepen our understanding of the substantial impact of NPM on social welfare professions and can enable these professions to develop effective responses to the substantial threats they now face. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright The Australian Sociological Association.]

title: Mandatory Identification Bar Checks: How Bouncers Are Doing Their Job
authors: Monk-Turner, Elizabeth; Allen, John; Casten, John; Cowling, Catherine; Gray, Charles; Guhr, David; Hoofnagle, Kara; Huffman, Jessica; Mina, Moises; Moore, Brian
abstract: The behavior of bouncers at on site establishments that served alcohol was observed. Our aim was to better understand how bouncers went about their job when the bar had a mandatory policy to check identification of all customers. Utilizing an ethnographic decision model, we found that bouncers were significantly more likely to card customers that were more casually dressed than others, those who were in their 30s, and those in mixed racial groups. We posit that bouncers who failed to ask for identification did so because they appeared to know customers, they appeared to be of age, or they took a break and no one was checking for identification at the door. We found that bouncers presented a commanding presence by their dress and demeanor. Bouncers, we posit, function in three primary roles: customer relations, state law management, and establishment rule enforcer. Adapted from the source document.

title: PT: Dilemmas of Bureaucratization
abstract: An examination of the basic policy problems caused by the internal institutionalization & bureaucratization of Brazil's Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT [Workers' party]). With 80% of the PT composed of former participants in collective action groups (social movements, student movement, revolutionary leftists), the PT instituted a grass-roots approach as the only means to reach consensus. However, when this unifying move led to the isolation & eventual expulsion of nonconformist factions in its revolutionary culture, problems with the definition of a political program & strategy appeared. Other shifts in internal structure resulted from the PT's decision to join Brazil's multiparty political system. Administrative solutions adopted by successive congresses of the PT toward controlling these problems are reviewed. 12 Figures. J. Sadler

title: TECHNOLOGICAL INNOVATION AND THEORETICAL FUNCTIONS OF PRIMARY GROUPS AND BUREAUCRATIC STRUCTURES
abstract: Bur'tic structures are ideally suited to deal with problems requiring technical knowledge or large-scale capital investments. Primary group structures are most able to handle problems requiring little technical knowledge, eg, where knowledge is so simple the ordinary person can do it as well as the expert, where knowledge is lacking so experts cannot be trained, where knowledge is so complex it cannot be put together in time to make a decision. In principle, technology is as likely to take tasks now handled by experts & simplify them so the ordinary person can deal with them as it is to take tasks now handled by ordinary individuals & show how they can be more effectively handled by experts. Therefore, in principle, technology is not likely, after its first stage, to reduce functions of either the primary group or the bur'cy. More characteristic will be stress on continuous change. AA.

title: Reforming Medicaid through Contracting: The Nexus of Implementation and Organizational Culture
authors: Romzek, Barbara S; Johnston, Jocelyn M
abstract: Investigates the administrative experience resulting from the intersection of two popular public management trends -- social service reform & contracting out -- offering a case study of a reform in which KS contracted with nonprofit agencies to provide Medicaid case management services. Implementation of the reforms entailed substantial changes in the roles & scope of administrative activities for the agencies involved & significant challenges to the administrative cultures of each. As a result, nonprofit agencies now play a more central role in state policy deliberations & encounter higher levels of interagency political conflict than they did prior to their contracting role. While some of the rationales for the policy reform have been realized, others have been more elusive, including cost savings & the single-point-of-entry organizing principle of the reform. Implementation challenges due to turf issues, tensions over external monitoring, & differences in administrative cultures have contributed to a lack of policy subgroup cohesiveness, which could facilitate intra- & intergovernmental relationships. 1 Exhibit, 1 Appendix, 53 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Politics, Public Administration, and Agricultural Development: A Case Study of the Sierra Leone Industrial Plantation Development Program, 1964-67,
abstract: Lack of communication & cooperation between specialists, administrators, & government officials results in the failure of many government sponsored development programs. The events leading to the failure of the Sierra Leone Industrial Plantation Development Program (1964-1967) are analyzed to demonstrate this concept. Plantation development was planned for the Northern province by the Prime Minister in an attempt to win over people affiliated with the opposition party. Although administration of the program was turned over to the Sierra Leone Produce Marketing Board (SLPMB), responsibility for decision making was transferred to the Prime Minister's office. Interference in the project by the Prime Minister caused a breakdown in communication between his office & the SLPMB. Further administrative problems were caused by a conflict that arose between the SLPMB & the Ministry of Agriculture & Natural Resources. Financial problems arose when the support that was expected did not materialize. The use of the little money that was available was not well planned for & most of it was wasted. Technical errors resulted in the inappropriate choice of sites for development & for the crops grown. When the program was evaluated it was recommended that the project be abandoned. Failure of the project was due to political intervention, lack of financial support, & technical errors. Projects supported by government or public agencies would be more successful with increased administrative capacity, adequate financial support, good technical skill, political leadership, & a minimum of political interference. 5 Tables. M. K. Razo.

title: The System of Sustainable Degradation
abstract: Following the lead of Gro Harlem Brundtland, the World Commission on Environment and Development declared sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The system of sustainable degradation tacitly responds to the stresses in the 'conditions of capitalist production'8: first, as the 'external physical conditions,' or natural elements required for constant and variable capital; second, as the 'labor power' of workers entangled in their own personal conditions of production; and third, as the 'the communal, general conditions of social production.' Today 'external physical conditions' are discussed in terms of the viability of ecosystems, the adequacy of atmospheric ozone levels, the stability of coastlines and watersheds; soil, air and water quality; and so on. 'Labor power' is discussed in terms of the physical and mental well-being of workers; the kind and degree of socialization; toxicity of work relations and the workers' ability to cope; and human beings as social productive forces and biological organisms generally.

title: Research on Research and Some Problems of Research Bureaucracy
abstract: Sociologists, especially American sociologists, tend to regard the sociology of science as part of the sociology of knowledge, concerned with defining the nature of scientific ideas, & with their relation to other kinds of ideas & to other factors. However, this ideocentric approach has been replaced in part with concern for other aspects of science than its character as a form of knowledge. Research on the objective socioeconomic, organizational & operational characteristics of institutionalized & professionalized research activity has become increasingly important in the sociology of science. The material demands of science & society on each other, the investment of society in the research establishment, national & industrial research policies, & related issues are further subjects awaiting sociological investigation. One part of this domain is the structure & function of contemporary research bureaucracies. Review of data from personnel files of the 38 full-fledged research institutes of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences suggests that "big science" is associated with an increased share of total personnel being devoted to administrative roles at research institutions. 1 Table. Modified HA

title: The Change in Public Organizations
abstract: Discusses problems facing modern governmental administrations around the world, & asserts that the public sector worldwide is currently facing crisis due to lack of money, poor decision-making capacity, & loss of political trust. Rapid industrialization & standardization of the global economy have led to a need for rapid transformation in both public & private sectors. Private enterprises have kept up with this transformation quite well, whereas governments have not. It is concluded that the public sector must model the experience of the private sector to participate in the modern global economy. M. Wagner

title: Social Capital and Interinstitutional Cooperation: Research Evidence from the Case of E-Government
abstract: The article explores the topic of interinstitutional cooperation in the policy area of e-government. Presenting some data from a 2001 survey on Italian municipalities, it shows differences among Italian regions in levels of interinstituional cooperation. Why do such differences exist? The correlation between regional levels of interinstitutional cooperation & regional stocks of social capital (or "civism," as measured by Robert D. Putnam) suggests that social capital could be used to answer this question. The correlation is also the starting point to reflect on the controversial link between social capital & politics. The article criticises those uses of the concept of social capital that ignore the role of politics & institutions & encourages development of the study of "deviant" cases (e.g., Basilicata, where, despite low levels of social capital, regional government fosters fruitful cooperative relations with municipalities) in order to better understand the role of political variables in their relation with the social context. Tables, Figures, References. Adapted from the source document.

title: CONCEPTIONS OF BUREAUCRATIC ACTION AND RELATIONS BETWEEN POLITICS AND ADMINISTRATION
abstract: The main assumption underlying the study is that a comparative analysis of public bur'tic action must adopt a functional approach, such as to identify & take into signif account those decision-making processes of bur'tic elites that partake of a pol'al nature. In a contrary manner, either implicitly or explicitly, a great body of literature dealing with public bur'cies accepts & sets forth value-loaded & ideological conceptions of admin'ive action in which bur'crats are seen as obedient & value-neutral servants of the pol'al decision-makers. These conceptions are analyzed & related to their historical, heuristic, & disciplinary matrix, & their inability to explain admin'ive action comprehensively is then discussed. The conceptions analyzed are: (a) that stemming from the implicit values imbedded in the formal Sch of public law, & acritically accepted by a large section of pol'al sci, which took shape during the 19th cent; (b) the scholarly systematization of reform movements esp active in the UK & the US; (c) the behavioral approach to admin'ive decisionmaking which, from the acceptance of some neo-positivistic postulates about the logical separation of facts front values, reaches conclusions to the effect that a logical separation of pol from administration is also necessary &, therefore, the decisional processes of admin'ors are to be analyzed independently of their ideological & pol'al implications. AA.

title: Politics, Public Administration and Canada's Aging Population
abstract: Aging policy is determined in very large measure by politicians & bureaucrats at all levels of Canadian government. Yet the political & administrative implications of aging have been neglected in the Canadian literature on gerontology. Focus here is on the aging process from the perspectives of political science & public administration. Particular attention is given to the political power & behavior of Canada's elderly & to political & administrative structures involved in policy formation & implementation in the field of aging. 1 Table, 28 References. HA.

title: Individualism, Civic Virtue, and Public Administration: The Implications of American Habits of the Heart
abstract: The increasing intensity of US individualism & the corresponding decline of a sense of community have been documented by Robert N. Bellah et al in Habits of the Heart: Individualism and Commitment in American Life, Berkeley: U of California Press, 1985). One striking implication of this trend is that public administration is becoming lost in the wilderness of individualism. The regime values of modern US politics dictate an emphasis on power & on the clash of individual interests, to the detriment of administrative effectiveness. However, public administration is in actuality founded on the other side of a constitutional duality of power & morals. Public administration relates directly to conceptions of classical republicanism, civic virtue, & cooperative effort. The true constitutional model of public administration derives from federalists & antifederalists alike in a system of modern politics & classical administration. This model is essential to the continuing viability & effectiveness of public administration in a representative democracy. 25 References. HA

title: The Significance of Ombudsman in Local Welfare: The Case of a Residential Community
abstract: Recently, it has been discussed again whether the progress of welfare society presents more advantages than disadvantages. At the same time, however, the question of reconstruction of the welfare state has to be raised. This paper, as a case study of a residential community, discusses the role & task of local administration in the change of welfare conditions. The public residential complex that houses the community is constructed as a model of welfare society & includes households that include the aged & the handicapped as members. Trouble occurred involving a handicapped member, which made her isolated in the community. An ombudsman institution of the local government played a part in settling the trouble. Through reviewing the pros & cons, this paper examines the function of the system, clarifying the roles asked of the administration in the development of welfare society, & discusses the sociological task accompanying such issues. 35 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Balance & Administrational Law
abstract: The development of politics, economics & culture in modern society have effectively controlled administrative domineering so as to ensure the people's rights. Social development should be with enlarging administrative power & binding people's rights. For suiting the needs of the social development, modern administrative law in all the countries of the world to varying degrees have leaped across the laws of management & power-controlled. The law of balance step by step has become the key tide of world administrative laws. The administrative law in China naturally is one of laws of balance. So the administrative law in China should not only be controlled but be ensured; the people's right is not only be ensured but be bond. The administrative law & people's right should be bond each other & also balanced each other. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Organizational Contradictions in Public Bureaucracies: Toward a Marxian Theory of Organizations
abstract: A Marxist alternative to organizational theory as now constituted is outlined. The concepts of 'productive forces' & 'SR of production' can be applied to such conflicts as those between organizing activity & organizational structures, manifested in conflicts between organizational control structures & new forms of work organization. A further application could be to recognition of the contradictions among such dimensions as labor power, skills, & knowledge; complexity of task structure; technology; DofL; control of labor through cost accounting & hierarchy; & organization of labor in various forms. Organizational contradictions are described for work organizations in general, & for public service bureaucracies & law courts in particular. Administrative & technical strategies for increasing juridicial efficiency, for example, come in conflict with the struggle of the judicial elite to maintain its authority. This analysis illustrates the Marxist method in general. Modified HA.

title: The Emergence of "Situated Role" in a Bureaucratic Setting: Role Reduction and the Limits of Social Reform
abstract: The relation between formally stated roles & actual practices in a federal German agency concerned with vocational counseling is analyzed through ratings of jobs, interviews, & classifications of activities as frequent/infrequent & desirable/undesirable, by 50 workers in one state. Activities formally required can be classed in concentric sets: (1) important; (2) actual, including important & frequent; (3) individual, including actual & desired; & (4) formal, including individual & ignored. The proportion of the formal set excluded from actual activities is taken to measure role reduction. More than 60% of activities were so excluded. Analysis of interviews reveals a predominant concern with bureaucratic role aspects (71%) with some concern for professional role aspects (29%). Concern for bureaucratic aspects may serve to reduce the cognitive dissonance following from not carrying out the formally legislated role. 1 Figure, 5 Tables. Modified HA.

title: REFLECTIONS ON BUREAUCRATIC CORRUPTION
