title: The Politics of Labeling Organizational Problems: An Analysis of the Challenger Case
abstract: Situations within organizations become problems through a process of construction determined by organizational & social filters, two dimensions of which include: (1) bureaucratic filter labeling the situation from operational to strategic; & (2) the scope filter labeling the situation from routine to exceptional. These two dimensions are independent, but together they provide a framework that can be used to represent the dynamics of escalating & deescalating competing interests. The framework is used to analyze the dynamics of the Challenger space shuttle disaster. 9 Figures, 13 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: "Whose Needs Are Being Served?" Quantitative Metrics and the Reshaping of Social Services
abstract: In this article in the forum on Quantitative Indicators, the author questions the hegemony of statistical data as the basis for Canadian political, social, & economic decision-making to argue that current management models are paving the way for reliance on low-wage, temporary, & unpaid workers. A discussion of the management/worker/client dynamic in care work contextualizes a critical examination of the New Public Management (NPM) & other performance based management models that advance the priorities of budget-cutting & pro-market rationality, decrease client care & access. The perverse incentive to increase efficiency in public & nonprofit services is antithetical to increased profit is reflected in worker resistance to the NPM, & the complexities of the conflicting power structures described by Abu-Lughod. The author concludes that quantitative metrics in the social services expand bureaucracy & contribute the standardization of work, & the deskilling of the workforce. References. J. Harwell

title: Bureaucracy and Contemporary Society
abstract: The development of bur'cy is the necessary consequence of the increasing powers of the contemporary state, which is itself the result of the needs of the econ order. This bur'cy is, by its very nature, composed of a portion of the bourgeoisie, though it does not always remain connected with this class, & tends to become independent, & sometimes even becoming associated with the Wc. As a general rule, the bur'cy wields the power of a state which is alienated from society. However, state bur'cies are not the only kind of bur'cies. There are business bur'cies, & even bur'cies of unions. In every such instance, the bur'cy does not represent any particular class, but instead represents a group that enjoys a relatively great degree of independence. The only way of preventing the bur'zation of the socialist state is by making the withering away of the state a reality. Tr by J. A. Broussard from IPSA.

title: Professionals of Policies for Fighting Unemployment in France: The construction and de-construction of professionalism
abstract: The increase in unemployment that occurred in France at the end of the 1970s is one aspect that has favoured the creation of jobs specializing in the field of social welfare for the unemployed. This paper focuses on the analysis of the professional group of advisers specializing in job seeking. The first section traces the circumstances of the emergence of such a group and explains the heterogeneity of these advisers who seem, nevertheless, to have developed a specific common expertise and the same interpretation of their professionalism. In the second part, the activity of these professionals is situated in the larger framework of unemployed policies which result from a combination of international, European and national influences. The study of recent changes to unemployment policies reveals the effects of the 'macro' on the 'micro' level. In the third section, it is explained that new measures of social welfare for the unemployed tend to challenge the moral and deontological principles of these advisers whose professional identity and professionalism are challenged. These challenges to their identities are due to the intensification of the follow-up of the unemployed and to the application of bureaucratic, monitoring and measurement techniques and logic to assess the efficiency of the tools for promoting a quick return to work. Adapted from the source document.

title: THE CIVIL SERVICE OF THE ANCIENT WORLD
abstract: A study of the civil services of 3 ancient states: Egypt, Athens, & Rome. Those of Egypt & Rome had many common elements: a hierarchical form of org, full-time professional staffs, soc stratification of the service, clearly marked paths of promotion, & relative security of tenure. Both, moreover, finally became oppressive & burdensome to the people. Scarcely any of these elements were present in the civil service of 5th cent Athens. Instead there were amateur boards, selection by lot, rotation in office, & an almost complete absence of professional staffs. Athenians valued responsiveness in gov more highly than efficiency, & under their conditions had, in truth, no great need for gov'al efficiency. The Athenian system, however, would have been wholly inadequate for Egypt & Rome. AA-IPSA.

title: Ethics and the Public Administrator
abstract: An overview & analysis of the practical problems of developing & implementing a code of ethics for public administrators, addressing three key issues: (1) What are public ethics & where do they come from? (2) What are the central ethical issues facing public administrators? & (3) Are there practical tools & guidelines to assist public servants to be both ethical & effective public managers? A plea is made for consideration of ethical issues, & five general ethical principles for public administrators are presented. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bringing Power Back In: Collective and Distributive Forms of Power in Public Participation
abstract: Much public participation research is built on the assumption that participatory arrangements empower citizens and disrupt existing power structures. This article challenges that claim. Drawing on one participatory venue considered most likely to empower citizens in Basel, Switzerland, the study shows that meaningful collective power has been conferred to citizens. However, resourceful and organisationally privileged actors have influenced the impact of citizen's demands on public decision-making in significant ways. The study concludes that the production and implementation of collective power deriving from citizens depends on distributive power sources residing in governments and bureaucracies. As a result, participatory arrangements that aim to direct state action have to conform to some extent to the rules and structures underlying ordinary policy-making. The case study highlights the intertwined relationship of the 'power to' and the 'power over' and shows how the interplay between these two forms of power places conditions on the empowering potential of participatory arrangements. Adapted from the source document.

title: MECHANISMS OF DISABILITY DISCRIMINATION IN LARGE BUREAUCRATIC ORGANIZATIONS: Ascriptive Inequalities in the Workplace
authors: Robert, Pamela M; Harlan, Sharon L
abstract: Studies of workplace discrimination have typically focused on empirically unobservable motives to explain ascriptive inequalities associated with class, gender, and race. Such studies usually have overlooked disability as an ascriptive status, and have offered little systematic research on the central question of this study: How, through what mechanisms, does disability discrimination operate in large, bureaucratic organizations? The in-depth personal interviews upon which this study is based reveal that interpersonal mechanisms of discrimination manifest as blatant and subtle acts of marginalization, fictionalization, and harassment. However, such interpersonal acts of discrimination would likely be less frequent or less consequential if not for the organizational mechanisms of tolerance and encouragement. The authors conclude that one of the central promises of the Americans with Disabilities Act, full inclusion and participation of people with disabilities in the workplace, is unlikely to be realized without renewed pressure for legislation that explicitly specifies the nature and extent of work organizations' responsibilities for creating a nonhostile environment and the consequences of not doing so. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Formal and Rational Authority. Some Notes, Hypotheses and Applications
abstract: Parsons questioned the analytic precision of M. Weber's legal-rational type of authority in bur'tic org's. It is proposed that 2 separate types should be distinguished: rational & Legal (or formal) authority. The basis of legitimation for the first is the effective utility of the person in authority, ie his technical competence to perform. On the other hand, legal authority is invested in an individual on the basis of a normative or legal structure. Another diff between the 2 rests on the premise that formal authority derives from the org, whereas rational authority may find its source of legitimation outside the org. In the case of formal authority, the org defines the boundaries within which domination is exercised. For rational authority, the power utilized depends on the capability of the individual to accomplish effective action. Utilizing these 2 types of authority as dimensions, R. Dahrendorf's conflict model may be employed to predict the nature of the relationships between 2 authority figures. A typology of authority types may be derived. HA.

title: Bureaucracy in the Hospital: An Empirical Test of Hall's Theory in One Organizational Type
abstract: In a study of 6 general hospitals in the Netherlands, R. Hall's dimensional model of bureaucracy was tested for its applicability within one type of organization. A pilot study with a group of 99 staff nurses generated a reliable version of the original questionnaire, translated & adapted to hospital organization. Individual analysis showed that the dimensional model was only partly represented by the facts & the 6 dimensions were not found to be independent. In the main study, only 5 dimensions, corresponding to 32 items, were kept. Nurses (number of cases = 442) representing 31 departments in 6 hospitals were interviewed. Of the respondents, 50 to 60% were students. Data were analyzed at the group level. Results show that the dimensions of hierarchy of authority, interpersonality, & rules/procedures are reliably measurable. Again, independence was not found. It is suggested that within this type of organization, bureaucracy might better be handled as a unit concept. The scale is judged valid to an acceptable degree. Before firm conclusions about the applicability of the dimensional model can be drawn, further research within other homogeneous groups of organizations will be needed. 7 Tables. Modified HA.

title: How Neopatrimonialism Affects Tax Administration: a comparative study of three world regions
authors: Von Soest, Christian; Bechle, Karsten; Korte, Nina
abstract: Neopatrimonialism is a concept that has predominately been applied to describe governance in sub-Saharan Africa. Recently, however, it has also been used to describe governance in states from other world regions. However, scholars have rarely attempted systematically to compare neopatrimonial rule in different regional settings. This paper aims to narrow this gap by examining the effect of neopatrimonialism on the tax administration as a core state function in six countries from three different world regions: Argentina, Venezuela, Indonesia, the Philippines, Kenya and Zambia. We conclude that neopatrimonialism is a valuable concept for comparative area studies with the potential to foster dialogue on the 'state in operation' across the regional divide. Nevertheless, several indicators are more valid for some world regions than for others. We find that there is no systematic relationship between neopatrimonial trajectories and the strength of tax administration. Individual actor decisions influence the outcomes of neopatrimonialism substantially. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Toward Efficient Social Management. Some Key Questions
abstract: Analyzes "social management" & its meaning, & explores some of its main problems. Its principal lineaments are summarized, drawing attention to the need of its having priority in Latin America. Adapted from the source document.

title: The First Reorganisation of the CPSU Central Committee Apparat under Perestroika
abstract: Discusses the first reorganization of the Soviet Communist Party's (CPSU's) Central Committee apparat under General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika reforms. Although Gorbachev's agenda mandated the creation of Central Committee commissions, the demolition of economic branch departments, & the reduction of the apparat workforce, it is noted that most government bureaucrats & released apparat officials gained new positions. The reformed Central Committee apparat was instructed to relinquish decision-making & policy implementation functions & commence developing policy & political strategies to handle the impending social, economic, & political crises facing the USSR; despite the dismantling of the economic, cultural, & ideological spheres, it is contended that the military & industrial spheres maintained a vast infrastructure after reorganization. It is concluded that apparat reorganization produced a hostile atmosphere, leading to a more contentious succeeding reorganization effort. 8 Tables. J. W. Parker

title: Japanese Bureaucracy in Transition: Regulating Deregulation
abstract: The article draws attention to the implications for the Japanese national bureaucracy of the current economic crisis of the country & of its possible passage, after having been characterized as a developmental state, to a new regulatory state. This passage is best epitomized by the liberalization & deregulation policies recently adopted. In this context the questions examined are whether the bureaucracy will accept being the sacrificial scapegoat & how this could possibly take place. The argument advanced is that the bureaucracy is probably in the best position to control its own demise which means that in so doing it may well simply become its own successor. The most effective way it has to do so, is to regulate the process of deregulation under way. Further attention is then addressed to the Three-year Program for Regulatory Reform & to a number of specific deregulation measures. Although some major changes introduced or being advocated in the Japanese civil service may deeply affect the bureaucrats' status & influence, what emerges is that, so far, the role the bureaucracy has played in planning & carrying out deregulation has remained quite central. 39 References. [Copyright 2002 Sage Publications Ltd.]

title: Women in Public Administration in the Federal Republic of Germany
abstract: WOMEN IN THE LABOR FORCE IN WEST GERMANYSince the end of World War II, women have constituted over one-third of all employed persons in the West German labor force. Women still suffer numerous disadvantages in working life, and their position in the labor market is by no means secure. Women earn 34 percent less than men. Most female blue-collar workers (94 percent) are unskilled or semiskilled as opposed to only 42 percent of their male colleagues. More than half of all women presently work in only six occupations (office workers, retail clerks, health services, janitorial occupations, agricultural occupations, teachers). Of those women working in industry, commerce, and insurance, 54 percent had no sphere of decision-making or responsibility of their own on the job, as compared to only 15 percent of male employees in these areas. Finally, roughly one-third of all working women have part-time jobs (34 percent in 1983), and two-thirds of all working women report interrupting their employment for family reasons.For a complete reprint of this article contact Haworth Press by telephone (1-800-HAWORTH) or EMail (getinfo@haworthpressinc.com) Article copyright The Haworth Press, Inc.

title: Autarchy, Self-Government, Autonomy
abstract: 'Autarchy' is a good example of a concept that evolved from a juridical one to one that applies to institutions. Since the beginning of the 19th cent, the doctrine of Sebstverwaltung has emerged from Prussian reform movements. The development of European legal codes shows that admin'ive powers are developing independently of the State & even of local gov's; an evolution which is diff even from the Anglo-Saxon type of selfgov. Certain innovations in the new Italian constitution reveal more precisely the notion of 'autarchy'. These innovations consist of the creation of regions & the special emphasis placed on the body of legal codes. This constitution implies both a new type of participation of the citizens in administration of the society, & also a relative independence of the citizens from the State. This gov'al form is, therefore, diff from both Selbstverwaltung & autonomy. Tr by J. A. Broussard from IPSA.

title: The nation-state, identity management, and indigenous crafts: Constructing markets and opportunities in Northwest Costa Rica
abstract: What are the roles of international tourism and global markets in the economic development of indigenous communities producing traditional "authentic" handicrafts? To what extent do state economic and cultural-political interests intervene in the structuring of cottage-industry markets? Are opportunities to enter the global handicraft market limited to communities "blessed" with indigenous artisan traditions? To answer these questions, the article presents ethnographic and historical evidence from two Costa Rican communities comprising about 1,200 individuals. These communities produce ceramics representing the Chorotega tradition and generate most of their incomes from selling handicrafts. The article contributes to the sociology of markets by documenting the historical contingencies and cultural understandings that facilitate and constrain opportunities in the global economy. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: A Defense of Professionalism: A Response to Fusco and Baizerman
abstract: Fusco and Baizerman (2013) criticized professionalization efforts for assumptions about improved outcomes, 'reducing' youth work to skills, 'controlling behavior,' bureaucratization, depersonalized services, a neoliberal focus, removing practice wisdom, and a 'telos of ...scientifically based youth work' (p. 189). They do not provide evidence or arguments for these claims. Academics benefit from professionalization, and it is curious to oppose efforts to provide those benefits to others. We believe that they and their colleagues, in the same issue, have misread other authors on key ideas and present an incomplete and rather one-sided representation. They conflate professionalization and professionalism. They conflate the industrial aspects of professionalization with the ethical aspects. They have overestimated the potential harm of professionalization and underestimated the harm being done by uninformed youth work practices. They misinterpreted social history-and Aristotle. They have incompletely cited other writers about professionalization. Professionalization and professionalism are not guarantees of anything, but our critique of them needs to be coherent, consistent, and based on arguments and evidence. Adapted from the source document.

title: Coexisting principles and logics of elder care: Help to self-help and consumer-oriented service?
authors: Dahl, Hanne Marlene; Eskelinen, Leena; Hansen, Eigil Boll
abstract: Healthy and active ageing has become an ideal in Western societies. In the Nordic countries, this ideal has been supported through a policy of help to self-help in elder care since the 1980s. However, reforms inspired by New Public Management (NPM) have introduced a new policy principle of consumer-oriented service that stresses the wishes and priorities of older people. We have studied how these two principles are applied by care workers in Denmark. Is one principle or logic replacing the other, or do they coexist? Do they create tensions between professional knowledge and the autonomy of older people? Using neo-institutional theory and feminist care theory, we analysed the articulation of the two policy principles in interviews and their logics in observations in four local authorities. We conclude that help to self-help is the dominant principle, that it is deeply entrenched in the identity of the professional care worker and that it coexists with consumer-oriented service and without major tensions in the logics identified in their practices.

title: The Administration of Poverty: Lessons from the "Welfare Explosion" 1967-1973
authors: Ritti, R Richard; Hyman, Drew W
abstract: The public assistance caseload literally exploded during the late 1960s, a period of unprecedented economic prosperity & record low unemployment. The reasons for this anomaly are examined, using the Pennsylvania Dept of Public Welfare (DPW) as an example. The Pennsylvania (DPW) caseload is compared with Pennsylvania unemployment, & migration as well as DPW management, etc. Various popular explanations for the growth of the caseload were rejected, including "welfare cheating" & mismanagement. Instead, the rise in caseload was attributed to the redefinition of the "product" of the DPW, for 'poverty is not merely a condition of relative deprivation," but a socially determined status, defined formally & informally according to the era & the political environment. 3 Figures, Appendix. Modified HA.

title: UK African Policy in the Post-Cold War Era: From Realpolitik to Moralpolitik?
abstract: The end of the Cold War led Western states to review their policies towards Africa. Against this background, the British government under John Major stressed the need for'new thinking' while the Blair administration promised to give'a new priority' to Africa. This article examines how far Britain has in practice adapted its African policy to the challenges of the New World Order. It evaluates and explains the changes which have taken place, focusing on the'multilateralisation' of UK-African relations and on Britain's new-found willingness to intervene in African affairs. Finally, it looks at'ideological' differences between the Major government, which based its policy on realpolitik, and the Blair administration, which has adopted a'third way' stance on African policy. While these differences should not be overstated, they have marked an identifiable change in Britain's response to Africa's challenges.

title: The Family Support Act: Defining the Social Contract in New York
abstract: The Family Support Act of 1988 was to offer a new relationship between the state and the dependent poor, but underlying philosophical conflicts over the role of government and the individual threaten the program's success.  The administration of the program in New York State is profiled.

title: The Institutional Reaction to Child Mental Illness: Co-Deviant Labeling
abstract: The findings of a study of the bureaucratic processing of emotionally disturbed children are reported. Emphasized are the components of bureaucratic decision making & evaluation that determine the biographical documentation of clients constructed by mental hospital staff. The staff was primarily Coll-educated, 25 years old, with little formal training in clinical psychology or psychotherapy. The 17 children in the program were between the ages of 6 & 12 years & represented a range of behavior problems from character disorders to severe schizophrenia or psychosis. Data are based on a content analysis of staff-written clinical documents written about each of the 17 children. These documents included prepatient evaluations, inpatient evaluations, & final evaluations of the child's career in the institution. Bureaucratic practitioners of child psychotherapy engage in codeviant labeling: placing responsibility for the child's pathology on the parents & casting the parents into the role of copatients. Institutional evaluation ostensibly designed for the recipient of service -- the child -- is extended to the child's parents, most often without their knowledge. Copatient labeling is shown to affirm the ideological assumptions of institutional staff. Modified HA.

title: LOCAL BUREAUCRACY IN THE SOUTH AS A SOCIAL GROUP
abstract: Communal admin'ors are studied as a socio-professional group, employed by the public, within a particular admin'ive structure, at a given hierarchical level, in the south of Italy. Data from an empirical res project conducted via questionaires & interviews among 261 secretary-generals, head engineers, & comptrollers, employed by local community administration's in the south are presented. The study was carried out at a moment when the communities examined faced a financial deficit. The typical careers of the 3 types of admin'ors are described & related to the ED & industr development of the south & the problems connected with it. Demographic & econ data on the communities they serve are presented & data on birth place, employment, age, class background, paternal occup's, educ, att's, & experience are supplied in 17 tables. The admin'ors' satisfaction & dissatisfaction with their offices, their opinions re the most urgent problems of the local community, re factors which contributed to their admin'ive careers, & their ideas on what constitutes an ideal local public functionary, were also analyzed. The bur'tic-pol'al conflict, expressed in terms of `technicians or technocrats,' is discussed. It is concluded that the authoritarian tendencies of the functionary are reconfirmed by the value & prestige attributed to local authority. Authoritarianism was not found to be r'ed to any particular pol'al ideology. However, the majority of admin'ors believed in state intervention into the economy. Asked to identify the most important needs of the region, many simply answered, 'modernization.' The position of the local admin'or was found ambiguous: he maintains his power through traditional authoritarianism, but carries out the role of modernizer. M. Maxfield.

title: Justice, Inequality, and the Market: Soviet Sociology in the Transition to Capitalism
abstract: This essay examines the role played by Soviet sociology in the USSR's transition to capitalism. It analyzes the discipline's contribution to the critique of Soviet socio-economic life during the 1980s, identifying the emergence of two divergent viewpoints within Soviet sociology over the relationship between inequality, the market, and the goals of a socialist society. The essay explores how these viewpoints intersected with the implementation of economic reforms by the Gorbachev regime, arguing that the dominant forces within Soviet sociology ultimately helped the party-state bureaucracy craft the legitimizing ideology of perestroika by insisting that growing social inequality and market-based mechanisms of distribution were the very embodiment of socialism. After enduring a politically fraught and semi-pariah existence for much of its history, Soviet sociology enjoyed a belle epoque as it helped the ruling elite navigate the transition to capitalism. [Reprinted by permission; copyright Sage Publications Inc.]

title: Migrations, sovereignty, social rights: Protecting and expelling foreigners in Europe since the early 19th century
abstract: The late nineteenth century in Europe saw less the apparition of state management of migrations than a change of system. The "protection of national labor" through identification techniques and border control came to replace the older regime of ex post facto regulation based on the notions of usefulness and subsidiarity (foreigners could be expelled if destitute and ineligible for local welfare). In reaction to this new institutional xenophobia, social reformers, soon helped by the International Labour Office, pushed for bilateral treaties and international conventions guaranteeing migrants similar rights (for unemployment, old-age pensions, labour protections, and so on) as nationals. These transnational negotiations helped the emergence of the welfare state; they also put in a new perspective the practice of state sovereignty in an area where the Treaty of Gotha of 1851 is still regularly invoked to manage refugee flows. Adapted from the source document.

title: Certain Sociological Problems Connected with Western European Integration
abstract: The process of integration taking place in western Europe in the form of the Common Market gives rise to certain questions regarding the problems which might arise from the formation of an international bureaucracy. The nature of the goals involved is an important factor in any such integration problem, since each member's desire to cooperate in the formation of joint policies is directly proportional to the degree to which common & individual interests will be upgraded. The success of the integration process is dependent on the ability of the members to shift their respective economic & political viewpoints to a new central base, & to alter their systems of values. The simple conformity of one national value system to another does not constitute social integration. Modified HA.

title: The Political Technologies of Caste: Manufacturing a Caste Certificate in a Mumbai Slum
abstract: This paper describes the political technologies of a caste certificate regularly employed by a Denotified Tribe, the Kunchikorves, in the Mumbai slum of Dharavi. The author demonstrates how the Kunchikorves mobilise kin and affine relations and engage with different organs of the state in an effort to authenticate their caste status. These ‘caste certificates’ are needed to make use of reservations policies to get government jobs and higher education. Municipal jobs and promotions are desirable as the basis for secure employment and upward mobility. Describing the circuitous methods by which the Kunchikorves obtain such authenticating documents, this paper notes that caste identity, while not hinging on notions of purity or pollution, is still an important vehicle for collective identification in contemporary India. The post-colonial state can be said to have extended and elaborated the colonial state's enumerating and objectifying imperatives when it comes to group identity. Groups such as the Kunchikorves are complicit in these objectifying measures, and actively seek out authenticating proofs of an identity that was originally pejorative, arbitrary and imposed. This paper argues that the Kunchikorves’ manufacturing of caste certificates secures them a job, while at the same time bequeathing them a caste categorisation necessarily mediated by processes of bureaucratic authentication.

title: Employees with Caregiving Responsibilities: The Example of Two Employers in Switzerland
authors: Radvanszky, Andrea; Craviolini, Julie; Bischofberger, Iren
abstract: In the future, more persons in the workforce will provide care and assistance to a family member while being employed. Little is known about this group in Switzerland. Comprehensive research has to be conducted on the phenomenon of the reconciliation and the interrelation of pertinent indicators. This paper describes a multivariate analysis of factors influencing the commitment and extent of family care, based on two surveys among employees in a public administration and a private company. Age, gender and wage level are relevant factors for the commitment to care, while characteristics of specific care situations correlate with the provided extent of care. Also, divergences between the two employers illustrate the effect of structural variables, allowing a closer insight into measures supporting reconciliation between work and care.

title: The Structure of Betrayal: Trade Union Bureaucracy and Public Sector Struggles in British Columbia
abstract: After the Liberal Party won a large majority of seats in British Columbia's legislature in 2001, it quickly moved the province into a program of financial retrenchment, making deep cuts in both business & personal income taxes. This action resulted in massive public sector cutbacks within months, especially in health care. In Jan 2002, the provincial government broke the established collective agreements with health sector workers & initiated plans to contract out some services. The workers went on strike. In post-strike negotiations, the Hospital Employees' Union (HEU) proved ineffective in protecting its members' jobs & wages. HEU officials claimed that they had been forced to make "wise but difficult decisions." Activist members contended that the HEU was committed to "social democratic electoralism." David Camfield, in a Labourarticle, blamed the HEU's failure on the character of "labor officialdom"; the union cared more about protecting its institutions than its members. The author draws on an Open Marxist perspective to consider these three narratives & demonstrates how they each "disarticulate structure from struggle, reifying class antagonism under ossified institutions that in some way transcend & determine the shape of struggle.". S. Stanton

title: "A Shockingly Premature Death." The Passing of Pope John Paul I and Its Interpretations in the Media
abstract: In the morning of 29 September 1978 John Paul I was discovered dead. One of the shortest pontificates in history ended after 33 days. The Vatican announced that the 65-year-old pope died of a heart attack according to God's unfathomable providence. The sudden papal death gained worldwide media attention. Two issues were extensively discussed in the press: Firstly, what meaning might lie in the premature death that ended the pontificate after such a short time. Secondly, there was speculation on possible alternative explanations for the pontiff's lonely end, because the official cause of death was promptly questioned by the newspapers. In their opinion the stress of the office and the strains of the curial bureaucracy decisively weakened the pope's fragile health. Journalists reckoned that he left a remarkable legacy: His unique personality was reflected in the extraordinary circumstances of his death. These characteristics would determine the election of his successor. Adapted from the source document.

title: Brokering Power and Property in China's Townships
abstract: This paper concerns the process of power at the periphery of state bureaucracy with a focus on township governments & their land development projects in the last two decades. I argue that townships at the bottom of the state bureaucracy operate like power brokers between the state & the village. When dealing with the formal party-state system above them, the township's delegated power is highly uncertain. Townships choose to maneuver in the unspecified legal & administrative zone to bypass the scrutiny of the supervising government. When it comes to the village below them, the township's power is under-defined, & therefore can be stretched to intensify & centralize the grips over village resources & land. In both cases, township officials strategize to maximize their control of village land & profit from the booming land-lease market in China's fast industrializing & urbanizing areas. Townships' land deals reflect the general power process of decentralization. Their brokerage of power corresponds directly with that of property rights in post-reform China. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: THE PROBLEM OF BUREAUCRACY IN MODERN AMERICAN SOCIOLOGY
authors: Dmitriev, V A; Orlov, V A; Yakovlev, V N
abstract: Some conceptions of US sociol'ts re the soc phenomenon of bur'cy are examined & some methodological mistakes which they are seen to have made in the study of bur'cy are pointed out from a Leninist-Marxist point of view. Particular reference is made to R. K. Merton, SOCIAL THEORY AND SOCIAL STRUCTURE (see SA 6037), P. M. Blau, BUREAUCRACY IN MODERN SOCIETY (see SA 5565), Paul E. Matt, THE ORGANI- ZATION OF SOCIETY (see SA 0202/B7501), D. Martindale, IN- STITUTIONS, ORGANIZATIONS AND MASS SOCIETY, Boston, Mass, 1966; D. Bell, THE END OF IDEOLOGY (see SA A1008), & others. It is observed that the bourgeois soc sci'ts confine themselves to the description of bur'tic mechanisms & their soc consequences, although the nature of bur'cy is embodied in the structure of capitalist society. The influence of burley on personality, according to the findings of the above mentioned US sociol'ts, is analyzed in detail. Modified HA.

title: Policy Outputs and Bureaucracy: The Roles of Need, Demand, and Agency Structure
abstract: The effect of bureaucratic structure on policy adoption is investigated relative to noise abatement policies of all publicly owned air carrier airports in the US. Data were gathered through a 1972 survey involving questionnaires sent to airport managers or chief executives (N = 139 Rs). A study of need & demand variables reveals that noise abatement policies are shaped by public demand & community needs. Internal, administrative, & executive characteristics of the policy-making unit, controlling for the need/demand variable, indicate that the presence of a legal staff & expenditure autonomy are the only structural factors facilitating policy outputs at local airports. These factors, however, are considered as falling under the rubric of need & demand. Findings indicate that the structure of the bureaucracy has little effect on policy outputs, after controlling for the impact of community needs & political demands. 3 Tables, 34 References. D. Graves.

title: Comment on Price's "The Study of Organizational Effectiveness"
abstract: 2 comments on J. L. Price. (See SA 0624/F9258). (1) Leland C. McCormick charges Price with neglecting several important issues, ie, those of comparison, validity, & triangulation. Measuring effectiveness by asking org'al members to rate themselves on a scale of effectiveness is considered inadequate if R's are not asked on what they are basing their judgments of effectiveness. Moreover, while major decision-makers can offer valuable information about org'al goals members from all levels of the org should be queried concerning the goals because some goals derive from the day-to-day encounters of these members. These comments are not intended as a criticism of the goal-attainment model or of efforts to measure org'al effectiveness. (2) J. Kenneth Benson (U of Missouri, Columbia), also points out problems with the goal approach in measuring & conceptualizing org'al effectiveness. Price's proposed measure of effectiveness is seen as premised upon a faulty conception of org'al phenomena. It assumes (a) that there is uniformity in the meanings R's attach to words designating core activities like "teaching" & "nursing care," (3) that the R has information & computational skills permitting him to synthesize the diverse activities in the org under the rubric of "teaching" or "nursing," & (4) that there is normative consensus in the org re what constitutes a quality performance of designated tasks. James L. Price REPLY TO McCORMICK AND BENSON, asserts that he does deal with the question of validity & rejects McCormick's suggestion that org'al effectiveness should be measured as based on the goals of the total membership. Goals are determined by the individuals who allocate org'al resources. Benson's criticisms are also rejected. M. Maxfield.

title: Financially and Socially Weak Citizens and Their Encounter with the Legal System
abstract: Between the legislation for & the implementation of laws, much can occur, often resulting in a significant change in goals-or `goal warp'. Programs to help the poor in the US often provide little real help to those who need it. Part of the problem lies in that the `top' of the system has no real notion of what is going on at the `base'. A common misconception is the belief that the poor are not willing to work & to better their condition. Much research is needed to determine what the needs of the socially weak citizen are, & how those needs could best be met. The situation is complicated by the fact that administrators do not always correctly understand the goal message, again leading to goal warp. It may be possible to avoid some of these mistakes by reviewing past programs & determining why some were successful & others were not. Further improvements might be made by soliciting client input into the process, although the exact nature of that input must still be more closely delineated. Various criteria might be used to evaluate such programs, such as feasibility, net achievement, duration, coordination, satisfaction of the client, & others. P. Tiersma.

title: Current publications abstracts -- The AIDS Bureaucracy: Why Society Failed to Meet the AIDS Crisis and How We Might Improve Our Response by Sandra Panem
abstract: Review.

title: The Need for a System of Evaluation in Public Administration
abstract: In a discussion of evaluative systems for policies in Norwegian public administration, in particular government intitiatives in the 1980s, the importance of the efficient organization of efforts to evaluate within the govermental ministry is emphasized. Three initiatives directed at producing information about the results of policies & programs are discussed: the 1982 resource productivity campaign, the plan of action for user-minded public services, & governmental budgetary systems reform. Evaluation-related problems range from disagreement on methods & procedures to acceptance of & compliance with results. 4 References. J. Sadler

title: In defence of amateurism--On not professionalizing ethnic and racial studies
abstract: This piece suggests that the field of ethnic and racial studies is too diverse in theoretical and methodological approach and subject of study to constitute its own discipline. Instead, ethnic and racial studies remains a loosely defined space of interdisciplinary exchange. There is a sense of community among researchers in this field, but teaching continues to be organized to meet the imperatives of different home disciplines. This article argues that in these times of increasing bureaucracy, standardization and managerial intrusion into academic life, there is a positive benefit in retaining a relatively open space of inquiry where we can consider the construction of contemporary social boundaries. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Community Action against Poverty: A Study in Emergent Conflict
abstract: The federal antipoverty programs instituted in the early 1960s have had the unexpected consequence of generating conflict over the control of federally supported local programs. This is illustrated by data gathered in interviews with 25 persons directly associated with the Economic Opportunity Council (EOC) of Champaign County, Ill, conducted in spring of 1971. The three major groups involved in administration of the EOC were the governmental bodies, local community agencies & organizations, & the poor themselves. The local governments, represented principally by the County Board of Supervisors, found the program unsatisfactory, since they were accustomed to regarding aid for the poor as charity, which was the personal responsibility of each township supervisor; they wanted a program run with a low budget & professional management. The organizational representatives saw a need for administrative effectiveness, which the hiring of the poor interfered with, but also saw the supervisors as unable to deal with the poor. The representatives of the poor underwent constant turnover, & whether they were actually representative of the poor is uncertain; they were most concerned with building a political power base in the program for the poor. A series of conflicts led the County Board of Supervisors as a whole to drop sponsorship of the EOC. The EOC appears to have served, while it lasted, as a training ground for leadership & as an arena for the expression of issues of institutionalized power. W. H. Stoddard

title: Seeking salvation: Moral economies and management at the Morozov mills, 1885-1905
abstract: Moscow's most famous textile dynasty, the Old Believer Morozovs, pioneered not only new technology, but also ways of managing their peasant-workers. This article focuses on the distinctive approaches of the two rival families who owned neighbouring factories: the Savva Morozov Company and the Vikula Morozov Company. In these factories the Morozov families desired to create a 'moral community' using the spiritual discipline of the Old Believer faith to bond workers and management to productive goals. But their peasant-workers also brought to the factories their own 'moral economy' assumptions about the duties and obligations of worker and master. The article visits three sites where the developing management practices of these two competing factories are expressed: clan rivalry and mentalities; labour-management conflict; and the battle between bureaucracy and factory over contested taxes. The identities of the rival families - one pious and private, the other publicly political - symbolize their different approaches. Nevertheless, it is their conflicts with labour and the tsarist bureaucracy which most vividly illustrate the significant role of moral economies in management practice. Moral economies and the Old Believer experience of the Morozovs provide keys to understanding the 'special worlds' of their factories and the relationships between management, labour and bureaucracy. Our salvation is in work. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Organizational Boundaries and Organizational Affiliates
abstract: Previous work on org's & inter-org'al relations has not dealt in sufficient depth with the problem of defining org'al boundaries. Simple appeals to a "roster of members or employees," when examined in detail, prove inadequate to capture the naturllly occurring variety of org'al affiliates & the problems they pose for defining an org's boundaries. "Analytical members" of an org are defined here as org'al goal-directed service-producing affiliates who share in the group identity & COMM network to some degree. Several other kinds of "non-service" affiliates of an org are also delineated: contributors, suppliers, users & various types of constraint affiliates, (official members, ultimate econ claimants, superordinate controllers, external cooperators). Org'al boundaries are then defined as the analytical distinction between an org's analytical members & all other persons & groups. Some implications for future res are suggested. AA.

title: Race, gender, and bureaucracy: Civil War army nurses and the Pension Bureau
abstract: When legislation was passed to give pensions to army nurses who served in the Civil War, it favored middle-class white women and not the black and working-class women who were more likely to need it.  The gender and racial discrimination to which female hospital workers were vulnerable both during their service and when trying to get pensions is examined.

title: Mine, Yours or Theirs? Accountability in the New NHS
abstract: Assesses recent changes in the British National Health Service (NHS) to ascertain whether they have made this once popular public service more accountable to its users & less bureaucratic, in an attempt by the Conservative government to orient the NHS to market incentives. A serious definitional problem exists in determining whether these changes have made the NHS more accountable, because the "accountable" can be taken to mean a concentration on the relationship between producers & consumers, & faithfulness to certain moral principles. This ambiguity has caused disparity in perceptions of the public & of management workers. The public perceives the changes as putting management into the hands of persons unresponsive to their needs; but this sentiment conflicts with studies suggesting that management workers consider themselves to be altruistic & committed to the values of voluntary work. Recommendations for improving the disparity between the public's & management's perception are discussed. 26 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: American Bureaucracy in a Changing Political Setting
abstract: Three major changes in US political culture led to the diminishing influence of bureaucrats in designing & implementing national policy: (1) the divided nature of government, with a Republican presidency & Democratic Congress; (2) the ascending role of political movements & interest lobbies in US politics; & (3) the new nonincremental style of decision making. It is suggested that bureaucracy has an important role to play in the policy process. Its capacity to learn from past mistakes & to conceive effective solutions is emphasized & contrasted with the political sphere's tendency to execute quick fixes. Bureaucracy also has an important role in conserving professional norms, & in functioning as an early-warning system. 31 References. I. Shagrir

title: Educational Policies and Systems Evaluation
abstract: After a short description of the history of school system evaluation, the author examines the main questions related to the implementation of the educational policies evaluation: a) the change of attitude needed inside the public administration as a consequence of the use of evaluation; b) the relationship between evaluators & policy makers; c) the goals of school system evaluation; d) the targets of evaluation; e) the relationship between external ed internal evaluation: f) the use of indicators. Finally it is presented the model followed by the school system evaluation Committee, which operates in the Trento region since 1992. The Committee has introduced gradually the idea of evaluation, beginning with the evaluation of the general system, then introducing schools self evaluation (which is now operated by almost all the Trento schools) to arrive finally to put forward the idea of school external evaluation. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: New Spaces for the Local Welfare State? The Case of General Relief in Los Angeles County
authors: DeVerteuil, Geoffrey; Lee, Woobae; Wolch, Jennifer
abstract: The current "hollowing out" & devolution of the national welfare state produces new spaces for the local welfare state, theoretically allowing more leeway to dismantle, privatize, further devolve, or even experiment with new local bureaucratic structures. At the same time, national devolution places greater burdens on local resources. Over the past twenty years, a series of theoretical frameworks have been proposed to understand local welfare strategies under these concomitant opportunities & pressures, including street-level bureaucracy, shadow, & workfare states. Despite the usefulness of these frameworks, they have rarely been applied to the long-term evolution of specific local programs. A particularly glaring omission is General Assistance, which constitutes a major component of many local welfare states. To address this gap, we examine the past 20 years of General Relief (GR) policies in Los Angeles County. GR is a locally funded mandatory program that provides aid of last resort for indigent individuals. In the face of exploding demand & rising expenditures, & unable to directly eliminate the program, the County employed a variety of strategies designed to ration services & depress demand. In the 1980s, these strategies were articulated through low-level & indirect bureaucratic disentitlements, including quality control & spatial consolidation. By the 1990s, the County took a more direct route, cutting benefits in 1993 & imposing time limits & workfare in 1997. Despite severe constraints, the evolution of GR strategies in Los Angeles County does suggest the emergence of genuinely new regulatory spaces, including a diminution of outlays, counterbalanced by the increasing micromanagement of clients & the materialization of a workfare & even shadow state. At present, the local welfare state in Los Angeles County combines the convolution of Franz Kafka with the misery of Charles Dickens. While our review goes some way in redressing the critical lack of local case studies, there remains a need to investigate instances of new local regulatory spaces, to understand in depth the engagement of various strategies, mechanisms, & even resistance. 2 Figures, 54 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Policing "Perversions": Depo-Provera and John Money's New Sexual Order
abstract: The use of the drug Depo-Provera (medroxyprogesterone acetate [MPA]) in the treatment of sexual minorities, such as sadomasochists, transvestites, sexually active children and teenagers, and adults sexually attracted to minors, is the latest development in a long tradition of dangerous and crude experimentation by psychiatrists and clinical psychologists with biodeterministic and reductionist views of human sexuality. Among them is clinical psychologist John Money, whose zealous advocacy of such treatments ignores or downplays critical issues of ethics, informed consent, and the side effects of the drug. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has failed to effectively regulate such uses of Depo-Provera. Public outcry, more stringent regulation, and a new acceptance of the rights of sexual minorities are necessary to forestall the imposition of a repressive, new sexual order.For a complete reprint of this article contact Haworth Press by telephone (1-800-HAWORTH) or EMAIL (getinfo@haworthpressinc.com). Article copyright The Haworth Press, Inc.

title: Becoming a Nonexpert and Other Strategies for Managing Fieldwork Dilemmas in the Criminal Justice System
abstract: In this article, the author presents three fieldwork strategies for managing role conflict in criminal justice settings. One of the most critical issues for ethnographers immersed in fieldwork is balancing the tension between the researcher and participant-observation roles. Ethnographers in criminal justice settings as well as other types of street-level bureaucracies are commonly confronted with dilemmas involving physical risk, highly sensitive data, marginalized clientele, and the exploitive use of power and domination by institutional gatekeepers. Researchers venturing into challenging fieldwork settings, such as criminal justice environments, must be highly attuned to the constraints and opportunities for collecting data. The author argues that these strategies can augment ethnographers' "data collection toolkit" to better address fieldwork problems. In addition, deploying these strategies can help to reveal unforeseen findings in the study.

title: Public-Sector Management Today: Advanced Differentiation and Early Institutionalization
abstract: Four central questions concerning a conceptually & politically turbulent & troubled area of inquiry & practice -- public sector management (PSM) -- are addressed: What is PSM? How has it been approached? What complicates PSM research? What are some immediate research priorities? Four major approaches to PSM are examined, & debate over its generic vs particularistic character is summarized. Problems with encompassing policy development & implementation within PSM concepts are reviewed, & methodological & theoretical research issues are identified. Focus is descriptive rather than prescriptive due to the current state of the field. 81 References. Modified HA

title: Urban crime trends and patterns in Ghana: The case of Accra
abstract: The study examined the broad crime trends and patterns, and the conditions under which crimes flourish, the crime incidence rates per 1,000 of population, and crime among the four police divisions of Accra, Ghana. Where crimes clustered the most and the times some crimes were committed were examined using the official police data. The study suggests that crime in Accra has been accentuated by rigid centralization of government bureaucracy, the nature of Ghana's economy, routine activities, lifestyles, and opportunities fostered by social change. Overall, the Accra Central Police Division recorded the highest volume of crimes, followed by the Nima, Kaneshie, and Kpeshie Divisions. The highest property offenses were recorded within twelve miles of the city center--the area most congested and heavily concentrated with socio-economic and routine activities. Calls for the adoption of situational crime prevention methods and strategies to reduce the incidence of crime in Accra have been made.

title: Kilombos of Brazil: Identity and land entitlement
abstract: As a result of the Afro-Brazilian social movement's pressure, Brazil's post dictatorship constitution, promulgated in 1988, included a provision granting land rights to the surviving kilombo communities that exist throughout the country. Although these communities were formed in many different ways, judicial interpretation of the constitutional provision has restricted the right to those deemed to be descended from groups that escaped or rebelled violently against enslavement. This interpretation violates the original intention of the provision and raises the issue of how to define the collective identity of Afro-Brazilian kilombo communities. Bureaucratic procedures designed to ensure proof of rebellion or escape, as well as interagency conflicts in land tenure administration, further complicate the implementation of the constitutional right. The 3rd World Conference Against Racism instigated political pressure to overcome these obstacles and interagency cooperation may herald positive changes in the future. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The grammar of colonial distinction. The organization of education staff member in French East Africa [1903 -- end of the 1930's]
abstract: This article examines the efforts undertaken by the colonial state to assign a clear-cut position in the colonial bureaucracy to the educated elite working for the administration, particularly elementary schoolteachers. The article reveals the problems involved in trying to fit African civil servants into colonial categories. As such, they formed a borderline group with uncertain contours & positions, a ferment of tensions that upset the definition of the colonial dualities of subject & citizen, native & European, colonized & colonizer. Adapted from the source document.

title: Globalization in Retreat: Capitalist Overstretch, Civil Society and the Crisis of the Globalist Project
abstract: Discusses the retreat of corporate-driven globalization to argue that the process of "reconstruction' takes place at two levels: the global, & the national/local. Reflection on personal experiences with multilateralism at World Bank, IMF, & World Trade Organization meetings describes the loss of legitimacy of key multilateral institutions that politically support corporate driven globalization. Further indicators of the crisis of the multilateral system of world economic governance identify the maintenance of national economies, & the fact that states still do matter. Six factors responsible for the stall of globalization indicate deep tensions in the global empire. Any alternative agenda to globalization must dis-empower centralized neoliberal bureaucracies at the global level, & move towards regulation & institutionalization of fair trade at the national or local levels. References. J. Harwell

title: Bureaucratic Rigidity Revisited
abstract: A review of the empirical research on rule rigidity in an attempt to determine whether rigid obedience to rules is an inevitable consequence of exposure to bureaucratic organizations. While no evidence is found to support the theory that mechanistic bureaucracy produces rote rule adherence, some evidence indicates that rule adherence is associated with a lack of education or formal responsibility, employment in the formal sector, employment in the public sector, & other factors that may contribute toward greater personal insecurity. Other evidence suggests that physical proximity & personal contact have greater impact on behavior than organizational rules & procedures, & that what rule rigidity exists may be tacit in internal organizational control struggles. 30 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Toward a Theory of the Public for Public Administration
abstract: Five social science perspectives on the public -- the pluralist, public choice, legislative, client, & citizen perspectives -- are used to build a general theory of the public in public administration. Such a theory must: (1) have its basis in the Constitution; (2) incorporate a notion of virtuous citizenship based on citizen understanding of moral philosophy, belief, individual moral responsibility, & civility: (3) develop & maintain systems & procedures responsive to collective & noncollective publics; & (4) be based on benevolence & love. In Some Tensions in the Notion of "The Public as Citizen": Rejoinder to Frederickson, Camilla Stivers (Evergreen State Coll, Olympia, Wash) identifies tensions & problems inherent in Frederickson's theory. 1 Table, 29 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Selling the Unemployed: The Performance of Bureaucracies, Firms and Non-Profits in the New Australian "Market" for Unemployment Assistance
abstract: Major changes to the organization of welfare programs indicate the emergence of a new welfare state (NWS) model which claims to put an end to the traditional "one size fits all" ideal of universality & standardization. The stated aim of such arrangements is to improve service for the client, reduce costs for the taxpayer, & lift the performance of the system as a whole. The Labour government reform of the Australian employment assistance system between 1994 & 1996, & the Coalition's first modifications of this scheme in 1997, provide a means to investigate the performance of a NWS system which uses private & public agencies to provide a basic, mandatory employment assistance service. Using verified data on the comparative performance of public, private, & nonprofit agencies & qualitative data on a study of Best Practice among high-performing agencies, the study shows that this system produces greater service variation than the previous universal service system. Overall, the system also does better in achieving employment & education outcomes with long-term unemployed clients. However, the study shows that such outcomes differ between different classes of client & between different types of service provider. In particular, outcomes are lower for the more disadvantaged, & are higher for those who have training programs available to support them. 6 Figures, 41 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Dysfunctions in Public Psychiatric Bureaucracies
abstract: Described are common dysfunctions in public psychiatric organizations according to the Weberian model of bureaucracy. Dysfunctions are divided into the categories of goal displacement, outside interference, unclear authority structure & hierarchy, & informal relations in the workplace. Emphasized are the bureacratic nature of public psychiatry & the need for mental health professionals to understand the dysfunctions of the organizations in which they work, including the impact of these dysfunctions on the provision of quality care. 32 References. HA

title: URBANIZATION AND GOVERNMENTAL ADMINISTRATION IN LOWER BUCKS COUNTY
abstract: Within M. Weber's and L. Wirth's conceptual frame of reference for urbanism it is hypothesized that, as a result of the introduction of industry and housing into Bucks County, Pa., centralization, increased regulation and control by gov. will gradually overcome the inertia of traditional beliefs in personal independence and small community autonomy. Analyzed are data of initial impact of urbanization due to rapid industrialization on the local governmental units of 18 minor civil divisions in Lower Bucks County: (1) Rate of pop. growth and development of large scale housing projects such as 'Levittown' and 'Fairless Hills.' (2) Development in school facilities, police protection, planning and control, and the pattern of increased governmental regulations. (3) The emerging pattern of governmental centralization and the 2 main status quo protecting forces: hard-headed self-interest of local citizens and officials, and a provincial sentiment tending to mistrust all 'big city' or 'large-scale' influence. It is concluded that, incipient urbanization has introduced problems in local gov. On the whole, government is playing a larger role in the life of each local community. Though the situation was fluid at time of study, a trend toward some form of consolidation of the local units was discernible. The eventual form consolidation will take is unpredictable, inevitably a balance between a so-called rational solution and conflicting local interests will be struck. M. R. Gunther.

title: The paradox of diversity: The construction of a multicultural Canada and "women of color"
abstract: The concept of diversity, as the central concept of the discourse of multiculturalism, has become common in Canadian politics and cultural life. This is so much the case that even the corporate sector has adapted its talk of profit to multiculturatism and diversity, while the Canadian government and public institutions have set up major administrative bureaucracies in their names.

title: Below Average. Only on Paper
abstract: The author declares that bureaucracy is capable of causing any good to turn into a harmful event. The following article analyzes education stages in Russia up to a current stage taking into consideration its painful attempts for breakthrough challenged by bureaucratic motives. The author lists a few statistics that reveal numbers of children not attending schools, among which he particularly lists children from low-income families, countryside scholars, and handicapped kids. Finally, the article provides a few facts from educational campaigns enforced/not enforced due to various parties' negligence in the government. It is peculiar to note that some parties, instead of raising hands or voting against, did not participate at all. Adapted from the source document.

title: Informed consent, anticipatory regulation and ethnographic practice
abstract: In this paper we examine the application of informed consent to ethnographic research in health care settings. We do not quarrel with either the principle of informed consent or its translation into the requirement that research should only be carried out with consenting participants. However, we do challenge the identification of informed consent with the particular set of bureaucratic practices of ethical review which currently operate in Canada, the US and elsewhere. We argue that these anticipatory regulatory regimes threaten the significant contribution of ethnographic research to the creation of more efficient, more effective, more equitable and more humane health care systems. Informed consent in ethnographic research is neither achievable nor demonstrable in the terms set by anticipatory regulatory regimes that take clinical research or biomedical experimentation as their paradigm cases. This is because of differences in the practices of ethnographic and biomedical research which we discuss. These include the extended periods of time ethnographers spend in the research setting, the emergent nature of ethnographic research focus and design, the nature and positioning of risk in ethnographic research, the power relationships between researchers and participants, and the public and semi-public nature of the settings normally studied. Anticipatory regulatory regimes are inimical to ethnographic research and risk undermining the contribution of systematic inquiry to understanding whether institutions do what they claim to do, fairly and civilly and with an appropriate mobilisation of resources. We do not suggest that we should simply ignore ethics or leave matters to the individual consciences of researchers. Rather, we need to develop and strengthen professional models of regulation which emphasise education, training and mutual accountability. We conclude the paper with a number of suggestions about how such professional models might be implemented. [Copyright 2007 Elsevier Ltd.]

title: PROFESSIONAL BUREAUCRACY AND THE LARGE WALL STREET LAW FIRMS
abstract: M. Weber thought that bur'cy, which has formal internal controls, was the most rational & effective way to run large scale org's. A. W. Gouldner developed Weber's 2 implied types of bur'cy in observing that there were 3 types: `Mock' (rules imposed from the outside & neither management nor labor agrees with them), `Representative' (formal norms which all groups in an org accept & follow), & 'Punishment- Centered' (rules formulated by either labor or management & enforced by one on the other). Examination of the soc structure of large law firms, which operate successfully with few formal internal controls, indicates additional factors affecting the functioning of bur'tic org's. Open interviewing was conducted with 170 attorneys from 19 of the 21 largest New York firms & with 34 attorneys from 3 firms of the same magnitude outside New York. When 101 members of the sample were asked to explain why their org worked even though it seemed to be loosely structured, 85.2% gave professional-org'al considerations as one of their answers; 47.5% specifically mentioned professional responsibility. This points to the function of formal (canons of professional ethics, rules of the courts) & informal (colleagual help, reluctance to talk about other lawyers, disputatious behavior without conflict) external professional controls, which is to provide guides for behavior & make it unnecessary for the firm's formal org to formulate its own regulations. The acceptance of these vocational norms probably starts with the decision to become a lawyer, is increased by entrance into law Sch, & is further boosted when practice is begun. These observations disclose a 'Professional' bur'cy, a 4th type or dimension which differs from Gouldner's models in that while these controls are external they are not Mock because lawyers agree with them, & while they are Representative they do not pass current everyday scrutiny but are accepted because of a long socialization process. The Punishment-Centered aspect is minor because rules are seldom violated. The large Wall Street law firms function effectively though they are loosely organized, in large part, because they accept these informal & formal external professional rules. This, in turn, has the effect of strengthening the idea that they are loosely organized, since those involved do not consider the outside rules as rules of their firm. The result of this complex is that management does not have to enforce as many rules, & lawyers working in what they consider a relatively rule-free environment feel that initiative, independence, & professional responsibility are being sponsored. Once isolated, `Professional' bur'cy may be used as a tool for further studies such as analysis to determine whether external occup'al rules exist for all occup's, & analysis of the implied statement that the greater the external control, the less the need for internal control. P. D. Montagna.

title: Social assistance in China and Sweden: how policy intentions are translated into local practices
authors: Lindqvist, Rafael; Tang, Jun; Li, Jing
abstract: This article compares social assistance policies in China and Sweden, with a special focus on the means of translating policy intentions into local practices. Unlike China, Sweden has laws regulating social assistance, which is intended to ensure a "reasonable standard of living." Though considered a legal right, assistance is Sweden is means-tested. While social assistance claims are dealt with by the welfare bureaucracy in Sweden, in China the process of application involves the input of cadres, administrative officials from different levels of government, and neighbours. The challenges facing Sweden are to find ways to cope with long-term social assistance and to help recipients find work. The challenges facing China are to establish a social assistance law and standardized management procedures, and to incorporate the resources of social work. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: BUREAUCRATIC POWER
abstract: The distinction between the pol'al & the admin'ive is difficult, due to functional interferences between these 2 notions & the subordination of administration to gov. It is undeniable, however, that a transfer of power from pol to administration is progressively operating. administration forms a State within the State, with its costumes & instit's & a `reason of admin' which doubles the `reason of State'. One finally comes to a distinction between constitutional (CONS'al) powers & extra-CONS'al or para-CONS'al powers. The definition of the respective spheres, & the admin'ive & pol'al responsibility, which permit contribution of some order in this evolution, are still insufficient. administration can thus, without risks, continue to acquire a rhythm, inertia & finality of its own, accenting its tendencies to self-conservation & expansion. It would be important to give a public statute to constitute a counterbalance to the functionary statute. tr fr IPSA by M. Farber.

title: The Perceived Inequity of Systems
abstract: A review of an eclectic literature suggests that systems are perceived to be inequitable by members & clients when systems function as special purpose tools, interacting subsystems, arbiters of meaning, regulators of behavior, mass producers, symbols, & amoral entities. Cognitive & motivational biases lead system clients to perceive of systems as less equitable than do system administrators. Perceived inequities result in unmet expectations, reactance & activism, increased resentment, reduced system legitimacy, & decreased initiative & trust. While it appears that perceived inequities are institutionalized in systems, informal subsystems, deinstitutionalization, & promotion of an organizational culture hold potential as remedies. Also, since it is the system's complexity & dynamism that engender the most inequities, a holistic process approach would be of value. 1 Table, 1 Figure, 117 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: United States -- Thinking about Political Corruption by Peter deLeon / Politics and Bureaucracy in the Modern Presidency: Careerists and Appointees in the Reagan Administration by Robert Maranto
abstract: Review.

title: Trust, Control and Post-Bureaucracy
abstract: This paper is a contribution to the analysis of intraorganizational trust. From a discussion of concepts of trust, we suggest that trust is something that is constructed for & by people in organizations, thereby producing some degree of predictability. Trust is a precarious social accomplishment enacted through the interplay of social or discursive structures, including those of work organizations, & individuated subjects. We argue that bureaucratic organizations effected this construction in such an efficient manner that it "disappeared" as an issue for organizational theorists, but that shifting organizational forms have reopened it. We suggest that the advent of corporate culturism in the 1980s offered one kind of reconfiguration of trust in organizations. However, subsequent extensions of organizational reform have undermined corporate culture as a way of constructing trust. These extensions, which, with some caveats, may be called postbureaucratic, have brought with them new potential bases for trust, & hence control, in organizations. We explore these in two ways. First, we discuss how various types of managerial languages & techniques have the capacity to provide a global "script" through which particular local contexts can be made sense of, & which allow possible subject positions & identities to be secured. Second, we develop this discussion with reference to two different kinds of employees whose work is in some senses postbureaucratic: accountants & consultants in Big Five firms, & temporary workers (temps) working through agencies to provide clerical & other services. In a conclusion, we comment on the durability of postbureaucratic modes of trust. 74 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Cultures of expertise and technologies of government: The emergence of think tanks in Chile
abstract: This article analyses the relation between the formation of a corpus of technologies of government and the establishment of bodies of actors that lay claim to this type of knowledge. In order to investigate this phenomenon, I examine the major milestones in the emergence of think tanks in Chile with the intention of uncovering not only the political aspects of technologies of government but also cultural ones, which come into play through people's beliefs and practices. I approach think tanks in the following three ways, which appear to be different dimensions of the same phenomenon: (a) as global assemblages; (b) through the genealogy of their emergence and (c) within their spheres and 'sites' of activity. Despite their differences in ideas and values, think tanks share the characteristic of being sites where neoliberal governmentality can be reproduced through a migratory technology of governing that interacts with situated sets of elements and historical conjunctures. The effects of this phenomenon are manifested in the establishment of a market for expertise opened up by think tanks, 'freed' from state bureaucracy and underpinned by a logic of competition that is supported by networks that blur the boundaries between public and private institutions. [web URL: http://coa.sagepub.com/content/36/2/145.abstract]

title: By the Book: An Academic Memoir
abstract: KEYWORDS. Autobiography, family sociology, research, gender, careersFOREWORDI did not plan to become a professor when I was young, but perhaps it was inevitable. All my life my surroundings have included academicians and books. Certainly not by the book, however, is the spelling of my first name and its pronunciation. My first name, Joan, is pronounced as if it were spelled Joanne. However, I have never thought of changing my parents' spelling. The pronunciation of my first name is one means I have for separating the people who know me and I care about from those I don't. I also have no middle name, and that has given various bureaucratic organizations problems. When I applied to enter the University of Chicago as a freshman, for example, those folks were concerned enough to give me the middle initial N. They assured me that it stood for "no name." So truly, as far as I am concerned, what's in a name? But with respect to my living my life by the book, that is worth an examination.For a complete reprint of this article contact Haworth Press by telephone (1-800-HAWORTH) or EMail (getinfo@haworthpressinc.com). Copies are available from: Haworth Document Delivery Center, The Haworth Press, Inc., 10 Alice Street, Binghamton, NY 13904-1580. Article copyright The Haworth Press, Inc.

title: Natural Justice and the Big Public Inquiry: A Sociological Perspective
abstract: Discussions within the field of academic public administration of procedural reform of the public inquiry system have taken an overly formal view of procedures, & have failed to fully understand widespread criticism of "big public inquiries" from those who participate in them. The central problems with the existing public inquiry process are reviewed.
