The ideas of Basil Bernstein ("On the Classification and Framing of Educational Knowledge" in Hopper, Earl [Ed], Readings in the Theory of Educational Systems, London: Hutchinson, 1971) on the classification & framing of knowledge offer a perspective from which it is possible to study natural justice in big public inquiries in a sociological rather than a purely legal sense. This perspective is illustratively applied to the Moss Moran inquiry into the proposal of Shell/Esso to build a petrochemical complex in Fife, Scotland. Modified HA

title: Politics in the Information Society: Electronic Administration and Government
abstract: This article presents a brief analysis of the use & application of Information & Communication Technologies (ICTS) to the political system of advanced democracies. First, we present a summary of the basic attributes of information society. The equation ELECTRONIC DEMOCRACY = E-ADMINISTRATION + E-GOVERNMENT is used to discern the different levels of politics. After that, we analyze how ICTS work at the level of concrete policies (c-administration), politics & governance (c-government). Adapted from the source document.

title: Tensions of European Governance: Politicized Bureaucracy and Multiple Accountability in the European Commission
abstract: Explores, from a neoinstitutionalist perspective, the function of the European Commission as a reflection of developing societal values & tensions in terms of the politicization of institutionalized contradictions. It is argued that the multiple accountability of the commission to European Union member states & their citizens while acting as a politicized bureaucracy has created a multiorganization amalgamation of contrasting logics (bureaucratic, political, diplomatic, & democratic). Resulting conflict among methods of problem solving suggests the need for a study of the contradictions & their resolutions. 2 Figures, 68 References. P. Schlachte

title: Reforming Welfare Bureaucracies: The Seebohm Report Outcome
abstract: An analysis of several critical unresolved issues facing social services departments (SSDs) that were established in England & Wales following the publication of the important 1968 Seebohm Report. Three main issues are discussed: (1) the boundaries of welfare bureaucracies; (2) the impact of qualitative organizational change; & (3) the dilemma of social conscience administration. SSDs were set up within an era dominated by the "social conscience" policy -- an optimistic belief that the central problems of welfare have been solved, & that change is cumulative & in the direction of greater generosity & wider purpose. However, an alternative analysis of SSDs leads to the concept of social breakdown, a state resulting in institutionalization. This is distinguished from another category of needs, social discomfort, which embraces problems of isolation & loneliness. Questions are raised as to the appropriateness of governmental intervention in "discomfort" problems, & the failure of government to intervene in all the categories of breakdown. The establishment of the new SSDs, which replace smaller & less complex agencies, is analysed as a qualitative organizational change. In particular, the phenomena of "missing" levels of work & lack of administrative capacity are discussed. Examples of the conceptual challenge to current administrative beliefs are given, & an outline of a theory of levels of response to social need is provided, with illustrations. Modified HA.

title: On being a strength coach: Child welfare and the strengths model
authors: Noble, Dorinda N; Perkins, Kathleen; Fatout, Marian
abstract: Strength coaches help athletes assess their strengths and build on them. Likewise, social workers dealing with children and families in the child welfare system, rather than looking for pathology, can learn to help clients discover and develop their strengths, even while dealing with a child welfare bureaucracy. This article gives examples of the strength coach approach.

title: Integrating social work and public health education: A clinical model
abstract: In Florida, the need for clinically oriented social workers with expertise in planning and evaluating maternal and child health programs has led to the establishment of a joint master of social work and master of public health degree program. This program has a clinical social work concentration combined with a public health concentration in maternal and child health content, administration, and research design. The philosophy and development of the program, the course content and degree requirements, the field placement content, issues regarding student acceptance and advisement, faculty appointments, and program directions and goals are discussed. Descriptions of both the social work and public health programs that operate the joint-degree curriculum and the differing perspectives are outlined as well as skills that students obtained through their participation in the program.

title: Weber and the Sociology of Revolution
abstract: Weber wrote about the Russian revolutions of 1905 and 1917 while they were in progress. Analytically, he held that revolution is a non-legitimate form of change, insofar as the source of legitimate power is the authority of military command in a community of fate organized for foreign war. He thus adumbrates some aspects of contemporary state-breakdown theory, in which revolution hinges upon geopolitical strain and fiscal crisis splitting elites. Yet Weber remained closer to classic Marxian theory of revolutionary interest groups mobilized from below. He broadened interest groups to include status groups as well as economic classes. His description gives leads for a theory of revolutionary process centered on alliances and splits, bandwagon effects and turning points, and the volatility of revolutionary ideas arising from the social organization of full-time political militants. Weber predicted structural change in Russia leading to bureaucratic dictatorship.

title: Exploring the Strategic Prevention Framework (SPF) and its Application to a Comprehensive Substance Abuse and HIV/AIDS Prevention Initiative: Evidence from Project C.O.P.E. (Communities Organizing for Prevention and Empowerment): A Model Substance Abuse and HIV/AIDS Prevention Initiative Targeting Urban Minority Youth in the Northeastern United States
abstract: The inextricable link between substance abuse and HIV/AIDS poses a serious public health threat in the United States. Of particular concern has been the detrimental impact that this crisis has wrought on urban centers, where people of color, particularly racial and ethnic minority youth, are disproportionately impacted by this twin epidemic. The U.S. federal government has made a concerted effort to fund demonstration projects through its Minority AIDS Initiative (MAI) in geographic areas with high rates of substance abuse and HIV/AIDS prevalence, with the specific intent of introducing culturally-resonant, model prevention protocols with proven effectiveness. Responding to this public health emergency, the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), Center for Substance Abuse Prevention (CSAP), introduced the Strategic Prevention Framework (SPF) to guide prevention planning and implementation efforts throughout the U.S. This paper illustrates the five steps of the SPF (e.g., assessment, capacity, planning, implementation, and evaluation) by describing its application to Project C.O.P.E. (Communities Organizing for Prevention and Empowerment), which is a comprehensive substance abuse and HIV/AIDS prevention program located in the northeastern United States.

title: Social Surveillance and the Rise of the `Police Machine'
abstract: In this paper, I explore the development of police as part of a modernist power/knowledge nexus, an essential feature of which is an ordered totality: designed, predictable and controllable. I argue that police was connected to a form of power, originally extraneous to the State, but which, in the eighteenth century, was eventually absorbed into a set of state techniques, that may best be termed pastoral. I examine how `police intellectuals' refined, reshaped and added to the meaning of police by transforming it from a condition of government into a techne of social order, a `police machine', if you will, charged with the effective and efficient administration of the general ensemble of a population. I concentrate on the writings of Patrick Colquhoun because he was a chief strategist of police in the transition to a liberal police in a modern world. A critical approach to the understanding of police and its relation to classical liberalism, I conclude, warns against accepting fast theoretical divides and contrasts between pre-modern and modern forms of power and government.

title: The Italian Labour Market as Perceived by Outstanding Upper Secondary School-Leavers
abstract: The article reports a set of findings drawn form a larger research programme, promoted by Italy's National Federation of Knights of Labour, aiming to supply a profile of social characteristics and the tertiary education choices of particularly gifted students, who are contacted one year after having earned their upper secondary school diplomas. More specifically, results reported here concern the incidence of meritocracy in the determination of workers' income and in other social contexts (including the labour market), as well as among outstanding upper secondary school-leavers' employment expectations and their representations of the 'ideal job'. Findings show that numerous criteria are deemed acceptable for establishing fair pay; Italy is perceived as largely non-meritocratic place, especially as regards politics, public administration, and taxation, but also insofar as its labour market is concerned; the 'ideal job' features stability (permanent, open-ended contracts), use and acquisition of skills, and gender parity. Adapted from the source document.

title: From Sheriff's Deputies to Immigration Officers: Screening Immigrant Status in a Tennessee Jail
abstract: This article contributes to emerging literature documenting the devolution of immigration enforcement authority by focusing on the implementation of the 287(g) program in Davidson County, Tennessee. It outlines how deputized immigration officers do their work as well as the ways they come to think about their roles in the larger immigration bureaucracy. Immigration officers see themselves as objective administrators whose primary responsibilities are to identify and process immigrants for removal, but who are not responsible for their subsequent deportation. While immigration officers never waiver about their obligation to uphold the rule of law, alternate narratives emerge depending on how they feel about the immigrants they encounter. These frames range from pride at identifying "criminal aliens" to guilt for processing immigrants who had been arrested for very minor violations. Ultimately, this work shows deputized immigration officers act as extensions of the federal government rather than as independent agents. Adapted from the source document.

title: Intellectuals, International Relations and the Constant Emergency
abstract: In this essay, I return to Hans Morgenthau's and Hannah Arendt's writings on the Vietnam war and US foreign policy, which explored questions of bureaucracy, technology, emergency. On one level the essays they wrote illustrate the extent to which the discipline of International Relations (IR) has now caught up with the analyses of politics and war that they were developing in the 1960s and 1970s. We begin to see how lines of thought in Morgenthau's writing connect directly with the work of a younger generation of scholars interested in the work of intellectuals like Giorgio Agamben on the dangers of a security-obsessed politics in a 'state of emergency' or 'state of exception', or how Arendt's and Morgenthau's work on bureaucracy and war is explored in contemporary work; from a pedagogical perspective, drawing out these connections creates the possibility of a different, potentially more subversive, way of introducing students to the discipline of IR. Adapted from the source document.

title: American Patrimonialism: The Return of the Repressed
abstract: Patrimonialism, until fairly recently, seemed an archaic social form, largely replaced by bureaucratic rationalism. That confident view of modernity, in the histories that Max Weber and his followers wrote, deserves to be challenged as patrimonial regimes reappear in states and firms throughout the world. This article is my attempt to mount that challenge. I first revisit Weber's conception of patrimonialism and discuss how gendered and elitist studies of early modern. Europe require a reevaluation of patrimonialism's dynamics and resilience. I then present an overview of evidence for the return of patrimonialism and of ideological justifications for its legitimacy, focusing on the US. Since Weber and his successors all see patrimonialism and bureaucracy as incompatible, it is necessary to develop a theory of how the dynamics of elite conflict within bureaucratic, capitalist societies can generate patrimonialism. I do so in the penultimate section of this article, and I then explore the implications of that theory for predicting the future course of patrimonialism in the 21st century. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Power to Negotiate: The Prison Worker as a Street-Level Bureaucrat
abstract: As street-level bureaucrats in a so-called frontline organization, prison workers regularly encounter situations in which they have to make immediate decisions about their clients, the prisoners. For that purpose they have great discretionary freedom. Except in the case of statutory (basic) rights of prisoners, this discretionary power allows them to interpret day-to-day situations & so deviate from semi-official regulations, a practice known in the Netherlands as gedogen. This article focuses firstly on the consequences of prison workers' discretionary powers on the daily practices of a penitentiary institution; & secondly, on how these practices influence the power relationship between prisoners & their 'guards.'. 14 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Voice, Choice and the Question of Civil Democracy in the Swedish Welfare State
authors: Saltman, Richard B; von Otter, Casten
abstract: The welfare state democracy of Sweden is examined with particular emphasis on the absence of formal participatory influence over civil institutions. Efforts at participatory reform are explored, including the introduction of cooperative self-managed service delivery, reconfiguration of the internal structure of Swedish social services, & increased citizen involvement in the design & delivery of community-based systems. Reform efforts are discussed from the perspective of voice & the alternative of exit, considering private sector provision of services. The need to broaden the Swedish working definition of democracy beyond direct public influence over social, political, & economic institutions & the private commodity market is emphasized. A process model of constituent components of current Swedish welfare democracy is developed, & the role of choice among alternative public sector human services discussed. 1 Figure, 34 References. D. Generoli

title: Becoming Traditional: Socialization to Bureaucracy among American Immigrants in Israel
abstract: One aspect of the acculturation of US immigrants in Israel is explored -- their socialization to Israeli bureaucratic norms & practice -- based on intensive interviews with 19 immigrant families, followed by a survey questionnaire administered to an additional 100 Rs in the Jerusalem area. Previous research focused on immigrants of Afro-Asian ("Oriental") provenance, & an equivalence was drawn between bureaucratic socialization & psychologial modernization. This equivalence is tested by examination of the US immigrants' case. In focusing on certain bureaucratic strategies & tactics learned by immigrants as clients, it is argued that their acculturation entails not "modernization" but "traditionalization." A distinction is drawn between instrumental & expressive traditionalization, & the implications of this distinction for conceptualizing the wider process of individuals "becoming modern" are discussed. 2 Tables, 21 References. Modified AA.

title: Eyesight and Governance in Britain: Bureaucracy and the Senses in the 1920s
abstract: Eyesight became a public concern to an unprecedented extent in 1920s Britain. This article discusses a number of enquiries made in these years into the causes of the impairment of eyesight, related legislation and some industry field studies. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Sociology of Professions and the Profession of Gender
abstract: A review of literature on the gendering of organization & bureaucracy suggests that a key issue for consideration is not so much the exclusion of women from professional work, but rather their routine inclusion in ill-defined support roles. This adjunct work of women facilitates the fleeting encounter of professional practice, thereby resting on, & celebrating, a specific historical & cultural construction of masculinity & a masculinist vision of professional work. In an era where professions are under unprecedented public scrutiny, sociological attention to their renewal needs to recognize that a key feature of profession, as presently defined, is that it professes gender. 83 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Effects of Bureaucratization and Commitment on Resource Mobilization in Voluntary Organizations
authors: Torres, Cruz; McIntosh, William Alex; Zey, Mary
abstract: An examination of the relationships, in voluntary organizations, between: bureaucratic control & commitment; commitment & resource mobilization; & all bureaucratic control & commitment variables & resource mobilization. The analysis is based on a case study of the food-pantry system, which operates centers in an economically depressed region of the Rio Grande Valley of southern Tex to supply food to the needy. Interviews were conducted with all directors of the 17 centers & most of the volunteers (N = 66). The results suggest that commitment, defined as loyal involvement with the organization, & local autonomy positively affect resource mobilization; a formal bureaucratic structure appears not to influence the impact of commitment on resource mobilization. 2 Tables, 1 Figure, 1 Appendix, 57 References. J. W. Stanton

title: Reading Bauman for Social Work
abstract: This article draws on the social theories of Zygmunt Bauman to provide some analytical purchase on the state of contemporary social work. It outlines key themes in Bauman's writing and considers features of current social work practice against these. The starting point for Bauman's work is his explication of modernity and in particular the shift he identifies from what he calls 'solid' to 'liquid' modernity. The implications for social work within solid and liquid modern imaginaries are considered. Essentially, modernity, in its dominant guises, conceives of social work as a technical-rational endeavour whereas Bauman would argue that it is an irredeemably moral one. The moral dimension, however, is swept aside by the bureaucracy of solid modernity and by the neoliberal tenets of liquid modernity. This creates a growing dissonance between the original ethical impulse that brings people into social work and the job they are increasingly expected to do. Bauman argues that an ethical stance involves social workers 'being for' those they work with. It cannot come about through recourse to rules and codes but ultimately relies on workers taking personalised and situated moral positions. Adapted from the source document.

title: Public Finances in 1985
abstract: Examined is the evolution of public financing in France between 1963 & 1978, as compared to the provisions contained in two government reports of 1963 & 1970. Based on this analysis, future developments are predicted. Discussed are changes within administrative, local, & military sectors, as well as in methods of financing. Maintaining the progress of real value of social benefits in relation to any of the other economic sectors entails a growing need for financing of public administration. While there are no official projections for 1985, proposed are two possible solutions to the crisis caused by slower economic growth: increase in compulsory taxation, & reduction of spending in certain sectors. Discussed are four main tasks of public financing: securing services not otherwise provided by private enterprise, substituting public choice in the matter of national resources, securing national solidarity in the realm of redistribution, & regulating economic activity. 5 Tables, 5 Figures. I. Irwin-Zarecka.

title: A Study of Management's View of the Motivation of Workpeople
abstract: A random sample of 30 employees of Corp's which are members of the Instit of Production Engineers were asked to rank 8 factors considering their own work motivation. Factors included such items as "money or econ security," "status in society," "shorter work hours," & "a position of trust." Findings were compared with those of E. N. Corlett, "Production Engineers, Their Education and Their Work," The Production Engineer, 1965, Feb. It was hyp'ed that the manag people would differ from the workpeople & that the diff in viewpoint would be influenced by (a) the age of the manager concerned; (b) length or type of educ background; (c) whether or not the man had served an apprenticeship or had had line manag experience; (d) the type & size of the Co he was working in; & (e) his position in the Co. Interviewees were also asked, after a series of questions on shop floor problems to rank a series of suggestions they considered the most powerful motivating forces. It was found that those who worked in smaller, single Co firms showed a greater degree of common motivation between executives & shop floor personnel, while in larger public Co's there was a wider degree of diff. It would appear that the size & structure of the org in which a person is employed is more important in his views on motivation than past experience or any of the other factors studied. l Diagram, 4 Tables. Modified HA.

title: Making History Public: Indigenous Claims to Settler States
abstract: Differences between historical practices are not valued symmetrically by courts and tribunals that investigate claims, or by state bureaucracies that negotiate settlements, or by most historians trained in the academic disciplines. Oral histories and traditions continue to be disputed according to the standards of verifiability and reliability that have been developed in the disciplines of law and of history to test documentary evidence. However, in the democratizing, multicultural moment in which indigenous claims have made such a national impact, ways of evaluating oral histories have become central to disputes about what happened. Here, Johnson argues as to why disputes about what counts as history, and how different kinds of historical practice can be evaluated, are disputes about how local pasts can be transformed into public history.

title: Contentions and contradictions of tourism as development option: The case of Kerala, India
abstract: Although the state of Kerala in India has been regarded as a 'model of development', its achievements may be unravelling thanks to a host of internal and external problems. The government and the bureaucracy now project tourism as 'an engine of growth'--an excellent source of foreign exchange and employment--to revive the local economy. Opposition to large-scale tourism projects by environmental and labour activists is often dealt with through undemocratic means. This article points to a less than sanguine role for tourism in the local economy and the dynamics that work to exaggerate tourism's share in the economy in an emerging context of governmental failure, political crisis and interest group consolidation. Lessons are drawn to revisit the debate on tourism and development.

title: Organizational learning in United Nations' peacekeeping exit strategies
abstract: This article illustrates how organizational learning can explain the shift in United Nations' peacekeeping exit strategies from the election-based approach of the 1990s to peacebuilding. Conceptualizing learning as an ideal-type, three-step process, of knowledge acquisition, interpretation and institutionalization, the analysis reveals the impact of new knowledge on institutional change. It demonstrates how knowledge acquisition became systematized within the United Nations' Secretariat especially after 2000, with the active promotion of boundary-spanning activities. The analysis then shows how a shared understanding of the role of peacebuilding for exit strategies was developed by the organization's bureaucracy and intergovernmental bodies in the interpretation step. Finally, it highlights how the establishment of the Peacebuilding Commission institutionalized the transition to peacebuilding as the new exit strategy and how new learning capacities were created. By conceiving the interaction between international organizations and their external environment as a dynamic relationship, the analysis confirms the potential of organizational learning theories for explaining institutional change in international relations. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright NISA.]

title: Adaptation of a political bureaucracy to economic and institutional change under socialism: The Chinese State Family Planning system
authors: Merli, M Giovanna; Qian, Zhenchao; Smith, Herbert L
abstract: In China, the transformation from a centrally planned economy to one dominated by market forces has been characterized by the devolution of authority from the center (Beijing) to localities. This is as true of the enormous state bureaucracy associated with the control of fertility as it is with the economic bureaucracies more often studied in transitional societies. Using observations from several field sites, the authors document how county-, township-and village-level family planning cadres have gone from being agents of the state to autonomous actors who must negotiate between the ongoing demands of the central bureaucracy and the new opportunities available in the locales in which they work and dwell. They suggest that any serious change in the draconian restrictions on fertility that have obtained in China for almost thirty years is likely to derive from initiatives at the local level. Local actors (cadres) have already begun to adjust to the tensions between responsibilities and available resources that have tended to induce paralysis in the upper levels of this long-standing state bureaucracy. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Retrotopia: Critical reason turns primitive
abstract: The collapse of the Communist regimes and the failure of the anti-bureaucratic critical left may be traced back to the same roots.  Around the middle of the 1960s the critical left turned away from a future-oriented utopia and discovered anthropology, the peasants and the primitive as an anti-capitalist, anti-bureaucratic, anti-centralist, anti-consumerist alternative.

title: Warlord, Social Welfare and Philanthropy: The Case of Guangzhou under Chen Jitang, 1929-1936
abstract: This study highlights the administration of social welfare & philanthropy in Guangzhou in the 1930s. It aims to elucidate three important points about state-society relationships under warlordism. First, a warlord could not afford to ignore the needs of society, for satisfying such needs (or at least making attempts to satisfy such needs) was vital to the credibility & survival of his regime. Second, a warlord would have little problem funding social welfare projects, for he always had recourse to extrabudgetary sources of revenue to finance desired undertakings. And third, the administration of social welfare & philanthropy by a warlord was an integral part of his drive toward total control of state & society. Indeed, care & control made up the two sides of a warlord's strategy of governance: care laid the foundation of stable rule, whereas control served as the means to safeguard this foundation. 7 Tables, 77 References. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright 2004.]

title: Critical review of older adults' caregiving-related programs and policies in South Korea
abstract: In light of the considerable contribution of older adult caregivers to South Korean society, we examine current caregiving-related policies and explore potential paths forward. Caregiving-related policies were analyzed in terms of service delivery system, eligibility, and benefits, including Public Long-Term Care Insurance, the National Basic Livelihood Security Act, Respite Care Service, the Formal Caregiver Program, and the Elderly Caring for Elderly and Children Programs. Findings indicate that older caregivers do not receive sufficient governmental support, and that most of the programs do not specify the explicit identification of older caregivers in benefits. Service benefits that do exist are generally limited to low-income caregivers, and the quality and quantity of these services are questionable. Negotiating bureaucracy to use these services is a particular challenge for older caregivers. We conclude that the current caregiving system has not been formally institutionalized to meet the specialized needs of older caregivers. A comprehensive needs assessment of older caregivers is necessary to develop social interventions tailored to their well-being. Adapted from the source document.

title: Sameness, Bureaucracy, and the Myth of Educational Equity: The TAAS System of Testing in Texas Public Schools
abstract: The verdict in the case of GI Forum et al. v. Texas Education Agency et al. is examined for the ways in which it undermines the concept of equitable access to education by the acceptance of "sameness" as a standard for equity. The implied comparability in a state testing system masks the educational inequities behind the test scores. The verdict also undermines equity as a legal standard by excluding from admissible testimony empirical evidence of those bureaucratic processes that create new inequities: the test prep & the artificial manipulation of students' grade-level designations that produce school-level test scores to the detriment of the quality of education provided to Latino & African American students. 19 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: BUREAUCRATS AS HEROES
abstract: Values and perspectives are the central concepts of the sociologist, writer, and the critic. Literature generally and the novel specifically, can be analyzed sociologically in terms of the symbolic act as developed in the work of John Dewey and George H. Mead. The object and viewer in literature, as in social situations generally, represent sets of values. The sociological analysis of literary perspectives consists of the identification of the values involved, and of the manner in which writers have related them. Ways in which such an analysis may proceed are suggested. Sociological analysis of the novel usually focusses upon the hero since 'the hero constitutes the novelist's strategy for encompassing the value situation.' When the value system of the writer and that represented by the hero are congruent, the hero figure tends to be ritualistic. American literature since the realisitc movement has been a literature of protest and rejection and, as such, highly critical of American culture. A group of recent American novels centering about bureaucratic relationships are analyzed in terms of the general approach indicated above. The captain of industry is discussed as a literary hero and the intellectual-'the symbol manipulator'-as bureaucrat is analyzed in terms of the intersection of value systems. Writers of bureaucratic novels emphasize the importance of non-rational 'enforced personalization' elements in bureaucratic success. Another theme is that of exploitation as a road to successful bureaucratic mobility. The resolution of bureaucratic value conflict is seen to follow two lines: the romantic resolution in which the hero rebels against the bureaucracy, and the tragic, in which he succumbs to it. R. Murphy.

title: The Brazilian Public Management and Citizenship Program
abstract: The Public Management & Citizenship award is a joint effort by the Ford Foundation & the Fundacao Getulio Vargas in Sao Paulo, with the additional support of the Brazilian National Economic & Social Development Bank (BNDES). The award program seeks to identify & disseminate innovative initiatives from Brazilian local & regional governments. Since 1996, 5,000+ programs have taken part in the annual awards cycle. The experiences of the program over the first six years has contributed to the identification of new policy types & areas of management systems, decision making, & public services provision. 22 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: THE PROFESSIONAL WORKER IN THE BUREAUCRACY
abstract: An examination of the relations between professional soc workers & the bur'cy in which they operate. Conflict situations arise between them because the requirements of bur'cy may be an impediment to service, professional workers resent bur'tic authority, colleague relations are affected by bur'tic procedures, & relations with the clients are similarly affected. Also certain types of soc workers-the 'victim,' the 'immature professional,' & the 'reformer'-are more likely than others to clash with bur'cy. The dynamic aspects of the professional worker's adjustment to bur'cy are examined, & the following areas of remedial admin'ive action are suggested: (1) development & refinement of the distinction between professional & admin'ive competence; (2) increase of the worker's autonomy in the org; (3) development of prestigeful & rewarding opportunities in the professional field; (4) changing the structure of the org; & (5) re-definition of the goals of the org to give more opportunity to the soc worker. I. Langnas.

title: Administration, Bureaucracy and Bureaucratism
abstract: Four meanings of the term bureaucracy are distinguished & analyzed: (1) the membership of a bureaucratic organization; (2) the formalized, rigid, conceited behavior of such members toward nonmembers; (3) a type of administration & organization, including decision-making patterns; & (4) usurpation of others' rights by state bureaucrats, managers, or other members of elite groups. A distinction is made between oligarchy as a result of political division between elites & masses & bureaucracy as the rule of professional experts & their method of administration. The Yugoslav system is a mixture of oligarchy, bureaucracy, & democracy. Two general points are argued: (A) the bureaucratic method of administration is not necessarily efficient & rational; & (B) politicians & capitalists are not necessarily powerless outsiders while bureaucrats & managers are powerful experts, as asserted by Max Weber. Modified HA.

title: Work Values: A Study of Managers
abstract: Data gathered from 308 M middle-level managers in 5 Northwest business firms on work values & managers' outlook if their careers were to terminate below top executive level are analyzed. Data indicate that org'al rank & progression were important concerns to the managers in this study. Advancement in the occup'al hierarchy appeared as less central a concern than assumed. Managers considered org'al rank achieved at the expense of mental stress as no success & agreed that it was preferable to remain in a modest position with less stressful duties. Those who placed career satisfaction upon upward mobility in the org'al hierarchy tended to be young. It is suggested that the strong emphasis in sociol'al & psychol'al literature on occup'al position as a crucial determinant of self-respect may be a distortion. For the middle-manager stratum here studied, non-stressful work was at least as important as maximizing occup'al rank, if not more so. Emphasis on maximizing occup'al rank appears to be consistently influenced by (1) age, & (2) the distance between initial level of LF entry & present position in manag. 2 Tables, 2 Figures. Modified HA.

title: Culture and Conformity: An Essay on Individual Adaptation in Centralized Bureaucracy
abstract: The cultural aspects of interpersonal relations in large bureaucracies are examined with participant observation & interview data from a field study of a large telephone company. The data reveal that "strong demands for conformity" dominated superior-subordinate relations, & serve as the main integrative mechanism for individuals vis-a-vis the managerial hierarchy. Managers were publicly deferential to superiors, yet employed "secret networks" & "hidden agendas" as means to protect themselves & to attain power. "Breaking ranks" was considered necessary to achieve outstanding results. It is emphasized that the cultural factors particular to an organization must be examined together with the more formal, structural features on which studies of management typically focus. 22 References. B. Heitman

title: Crabgrass and Bureaucrats
abstract: Personal experience in dealing with government bureaucracies offers a basis for questioning many commonly held assumptions about their operations. In many cases, citizens & elected officials end up acting as servants of their own appointed or hired officials. Bureaucrats can survive, whether or not their activities are useful, because they are able to outlast elected officials who might want to remove them, & thus are able to gain a basis of information & influence better than that available to elected officials. Self-serving bureaucratic activity is an inescapable problem of bureaucratic government. There is no simple solution, but certainly the need for a solution should be recognized. W. H. Stoddard.

title: Why we must attack Iraq: Bush's reasoning practices and argumentation system
authors: Chang, Gordon C; Mehan, Hugh B
abstract: This three-part article describes the reasoning practices and argumentation system deployed by the Bush administration to build a case for the war on Iraq initiated in 2003. First, it analyzes the elaborate description of Saddam Hussein's evil character presented by the Bush administration and the political implications that followed from it. Then, it analyzes the methods by which these understandings were utilized to argue that Saddam Hussein's regime (1) possessed weapons of mass destruction and (2) had collaborative relationships with terrorists, including al-Qaeda. Last, it explains how the Bush administration creatively used event-sequencing strategies and syntactical formations to help forward their accusations in public against opponents who argued that the Bush administration had lacked evidence for its claims. The overall analysis demonstrates that an argumentation system was built through a dialectical process whereby one way of speaking, thinking, and acting helped to legitimize and `afford' subsequent ones.

title: Opportunists, Predators and Rogues: The Role of Local State Relations in Shaping Chinese Rural Development
abstract: Chinese rural enterprises have developed in various ways in different parts of the country, giving rise to competing explanations of the variation in terms of the role of structure, historical legacies, norms, bureaucratic controls & agency. A new analysis seeks to resolve these contradictions by placing development in the context of township & village cadres' relationships. Townships can either enforce village compliance with county policy or not, & can promote economic development or not, resulting in bureaucratic controls working where compliance is enforced, & norms & agency guiding development where they are not. Perverse incentives allow compliance without achieving larger goals of economic development, & can trap villages in opportunistic or predatory townships. While structure & historical legacies do constrain development in general, inter-level relationships are key to understanding micro-variations. Village wealth & village elections further empower the village level & give agency greater salience. 1 Table, 2 Figures, 1 Appendix, 63 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Zygmund Bauman: A Sociologist between Modernism and Postmodernism
abstract: Lately Zygmund Bauman has been one of the most important thinkers that contributed to sociological theory. He is regarded as one of the most important postmodern society theorists with his effective critique of modernism. He owes his popularity to his critique of modernism. His critique especially focuses on the theory that enlightenment based progressionist worldview of modernism has reached a deadlock. In other words, he announces the falling of "Modernism Project" based on "instrumental reason culture." Postmodernist notion has been the most important intellectual background lately because modernism has broken its promise. Bauman has also directed his attention to postmodern perspective & the notion of 'other'. He has probably given his attention to postmodernism not only for his own background but also for his testimony to the present age. In this article, Bauman, who is one of the most important actors, his critique of modernism & his postmodern position is analyzed & his intellectual curiosity as a sociologist is followed. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Politics and Government: A Background to Corruption in Public Administration in Developing Countries
abstract: The study of corruption is important to scientist & citizen alike, & it may fruitfully be pursued along ecological lines, focusing on the interrelationship of politics & administration. If politics is defined in terms of values, power, & public policy, then an administrator may be considered a 'politician' in many respects, although he is operating in a more structured context & subject to different norms (administrative output-culture vs politician's input-culture). Whether one defines corruption as the violation of norms, as self-interested behavior, or as a transaction, the various forms of corruption may be explained by the confusion & overlap of politics & administration. Official positions may serve as spoils, they may be used as a political resource, or corrupt loyalties may guide an administrator's behavior; the latter may be related to the informal organization within the bureaucracy or to the social & political environment. In developing countries, internal bureaucratic competition & environmental needs for corrupt influence on public policy are especially strong because of social conflicts, disruptive contact between traditional & western norms & roles, & because of an increasing impact of the national administration upon the culturally distant local communities. Cultural confusion & political exclusion of many groups leave corruption as the only effective means to influence public policy at the output stage. AA.

title: Bureaucratic Approaches to the Bureaucracy: A Conference Report
abstract: A report on the First International Conference on Comparative Historical & Critical Analysis of Bureaucracy, held by the Gottlieb Duttweiler Instit fur wirtschaftliche & soziale Studien in Zurich, Switzerland, 4-8 Oct 1982. Four main themes were explored: comparative historical analyses, theories of bureaucracy & rationalization, the bureaucratization of culture, & alternatives to bureaucracy. Papers presented are briefly noted & reviewed. A number of disputes took place among anti-Marxists, non-Marxists, cultural Marxists, & orthodox Marxists. W. H. Stoddard.

title: The French Riots of November 2005. Elements of Analysis of Political-Administrative Management and Forms of Participation
authors: Cicchelli, Vincenzo; Galland, Olivier; Maillard, Jacques de; Misset, Severine
abstract: In November 2005, France was affected by urban riots in a large number of suburbs & towns. Based on a fieldwork made between April & September 2006, this article aims to make an analysis of the disorders exploded in Aulnay-Sous-Bois (a town in the north of Paris). First of all we examine the governmental responses, the management of the crisis at the local level & some serious problems encountered by the police in quelling conflicts at the beginning of the unrest. Then, through the analysis of interviews with both twenty young people, involved or not involved in the encounters with the police, & twenty adults, we have demonstrated that, in spite of some arguable statements, the riots were not caused by racial conflict. Some relevant causes have been argued as urban segregation & discriminations, the feeling of everyday harassment of the police, the lack of perspectives in the integration of labor market & also the scope of the rivalry & competition between young inhabitants of the areas for scoring the "best performance.". Adapted from the source document.

title: New Public Management and Social Work in Sweden and England: Challenges and Opportunities for Staff in Predominantly Female Organizations
authors: Berg, Elisabeth E B; Barry, Jim J J; Chandler, John J P
abstract: Purpose - This paper aims to explore the issues for middle-level social work managers arising from the development of the new public management, with its emphasis on the intensification of work, the measurement of performance in service delivery, and cost efficiencies. This is commonly thought to have affected those working in human services such as social work adversely. This paper explores the nature of these consequences, from the point of view of those centrally placed in its implementation. Design/methodology/approach - The methodology adopted in this paper is designed to acknowledge and explore the perceptions of middle-level social work managers as they contribute to the social construction of the new public management. This is accomplished through in-depth interviews with a sample of their number in Sweden and England. Findings - The findings reveal that social work managers are not only comfortable dealing with budgets but also enjoy the autonomy this affords them in their relationship with their subordinates. The findings also reveal that they appreciate the benefits of the more generalised knowledges of management, used in their work with junior colleagues, who they attempted to lead rather than manage and who they respected as colleagues. This has further implications: the possibility of new career opportunities for these predominantly women managers. Originality/value - The managers in social work see the knowledges gained from their position as managers as transferable to other areas of the public and private sectors, thereby opening up new career opportunities. They were also found to enjoy dealing with budget issues, contrary to earlier studies. Adapted from the source document.

title: A Joining between Two Public Policies on Environmental Education and on Old Aged People
authors: Machado, Rosangela Fatima de Oliveira; Velasco, Fermin de La Caridad Garcia; Amim, Valeria
abstract: In this paper we discuss the convergence of two public policies: the National Policy of Environmental Education & the National Policy for Old Adults. We show a comparative view of the similarities & the contradictions in the application of those policies by the public administration. Analysis of those policies indicates possibility of communitarian & institutional works where old aged ones could develop a relevant social role based on their past & present experiences, contributing to environmental sensitization of next generations. In this approach, we propose that old aged people -- considering the summed experience -- can act as advisor of an environmental education that offers to next generations a way to change personal concepts on environmental preservation, as a interdisciplinary inclusive work. To deal with those two public policies is a way to clarify & accelerate the implementation of key practices focused on improving personal life, environmental quality & interpersonal relations. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: State Capacity, Policy Feedbacks and Affirmative Action for Blacks, Women and Latinos
abstract: Analyzes archival documents from the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to argue that affirmative action resulted from a US bureaucratic rationality & not from the popularly perceived interest group & lobby activities of blacks, women, & Latinos. A historical-institutionalist approach to political sociology is applied to the examination of affirmative action's formation & the role of the state as a creative policymaker. It is contended that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission operated not according to any formal law or state structure, but under the common assumption of which groups were discriminated against & a rationality founded on quantitative procedures & substantive justice. 72 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucratic Strategies of Exclusion: Land Use Ideology and Images of Mexican Farmworkers in Housing Policy
abstract: This article examines how land use ideology and popular images of farmworkers contribute to the housing crisis for Mexican farmworkers in Fresno County, California. Despite the desperate need for affordable housing in the rural areas of Fresno County, local policy makers either have failed to aid or have actively discouraged attempts to increase the stock of affordable housing. Through an ethnographic examination of public policy decision making about residential construction on the west side of Fresno County, I document how public officials make policy decisions based on both a land use ideology that rationalizes governmental failure to serve Mexicans working in the agriculture industry and portraits of farmworkers and farmworker families that reflect stereotypes and nationally relevant population characteristics rather than regionally specific realities. This ideology and these stereotypical profiles operate to render invisible portions of the Mexican farmworker population who have been working in the area for decades and diminish affordable housing opportunities. Adapted from the source document.

title: Neoliberalism, New Public Management and the Human Service Professions: Introduction to the Special Issue
authors: Connell, Raewyn; Fawcett, Barbara; Meagher, Gabrielle
abstract: This special issue of the Journal of Sociology includes papers contributed to a workshop in 2008, called 'Sisters of Sisyphus', about New Public Management (NPM) and the human service professions. This workshop arose from discussions about the impact of neoliberalism on the welfare state, and specifically on its workforce. 'Neoliberalism' broadly means the project of economic and social transformation under the sign of the free market. It also means the institutional arrangements to implement this project that have been installed, step by step, in every society under neoliberal control. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright The Australian Sociological Association.]

title: Inclusion in Employment: Characteristics within the Context of the Andalusian Experience
authors: Miedes Ugarte, Blanca; Asencio Coto, Ma Jose
abstract: The article analyzes the concept of economic inclusion by way of investigating, in detailed fashion, relevant developments in Andalusia, while emphasizing the economic importance of low-income sectors of the workforce. Public services aimed at this population tend to engender a negative reaction, as these services tend to be homogenized, rather than geared toward the needs of specific sub-sectors. The chief culprit in these instances is acknowledged to be the state bureaucracy, the response of which to the problems of lower-class citizens has been problematic. The marketplace, in general, for economic reasons, has proved equally ineffective in addressing & resolving the relevant issues, thus adding to the economic crisis. The article praises those entities that have developed mechanisms for absorbing the most disadvantaged members of the workforce. Chief among these has been the Andalusian Association for Inclusion in Business. R. Young

title: History and Career in a Bureaucratic Labor Market
abstract: Presented are a synthesis of theoretical statements on the determinants of socioeconomic achievement within bureaucratic internal labor markets & an empirical examination of resultant predictions. Official personnel records from a 1% sample of white-collar United States civil service employees, along with secondary survey data, are used to analyze careers of persons who entered civil service employment from 1 Jan 1963 through 31 Dec 1973. Five successive entering cohorts are differentiated, & a model of socioeconomic achievement is estimated for each incorporating key characteristics of bureaucratic labor markets not previously used in such models. This model supports a Weberian view of bureaucratic labor markets as highly rationalized personnel systems, although ascriptive characteristics also affect federal service career success. Important organizational & historical effects are revealed by cohort analysis; these effects are interpreted as demonstrating the influence of variations in opportunity structure on socioeconomic achievement. These findings show a need for greater attention to the relationship between individual biography & societal history. 5 Tables, 1 Figure, Appendix. Modified HA.

title: Doing 'Serious Case Reviews': The Views and Experiences of NHS Named and Designated Safeguarding Children Professionals
authors: Peckover, Sue; Smith, Sue; Wondergem, Fiona
abstract: Serious Case Reviews (SCRs), undertaken when a child has died or been seriously harmed, are an important feature of child protection in England. They are substantial exercises, but little research has examined the everyday work processes associated with their production. This study, undertaken during 2011, explored the views and experiences of NHS Named and Designated Nurses and Doctors for Safeguarding Children about their involvement in SCRs. Nineteen telephone interviews were undertaken and the data thematically analysed. The study found that doing SCRs involved additional work and staff did not always feel fully supported or prepared. Doing SCRs is a rigid and bureaucratic process which sometimes detracted from the case itself. The study also found mixed views about the value of SCRs and the extent to which they promote learning and child-centred practice. The findings contribute to overall understanding of how this process is undertaken, and help open up to scrutiny the work required and the challenges generated for those involved in SCRs. Copyright © 2013 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.'Doing SCRs is a rigid and bureaucratic process which sometimes detracted from the case itself'Key Practitioner Message:SCRs are substantial exercises; little previous research has examined their production.Undertaking SCRs requires considerable time, effort and can be emotionally difficult; NHS staff involved in their production face challenges in doing this work.Producing SCRs may distract from the value of the outcomes and the extent to which they promote learning and child-centred practice.

title: THE CRISIS OF MODERNIZATION IN THE ARMY
abstract: Since the end of WWII, the French army has been undergoing an acute crisis which sheds doubt on its structures & traditions. Man, rather than being the primary instrument of combat, has become the servant of the new military (MIL) technology. A MIL technocracy must inevitably develop to deal with the problems of specialization & increasingly complex forms of association. MIL planning will increasingly become the province of `brain trusts,' operating behind the screen of bur'cy. Numerous individuals, however, enter MIL service by reason of their desire for direct action & attracttion toward the 'commando' ideal & are antipathetical toward 'technological' virtues, bur'cy, intellectuals, & 'salon generals.' A second group opposes the 'inhumanity' of modern methods of warfare. The present army contains partisans of both the old & the new M styles, & the conflicts between them are often severe. M. M. Ito.

title: Le français au Zaïre: Langue "supérieure" et chances de "survie" dans un pays africain
abstract: RESUMOLa franca kiel prestiĝa lingvo en Zairio: la probablo de gia pluvivo en afrika medioFoje oni nornas Zairion la dua francparolanta lando de la mondo. Estas vere, ek-zemple, ke Zairio havas enlogantaron de preskaǔtridek milionoj. Sed estas egale vere, ke nu r unu zairiano el dudek kvin kapablas paroli la francan kaj nur unu el cent tridek kapablas gin skribi funkcie. Kiel la oficiala lingvo de Zairio, la franca elstaras super pli ol tricent indiĝenaj lingvoj kaj super la kvar naciaj lingvoj, nome la ciluba, la konga, la svahilia kaj la lingala. Gi estas la lingvo de publika administrado kaj inter-naciaj rilatoj kaj la medio de instruado. Sepdek kvin procentoj de la programoj en nacia televido kaj radio realigas en la franca. Tiel, la franca estas elita lingvo.Esplorante kiel la franca atingis sian nunan situacion en Zairio, tiu ci artikolo pesas la eblecojn, ĉu ĝi pluvivos, en la postsekvo de zairiaj kulturaj kaj ekonomiaj politikoj. Gi ekzamenas kiel eǔropaj lingvoj en Afriko generale kaj Zairio aparte povus inte-grigi harmonie en la socia evoluo, samtempe ludante kiel iloj por akiri sciencan kaj teknikan scion kaj antaǔenigi internaciajn rilatojn.SUMMARYFrench as the Language of Prestige in Zaïre: The Odds for Its Survival in an African ContextZaire has sometimes been referred to as the second francophone country in the world. It is true, for instance, that Zaïre has a population of nearly 30 million. But it is no less true that only 1 out of 25 Zaïreans can speak French and only 1 out of 130 can efficiently write in French. French, as the official language of Zaïre, overshadows not only more than three hundred indigenous languages but also the four national languages: Ciluba, Kikongo, Kiswahili, and Lingala. It is the language of public administration and international relations and the medium of instruction. Of programs on national television and radio, 75% are carried out in French. Thus, French is an élite language.Exploring how French came to be what it is in Zaïre, this paper evaluates its chances of survival in the aftermath of Zairean cultural and economic policies. It examines how European languages in Africa in general and in Zaïre in particular could be integrated harmoniously into the social development while still serving as a means to acquire scientific and technological knowledge and to promote international relations.

title: A Program Evaluation of Los Angeles ACORN's Welfare Case Advocacy
abstract: Bureaucratic confusion & client dissatisfaction since the 1996 changes in welfare policy opened opportunities for third party advocacy on behalf of welfare clients. This paper evaluates Los Angeles ACORN's case advocacy program for welfare clients. Outcomes analyzed include client satisfaction with ACORN's advocacy & effects of the program on welfare clients who later became ACORN members. Ninety-one percent of clients surveyed (N = 99) stated they were satisfied with the resolution of their welfare case complaint. Eighty-eight percent of respondents stated ACORN did a better job resolving their problem compared to the welfare department. Unique aspects of the program include peer advocacy & opportunities for welfare recipients to join ACORN & work on welfare policy changes among other issues. Tables, References. Adapted from the source document. COPIES ARE AVAILABLE FROM: HAWORTH DOCUMENT DELIVERY CENTER, The Haworth Press, Inc., 10 Alice Street, Binghamton, NY 13904-1580

title: Making Up Managers: Bureaucracy, Enterprise and the Liberal Art of Separation
abstract: Contemporary managerial discourse criticizes bureaucracy for its lack of market & entrepreneurial orientation, particularly its adherence to procedure, hierarchical sub- & supraordination, & lack of moral enthusiasm. Bureaucracy is characterized as a vehicle of public good, but an obstacle to effective provision of goods & services. In many respects this critique is misplaced, because it ignores the constitutive relationship between forms of bureaucratic administration & liberal democratic government, & values efficiency over fairness. Bureaucracy's adherence to market & entrepreneurial principles would likely result in unequal treatment of citizens & social injustice. It is concluded that the rationality of bureacracy has a strong moral basis. 38 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Politics of Public Expenditure in Malta
abstract: This study offers an 'insider' perspective on the politics of public expenditure in Malta between 1996 and 2001 focusing on a five year period which, in a number of ways, represented a major watershed in the history of Malta's politics. Two elections led to changes of government and to the adoption of two radically different styles of public expenditure management. A short period of Labour Party Government, distinguished by comparatively tight public expenditure control, was swiftly followed by the return of the Nationalist Party. In contrast, the Nationalist Government downgraded the importance of public expenditure control. These developments are found to be indicative of a characteristic pattern of politics defined by clientelism. Outcomes are frequently paradoxical. Analysis of public expenditure evidence reveals that government room for manoeuvre can be substantial at programme level but is significantly more limited and constrained in relation to overall expenditure parameters. Adapted from the source document.

title: Democracy and Bureaucracy: Towards an Understanding of the Politics of Educational Action Research
abstract: After describing the key elements of the dominant paradigm in educational action research, in particular, its emphasis on participatory, collaborative enquiry & its prodemocratic educational stance, an argument is developed that revolves around two themes. (1) The paradigm is clarified as a democratic political agenda by comparing & contrasting it with other critiques of bureaucracy, eg, those deriving from neoliberalism & neoconservatism. (2) The problematic & contradictory nature of this agenda is explored, with particular reference to the foundationalism of bureaucratic rationality & similar problems of grounding in relation to democratic rationality. An attempt is made to suggest a way forward for the movement based on an explicit understanding of a democratic political order, & a thoroughly "ironic" & nonfoundational approach to research & education. 28 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: PPPs and the Changing Public Sector Ethos: Case-Study Evidence from the Health and Local Authority Sectors
authors: Hebson, Gail; Grimshaw, Damian; Marchington, Mick
abstract: This article explores the extent to which a new contractual approach to delivering public services, through public private partnerships (PPPs), is transforming the traditional values underpinning the public sector ethos among both managers & workers. Drawing on two detailed case studies of PPPs -- a Private Finance Initiative in the health sector & the outsourcing of housing benefit claims in the local government sector -- we identify a range of new pressures impacting on five key elements of a traditional notion of the public sector ethos. Our findings demonstrate that the contractual relations of PPPs have led to a clear weakening of traditional notions of managerial accountability & bureaucratic behaviour, reflecting both a shift to new lines of accountability (private sector shareholders) & a vicious circle of monitoring & distrust between partner organizations, in place of the old faith in bureaucratic process. Among workers, certain traditional values -- especially a concern for working in the public interest -- continue to inform the way they identify with, & understand, their work in delivering public services. However, the cost cutting & work intensification associated with PPPs present a significant threat to these values. The article identifies examples of short-term resilience of the traditional public sector ethos, as well as developments that threaten its long-term survival. 1 Figure, 26 References. [Copyright 2003 Sage Publications Ltd.]

title: From Bureaucracy to L'Imaginaire: Cornelius Castoriadis' Immanent Critique of Marxism
abstract: A critical survey of the work of French social theorist Cornelius Castoriadis is presented, with particular attention paid to his critique of Marxism, & his development of a social ontology, L'Institution imaginaire, which presents social life as a dialectical struggle between creativity & identity. Perceiving modern capitalism as a bureaucratic social regime, Castoriadis finds that Marxism inadequately accounts for this social formation. He also faults Marxism on political & philosophical issues, & finds it incompatible with revolutionary rhetoric. Ironically, Castoriadis's own theory incorporates basic Marxist notions & renders his critique problematic. In What Is Important, Cornelius Castoriadis expresses concern for the gap between workers & intellectuals who write for workers, workers' failure to recognize their own importance, & the mistaken adherence to capitalist ideology revealed by both intellectual rhetoric & worker attitudes. In Hierarchy of Salaries and Incomes, Castoriadis examines the concept of worker control of production, or self-management, the arbitrary forces that determine income hierarchies & inequities, & misconceptions about the justification for hierarchies, eg, those held by workers. Modified AA.

title: THE DEVELOPMENT AND DECLINE OF PATRIMONIAL AND BUREAUCRATIC ADMINISTRATIONS
abstract: M. Weber's broad-gauge theory of the development of admin, though largely neglected by soc sci'ts is still useful. By confronting Weber's theory with recent empirical work, an attempt is made to evaluate its present sci'fic status. Weber's failure to forecast correctly the current decline of bur'cy in US society is only one of the shortcomings of his theory. But it achieves much, raises many researchable problems, & deserves reclaiming & refining. AA.

title: Embarking on self-directed support in Scotland: a focused scoping review of the literature
authors: Manthorpe, Jill; Martineau, Stephen; Ridley, Julie; Cornes, Michelle; Rosengard, Ann; Hunter, Susan
abstract: This article presents findings from a focused scoping review of the published literature on self-directed support (SDS), the term adopted by the Scottish Government to refer to its policy to improve social care outcomes and choices for people using publicly funded services and to distinguish it from personalisation, the term more commonly used in England, and from consumer-directed-care and cash for counselling. The review was undertaken to inform an evaluation of the early adopters of SDS, funded by the Scottish Government 2009-2011, and was updated with later literature. It focused on the evidence base available to inform the Test Sites' (pilot local authorities) efforts to reduce bureaucracy or 'red tape' for people choosing their own social care and support; the available evidence about leadership and training to support these changes and about the use of specific transitional funding to ease the process of implementation. The findings of the literature review around these three themes are presented and discussed. The article concludes with a discussion of the potential for such focused literature reviews to inform policy-makers, researchers, and social work practitioners across Europe of the options available when seeking to combine rapid yet rigorous approaches to evidence. Adapted from the source document.

title: Broken Hierarchies, Quasi-markets and Supported Networks -- A Governance Experiment in the Second Tier of Germany's Public Employment Service
abstract: From 2005 to 2015, the German government implemented a special programme for jobseekers aged 50 plus and receiving minimum income benefits. Descriptive comparisons and econometric evaluation indicate that this programme was more effective and cost-efficient than the German jobcentres' standard operations. However, our evaluation did not ascertain any particular instrument or technique which would explain this accomplishment. Rather, the formula for success appears to be hidden in the governance and design of the programme which differed markedly from routine support. Network-type governance mechanisms as applied in this programme appear to have served as an expedient in circumstances where hierarchical steering is no longer feasible. This article explains how the governance dilemma of the German Public Employment Service's 'second tier' (serving recipients of minimum income benefits) probably triggered the innovative approach so successfully pursued in the programme under consideration. The analysis is concluded by proposing some conceptual clarifications for the long-standing debate about hierarchies/bureaucracies, markets and networks in the governance of welfare programmes. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Mexican State and Democracy: The Ambiguities of Corporatism
abstract: The bureaucratic-authoritarian approach (eg, see O'Donnell, Guillermo, El estado burocratico-autoritario: Argentina, 1966-1973 [The Bureaucratic-Authoritarian State: Argentina, 1966-1973], Buenos Aires: Editorial de Belgrano, 1982) to the authoritarian state is discussed, focusing on its main analytical dimensions, hypotheses, & theoretical underpinnings, the feasibility of applying this model to the Mexican case, & its eventual utility for explaining the process of policy making in Mexico. It is concluded that O'Donnell's bureaucratic-authoritarian state model is not appropriate to understand the Mexican state. Civilian domination in Mexico, based on a government party, presidentialism, a mystifying government rhetoric & an ideology based on a popular revolution, & active, although carefully monitored & controlled, participation of workers, does not fit very well with the bureaucratic-authoritarian state model, which is considered a system of political exclusion, sharp denial of the citizenship, a high level of repression, & attempts to depoliticize via technocratic officialdom. 89 References. Modified AA

title: The Personal Side of Street-Level Bureaucracy: Discrimination or Neutral Competence?
abstract: Despite much evidence that municipal services are delivered usually without significant SC bias, suspicions remain that administrators discriminate against the disadvantaged, particularly in one-to-one citizen-administrator interactions. Evidence of that possibility is developed by examining how helpfully & courteously citizens feel they have been treated on a broad range of contacts with the municipal bureaucracy in Cincinnati, Ohio. Data from telephone interviews with 3,334 adult residents suggest some areas of possible racial discrimination in bureaucratic treatment of citizens but no discrimination by income. In addition, much of the apparent racial discrimination results from blacks bringing more difficult problems to the bureaucracy, not from bureaucrats giving less consideration to them. Municipal administrators appear to exercise neutral competence in their dealings with citizens. 5 Tables, 23 References. Modified HA

title: Bureaucratic Promotion Criteria
abstract: Three hypotheses regarding the relative significance public bureaucracies assign to evaluations, examinations, & seniority in making promotions are examined. The control proposition asserts that the bureau's authority structure state is an important factor; the technical uncertainty proposition assumes that nature & variety of organizational skills & tasks play a dominant role. Against these propositions emphasizing emergent internal structural conditions, a legal-institutional null hypothesis is posed, explaining promotion criteria in terms of extraorganizational constraints & conditions imposed by civil service regulations & regional differences in experience with merit systems. Based on the Meyer's Finance Bureaucracy Panel Study, two waves of data (1960, 1972) were obtained throughout the US for 240 city, county, & state finance departments. The dependent variable was measured by determining on a scale of 100 points the relative importance of seniority, evaluations by superiors, & examinations in determining promotions. The control proposition indicators measured were executive succession, turnover rate, & length of employee service. Technical uncertainty indicators included professionalization, specialization, functional complexity, & task routinization. Legal-institutional indicators were determined by a dummy variable indicating whether most placements to entry-level nonsupervisory jobs were obtained by civil service or other means. Results indicate that length of service & the professionalization of a bureau's skill structure were the only internal conditions associated with promotion criteria. As an extraorganizational factor, the most powerful predictor of promotion criteria was the governance of a bureau's personnel practice by civil service regulations. While the results provide some support for the control & technical uncertainty propositions, they underscore the significance of extraorganizational factors. The significant effects of regional differences are of special interest because they indicate the degree to which intraorganizational advancement criteria are ultimately shaped by the SE & cultural environment. 1 Figure, 5 Tables. Modified HA.

title: Singapore: The State and the Culture of Excess
abstract: Apparently unsatisfied with the legitimacy acquired from successfully delivering social and efficient administration, the PAP or People's Action Party, which has been in power since Independence, needs to boost its moral authority by personifying the values of sacrifice and incorruptibility in order to command popular support.  [...] the government understands that invoking "community" as a political ideology crucially secures its rule via "moral authority".

title: Between risk and emergency: The increasing police approach in social interventions strategies
authors: Avila Cantos, Debora; Garcia Garcia, Sergio
abstract: Many voices warn us of the eminent end of the social model that shaped the Welfare State as we know it. The disappearance of certain social policies, however, does not mean that others do not appear with great force. In fact, the crisis is none other than the maximum expression of a transformation that has been inching its way forward for years: the appearance of a specifically neoliberal social policy that, while incorporating many elements of the Welfare State, introduces new logic in government and social management. This article is the result of a dialogue between the works of those whose names appear above. Our intention is to untangle what we consider to be one of the central transformations in social policy on the neoliberal path: the shift towards an ever-increasing police-like approach in the management of the population. This shift (which actually goes two ways as it includes on the one hand, the make-over of police to make them appear more like social work professionals, while at the same time, the introduction of a police-like mindset into the social intervention sector), directly responds to the demands of the new government philosophy that is brought forth by neoliberal social policies. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Civil-Military Divide in Protracted Small War: An Alternative View of Military Leadership Preferences and War Termination
abstract: This article examines the basis of military leadership preferences toward war termination, and thus the basis of the associated civil-military divide, within the context of protracted small war. The conventional wisdom posits military leadership preferences as a near-constant in favor of persistence and thus expects a dominant pattern of military obstructionism. However, such a pattern does not hold empirically across the population of small wars. This gap between expectation and evidence derives at least in part from the limits of the bureaucratic-organizational model, focused on the military's desire for resources, autonomy, and influence, that underlies the conventional wisdom. In contrast, this article suggests an alternative model privileging the demands of institutional legitimacy. The legitimacy motive as conceptualized here is particularly salient to the small war context. It accordingly provides a foundation for better understanding variation in military leadership preferences toward war termination and thus variation in the direction and intensity of the civil-military divide. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Bureaucracy and Modernization in China: The Maoist Critique
abstract: A comparison of the conceptions of org held in the West, particularly those stemming from Weberian rational bur'cy, with the Maoist org'al ideal extolled in China. After analyzing the traits distinguishing the Maoist ideal from these Western conceptions, the author examines the utility of the Maoist ideal as part of a broader strategy of modernization. On the basis of logic & the available empirical evidence, it is concluded that the Maoist ideal is neither utopian & irrational nor the best solution to the org'al problems of modernization in all circumstances. AA.

title: Standing by themselves: Caregivers' strategies to ensure the right to education for children with disabilities in Orange Farm, South Africa
authors: De Sas Kropiwnicki, Zosa O; Elphick, Jean; Elphick, Rosalind
abstract: This article describes the strategies employed by caregivers in accessing the right to education for their children with disabilities in Orange Farm, Gauteng. Children with disabilities are one of South Africa's most vulnerable population groups. Despite enabling legal and policy reform, children with disabilities face unconstitutional attitudinal and environmental barriers to accessing the nonprogressive right to a basic education. This case study examines the caregivers' self-efficacy, agency and the opportunity structures within which they are operating using an interdisciplinary theoretical framework and a qualitative methodology. The article will provide detailed examples of the agentic strategies that caregivers devise, in the face of hostile and unaccommodating bureaucratic institutions, disjointed referral mechanisms, discriminatory norms, stigmatising discourses and unjust power relations.

title: A Silent Revolution by Procedures: Processes of Bureaucratic Integration in the European Community
abstract: The system of the European Community (EC) rests on an order of law with a legitimacy of its own, which is becoming autonomous from the laws of member states & constitutes an administrative body that is developing a distinct functional elite with strong technocratic orientations. It is argued here that the EC's policy-making process, both in content & procedures, is strongly defined by bureaucratic policies.
