CROZIER'S WORK (SEE SA 13:2/65B5079), WHICH OBSERVES THAT ORGANIZATIONAL MODELS ARE CLOSELY CONNECTED WITH INSTITUTIONAL MODELS SUCH AS THE SYSTEM OF EDUCATION OR THE POLITICAL SYSTEM OF A COUNTRY. RESULTS ARE THEN PRESENTED & ANALYZED FROM J. P. DAUBIGNEY & J. J. SILVESTRE, ("COMPARAISON DE LA HIERARCHIE DES SALAIRES ENTRE L'ALLEMAGNE ET LA FRANCE" COMPARISON OF THE SALARY HIERARCHY BETWEEN GERMANY AND FRANCE , AIX-EN-PROVENCE, FRANCE, LABORATORY FOR ECONOMICS & SOCIOLOGY OF LABOR, 1972.) THEY REVEAL 2 'NATIONAL TYPES' OF SALARY STRUCTURE & WORK HIERARCHY RELATED TO DIFFERENT EDUCATION SYSTEMS. MORE WORK IS NEEDED ON THE RELATIONS BETWEEN ORGANIZATIONS & SOCIETY. 3 TABLES. M. MAXFIELD.

title: Knowledge, Practice, and Political Community: The Making of the "Custom" in Turkey
abstract: This article begins with the observation that the honor crime (the murder of a woman by her family because of actual or deemed sexual acts that are considered an offense to the culturally defined terms of family honor) has received increasing attention in Turkey during the last decade. Although Turkish feminists have long worked to raise awareness of the gendered inequality and violence involved, their efforts until recently were met with stark silence. The increased attention given to honor crimes involves little interest in the patriarchal excesses that affect women across class and ethnic groups in Turkey, tending to focus attention, rather, on an essentialized "Kurdish" or "Eastern" culture as the main dynamic behind honor crimes. Blame for the practice is attributed to the intractable customs of backward peoples, customs that are disconnected from discussions of capitalism, state bureaucracy, armed conflict, or familial practice prevalent in Turkey's public sphere. Drawing on extensive archival research and fieldwork, the author argues that the recent focus on the "custom" is symptomatic of a shift from a developmentalist/assimilationist to a cultural/racial imaginary. By looking at the intricate web of practices, meanings, institutions, and policies that make up the Turkish public sphere, this article sheds light on how the custom came to be recognized in Turkey and how familial modes of conduct influence current modes of governing minorities. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Performing 'Legitimate' Torture: Towards a Cultural Pragmatics of Atrocity
abstract: Scholars have traditionally explained away torture as an act of monstrosity. Hannah Arendt has proposed instead a socio-cultural explanation of the phenomenon. Modern rationality, she suggests, constitutes the legitimacy principle that grounds the bureaucracy of repression and that perpetrators can ultimately tap into for the purpose of justifying their deeds. I will suggest, instead, that modern technical rationality is per se not sufficient to justify torture. Rather, to do so, it must undergo a profound transformation as a result of its being linked to deeper moral logics. Linkage, in turn, is a matter of cultural performance. To tackle the question of legitimacy in torture, it is therefore necessary to address its cultural pragmatics. Jeffrey Alexander's latest work on social performance can help in this respect. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications and Thesis Eleven Co-op Ltd, copyright holder.]

title: Approaches to Organization Theory
abstract: The major concepts & most recent trends which have occurred under the headings of systems theory, contingency theory, & subjective-interaction theory (or action approach) are outlined. Recent classifications of contributions to org theory are referred to. Criticisms of functionalism & the systems approach in sociol are reviewed. Alan Dawe (1970) sees the sociol of soc systems & the sociol of soc action as 2 diff disciplines. The latter approach generally rejects the systems model, eg, D. Silverman (THE THEORY OF ORGANIZATIONS: A SOCIOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK, London: Heinemann, 1970). Action theory is based on 3 principles: (a) sociol is concerned with "meaningful action" & not just behavior; (b) particular meanings persist through their reaffirmation in actions; (c) actions can also lead to changes in meanings. The action model looks at roles, relationships, structure, & process. A final category of approach considered is the study of org'al goals. Contemporary work on org'al goals can be subdivided into 3 approaches: (1) those who take a "systems" perspective of the org'; (2) descriptions of goal-oriented behavior which take account of the individual & his motivations, his meaningful actions, his role, & his decision-making process; (3) "action theory" interpretations of goal-oriented behavior. It is concluded that, on the surface, the 3 main trends seem to have little in common; however, a convergence is found in the recent work of some; eg, systems theorists such as Walter Buckley (SOCIOLOGY AND MODERN SYSTEMS THEORY, Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Prentice-Hall, 1967) feel that their model of a soc system must emphasize that patterned interactions arise from meanings & alternative responses to information & are temporary adjustments open to redefinition. Action theorists see the need for action theory to develop concepts to cope with large-scale phenomena. Studies of goals in org's have progressed toward interpretations consistent with the trends in the other 2 Sch's. Contingency theory at present is the least integrated with the other approaches. A Bibliog. M. Maxfield.

title: Social Work with Children and Families: Challenges and Possibilities in the Neo-Liberal World
abstract: The 1970s saw social work as the rising star of the human service professions in the UK. Since then, the profession has been under attack from the media and politicians, this coinciding with changed ideological, political, economic and social circumstances. Practitioners' expertise and effectiveness were questioned and they were blamed for scandals, notably in relation to abused children. There have been changes in their organisation and practice whereby a profession based on knowledge, understanding and skills has become a so-called profession with managers now dominating what practitioners do. Relationship-based work has been transformed into a bureaucratic focus on the assessment of risk and rationing of resources and services, together with a more controlling, moral policing role. Focusing on developments in England in relation to children and families, I argue that, although what remains is a limited version of social work's possibilities, there remains scope for a radical/critical practice that involves working alongside users on the problems they face. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Evaluating a Federal Experiment in Bureaucratic Reform
abstract: A contextual evaluation model was used in assessing a federal program that develops cooperative policy experiments with other government agencies. The two-year Experimental Technology Incentives Program (ETIP) study was commissioned by the National Academy of Sciences to determine whether such a program could stimulate useful changes in the federal bureaucracy. ETIP chose to experiment with minor changes in four policy areas: procurement, regulation, government subsidy, & research & development. Program alterations resulted from the findings; its methodology offers an alternative to traditional evaluation strategies. Modified Author Summary.

title: COMMUNICATION AND REASON: THE CRISIS OF OUR CIVILIZATION
abstract: The evolution of modern society has placed enormous responsibilities on the shoulders of managers of men and women requiring that, we transcend the modern and medieval challenges for effective communication to achieve unity in diversity. This condition is necessitated with the increase of multiplicity of human interests and aspirations. The collapse of ideological forces built on logocentric Greek metaphysics and epistemology glorified rationality and reason above any other transcendental structures of man. The inevitability of arrogance, imposition and supremacy appropriated to reason and rationality made man to become a slave to structures of bureaucratic red tapism that have affected our intellect. The mission of bureaucracy is to achieve efficiency but this goal has been frustrated by the application of reason as the ultimate legislator of results. To this end the communitarians have suggested rational consensus to achieve order and social stability in decision making. This paper therefore addresses the basic problems of rational consensus through communication. Adapted from the source document.

title: Regional Labor Unions in Social Dialog
abstract: A case study methodology was applied in the research project "Deyatel'nost' profsoyuznykh struktur v sovremennoy Rossii: trudovye otnosheniya, sotsial'noe partnerstvo i politicheskoe predstavitel'stvo" (The Functioning of Labor Unions in Contemporary Russia: Labor Relations, Social Partnership, and Political Representation), carried out by the Samara Institute of Comparative Studies of Labor Relations. The nature of trilateral interactions & negotiations between regional labor unions, representatives of regional/federal government, & employers was investigated, finding that labor unions either enter into such relationships as an unequal partner, & often the weakest party of the three, or surrender their role altogether relinquishing their bargaining responsibility to the central level of the union organization. Government representatives play a dominant role, which resembles the situation during the Soviet era when labor unions performed only a symbolic role & functioned as an integral part of the government bureaucracy. This further undermines the credibility of labor unions in the eyes of workers, results in a highly dissatisfied & eroding membership, & leads to low effectiveness of their bargaining power. The closeness between the government & labor unions also distorts the role of the later as they are often manipulated by the former into solving social & labor conflicts benefitting parties other than the workers. 9 References. Z. Dubiel

title: Goals and Structures of Education
abstract: The process of restructuring educ'al instit's (viz, the U) is necessarily proceeding slowly & with difficulty, because: (A) goals & expectations are diffuse & implicit, & (B) restructuring the U meams also restructuring society. Soc sci could facilitate the discussions by clearing up the goals & expectations. A typology of educ'al org is possible, in which 2 types of references are contrasted: (1) the professional model focusing on "expertness," with a hierarchical structure, & (2) multi-functionality with a 'multihierarchical' structure. The latter structure is better adapted to the new type of student & will open possibilities for spontaneity, flexibility & creativity. Educ by interdisciplinary projects could be the org'al structure to effectuate the self-determination model of educ. AA.

title: Voluntary Organizations as New Street-level Bureaucrats: Frontline Struggles of Community Organizations against Bureaucratization in a South Korean Welfare-to-Work Partnership
abstract: In recent years, the role of voluntary organizations in welfare partnership has received considerable critical attention from scholars working in the field. While mainstream debates have valued state-voluntary sector partnership as participatory governance, critical studies have argued that it leads voluntary organizations to serve as a shadow state. The present study, however, contends that partnership does not necessarily entail participatory welfare or the complete subordination of the voluntary sector to the state's bureaucratic system. Rather, as new street-level bureaucrats, voluntary organizations can exercise a degree of autonomy on the frontline despite the bureaucratic constraints engendered by partnership. Through an ethnographic analysis of Korean community organizations engaged as frontline agencies in a welfare-to-work partnership, this study unveils how the former have recreated democratic and inclusive environments in a particular policy setting by organizing non-work activities and transferring administrative authority to recipients. Delineating such street-level practices, this article demonstrates that state-voluntary sector partnerships may be sites of struggle where voluntary organizations continuously strive to actualize participatory governance in diverse and indirect ways. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Institutional Logic of Collusion among Local Governments in China
abstract: A salient organizational phenomenon in the Chinese bureaucracy is collusion among local governments in response to policies and directives from higher authorities; local governments often form alliances to compromise the original intention behind state policies. There are thus significant and persistent deviations and goal displacement in policy implementation. This article develops an organizational analysis and theoretical explanation of this phenomenon. It argues as follows: Collusion among local governments, though informal, is generated and perpetuated by the institutional logic of the Chinese bureaucracy, results from organizational adaptation to its environment, and hence acquires legitimacy and becomes highly institutionalized. In particular, the institutional logic of the Chinese bureaucracy has generated three organizational paradoxes--uniformity in policy making and flexibility in implementation, incentive intensity and goal displacement, bureaucratic impersonality and the personalization of administrative ties--which provide legitimate bases for collusion among local governments. Bureaucratic collusion has been greatly exacerbated in recent years because of the unintended consequences of the centralization of authority and the enforcement of incentive mechanisms in the bureaucracy. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright holder.]

title: Reform at Mexico's National Autonomous University: Hegemony or Bureaucracy
abstract: Although there seems to be a general consensus regarding the need for reform at Mexico's National Autonomous University (UNAM), most attempts in the last 25 years have failed. Here, the limitations & obstacles for university reform at UNAM are analyzed, highlighting established power relations & the bureaucratization process as the main political & structural limitations on change. The dominating system at UNAM is analyzed in historical perspective, emphasizing the cultural elements in the conformation of the dominant discourse & alliance. Confrontation & conflict in the university & against external power structures are shown to be permanent components in the modern history of UNAM. A legitimacy crisis in the governance structure is argued in terms of the erosion of the prevailing dominating system, expressed in the open manifestation of inherent contradictions through social conflicts directed against the bureaucracy; the permanent challenge to rules, regulations, & established procedures; the lack of academic leadership; & internal dissent & deficient articulation in the dominant block. The building of a new hegemony at UNAM (through a redefinition of the concept of university reform, reconstruction of the social fabric, establishment of new constituencies, rebuilding of collegial relations, & founding of a new pact with the Mexican State), is shown to be a unique path toward reform. 29 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Organization Child: Experience Management in a Nursery School
abstract: This paper proposes a relationship between the structure of educ & the major instit'al forms of a society. It posits that in a society characterized by a predominance of bur'tic org's the criteria for health & maturity in a popular psychol'al perspective (neo-Freudian ideology) may correspond with the demands of bur'cy; that the practices of one nursery Sch in implementing this ideology create bur'cy-like experiences for the children in it; & that the behavior of the children in the Sch reflects their experience of a phenomenologically bur'tic world. These propositions are based on participant observation in an Amer nursery Sch for 7 months in a Midwestern town. There were 3 classes of about 20 children each; the children generally came from professional fam's, & the teachers were Coll graduates. The org'al society & concepts of psychol'al health accepted in the 1950's & 1960's are explicated. More permissive, love-oriented techniques which emphasize soc adjustment have been substituted for strict independence demands at early ages, which formerly stressed self-reliance & achievement. Adjustment & belonging rather than competition are stressed by bur'tic parents. The nursery Sch implemented its conception of an appropriate set of experiences for the child. This involved dealing with the children & structuring the environment in such a way as to limit anxiety-producing experiences. Modified HA.

title: Participation, Alienation, and Bureaucracy
abstract: In the post-war period, the works of George Friedmann & Elton Mayo have stimulated empirical research & theoretical study of the problems of human work. Concepts of alienation & participation have dominated in these studies, & in those by P. Blumberg. The "alienation-participation" model elaborated by Blumberg in SOCIOLGIA DELLA PARTECIPAZIONE OPERAIA (Sociology of Worker Participation, Milan, Italy: Franco Angeli, 1972), can be generalized by taking it out of the manual work setting & applying it to society as a whole: not only is the problem of worker's participation is raised here, but the general problem of participation as it involves all social institutions. In the epoch of "HR," there is an acute confrontation between the role of the worker & that of the citizen. The work of R. Bettini on elaborating the "Italian models of participation of the citizen in Public Administration" is referred to as an example of positive effort to integrate theoretical contributions in the field made so far. The recent examples of theoretical advances made by the science of administration show a tendency to confront the problem of interorganizational rapport, but the organization theory attempts to broaden the notion of organization to encompass administrative action & the Durkheimian suggestion of "internal participation." S. Karganovic.

title: Critical Notes toward a Theory of State Bureaucracy
abstract: An attempt to fill the gap in the literature concerning the evolution of state bureaucracy in Latin America & the complexity of its relationship to civil society. Two types of problems are discussed: (1) deficiencies in the existing literature on the analytical level, ie, with respect to the interaction of the major social processes & the dynamics of the state bureaucracy; & (2) the conflicting role of the state bureaucracy in capitalist society, ie, as guardian of the universal order & servant of the dominant class. S. Karganovic.

title: Fairness in Context
abstract: This article is a contribution to the occasional series dealing with a major book that influenced the author. Previous contributors include Stewart Macaulay, John Griffith, William Twining, Carol Harlow, Geoffrey Bindman, Harry Arthurs, and Andre-Jean Arnaud.It describes the author's original encounter and subsequent dialogue with Bureaucratic Justice , by Jerry L. Mashaw which transformed his thinking about administrative justice and shaped the research he conducted over the next 25 years. The article assesses the strengths and weaknesses of Mashaw's approach to administrative justice, describes the author's attempts to modify and extend Mashaw's approach, outlines four case studies conducted by the author, and describes how the United Kingdom government has recently adopted an approach to administrative justice that is very similar to Mashaw's. The article concludes by considering the implications of Mashaw's approach for researchers and policy makers who wish to promote the idea that governments should attempt to treat people fairly. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: A Citizens' AIDS Task Force: Overcoming Obstacles
abstract: This article analyzes the experience of a state-wide Task Force on AIDS using grassroots techniques to construct policy responsive to the needs of people living with HIV. The four primary obstacles to effective policy making were the need (1) to include disenfranchised groups; (2) to avoid the domination of governmental bureaucracy so that community-based organizations could offer solutions, as well as services; (3) to overcome resistance to anonymous testing; and (4) to reach "hard to reach" populations. Task Force members' perspectives colored what were deemed appropriate policies. Members tended to polarize into two groups: those community-based groups and individuals who focused on the needs of people with HIV on one side, and on the other side, more institutional players who wanted to identify and isolate "HIV carriers." The article closes by analyzing the resulting HIV Omnibus Bill. Those who focused on the needs of people with HIV seized the opportunity to draft and successfully pass an omnibus bill through the Arizona Legislature. This success demonstrates that highly organized communities can affect policy making, even to the extent that it offsets more institutionalized power.For a complete reprint of this article contact Haworth Press by telephone (1-800-HAWORTH) or EMAIL (getinfo@haworthpressinc.com). Article copyright The Haworth Press, Inc.

title: Conversation and Knowledge in Bureaucratic Settings
abstract: An account of discourse & bureaucratic process must of necessity confront the question of linkages between the macrostructures of a social order & the microstructures of any communicative act. Focusing on theoretical & analytic issues, a discussion is presented of how the concept of index can be used to provide a capacious yet coherent account of communicative context, one that can be integrated into the more general characterization of social relations provided by the study of institutional ideologies. The argument is illustrated with materials taken from educational studies. Ability grouping & prescriptivism are concentrated on, analyzing both as ideologies that engender a structuring practice with demonstrable effects on the organization of face-to-face communication as well as on the general form of bureaucratic institutions. 44 References. HA

title: Bureaucratic and Political Corruption in Africa: The Public Choice Perspective
abstract: Emizet reviews 'BUREAUCRATIC AND POLITICAL CORRUPTION IN AFRICA: THE PUBLIC CHOICE PERSPECTIVE' by John Mukum Mbaku.

title: Birth and Death Processes of Governmental Bureaus in the United States
abstract: The birth & death process is a classical exponential for governmental bureaus in the United States. The number of bureaus, outside the defense & postal services, is approximately equal to P sub o to the (b-m)t power, where P sub o is the number of bureaus at some time zero, b = .0217 is the birth rate, & m = .0043 is the death rate for time in years. This suggests an absence of predators but no shortage of sustenance for bureaus. The growth in the number of bureaus is not controlled in the executive departments of the United States government; there were 175 such bureaus in 1923 & 394 in 1974. 3 Tables. AA.

title: A BALANCE THEORY OF COORDINATION BETWEEN BUREAUCRATIC ORGANIZATIONS AND COMMUNITY PRIMARY GROUPS
abstract: This theory is based on the idea that both bur 'tic & community primary groups are essential for achieving most tasks in our society. At the same time they have antithetical atmospheres. Therefore, they are best linked when they are at some midpoint of SD. If they are too close, there will be conflicts because of their atmospheres. If they are too far, they will not be able to coordinate to solve their mutual problems. 8 possible mechanisms of coordination are suggested which can link bur'tic org's with community primary groups. The theoretical bases for determining which of these mechanisms tend to close SD & which tends to open distance, & kinds of bur'tic structures which can tolerate each type of coordinating mechanism are indicated. AA.

title: The Context of Public Bureaucracies: An Organizational Analysis of Federal District Courts
abstract: An organizational approach to the study of dispositions in the US District Courts is outlined, focusing on the pressures created by the combination of an increasing demand for service & a relative decline in resources. The functions of courts are identified as adjudication, judicial administration, & policy making. Courts are described in terms of eight organizational characteristics: (1) networks of organized activities with a mixed collegial & bureaucratic authority structure & informal political processes of coordination, (2) heteronomous, (3) a labor-intensive professional service, (4) a branch of government, (5) nonspecialized, (6) passive, (7) vertically & horizontally interrelated with other organizations, & (8) tasks influenced by the demographic, economic, & legal-governmental characteristics of the jurisdictional environment. Theoretically, the output (eg, the volume & nature of dispositions) of courts is determined by the environmental profile & the complexity of the task structure, with fiscal resources & organizational structure as intervening variables. These major organizational dimensions & variables are illustrated with data on the six District Courts of the Second Circuit. A preliminary statistical analysis presents the effects of the jurisdictional environment on various types of filings in all US District Courts in 1950, 1960, & 1973. The results confirm one aspect of the increasing involvement of government in the economy & society: that which is mediated by the federal courts. Increasing governmental presence is evidenced in civil litigation involving the US government as defendant & plaintiff, as well as in the contextual effects on filings of governmental agencies at the federal, state, & local levels. Three types of responses to this crisis of the judiciary are presented: (A) the judicial response, emanating from the law-finding & adjudicatory role of courts, (B) the bureaucratic response, reflecting the progressive transformation of adjudication into administration, & (C) the technocratic response, emerging as a synthesis of adjudication & administration & stressing the policy-making function of courts within the context of the modern American political economy. 8 Tables, 1 Figure. Modified HA.

title: Ethnic Chinese Muslims in Indonesia: An Unfinished Anti-Discrimination Project
abstract: Indonesia is a nation with the world's largest Muslim population. However, ethnic Chinese Muslims constitute a very small minority since the population of ethnic Chinese themselves is very small in Indonesia. For over three decades, Chinese identity in Indonesia has been on the decline, and almost lost due to state repression. There was little room for the Chinese to articulate and express their socio-political interests and identity, including their traditional culture. This paper is an attempt to investigate state discrimination practices against ethnic Chinese, including the Muslims in particular, as a minority group in Indonesia in the post-enactment of the new Citizenship Bill No. 12/2006. The paper argues that even though all ethnic groups are constitutionally guaranteed equal citizenship status, the enactment of the Bill did not automatically eliminate state discriminatory practices at all levels of the bureaucracy from national to local against the Chinese, including particularly the ethnic Chinese Muslims. To guarantee their socio-political security, Chinese Muslims therefore adopted cultural approaches, intensively coordinating with religion-based organisations, including Muslim mass organisations and Islamic non-governmental organisations. Ethnic Chinese Muslims find these cultural approaches important and effective for protecting themselves from any possible anti-Chinese sentiments and discriminations as well as exploitation from either the local communities or the state bureaucracy. Adapted from the source document.

title: Ibn Khaldun's Fourteenth Century Views on Bureaucracy
abstract: A description of the function & dysfunctional behavior of fourteenth-century bureaucratic organizations headed by dynastic rulers, as incisively analyzed by Ibn Khaldun, an outstanding Arab social scientist of that era. Initial dynamics produce good leaders, close to the people; however, economic development brings about corruption & decadence, & a weakening of the administration, now burdened by obsequious "protective strata." The dynamics of change inevitably lead to the fall of dynasties, with new ones waiting in the wings. Ibn Khaldun made some peerless observations, set in the context of his time, but applicable also today. The relationship of his remarks to several modern economic theories is indicated. 26 References. AA

title: Circumventing the Imposed Ceiling: Art Education as Resistance Narrative
abstract: This article stems from a story of arts education advocacy in the midst of a bureaucracy that misunderstood the purpose of art education at the launch of a new elementary school. Contemporary visual arts education practices overlap a unique period of change in neighboring social science disciplines, a turn of the tide that involves the embrace of narrative methods to rewrite prevailing working models and paradigms of social science practice. Here at the start of the 21[superscript]st[/superscript] century, art education continues to be practiced in the thrall of a scientific paradigm that misunderstands the greater potential of the arts in education, often imposing a ceiling ill-fitted for arts praxis, arts-based research, or arts pedagogy. The author argues that art education is also at a turn of the tide and surmises some of the unexpected outcomes when new and ex-centric stories of learning and a "pedagogy of possibility" are more thoroughly explored, allowing practitioners to fully rethink an art education practice without taxonomic ceilings and within the shelter of the unexplored labyrinth. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright holder.]

title: Educational credentials, elite dualism, and elite stratification in China
abstract: Despite the general consensus on the importance of university degrees in leadership selection, researchers in elite studies have not focused on how education differentiates and stratifies elites. Using a 1994 data set on top Chinese leaders, Zang shows different effects of educational credentials on elite stratification in two major bureaucratic structures in China.

title: The Struggles of Public Intellectuals in Australia: What Do They Tell Us About Contemporary Australia and the Australian 'Political Public Sphere'?
abstract: In the light of Markus's notion of the decent society, this contribution examines the challenges facing public intellectuals in Australia's contemporary political public sphere. It observes, firstly, that Australia has a distinctly Benthamite political culture that listens more to bureaucratic solutions than to metaphysics, history and arguments grounded in human rights. It explains, secondly, how public opinion gives voice to underlying norms and should thus be treated as the starting point for intellectual activism. Thirdly, the article looks into confusion on the criteria for political deliberation in contemporary Australia. Consideration is then given to the growing constraints imposed on public intellectuals through various new forms of censorship and closure. The conclusion uses the gathering debates on adjustment to climate change to illustrate how public intellectual activism can break new ground. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Bureaucracies and Community Planning
abstract: Personal observations made while working in several Wash, DC agencies make possible an unusual opportunity to compare some sociological concepts & theories about bureaucracies with the realities of bureaucratic life. 4 propositions about public bureaucracies can be put forth. (1) They are usually pluralistically organized, rather than monolitic. (2) Because of diffusion of power, they have greater difficulty initiating collective action & bringing it to a successful conclusion than they do preventing such action. (3) Because of their difficulties in achieving collective action, public bureaucracies are almost incapable institutionally of solving the problems of communities. (4) Major modifications must be made in the way American public bureaucracies function if comprehensive solutions to community problems are to be implemented. This latter point will not be easily or readily accomplished. One useful long-term solution might be to combine the philosophy built into the Allied Services Act with revenue sharing--with the states & local governments determining how to implement federal priorities. Modified HA.

title: Confidence in the police: Balancing public image with community safety - A comparative review of the literature
abstract: Examining the evolution of British and Australian policing, this comparative review of the literature considers the historical underpinnings of policing in these two countries and the impact of community legitimacy derived from the early concepts of policing by consent. Using the August 2011 disorder in Britain as a lens, this paper considers whether, in striving to maintain community confidence, undue emphasis is placed on the police's public image at the expense of community safety. Examining the path of policing reform, the impact of bureaucracy on policing and the evolving debate surrounding police performance, this review suggests that, while largely delivering on the ideal of an ethical and strong police force, a preoccupation with self-image may in fact result in tarnishing the very thing British and Australian police forces strive to achieve -- their standing with the public. This paper advocates for a more realistic goal of gaining public respect rather than affection in order to achieve the difficult balance between maintaining trust and respect as an approachable, ethical entity providing firm, confident policing in this ever-evolving, modern society. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Formal Organizations Faced with Conflict in Recent US Sociological Studies
abstract: Up to the present, the sociol of US org's has almost totally ignored the problems of conflicts, concentrating on command structures & leadership. The antagonisms which actually characterize US society have led to a consideration of conflictual data. The Dec, 1961 issue of Administrative Science Quarterly, furnishes an example of this evolution. One discovers therein diverse theories which are useful to compare with the first-mentioned current of res. Traditional sociol, which leaves serious conflicts by the wayside, is not extensive enough to allow the interpretation of current antagonisms & instit'al crises. IPSA Tr by A. Potter.

title: Sociological Analysis of Professionalism: Past, Present and Future
abstract: For a long time, sociological analysis of professional work has differentiated professionalism as a special means of organizing work and controlling workers and in contrast to the hierarchical, bureaucratic and managerial controls of industrial and commercial organizations. But professional work is changing and being changed as increasingly professionals (such as doctors, nurses, teachers, social workers) now work in employing organizations; lawyers and accountants in large professional service firms (PSFs) and sometimes in international and commercial organizations; pharmacists in national (retailing) companies; and engineers, journalists, performing artists, the armed forces and police find occupational control of their work and discretionary decision-making increasingly difficult to sustain. This paper begins with a section on defining the field and clarifying concepts. This is followed by a second section on the concept of professionalism, its history and current developments. The third section discusses convergences between Anglo-American and Continental European systems of professions and the general, wider applicability of particular explanatory theories and analytical concepts in the field. Section four examines internationalizing processes affecting professions. Markets for professional services are increasingly international and professional regulation is now a matter for international professional federations as well as national and regional states. The final section provides summary and considers consequences for aspects of professionalism as an occupational value in the global world. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Politics and Bureaucracy
abstract: The expanding role of the state, & the increasing delegation of political decisions & authority, make it clear that politics & administration have become enmeshed. Organizational interests, including intraorganizational conflict & interorganizational competition, are examined. The role of bureaucrats in the formulation of policy is considered, along with the public image of the technocrat & the functions of bureaucracies as mediators & participants in interest-group politics. The term "hybrid" is applied to civil servants who have achieved clearly political positions. It is argued that the role of bureaucracy should be analyzed in the context of the political system. 64 References. F. S. J. Ledgister

title: Under the Rainbow: Migration, Precarity and People Power in Post-Apartheid South Africa
abstract: The article focuses on systemic drivers of poverty, inequality and precarious livelihoods. It discusses the transformation of South Africa's labour force management and its migratory system from a centralized management of unfree labour by the apartheid state bureaucracy, to a post-apartheid state of precarity, driven by 'flexploitation'. The nexus of precarious work and a fracturing citizenship is seen to represent a duality of flexibility linking practices of employment and labour control to areas like welfare benefits, citizenship status, political participation and informal livelihoods. This is applicable to migrants and natives alike, but with migrants being particularly flexible. The author connects the issue of precarity with politics of xenophobia seen as a stratagem for the retaining of hegemony confronting looming labour struggles and an insurgent citizenship of the poor. The argument revolves around precarity as representing a rallying point for resistance as well as a social condition.

title: Rules, Red Tape, and Paperwork: The Archeology of State Control over Migrants
abstract: Conventional accounts of a drastic shift to migration restriction after World War I following a golden era of free movement obscure crucial processes of state formation around matters of administering migration. How and with what consequences did state control over migration become acceptable and possible after the Great War? Existing studies have centered on core countries of immigration and thus underestimate the degree to which legitimate state capacities have developed in a political field spanning sending and receiving countries with similar designs on the same international migrants. Relying on archival research, and an examination of the migratory field constituted by two quintessential emigration countries (Italy and Spain), and a traditional immigration country (Argentina) since the mid-nineteenth century, this article argues that widespread acceptance of migration control as an administrative domain rightfully under states' purview, and the development of attendant capacities have derived from legal, organizational, and administrative mechanisms crafted by state actors in response to the challenges posed by mass migration. Concretely, these countries codified migration and nationality laws, built, took over, and revamped migration-related organizations, and administratively encaged mobile people through official paperwork. The nature of efforts to evade official checks on mobility implicitly signaled the acceptance of migration control as a bona fide administrative domain. In more routine migration management, states legitimate capacity has had unforeseen intermediate- and long-term consequences such as the subjection of migrants (and, because of ius sanguinis nationality laws, sometimes their descendants) to other states' administrative influence and the generation of conditions for dual citizenship. Study findings challenge scholarship that implicitly views states as constant factors conditioning migration flows, rather than as developing institutions with historically variable regulatory abilities and legitimacy. It extends current work by specifying mechanism used by state actors to establish migration as an accepted administrative domain. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Linking Organization and Mobilization: Michels's Iron Law of Oligarchy Reconsidered
abstract: The key assumptions of Robert Michels's iron law of oligarchy (1908) are specified & tested using two data sets that focus on collective protest & the evolution of organizational features of German new social movement groups, 1950-1994. With some significant exceptions, the data support Michels's theory. Movements tend to become more centralized-bureaucratic & more moderate in their actions over time. There is also a negative correlation between bureaucratization & radicalization. Findings suggest that informal groups are more radical than formal organizations. Also, new social movements that are less formalized & centralized tend to be more radical in their protest actions than older movements. Within the new social movements themselves, those that are less formalized & centralized tend to be more radical. However, both theoretical reasoning & close inspection of the data lead to the conclusion that there is no such thing as an "iron law" at work. Informal groups can be moderate in their activities, & formal groups can tend toward radical action. Also, some of the national environment organizations investigated became more moderate over time while others did not. Groups do not necessarily become more orderly with age. Organizational features influence but do not determine forms of action. 9 Tables, 1 Figure, 56 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Autonomía integrada y el poder discrecional de las burocracias: evidencias de un programa de riesgo geológico en Belo Horizonte, Brasil/Embedded autonomy and discretionary power of bureaucracies: evidences from an urban geological risk management program in Belo Horizonte, Brazil
authors: Higgins, Silvio SaIej; Pinto, Ana Marcelu Ardila; Bragato, Josiane
abstract: During its redemocratization process, Brazil was the stage for social struggles for urban reform and the right to decent housing for the poor. Among the large state capitals, Belo Horizonte stands out for having a specific program for resetting families in situations of geological risk: the Structural Program for Risk Areas (PEAR). We conduct a sociological analysis of the flexible action of the PEAR bureaucracies working in low income communities. Armed with the concepts of embedded autonomy and street- level bureaucracy, we identify the agendas of behavior that emerge from tension in the exercise of the functions of this bureaucratic corps: the PEAR employees coordinate collective action and mediate conflict, while they administer scarce resources.

title: The Politics of Control in Kenya: Understanding the Bureaucratic-Executive State, 1952-78
abstract: Colonial rule in Kenya witnessed the emergence of a profoundly unbalanced institutional landscape. With all capacity resided in a strong prefectural provincial administration, political parties remained underdeveloped. The co-option of sympathetic African elites during the colonial twilight into the bureaucracy, the legislature & the private property-based economy meant that the allies of colonialism & representatives of transnational capital were able to reap the benefits of independence. In the late colonial period these elites not only attained the means of production, they also assumed the political & institutional capacity to reproduce their dominance. The post-colonial state must therefore be seen as a representation of the interests protected & promoted during the latter years of colonial rule. Under Jomo Kenyatta, the post-colonial state represented a 'pact-of-domination' between transnational capital, the elite & the executive. The ability of this coalition to reproduce itself over time lay in its capacity to demobilise popular forces, especially those elements of the nationalist movement that questioned both the social & economic cleavages of the post-colonial state. Whilst Kenya may have experienced changes to both the executive & legislature, the structure of the state itself has demonstrated remarkable continuity. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Max Weber's Sociology of Law: Judge as Mediator
abstract: The substantive underpinnings of Max Weber's 'Sociology of Law' and the standing of judges therein are discussed. Foregrounding his conception of the administration of justice, perennial concern with the correlation between personality and the structure of domination, and account of legal rationalization, his discernment of the vital adjudicative role assumed by judges and the bearing of their personal qualifications is elucidated. The focus is placed on Weber's putatively negative assessment of the Common Law. Reading his appraisal of precedent and the charismatic stature of the judge in light of his theory of casuistry and critique of bureaucracy, it is shown that his examination implicitly extols the English administration of justice. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright]

title: Development and the State in Post-Colonial Algeria
abstract: After briefly reviewing four stages of state formation in Algeria, the role of the bureaucracy in development is assessed. It is shown that the state owns the significant means of production & has used the bureaucracy to implement its statist model of development. In so doing, it has emphasized the development of heavy industry & the use of the most advanced technology to promote it. Despite initial high hopes, this model has failed to create jobs for the bulk of the population, led to a heavy reliance on foreign capital, & created large pools of un- & underemployed. Though these problems were staved off for two decades when high oil prices shaped the relationship between bureaucracy & development, the decline of oil prices in the 1980s caused major unrest & turmoil, creating an economic crisis that the state & its bureaucracy are still trying to manage. Modified HA

title: BUREAUCRATIC DI-MORPHISM
abstract: A critical examination of the problems of bur'cy, esp in Italy; in 2 parts-theoretical & practical. The theoretical part proposes a dual concept of bur'cy, adumbrated in M. Weber's distinction between wertrational (rational with reference to values; & zweckrational (rational with reference to purpose). Modern analyses of bur'cy (A. Gouldner, A. Etzioni, etc) yield a distinction between a hierarchical line, where promotion is in accordance with traditional standards, & a technical staff, with promotion based on competence. To test these ideas, an enquiry into the Italian civil service was conducted for the Italian Instit for the Sci of Public Admin (ISAP) in 1964. The bur'cy was tested for 5 variables: impersonality of relations; formal rules: specialization of tasks; standard procedures; alternatives of training & control. In each case, the bur'cy was found deficient in 'staff' factors & fixed in the 'line' tradition. Impersonality is made impossible by traditional personal ties; specialization is summary & approximative; regulations are arbitrary; standards are reduced to irrational following of precedents; the training-control alternative is vitiated by concentration of responsibility & a chaos of consultative commissions. I. Langnas.

title: Who Decides? Who Implements? Political Structure, Governance and Rural Development in Meghalaya, India
abstract: Rural Development is one of the major objectives of India's planning and development. Since 1950 the central government has formulated various rural development programmes or schemes and state governments implement them. The paper explores, whether or not the political structure and governance is serious or competent enough to promote rural development. The paper examines this question based on field-based interactions in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills Districts, and consulting secondary materials. The paper demonstrates that the political structure and governance for rural development is centralised, and controlled by elected representatives and the bureaucracy. The outcome shows that rural development is not taking off, as it should; instead, it is benefiting only a few people at the expense of the rural poor; and the causal factor is the existing political structure and governance. Adapted from the source document.

title: Particularism Reconsidered. Orientation of Action and Institutional Context
abstract: Given that particularism is perceived negatively in contemporary sociology, a particularism freed from such prejudice is considered. The theoretical tradition of social action has given form to the particularism-universalism dilemma, centered in the approaches of Max Weber & Talcott Parsons. In arguing against the prejudice against particularism, the post-Weberian critique of bureaucracy is used, which underlies the diversity of strategic uses the actors can give to particularism & universalism, & points to the existence of both beneficial & perverse particularisms & universalisms. It is shown that both universalism & particularism are equivocal categories that embrace phenomena with very different consequences & meanings. The case of recruitment of university professors in Italy & England is discussed to determine the institutional conditions supporting a distinct kind of particularism. 33 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Research and the Firm in British Industry, 1919-39
abstract: A study based on private papers of Co res dept's & extensive interviews with directors of res of the 1930's which argues that private firm res as opposed to that of the DSIR & other agencies was the leading engine of technical change in British industry in the interwar yrs. Although there were developing res dept's in Britain from the 1890's, the chief spurt of their formation was in the early 1920's. War experience & profits, entrepreneurial succession, the difficulty of modifying large-scale production, & product diff'iation were seen as factors behind this. By 1938 at least (Pounds Sterling)5.4 million was being spent on R&D by private firms. The leading areas were chemicals, engineering & food, & the largest spenders were drugs, electrical engineering & oil. Expenditures ranged from 0.15 to 0.29% of nat'l income. Capital saving was more important than labor saving, but factor prices were not an important element in the motivation of res except possibly in metallurgy. Technical quality was usually a predominant consideration. Res dept's were receptive to outside ideas & through them advances permeated rapidly within the same industry. Industries varied considerably in their use of res assoc's & U's, ranging from the highly engaged food industry to the relatively disengaged photographic & tire industries. With the electrical & dye industries there was a shift in the locus of res from outside to inside the firm. There was a good deal of co-operation between res dept's, esp in engineering & food. Res dept's were also valuable as entrees for graduates into industry, about 33.3% of R&D personnel being graduates. They were also managerial seed beds & a useful sphere for women graduates. Res'ing firms had usually 1,000+ employees, taxation (contrary to common belief) was not an inhibitor of res, nor was the depression, but accountancy att's were. The development of high-level sci outside the U's for the first time was ultimately vital for the ensuing war. AA.

title: "Guten Tag, hier spricht Ihr Bürgerservice, was kann ich fur Sie tun?"; Restrukturierung im KundInnenservice des öffentlichen Sektors und die Auswirkungen auf die Qualität der Beschäftigung
abstract: The aim of this article is to examine a specific aspect of restructuring in the public sector: the implementation of call centres in customer service and its effects on job quality. The trend to organise customer service through call centres gained worldwide importance back in the 1990s. In the public sector it emerges only recently in connection to strategies of 'new public management'. The article presents five international case study organisations from the public sector from Austria, Italy, Great Britain, the Netherlands and Sweden. The article concludes that the implementation of call centres or the outsourcing of customer service to private service providers has severe consequences for the quality of employment in the public sector and in the new -- female dominated -- service sector jobs. This concerns in particular the following three aspects: fragmentation of employment, qualification versus standardisation and interest representation.[PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: SOCIAL INTEGRATION BUREAUCRATIZATION AND THE PROFESSIONS
abstract: The central problem of modern society is the integration of differentiated activities into some kind of meaningful whole. Using occup'al roles as basis and grouping them according to T. Parsons into professional, executive, & labor roles, the relationship to bureaucratization is discussed. In Coll's and U's despite the manifestation of a 'group of equals' pattern, there are stronger pressures towards bureaucratize than in law and medicine. The 'free' professions, crafts, & enterprises seem to be undergoing modification in favor of emerging bureaucratic structures. The paradox is posed that though the functions of executive roles is that of coordination and integration, this is achieved in limited areas, while professional roles (such as law & science) focused on technical competence seem to offer the likeliest bases for societal integration. L. P. Chall.

title: The growth of bureaucracy and alienation in colleges of higher education
abstract: The brief history of colleges of higher education has been characterized by external threats and deep-seated internal conflicts. This article is based mainly upon our combined total of over 30 years as sociologists teaching in colleges of higher education. During the past 20 years we have, therefore, had first-hand experience of the constantly changing and invariably conflicting demands which have been made upon college staff. As participants in this process, it is our impression that colleges have responded to these external pressures in a swift yet disappointingly compliant fashion and in so doing have failed to establish a sufficiently distinctive role.

title: An exploratory study on the potential of social enterprise to act as the institutional glue of network governance
abstract: This study combines two topics of contemporary salience for public administration: social enterprise and governance networks. While operating at different levels, both are institutions which attempt to draw together the three pillars of state, market, and civil society. Nevertheless, the respective literatures focus on particular aspects of the three pillars. We connect the two concepts and suggest that some social enterprises can act as the institutional glue of networks due to their ability to benefit organizations in each of the three sectors. This requires social enterprises to have the managerial capacity to diffuse social know-how, and is facilitated by the trust of other organizations and a supportive policy framework. The links are explicated at the conceptual level before providing evidence from South Korea and the UK. Finally, research propositions are offered, which suggest new avenues for future research. [Copyright Elsevier Inc.]

title: A Preventive Approach to Bureaucracy: The Dialectical Organization as a Model for Citizen's Advocacy and Ombudsmen
abstract: Dialectical organizations & citizens' advocacy programs have been suggested as remedies for inherent problems of bureaucracies. "Dialectical organization" is the ideal-type opposite of bureaucracy. Its goals, use of authority, structure, organization, location, staffing, client relationships, & operating procedures are antithetical to the bureaucratic form. "Citizens' advocacy" refers to access, steering, & ombudsman-type complaint-handling programs, providing third-party advocates for citizens in order to counter certain dysfunctional aspects of the modern bureaucratic state. Since citizens' advocacy programs are, in essence, in a conflict relationship with bureaucracies, they should be organized on dialectical principles if they are to maintain their advocacy stance & orientation. The Pa Governor's Branch Office experiment with such a program provides an empirical operationalization of the concept & is instructional regarding the form & content of such organization. 1 Table, 1 Figure, 22 References. AA.

title: Reshaping New Spain: Government and Private Interests in the Colonial Bureaucracy, 1531-1550
abstract: Schwaller reviews Reshaping New Spain: Government and Private Interests in the Colonial Bureaucracy, 1531-1550 by Ethilia Ruiz Medrano.

title: J. D. Kingsley, Representative Bureaucracy
BUREAUCRACY, BUREAUCRATIZATION, AND DEBUREAUCRATIZATION
abstract: Analysis of bur'tic org's as instruments for efficient & effective implementation of goals on the one hand, & for gaining, maintaining, & exercising power on the other are usually separate in the literature & have employed diff sets of concepts & assumptions. Some ways are suggested through which analysis of both these major problems can converge. This can be done through analysis of the conditions which give rise to the development of bur'tic org, analysis of such org's as composite soc systems that are in continuous interaction with their environment, & analysis of the forces in this environment that impinge on these org's. On the basis of these analyses some preliminary hyp's about conditions of development of processes of bureaucratization & their relation to internal structure of bur'tic org's are proposed. IPSA.

title: SCIENTISTS VERSUS ADMINISTRATORS: AN APPROACH TOWARDS ACHIEVING GREATER UNDERSTANDING
authors: Tarkowski, Z M T; Turnbull, A V
abstract: Professional sci'ts & professional admin'ors often lack sympathy for each other's points of view, esp in large org's. The Treasury organizes conferences on org & management for senior sci'fic & professional officers & admin'ors. One obstacle is lack of a common language; sci'fic officers have little knowledge of the admin've machine, & admin've officers no experience of sci'fic res & the sci'fic outlook. Similarly there are marked psychol'al diff's in the 2 points of view, sci'fic res entailing an intellectual enthusiasm & attitude that contrasts with the admin've officer's preoccupation with protecting his minister, avoiding mistakes, & coordinating conflicting interests. One method of breaking down barriers in communication is case study methods of training for junior officers. This must be carefully & realistically carried out, & has been done successfully on lines detailed in this article_ TPSA.

title: Integrating Agriculture and Environment in Spain. On the New Spanish Ministry of Environment and Rural Areas and Fishery
abstract: This article analyses some factors explaining the creation of the new Ministry of Environment & Rural Areas, & Fishery in Spain, which has implied the suppression of the former ministries of Agriculture & Environment. The author thinks this decision of President Zapatero could be explained by the political & economic changes that are undergoing the international markets of foods & that are opening a new political scenario where the farming production becomes a priority again for national governments. The author also considers that after two decades in Spain where the separated management of agriculture & environment in two different government departments had provoked negative effects on the development of natural areas. This is another reason why the President Zapatero has decided to integrate again environment & agriculture in a new minister. Finally, the author thinks the existence of this new Ministry of Environment & Rural Areas, & Fisheries, makes change the old scenario of social interlocution where farmer's unions had the monopoly of representation of agricultural interests, & ecologist organizations that of environmental interests. He beliefs that new scenario will be more open & pluralist than before, allowing other interest groups to participate in the dynamics of interlocution. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucratic Agriculture: Planned Social Change in the GDR
abstract: A critical view of recent organizational change in rural society in the German Democratic Republic (GDR), including the formation of specialized production cooperatives & a more intensive vertical integration in the agroindustrial complex. This more centralized, bureaucratic structure is explained in relation to the historical development of the mode of production, particular immediate problems, & the ideological orientation of the leadership. In contradiction to the harmonious, functionalist interpretation of GDR authors, most contemporary developments serve to expand the bureaucracy, & are likely to increase alienation, thus deepening contradictions in the rural sector, despite certain material achievements. Although before the war, farming areas in the (present-day) GDR were more productive than those of the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG), the reverse is now the case. While some of the deep problems that emerged immediately after collectivization have been overcome, most production comparisons still favor the FRG. The lack of commitment on the part of farmers is explained by their low input on the local level, all major decisions being reserved for central agencies. Thus, genuine progress in eliminating some forms of exploitation has been accompanied by political alienation. 1 Table. Modified HA.

title: Evaluation in Italy: Experience and Prospects
abstract: The management of public affairs in Italy today is characterized by a demand for transparency & accountability, & by a desire to learn to manage the available instruments of intervention. These emphases highlight the need to evaluate the effectiveness & results of policies & programs, which is not, however, matched by adequate knowledge of the methods or by sufficiently creative approaches. This social deficit in evaluation has both a cultural & an organizational origin, discussed here. 9 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: AUTONOMY AND BUREAUCRATIC ORGANIZATION
abstract: Autonomy is regarded as an important dimension of professionalism. A number of investigators claim that bur'tic org limits professional autonomy. This study was undertaken to determine empirically the validity of this claim. The relationship between bur'tic structure & degree of professional autonomy within the client-professional relationship was examined by systematically comparing the perceived autonomy of professionals in 3 types of bur'tic settings, non-bur'tic, moderately bur'tic, & highly bur'tic. The data revealed that those professionals associated with the moderately bur'tic setting are most likely & those in the highly bur'tic setting are least likely to perceive themselves as autonomous. These findings do not support the contention that bur'cy is necessarily detrimental to professional autonomy. HA.

title: Among the Beasts of Burma: Animals and the Politics of Colonial Sensibilities, c. 1840-1940
abstract: According to imperial writings, the Burmese were too close to animals, both physically and emotionally. It was claimed that some Burmese people had innate connections to animals, notably elephant-drivers with their elephants. British writers were also intrigued but disgusted by what they deemed to be inappropriate interactions with animals, recounting apocryphal tales of women breastfeeding orphaned non-human mammals. But despite these negative portrayals of human-animal relations, imperial texts also betray their authors' own material and sentimental ties to animals. Their adoration of their pets and their sufferance of pests both served to embed them in the colony. Using insights drawn from animal history, sensory history, postcolonial theory and historical geography, this article explores how these felt encounters with animals were mediated in colonial discourse. I argue that uncovering these hitherto overlooked affective colonial relationships with animals is necessary to contextualize histories that have primarily focused on the emergence of scientific and bureaucratic imperial representations of nature.

title: Public-Sector Management Today: Advanced Differentiation and Early Institutionalization
abstract: Four central questions concerning a conceptually & politically turbulent & troubled area of inquiry & practice -- public sector management (PSM) -- are addressed: What is PSM? How has it been approached? What complicates PSM research? What are some immediate research priorities? Four major approaches to PSM are examined, & debate over its generic vs particularistic character is summarized. Problems with encompassing policy development & implementation within PSM concepts are reviewed, & methodological & theoretical research issues are identified. Focus is descriptive rather than prescriptive due to the current state of the field. 81 References. Modified HA

title: Social Administration Digest: Number Twenty-Six
abstract: The social administration digest reports on various events, publications, & news items that occurred during the months of Feb to Apr, 1977, concerned with the following subjects: social security & income maintenance; public health & the national health service; education, school welfare & youth & community services; housing & Ur development; local authority social work, social services & allied personal services; law & treatment of the offender; employment services; race relations; voluntary effort; & local government. G. Simpson.

title: The relationship between bureaucracy and workplace friendship
authors: Mao, Hsiao-Yen; Chen, Chien-Yu; Hsieh, Ting-Hua
abstract: The relationship between bureaucracy and workplace friendship remains largely unknown in the organizational literature on workplace friendship. Competing hypotheses for that relationship were proposed. On one hand, bureaucracy's characteristics indicate bureaucratic organizations' attitude is unfavorable to, and thus detracts from, workplace friendship. On the other hand, those characteristics lead to employees' negative feelings at work and thus promote their workplace friendship. Data collected via a questionnaire survey of 408 employees in the medical, education, governmental, and banking sectors show that bureaucracy is negatively related to workplace friendship. Our finding provides an organizational perspective, a different angle from the factors of employees' perspective in the extant literature, from which to view and manage the issue of the decrease of workplace friendship in the organization. Adapted from the source document.

title: Why the Soviet Bureaucracy Is Not a New Ruling Class
abstract: In 'Is There a Ruling Class in the USSR?' (see abstract in this section) Paul M. Sweezy discusses the Russian Revolution in terms of the Trotskyist interpretation of Marxism. Sweezy has criticized the thesis that the fate of the USSR & the issue of its developed bureaucracy remain unsettled questions; he has claimed that long-term extensions of the theory are mistaken. Sweezy is himself mistaken in his priority on the issue of time, when basic questions are really of contemporary trends of development. While there has not been a victorious proletarian revolution in an advanced country, there have been significant post-World War II gains by the proletariat worldwide. The social crises evinced in the USSR & in the Western capitalist nations are not Marxist ones, but are those of the bureaucratic dictatorship. In Paul Sweezy Replies to Ernest Mandel, Paul M. Sweezy frames a question about true ownership of the state following the abolition of private property & the disappearance of the bourgeoisie. Three possibilities are discussed: (1) a state owned by the proletariat, (2) one owned by an administrative or bureaucratic staff, or (3) one controlled by a ruling class. Criteria for a new theory of class are provided which are not considered in Marxism. D. Dunseath.

title: Trust and Managerial Problem Solving
abstract: The paper presents a model of trust & its interaction with information flow, influence & control, & reports on an exp based on the model to test several hyp's about problem-solving effectiveness. The S's were managers (N=64) & the independent variable was the individual manager's initial level of trust. Groups of business executives were given identical factual information about a difficult mfg-marketing policy program; half the groups were briefed to expect trusting behavior, the other half to expect untrusting behavior. There were highly signif diff's in effectiveness between the high-trust groups & the low-trust groups in the clarification of goals, the reality of information exchanged, the scope of search for solutions, & the commitment of managers to implement solutions. The findings indicate that shared trust or lack of trust apparently are a signif determinant of managerial problem-solving effectiveness. Modified HA.

title: Anatomy of a Care Manager
abstract: The article considers the impact of the NHS & Community Care Act (1990), & the redefined role of 'care manager', upon social work. It draws from a three-year ethnographic study of five area teams; one based in inner London & the others, including a hospital team, based in the north of England. Particularly it uncovers the considerable impact of intense bureaucracy, circumscribed budgets & the consequential removal of the care manager from the community. The article also questions any 'seamless service' in work with other professionals & raises doubts as to whether need is even being partially met. Care managers are rarely able to utilize the skills that they develop during the Diploma in Social Work course. Frustration is felt on behalf of staff in the area office, who are now working under considerable strain, with little recognition, within what resembles a new emergency service. It is hoped the article is able to draw attention to the consequences of the continued deskilling of social work & retrenchment of what little remains of welfare. 28 References. [Copyright 2003 Sage Publications Ltd.]

title: A CLASS ANALYSIS OF THE BUREAUCRATIC PROCESS IN MALI
abstract: The impact of colonization had varying results according to the native soc structures which it met & according to the degree of econ transformation which it brought about. In Mali, prior to French colonization, a native aristocratic & slave society was in the process of developing. This development was frozen by the conquest, but the hitherto dominant aristocracy was maintained in an inferior, menial gov position. The lack of industr development did not permit the emergence of capitalist classes, while admin'ive growth gave rise to a comparatively numerous & able bur'cy. African trade remained in the hands of a rich but illiterate Malian bourgeoisie. The colonial crisis abruptly brought these forces into competition for power. with the victory of the bur'cy as the outcome. The Malian case illustrates the fact that the concept of SC is a valid instrument of analysis, given that the soc evolution of dependent countries is not considered in isolation but as part of the broader soc system constituted by the econ sphere of influence of the dominant foreign power. IPSA.

title: MITIGATED BUREAUCRACY
abstract: The Philippine gov, bur'tic in org, is both paternal & personal. This coexistence of paternalism & bur'cy is rooted in the perceived right to appeal to an authoritative gov official; the general nature of dominant subordinate relations in society; & the high degree of 'familism.' The prevailing concept of gov is thus founded on Filipino culture patterns which predate the Spanish & US occup's. D. Cooperman.

title: On Socialist Bureaucracy
abstract: The organizational & management conditions of the communist countries justified Max Weber's forecast of intensifying bureaucracy, simultaneously refuting the fundamental hypotheses of Marxist ideology. Yet the bureaucracy encountered in Eastern Europe differs substantially from the Western type of bureaucracy described by Weber. Communist bureaucracy was distinguished by its ideological dominance & monopoly of power held by the Communist party. Additional features included centralization of authority, the doubling of management & control in the party hierarchy, the politicization of bureaucracy, the restriction of skills by political limitations, & the consequent dilution of inter- & intraorganizational authority relations. In Hungary it will be much easier to freely elect a new parliament than to develop a professional, functional, & efficient bureaucracy. Adapted from the source document.

title: Divination and Power: A Multiregional View of the Development of Oracle Bone Divination in Early China/Comments/Reply
authors: Flad, Rowan K; Allan, Sarah; Campbell, Rod; Chen, Xingcan; Falkenhausen, Lothar von; Fang, Hui; Fiskesjö, Magnus; Jing, Zhichun; Keightley, David N; Kyriakidis, Evangelos; Smith, Adam; Peek, Philip M
abstract: Divination is a ritual practice frequently employed as a source of social and political power. Elaborate forms of divination can be crucial to state control and have widespread influence. In ancient China as elsewhere, divination was the domain of ritual specialists who used their skills to mediate uncertainty, but the role that these specialists played in society differed considerably from one place to another. An examination of divination remains from the Neolithic, Shang, and Zhou periods of China suggests that more elaborate divination procedures are associated with bureaucratic institutions as a source of state power. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Barriers to the Process of Awarding and Implementation of EU Funds and Systemic Mechanisms in the Late Welfare State. The Case of Poland
authors: Bukowski, Andrzej; Gadowska, Kaja; Polak, Paulina
abstract: The article deals with the issue of structural & cohesion funding by the European Union in Poland. Although all funds earmarked for the first programming period 2004-2006 were allocated, the process posed certain problems. Therefore, in our paper we point to the weaknesses of the system & some of the hindrances to efficient fund allocation: faulty institutional & legal framework, bureaucracy, corruption & personnel deficits. We base our findings on a research incorporating 150 in-depth interviews carried out in four regions of Poland. Referring to Niklas Luhmann's theory of autopoietic systems, we present a sketch of an unevenly differentiated political system, in which administration & politics prevail over the underprivileged public, incapable of counteracting trends of politicization & bureaucratization. By showing the evolution & reproduction of the system, we relate to its deficits & their impact on the future use of the EU funds inflow. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: 从“官吏分途”到“群体三分”：中国地方治理的人事结构转换及其政治效应——对周雪光《从“官吏分途”到“层级分流”：帝国逻辑下的中国官僚人事制度》一文的一个补充 / From Stratification between Officials and Staff to Three Group Divisions: Personnel Management Structure Change and Its Political Impact in Chinese Local Governance - A Complement to Xueguang Zhou's "Between 'Officials' and 'Local Staff': The Logic of the Empire and Personnel Management in the Chinese Bureaucracy"
abstract: The institutionalized stratification between officials and staff in imperial China has its continuity and transformation in modern Chinese state bureaucracy. One example is the compartmentalization of three groups in Chinese bureaucracy: bureaucrats, derivative staff, and employed staff. This "three-group" structure is more in the same spirit with "stratification between officials and staff" than "stratification at different levels", the two cornerstones of imperial local and grassroots governance as discussed in Xueguang Zhou's works. Under the inflexible "personnel quota" system, bureaucrats and derived staff are a constant in the structure while employed staff is a changeable variable. The difference among three groups resembles the difference between officials and staff in imperial China. The bureaucrats and derivative staff are elites or cadres sorted through the system of stratification at different levels and they are the key players in local governance in today's China. In addition to its historical root, this "three-group" structure is a result of the interaction between the "visible hand" of the state and the "invisible hand" of market. People who belong to the first two group are not only "rational men" but also men driven by their political mission and commitment. This explains the phenomenon of "mobile officials" and "immobile staff", thus is a complement both to Zhou's "stratification at different levels" and to the so-called "tournament model". We hope this study provides an important theoretical perspective for understanding contemporary China's transition and rise.

title: The Fraser Government's "Uranium Decision" and the Foundations of Australian Non-Proliferation Policy: A Reappraisal*
abstract: The Fraser era represents a defining moment in Australia's approach to the issues of uranium exports and non-proliferation policy. In contrast to some well-established positions in the literature, this essay argues that the Fraser government's August 1977 decision to approve the export of uranium was framed not only by domestic political considerations stemming from the Ranger Environmental Inquiry but also by important international factors. In particular, I argue that the non-proliferation initiatives of the Carter administration presented the Fraser government with an opportunity to portray the export of Australian uranium as means to strengthen the non-proliferation regime and enhance Australia's influence. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Instituting Europe: Germany, the Union, and the Legacy of the Short Century
abstract: Asserts that the large questions confronting Germany & the European Union after the 20th century are cultural differences in each country's population & how leaders deal with the powerful European Union bureaucracy in Brussels. After 1989, European countries have seen large growth in the immigrant population. The rise of ethnonationalism after the fall of the Berlin wall is examined, & it is argued that new mythologies must be created to avoid the dangers of ethnopolitics. Werz suggests looking to the US, as it has made much use of invented tradition to create a cohesive nation out of disparate ethnic groups.
