The purpose of business leaders is to create loosened communities where people should feel a sense of duty & where, at the same time, a sense of being unique & competitive should remain strongly embedded in individual rationales. 68 References. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright 2003.]

title: Refugee Voices: Exploring the Border Zones between States and State Bureaucracies
abstract: Settled people have been forced to move and nomads have been coerced into settling for as long as there has been history. Until the emergence of the Westphalian concept of the nation (where the state corresponded to the nation, groups of people united by language and culture), movement and mobility were largely recognized and accommodated. However, most contemporary academic disciplines as well as public institutions adopt a particular sedentist perspective on the nation-state. It is commonly recognized that people are displaced and move when political states collapse; they return when political security is restored. The liminal “state” outside the defined territory of the nation-state, where the displaced are found, is regarded as a threat to the world order.1 Predominant theory has been that people must be tied to territory, and thus the durable policy solutions advanced are frequently about resettlement. Reality does not support either current forced migration theory or humanitarian aid practices, however, and an epistemological change in thinking about forced migrants is urgently required. This means looking beyond the nationstate— the purview of most academic work in this area— and beyond traditional barriers between disciplines, to give cross-disciplinary attention to the self-expressions and experiences of forced migrants. Furthermore, the forced migrant creates a dilemma in how aesthetic expression is displayed, as their forms of expression cannot be squarely identified with one state or another. The dispossessed and displaced are changed by their experiences in the grey zones between states, and their migrations cannot be neatly catalogued as belonging to one state or culture.

title: Conception of Bureaucracy of Alfred Weber
abstract: The conflict between the demands of the bureaucratic mentality & principles of bourgeois liberalism was the primary concern in the works of Alfred Weber (1868-1958), whose historical sociology of culture was based more on cultural morphology than on analytical empiricism. Special attention is given to his analysis of the mushrooming bureaucracy of Germany at the turn of the century, where there was a lack of democratic traditions & where the semifeudal nobility used the bureaucracy to help preserve its position. Weber's solutions to the problem of bureaucracy were hopelessly utopian. Similarities to Max Weber & Franz Kafka are noted. 9 References. G. Prostakov

title: Abjection and Organization: Men, Violence, and Management
abstract: The impact of nonorganizational experiences of violence on the behavior of men in organizations is examined from a theoretical background of psychoanalytic & object relations theory & theories of masculinity. Bureaucracies attempt to deny the emotional dimension of their behavior & decision making, creating abjection -- denied experience that cannot be fully suppressed by the subject. The abject is defended through symbolic investment in the ego ideal, manifested in stylized or exaggerated ideas of masculinity or femininity & narcissistic & addictive behaviors. By coming to terms with the denied & unacceptable aspects of themselves & their experience, men in organizations can break this cycle of reproduction of dysfunctional behavior. The psychodynamics underlying the development of abjection, investment in the ego ideal, & narcissistic & addictive behaviors are examined through analysis of film, literature, & biographical data. 41 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Organizations, Internal Labor Market Policies, and Gender Inequality in Workplace Supervisory Authority
abstract: It is generally assumed that bureaucratic labor policies associated with internal labor markets (ILMs) both promote the efficient use of workers' skills & foster equality in the workplace by publicizing managers' decisions & increasing their accountability. Here, survey data from a national probability sample of 727 US workplaces are used to test these assumptions about ILM policies with regard to gender inequality in workplace supervisory authority. Supply-side & occupational segregation are also considered as explanations. Results indicate that occupational segregation accounts for most of the gap in supervisory authority, while purely human capital accounts are insufficient. Other results are consistent with an institutional interpretation -- that organizations adopt ILM policies to symbolically comply with both regulatory bodies & public ideals about workplace opportunity. 5 Tables, 31 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Technical Progress in Bureaucracies
abstract: Asks whether incentives exist to implement technical progress into public goods production as may be observed in the private sector. It is suggested that depending on bureaucrats' preferences two results can be obtained: (1) if bureaucrats maximize their budget or if output or the classical production factors enter their utility function, research & development (R&D) will be used efficiently due to cost reductions increasing the bureaucrats' budget or utility; (2) if bureaucrats prefer R&D as an end itself, they will use this factor like other factors by more than the efficient amount. In both cases an allocative inefficient output of the public good is produced. In result, society cannot benefit from gains by technical progress since net social welfare is appropriated totally by bureaucrats, even if it is increased by R&D efforts. 10 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Together We Shall Be Heard: Exploring the 1981 "Solidarity Day" Mass March
abstract: This article provides the first detailed examination of the "Solidarity Day" march, which was held on September 19, 1981, in Washington, DC. Well funded and well organized, Solidarity Day was a mass protest against President Reagan's policies, particularly his cuts to social programs. Although the march was initiated by the AFL-CIO, participants came from 250 organizations, including 100 unions and a variety of civil rights, religious, and civic groups. Despite an impressive turnout of at least 260,000 people, Solidarity Day has received little scholarly attention. Drawing on unutilized archival records, this article argues that Solidarity Day was a protest that deserves more scholarly-and public-recognition. Solidarity Day showed that the AFL-CIO, which has often been viewed as bureaucratic and conservative, could mobilize mass street protests. It also boosted the morale of many union members, helped to strengthen the leadership of AFL-CIO president Lane Kirkland, and set the precedent for a different kind of AFL-CIO, one that was much more connected to its members. While Kirkland proved unable-or unwilling-to fundamentally reorient the AFL-CIO toward grassroots activism, these ideas were ultimately carried through by John Sweeney, a reformer who won the federation's presidency in 1995.

title: Globalization and the Reconstitution of Local Gender Arrangements
abstract: This article explores how globalization shapes the construction of masculinity among nationalist Indian men, filmgoing men in India, and diasporic Indian men in Fiji. These men are often attracted to transnational media depictions of male violence as the basis of male identity. But bureaucratic transnational forms and transnational media celebrations of cosmopolitan lifestyles also engender anxieties about national identity. Men often handle these anxieties by rooting their own national identity in women's acceptance of food habits, clothing, and gender subordination that men regard as traditional. Although participation in bureaucratic economies is an important source of men's anxieties about globalization, men address these anxieties in the realm of interpersonal gender relations over which they have some control.

title: Strategic Public Management: Case Study of Thailand's Office of the Board of Investment
abstract: Explains how Thailand's Office of the Board of Investment applied the concept of strategic management to cope with external threats & enhance its organizational capacities, shifting from a rule-based authority structure, which granted tax incentives & privileges, to a new form of governance involving provision of information & related services necessary for investment promotion. Organizational restructuring, work process redesign, strong leadership, empowerment, performance measurement, & human resource development were key factors in this successful bureaucratic reform. A lesson drawn is that public organizations can & should be transformed to become more flexible, innovative, & results oriented. 4 Figures, 11 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Organizational Response to Disaster: A Typology of Adaptation and Change
abstract: A time sequenced model of bureaucratic adaptation to a disaster episode is derived from one developed by J. R. Brouillette & E. L. Quarantelli (originally abstracted as SA D8938/ASA/1969/0187). The Brouillette & Quarantelli model does not allow analysis of dynamics of organizational change, nor does it account for planning & normative orientations of disaster subcultures. Using A. H. Barton's taxonomy of disaster phases (Communities in Disaster: A Sociological Analysis of Collective Stress Situations, Garden City, NY: Anchor Books, 1970), a typology is derived that accounts for disaster as a process & includes the expected influences of planning. With this dynamic model, short-term, particularistic, adaptations of the organization can be distinguished from long-term, universalistic, organizational change. The model is then tested on an empirical example based on a recent major flood. Results showed that the typology was applicable; however, some questions were raised as to the generalizability of Barton's typology. Recommendations are also made concerning difficulties encountered in applying the typology. 8 Figures. Modified AA.

title: Patrimonial Alliances and Failures of State Penetration: A Historical Dynamic of Crime, Corruption, Gangs, and Mafias
abstract: The historical shift from patrimonialism to bureaucracy is the key organizational transformation of the past thousand years. Classically, patrimonialism was organization based on private households, plus alliances among them. But there are two types of patrimonial organization: expanded households and patrimonial alliances or pseudo-tribes. The latter include ad hoc warrior coalitions, frequently organized as fictive kin. The main historical cause of the shift from patrimonialism to bureaucracy was the military-fiscal revolution and ensuing state penetration into society. But patrimonial politics did not entirely disappear. In some areas, the state fails to penetrate, leaving the possibility of mafia-style organization. Elsewhere, political machines are a mixed form of incomplete bureaucracy. Gangs are patrimonial organizations, growing in dialectical conflict with bureaucratic penetration and efforts at control. Through a comparison of American, Sicilian, and Russian mafias, the questions considered are whether crime organization recapitulates the history of the state, why some gangs become bigger than others, and why organized crime succeeds or fails in varying degrees. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright The American Academy of Political and Social Science.]

title: Bureaucracy versus high performance: Work reorganization in the 1990s
abstract: During the time of increased work reorganization, I investigate the components of bureaucratic and high performance work systems and the sources of variation in an organization's adoption of bureaucratic and high performance practices. Findings from the 1996 National Organizations Survey suggest that the degree of workplace formalization, level of hierarchy, and number of departmentalization strongly indicate bureaucratic organizations, but the alleged high performance indicators of teamwork, skill enhancement, job autonomy, and innovative pay structures do not cohere to identify high performance work systems. Instead, teamwork and skill enhancement cluster to indicate one type of high performance work system, whereas job autonomy and performance-based pay constellate to identify another type. Multivariate analyses reveal that institutional mimetic isomorphism is the major factor that compels organizations to implement a certain work system. Organizations mimic their peers in their strategic adoption of different work systems. In addition, foreign market competition increases organizational adoption of teamwork and training programs to enhance skills. [Copyright 2008 Elsevier Inc.]

title: Effective Emergency Management: Reconsidering the Bureaucratic Approach
authors: Neal, David M; Phillips, Brenda D
abstract: The command & control approach is compared with the emergent human resources model approach to emergency management. Four decades of systematic research show that a rigid, bureaucratic command & control approach to emergency management generally leads to an ineffective emergency response. It is suggested that flexible, malleable, loosely coupled, organizational configurations can create a more effective disaster response. 48 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: A REPLY TO AN IDEOLOGICAL CRITICISM
authors: ELLEMERS, J E; HOEVEN, AUG TER
abstract: A reply by the authors to a critique of SA 2148/D2913 by P. Plodger (see SA 2148/D2922). It contains their answers to 4 points made by Ploeger: (1) there is no agreement on the definition of soc work, even among experts; (2) in the Netherlands, as in other countries, the instit'al org of soc work has preceded the professionalization of soc workers; (3) source material about systematized soc work was used; no documentation exists on soc work of the informal kind; (4) bur'ization as such is not condemned; its results are merely presented as far as soc work is concerned. I. Langnas.

title: Bureaucracy and Citizen Participation in a Metropolitan Area
abstract: Four citizen participation committees established in New York City during the early 1970s are examined to assess the degree to which such mechanisms influence the structure of local bureaucratic power. The success of participation is discussed in terms of the visibility of & access to bureaucratic decision making & information provided by the committees; changes in the use & control of the social services provided are also described. The emergence & functions of the New York Community Mental Health Center Advisory Board, the Community Planning Boards of the 1974 Housing & Development Act, the Employment & Training Planning Council, & the Community Boards of the 1975 civic decentralization are described. While all these committees are seen as contributing to a decrease in discrimination against the underprivileged, none are viewed as appropriating decision making from the institutional bureaucracies; in fact, a tendency toward absorption by the latter is identified, as is the later emergence of client-representative relations. Modified HA.

title: The Ritual of Reorganization in a Public Bureaucracy
authors: Stull, Donald D; Maynard-Moody, Steven; Mitchell, Jerry
abstract: An examination of the paradox that reorganizations are common in modern bureaucracies even though they have been found to have few instrumental effects. Data obtained via field research & interviews (N not specified) conducted in a state regulatory agency reveal that while reorganization had little instrumental consequence, it did provide the context for a power struggle between the administrative & occupational spheres of authority. In fact, reorganization proved to be a highly ritualized arena for significantly altering the agency's informal structure by replacing an entrenched dominant subculture. By examining the symbolic & ritualistic nature of this process, the analysis looks beyond the ineffectual manifest functions of reorganization to uncover its latent power functions. 1 Table, 42 References. Modified HA

title: Organizational Size and Bureaucratic Structure
abstract: Patterns in the evolutionary development of bureaucratic organization are analyzed as functions of the interplay between four structural dimensions: work-flow interdependence, hierarchical shape, administrative intensity, & mechanisms of control. Three stages of growth, marked by distinct configurations of these four structural dimensions, are associated with increases in organizational size. The growth stages are derived as ideal types that are constructed on the basis of technical rationality. These technically ideal types are compared to Max Weber's bureaucratic ideal type, & some terminological confusions in the organizational literature are identified. 2 Figures, 85 References. HA

title: Controlling Nature, Disciplining Human Nature: Floods in Singapore and Metro Manila, 1945-1980s
authors: Loh, Kah Seng; Pante, Michael D
abstract: A history of urban floods underlines the state's efforts to discipline people as well as to control floodwaters. Researchers focus on two big cities in Southeast Asia -- Singapore and Metro Manila -- in the period from after World War II until the 1980s. During this period, both cities traversed similar paths of demographic and socioeconomic change that had an adverse impact on the incidence of flooding. Official responses to floods in Singapore and Manila, too, shared the common pursuit of two objectives. The first was to tame nature by reducing the risk of flooding through drainage and other technical measures, as implemented by a modern bureaucracy. The second was to discipline human nature by eradicating bad attitudes and habits deemed to contribute to flooding, while nurturing behavior considered civic-minded and socially responsible. This article argues that in controlling floods -- that is, when nature is deemed hazardous -- the state needs to accommodate sources of authority and expertise other than its own. Adapted from the source document.

title: Critical Approaches to the Study of State Bureaucracy: A Latin-American Perspective
abstract: Suggested is an analytical perspective showing those substantive & environmental factors which give the state bureaucracies of Latin America their specific character. Pointed out is the emphasis placed on private organizations by those dealing with administrative & organizational questions, & its consequences for a study of state institutions. Taking state machinery as a separate unit of analysis, considered is its field of competence & action as an arena where political conflicts & historical processes take place, through a complex set of interactions that make the boundaries between state & civil society unclear, & increase the heterogeneity of the bureaucracy. The role of the state is reviewed, noting the intrinsically conflicting nature of the bureaucracy's functions & the way in which its performance & productivity should be understood. Bibliography. Modified AA.

title: Child Welfare Practice in Organizational and Institutional Context
authors: Smith, Brenda D; Donovan, Stella E F
abstract: Child welfare policy changes have intensified the need for effective child welfare practice, yet little is known about the everyday practices of frontline child welfare caseworkers. Based in Michael Lipsky's theory of street-level bureaucracy, this study explores child welfare practice through interviews with frontline caseworkers and observations in juvenile court. The study suggests that best practices in child welfare are compromised not only by organizational pressures, such as time limitations, but also by pressures to conform practices to the expectations of powerful institutions in the organizational environment. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Officialdom of Educational Systems
abstract: In Anmerkungen zu Theodor Geigers "Burokratisierung des Erziehungswesens" (Introduction to Theodor Geiger's Burokratisierung der Erziehungswesen), Klaus Rodax (Konigschaldinger Str 42, D-8390 Passau Federal Republic Germany) introduces this previously unpublished paper, written 1932/33. It is argued that Geiger's achievement in social sciences & especially in the field of sociology of education were highly influenced by his ideology-critical perspectives. In this theoretical comment on Max Weber's discussion of "officialdom," emphasis is placed on the ideological emancipation of content of function (Funktionsinhalt) in regard to officialdom. The discussion is illustrated by the example of the historical development of educational systems. Adapted from the source document.

title: Towards monopolisation and re-nationalisation of European social science research? Some critical remarks on the 6th Framework Programme
abstract: With the launching in December 2002 of the first calls of the "6th Framework Programme of the European Community for research, technological development and demonstration activities, contributing to the creation of the European Research Area and to innovation (2002 to 2006)", it is very timely to have a critical look at its reality and its potential impact on the European Research Area, in particular with respect to the social sciences. It is argued that it is by no means guaranteed that the Framework Programme will be able to mobilise the creative research potential within and outside the European Union and include the best European researchers. There is a significant danger that the Framework Programme will lead to a monopolisation of research activities within bureaucratic national research institutes (and within the networks they build) and greater political influence on research, especially by the member states and their National Research Institutes. This endangers the existing European Research Area as manifested in the open and flexible research networks that have proven their capacity in the 4th and 5th Framework Programmes. The article will start from the history of the 6th Framework Programme up to its first implementation, describe the First Call and its impacts on consortium building, and finally draw some preliminary conclusions. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Organizational Rehabilitation through Rehabilitating People: Transcending the Original Structure of a Project
abstract: This paper presents a description of & reflections about an action research process in a local authority. The focus of the project is on the introduction of a new approach to the rehabilitation of staff. The new approach requires collaboration between departments, which is a great stumbling block in the bureaucratic structure & culture of the organization. The project describes & discusses how, through a gradual joint focusing on the rehabilitation of individuals, the departments concerned became aware of the fact that they were also engaged in a process of rehabilitating the organization. Various aspects of the importance of the relationship between the researcher & the organization are brought to the fore. 1 Appendix, 23 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: System Size and Structural Differentiation in Formal Organizations: An Alternative Baseline Generator
abstract: The baseline model for B. H. Mayhew, J. M. McPherson, R. L. Levinger & J. F. James (see SA 21:5/73G4149) which generates P. M. Blau's 2 major theoretical proposals relating size & structural diff'iation in formal org's (see SA 18:7/70E5782), is shown to be based on an assumption which limits the model's applicability to only hierarchical org's. An alternative baseline model is developed which does not make this assumption & which fails to yield Blau's second proposition as a logical consequence. Modified HA.

title: Individual Freedom and Capitalist Power Relationships
abstract: Power -- its nature & exercise -- in capitalist society is analyzed in Weberian terms as being of the legal type, & therefore projecting itself as bureaucratic authority. An analogy is drawn between the impersonal rationality of bureaucratic rule in the political sphere & the equally impersonal direction of capital in the SE sphere. S. Karganovic.

title: Bureaucratic Regulation and Farmer Protest in the Michigan PBB Contamination Case
authors: Coyer, Brian Wilson; Schwerin, Don S
abstract: The representation of farmer grievances when established political channels break down is examined. The source of farmer dissatisfaction examined is the Mich regulatory response to polybrominated biphenyl (PBB) contamination of livestock feed & animal products from 1973 to 1978. The established political actors are Michigan Farm Bureau Federation, Mich Dept of Agriculture, Governor William Milliken, & the Michigan State U Cooperative Extension Service. Breakdown in established representation occurred when farmers perceived the bureaucratic & organizational interests of the farm establishment to be hostile to their own. Writers on the regulatory process have explored the thesis that regulatory agencies become "captured" by those they presume to regulate. In the PBB incident, the farmers affected, whether or not they had "captured" the agencies, were unable to displace the burden of regulation to society as a whole, but had to bear the costs themselves. Survey data collected by mailed questionnaire from 407 farmers in 24 counties are used to examine reactions. Complaining is not explained by farm income, farm size, education, age, or sex, possibly because of high issue salience; dissatisfaction does explain complaining. Bureau conversion of dissatisfaction into complaints varies with bureaus. Farmers seek general relief as a class, not merely individual relief, & turn to the electoral process when unable to get results through complaining. 4 Tables, 2 Figures. Modified HA.

title: A Neo-Weberian Theory of the Firm
abstract: The field of organization studies harbors two types of theory of the firm: 'why' and 'how' theories. The former seeks to explain why firms exist despite the availability of institutional alternatives, whereas the latter explores how firms meaningfully connect the actions of many interdependently operating individuals to collective outcomes. Since the two approaches are complements rather than substitutes, the field would benefit from the development of a parsimonious theory that integrates 'why' and 'how' perspectives. It is argued that Max Weber's writings on bureaucracy, and especially his focus on the organization as a collective actor governed by rational-legal decision rules, provide a meaningful conceptual background structure for such a theory. Specifically, through a rational reconstruction of certain elements of the Weberian legacy, a neo-Weberian theory of the firm is constructed here that simultaneously provides reasons for the existence of the firm and explores the nature of cooperation within the firm itself. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: The Economic Conditions of Black Employment in Municipal Bureaucracies
abstract: The degree to which blacks have penetrated municipal civil service bureaucracies is explored on the basis of municipal statistics for 49 US cities for 1973 & 1978, & is found to vary positively from city to city as a function of several economic factors: the health of the local private sector, the relative scarcity of prestige jobs for blacks in private industry, & weak or absent public employee union coverage. To the extent that bureaucratic employment provides access to policy making, blacks are increasingly laying claim to a significant share of the governance of economically healthy cities, more so even than in the fiscally precarious cities governed by black mayors. It is in these economically healthy cities that true possibilities for biracial local government exist. 4 Tables, 24 References. Modified HA.

title: Understanding Organizations Through Language; Discourses of Post-Bureaucratic Organization
abstract: Jones reviews Understanding Organizations Through Language by Susanne Tietze, Laurie Cohen and Gill Musson and Discourses of Post-Bureaucratic Organization by Rick Iedema.

title: Irresponsible Organizations: The Theory of Court as Organization
abstract: The study presents a theory of irresponsible organizations. According to our definition, an organization (focal one) is responsible if it hurts the interest of others (other organizations), others can re-hurt the interest of focal organization. The irresponsible organizations are immune to the re-hurting trials: cannot be re-hurt. This definition fits many types of bureaucracies, or the courts. The theory of irresponsibility of organizations helps to sketch a new organization theory of power. It is important to emphasize that the definition of responsibility & irresponsibility is not an ethical one, but one based on the power. In interorganizational conflicts, it is extremely useful to differentiate the actors according to how they can win or lose during the conflicts. Responsible organizations can win & lose too, but the irresponsible organizations can win only. So the risk of different actors, & the behavior of them can be differentiated according to their positions on the responsible-irresponsible scale. The first half of the article introduces the reader into the theory of irresponsible organizations (as a part of the theory of power). The second half of the study deals with the court as an irresponsible organization. This paper is an introductory part of the theory of court as organization. 27 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Experts and Specialists in Bureaucratic and Professional Organizations
abstract: Comments on P. J. van Delden's "Professionalisiering als organisatiestrategie" ([Professionalization as an Organizational Strategy] 1993), awarded the Professional Publication Prize in Jun 1994 by the Council for Organizational Office of Advice in Amsterdam, Netherlands. Special praise is given for his treatment of organizational contingencies, the perspective of professional experience, bureaucratic & professional forms of organization, the development of professional insights, the enhancement of technical competence, & the difference between image & reality in professional organizations. M. Meeks

title: Paying for Service: Service Learning as a Challenging Student Experience
abstract: Service Learning (SL) is a pedagogy aimed at combining academic studies and volunteer community action. The advantages of SL are numerous and are discussed elsewhere. The article points to some of the less studied aspects of service learning programs: the price that students pay for their volunteer service in the community. The discussion will be based on experiences of students in a Community Interpreting course in an Israeli University, where bilingual students volunteer as interpreters in public institutions and NGOs. In their reflective reports from 2008 - 2011, the students reveal problems encountered in marketing their cultural capital, facing bureaucracy, coping with difficult emotional situations and cultural differences, and handling ethical dilemmas. The study will conclude with possible explanations for these negative effects, and offer suggestions of ways for the organizers of the volunteer work - be they faculty, volunteer coordinators or NGOs, to help volunteers give more and pay less. Adapted from the source document.

title: Gender difference in occupational stress: A study of the South Korean National Police Agency
authors: Kim, Jeong L; Wells, William; Vardalis, James J; Johnson, Sharon K; Lim, Hyungjin
abstract: Using survey data from 512 sworn police officers in the Korean National Police Agency, this study explores the impact of five job characteristics, organizational environment, and external environment on stress experienced by male and female police officers in South Korea. Data analyses show that female officers experience statistically significant elevated degrees of somatization and anxiety. The level of organizational bureaucracy has statistically significant impact on both male and female officer's somatization and anxiety, and male officer's depression. In addition, the level of community relationships has statistically significant impact on somatization, anxiety, and depression for male officers, but only on anxiety and depression for female officers. The effects of task identity and autonomy on different measures of work-related stresses differ between the two gender groups. Findings of the current study support previous police stress literature in general. Implications, limitations, and directions for future research are discussed. [web URL: http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1756061615000701]

authors: Petersen, Trond; Spilerman, Seymour; Dahl, Svenn-Age

title: Displaced Persons and the Politics of International Categorisation(s)
abstract: Between 1947 and 1952 170,000 Displaced Persons (DPs) arrived in Australia as International Refugee Organisation (IRO)-sponsored refugees. This article sets out the international historical and political context for the migration of DPs to Australia, and interrogates the "bureaucratic labelling" inherent in the category "Displaced Persons". The post-war refugees were presented internationally as "Displaced Persons", "refugees", "political refugees" and eventually, in an effort to solve the population crisis, as potential "workers" and "migrants". This article will describe the historical origin of the terms "Displaced Persons", "refugees", "political exiles" and "migrants"-- terms which were, and continue to be, relevant and problematic. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: INTERNAL CONTRADICTIONS IN BUREAUCRATIC POLITIES
abstract: A preliminary analysis of the main patterns of change in bur'tic polities, drawing examples from the ancient Egyptian Empires, the Sassanid Empire of Persia the Chinese Empires from the period of Han onwards, the Roman & Byzantine Empires, the age of Absolutism in Europe, & the Spanish Amer Empire. The major aims & policies of the elites, made up of the head of state on the 1 hand, & the upper pol'al group connected with him on the other are reviewed: (1) the aims of 'concentration of resources ... & the increase & regulation of free-floating resources, give rise to a variety of econ policies: the formation of monopolies; attempts to control manpower; & taxation policy, which may also regulate the ratio between land & pop, serve as a levelling instrument, & control the investment-potential of the financially active groups. (2) In the field of stratification, referring to the distribution of honor & prestige within the society: there were attempts to make king or emperor the main dispenser of soc prestige; to limit the power position of any high status groups & esp of the aristocracy; & to make the middle & lower strata dependent on the centFal authorities, freeing them from the aristocratic elements. (3) In the legal field the elites codified law, & reduced the sphere of civil procedure & enlarged that of criminal jurisdiction. (4) An endeavor was made 'to maintain direct channels of communication with the more active ... groups of the society, & to control those centers of learning & cultural creativity in which such cultural & religious symbols & values were created & could be transmitted to the various strata,', & (5) in the pol'al field the ruling elite aimed to diminish the pol'al power of any group which might compete with it. However, in few cases were their basic aims successfully & continuously implemented, due to marked internal contradictions: (a) where the economy is relatively undifferentiated, the 'free' resources available are insufficient for given pol'al goals, (b) where econ development is relatively high & traditionalism relatively low, there may be an inherent incompatibility between the value orientations of ruling elites & potential supporters, & (c) elites were often suspicious of the groups from which resources came, & there was a contradiction between short & long range aims, & 'consequently a tendency to regiment the free resources in such a way as to exhaust them. E. Weiman.

title: Reflections on the Changing Tendencies of the Bureaucratic-Authoritarian State
abstract: The expression "bureaucratic-authoritarian" serves to distinguish the kind of state under consideration from others which are also authoritarian, eg, traditionalist, populist, or fascist. The defining characteristics of the bureaucratic-authoritarian state are (1) top positions in the government are held by individuals who had previously occupied responsible posts in other bureaucratic institutions, eg, armed forces, lower echelons of government, private corporations; (2) popular groups & their allies are barred from access to the state apparatus; (3) the desire to participate in economic management on the part of the popular classes is postponed into the indefinite future; (4) social & political questions are reduced to "technical" problems, ie, the depoliticizing tendency is pronounced; & (5) the emergence of this type of state coincides with the process of "entrenchment" of peripheric capitalism (or dependent capitalism) which may, nevertheless, show extensive industrialization. The emergence of the bureaucratic-authoritarian state is fundamentally the result of the abrupt politicization of the popular classes which is perceived by other classes as a threat to sociopolitical continuity. The period immediately preceding the installation of this regime typically shows an economic crisis including but not limited to high inflation, decline in production & gross national product, flight of capital, balance of payment deficits, etc. The cases of Chile & Argentina are contrasted as examples of different conditions which may still conduct ultimately to the installation of the bureaucratic-authoritarian regime. The broad alliance of the privileged classes, which brought about the installation of the bureaucratic-authoritarian regime typically disintegrates soon after its successful establishment. Many of the groups which supported the coup now find out that they are not among its direct beneficiaries once the integration of the local economy with the requirements of international finance capitalism begins to occur. 2 Charts. S. Karganovic.

title: SPORT AS INSTITUTIONALIZED CHARISMA
abstract: Allen Guttmann has developed an ideal type descriptive of the transformation from medieval leisure to modern sport. His method of type construction and its substantive components are replicas, shaped for the study of sport, of Weber's concept of Western rationalization. The rise of the Gaelic Athletic Association in late 19th-century Ireland represents the principal empirical universe used to assess the validity of Guttmann's ideal type. The Irish case study suggests that modern sport, at its historical moment of incorporation, was as much a project of irrational elements and affective rationality as it was instrumental action. Using the writings of Weber as a source and the early history of Irish sport, it is suggested that modern sport be conceived as a multidimensional institution existing in tension with bureaucratic and charismatic forms of control.

title: In the Picture or Off the Wall? Ethical Regulation, Research Habitus, and Unpeopled Ethnography
abstract: This article focuses on two unintended consequences of ethical regulation of social enquiry: the exclusion of participants and, subsequently, a transformation of research practice. An ethnography of corridor life in a large university building forms the basis of the discussion. Originally intended as a pilot for a broader study of informal networks of power, the project's aim seemed unachievable. External ethical bureaucracy engendered an overdeveloped sensitivity to doing wrong, resulting in a bizarre form of reflexivity. The first consequence of ethical constraint is, paradoxically, the exclusion of participants and their worlds, as research projects are ever more tightly framed. However, forced to reflect on her research habitus, the author discovered that a conventional qualitative research focus on participants' narrative/biographic accounts and face-to-face interaction can be similarly restrictive. In conclusion, the author discusses how practicing an unpeopled ethnography can open up space for democratic, innovative research within the confines of current ethical regulation.

title: The Computer Metaphor Bureaucratizing the Mind
abstract: The development of the computer, its antecedents, & its cultural metaphors are analyzed along with the computer's relationship to the bureaucratic organizations, labor processes, & managerial ideologies of capitalist societies. It is argued that the pretechnological development of capitalism created a need for mechanization & computer technology, as exemplified by the designs of Charles Babbage in the 1820s, who related the division of labor to computational machinery. Since then, this division of labor & striving for efficiency has been linked to computer technology, bureaucracy, control mechanisms of management, & the military. Implications of this development include: loss of employment, political unrest, & reorganization of social relations. The role of artificial intelligence in this process is discussed. 61 References. A. Cole

title: The Passive Protest of the Political Bureaucracy
abstract: An examination of the political bureaucracy, ie, the entire body of civil servants, in Mexico. It is argued that, over the past three decades, a phenomenon of passive protest has been observable at all levels of this group (though not in the other branches of government, eg, the police or the army), which is the counterpart of more overt conflicts between the state & other groups of workers. The nature of this protest, which is described as unconscious sabotage, & the reasons for it are discussed. Statistical information concerning civil servants (their occupations, length of employment, educational level, salaries, etc) & legislation & contracts relating to public employees & other workers are examined. It is argued that the political bureaucracy is a social category, defined in relation to the state, & its protest must be considered a relevant social & political phenomenon. 10 Tables, 39 References. C. Waters

title: A FUNCTION OF BILATERAL KINSHIP PATTERNS IN A NEW ENGLAND INDUSTRY
abstract: An illustrative analysis of a New England brick company, using the principles of bilateral kinship for (a) the org of task accomplishments, (b) patterning of authority relationships, & (c) recruitment of labor. It is concluded that: (1) kinship models of org are found in certain industries involving hard labor, a minimum of skill, seasonal employment, & unique ecological conditions. (2) The equilibrium of the kinship & ecological systems in the company studied was maintained more by ritual or symbolic, rather than rational or functionally productive, aspects of soc behavior. (3) The use of bilateral kinship as a model depends upon the nature & size of the industrial org & of the family. (4) Inefficiency results from conflict between the symbolic expression of bur'tic values & familistic values. (5) The distinction between the formal or instrumental org which defines the occup'al roles of the participants & the informal or expressive org is difficult to maintain in the group studied where the 2 systems merge. R. Goldwater.

title: Bureaucratization in the US Department of State
abstract: An attempt is made to consider the question of bureaucratization in the individual governmental agency. Departing from an experiment in debureaucratization, the origins of 2 core components of bureaucracy--hierarchy & rules--in the US Dept of State are traced. The discussion emphasizes the interaction between the internal structure of a public organization & 2 sets of environmental factors: the power setting & the operating environment. This interaction produces a high degree of message generation, top-down demands for accountability & control, & bottom-up pressures for clearance & guidance. These conditions lead to a heavy message volume & a high degree of centralization which, in turn, bring on communications overload. Bureaucracy increases as overload is handled through hierarchical differentiation & the proliferation of rules. HA.

title: Weak Theme -- Weak Politics. Why Does the Politics of Engagement Remain in the Shadows in Germany?
abstract: The lack of political instincts in the ministerial bureaucracy can have far reaching effects, as evidenced by the reaction to a planned elimination of tax breaks for businesses supporting community purposes in Germany. Widespread abstinence of businesses in the field of furthering commitments, the exploitation of honorary officials & volunteers to fill holes in the social system, & the half-hearted development of a policy for citizen engagement create an interrelated problematic cycle that belies the myth of corporate citizenship. While the Commission of Inquiry is intended to inform & advise Parliament & is heading in the right direction, in avoiding conflict & failing to offer any concrete suggestions, they have created a weak case that does not inspire mobilization. L. Kehl

title: Bureaucratic Organisation of Professional Labour
abstract: Those who reject the proletarianization of professional labor argue that making professional employees subordinate to nonprofessional administrators in a bureaucratic organization compromises their professional status. They claim that professionals tend to identify with their profession rather than with the employing agency & control their own certification & performance standards, so any movement to salaried employee status is problematic. A conflict arises between the autonomy of professionals & the control of administrators. A literature review examines structural features of professional bureaucracies, the characteristics of professional employees, & the nature of professional knowledge, & raises doubts that bureaucratic organization undermines professionalism. 56 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Brexit, Post-liberalism, and the Politics of Paradox
abstract: Britain's vote to leave the EU is part of a tectonic shift in Western politics. An alliance of socialists and conservatives rejected the status quo of remote bureaucracy, mass immigration, and multiculturalism in favor of more self-government and the protection of settled ways of life. A similar realignment is underway in European countries such as Austria, Italy, the Netherlands, and France, where it could see anti-EU parties force similar referenda or even seize power altogether. Here, Pabst provides compelling insight into the texture of the vote as well as to the parallelism between Brexit and the Trump phenomenon in the US.

title: The twists and turns of institutional innovation in small island developing states: the case of Tuvalu
abstract: The question of institutional reform in small island developing states (SIDS) has so far attracted two general perspectives. The predominant approach prescribes neo-Weberian principles such as de-politicisation, neutrality, 'professionalism', continuity and anonymity, and rational-bureaucratic structures. Critics highlight contextual specificities and maintain that Weberian principles are not plausible amid key constraints in SIDS including low human and logistical capacity, pervasive inter-personal and cross-cutting relations, and difficulty in attaining anonymity in public affairs. This debate remains largely intuitive, without the requisite empirical insights about the peculiar institutional trajectories and incentive structures driving change and continuity within SIDS. This paper provides a critical examination of the enduring quagmire of institutional development in SIDS based on a comprehensive account of the experience of Tuvalu.

title: Staff-Attitudes in the New Tunisian Industry
abstract: It is hyp'ed that in developing countries industr'ization not only means the transmission of a modern technology but also a cultural configuration of roles, att's & aspirations which the agents of industr'ization have to internalize. Its general characteristic can be considered as being rationality. At its bounds, industr'ization could be defined as the coincidence of an operational technical rationality & the cultural rationality. The staff of the new industry are considered as the agents who have internalized this technical & cultural rationality to the highest degrees. Here the analysis concentrates on the way these agents meet the contradiction inherent in the implantation of an industry into a preindustr society & a dominant Ru setting. The expression of this contradiction is the tension which can be observed on various levels: between enterprise or staff & environment, between the conception of industry & the reality of daily life, between aspired ways of living & necessary limitations imposed by the preindustr environment, between traditional & intended modern society. A. Schmalfuss.

title: Dyadic Nexus Fighting Two-Front Battles: A Study of the Microlevel Process of the Official-Religion-State Relationship in China
abstract: This article provides a microlevel perspective of the interacting dynamics between religion and the Chinese state, demonstrating how religious leaders and local officials negotiate with each other pragmatically, continually withstanding pressure from hardline religious masses and state bureaucracy. This perspective, constructed using qualitative data on the True Jesus Church, also helps to answer a critical empirical question left open in scholarly discussions: When and how does the state regulative power on religion come to the fore in the economic reform emphasizing pragmatic religion-state cooperation? The findings show how religious leaders and local officials have become pragmatic, cooperating to form a dyadic nexus that tackles regular affairs in a practical way, though it may run the risk of fracture when lay members and bureaucratic superiors pressure leaders and officials, respectively, to take hardline positions. The leaders and officials have continually fought two-front battles while shuttling between negotiations with their nexus partner and aligning with their hardline sources of pressure. This study may shed light on future research of the Chinese religion-state relationship in general by illustrating a microlevel, integrative, dynamic approach. Adapted from the source document.

title: How Culture and Economy Meet in South Korea: The Politics of Cultural Economy in Culture-led Urban Regeneration; [1]
abstract: This article investigates the ways in which cultural economy is formed through negotiation and interaction between local actors in the case of culture-led regeneration in Gwangju, South Korea. It looks at the dynamics between the bureaucrats' pursuit of economic growth in the city and the efforts of civil society to maintain a strong political spirit throughout the regeneration process. Through in-depth interviews with various participants and archival analysis, the politics of cultural economy are examined in relation to the Gwangju Biennale and the City of Culture project. The findings show that in these two cases bureaucrats were the dominant force, a tendency that instrumentalized culture. They also illustrate that this dominance brought about resistance from civil society. However, in the process of both engaging in conflict and working with each other, the different discourses of economic growth and cultural meaning were integrated, and in the process mutual learning and adaptation took place among members of the two groups. Civil society also faced cleavages resulting from different approaches to how to collaborate with the bureaucrats and its ensuing self-reflection on communicative value enhanced its rehabilitation. The article argues that the politics of cultural economy is dynamic, involving processes of renegotiation, adaptation and self-realization. It also offers the possibility of a new arena for the public sphere. Civil society plays a critical role in the integration of culture and economy.[PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Knowledge-Intensive Organisations: Women's Promised Land? The Case of the Irish Software Companies
abstract: This article investigates the contention that the organisation of work and the model of industrial relations in knowledge intensive companies are less iniquitous for women than in other industries. It does so by analysing a series of biographical interviews conducted with a number of women working in the Irish software sector. In contrast to bureaucracies, knowledge intensive companies promote time flexibility, collaborative work environments, immediate human relations, autonomy and performance-related career progression. These features are generally deemed to be less prone to the reproduction of gendered practices and values and to facilitate women's dual role in society. The findings of the empirical investigation suggest that the process of feminisation of the Irish software companies has not been matched by a distinctive process of recognition of the gendered nature of workplaces; as a consequence, they are failing to accommodate female presence in the industry. Whilst no clear discriminatory behaviours and practices emerge in the sector, new and different forms of inequality have come to surface in the industry.

title: Assessing One-stop-shop Best Practices for South African Investment: A Comparative Case Study of Mauritius and Egypt
abstract: One stop shop (OSS) models are an investment process that came about to create a centralised place for the voluminous documentation required in international trade between companies. Bureaucracy has proven to be a major barrier to the development of international trade, particularly in African countries that still lag behind in industrial growth and development. South Africa needs to establish a one-stop-shop model for incoming investors soon, particularly since the Department of Trade and Industry submitted a Special Economic Zone Bill last year. The focus of this article is to examine challenges and prospects of one-stop-shop models through a case study analysis of Mauritius and Egypt, both of which have implemented such processes with relevant investment experiences that South Africa can draw from. Adapted from the source document.

title: PRESSURES AND DEFENSES IN BUREAUCRATIC ROLES
abstract: Line-bur'crats may be exposed to conflicting pressures from superiors & from clients. In that case they are in need of defenses to reduce pressures or alleviate their impact. A societal ideology may serve as individual defense; moreover, the org'al unit as a whole may develop structural mechanisms of defense. 2 such mechanisms, joint defense & buffer defense, are discussed. The existence of buffer defense makes it possible for bur'crats to resist both superiors & clients, & act according to independent criteria; the absence of any type of defense may lead to erratic behavior, where the bur'crat bows to whatever pressure is momentarily strongest. HA.

title: Family Intervention Projects: A Site of Social Work Practice
abstract: Family Intervention Projects (FIPs) provide intensive support to 'problem families' and are a core element of the Government's Respect Action Plan (2006). Drawing on recent research findings from an independent evaluation of the FIP 'Signpost', this paper aims to offer a new insight into our understanding of FIPs. The paper draws attention to two key points. First, the organizational context within which Signpost has emerged is one dominated by a social work ethos. It is suggest that the FIP has been implemented in a way which has provided social work professionals with an opportunity to engage in the kind of creative practice that proceduralization, bureaucracy and managerialism have made impossible to achieve in mainstream social work arenas. Following on from this, the paper emphasizes the limitations of evaluating anti-social behaviour policy effects without due consideration of the local policy and practice context within which policies are embedded. The paper is not intended to discount important critical reflections on FIPs, but seeks to illustrate the gaps that can open up between political rhetoric and policy effect, demonstrating why we should not be too quick to foreclose the possibilities afforded to vulnerable families by this type of intervention. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: SOCIAL STRATIFICATION IN CONTEMPORARY CZECHOSLOVAKIA
abstract: Results are presented of an extensive sociol'al-statistical survey of soc stratification in Czechoslovakia in 1967. The operationalization of major variables is described. The problem of the dominant stratification is solved in favor of the following group of cultural variables: complexity of work, educ, style of life. The taxonomic analysis reveals 4 major strata & 3 large inconsistent groups. An unexpectedly high 'subjective' manifestation of objective stratification is another finding of the res. A preliminary interpretation in terms of relation to types of soc stratification leads to the conclusion that relations of the socialist, egalitarian, bur'tic, & technocratic types played the most signif role at the time when data were collected. Several general judgments are advanced re the relation of actual soc stratification found in Czechoslovakia in 1967 & to the 'Ideal types' of soc stratification. It is stated that soc diff'iation in Czechoslovakia in 1967 was pronouncedly noncapitalist. Soc diff'iation was of a pronouncedly gradual character. Moreover, Czechoslovak society in 1967 was not even a society of the worker type. Findings further suggest that it was the bur'tic type of org that played a signif role in the society. Relations of an egalitarian type had great weight in the soc arrangement of the country. The technocratic (culturocratic or meritocratic) type of arrangement also proved to be rather signif. A realistic form of socialism began to arise as a noncapitalist (ie after abolishing the capitalist form of inequality) variant of an industr society, based on achievement & stratified & consequently diff'iated also in interests & views. Modified HA.

title: From the Royal House to the State's Logic: A Model of the Genesis of the Bureaucratic Field
abstract: Explores the historic process dynamics & unique traits underlying the transition from dynastic regime to modern rational, bureaucratic state. Analysis of the transitional process focuses on actors with divergent interests & their intrigues for legitimate control & manipulation of public wealth. While it is important to map the logic behind the institution of the relatively autonomous, politicoeconomically independent administrative field that constitutes the modern bureaucracy, equally indispensable is an examination of the imaginary symbolic & rational implications of various bureaucratic instruments (ie, the signature, office, seal, certificate, register) used to establish impersonal, interchangeable power. Adapted from the source document.

title: Expanding Choice in Long Term Planning for Family Futures
abstract: KEYWORDS. Caregiving, Choice, Decision making, Opportunities, Problem solving, Management, Risk, Equity, Life course, Generational relationships, Family planningINTRODUCTIONWe are living our lives around and among crises and challenges. Planning for our futures is done with an awareness of the many imponderables and the unknowns that shape our destinies. The responsibility, that individuals and their families have for shaping their own lives and providing for their futures, has become more important because of demographic, social, economic, and technological changes. In addition, families need to become more effective in influencing the larger society and bureaucratic institutions in terms of long term outcomes of policies and programs. Although there is increased opportunity for choice and planning, families need new strategies for dealing with the complexities, changing situations, and finding the relevant and useful information critical to estimating outcomes and assessing the effectiveness of actions. The role of professionals and agencies serving families must be re-examined in light of these changes. Often, the assumption has been that experts' programs, or interventions could replace individuals and families in making decisions that direct long term outcomes. In fact, it is clear that work and community institutions have much shorter time lines and interests than the individuals and families who use these programs. When employers are dominated by the bottom line on a quarterly basis, government has only a yearly budget process, and voluntary, non-profit groups are funded on a project or contributory approach, their evaluation and planning activities are constrained and consideration of long-term outcomes are pushed into the background. The accounting of costs and benefits seldom includes consequences over the lifetimes of clients in these bureaucracies. It is well to remember that is the individuals and their families that absorb the costs of short falls in economic and social institutions.For a complete reprint of this article contact Haworth Press by telephone (1-800-HAWORTH) or EMail (getinfo@haworth.com) Article copyright The Haworth Press, Inc.

title: Beyond Structure: The Role of Social Accounts in Implementing Ideal Control
authors: Cobb, Anthony T; Stephens, Carroll; Watson, George
abstract: In order to survive, the contemporary organization must quickly adapt to its ever-changing markets & environment. The methods of structural control associated with the bureaucratic organizational form impede such adaptation. As a result, organizations are supplanting structural control with newer means of control -- the control of ideas. Drawing on & extending social accounts theory, the authors explore how social accounts are used as one method to help to gain control of ideas, lessening management's dependence on bureaucratic structures. The article exemplifies the managerial use of social accounts by reviewing the text of a videotape used by one organization in its attempt to influence workers' ideas about management, unions & their own interests in order to keep the organization union free. The authors conclude with a discussion of how managerial uses of social accounts can be resisted by workers. 125 References. [Copyright 2001 Sage Publications Ltd.]

title: BUROCRATIC RELATIONSHIPS AND SOCIALISM
abstract: An examination is made of the relations between socialism & bur'cy-first presented as a paper at the 6th Congress of the Internat'l Sociol'al Assoc at Evian in 1966. Soc rebellions, from the German peasant revolt led by Thomas Muenzer in the 16th cent to the Paris Commune, fought for a society without burley, for which J. J. Rousseau prepared the theoretical foundations. V. I. Lenin believed in a society in which workers could govern themselves without bur'cy. But the realities of power forced him to admit in conversations with L. Trotsky & N. I. Bukharin (1920), & in a letter to a young fighter against bur'cy, M. D. Sokolov, that the USSR was 'a workers' society with bur'tic blots.' Bur'cy is part of all socialist countries today; it is largely a negative phenomenon because it has developed a particular interest of its own. But it need not be a wholly negative phenomenon & the following ways are suggested to develop its positive aspects: (1) pressures on specialized admin'ors to effect a sharing of power; (2) promotion of a healthy mobility in all spheres of admin; & (3) a democratized public life which is the best antidote to a bur'tic monopoly. I. Langnas.

title: BUREAUCRACY AND POLITICAL DEVELOPMENT
abstract: A critical discussion & evaluation of BUREAUCRACY AND POLITICAL DEVELOPMENT, edited by Joseph La Palombara (see SA 0715/B3371). Theories & concepts of the book, which contains a collection of papers by soc sci'ts re the role of bur'cy in modern econ development & pol'al change are considered. It is summarized that the book suggests: (i) that 'change is essentially the outcome of modifications in the amount of information available to a society & the way that information is converted into energy'; (ii) 'a model of bur'cy would classify public admin'ive systems according to how they relate to the critical sectors of cultural maintenance & transmission, nat'l integration, systematic goal gratification & environmental transformation'; (iii) a somewhat similar sf model would view bur'cy re the manner in which it handles the flow of demands & org's that interact with the pol'al system. M. Maxfield.

title: Historicising 'asylum' and responsibility
abstract: Territorial rule 'begins' with an assertion of who deserves protection and who does not. The question of responsibility and its limits is integral to the making and maintenance of a nation state. But a modern refugee rights regime externalises the question of asylum. Asylum claims are made by strangers dealt with by bureaucracies. How has this come to pass? How has responsibility become thought in terms of the territorial state and the society and order it begets? In this article, I try to make the case through a historical example that asylum is not external to the constitution of the nation state, rather territorial rule begins by figuring out who to protect and who not to. At the core of these ideas about protection and responsibility is a notion of political subjectivity, which is graduated, hierarchical and centred on the state. The privileging of an ahistorical idea of how political subjectivity has been so limited has contributed to the externalisation of asylum, where the troubling questions of to whom we are responsible and whom not barely figure because asylum claims become the subject of a technicalised procedure. In this article, I focus on the British colonial authority's encounter with native slaves seeking asylum in Perak. Adapted from the source document.

title: Holding Government Bureaucracies Accountable
abstract: Kearns reviews "Holding Government Bureaucracies Accountable" by Bernard Rosen.

title: Bureaucrats as "Social Engineers": Federal Welfare Programs in Herbert Hoover's America
abstract: Historians studying twentieth-century US reform often seek to analyze the ideologies of political leaders separately from the institutions that these same leaders created. Such emphasis on ideas, as opposed to actions, has led "revisionist" US historians to argue that the presidencies of Herbert Hoover & Franklin D. Roosevelt were "conceptually continuous." Based on historical studies & government documents & reports, an examination of the major social welfare programs undertaken by the US federal government in the 1920s disputes this claim. Examination of the operations of the federal bureaucracy instead of the rhetoric of politicians demonstrates the existence of decided policy differences between the Hoover & Roosevelt eras. Background is provided for increased understanding of some of the policy implications of the US's contemporary welfare debate -- particularly concerning "rehabilitation" strategies & rationales for action in the social welfare field. Modified HA.

title: The Juárez Wives Club: Gendered citizenship and US immigration law
abstract: When US citizens sponsor their undocumented spouses for lawful status, they find themselves at the center of immigration petitions. They are invasively scrutinized, treated with bureaucratic indifference, and separated from their loved ones. As this "politics of exception," which often targets migrants, is unleashed on US citizens, they learn that their citizenship offers little protection from dehumanizing treatment. Instead, restrictive immigration criteria, designed in theory to boost the value of US citizenship, in practice dehumanize US citizens and can alienate them from feelings of national belonging. This contradiction inevitably emerges when shared lives disrupt the boundaries of citizenship status, illuminating inconsistencies in normative conceptions of citizenship itself. / Cuando los ciudadanos estadounidenses piden para sus conyuges indocumentados un cambio de estatus legal, caen en el ambito de los procedimientos de inmigracion. Se les examina de forma invasiva, se les trata con indiferencia burocratica y se les separa de sus seres queridos. Cuando esa "politica de excepcion", que normalmente se dirige en contra de los inmigrantes, se aplica a los ciudadanos estadounidenses, estos aprenden que su ciudadania no les protege de tratos inhumanos. De hecho, los criterios restrictivos de inmigracion, disenados en teoria para aumentar el valor de su ciudadania, en la practica les deshumanizan y pueden hacer que se sientan despojados de sentimientos de pertenencia nacional. Esta contradiccion surge inevitablemente cuando las vidas compartidas traspasan las fronteras del estatus de ciudadania, poniendo al descubierto las incoherencias en las concepciones normativas de la ciudadania misma. [web URL: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/amet.12309/full]

title: Beyond Serving State and Bureaucracy: Problem-Oriented Social Science in (West) Germany
abstract: The use of social science knowledge in politics & administration in West Germany is examined. Though problem-oriented social science existed in German politics in the eighteenth century, policy sciences largely vanished from public administration in the late nineteenth century with the trend toward decreasing state interventionism. Social science was replaced by law as the profession of the state, & until after WWII, the orientation of German social science academia was detachment from society. In the late 1960s, social scientists & political actors joined together to reform the policy apparatus within the bureaucracy & to emphasize the need to intervene in practical affairs. Such intervention requires analysis of the interdependence of scientific & societal development from an action perspective. 62 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: How Institutions Form: Loose Coupling as Mechanism in Gouldner's Patterns of Industrial Bureaucracy
abstract: This article uses a mid-century text to reengage a late-1970s concept to answer a new century question. The authors return to Alvin Gouldner's classic (1954) study Patterns of Industrial Bureaucracy to reexamine the "coupling" concept in contemporary institutionalism in a way that engages the following question: How do new institutional forms emerge? Based on Gouldner's detailed observations of work in a gypsum mine, the authors argue that coupling processes are key mechanisms in the emergence of institutional forms. Examining coupling as a dynamic process and activity helps us to understand how the institution of bureaucracy emerged in the gypsum mine and interacted with previous social orders of authority and control. Gouldner's account of coupling at the mine is a story of formal and informal power struggles and active conflict over meaning, bringing the process of local institutional formation into sharp relief. References. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright 2006.]

title: European Union transgovernmental networks: The emergence of a new political space beyond the nation-state?
abstract: Does the European Union (EU) represent a new political order replacing the old nation-states? The assessment of the real character of political orders requires the identification of political key actors and of the specific structure of their interactions. Transgovernmental networks have been considered to be one of the most important features of EU integration. Unfortunately, the network structures, processes and the impact of these informal horizontal inter-organisational relations between nation-states are mostly unknown. The main objective of this article is to measure and explain the selective pattern of informal bilateral relations of high officials of the EU Member States' ministerial bureaucracies on the occasion of an EU Intergovernmental Conference. The quantitative data used rely on standardised interviews with 140 top-level bureaucrats. The statistical estimation of network choices is based on recent developments of exponential random graph models. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: INTRODUCTION TO THE BASICS OF SYSTEMIC ANTI-CORRUPTION PREVENTION
authors: Sukhodolov, Aleksandr P; Moscovtsev, Aleksandr F; Kopylov, Aleksey V; Frolova, Evgeniya E
abstract: Systemic anti-corruption prevention presupposes the use of a corresponding conceptual approach to modeling a complex of factors facilitating corruption. The authors state the social inclusion of corruption, i.e. the inclusion of these factors in key social mechanisms when, under certain conditions, the mechanisms themselves turn into a corruption-generating factor. According to them, the corruption relations matrix is basically composed of a set of structural elements that are common to any other social relations' types: hierarchy, market, patrimonial relations, i.e. these are the same ways of economic coordination and social integration that interact to form the diversity of specific synthetic social orders. Only the combination of the above-mentioned elements in specific situations, conditions, organizational forms could challenge or violate the legitimacy of a more general social order, which is, as a rule, formally represented in the system of social relations by the state, bureaucratic, hierarchical order. In this connection, the authors systemically develop the idea that the source of corruption relationships is not a simple collision or even an interlocking, blending of different social orders. Each social order is, in itself, legitimate within its own local boundaries. The illegitimacy of some situational complex order can only be established as a result of a special assessment procedure. This procedure includes putting a certain order - in this case, the bureaucratic one - in the dominant position and determining the boundaries of its blending with other social orders. The whole corruption problem is contained in the answer to one question: is the bureaucratic organization, being the dominant structure, able of enforcing its specific order and values? The specific character of corruption relationships, according to the authors, consists in serving a complex social order arising from the blending of the bureaucratic, market and patrimonial orders in situations when the domination of the bureaucratic order and its public legitimacy are violated. At the end, the authors conclude that the problem of researching corruption and measures of counteracting it, including the development of complex anti-corruption programs, is insoluble unless this phenomenon is viewed within the framework of modern society's development. Such a vision demands the use of adequate categorial instruments that should be interdisciplinary in their essence and should be developed through the efforts of most social sciences.

title: Research Ethics between Science, Privacy and Bureaucracy
abstract: The paper examines key ethical dilemmas that arise between researchers & participants, while demonstrating difficulties in solving them & highlighting their contextual nature. The first part discusses confidentiality, anonymity & informed consent, three principal steps in protecting research subjects, & the difficulties of implementing them in social research. It proceeds to review emerging ethical issues on the Internet, a new research medium, & ends with a discussion on the bureaucratization of ethical procedures & the risks the process brings. The paper concludes that, due to the diversity of methods & research situations, contextual decision-making fits the social sciences better than a universalist approach. Accordingly, ethical regulation based on rigid deontological principles may hamper social research. Adapted from the source document.

title: Production Efficiency Versus Bureaucratic Self-Interest: Two Innovative Processes?
abstract: A report is offered of a study of technological innovations in state & local government agencies. Data were gathered from an aggregate analysis of 140 previously-published & unpublished case studies in which a closed-ended questionnaire was to extract information from the case studies. It is concluded that government innovations may entail two distinct but interrelated processes: (1) the production efficiency process which emphasizes service improvements but does not necessarily lead to enduring incorporation of such innovation & (2) the bureaucratic self-interest process which emphasizes incorporation even where the innovation may not have produced a demonstrable service improvement. 7 Tables. Modified HA.

title: Capitalism, Bureaucracy and Male Homosexuality
authors: Greenberg, David F; Bystryn, Marcia H
abstract: An examination of the impact of the rise of capitalism & the development of bureaucratic forms of social organization on social responses to M homosexuality. AA.

title: Personal and Role-Related Factors in the Development of Organizational Commitment
authors: Hrebiniak, Lawrence G; Alutto, Joseph A
abstract: This res examines the relationship between personal & role-related factors & commitment to the employing org. The S's are 318 elementary & secondary Sch teachers & 395 registered nurses employed, respectively, in 2 Sch districts & 3 general hosp's in western New York State. While there is evidence that commitment is diff'ially related to such personal variables as sex, marital status, & father's occup, the results of multivariate analysis show the primary importance of role-related factors in explaining org'al commitment. The signif of role tension, yrs experience in the org, & dissatisfact ion with the bases of org'al advancement suggest that commitment is an exchange & accrual phenomenon, dependent on the employee's perception of the ratio of inducements to contributions & the accumulation of side bets or investments in the employing system. It appears that for teachers & nurses the question of org'al interference with professional activities is not sufficiently salient to affect org'al commitment. In addition to emphasizing the org'al career of the professional employee, the study expresses agreement with authors who have argued that a lack of tension & ambiguity in the performance of org'al roles could be properly regarded as an org'al asset. Modified HA.

title: Innovation in Professional Organizations
authors: Delbecq, Andre L; Pierce, Jon L
abstract: To determine whether innovation correlates of bureaucratic organizations apply to medical organizations, 30 multispecialty fee-for-service medical groups from a midwestern state were studied by interview & questionnaire in 1975. Modal group practical size was 15 physicians. Innovation is seen in 4 phases: informal discussion, formal proposal, adoption, & implementation. Innovation was assessed by asking respondents to rate their organization's innovation phase with respect to 87 identified medical innovations. Structural, attitudinal, & affective response correlates were measured.
