abstract: Introduction to special journal issue "Patrimonial Power in the Modern World.".

title: “A New Health Order as Part of the New Social Order”: The Strategic Response of the WHO to its Member States
abstract: This article explores the range of responses available to international bureaucracies when confronted with demands made by their member states through the study of the World Health Organization (WHO) during the 1970s and 1980s. I show that the WHO bureaucracy successfully addressed the demands of developing countries for health policies compatible with a more equitable world economic order, but in a way that preserved the bureaucracy's own agenda and without upsetting the opposite coalition of wealthy countries. Drawing on insights from the sociology of organizations, this article shows that externally dependent international bureaucracies are able to preserve their autonomous agenda by strategically reframing countries’ demands before responding to them.

title: Participation in the "Glasshouse"
abstract: Participation has always been considered an important feature of the democratization process of state bureaucracy. In Italy, this experience has sometimes been opposed & sometimes solicited by the administration itself. Two participation patterns unfolded in the 1990s, one centered on the citizen's role & the other on unions' involvement, the latter especially conspicuous following new labor union laws in 1993. The administration & unions have been cyclical in their participation, in legal & political contexts, either open (1970s) or closed (1980s) to participation. The administration solicited more citizen participation in the 1990s as a result of its attempts to restructure itself into a "transparent glasshouse.". 13 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Rethinking State-Society Relations in Vietnam: The Case of Business Associations in Ho Chi Minh City
abstract: The growing private sector in the post-reform Vietnamese economy and its new forms of mobilisation have led to newly emergent social forces that have shaped internal state agendas and political deliberations. With a view to exploring the nature of institutional change in Vietnam, I argue that business associations have played a crucial intermediary role between the state and the private sector over past decades. These associations and the spaces of governance that they constitute are neither characteristic of autonomous actors as suggested by liberal theory nor a form of state corporatism. This paper adopts the "state-in-society" approach, which contends that the state and society should be considered through new governance spaces within the state. These spaces create institutional mechanisms for interaction between the government and business, and provide a framework for deliberative engagement between state and nonstate actors. This framework will be tested through an examination of associations of small and medium enterprises in Ho Chi Minh City and their connections to the city authorities. I argue that business associations will be accommodated by the state and will coalesce with existing bureaucratic interests. This proposition contributes to the new research agenda that applies the state-in-society approach to post-socialist institutions. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: POLITICAL ATTITUDES OF THE HIGH BUREAUCRACY IN WESTERN EUROPE
abstract: THE POLITICAL ATTITUDES OF BUREAUCRATIC FUNCTIONARIES ARE EXAMINED AGAINST THE CLASSICAL IDEAL OF POLITICAL NONINVOLVEMENT. THE U OF MICHIGAN STUDY ENCOMPASSED GREAT BRITAIN, GERMANY, & ITALY. IN GREAT BRITAIN THE MAJORITY OF R'S WERE AT THE UNDERSECRETARY LEVEL, IN GERMANY SECTION CHIEFS. THE BUREAUCRATIC ELITES IN THE 3 COUNTRIES ARE COMPOSED OF MIDDLE AGED FUNCTIONARIES, LONG EMPLOYED IN ADMINISTRATION, U EDUCATED, WITH A MC OR UMC BACKGROUND, & MOSTLY M. THE ITALIAN HIGH BUREAUCRACY IS DISTINGUISHED BY LONG YEARS OF SERVICE & A RELATIVELY HIGHER AGE STRUCTURE. WITH REGARD TO POLITICAL ATTITUDES, IN RESPONSE TO THE STATEMENT THAT "IN SOLVING SOCIAL PROBLEMS IN MODERN SOCIETY, TECHNICAL CONSIDERATIONS SHOULD CARRY GREATER WEIGHT THAN THE POLITICAL," 77% OF THE ITALIAN, 22% OF THE BRITISH, & 49% OF THE GERMAN R'S ANSWERED "YES." WITH RESPECT TO "THE INTERFERENCE OF POLITICIANS SO AS TO COMPETE WITH THE PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION IS AN ELEMENT OF DYSFUNCTION," 83% OF THE ITALIAN, 43% OF THE GERMAN, & ONLY 9% OF THE BRITISH R'S AGREED. THE ITALIANS SHOW A SLIGHTLY GREATER PREFERENCE FOR PLURALISTIC INSTITUTIONS THAN THE GERMANS & THE BRITISH. 90% OF THE POSTS IN THE ITALIAN BUREAUCRACY ARE TAKEN UP BY PROFESSIONALS WHO STAY BASICALLY ABOVE POLITICAL CONFLICTS; OF THE ENGLISH R'S ONLY 32% SEE THEMSELVES SITUATED ABOVE POLITICAL CONFLICTS, & 38% OF THE GERMANS. IN RESPONSE TO THE STATEMENT THAT "POLITICAL PROPAGANDA IS NOT ABSOLUTE & THE STATE SHOULD LIMIT IT RIGOROUSLY," IN BRITAIN 3% AGREE, 19% AGREE, WITH RESERVATIONS, 40% DISAGREE, WITH RESERVATIONS, & 38% DISAGREE. IN GERMANY, 8% AGREE, 25% AGREE, WITH RESEARVATIONS, 37% DISAGREE, WITH RESERVATIONS, & 30% DISAGREE. IN ITALY, 36% AGREE, 21% AGREE, WITH RESERVATIONS, 12% DISAGREE, WITH RESERVATIONS, & 31% DISAGREE. THE ATTITUDE TOWARD POLITICS IS CORRELATIVE TO THE BUREAUCRAT'S ADHERENCE TO THE VALUES OF POLITICAL EQUALITY & POPULAR PARTICIPATION IN THE MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC AFFAIRS. 7 TABLES, 1 FIGURE. MODIFIED HA.

title: Dereliction at the South African Department of Home Affairs: Time for the anthropology of bureaucracy
abstract: In this article, I consider how a temporal reorientation of bureaucracy studies -- from retrospective analysis of outcomes to prospective analysis of states of possibility manifest in moments of bureaucratic waiting -- could help students of bureaucracy to think non-normatively about the relationship between policy and practice. I draw on ethnographic fieldwork with low-level officials at visa permitting offices of a South African immigration bureaucracy to explore how time textures everyday bureaucratic processes and configures one's understanding of what is possible in bureaucratic encounters. I develop the concept of "dereliction" to describe the ambiguous condition of hope and despair experienced by people engaged in bureaucratic encounters, illuminating the technologies that produce and manage this ambiguity, such as counters, cubbies, and temporary extension permits. While previous authors have shown that bureaucracies work to capture and control time, I shed light on a somewhat different sort of power: bureaucracies' ability to orient people toward the future.

title: The Role of Laymen in Bureaucratic Decisions. (Theoretical Conclusions of a Research in Sociology of Law)
abstract: Using data from two studies conducted in Hungary, the participation of nonprofessionals in governmental decision-making is assessed on three levels: (1) the effects of social preconditioning, (2) the influence of the organizational conditions under which the decisions are made, & (3) the social significance of such participation. The greatest problem encountered in the use of nonprofessionals is the latter's lack of professional expertise which contributes to a low level of organizational adaptation. However, this lower level of organizational involvement on the part of the nonprofessional allows him to act as a more effective intermediary between government & the public. 1 Figure. Modified HA.

title: ORGANIZATION SIZE, COMPLEXITY, AND ADMINISTRATIVE SUCCESSION IN HIGHER EDUCATION
abstract: One aspect of the theory re optimum size for bur'tic org's is explored: ie, the effect of org'al size & complexity upon the f of succession of admin'ive officers. Some previous studies are mentioned. The 'size-succession-bur'ization hyp' is tested in the setting of Coll's & U's under introduction of the element of org'al complexity as a factor influencing succession. Complexity is defined as the N of specialized & diff'iated tasks performed by personnel in an org & the integration of the diff'iated parts through the elaboration of codified procedures, ie, rules for the operation of the org. The measurement of org'al complexity is difficult but it is felt that this approach resuits in a more direct index of those aspects of bur'ization that are related to succession than is obtained by using only org'al size. The data for the study are drawn mainly from the EDU- CATION DIRECTORY OF THE OFFICE OF EDUCATION, Washington, DC: US Gov Printing Office, 1948-49, 1955-56, & 1962-63 Ed's. Size, complexity, & succession rates were measured for 2 periods. Findings in general indicate that large instit's stit's experience higher succession than small instit's. However, there was less support in the way of statistical signif for the obtained diff's. Size & succession are not related in a monotonic fashion. Middle-size instit's have lower succession rates than either the large or small instit's. 2 of the 3 measures of org'al complexity were also found to be associated with succession in the predicted direction. Sch's that were implicated in larger bur'tic structures (denominational & pub- , lic instit's) had higher rates of succession than independent Sch's; & Sch's with graduate programs had higher rates of succession than Sch's without graduate programs. These relationships were found to hold in a majority of comparisons in- G' dependent of the size of the instit. Growth rate was found to produce relationships opposite to those hyp'ed; it was inversely related to succession, as the rapidly growing instit's had lower succession rates than stable or modest growth instit's. It is suggested that growth might be a better index of org'al effectiveness than complexity. In general it appears that factors quite diff from complexity & size may influence succession in instit's of varying size. M. Maxfield.

title: Getting at the Live Archive: On Access to Information Research in Canada
Fluid adaptation of contested citizenship: second-generation migrant Turks in Germany and the United States
abstract: This paper explores belonging in the context of legal citizenship for second-generation Turkish immigrants in Berlin and in New York. Fluid adaptation refers to the discursive boundaries of immigrant identity articulations, the contextual and shifting adjustments immigrants make to their sense of belonging. Immigrant belonging, gauged by 'encounters' with bureaucracies and participatory expressions, is shaped in large part by the receiving state's legal framework and citizenship status. Belonging is complicated by racialization and exclusion, and affected by intersectionalities of immigrant experience. Limited citizenship models necessitate deployment of fluid and alternative membership models. Alternative forms of belonging underscore the power of the nation-state in delimiting belonging. Adapted from the source document.

title: Chronology, Succession, and Sovereignty: The Politics of Inka Historiography and Its Modern Interpretation
abstract: Western scholars have long identified the existence of writing systems as a near-universal characteristic of high civilization, with Tawantinsuyu, the Inka empire, representing the only significant exception. Although writing was absent in the pre-Hispanic Andes, there existed the means of recording administrative information & preserving narratives of the past. Inka imperial overseers & specialized record-keepers produced tribute levies, population counts, & assessments of provincial development potential, using a system of knotted cords (a khipu) as their principal device. Such records fulfilled bureaucratic & administrative functions that were satisfied in other societies by writing; however, the maintenance of narratives of the Inka past contrasts with these practices in its hybrid use of oral tradition in consultation with similar record keeping devices. Tables, References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Sociological studying of religion and 'atheisation' of population, 1960-1970-es
authors: Klimova, S M; Molostova, E S
abstract: The article examines the theory and practice of sociological study of the phenomenon of religiousness in the USSR in 1960-1970-es. The philosophical and ideological assumptions, tasks put forward by the party bureaucracy before the sociology of religion, the role of the scientific atheism, atheist propaganda and their influence on the sociology of religion are considered. The article shows the typical classifications of religious consciousness, tools of mass surveys (questionnaires); the results of informal interviews and participant observation among believers that are kept in the Russian Archive of Socio-Political History. In particular, the authors come to the conclusion that theoretical concepts and empirical research were, to a large extent, determined by ideological order. Adapted from the source document.

title: McJobs and Pieces of Flair: Linking McDonaldization to Alienating Work
abstract: This article offers strategies for teaching about rationality, bureaucracy, and social change using George Ritzer's The McDonaldization of Society and its ideas about efficiency, predictability, calculability, and control. Student learning is facilitated using a series of strategies: making the familiar strange, explaining McDonaldization, self-investigation and discovery, and exploring and implementing alternatives. Through assignments, class exercises, and films, students contextualize modernity and its unintended negative consequences by viewing McDonaldization though the lenses of work and jobs. These strategies provide a framework to help students understand key concepts, critique McDonaldization, and formulate positive ways to cope with Weber's iron cage. Adapted from the source document.

title: Postmodernism and the source of military strength in the Anglo West
abstract: Believing that cultural change must be rapid and thorough, many analysts are calling for a revolution in military culture as a necessary condition for a broader revolution in military affairs. This article argues for cultural reform in Anglo-Western armies, although much applies to other nations and other branches of service. Army transformation must draw upon the source of military strength in the cultural heritage of the host society. In the Anglo West, social capital, societal discipline, modem bureaucracy, and professionalism provide the foundation for military cohesion, discipline, efficiency, innovation, and legitimacy. Modern armies require postmodern reinvention to correct for misapplied modernism that has led to personnel turbulence, careerism, and factionalism. Although the source of economies of scale, modern bureaucracy can also undermine social stability and inhibit adaptability. Stages of psychological maturation parallel the stages of professional awareness required for balance among army stakeholders. The article concludes by suggesting a new force structure, personnel strategy, and governance system that emphasizes stability, local reputation, productive bureaucracy, professional streaming, and legitimacy for the military social contract. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Political Dynamics and Bureaucratic Career Patterns in the People's Republic of China, 1949-1994
abstract: Bureaucrats & bureaucratic organizations are at the center of political & economic institutions of state socialism. This study examines the link between political dynamics & bureaucratic career patterns in the People's Republic of China to shed light on the evolution of state socialist bureaucracy. The author argues that political dynamics induced by shifting state policies & tensions between state & bureaucratic interests led to the recruitment & promotion of separate cohorts of bureaucrats with distinctive characteristics & divided loyalties. Using the life histories of a representative sample drawn in 20 cities in China, I examine patterns of access to the Chinese bureaucracy & promotion patterns during the period from 1949 through 1994. The evidence shows varying selection criteria over time & two distinct patterns of promotion between national bureaucratic systems & within workplaces. These findings portray an image of bureaucrats as highly differentiated groups rather than a homogeneous ruling class. 4 Tables, 38 References. [Copyright 2001 Sage Publications, Inc.]

title: Controls of Knowledge Production, Sharing and Use in Bureaucratized Professional Service Firms
abstract: One of the main obstacles to the current bureaucratization trend in large professional service firms (PSFs) is the organic nature of professional knowledge production, sharing and use. Centralized knowledge management (KM) systems aimed at codifying 'best practice' solutions to recurrent client questions for large-scale reuse are a common strategy increasingly employed to overcome this obstacle. Using a socio-ethnographic case study of a business law firm in Paris, this research examines whether the use of centralized KM systems in bureaucratized PSFs contributes to a shift in power from professionals to managers. More specifically, are administrative controls over knowledge resources increasing, or do professionals retain power (i.e. some level of social and self-control) over knowledge production, sharing and use? The results of this study indicate that, far from losing ground, professionals' social and self-controls have been reinvented and reformed in a bureaucratized context. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: Better Expert than Orthodox: Reply to Shenkar
abstract: In a response to O. Shenkar's critique ("Rejoinder to Clegg and Higgins: The Chinese Case and Radical School in Organization Studies," Organization Studies, 1989 10, 1, 117-122) of Stewart R. Clegg's & Winton Higgins's work on the Chinese Cultural Revolution (see SA 35:4/88T7499), Shenkar's previous work (see SA 33:2/85O6424) is analyzed. Shenkar saw the Cultural Revolution as indicating the functional necessity of bureaucracy: it was the absence of the latter, he argues, that created the chaos of the former. While agreeing on the interpretation of chaos, the causality of his argument in accounting for it is rejected. Aspects of Shenkar's methodology, especially its reliance on Mao Tse-Tung's "Twenty Manifestations of Bureaucracy," are criticized. It is argued that bureaucracy & democracy are not antithetical, nor is organization feasible without rules or divsions of labor. 8 References. Modified AA

title: The negotiation of Takapuneke: conflicting notions of value of a tapu site
abstract: Struggles over indigeneity in Aotearoa/New Zealand have their roots in events that occurred before the creation of the nation. Ten years before the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi, the founding document of relations between Maori and colonial Britain, there was a massacre at the site of Takapuneke. The event helped to give birth to the nation and immediately started the struggle of Maori indigeneity against the increasingly politically dominant colonials. There are parallel struggles in contemporary New Zealand, as the country debates and attempts to rectify the concept of a bi-cultural society. These on-going struggles can help us understand how Maori are able to exercise agency and engage in practices that allow them to promote their indigeneity. The contemporary events around the site of the massacre at Takapuneke will illustrate such a struggle between the local Maori at Onuku and three bureaucratic and civic organizations.

title: Hunters and bureaucrats: power, knowledge, and Aboriginal-state relations in the Southwest Yukon
abstract: Westman reviews Hunters and bureaucrats: power, knowledge, and Aboriginal-state relations in the Southwest Yukon by Paul Nadasdy.

title: INDUSTRIALIZATION AND LABOR UNIONISM IN BRAZIL
abstract: The history of Brazilian workers' unions covers 2 distinct pe periods. The 1st, which ends in 1935, is that of anarchistic, Communistic, & traditional socialist unionism. The 2nd is marked by the org of bur'tic unionism imposed by the Ministry of Labor, between 1935 & 1950. Brazilian unionism thus presents itself today as a system of bur'tic assoc's created before the development of industrialization, & comprising very heterogeneous groups of individuals, both Ru & Ur. In addition, industrialization does not reduce the utilization of paternalistic values values & norms. Tr from IPSA by L. Gimenez Melo.

title: Patronage and Bureaucratic Control -- The Case of the Naval Officer in English Society 1780-1850
abstract: An examination of the problem of explaining how the process of bureaucratization takes place in relation to the historical development of the occupation of naval officers as a branch of the British State, & the changes in the ways in which it was controlled. Bureaucratization is taken to involve the interdependent processes of: (1) the impersonalization of rules, & thus, the movement away from forms of control deriving from relations of personal, political dependence, (2) the specialization & permanence of officials' positions, (3) the centralization of power over officials' positions, & (4) the decentralization of specified authority. By 1815 the occupation of naval officer had developed certain bureaucractic characteristics, but the principle form of occupational control stemmed from patronage relations of personal, political dependence, which alternated between centralized & decentralized forms. Patronage is seen as a basic principle of the social structure in this period. Using evidence from officers' letters & Admiralty documents, it is argued that in the post-1815 period certain candidates established the conditions for a further push in the direction of bureaucratization. These conditions were, first, at the level of general social structure, the extension of industrial capitalism which involved (A) basic shifts in economy-polity relations in English society, & (B) shifts in relations between States as a consequence of external political & strategic commitments posed by the expansion of the British Empire; secondly, at the occupational level, this period witnessed: (C) a decline in the efficiency of the officer corps, & (D) significant changes in the nature of naval warfare. These two sets of conditions reinforced each other, in that the expansion of industrial capitalism altered the setting of & permitted technical changes in, naval warfare, & the economy polity shifts altered the political atmosphere in where the problems of officers' effectiveness were viewed. As a result the government, via the admiralty, was constrained to introduce policies that resulted in shifting the control of naval officers away from patronage, towards more bureaucratic forms, a process that was to continue throughout the nineteenth century. AA.

title: Educational provision for refugee youth in Australia: left to chance?
abstract: This article investigates how education bureaucracies in Australia use languages of categorization and promote community partnerships to construct and govern the refugee subject. We use a framework of governmentality to analyse education policies and statements emerging from two levels of government -- Commonwealth and state. Drawing on web-based materials, policy statements and accounts of parliamentary debates, the article documents the ways in which refugee education continues to be subsumed within broader education policies and programmes concerned with social justice, multiculturalism and English language provision. Such categorizations are premised on an undifferentiated ethnoscape that ignores the significantly different learning needs and sociocultural adjustments faced by refugee students compared with migrants and international students. At the same time, educational programmes of inclusion that are concerned with utilizing community organizations to deliver services and enhance participation, point to the emergence of `government through community partnerships' -- a mode of governance increasingly associated with advanced liberal societies.

title: Organizational Design as Public Policy
abstract: An exploration of whether policymakers & analysts discover & prescribe organizational forms that will enhance attainment of desired policy outcomes, based on analysis of 2,199 resolutions & bills proposed or enacted by the state legislatures of Fla, Iowa, Mich, & NJ between 1956 & 1978, & data from House & Senate files on the legislators who proposed them (N = 921) & the committees that handled them. Past theoretical treatments of reform through reorganization are critiqued, & an alternative understanding of government organizations -- the governance model -- is introduced, which provides a more satisfying conceptual language for thinking about public organizations & expands the range of potential structural forms. The relationship between organizational governance & the essentially hierarchical nature of government agencies is also examined, & implications for efforts to formulate organization policy are discussed. 2 Tables, 93 References. Modified AA

title: Can Business Beat Bureaucracy?
abstract: An examination of the trend among major corporations in the last decade that has involved cutting layers of management & encouraging decentralized teamwork. This transformation, it is suggested, can be traced to innovations in both managerial & blue-collar work starting in the 1950s. However, the rhetoric of debureaucratization, participation, & empowerment refer not to a unified phenomenon, but to four visions: a cleaning up of the bureaucracy to eliminate unneeded rules & layers; the creation of a unified community, or culture, which draws employees into a closed circle of shared commitment; a vision of the corporation as a market, with many "profit centers" & with each part relating to the others as "customers"; & an open, consensus-based teamwork, with employees constantly reforming their internal associations to meet changing demands. Each vision is reflected in changes currently underway, but, it is argued, only the fourth -- the associational model -- holds promise for employee empowerment. L. Baker

title: THE EFFECTS OF POLITICAL CHANGE ON THE ROLE SET OF THE SENIOR BUREAUCRATS IN GHANA AND NIGERIA
abstract: It is argued that the role of senior bur'crats in both developing & developed pol'al systems is multifunctional, & that changes in the personnel, structures, & goals of a pol'al system affect the multifunctional content of the senior bur'crats' role. R. K. Merton's concept of role set is utilized to demonstrate how pol'al changes in Ghana & Nigeria have affected the role of the senior bur'crats in these 2 systems. From these 2 examples a set of tentative propositions is advanced on this subject, & an effort is made to relate these to G. Homans' theory of elementary soc behavior. HA.

title: Individual Discretion and Organizational Accountability: Evaluating the Performance of Public Bureaucrats
abstract: Individuals within organizations have to confront the conflict between being accountable for their performance and trying to maintain autonomy and exercise discretion when accomplishing complex tasks. It is usually assumed that individuals, particularly professionals, face complex tasks that are difficult to evaluate and will resist attempts to control their performance through organizational rules. However, routinizing tasks and decentralizing decision-making authority to the individual may clarify rules and give individuals some control over their jobs, making the individual more amenable to the evaluation of performance. Hypotheses concerning the somewhat conflicting demands of job complexity and organizational control were tested by analyzing attitudes towards a performance appraisal system undergoing change in two United States federal agencies. Changes in attitudes were measured by a LISREL panel analysis over five points in time.

title: The Commission for Racial Equality, British Bureaucracy and the Multiethnic Society
abstract: A book review of The Commission for Racial Equality, British Bureaucracy and the Multiethnic Society by Ray Honeyford is presented.

title: The Class Position of Scientific Workers
abstract: Scientific workers can be considered in 2 lights, according to a class analysis or one which defines them as an elite. After considering these 2 approaches, the concrete work relations engaging the scientific specialist in the framework of a theory of bureaucracy is examined. The scientific workers' source of power within the productive organization is then explored. At the base of these different views on the position of the scientist in the production lies their conceptions of the source of impetus for further SE development. The advocates of technocracy assert that since technological know-how & organization are the new motive forces of the postindustrial revolution, the development of knowledge replaces economics per se at the foundation of historical development. For A. Touraine, the foundation is the will to continual growth, a political, not economic impetus since industrial capitalism has raised western society above need. In this view, alienation & not exploitation is the basis of class opposition. Neo-Marxist analysis, however, indicates that the need for growth is an economic one, & that the bureaucratic forms of productive organization in which the scientific worker is integrated are the same as the other workers, even though, as a group crucial to the capitalist program, they are privileeged & do not therefore share the same conditions as the other workers. Although perhaps not as economically exploited in terms of salary & work conditions, they exist in the same structural relation as the nonscientific workers to the capitalist interest of continual expansion & inc;easing efficiency, without for a moment being responsible for the direction of the enterprise. E. Holland.

title: Collaboration and Competition in Two Colonization Projects: Toward a General Theory of Official Corruption
authors: Bunker, Stephen G; Cohen, Lawrence E
abstract: Analyses of corruption in bureaucracies in underdeveloped countries have frequently attributed causation to particular political, cultural, or social-structural factors, without taking into account the different degrees of corruption in different frames. Here, it is proposed that the degree of antagonistic surveillance or collaborative exchange within & between bureaucratic agencies is a key determinant of the incidence of official corruption. Two development projects within the same geographical, political, administrative, & temporal frames in Brazil are compared to examine this proposition. Analysis of Ru development projects along the Trans-Amazon Highway indicates that antagonism between agents of different bureaucratic agencies serves to reduce corruption by ensuring the mutual vigilance of the actors involved, & by preventing the opportunities for collusion or acquiescence that are necessary for corruption to occur. The generalizability of this proposition beyond developing countries is considered, & policy implications are discussed. 35 References. HA.

title: Anatomy of a Care Manager
abstract: The article considers the impact of the NHS & Community Care Act (1990), & the redefined role of 'care manager', upon social work. It draws from a three-year ethnographic study of five area teams; one based in inner London & the others, including a hospital team, based in the north of England. Particularly it uncovers the considerable impact of intense bureaucracy, circumscribed budgets & the consequential removal of the care manager from the community. The article also questions any 'seamless service' in work with other professionals & raises doubts as to whether need is even being partially met. Care managers are rarely able to utilize the skills that they develop during the Diploma in Social Work course. Frustration is felt on behalf of staff in the area office, who are now working under considerable strain, with little recognition, within what resembles a new emergency service. It is hoped the article is able to draw attention to the consequences of the continued deskilling of social work & retrenchment of what little remains of welfare. 28 References. [Copyright 2003 Sage Publications Ltd.]

title: Faire la «guerre contre la drogue». Relations asymétriques et adoption d'un régime répressif/Making the "War on Drugs": Asymmetric Relations and the Adoption of a Repressive Regime
abstract: At first glance, the adoption of a repressive agenda against drug trafficking by dependent countries appears as a clear sign of the influence of hegemonic states over world affairs. However, even if this asymmetry is real, the importation of repressive norms and law enforcement instruments is intrinsically linked to internal political and bureaucratic dynamics. Based on a case study of the progressive involvement of the Colombian state in the war against drugs from the late 1970s to the early 1990s, this paper proposes a reflection on the ways in which internal politics and international relations can be intertwined. The method of analysis essentially rests on retracing links between the international and the emergence, politicization, and transformation of drugs into a public problem -- that is an assessment of the relationship between endogenous games, on the one hand, and international processes and resources on the other.

title: What Is Bureaucracy?
abstract: The theory of state is analyzed through its development in the writings of 3 theorists: (1) the later writings of Marx with their emphasis on historical theory, (2) the STATE AND REVOLUTION by Lenin (no publishing information available) which closely follows Marxian principles, & (3) Trotskyist ideas of social democracy & labor aristocracy. The concept of bureaucracy in modern society is examined with reference to M. Weber's analysis of commonalities among bureaucracies, & his typification of bureaucracy based on his theory of the general nature of bureaucracy. The definitions advanced by Weber are supplemented with the ideas of other theorists such as A. Touraine, & M. Crozier. 3 examples mentioned by Weber are presented to illustrate aspects of bureaucracy. Difficulties inherent in the writing of a formal definition of bureaucracy are described; they are manifest in the imprecision & ambiguity which exists (in current literature) concerning the phenomena. Some conclusions are drawn pertaining to the bureaucrat in his functionings in the areas of administration, hierarchal power relations, exploitative SR, sphere of addressed, & principles for the guidance of discussions of bureaucracy are outlined. The described text is related to present day situations & modes of thought. C. Grindle.

title: The Social Organization of Knowledge and Its Consequences for Discourse in Bureaucratic Settings
abstract: In a recapitulation of the principal themes of the articles collected in this issue (see abstracts in SA 36:5), the notion that in bureaucratic settings knowledge is socially organized in ways that have similar consequences for discourse organization is examined. All articles share the viewpoint that the knowledge of bureaucratic constraints is socially organized & differentiated in terms of the role distinction between bureaucrat (insider) & client (outsider). Insiders are privy to knowledge of institutionally defined constraints on discourse whereas outsiders have less such knowledge & vary in their expectations. Brief outlines of the papers are presented to identify the particular aspects of the relationship between social & communicative organization examined. It is concluded that the insider's contribution to discourse management is shaped by the knowledge necessary for functioning as a representative of the bureaucracy, but this knowledge is not shared or transmitted to the outsider. 12 References. Z. Dubiel

title: BUREAUCRACY
abstract: A continuation of SA A5345. Selling through mass COMM's in the US relies heavily on a continuing study of an expanding & diverse market by experts trained in mass culture. The means of COMM - nat'l radio & TV networks, magazines & newspapers, motion pictures, etc - gear their advertising & program content to the results of studies of the makeup of the mass audiences & readership. Modern advertising incorporates the conclusions of psychol'ts like S. Freud & uses the simple message aimed at high ideals found successful by such propaganda masters as Lenin, Goebbels, & before them by the French revolutionaries. The studies try to determine what the latest taboos & prejudices of the mass audience happen to be. Efforts are made not to offend minority groups or pressure groups, & as a result, both the broadcasting industry & the publishing industry have imposed self-censorship. These restrictions have produced 'the artist for the masses,' an artist who 'works for a salary, a price, a commission, who must obey certain norms of style & taboos imposed by admin'ors without artistic capacity ... .' The result is a certain sameness in programming & literature. It is concluded that a knowledge of the market is necessary, but despite enormous efforts to acquire the necessary understanding, a great deal remains to be learned. Modified AA.

title: CORPORATE SIZE, BUREAUCRATIZATION, AND MANAGERIAL SUCCESSION
abstract: 2 studies of the largest & smallest business corporations among the top 500 were conducted. The positions of board chairman, president, treasurer, controller & secretary were examined over a 10-yr span to determine whether succession had taken place in each office. The findings indicated that f'cy of succession was positively related to size of firm. An explanation proposed suggested that the process of succession may be radically diff in form & org'al consequence for the large, bureaucratized system than for the smaller, less bureaucratized one. Greater size necessitates increased bureaucratization & this increases the likelihood that succession will be rationally treated by being routinized. Without f succession bur's tend to lose that degree of flexibility which they esp need. Enlarged AA.

title: Ritzer, Rationalization, and Risk
abstract: Bureaucracy was Max Weber's paradigm of rationalization; Ritzer's is the fast-food-restaurant, suggesting a modified form of rationalization is ascendant in contemporary society. Sources of possible difficulty in & for Ritzer's McDonaldization thesis are discussed: ambiguous formulation, unsubstantiated causal claims, & seeming countertendencies of risk, post-Fordism, & of tradition in science. 28 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Thin versus Thick Democracy in Education: Porto Alegre and the Creation of Alternatives to Neo-Liberalism
authors: Gandin, Luis Armando; Apple, Michael W
abstract: In this article, the authors describe the ways in which a set of policies has had what seem to be extensive & long lasting effects precisely because these policies are coherently linked to larger dynamics of social transformation & to a coherent strategy that aims to change the mechanisms of the state & the rules of participation in the formation of state policies. They describe & analyze the policies of the "Popular Administration" in Porto Alegre, Brazil but, more specifically, they focus on the "Citizen School" & on proposals that are explicitly designed to radically change both the municipal schools & the relationship between communities, the state, & education. This set of polices & the accompanying processes of implementation are constitutive parts of a clear & explicit project aimed at constructing not only a better school for the excluded, but also a larger project of radical & thick democracy. The reforms being built in Porto Alegre are still in formation, but the authors argue that they have crucial implications for how we might think about the politics of education policy & its role in social transformation. 27 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Exploring the Metropolitan Trap: The Case of Montreal
abstract: This article analyses the normative dimension of metropolitan governance in the case of Montreal. According to the main schools of thought (the reform school, the public choice school, new regionalism and the rescaling approach), there is an ideal scale at which to achieve specific goals such as equality, efficiency, democracy and economic competitiveness. These ideologically oriented conceptions of metropolitan governance are assumed by actors and used as symbolic resources to build their own strategies, i.e. to support or contest institutional reforms -- what we call the metropolitan trap. The case of Montreal, which underwent two successive institutional reforms between 2000 and 2006, provides empirical evidence for this idea. Our analysis reveals that the Government of Quebec and local elected councils of Greater Montreal are trapped by these normative conceptions, especially the old regionalisms. However, scalar strategies do not compete equally, as the institutional context legitimates specific approaches to metropolitan governance. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: To Control or to Smash Bureaucracy: Weber and Lenin on Politics, the State, and Bureaucracy
abstract: Lenin & Weber were both critics of "bureaucratic" government, but they had very different analyses of the causes of bureaucratic rule & they drew very different conclusions as to where the solutions to the problem might lie. Weber saw the causes as lying in the organizational dynamics of bureaucracy & the state, especially in the drive for rational efficiency. The only partial solution was the creation of organizational forms which might help to contain the worst aspects of unconstrained bureaucratic rule. Lenin saw the causes of bureaucratization as embedded in the basic contradictions of capitalist society, in particular in the need for the bourgeoisie to suppress class struggle, & he saw the solution in the revolutionary reconstruction of the social order. The details of Lenin's & Weber's arguments are analyzed, the theoretical strengths & weaknesses assessed, & the political implications of the unresolved problems discussed. AA.

title: Namibia's Post-Apartheid Agricultural Bureaucracy Restructuring: The Agricultural Extension Service, 1990-1996
abstract: In posing these analytic queries, I wish to underline the real-world link between the policy process and institutional reform. A growing literature seeks to re-emphasize the significance of institutional behavior in policy studies and in comparative politics;3 in this article I suggest specifically that internal administrative reforms helped to generate changes in staff behavior that in turn represented a significant factor in the carrying out of new agricultural policy goals targeting the upliftment of communal area farmers. I do not seek to minimize the significance of macro-level policy decisions in determining these policy outcomes4 -- to be sure, the administrative changes were in part initiated by new policy priorities to lend greater attention to communal areas -- but at the same time I underline the crucial role of changes in internal organizational and personnel behavior in helping to assure mat the government's new policy priority of providing higher levels of service to communal area farmers was in fact implemented. I argue that policy implementation was achieved mainly in regard to the provision of (1) advanced crop seeds of the country's staple food crop -millet -- to agronomic farmers, and (2) cattle licks to communal area herders. I explain that these implementation successes were made possible, in part, through organizational restructuring and behavioral changes that took place within the agricultural sector of the civil service. In doing so, I emphasize the importance of examining the micro-level, behavioral changes in bureaucratic behavior in understanding the success of policy reform in contemporary Africa.5 Too often, policy analyses and studies of 'the African state' focus on broad national-level decisions without paying sufficient analytic attention to the human dynamics involved in restructuring bureaucracies which render the implementation of new policies possible. In this article, I prioritize the importance of changes in officials' behavior at the middle and lower levels of a state bureaucracy, and demonstrate that such an analysis can reveal key aspects of institutional dynamics mat bear significantly on the policy process. Adapted from the source document.

title: NOTES ON MERITOCRACY
abstract: In looking ahead to the mythical 'Yr 2000,' to a symposium to which this article is a contribution, questions are raised as to the resistances developing in a society which increasingly judges people on universalistic criteria & certifies them for soc roles on the basis of measured educ'al attainments. It is suggested that even if attainments of a nonprofessional or nonacademic sort were to be weighed & rewarded soc'ly, these would not be randomly distributed, so that even qualities like sympathy & courage would be more likely to go together with the qualities already measured & defined. There is some discussion of the generational turnover in a meritocratic society & of the obsolescence of senior men who must give way to more up-to-date younger ones more rapidly than they can gracefully be retired. But there is also discussion of the advantages of meritocracy in protecting the idiosyncratic & nonconformist member of an org, whose talents save him from having to be like his fellows in nonoccup'al respects. As what are called human resources become more important than other material resources, res on personality & instit'al res in personnel-processing instit's seems likely to grow. But so do resistances of an anarchic sort, based on surviving particularistic values, familistic, regional, & idiosyncratic. Young women are likely to continue to feel it is even more important to be attractive than to be brilliant, though the verdict of 'stupid' becomes more & more intolerable. But the US, even in the Yr 2000, is likely to be a less centralized society than other large-scale industr & post-industr states, so that the hegemony of nat'l or global standards will be delayed. AA.

title: Reframing child poverty: What lessons can we learn from the limitations of Labour's efforts to end child poverty?
abstract: The experience of poverty in the UK is the struggle to make ends meet, die frustration and debilitation of dealing with inflexible and unsympathetic bureaucracies, employers, landlords and creditors, and, for many, the shame and alienation that can come with it. It can mean facing pernicious material choices that in today's Britain are unimaginable for most of us, such as whether to put adequate food on the table or to heat the home. It can mean lack of dignity, absence of control and immense time pressures without commensurate reward. Poverty is often compounded and reinforced by other aspects of disadvantage, including challenging neighbourhoods, absence of support and a lack of assets. We believe that this is the context in which child poverty needs to be situated. Growing up in this kind of poverty has a profound impact on both childhood experience and life chances, at many different levels. For example, children from poor households have worse average educational outcomes and are much more likely to suffer from significant ill health, both in childhood and in adulthood. Adapted from the source document.

title: Alvin Gouldner's Challenge to Sociology and Marxism: The Problem of Bureaucracy
abstract: Aligned with the tradition of Western Marxism, the work of Alvin W. Gouldner animates a concern with the political implications of social scientific research. The Western Marxian theme of theory & praxis finds its fullest elaboration in his most recent work. This same theme also provides the theoretical impetus to Gouldner's early industrial organization studies -- Patterns of Industrial Bureaucracy (New York: Free Press, 1954) & Wildcat Strike (Yellow Springs, Ohio: Antioch Press, 1954). Vital to Gouldner's work is the notion that sociology must concern itself not only with what is but also with what human society might be. Gouldner's message is clear: The project of a critical social science cannot stop at mere "negativity," but rather must incorporate the insights of empirical sociology. Examination of his earliest work on organizations & bureaucracy shows that Gouldner has superbly woven these two traditions together & significantly advanced the progress toward developing an adequate critical sociology. In order to demonstrate Gouldner's intellectual lineage with Western Marxism, some translation is necessary. One of the goals here is to show that the tradition of empirical social science is translatable into the dialectical tradition of social analysis. Gouldner's empirical studies share the same "cognitive interests" -- although guided by a different style & method of investigation -- with Western Marxism. These insights are offered in his empirical analyses of the recurrent dilemmas of power, leadership, organization, & the fate of democratic aspirations in the modern world. Gouldner's work stands as a significant attempt by a US sociologist to rethink the central issues confronting sociology & Marxism. HA.

title: Quality Of Public Service Delivery In The Civil Service Of Macedonia: What Role For The Code Of Ethics?
abstract: The ongoing Public Administration Reform (PAR) process in Macedonia is being largely focused on public service delivery improvement. Despite the efforts, the Civil Service in Macedonia is being continuously criticized for the low level of its public services delivery. Main weaknesses brought in the focus involve various forms of unethical behavior of civil servants including, but not limited to, corruptive acts, inappropriate behavior in their daily communication with clients, and hesitations to serve the public interest as required by the constitution and the laws. The paper analyzes the role of the Code of Ethics for Civil Servants in the advancement of the quality of the services delivered to the citizens. It concludes that it has failed to make an impact in the public service delivery. It further elaborates that the marginal role results mainly from the lack of attention and focus on the Government's side in enforcing the document fully. Adapted from the source document.

title: TOWARD AN IDEAL TYPE OF BUREAUCRATIC ADMINISTRATIVE PARTICIPATION?
abstract: A REPLY IS MADE TO L. POTESTA (SEE SA 23:3/75H3616), WHO IS SUSPECTED OF REDUCTIONISM IN CRITICIZING THE AUTHOR'S PROPOSAL OF A 'POST-WEBERIAN' IDEAL TYPE OF ADMINISTRATIVE PARTICIPATION, OR OF "BUREAUCRACY WITH ADMINISTRATIVE PARTICIPATION." THIS THEORY IS AN ALTERNATIVE TO STATE CORPORATISM, SOVIETISM, GUILD SOCIALISM, & OTHER FUNCTIONAL REPRESENTATION SYSTEMS. IT IS CHARACTERIZED BY 3 MAJOR FEATURES: (1) THE POSITIONING OF THE CITIZEN IN THE FOCI OF ADMINISTRATIVE DECISION-MAKING, PRESUMING DEMOCRATIZATION OF ALL PUBLIC DECISION-MAKING PROCESSES, (2) THE DEBUREAUCRATIZATION OF PUBLIC ORGANIZATIONS AS THE END RESULT OF PARTICIPATION, & (3) THE REVIVAL OF THE WEBERIAN OBSERVATION OF THE POLITICAL & JURIDICAL IMPORTANCE OF THE 'BUREAUCRACY' AS AN ADMINISTRATIVE APPARATUS. A RETURN TO THE WEBERIAN CONCEPT OF BUREAUCRACY WOULD HAVE A SALUTARY EFFECT. FOR WEBER THE BUREAUCRACY WAS NOT AN END IN ITSELF, BUT JUSTIFIED IN THE NAME OF THE CITIZEN. S. KARGANOVIC.

title: The Female Being and the Management of School Establishments in Quebec
abstract: Contrary to what has been happening in the private sector in Quebec, the number of women in high administrative positions in the public sector -- particularly education, a traditionally female(F)-dominated field -- has actually declined since 1960. Here, time-use questionnaire data obtained from 70 male & F educational directors are used to describe gender differences in administrative roles, activities, & responsibilities. The social invisibility of F administrators is discussed, & the contradictory roles that are thrust on them are examined. Factors in the professional environment that limit F administrators' access to financial, cultural, & information resources are identified. K. Hyatt

title: Devolution and Recentralization of Welfare Administration: Implications for "New Federalism"
authors: Adkisson, Richard V; Peach, James T
abstract: When the Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) program was created, participating states were made responsible for the administration of the program. States could choose between administering the program themselves or allowing local administration under state supervision. Initially, 32 of the 50 states (64%) opted for the state-supervised, locally administered structure. By 1990, only 15 states (30%) were operating under state-supervised systems. Amid decades of talk about federal-to-state decentralization, 17 states have chosen to centralize their welfare administration systems. This choice is an important one as there is substantial evidence indicating that administrative structure is an important determinant of program delivery costs & equity. This article uses a logit model to identify the characteristics that have influenced state choice of administrative model. The results suggest that decisions to centralize welfare administration have been systematic choices, driven by geographic, demographic, economic, & political considerations unique to each state. 4 Tables, 13 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Dynamos And Virgins Revisited: Women And Technological Change In History. Edited by Martha Moore Trescott
abstract: This collection addresses a heretofore underresearched topic: the historical interaction of women and technology. The pursuit of such a focus is, of itself, laudable. It is reminiscent of the recent development of interest in women and the organization (such as the work of Denhardt and Perkins, "The Coming of Death of Administrative Man" in Public Administration Review; Kanter, Men and Women of the Corporation; and Hennig and Jardim, The Managerial Woman). For too long, the study of the history of technology has ignored not only the role of Women in the process but the effects of technological advances on women as well. It is as if women sat out the industrial revolution.This anthology derives from the organization, Women in Technological History, founded in late 1976. Several of the essays originated in that forum. The introduction is worthy of a close reading, for editor Trescott and the central contributor, Cowan use it to integrate the thematic threads. The book has a dual focus: 1) women as active participants in technological change (not only as workers and operatives but as inventors, scientists and entrepreneurs as well), and 2) the effects of technology on women in the more private spheres of life (as homemakers, childbearers and rearers).For a complete reprint of this article contact Haworth Press by telephone (1-800-HAWORTH) or EMail (getinfo@haworthpressinc.com) Article copyright The Haworth Press, Inc.

title: Does democracy produce quality of government?; [1]
abstract: This article analyses the effects of political regimes over state capacity or the quality of government (QoG): Do democratic states perform better than authoritarian ones? Previous studies point to a nonlinear relationship between democracy and government quality. It is argued here that QoG is a function of both forces of supply  (leaders who have the power to make reforms) and demand  (citizens' desire for mid- to long-term investments over short-term needs), the latter of which is a function of economic development. In democratic states, leaders have stronger incentives to improve QoG after a certain degree of wealth is reached, while in poorer countries they have little incentive for long-term bureaucratic investments. Thus it is predicted that the relationship between democracy and QoG is conditional, based on economic development. With over 125 countries in the sample, this hypothesis is tested using time-series panel data and spatial models, and strong empirical support is found.

title: Notes toward a Study of the Mexican Bureaucracy
abstract: Some approaches to the study of the Mexican bureaucracy are discussed. One line of research in this area focuses on administrative processes, clientism, & jurisdictional dysfunctions & contradictions. A more fruitful approach is suggested based on the internal analysis of the bureaucracy in its social context. A brief survey of the growth & function of the bureaucracy from the colonial period to the modern day in Mexico is presented. S. Karganovic

title: The Intellectual Crisis in Philanthropy
abstract: Defenders of modern philanthropic freedom often defend donor intent and celebrate voluntary action. Nevertheless, donor intent and voluntarism have often undermined the conditions of constitutional freedom. This paper proposes that philanthropy currently suffers an intellectual crisis very much like the intellectual crisis in public administration diagnosed by Vincent Ostrom. The Common Core State Standards initiative is a case study of the problems of epistemic drift in philanthropy and raises questions about whether merely defending donor intent and voluntary action for their own sake is sufficient. To escape philanthropy's current intellectual crisis requires a clearer consideration of the epistemic choices that shape donor intent and voluntary action. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Black International Conspiracy as Security Dispositive in the Netherlands, 1880-1900
abstract: In this paper we introduce the fight against anarchism at the end of the 19th century as a security dispositive. An analysis of the emergence of the dispositive of the Black International conspiracy and the rise of new modes of governance in the wake of the fight against violent anarchism in the Netherlands is presented as a bottom-up process of securitization, enabled by two remarkable episodes of anarchist activities in the Netherlands in 1894 and 1895-1898. Regional prosecutors and police commissioners capitalized on this (foreign) anarchist threat to instigate large-scale police reforms in terms of bureaucratization, standardization and centralization. New technologies of imagination, imported from abroad, helped to advance these processes of securitization and modernization. Adapted from the source document.

title: Woven worlds: Material things, bureaucratization, and dilemmas of caregiving in Lutheran humanitarianism
abstract: In this article, I examine the transition from charitable assistance to a professional model of humanitarianism in one American Lutheran agency that emerged from colonial missions to Madagascar. The agency, "International Health Mission" (IHM), primarily supplies medical technologies to Lutheran clinics in Madagascar, Tanzania, and Cameroon. I argue that popular material devices of relief provision, such as handmade bandages, tie the Christian humanitarian project to older notions of Lutheran faith as caregiving and pose special challenges to the bureaucratic model of aid delivery espoused by IHM. Casting renewed scholarly attention on materiality sheds light on the unique dilemmas facing faith-based aid agencies that strategically merge political discourses of humanitarianism with religious motivations for their work. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Recordkeeping as a Technology of Power
abstract: Discusses recordkeeping as a technology of social control peculiar to bureaucratic organizations, & outlines five types of information systems; archival, statistical, administrative, intelligence, & evaluation. The subject submits personal data to an organization in return for a service or a product. The data are manipulated by the organization to form a voluntary market-based system. Advances in technology allow more massive data manipulation, including combining data sets. The argument is made that the legal framework for protecting personal privacy contributes to the construction of such information systems because it legitimates them & encourages individuals to participate. The problem with the current protection against data surveillance is that it fails to limit the power of organizations in manipulating the information for their own use. 69 References. A. Cohen

title: Public Enterprise Management Training in Least Developed Countries of the Asian and Pacific Region
abstract: Since planners have long held that the goal of national development cannot be achieved by relying on the private sector, governments are becoming increasingly involved in promoting SE development, & public enterprises have thus been increasing in importance. However, there is a growing feeling that their performance has been less than satisfactory. Thus, the UN Economic & Social Commission for Asia & the Pacific has undertaken to design & conduct training programs focused on the specific needs of least developed countries in this region, as an effort at human resource development. An in-country approach was taken to provide public enterprise management training facilities. A draft curriculum is described that was prepared for a public enterprise management training program for senior managers & executives in the Maldives. 2 Tables, 10 References. HA

title: The French-Style Americanization of Homelessness in Bordeaux
abstract: Although homelessness, which first appeared in the United States, did not reach France until the 1990s, it progressively took root as an inescapable structural feature. Its American anteriority justifies considering whether the phenomenon in France is similar. Among the challenges, there is the sheer scale of the problem, the underlying gravity of the housing and job-market situation, the disengagement of the welfare state, and repressive management of the homeless. This study focuses on the main characteristics of homelessness, the extensive transformations in the treatment of the homeless, and the management of their visibility in public spaces. From an in-depth case study in Bordeaux, we can see how management of the homeless in public spaces corresponds to a new logic. It is no longer based on repression, but on an approach that involves the homeless in programs aimed at giving them an urban role in the form of street cleaning and participation in street arts. This new policy corresponds to a certain definition of neoliberalism in which homeless individuals themselves are the consenting instruments of this form of urban governance.

title: "McJustice": On the McDonaldization of Criminal Justice
abstract: This essay examines the "McDonaldization" of criminal justice or "McJustice." In doing so, it provides another useful way of understanding the development & operation of criminal justice in the United States. The McDonaldization of various social institutions has succeeded because it provides advantages over other, usually older, methods of doing business. It has made McDonaldized social institutions bureaucratic & rational in a Weberian sense &, thus, more efficient, calculable, predictable, & controlling over people (often by nonhuman technologies). The principal problem with McDonaldized institutions, & another characteristic of the process, is irrationality or, as Ritzer calls it, the "irrationality of rationality." A primary purpose of this essay is to expose some of the irrationalities of "McJustice" & to suggest some possible responses to them. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Theories of lean management: An empirical evaluation
abstract: Debates within organization theory traditionally argued the relative merits of bureaucracy but today there is broad agreement across different perspectives that bureaucratic organization is inefficient and outmoded. Despite their differences, post-bureaucratic and neo-liberal theories argue that organizations with relatively flat hierarchies and low management overhead are better adapted to current market requirements. Post-bureaucratic theory also argues that employees, as well as firms, benefit from leaner management structures. This paper investigates trends in managerial leanness, proposed explanations for such trends, and the consequences of leanness for firms and employees. Although there is a trend toward flatter management hierarchies, there is only weak support for current claims regarding both the causes and consequences of lean management. [Copyright Elsevier Inc.]

title: Intellectual Underemployment in Italian Public Bureaucracy
abstract: An analysis of intellectual employees in Italian public bureaucracy, with emphasis on quantification. Bureaucratic statistics between 1889 & 1927 are compared with data from 1954 to 1984. Analysis shows that the scope of this phenomenon is not caused by a statistical increase in intellectuals, but by the fact that Italian public administration is a sector that hires better-educated people, both in administration & technical fields. 6 Tables. Modified HA.

title: Ascription into Achievement: Models of Career Systems at Lloyds Bank, 1890-1970
authors: Stovel, Katherine; Savage, Michael; Bearman, Peter
abstract: Using optimal matching techniques to analyze the employment histories of three cohorts of GB's Lloyds Bank employees, 1890-1970, the tranformation of the structure of careers is explored. Full career histories were reconstructed from a random sample of 4,000 bank workers, & the rise of the modern achievement-based career structure of large bureaucratic organizations was traced. The breakdown of the traditional ascriptive, status-based system is modeled & then a more dynamic, achievement-based system is identified as its replacement. Traditional employment systems deliver social status to clerks by linking salary with tenure rather than the status of the position. In the new system, however, mobility came with achievement. As bank patronage diffused throughout the middle class & banks consolidated & expanded their branch networks, the need for local networks of employees decreased. Higher levels of integration introduced an increasingly competitive employment environment; the result was the modern male achievement-based career at the same time that women created a new tier of employees within the clerical ranks. Focusing on sequences of events demonstrates that social processes are marked more by discontinuities than gradual transitions. 3 Tables, 4 Figures, 1 Appendix, 58 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Corruption in the World of Politics
authors: Teofilovic, Nebojsa; Korajlic, Nedzad; Dautbegovic, Almin
abstract: Corruption is universal social phenomenon which directly causes decrease in political and economical power of each society, and prevention of it represents one of the leading challenges of contemporary democratic changes. Considering increasing presence of corruption in political and social life, dominant public perception is that society cannot function without it. Corruption appears as normal and acceptable social practice. These types of criminal acts are difficult to discover and complicated for investigation thanks to the support from bureaucracy, technocracy and plutocracy of given society. Adapted from the source document.

title: Beyond the Symbol of Public Consultation
abstract: The institution of consultation as a means of public participation in management decisions in Quebec, seen as a response to public activism, is criticized for lacking coherence & effectiveness & for being little more than a symbolic gesture. Consultation is defined in detail & distinguished from other modes of citizen participation & public relations. Three research projects studying the consultation process between 1979 & 1983 provide data on common problems & possible solutions. Problems center around lack of agreement on & imprecision about the role that consultation will play in the decision-making process. Some preconditions that are considered necessary for a successful consultation process, but which rarely are present, include: (1) a clear definition of how public power is to be manifested in consultation; (2) agreement on procedural rules; & (3) an informed public skilled in decision making. Modified HA

title: The State's Wish to Know and to Influence
abstract: The survey is one of the elementary modalities of State science. Describing & counting is already controlling. The example of statistics of manufacturing illustrates how, in France, under the Ancien Regime, an art of describing & classifying has gradually evolved, in step with the accumulation of experiences. Observation & inquiry procedures, surveys & statistics became slowly institutionalized, formalizing a true practical science of industrial counting. A new type of administrative agent developed: halfway between the assistant & the engineer; the manufacturing inspectors are both the eyes & ears of the State in the provinces. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Charismatic and the Bureaucratic Leaders
abstract: Typological studies of pol'al leaders presently classify them under 2 headings, charismatic & bureaucratic. These types have been defined & analyzed by the German, Max Weber, & by the American, H. D. Lasswell. This dichotomous classification has as its basis the classification of types which was developed especially by Max Weber. These types cannot exist in reality, & so in each instance it must be determined which of the 2 types the individual under consideration most closely resembles. The charismatic leader owes his position to his personality, while the bureaucratic leader owes his position to formal conditions. Analysis reveals that a situation of anomie helps the rise to power of charismatic leaders, while periods of peaceful development are best suited to interests of a bureaucratic leader. The present international situation, which ordinarily has strong elements of insecurity in it, can give numerous opportunities to charismatic leaders to come to power. Since these leaders are frequently inclined to make use of dictatorial methods, a development of this nature would naturally resemble that which occurred between the two world wars. This hypothesis presupposes a direct association between the theory of types of leaders & the theory of anomie. Tr by J. A. Broussard from TPSA.

title: Состояние здоровья в Европе и России: общественный контекст и социальные неравенства
authors: Rusinova, N L; V Safronov Safronov
abstract: Article is devoted to health differences in the European states and social inequalities in health in Europe. The analysis of the European Social Survey 2008 data (representative samples of the population of 28 countries) and statistics of World bank and WHO, carried out with methods of two-level logistic modeling, shows that in the postcommunist countries health is, as a rule, significantly worse, than in other parts of the continent. The reason of such differences is rather low level of their development (inefficient economy, welfare state, public administration) and low social integration. It is found also that health in Europe is structured on demographic and social variables, and such structuring depends on a macro context - a country level of social development. With growth of this level, social inequalities in health start smoothing out.

title: Local Administration in Lodz: Past, Present and Prospects
abstract: Since Poland's regained independence in 1918, the position of Lodz as the seat of local administration organs has had a specific character. Although over years the concept of state management tended to change, together with the models of local administration, which exerted an influence on the structure of local organs operating in the city, one thing remained unchanged: Lodz remained the seat not only of organs charged with city management, but also organs whose sphere of activity extended beyond the city itself, thus making Lodz the "capital" of larger territorial units. The present self-government system in Lodz raises many justified questions, all pointing to the necessity of abandoning the present formula of an integrated administrative district. The fundamental issue is the number of levels of the future local administration (two or three), & the levels at which self-government & the organs of central administration will be located. Another issue is equipping the administrative units smaller than the city with the self-government status. It would mean bringing the local government closer to the local community, conforming with a broader trend of views on this subject voiced in the countries of Western Europe & the US. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Use of Discretion in a 'Cinderella' Service: Data Protection and Access to Child-Care Files for Post-Care Adults
authors: Kirton, Derek; Feast, Julia; Goddard, Jim
abstract: This paper focuses on policy implementation and, in particular, the workings of 'street-level bureaucracy' in a small, marginalised area of welfare provision, namely post-care adults seeking access to their care records. The work arises from research mapping UK service provision in this area, via questionnaires and interviews with key actors in local authorities and voluntary organisations. The study was prompted by widespread but largely anecdotal evidence that practices and service provision for those seeking to access their care records varied enormously. While post-care adults may seek access to records for reasons similar to those of adopted adults (curiosity, information on birth family, medical information, care histories and experiences, search and reunion), there is a lack of comparable legal framework and service provision, with reliance instead on the 1998 Data Protection Act (DPA). The intersection of data protection and (child) welfare gives rise to a number of important tensions that are explored, such as those surrounding 'ownership' of files and their content, between rights to information and (paternalistic) welfare considerations, and whether the handling of requests should constitute an administrative or a social work task. Finally, we consider the findings, their wider contexts and implications for legal reform and policy change. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Le Travail Social entre Résistance et Innovation. Soziale Arbeit zwischen Widerstand und Innovation
abstract: Le travail social entre Résistance et innovation. Soziale Arbeit zwischen Widerstand und Innovation, edited by Sabine Voélin, Miryam Eser Davolio, and Mathias Lindenau. Interact, 2014, 386 pp., ISBN 978-3906413983.

title: The persistence of collectivity in digital protest
abstract: 'How are technology-enabled crowds activated, structured and maintained in the absence of recognized leaders, common goals, or conventional organization, issue framing, and action coordination?' The question Lance W. Bennett, Alex Segerberg and Shawn Walters ask in the 'Organization in the Crowd' article published on this issue of Information, Communication and Society is a crucial question for all those interested in the intersection between digital communication and social movements, as it has been manifested in a number of recent protest movements, from the Arab Spring, to Occupy Wall Street. Asking how 'crowds' hold together, without the presence of familiar forms of 'social glue', formal leaders, bureaucratic organizations and the like, is fundamentally posing the question of unity, coherence and order of protest action at a time of social complexity and 'liquidity' (Bauman, 2000). How do thousands of participants, often acting at a distance from one another come to perceive themselves, and to be seen by others as part of a common actor? How do dispersed internet users come to feel part of a collective actor that goes under the name of convenience of 'crowd'? Adapted from the source document.

title: Controlling children's lives: covert messages in child protection service reports
abstract: ABSTRACTThis article presents central findings from a detailed examination of written documents in 50 child protection cases from the Norwegian welfare state. In so doing, it explores issues related to the social consequences of document writing in welfare state services. Using a frame drawn from Foucault's theory of discursive rites, it looks at the writing of certain documents as ritual performances involving on the one hand, various chains of power and on the other, processes reinforcing ruling definitions of normality. The examination shows that documents do more than satisfy bureaucratic demands for record keeping about the delivery of child protection services. These records also serve as distributors of social identities and social positions for children and their families. Moreover, the examination also reveals the contours of a paradox whereby, activities intended to help and to protect some children often involve using these youngsters to reaffirm normality in society and to confirm the existing social order. These findings indicate that there is a need for greater sensibility to ethical issues involved in documents writing. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Intersection of War and Politics: The Iraq War Troop Surge and Bureaucratic Politics
abstract: This study examines the decision-making process of the George W. Bush administration which led to the decision in late 2006 to order the Iraq troop surge. The study analyzes whether the bureaucratic politics model of foreign policy decision making can accurately explain the events of the case. The study seeks to further test the explanatory power and descriptive accuracy of the bureaucratic politics model, while also attaining a more textured, academic understanding of the decision-making process leading to the Iraq troop surge. The decision to order the troop surge in Iraq is one of the more important decisions in post-9/11 U.S. foreign policy and continues to impact U.S. strategy in Iraq, Afghanistan, and overall military doctrine. Finally, the author endeavors to contribute to the further development and refinement of the bureaucratic politics model of foreign policy decision making. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: An Apology for Absence. A. Alberts' Fictionalization of Bureaucratic Existence
abstract: The literary oeuvre of the acclaimed Dutch novelist A. Alberts (1911-1995) consists of almost 20 novels, short stories, & memoirs on life in bureaucratic organizations. Starting from the novel, De vergaderzaal ([The Meeting Room] 1974), this article argues that Alberts's fiction on alienated civil servants & white-collar workers presents social scientists with an incisive analysis of Merton's "bureaucratic structure & personality." Three elements of bureaucratic existence can be distilled from his work in particular: the bureaucratic time regime, the formalized sociability, & the collective fantasy of escape. Not unlike his famous equal Franz Kafka, Alberts combined his work as a novelist with a life-long tenure in several bureaucratic organizations. His work, then, should be located in a wider field of texts that figure both as a reflection & comment on the administrative revolution that changed the face of Western Europe in the 20th century. 59 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The No/Name of the Institution
abstract: Anthropologists have lately sought a subject not containable within the institutions that the author analyze. This article suggests that people should do the same for institutionality.
