This study empirically investigates the extent to which institutional change - through paternity leave implementation at the company level - challenges gendered representations and practices of fatherhood. The study draws on a mixed methods case study conducted in a public administration which implemented a one-month paid paternity leave. Using register data about leave recipients (N = 95), we adopt a longitudinal and typological approach of leave uptake patterns by means of sequence and cluster analyses. In-depth interviews conducted with recipient fathers and managers working for the company (n = 30) enable an analysis of the implementation process and the meanings associated with paternity leave and fatherhood. Results show that paternity leave implementation challenged, in a limited way, gendered representations and practices of fatherhood. Fatherhood was made more visible within the company, but workplace characteristics and informal norms influenced fathers' leave uptake. Overall, motherhood and fatherhood were associated with different and specialized responsibilities. Fathers mainly had a secondary and temporary role with the newborn, while mothers were the central and taken-for-granted parent.

title: Descriptive dimensions of US occupations with data from the O*NET
authors: Hadden, Wilbur C; Kravets, Nataliya; Muntaner, Carles
abstract: Several authors have successfully used the Dictionary of Occupational Titles to construct scales measuring occupational work environments. The Dictionary, however, has been replaced by the Occupation Information Network or O*NET, which offers expanded content and higher quality data. This paper reports an exploratory factor analysis of the O*NET (version 4.0). Four factors are identified. Three factors are comparable to the results of earlier analyses: SUBSTANTIVE COMPLEXITY, PEOPLE VERSUS THINGS, and PHYSICAL DEMANDS. A fourth factor, BUREAUCRACY, is discovered that describes work in hierarchical organizations and oriented toward organizational policies and practices. O*NET variables and these factors can be linked to social studies via occupation codes and used as relatively objective and up to date assessments of work environments.  [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: New Right of Inquiry Is a Good Matter for All Parties Concerned
abstract: Any system of production, whether centralized or by means of private undertaking, entails risks; in a centralized system of production a mistake will have a more serious result because not only one Co, but a complete sector of the economy will carry the consequences. The new right of inquiry will be one of the measures to minimize the risks involved in a system of production by means of private undertakings. The foundation of this right is the common interest of both employers & employees in the undertaking & their mutual dependency. Authority in a undertaking will be based on the confidence of the employees in manag. If this confidence is doubled, it must be possible to call the manag to account. Such a right will be an essential element in the trend towards democratization of the undertaking. It is in line with other proposed forms of democratization in that it does not interfere with a quick-witted policy of the entrepreneur. Some critical remarks are made on the futile role of the ondernemingsraad (a council of contact between employers & employees), the dialectical relation between manag & trade unions as point of departure, the possibilities of demanding an inquiry for employees who are not org'ed or not org'ed in the recognized trade unions. The right of inquiry will have its most important function in a general prevention; the inquiry itself is a sanction that will seldom be applied. H. van de Belt.

title: Agency Leaders, Gendered Institutions, and Representative Bureaucracy
abstract: This study examines three central questions: Do women state agency heads establish priorities that advance women's interests more frequently than men agency heads? Among state agency heads with women-related top priorities, are there systematic differences between women & men in the influences on their priority choices? Do the organizational & political contexts in which agency leaders work explain variation in policy priorities? Analysis of data from a national survey of women & men department heads reveals that working in a redistributive agency affects whether a leader pursues a women-centered policy agenda, regardless of the leader's gender, other personal characteristics, or reported influences on priority choice. The authors conclude that the way representative bureaucracy actually plays out can be more fully understood if the tenets of social science theory on gendered institutions are incorporated into analyses of how representative bureaucracy works. 3 Tables, 2 Figures, 1 Appendix, 57 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Colonial Administration and Its Implications for Development Administration
abstract: Before WWII the colonial administrative system was a satisfactory mechanism for achieving the objectives of the colonial power. However, when many colonial countries were achieving independence, severe crises arose as they attempted to solve social & economic problems with the vestiges of a colonial administrative system. The reasons for these difficulties are best understood through F. Riggs's theory of "prismatic society," (Administration in Developing Countries: The Theory of the Prismatic Society, Boston: Houghton Mifflin Co, 1964). Societies experiencing postcolonial transition are prismatic because colonial rule superimposes elements of diffracted society on a fused one. Because of the complex interrelationships between all elements of the society, the concepts of public administration developed in a diffracted society do not work well. Ultimately, the questions are: What contribution can the colonial administrative machinery make to political, economic, & social development? What are implications of colonial administration for development administration? R. Johnson.

title: The contradictions of individualized activation policy: Explaining the rise and demise of One to One Service in Australia
abstract: Recent research has documented a trend towards the individualization of activation policies. This study reviews a radical Australian effort to personalize the delivery of activation policies called the One to One Service initiative, which was abandoned shortly after its introduction. The paper asks: what does the brief and tumultuous tenure of this initiative reveal about the role of the individual in contemporary welfare administration and activation policy? Based on a theoretical engagement with the works of Ulrich Beck, Elizabeth Beck-Gernsheim and Anthony Giddens, and an ethnographic study of frontline interactions in Centrelink, Australia's national benefits agency, the paper argues we should understand the rise and fall of One to One Service in terms of contradictions between two competing forms of contemporary welfare individualization, referred to as 'democratic relationships' and 'compulsory choice'. One to One Service represented a push for individualized, democratic relationships between staff and clients; yet it was undermined because policy makers chose to emphasize an alternative form of individualization premised on forcing recipients to take responsibility for their lives and move off welfare. The findings have implications for the individualization, street level bureaucracy, and activation policy literatures. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: Administrative Deviance and the Ideology of "Injustice"
abstract: A theoretical exploration of deviant behavior theories with special reference to R. K. Merton's theory of bureaucratic structures & the concepts of "anomie" & "deviance." According to Merton, bureaucratic inefficiency derives from ritualism & ultraconformism to the rules & methods to the point where sight is lost of the purpose. Merton's viewpoint is contrasted with that of M. Weber. It is suggested that a mere examination of the bureaucratic personality does not suffice; rather, the entire bureaucratic structure must be examined. While Merton's view has promoted a behaviorist view that has enlarged the conceptual horizon of the problem, he has not researched the central problem of the structural & functional attributes of the bureaucratic organization. North American sociologists such as P. Blau, M. L. Kohn, C. Perrow, & others who have explored this problem are discussed. It is concluded that American theories are based on a liberal ideology that has become liberalist & has been condensed into an "ideology of injustice." 1 Table. S. Whittle.

title: Whither Bureaucratic Influence?: A Cautionary Note
abstract: The diminishing bureaucratic influence theory of Francis Rourke (see abstract in this section of SOPODA 14:1) is critiqued, based on a review of the literature on bureaucracy. It is argued that, although Rourke identifies real trends in evaluations of bureaucratic advice & discretion, the diminishing influence theory is contradicted by current research. It is argued that a contingency theory of bureaucratic influence needs to be developed to explain current trends. 51 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Accounting for ethos or programmes for conduct? The brave new world of research ethics committees
authors: Boden, Rebecca; Epstein, Debbie; Latimer, Joanna
abstract: This paper examines the operation of power and its consequences arising from the growth of new ethical bureaucracies in universities. We use the UK as a case study to illustrate more general points about the globalised nature and impact of such bureaucratisation. Our focus is on the social sciences as this is where, we argue, the impact is likely to be most marked. The paper is organised in five sections. The first introduces our concerns. Section 2 traces the genealogy of these new regimes of control in the UK. We then problematise the new ethical bureaucracies, making an analysis in terms of the shift in the locus of power away from researchers to becoming centralised in bureaucratic structures. In section 4 we explore some of the ways in which researchers might respond to the changing regimes of ethical control. Finally, we offer considerations of the ways in which ethical governance of research might be differently conducted so as to avoid the adverse consequences of new regimes of control on research practice. Our aim is to provoke debate and thereby contribute to a platform from which to reassert ways to ensure that research is ethical and that do not interfere with the production and consumption of critical social science. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: More than the Politics of Decentralization: Local Government Reform, District Development and Public Administration in Zimbabwe
abstract: What is evaluated as central government decentralization to improve rural development may also be local government reform for improved district development. The challenge in analyzing such efforts is not to be preoccupied with an always-present politics of decentralization. Examined here is local government reform in Zimbabwe that has been equated with central government decentralization: the amalgamation of the countryside's two racially different local authorities. Lessons from the Zimbabwe experience have implications for similar efforts in postapartheid South Africa. 28 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Appreciating Cultural Differences: The Case of German Reunification
authors: Dunbar, Roger L M; Bresser, Rudi K F
abstract: Explores the influence of cultural differences on German reunification, arguing that the process has been interpreted differently by those from the East vs the West. Using E. H. Schein's (1992) framework, different & critical aspects of the respective cultures are identified, & their impact is illustrated through a case study describing the development of the Treuhandanstalt & through metaphors that highlight alternative interpretations of reunification. Discussed in conclusion are implications of this process for appreciating cultural differences in the reunified Federal Republic of Germany. 1 Table, 2 Figures, 55 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Political Optics and the Occlusion of Intimate Knowledge
abstract: In Seeing Like a State (1998), James Scott provides a comprehensive understanding of the optics of state power. He also shows how the bureaucratic logic of high-modernist official planning occludes the social and cultural worlds both of marginalized citizenries and of the bureaucrats themselves, and accurately pinpoints the pernicious reductionism that has accompanied the modernist state's self-proclaimed "cult of efficiency." As in his earlier work, however, Scott overgeneralizes the idea of "resistance"; he also, and concomitantly, underestimates bureaucrats' complicity with local populations and the consequent modification of bureaucratic schemes (including the construction of national heritage) in actual practice. These absences reflect a relative lack of ethnographic specificity in the analysis as well as a partially uncritical endorsement of the master narrative of Western history. 34 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: DEMOCRACY, BUREAUCRACY, AND OLIGARCHY IN PARTIES
abstract: After presenting the 'iron law' of oligarchy, as posited by R. Michels, the law is subjected to an empirical & logical analysis. The logical concepts are found to be indefinite & imprecise, which leads to the possibility of 2 interpretations, differing from each other, ie, 2 laws: (1) the iron law of bur'tion, & (2) the bronze law of oligarchization. It is noted that if the party members participate in party activity, (2) does not function. The empirical analysis results in an agreement with Michels. Particular problems, ie, apathy are discussed re a voting pop which has registered with a particular party, & nonpartymembers, & applied to diverse situations in the US, France & Italy. G. Di Bernardo (Tr & modified by E. Berliner).

title: Introduction: Bureaucrats in Uniform
abstract: This special issue deals with 'bureaucrats in uniform', an expression by which we like to designate the different administrative agents who have the task of enforcing the law through the legal use of violence, ranging from policemen to provincial and national guards, gendarmes, forest agents, customs officers, and so on. There are at least three reasons for studying this particular group of state agents. Adapted from the source document.

title: UNDERSTANDING OUR BUREAUCRACY
abstract: Possible explanations for some of the aberrations of Indian bur'cy & the nature of some complaints against it are explored: delays, irresponsibility, callousness, lack of imagination in decision making, endless 'paper-chases,' cumbersome & self-defeating procedures. Some misleading formulations & incomplete explanations of bur 'tic inadequacy are also examined: that the bur'cy is not development-oriented, that the specialist is subordinated to the generalist in admin, that inefficiency is a result of the financial control procedures. That this state of affairs is a legacy from the British is an incomplete explanation. Procedural & structural reform & revision of rules & regulations will not alone be adequate without a clear idea of the kind of civil service that is wanted. Preferred directions are the inculcation of cost-consciousness; a sense of urgency & concern for results; & a modernization & professionalization of the civil service. The attitude to training needs to be changed with a diff kind of civil servant in view-an official with managerial skills. IPSA.

title: COMMUNITY AND BUREAUCRACY IN THE MODERN WORLD
abstract: The modern community is composed of both bur'tic & primary group structures, & its identity & effectiveness are dependent upon a mix of the 2. The key distinction between the bur'cy & the primary group is whether the structure is regarded by the participants as instrumental or intrinsic. Structural diff's between the community & bur'tic models are classified in terms of leadership, action structure, & group patterns. As compared with the bur'cy, community participation is more likely to be comprehensive in interest, volunteer, peer-staff relations among participants, give & take in decision making, & flexible & permissive concerning role expectations. Signif types of interaction between community & burley are (1) mass contacts such as those provided through MM & regional & nat'l markets, & (2) the relationships between the community leaders, & the admin'ors & the specialists of the burley. As the community has lost its cultural distinctiveness, its identity must be provided in effective, local soc structures which supply many material needs & offer an intermediate level of group membership & participation between the primary group & the larger society. AA.

title: Bureaucracy, Contracts and Networks: The Unholy Trinity and the Police
authors: Fleming, Jenny; Rhodes, R A W
abstract: Over the past thirty years, police services in the UK and Australia have been subjected to a series of demands for change and reform. This article describes these reforms as a shift from command and control bureaucracy through markets to networks and argues that constant reform is a result of the unintended consequences of change. Many of these unintended consequences stem from the limitations and incompatibility of each of these governing structures. We show that the conflicts between the core ideas that distinguish each governing structure create dilemmas that render all reforms contingent. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Innovations in Trust: Patrimonial and Bureaucratic Authority in the Asante Empire of West Africa
abstract: Analysts of modern-day sub-Saharan Africa have argued that its "neopatrimonial regimes," descending from pre-colonial polities, translate badly to the scale of the nation-state and hinder democratic accountability. In this paper, I argue by contrast that the problem with today's failed or failing states is that they are not patrimonial enough, if we understand patrimonialism in classic Weberian terms as a system based on traditions of reciprocal interdependence between rulers and citizens, and characterized by personal but malleable ruling networks. I make this argument by showing how the Asante Empire in the 18th and 19th centuries shifted from a working model, incorporating both patrimonial and bureaucratic forms of authority, to an exploitative one that reneged on its traditional commitments to the wider public. The cause of this shift was the expansion of exchange with European nations as a rival avenue to power and wealth. This problem continues today, where African rulers are incentivized by the demands of global banks, the United Nations, and G20 governments rather than internal authority traditions, thus limiting their ability to establish locally effective and publically accountable hybrids of patrimonial and bureaucratic governance.

title: Lilia Ben Salem: "A Proposal for Sociology in Tunisia" An Interview with Sylvie Mazzella
abstract: Through an interview with Lilia Ben Salem, this articles retraces certain aspects of sociology in Tunisia : the considerable influence of the French university system on the Tunisian university system during the first decade of Tunisia's independence, the role played by the CERES, one of the first social science research centres, in the 1960s, the developmental approaches adopted in the 1960s, followed by the debates in the 1970s on the notion of cultural specificity, the effects of arabicising teaching & the professional outlook for sociologists at a time of employment saturation in public administration. Adapted from the source document.

title: Assessing Determinants of Bureaucratic Discretion: An Experiment in Street-Level Decision Making
abstract: Questionnaire data from an experimental study in which 96 newly hired social work graduate students & practitioners awarded public benefits & services to clients in a simulated training session indicate that factors extraneous to client need influenced award decisions. It was determined that organizational control/formalization, client characteristics, &, to a much lesser extent, professional field influenced the awarding of public assistance. In general, higher levels of financial assistance were offered in settings with less organizational control & to clients evoking more compassion. In contrast to some previous findings, social worker attributes were not influential award determinants. It is concluded that the everyday exercise of street-level bureaucratic discretion reflects competition between desires to standardize & individualize decisions. 5 Figures, 59 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Trust and Moral Motivation: Redundant Resources in Health and Social Care?
abstract: The government's modernization program for health & social care has introduced institutional arrangements that are characteristic of 'late modernity.' These support heightened surveillance of organizational performance & professional practice, increased bureaucratization of operational arrangements, instrumental decision making about service provision, & a drive to centralize consumer empowerment. Such developments are designed to (re)establish political & public confidence in professional interventions & services that are predictable, reliable, & safe. A focus on confidence, however, necessarily neglects the significance of trust for service users & providers. This article argues that privileging confidence over trust fails to acknowledge the role of uncertainty, morality, & discretion in the provision of care & has important consequences for service users, managers, & frontline practitioners. 108 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: "Sports is Politics": Swimming (and) Pools in Postcolonial Singapore
abstract: Almost immediately after Singapore's independence in 1965, sports became an agent of social engineering in the creation of the new nation, and the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) government pragmatically used the institution of sports in its nation-building enterprise. Based on an analysis of the speeches and press statements of Singaporean bureaucrats and civil servants from the 1960s to the 1980s, this article investigates the ruling elite's general perception of sports and regional sporting events, examining how such a perception influenced Singapore's local governance and strategic thinking in foreign relations. Although scholars have pointed out that sports were prominent in the nationalistic discourses of Singapore and in the projection of Singapore's international image, little about the history and development of individual sports in Singapore is known. The article argues that swimming was the premier sport of choice for Singapore's ruling elite in its projects of building bodies and the nation after independence, manifested in the swimming pools that the nascent nation strove to build in the residential estates outside the "colonial stronghold" of the central town district.

title: The Municipal Action Groups
abstract: The inability of the French political & administrative systems to control Ur development gave rise, in the middle 1960s, to the movement of the "Groupes d'action municipale" (municipal action groups--MAG) which, by means of creative action programs, attracted new social groups to political action. The movement has been most influential among Catholics, & new social groups such as professionals & technicians. Analysis of the social base of the movement shows that in 1973 61% regarded themselves as Christians. A composite portrait of a typical member, derived from various studies, would be: between ages thirty & forty, married, three school-age children, new in his present neighborhood, graduate degree, middle or high echelon employee, high income, ownership of living accommodations (often a private home), SS on the upswing. The MAG filled the vacuum left in the 1970s by political & trade union movements which failed to realize the importance of Ur problems. Ideologically, the MAG refuses partial reforms & demands "destabilizing" changes which would completely alter the existing system. There is increasing radicalization & acceptance of Marxist discourse: they regard the state as no longer representing the general interest & as having lost its claim to legitimacy. The aim of MAG is the formation of a new, active, & responsible citizen; wide-ranging grass-roots government changes are proposed. The general tendency is to create a structure which would parallel that of the political parties; MAG's political activity represents the sentiments & interests of the petty bourgeoisie & raises the question of whether this movement is anything but a stage in the process of renewal of old community elites. Modified HA.

title: An institution close to the public: the ombudsman in a dialog to promote a democracy of rights and responsibilities
abstract: A series of concrete cases drawn from the experience of the regional ombudsman in Italy's north-eastern region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia, describing the difficulty in communicating encountered by the public administration, highlights the fact that, like all communications, those that are of interest to the public sector have to be approached as a tool for interpersonal relations. As the word's etymology indicates, "communication" is a common action whose purpose is to seek a common understanding and a common experience, in this case of the law. As such, it is a tool that has the potential to consolidate the "democratic state governed by the rule of law", as when citizens are enabled to understand and get involved in "legal affairs", they are stimulated to overcome a vision of rights that sees them in terms of individualism. By favouring and promoting reciprocal understanding, the ombudsman facilitates the public administration's work in providing a service to which the public feels a sense of belonging, overcoming the traditional "vertical" model of administration as command and also becoming a tool for achieving subsidiariety, recuperating the dimension of private autonomy and of private responsibility on the part of private individuals or groups for pursuing interests of public relevance, as outlined in the Italian Constitution at Article 18, section IV. Adapted from the source document.

title: Organizing for social sustainability: governance through bureaucratization in meta-organizations
abstract: The difficulties nation states face when attempting to use traditional legal means to cope with transnational phenomena such as environmental degradation, international labor conditions, and global trade have created an opportunity for the emergence of new types of regulations. These rules are often issued by organizations that produce voluntary measures such as standards and action plans to influence the behavior of individuals and institutions. These are in many cases meta-organizations that have other organizations rather than individuals as members. They are important links in the process of creating and diffusing dominant definitions in the "ideoscape" of influential policy concepts such as sustainable development. This article explores how two meta-organizations, Fairtrade International (FLO) and Organic Forum, shape the concepts of fair trade and organic food by providing ideas and content to the ideoscape of sustainable development. We argue that this process takes place by governance through bureaucratization in which fair trade and organic food become formalized, precisely defined, and made visible. This in turn determines how -- or even if -- the social dimension of sustainability can be made into policy. Furthermore, we find explanations in these processes as to why the social dimension of sustainability tends to be the most underdeveloped. We conclude that bureaucratization is also a form of politics, although not one that is as easily recognizable as an open power struggle. Adapted from the source document.

title: Too Much, Too Little and Too Often: A Critique of du Gay's Analysis of Enterprise
abstract: Paul du Gay has articulated a persuasive analysis & critique of the enterprise discourse; he & a number of collaborators have analyzed the various managerial discourses & techniques through which employees are reimagined as entrepreneurs & organizations are to move from dysfunctional bureaucracies to models of excellence. While du Gay's critical position toward enterprise & the Foucauldian tradition on which he draws is supported here, it is argued that his analysis suffers from several flaws that are articulated around three themes: (1) His analysis claims too much for enterprise, & relies on a flawed dualism between enterprise & bureaucracy. (2) His analysis is overdeterministic & makes too little space for resistance & alternative discourses to enterprise. (3) He presents the same arguments too often, & his work is implicated in the constitution of the enterprise discourse as an accomplished fact in the academic community. 69 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Interests of Bureaucrats: Implications of the Asian Experience for Recent Theories of Development
authors: Kraus, Richard; Maxwell, William E; Vanneman, Reeve D

title: The Politics of Structure: Decentralization and Empowerment
abstract: Examines how the relationship between service bureaucracies & the people dependent on them can be made more fair. It is argued that legal remedies are generally ineffective & that privatization works only in rare cases of true competition. A third option is communitarian or participatory bargaining. Examples from health care, community-based care for the frail elderly, & worker safety illustrate how & under which circumstances this approach can empower people faced with bureaucratic resistance. It is contended that communitarian bargaining can work when those with power see that it is in their interests to share it. This involves changing professional ideology so that the dependent person is seen as a concrete part of the solution. Adapted from the source document.

title: Being Productive, Being Clever: The Enchanted Forest of Intellectual Property
abstract: Government rhetoric and policies exhort Australian universities to be 'productive' and to build a 'clever country'. Academic award restructuring is an important element in this re-shaping of Australian higher education, although the increasingly fashionable term 'intellectual property' enters higher education discourse and re-defines academic labour and the ways in which academics perceive themselves and their roles. It is argued that the term intellectual property carries within it a range of meanings extending beyond the legal world of patent and copyright and that this privatising and capitalising discourse has the capacity to transform universities. The individualising and formalising of academic labour goes against the tradition of university collegiality and, crucially, contradicts the processes by which ideas and skills are constituted within a university. Inappropriate intellectual property discourse has the potential to devalue university work by positing a model drawn from the world of the managerialists within the bureaucracy and private sector.

title: The Politics of Possession: The Proliferation of Partnerships in the Brazilian Amazon
abstract: Centered on one village, Aukre, this article discusses new types of intervillage ties and coordination in the Kayapo lands in Brazil. Present-day village politics are animated by a diverse array of old and emergent partnerships in the Amazon region. The Kayapo effort to preserve their homeland has resulted in communities' networking, articulating, and partnering with many different types of stakeholders as a response to the territorialization of their homeland and the increased bureaucratization of their livelihoods. Ethnographic data from one village suggests that current community relationships are part of a multilayered political and social landscape. Now, village ties are forged and maintained because of ramped-up transportation and communication within the territory, bureaucratic structures that demand consistent intervillage diplomacy, economic incentives that offer Kayapo communities opportunities for engagement and competition, and ongoing alliances to protect and defend the integrity of the Kayapo lands and their territorial boundaries. Adapted from the source document.

title: Black Boxes of Bureaucracy: Transparency and Opacity in the Resettlement Process of Congolese Refugees
abstract: To qualify for third-country resettlement, refugees must convince aid representatives that they have been individually persecuted and continue to fear such persecution. This article focuses on the official documents Congolese refugees collect as evidence of their persecution to bolster their resettlement claims before their refugee camp in Tanzania closes. To illuminate the creation, collection, and circulation of such documents, I trace one Congolese family's story as it is folded, literally and metaphorically, into an envelope that I hand-delivered to a United Nations High Commission for Refugees (UNHCR) resettlement official. Following this envelope led me to an investigation of the bureaucratic institutions involved, which both produce and then later receive the documents. I argue that the apparent transparency of the resettlement process facilitates and justifies its concomitant opacity. Adapted from the source document.

title: Academic Bureaucracy
abstract: Issues concerning the U as a bur'tic org are discussed, eg, "faculty power," the consignment of undergraduate students to the role of clients rather than constituent members of the org, etc. Ideas by M. Weber & Thorstein Veblen on bur'tic org's are referred to. U's are, structurally speaking, secondary rather than primary groups. A move away from secondary toward primary group values can only be justified at sub-group levels within the large U. Students & faculty members share a desire for more flexibility in the kinds of courses given & the approach to the subject matter. Large U's might consider proposals which attempt to provide, within the framework of a real Coll system, a number of educ'al options along a continuum from comtlete programming at one end to an almost totally unstructured curriculum at the other. This would seem to be the only way that primary group values & an individual-intensive educ'al experience can be provided for those who want it. Students must have as wide a range of choice as is possible re both content area & approach. M. Maxfield.

title: Bureaucratic Barriers to Service Delivery, Administrative Advocacy, and Mother Goose
abstract: Describes a 5-year administrative advocacy effort to address the negative consequences of categorical government funding on the development of integrated & comprehensive mental health & chemical dependency services for youth & their families. The discussion incorporates rational & irrational aspects of macrolevel practice. This recounting of the advocacy process -- presented in narrative form as a children's story to a group of legislators & government officials during a gathering celebrating the success of the effort -- is chronicled. While all of the events in this narrative are true, all locations & identifying information have been changed to accent the universal nature of the encounters described. 2 Tables, 20 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Fighting fraud: An evaluation of the government's social security fraud strategy
abstract: This article examines the government's strategy for dealing with social security fraud. The Social Security (Administration) Fraud Act 1997 has been enacted to facilitate the detection, prosecution and punishment of benefit fraud.

title: Governance as theory: Five propositions
abstract: Stoker attempts to bring order to the governance debate by concentrating on how the rise of governance challenges many of the more traditional notions of public administration.  Five propositions and associated dilemmas of governance are examined.

title: The Internal Structure of EPA Rulemaking
abstract: Twenty years ago, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) was put together rapidly & given unprecedented discretionary powers. The new agency, composed of bureaucrats culled from a range of existing programs, was to actively promulgate rules fundamentally affecting US industrial practice. Because of its abrupt birth & the enormous scope of its responsibilities, the EPA's decision-making structures are complex & continuously evolving. Interviews conducted over a 6-year period with 50+ EPA employees reveal that, due to the complexity of the issues addressed by the EPA, no one employee understands all the components of any decision. The consequences of the resultant team-oriented system of decision-making are explored, & the role of each subunit in the process is elucidated. The version of the team model used by the EPA is compared with other alternative models of bureaucratic decision making, eg, the hierarchical outside advisor, & adversarial models. It is concluded that, under the model, decision making is slow, & innovative suggestions rarely survive the consensus-building process. The agency is advised to develop a hybrid system relying on the team model, among others. 1 Table. K. Pizer

title: Perspectives on Policy, Planning and Administration Tasks in Spain and the United States
abstract: Scale data are used to compare preparation for roles in policy, planning, & administration among 82 graduate social work students in the US & 23 social service managers in Madrid, Spain. Special attention is given to tasks & activities emphasized by both groups. 5 References. Modified AA

title: European Policies: The Impact of National Administrative Traditions
abstract: Argues that a central problem for effective implementation of European legislation is the impact of national administrative traditions, since the formal & practical transformation of European Union (EU) law rests mainly at the national level. The interplay of national administrative traditions & EU policy implementation is described, noting that national administrative traditions prevalent in a policy field may differ from country to country. It is argued that implementation effectiveness depends on the "institutional scope" of EU adaptation pressure, which is not only affected by broad European requirements, but also by the embeddedness of the respective administrative traditions & national capacities for administrative reform. According to the degrees of adaptation pressure, different paths are distinguished, suggesting more or less effective implementation. 1 Table, 44 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Information Technology, Expertise, and the Politics of Bureaucratic Control in Africa
abstract: The growing adoption of computers in state bureaucracies across Africa has placed a high value on expertise in the field on information technology (IT). Experts are seen as the repositories of knowledge in the "information age." With the presumption that knowledge confers power, some analysts have argued that we are likely to see a "power-shift" from the "old bureaucratic elite" to the IT experts. This article assesses the veracity of this contention in the African context. It argues that there are efforts by some computer professionals to control access into the field, thereby giving "recognized" experts exclusive authority over computer-related expertise. The definition of knowledge & qualification, therefore, become social constructs that are meant to serve the parochial interests of a particular group. These efforts have, however, not translated into substantive control over the IT field. Furthermore, experts are unable to seize bureaucratic power. This is the consequence of a contingent configuration of social forces that they have had to contend with & that they have, so far, not been able to overcome. Among these are a lack of cohesion with the computer priesthood, the transcendent power of the "old bureaucratic elite," & the perception within most organizations that the role of computer experts is tangential to organizational activity & survival. 54 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucratic barriers to service delivery, administrative advocacy, and Mother Goose
abstract: This narrative describes a five-year administrative advocacy effort to address the negative consequences of categorical government fundIng on the development of Integrated and comprehensive mental-health and chemical-dependency services for youth and their families. The discussion incorporates rational and irrational aspects of macro-level practice.

title: Monitoring the Impact of Land Reform on Quality of Life: A South African Case Study
authors: May, Julian; Stevens, Thilde; Stols, Annareth
abstract: This paper outlines the approach that is utilized by the Monitoring & Evaluation directorate of the Dept of Land Affairs (DLA) in South Africa in assessing quality of life for Land Reform beneficiaries. The paper begins with an overview of the three Land Reform programs in South Africa & then outlines the original design for monitoring & evaluating quality of life for land reform beneficiaries. It then details the current Monitoring & Evaluation design being utilized, highlighting its strengths & weaknesses. The last section discusses some of the findings of the quality of life study undertaken in 1999. 3 Tables, 1 Figure, 18 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: A Decision Model for the Study of Public Bureaucracies
abstract: The concept "series of decisions" is introduced & defined as the total number of decisions made in the attainment of a goal. The series are analytically divided into 2 types of decisions, programming, & implementation--the 1st are those made during the process converting policy goals into programs, the 2nd, those made during the implementation of the programs. The distinction is important because different actors & institutions are involved in the 2 phases. It is hypothesized that the relation between the time of programming decisions & the time of implementation of decisions tends to be zero the less effective & the less numerous the organizations participating in the programming phase. A list of factors which could be useful in the process of testing & modifying the hypothesis is presented. The division of health environment of the health ministry of Colombia is used to exemplify the concept of "series of decisions" & to show the utility of the analytical distinction between programming & implementation decisions. The programs for 1970 of the Division of Health Environment were studied in detail, & their stages of implementation were checked at the end of the year. In 7 of 9 programs, the professional interests of the decision-makers were an influential factor. The influence of ideologies & value systems are subtle & difficult to detect in a highly technical division, but generally they can be observed in the selection of alternatives. There is very little knowledge about interbureaucratic decision-making, but this model can be a helpful instrument for systematic data gathering leading to theory building. 1 Table, 1 Figure. Modified HA.

title: The labor of surveillance and bureaucratized killing: new subjectivities of military drone operators
abstract: As the military's armed surveillance drones have become the iconic weapon of the early twenty-first century, they have also introduced radical transformations in the traditional labor of those who operate them - the pilots, crew, analysts, and commanders. In so doing, these transformations have engendered new kinds of subjectivity, with new ways of experiencing the work of surveillance and killing. This paper investigates the nature of these new subjectivities, how they are constructed through new technologies that combine surveillance with remote agency, the bureaucratization of killing, and the psychological implications for operators. It examines how scientific management strategies from Taylorism to business process re-engineering have contributed to reconstituting the subjectivity of drone pilots and sensor operators through decomposing their labor practices and reconstituting them within professionalized careers and technological systems of supervision and management. It also looks at how the decisions to use lethal force are themselves decomposed and distributed among individuals designated as responsible agents within the chain-of-command. In light of the creation of these new subjectivities, the paper examines the psychological stress experienced by those who occupy these new subject positions through an examination of several recent military studies, journalistic accounts, and a recent short film based upon an interview with a drone pilot, Omer Fast's 5,000 Feet is the Best (2011).

title: The "Political" Economies of Central America: Foreign Aid and Labour Remittances
abstract: A study of changes in the economy, bureaucracy, & class structure of Central America over the past ten years in terms of the influence of foreign aid & remittances from migrant workers. Strategies such as deregulating exchange rates, changing the composition of investment, & reducing food prices have helped improve the standard of living of the peoples of this region. Project administration has become a primary function of the state. The influx of foreign capital has favored decentralization & increased popular participation, though it has also weakened the ability of the governments to carry out policy. New social groups have been created, including families partially supported by the remittances of their family members working in other countries, foreign-financed military forces, public employees of newly formed agencies, & financial intermediaries who handle funds from abroad as well as domestic investments. 46 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Social Research on Bureaucracy: Limitations and Opportunities
abstract: It is asked, how can the sociol'st best study bur'cies which, as a result of their emphasis upon hierarchy & control, seek to hide their activities from public scrutiny? The limitations of the typical res design for investigating the normative order of a bur'cy are examined. Res procedures of journalists & related functionaries are studied in order to explore the role of assumptions about soc reality & of instit'al bases in the collection of information on bur'cies. The models of I. F. Stone, S. Hersh, J. Anderson & R. Nader are examined. Much of the sociol'al inquiry on bur'cy, it is found, assumes the existence of integration & a rational model with a free flow of information & a lack of hidden side. Many of the res procedures currently favored by sociol'ts are predicated upon these kinds of assumptions. For the study of bur'cy to advance, assumptions about human nature & soc reality demand re-evaluation. Concomitantly, greater appreciation of various kinds of evidence, drawn from diverse sectors of the system, is mandatory. In addition to interview data, the published accounts of journalists, the records of courts & Congressional committees, & the reports of bur'cies themselves all have a special role to play. E. Weiman.

title: Markets, Networks and the New Welfare State: Employment Assistance Reforms in Australia
abstract: Contemporary theoretical debates point to a transformation of societies & social organizations away from universal forms of mass production & consumption, organized through mass institutions, toward smaller, diversified, entrepreneurial units linked together by new forms of market & network coordination. This greater diversity is also held to be a feature of service users who require individually fashioned solutions to nonstandard problems & tailored products for their different tastes. Applications of these accounts of social & economic transformation to the public sector propose similar patterns to those evident in private industry & in regional communities. The large, standardized bureaucracy is seen to give way to decoupled, multiple-agency models of service delivery in a new type of welfare state. Here, data obtained 1994-1996 via interviews & surveys (N = 365) with service delivery staff in the Australian employment assistance sector, where transformations of this type have recently been sponsored by government, indicate that many of the key propositions of the post-Fordist account are valid. Smaller, nonunionized units dominate the new order, & services are devolved to the local level. However, a number of the expected patterns of flexible specialization, diversity, & networking are not found, suggesting marked differences & possible tensions between public- & private-sector forms of organizational development in the new order. 6 Tables, 1 Figure, 33 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROLS AND INNOVATION
abstract: The influence of admin'ive control procedures on org'al innovation is examined. It is noted that admin'ive controls assume 2 forms whose effects on innovation may differ: (a) activity control-the degree to which members of the org use procedures or resources specified by their superiors; (b) visibility of consequences-the ability & willingness to measure the consequences of org'al programs in terms of org'al goals. The following general hyp's are advanced: (1) innovation varies inversely with activity control because activity control reduces the search for new programs & abridges the individual's capacity & incentive to innovate; (2) innovation varies directly with visibility of consequences, since visibility of consequences allows the owner of an org to evaluate an innovation's effect on goal achievement & to reward & encourage successful innovators. 4 working hyp's were established & tested in a questionaire field investigation of 24 short-term voluntary hosp's in the Chicago, Ill area which ranged in size from 216 to 393 beds. The chief pharmacist in each hospital was asked to indicate on the questionaire whether any new drugs released by manufacturers between Jan 1962 & May 1964 had ever been ordered in his hosp. Org'al influences on f & promptness of the trial of new drugs, as well as activity control & visibility of consequences, were measured. The working hyp's were: the greater the control over Med staff activities (i) the less prompt the trials of new drugs & (ii) the less frequent the trials of new drugs, & the higher the visibility over Med care, (iii) the more prompt the trials of new drugs & (iv) the more frequent the trials of new drugs. Multiple regression analyses of the data were made & other factors affecting innovation were controlled. Hyp (iv) received support at the 0.5 level of signif, & the other hyp's were supported at the 0.10 level. The pattern of findings tends to confirm the general hyp's. Since hospital control over Med staff activities was found to be minimal, the relationship may be more pronounced in more tightly controlled org's. 2 Tables. M. Maxfield.

title: Managing Labor and Delivery among Impoverished Populations in Mexico: Cervical Examinations as Bureaucratic Practice
abstract: Birthing experiences for low-income and marginalized women have frequently been framed within explanatory models of authoritative knowledge and power dynamics. Many of these explanatory models have pointed out the structural violence inherent in the biomedical model of birth. The research on which this article is based suggests that clinicians' stressful work environment and class-based stereotypes of low-income women resulted in the routinizing of inhumane medical practices. Hospital overcrowding due to health reforms led to clinicians being primarily concerned with moving patients swiftly through the system. Clinicians increasingly relied on the cervical examination as a marker for labor's progress and a shorthand method to track cervical dilation. Using ethnographic data collected in the obstetrics ward of a public hospital in Mexico, in this article I explore the emergence of a bureaucratic routinizing of obstetricians' everyday practice. I provide a new understanding of the encoding and entrenching of everyday medical practices and their effect on the reproductive rights of women. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Organizational Response to Disaster: A Typology of Adaptation and Change
abstract: A time sequenced model of bureaucratic adaptation to a disaster episode is derived from one developed by J. R. Brouillette & E. L. Quarantelli (originally abstracted as SA D8938/ASA/1969/0187). The Brouillette & Quarantelli model does not allow analysis of dynamics of organizational change, nor does it account for planning & normative orientations of disaster subcultures. Using A. H. Barton's taxonomy of disaster phases (Communities in Disaster: A Sociological Analysis of Collective Stress Situations, Garden City, NY: Anchor Books, 1970), a typology is derived that accounts for disaster as a process & includes the expected influences of planning. With this dynamic model, short-term, particularistic, adaptations of the organization can be distinguished from long-term, universalistic, organizational change. The model is then tested on an empirical example based on a recent major flood. Results showed that the typology was applicable; however, some questions were raised as to the generalizability of Barton's typology. Recommendations are also made concerning difficulties encountered in applying the typology. 8 Figures. Modified AA.

title: The Dialectic of Size and Structure: The Case of Kenya's State Bureaucracy
abstract: Most of the available literature on Kenya suggests that the state bureaucracy has undergone little or no structural change since formal independence in Dec 1963. This claim is reevaluated through review of the literature & examination of empirical data on the Kenyan governmental structure. While many prominent & prestigious positions in the Kenyan state hierarchy have the same titles as during the colonial era, thus suggesting structural continuity, in fact the current bureaucratic structure is much more extensive & complex than that of 1963. At the same time, this cannot be attributed to any reorientation in the dominant ideology. 1 Table. Modified HA.

title: Conceptual Notes on the Public Interest for Public Administration and Policy Analysts
abstract: An argument is made for critical evaluation in public administration & political science. The current lack of publicly acknowledged standards of judgment results in poor direction provided to policy & research sciences. It is argued that the appropriate standard of evaluation is public interest, arising from interactions among private parties. The consequences of public interest can be assessed through projection & evaluation of agreed-upon values in "reasoned argument." Drawing on examples from twentieth-century US politics, the process of policy appraisal vis-a-vis public interest is described, with emphasis on the need for tests of generalizability & affordability. 14 References. C. Grindle

title: State Reform for Democratic Governability in Mexico
abstract: Provides an introduction to an issue of Politica Cultura on state reform in Mexico. Tables, Figures, Appendixes. Adapted from the source document.

title: Assessing Policy Implementation Success: Observations from the Philippines
abstract: Analyzes the establishment & start-up of the One Stop Shop Inter-Agency Tax Credit & Duty Drawback Center in the Philippines, with respect to the adoption of strategic management principles & techniques. The policy change agenda embodied in the center's creation is described, & developments during its first eight months of existence are outlined. The impact of bureaucratic complexity on the ability of center management & Dept of Finance staff to implement the policy reform agenda is explored. 1 Table, 17 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Rent Control Legislation and the National Housing Corporation in Tanzania, 1985-1990
abstract: Following a general overview of housing problems in Third World countries, discussed are difficulties faced by the Tanzanian National Housing Corporation (NHC) in its estate management functions that hinged on getting higher rents from its nearly 13,000 housing units, located mainly in urban areas. Rent revision proved difficult given the sociopolitical status of the NHC, as well as its subjection to the country's rent control legislation. Analysis highlights the problems of supplying public housing at realistic rents where the general public & government ideology support low rents. It also exposes the dilemmas faced by governments in dealing with NHCs, especially in African urban areas, where the NHCs can only house a tiny minority of households, at high cost to the public. 2 Tables, 46 References. Modified AA

title: The Holocaust-Anomic Hobbesian 'State of Nature'
abstract: Evidence is summarized attesting to the involvement of normal human beings in mass murder, interpreted in terms of 'identification with the victim,' as guided by H. Arendt's characterization of the Holocaust as 'the banality of evil.' Despite facts cited to demonstrate various motivations for the Holocaust, many contemporary approaches tend to conceal one distinctive & radically modern feature, ie, that the Holocaust was a bureaucratically administered extermination of a surplus population in the service of an abstract goal, creating Lebensraum for Germany within the New Order. This was possible only because the very impersonality of the bureaucratic spirit had been developed to a point where the pursuit of so abstract a goal no longer needed any morally compelling & therefore emotionally experienced legitimation at the level of its concrete human perpetrators. It is shown that: (1) the Holocaust occurred despite the absence of 'true believers' in any large number, (2) its single most important cause was a massive moral indifference among Germans in elite positions, (3) it could have been stopped with surprising ease, & (4) concentration camp guards & other staff often identified with their victims. Modified HA.

title: What the Party Wanted to Know: Citizen Complaints as a "Barometer of Public Opinion" in Communist Bulgaria
abstract: Authoritarian governments produce internal assessments of the quality of governance that allow them to identify and address brewing problems before they threaten regime stability. This paper provides a theory of how the information necessary to produce such assessments is collected. The empirical focus of the paper is on pre-1989 Bulgaria, which is used to illustrate how information-gathering channels in communist autocracies differ from those used in electoral autocracies. The theoretical argument of the paper is that citizen complaints rather than elections function as the main channel for gathering information on popular perceptions about governance problems in communist autocracies. Information compiled through the analysis of complaints is valued because it allows the leadership to identify problems with policy implementation, to track corruption, and to monitor the level of popular trust in the regime. Therefore, citizen complaints serve as a barometer of public opinion regarding governance problems. The archival materials on which this paper is based were accidentally discovered in the 2000s, when a closetful of about 2,000 files of the Information-Sociological Center of the Central Committee of the Bulgarian Communist Party was located during routine repairs of the Central State Archive in Sofia. These files, which were previously assumed lost, give scholars access to a treasure trove of material that provides a rare internal perspective on governance under late socialism. In conjunction with other formerly classified archival materials, they allow us to document what information on public opinion was collected and transmitted to the top leadership in pre-1989 Bulgaria. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Present Consequences and Lines of Correction, in the Educational System, of the Synchronic Isomorphism between [Feudal] Stratification and Initiation in Universities
abstract: The slow pace at which schools have adjusted & given adequate responses to "the profound problems of modern man" is explained by two hypotheses: (1) an explicative-descriptive hypothesis of dissonance, positing an isomorphism among stratified society, Us, & the bureaucratic school; & (2) a critico-explicative hypothesis, positing the interests of dominant social groups in the bureaucratic use of the stratified (academicist, structure from above, & nonautonomous) school. Truly humanistic interests require that the school be severed from its stratificatory dependence on & alliance with bourgeois interests. A. Ash.

title: Client Power and Italian Bureaucracy: Time Delay and Its Cost to Clients
abstract: There is a clear pattern of client inattention on the part of both public & private agencies brought about by the typical bureacratic structure in Italy. Observational data (total N = 180 30-minute observations) gathered in 3 settings -- a post office, a U information office, & small businesses -- in north central Italy show that failure to interchange functions on the job is a major reason for this client neglect. The result is that clients are required to wait an inordinately long time for services, which may have significant consequences. For those who are caught in emergencies or catastrophic situations, unnecessary waiting may dispossess them of their lives. Modified HA

title: Show Me the Money: The Benefits of For-Profit Charter Schools (aka EMOs)
abstract: The continued presence of educational management organizations (EMO) is explained as an inevitable and continued component of the public school landscape. This article discusses both why EMOs are here to stay and the benefits of EMOs in public education. Statistics are shared showing a 420% increase in the number of EMOs over the past 11 years as well as the Obama administration's commitment to choice and entrepreneurship in education. EMOs' role of providing a quality education option for students living in low-income urban neighborhoods and students of color was discussed using evidence and research showing that EMOs serve students of color in the urban centers of districts. In addition, the benefit of being free from the bureaucratic control of traditional public school districts is examined. Last, research findings that suggest significant academic gains for students attending EMO-run schools are presented. Together, these findings suggest that EMO-run schools are a beneficial component to the educational landscape. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Development and Trials of a Decision-Making Model: An Evaluation
authors: Peters, Michael; Marshall, James; Shaw, Robert
abstract: A description of an evaluation undertaken on contract for the New Zealand State Services Commission of a major project (the Administrative Decision-Making Skills Project) designed to produce a model of administrative decision making & an associated teaching/learning package for use by government officers. A philosophical model of decision making & the associated teaching/learning package in the setting of the New Zealand public service, where a deliberate attempt has been initiated to improve the quality of decision making, especially in relation to moral factors, are evaluated. 1 Figure, 2 Appendixes, 17 References. HA

title: THE MIND OF THE CAREER MAN
abstract: The management of public affairs is characterized by the joint yet divided responsibility of chosen representatives of the people, on the one hand, & of appointed admin've officials, on the other. To be in the service of the community lends stature to the career man in gov. To fit himself into the dual structure of responsibility is his hardest assignment. Reflecting the expert's view, he is likely to insist that the use of the admin've machinery should conform to his own judgment. Thus he may show inflexibility in meeting the demands of the policy-makers, instead of helping them to accomplish their program. The normal conditions of his soc existence place him on a Mc island where he is safe from the agitated seas about him. By keeping his world small, neat, & tidy, he can withdraw from the thunderous issues of politics & employ his nonpol'al status as a toga of righteousness. Instead of functioning as a generalist, attending to the general interest, he is more often a specialist & even a source of specialized pressure. These tendencies can be held in check only when the career man is guided by the counsel of integrity. His duty is toward the community as a whole. It is for him, looking at matters through the eyes of admin've experience, to identify for the policy-makers the ramifications & repercussions of emerging issues. He must hold before his pol'al masters the larger canvas, though he may not be graciously received. But integrity needs the support of spirit, esp of public spirit. Such spirit has to be generated. Only with thought & time can it grow into a guide toward the common good. AA-IPSA.

title: The Reorganization of U. S. Manufacturing Industry and Workers' Experience, 1880-1920: A Review of Bureaucracy and the Labor Process by Dan Clawson
abstract: Dan Clawson's Bureaucracy and the Labor Process (New York: Monthly Review Press, 1980, [see IRPS listing in this issue]) is evaluated as a study of US industrial relations from 1860 to 1920, focusing on its application of materials from Harry Braverman's Labor and Monopoly Capital (New York: Monthly Review Press, 1974). Braverman's model of class dynamics & proletarianization is reviewed; Clawson's focus on Taylorism as the "archetype of capitalist management" is critiqued, & empirical issues in managerial rationalization & skilled worker response are outlined. Particular attention is given to: (1) the limitations of the skill degradation model; (2) the impact of rationalization of unskilled labor; & (3) Clawson's neglect of ethnicity & gender factors & of the social bases of skill divisions. In Reply to Benenson, Dan Clawson defends his focus on the impact of worker struggles & their impact on the labor process; the emphasis on shop-floor conflict is seen as crucial to an understanding of options available to contemporary workers & of the supposed inevitability of work rationalization & bureaucratization. L. Whittemore.

title: Meltdown of the Public Interest and the Need for an Engaged Public Sphere: A Critical (Re-) Interpretation of the Nuclear Accident at Three Mile Island
abstract: We argue the need for a national public debate re-assessing the nuclear industry in light of recent Bush Administration initiatives for expansion of the nuclear industry in the US, and expressed support for nuclear power by Barack Obama. Specifically, we use a critical theoretical lens to re-examine the worst nuclear accident in US history at the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear power plant in 1979. Our three-part argument includes a focus on the conflicting imperatives in institutional and economic spheres; critique of the ideology of nuclear science and technology; and a discussion of processes by which the public sphere is de-politicized and, potentially, re-politicized. Through the critical re-interpretation of the TMI accident, we assert the essential importance of a deliberative, engaged public sphere.

title: La fabrique des indésirables: Pratiques de contrôle aux frontières dans un aéroport européen
abstract: Based on empirical research in a European airport, this article analyses how border guards control third-country nationals by advancing an anthropology of the power of border control as exhibited by the use of symbolic violence and discretionary state power. Leaning on the theories of street-level bureaucracies and organizations, we analyze the work practices, professional routines and organization of the work of border guards in order to show how border guards activate and constitute the border and the control of mobility. We argue that control at the airport is based both on the influence of the network-border and on a dramaturgical performance of bureaucratic governance, which is meant to create legitimate travelers and undesirable passengers, while circumventing potential protests of the latter and simulating accountability toward the broader public of citizens. As such, border control is more of a symbolic act than an efficient tool of immigration policy.

title: Information Technologies and Citizen Participation in the Venezuelan Toron: A Normative Analysis
authors: Fuenmayor Carroz, Jennifer; Avila Hernandez, Flor Maria
abstract: The 1999 constitution establishes citizens' right to freely participate in public affairs, be it directly or through their representatives. For this right to be effective, there has to exist an adequate flow of information from the state to its citizens & vice versa. The state needs to communicate how it administers its policies & how it can be accountable for them, so that citizens can participate in the flow of information, implementation of policy, & evaluation of local public policy. This article presents some proposals that deal with municipal public administration at the managerial level in order to guarantee an adequate information process, taking into account the new information & communication technologies. 16 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureacuracy and Immigrant Adjustment
abstract: The gap between client's expectations & behavior of officials in a bureaucracy are explored. In the specific case of the interaction between immigrant & official in Israel, a difference is suggested between immigrants from traditional vs modern countries. The former are more troubled by the official's conformity to bureaucratic norms, the latter, by the official's deviance from such norms. The study was based on a sample of 1,649 immigrants from North America. 4 hypotheses were tested: (1) Contact with the Israeli bureaucracy will be more problematic for American immigrants than other experiences. (2) Immigrants with knowledge concerning conditions in Israel (adequate anticipatory socialization) will have fewer problems with the Israeli bureaucracy than those with less knowledge. (3) Immigrants will describe their contact with bureaucracy as problematic in terms of deviations from bureaucratic norms rather than in terms of bureaucratic norms per se. (4) Those whose contacts have been problematic will tend to be low on subjective adjustment. Findings are presented which clearly support these hypotheses. 2 Tables. AA.

title: Negotiating Boundaries of Refugee Resettlement: A Study of Settlement Patterns and Social Support
abstract: This article analyzes aspects of the bureaucratic process of negotiating placement & social support by & for resettled refugees in Canada. Theoretical issues addressed include refugee resilience & effects of power structures on migrant networks. The article describes a qualitative study of underlying reasons for government-assisted refugee secondary migration to Ontario. The study demonstrates that refugees seek social support by moving from initial settlement sites to join extended family & analyzes how the resettlement bureaucracy, driven by political as well as humanitarian interests, attempts to control the process, in contradiction to refugees' preferences. The negotiation of placement & definitions of relevant social supports by bureaucrats & refugees are discussed. In conclusion, greater attention to refugee self-determination is suggested to improve settlement outcomes. 45 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The EU in search of its people: The birth of a society out of the crisis of Europe
abstract: The article argues that the 'crisis of Europe', triggered by market and governance dysfunctionalities (summarized as the Euro crisis), represents a 'critical moment' in the evolution of a European society. This society so far does not offer much resistance to such critical moments which is due to its incapacity to form a demos capable of acting together. The existing European society - and this is the basic claim - is nothing but the sum of individuals living in 'sub-European' (mainly national) groups. The evolution triggered by this critical situation opens pathways to turn these peoples of Europe into something more than being a sum of peoples governed by supranational bureaucracies. To decipher such processes a model is presented using Hirschman's idea of exit, voice and loyalty as mechanisms to generate social ties. Two points arise as crucial. The first is the observation that national societies which continue to provide foundational claims for people have turned into interest groups in the context of the European Union. This undermines not only the ontological nationalism still dominating the self-presentation of national societies in Europe, but it also offers evolutionary paths towards a society beyond national foundational claims in Europe. Yet it also provokes reactive processes such as the return to the self-contained nation (or even ethnic group). This is the core of the crisis of Europe. The systemic crises of the state and the market in Europe are speeding up an evolutionary process of people-making, the outcome of which could be either the regression to a people with foundational identities or to a people without foundational identities. The latter will be described as a postnational society, which would make an emerging European society the first really modern society. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: Contractual Legitimacy in Organizations and Governments
abstract: All org's & gov's rest, at least in part, on a legitimacy provided by the "pol'al contract," which involves an exchange of allegiance on the part of the followers in return for specific benefits conferred by the ruler. The ideal -- type of the pol'al contract envisions the pol'al community as a loosely -- bound "interestassociation" in relation to a leader who serves the community & whose scope of authority is strictly limited by the implicit terms of the contract & his ability to provide benefits & services. The pol'al contract can be observed in pol'al machines, mercenary uilitary groups, trade unions & professional assoc's, & in primitive societies, where the adherence of the members to the group & the leader is conditioned by the idea of benefits. In modern industr states the idea of contract produces a pol of interest -- group egoism in which society, org'ed as special interest -- groups, confronts the state with demands, but withholds the comprehensive allegiance necessary for the operation of gov. The prevalence of the philosophy of contact in the modern bur'tic state thus poses the most serious obstacles for the rational pol'al resolution of the crises of pollution, poverty, population, & war. AA.

title: The Relativization of the Bureaucratic Model and the Situational Organization
abstract: While the criticism of M. Weber's bureaucratic model has been primarily deterministic, projecting either the further spread of the bureaucratic organizational form or its gradual disappearance, it has contributed little to a theoretical penetration of the bureaucratic phenomenon. The basic assumption of the bureaucratic model is that it guarantees rationality of action in a cooperative social system through logical goal-orientedness as well as through economy of means. By posing the question of uncertainty, the structural-functionalist investigation makes relative both its model of control & its model of purposiveness, as well as its implication of independence as a closed system. The aim of the bureaucratic model of control (to reduce the variability of HB through structural means designed to secure the stability & continuity necessary for efficient performance) can be achieved only under certain conditions. K. Schmitt.

title: Outsourcing Schengen Visas
abstract: Outsourcing, a usual strategy in the management of private companies, is now also implemented by public administrations. In the recent past, consular services touching upon the emission of visas have more and more been given to outsourced service providers. This contribution details the reality of the outsourcing of Schengen visas. Beyond a mere description, this contribution highlights the motives behind the outsourcing and underlines a number of juridical and political problems concomitant to this trend: respect of EU laws, interest of visas' seekers, dependence on service providers, data protection, relations with other countries. The analysis is centred around Schengen's states policy but also includes revealing developments about the UK's experience in this domain. Adapted from the source document.

title: Determining 'truth' at the border: Immigration interviews, Chinese marital migrants, and Taiwan's sovereignty dilemmas
abstract: As Taiwan transitions from an immigrant-sending to an immigrant-receiving country, it struggles to build an immigration bureaucracy while its status as a sovereign nation-state is not recognized by much of the international community. Taiwan's largest immigrant group, marital migrants from China, are perceived as posing the greatest challenges to border control due to longstanding political tensions between the two countries and governmental and societal suspicions about Chinese spouses' marital motives. Based on research conducted with immigration officials and during immigration interviews at the border, this article interrogates the status of 'truth' in official efforts to determine definitively immigrants' marital intentions. It analyzes such truth demands in relation to Taiwan's anxieties about its national standing and the ability of an immigration bureaucracy to generate 'sovereignty effects'. Adapted from the source document.

title: Discourses on Death: Obituaries and the Management of Spoiled Identity
abstract: What do obituaries disclose about the death of persons who die of AIDS or where AIDS-related death is indicated? Obituaries meeting pre-established criteria were collected from a major metropolitan newspaper for a sixteen-month period in 1992 and 1993. A total of 184 obituaries were collected, content analyzed, and broken into three disclosure categories based on: 1) AIDS-related complications as published cause of death, 2) same-sex partner named as survivor, and 3) association with the AIDS cause or with the gay community. All three categories are stigmatized in the context of today's social norms. Discourse analysis revealed similarities and differences in topical and in subtextual themes and in varying degrees of identity management for the three categories. Descriptive findings suggest areas for further research and reveal much about the public management of death to counter the social stigma of "spoiled identity."

title: AFTER FUKUSHIMA: REFLECTIONS ON RISK AND INSTITUTIONAL LEARNING IN AN ERA OF MEGA-CRISES
