The 'historic classes' & public servants of bourgeois Hungary had fallen; the old econ & soc order had collapsed. The Soviet model for the building of communism was adopted. In the period 1948-1956 the cadre bur'cy of Hungary achieved its pinnacle. The cadres are formed by the leading members (occasionally the leading groups) of the party. They are the party's decisionmaking body & since the party has absolute governing power, they are the country's decision-makers. A cadre bur'cy is based on the centralization of all org's. Existence, functions, & leadership structure of all org's are determined by the leadership cadre. The concomitant potential for conflict in people's democracies is noted. Cadre bur'cy differs considerably from Max Weber's ideal type of bur'cy by this centralization, by the special function of the law under its particular norm system, stress on willingness to work & efficiency, subordination of professional qualifications, extensive control over the economy, a high degree of exchangability of cadres, insecurity of the individual cadre member's position, & a system of divisions in the cadre. Max Weber's type of bur'cy is contrasted with cadre bur'cy. Efforts are discerned in Hungary to abolish this cadre bur'cy or limit it, as exemplified by the approach of Hungarian Premier Imre Nagy (1953-1955), & the revolt of 1956. A restructuring of the admin'ive system is still underway, which among other things makes it possible for non-party members to fill admin'ive positions. Econ mechanisms & policies are also undergoing changes. These could eventually lead to the abolishment of cadre bur'cy in Hungary. Whether a new type of bur'crat will evolve remains to be seen. M. Maxfield.

title: An understanding of poverty from those who are poor
abstract: Participatory research in the study of poverty invites those living in difficult                 circumstances to participate in an analysis of their own livelihood situation. A                 participatory poverty assessment was facilitated with a small group of women who are                 members of a food co-operative in Niagara Falls, Canada and who live in poverty. The                 women explored together issues of well-being, the stress of living in poverty, the                 role of the social assistance system in shaping their lives and community attitudes.                 Important themes which emerged included an emphasis on social relationships, the                 impact of the pervasive scrutiny of the social assistance bureaucracy, the                 importance of community good will and the possibilities for community action. This                 article discusses the contribution of local knowledge to an understanding of poverty                 as well as the limitations of participation in changing social policy.

title: 1998 PSA Presidential address: The value of sociology
abstract: What is the value-added character of sociology? In an era of change and unease in higher education, can a case be made for sociology interms of intellectual and scholarly substance rather than in terms of bureaucratic and political considerations? As a scholarly and instructional activity, what is the value of sociology beyond what other disciplines have to offer?

title: The Surplus of Employment in the Post-al Real
abstract: A review essay on two books by Slavoj Zizek: The Sublime Object of Ideology (New York, NY: Verso, 1989); & Looking Awry: An Introduction to Jacques Lacan through Popular Culture (Cambridge: MIT Press, 1991 [see listings in IRPS No. 81]). Zizek's work is judged an exemplary post-al (postmodernism, - Marxism, -structuralism, -industrial, etc) practice that revives a regressive bourgeois idealism that seeks to suppress the historical & revolutionary knowledge necessary for social transformation. Zizek's analysis explains the social in terms of the psyche, using a psychic & rhetorical reductionism as it reintroduces the surplus of enjoyment as the base for the ideological superstructure. Zizek's identification of bureaucracy as the great social evil is compared to the exhortations of Ronald Reagan, Margaret Thatcher, & Rush Limbaugh against government interference of individual pursuits. His idealism substitutes enjoyment for labor as the fundamental locus for understanding ideology, the subject, & a conflicted social reality. 4 References. D. Schwartz

title: RELIGION, BUREAUCRACY, AND MODERN ECONOMIC GROWTH, A POSSIBILITY OF REVISING WEBER S THESIS
abstract: An attempt to revise Max Weber's thesis on the links between Protestant ethics & the spirit of capitalism, founded on evidence from the Netherlands & the Far East. Weber himself was aware that his thesis did not fit very well with the facts of the Dutch case. He noted that foreign O's attributed the Netherland's econ expansion in the 16-17th cent's to extreme Calvinism; but he also noted the role of patrician 'regents,' many of whom were 'Arminianists' or moderate Calvinists. The light that China & Japan may throw on the experience of the Netherlands is considered. It is noted that Robert N. Bellah, in his TOKUGAWA RELIGION had emphasized the role of Confucianism & samurai (noble) bur'cy in bringing about Japan's modern industr'ization. The Dutch historian Albert Hyma had similarly noted the role of Arminianism & gov bur'crats in fostering the early econ flowering of the Netherlands. The author's own study of Java confirmed his thesis that, in the Netherlands, 'the principal agent of econ progress. . .had been a sober & restrained humanism combined with loyalty towards the State.' This means a revision of Weber's thesis, not its rejection. For, as against the Marxist emphasis on the dominant role of econ forces, Weber showed the autonomous role of the spiritual forces of ideology & religion. I. Langnas.

title: Political Personalism in Germany. Sociological Aspects of the So-Called "Kohl-System"
abstract: So far, bureaucratic apparatuses have been important for the analysis of both dictatorial regimes & democracies characterized by a weak political party structure, like the US. This article will elucidate the political system of the Federal Republic of Germany, especially the so-called "Kohl System," by making use of Max Weber's type of administrative apparatus. I argue that highly organized state bureaucracies & mass parties embedded in a parliamentary system do not necessarily provide effective control against the arbitrary use of power by the chancellor & party leader. Rather, they tend to establish a two-track system: while the regular organization takes care of routine political business, decision making shifts to informal circles shaped & dominated by a single person & maintained by the personal will for power. The analysis shows that key components of the "Kohl System" include party adherence, as a means of political leverage, the cult of personality, cronyism, patronage, & back door funding. 55 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Trade and Bureaucracy in China under the Sung [10th-12th Century]
abstract: The status of middlemen (yaren, shikuai) & their role in the trade policies worked out by authorities during the first half of the Sung dynasty are analyzed. During this period, the first centralized state bureaucracy emerged; & trade as well as the means of credit thrived as never before. This growth associated & placed in competition two big networks, the only ones capable of covering the whole empire: civil servants & merchants. This connivance & rivalry fixed, for a long time, the forms whereby trade was controlled as well as the way that authorities, producers, & middlemen perceived the interlocking relations between public & private interests. 48 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Role of Bureaucracy in Policy Development and Implementation in India
abstract: A common perception -- that bureaucracy has always been dominant in Indian policy making -- is refuted. Three distinct phases in the evolution of the role of bureaucracy are described. Under British colonial rule, the bureaucracy was the government; its key features were the elitism & strong loyalty of the Indian Civil Service (ICS). Postindependence, under a comparatively strong & stable government, bureaucracy was less powerful, but served to provide advice, influence, & implementation. The ICS was replaced by the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), which was almost as elitist (replacing British upper class with Indian upper class); the British model of governance continued. In the third phase, the social composition of the bureaucracy has broadened to include members from lower strata, & wider geographic representation. However, a less stable government, lack of policy, & arbitrary shifts & changes in the bureaucracy have reduced the IAS to low-level civil servants. A major problem is the dichotomy between the planning & implementation processes, leading to a serious implementation gap. Cooperative & constructive efforts on the part of the political & bureaucratic leadership are urged to improve the acquisition & integration of knowledge & information, & to develop effective policy-making personnel. 2 Photographs. S. Dilts

title: "A New Health Order as Part of the New Social Order": The Strategic Response of the WHO to its Member States
abstract: This article explores the range of responses available to international bureaucracies when confronted with demands made by their member states through the study of the World Health Organization (WHO) during the 1970s and 1980s. I show that the WHO bureaucracy successfully addressed the demands of developing countries for health policies compatible with a more equitable world economic order, but in a way that preserved the bureaucracy's own agenda and without upsetting the opposite coalition of wealthy countries. Drawing on insights from the sociology of organizations, this article shows that externally dependent international bureaucracies are able to preserve their autonomous agenda by strategically reframing countries' demands before responding to them. [Copyright Elsevier Ltd.]

title: Non-Profit, For-Profit and Government Organisations in Social Service Provision: Comparison of Behavioural Patterns for Austria
abstract: Behavioral differences between nonprofit organizations (NPOs), government organizations (GOs), & private market organizations (PMOs) as social service providers in Austria are investigated using data on 4,380 nursery schools collected by the Austrian Federal Statistical Office, & on 512 retirement homes from an information brochure of the Austrian Council of Social Work. Three hypotheses regarding client, product, & price differentiation -- formulated on the basis of B. A. Weisbrod's undersupply model, ("Toward a Theory of the Voluntary Nonprofit Sector in a Three-Sector Economy," Phelps, E. S. [Ed], Altruism, Morality and Economic Theory, New York: Russell Sage, 1974), the differentiated demand approach, & the public finance argument on the redistributive role of government -- are tested & found to be supported by the data. NPOs & PMOs are shown to provide qualitatively better services, but also to charge significantly higher prices, than GOs. Other findings are detailed, & policy implications suggested. 7 Tables, 21 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: BUREAUCRACY, PROGRAMMATIZATION, POLITICAL POWER
authors: LA PALOMBARA, JOSEPH; Freddi, Giorgio; FERRARI, DORELLO; Cimmino, Salvatore
abstract: Part II of a round table (see SA 0624/C4169 on 5 major questions concerning the conditions & tasks of civil service in Italy. J. La Palombara criticizes the inadequacy of data available to the public admin, suggests the creation of a nat'l commission for econ planning within the Council of Ministers, & encourages exp'tion with new admin'ive structures, eg, dept's for industr development, Ur & agri'al planning, as well as a nat'l system of U instruction in the functions of public administration on a state level. G. Freddi advocates the employment of specialists at high levels of public administration & is concerned with the relationship of the bur'tic elite to pol'al power & pressure groups. D. Ferrari considers it important that the dept's of public service function exclusively within their defined scope. S. Cimmino demands that techniques & methods be developed to transform the system of public administration to correspond to the needs of the public. M. Maxfield.

title: The 'War' of Bureaucracy with Society
abstract: The war between bureaucracy & society is revealed in their respective values. Bureaucracy values precision, stability & predictability, while society values justice, oppression, happiness, death, & other unpredictable entities. Bureaucracy is mechanistic, society humanistic; these two opposing forces have led man to war with himself, torn between conflicting impulses towards organization & spontaneity. As a result of this conflict the individual can no longer form abstract concepts of self, but is held captive to external laws of behavior. People of Western societies have been converted to the habit of Aristotelian thought, which requires that a wide range of options be ignored in favor of a single perspective that makes the assertion of an 'absolute' truth possible. The effect of this line of thinking is to convert social humanity into a scientific community, replacing two-way social logic with one-way bureaucratic fiat. Bureaucratic thinking becomes a habit both in the individual & society, & is ultimately rationalized so that bureaucratic goals are perceived as superior to the ideals of the social person. It may be that the burden of remaining a human in a bureaucratic society is too great, & that survival necessitates the active embrace of prescribed thought. E. Goldberger.

title: An Appraisal of the Two Faces of Bureaucracy in Relation to the Nigerian Society
authors: Aluko, M A O; Adesopo, A A
abstract: This paper is an evaluation of the two faces of bureaucracy. The point of focus is on whether bureaucracy is desirable. The discussions in the paper show that there is no rose without its thorns as bureaucracy is characterized by both functions & dysfunctions. While bureaucracy provides greater organizational efficiency in work settings, it is at the same time creating an uncaring "iron cage" from which there is little escape in modern society. The paper concluded with the thesis that it may be impossible to dismantle bureaucracy, but it is important to reform it. 22 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Explaining Citizen-Initiated Contacts with Municipal Bureaucrats
abstract: Provides a comprehensive explanation of when & why citizens initiate contacts with municipal bureaucrats, using telephone survey data collected in 1995 from 2,257 residents of Atlanta, GA. Logistic regressions of 15 contact types reveal perceived needs as the most consistently significant predictor of most types. The influence of socioeconomic status over contacting is indirect. Prior research is drawn on to summarize knowledge about these contacts & the measurement problems that have plagued earlier research. 6 Tables, 1 Figure. Adapted from the source document.

title: Descriptive Representation by Gender and Race/Ethnicity in Municipal Bureaucracies: Change in US Multiethnic Cities, 1987-2001
authors: Miller, Will; Kerr, Brinck; Reid, Margaret
abstract: We explore the extent of employment inequalities between Latinas, African American women, and white (non-Latina) women (and their coethnics) in public sector managerial positions in multiethnic US cities. Our analysis of Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) data from 1987 and 2001 indicates that all groups of women suffer from underrepresentation at the administrator level, especially in agencies that have regulatory and distributive policy commitments, but that Latinas and African American women show the lowest levels of representation. Moreover, Latinas and African American women are substantially underrepresented among professional workforces in almost all municipal departments; however, white (non-Latina) women achieve parity in many cities. Among pairs of coethnics (e.g. African American females versus African American males), we find that males are usually better represented than females, but even in multiethnic cities large disparities remain between white males and all other groups in the ability to claim and retain the most prestigious municipal government positions. We are concerned that the continuing lack of progress made by members of traditionally disadvantaged groups may further compromise the representativeness and legitimacy of bureaucracies in many multiethnic cites -- and may also present a serious barrier to addressing important public policy challenges in these cities. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Marginality, ethnicity and penality in the neo-liberal city: an analytic cartography
abstract: This article draws an analytic map of the research programme pursued across my three books Urban Outcasts (2008), Punishing the Poor (2009) and Deadly Symbiosis: Race and the Rise of the Penal State (in press). In this trilogy, I disentangle the triangular nexus of class fragmentation, ethnic division and state-crafting in the polarizing city at century's turn to explain the political production, socio-spatial distribution and punitive management of marginality through the wedding of disciplinary social policy and neutralizing criminal justice. I signpost how I deployed key notions from Pierre Bourdieu (social space, bureaucratic field, symbolic power) to clarify categories left hazy (such as the ghetto) and to forge new concepts (territorial stigmatization and advanced marginality, punitive containment and liberal paternalism, hyper-incarceration and negative sociodicy) as tools for the comparative sociology of the unfinished genesis of the post-industrial precariat, the penal regulation of poverty in the age of diffusing social insecurity, and the building of the neo-liberal Leviathan.

title: Colored Identity: The Politics and Materiality of ID Cards in Palestine/Israel
abstract: In Palestine/Israel, different colored identification cards are mandated by the Israeli state apparatus to Palestinians in the West Bank, the Gaza Strip, East Jerusalem, and those who are citizens of Israel. The article traces the development of the bureaucracy of the Palestinian ID card since the establishment of Israel and suggests that modern-day ID cards in Palestine/Israel are physical and visible instruments of a widespread low-tech surveillance mechanism to control mobility and a principal means for discriminating, both positively and negatively, subjects' privileges and rights. ID cards are both the spaces in which Palestinians confront, tolerate, and sometimes challenge the Israeli state, and a mechanism through which Palestinian spatiality, territoriality, and corporeality are penetrated by the Israeli regime. Vital in the control and differentiation of Palestinian populations, what makes ID cards unique in the Palestinian/Israeli case is that their materiality is one of their most important and resonant aspects. The article describes various representations of the ID cards, for example in poetry and in murals, to show how they also function as sites of remediation, spaces and moments of renegotiation for their bearers, subject to counter-hegemonic representations, interpretations, and uses. As a special kind of material object, ID cards are an effective and low-tech means of surveillance and differentiation and an important nexus of Israeli power, demonstrating the institutional materiality of the state apparatus's constitution in subjects' everyday life; but they have also become important because they allow a poetics of political resistance. Adapted from the source document.

title: State Capitalism and New Developments in Social Class Structure
abstract: The progressive substitution of bur'cy by the bourgeoisie is today essentially a soc phenomenon. As a result, a classless society is springing up from this disappearance of bur'cy. A study of this process must include an analysis of the position, within the class structure, of the technical intelligentsia whose role is continually increasing. It would seem that a part of this intelligentsia is identifying itself with the bourgeoisie & another part with the proletariat, while the group in between has as yet not declared its allegiance. Tr by J. A. Broussard from IPSA.

title: The Elements of Political Science
abstract: Excerpts from Gaetano Mosca's Elements of Political Science (1953) are used to analyze the relationship between the social (group) type & world religions, on the one hand, & between the feudal & bureaucratic state on the other. The initial social types were formed as a combination of racial & cultural factors, whose uniqueness was maintained by the absence of communication between ancient civilizations. The relative isolation of ancient communities did not necessarily result in the integration of neighboring states, nor did it provoke the creation of a universal god. Buddhism, Christianity, & Islam facilitated the integration of culturally diverse peoples in feudal states while competing for political influence with them. Feudal organization of the state is defined as a sum of small self-sufficient social aggregates, while the bureaucratic state is characterized by the type of salaried state official & the separation of legal, military, & administrative functions. 28 References. A. Devic

title: PONAPE ISLANDS CENTRAL HIGH SCHOOL: A CASE STUDY OF BUREAUCRATIC ORGANIZATION AND CROSS-CULTURAL CONFLICT IN A MICRONESIAN HIGH SCHOOL
abstract: BUREAUCRATIC ORGANIZATION, CROSS-CULTURAL CONFLICT, & THEIR EFFECTS ON PERSONALITY FORMATION IN THE AMERICAN TRANSPLANTED HIGH SCHOOL ON PONAPE IN THE EASTERN CAROLINE ISLANDS ARE EXAMINED. PONAPE IS THE ADMINISTRATIVE CENTER OF 1 OF THE 6 DISTRICTS OF THE UN TRUST TERRITORY OF THE PACIFIC ISLANDS, UNDER THE DEPT OF THE INTERIOR OF THE US GOVERNMENT. THE FOCUS IS ON THE SCHOOL ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE AS A NETWORK OF CONTRIVED SOCIAL ROLES HELD TOGETHER BY: (1) PSYCHOLOGICAL BONDS EVOLVING FROM ADHERENCE TO THE FORMAL STRUCTURE & FROM RESISTANCE TO THAT STRUCTURE, & (2) THE INTERPLAY OF THESE FACTORS. THE FAMILY FUNCTION & THE FUNCTION OF SCHOOLS & GOVERNMENT CLASH. THE MAIN CONCERN IS WITH CHARACTERISTICS OF THE SCHOOL AS A COMPLEX FORMAL ORGANIZATION & THE EXPERIENCES OF ADMINISTRATORS, COUNSELORS, TEACHERS & STUDENTS AS PARTICIPANTS IN THAT ORGANIZATION. AN EXAMINATION IS MADE OF THE CHARACTERISTIC FORMATION IN THIS AUTHORITY SYSTEM. THE STUDENT IS LOW IN THE HIERARCHY AS THE RESULT OF CULTURAL & BUREAUCRATIC CONFLICTS. BEHAVIORAL ADAPTATION WITH FUNCTIONAL RATIONALIZATION IS HUMANLY ALIENATING. L. MESTMAN.

title: In the Picture or Off the Wall? Ethical Regulation, Research Habitus, and Unpeopled Ethnography
abstract: This article focuses on two unintended consequences of ethical regulation of social enquiry: the exclusion of participants and, subsequently, a transformation of research practice. An ethnography of corridor life in a large university building forms the basis of the discussion. Originally intended as a pilot for a broader study of informal networks of power, the project's aim seemed unachievable. External ethical bureaucracy engendered an overdeveloped sensitivity to doing wrong, resulting in a bizarre form of reflexivity. The first consequence of ethical constraint is, paradoxically, the exclusion of participants and their worlds, as research projects are ever more tightly framed. However, forced to reflect on her research habitus, the author discovered that a conventional qualitative research focus on participants' narrative/biographic accounts and face-to-face interaction can be similarly restrictive. In conclusion, the author discusses how practicing an unpeopled ethnography can open up space for democratic, innovative research within the confines of current ethical regulation. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright holder.]

title: VMG: City Building, Legitimacy and Governability. Towards an Ethical Praxis in Local Government in Venezuela
abstract: The paper analyzes, from an ethical perspective, the emerging governmental practices in Maracaibo Municipality (1995-2004), visible management government (VMO), & establishes guidelines for a VMG & ethical urban manager. In order to achieve these objectives, the city & ethics are analyzed in the postmodern context & the VMO in the recent history of Venezuela, Several authors were reviewed to establish the theoretical framework that was contrasted with the VMO in order to establish ethical characteristics. The article concludes pointing out that the praxis of the VMO, which governs the city in order to be perceived as "good government" & in this way legitimize itself based on performance & increased local governability, & also in order to be ethical, must be supported in a redefined practical manner such as: transversal reason that conceives of & assumes plurality with intellectual rigor & ethical responsibility & in an "urban ethical management model," based upon an ethic of agreed responsibility and solidarity capable of uniting the city based on legitimacy & governability. Tables, Graphs, References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucracy in the United States and Canada: Social, Attitudinal and Behavioral Variables
abstract: Using a random sample of high-level bureaucrats (N=475) in the US & Canada, the analysis compares Rs along such dimensions as SC, educational backgrounds & achievement, economic liberalism, political efficacy, & attitudes toward legislators. Canadians tend to have a lower regard for the competence of legislators, to rank lower on political efficacy, to rank higher on economic liberalism (defined as a preference for "big government"), & to include a higher proportion of individuals with educational backgrounds that characterize a "generalist" as opposed to a "specialist" preparation for their official roles. Almost 50% of both samples reported that they had created an interest group to make demands upon their own agencies. Regarding the influence of lobbyists in each system, whereas US bureaucrats tend to remain roughly equal regardless of tenure, in Canada, there is a linear tendency for officials to be more susceptible to such influence as tenure increases. 9 Tables. AA.

title: HIGHER PUBLIC SERVANTS AND THE BUREAUCRATIC ELITE IN CANADA
abstract: The bur'tic elite of Canada is analyzed in terms of 3 continua: rationalized/non-rationalized; rivalled/unrivalled; open/closed. It consisted in 1953 of 202 persons: senior publie servants of the rank of deputy minister or the equivalent, directors of branches in the more important branches or the equivalents, & senior executives of Crown corporations. It is probably the most highly trained group of men in Canada, 78.7% having U degrees & 43.6% post-graduate training, chiefly in law, sci & engineering, & the soc sciences; 18.3% have taught in a U. Only 23.8% have spent all & only 52.9% more than 50% of their working lives in the public service. 39% were outsiders at the time of their appointment to senior positions & of the 1953 group, 15 had by 1957 moved to other institutional structures. 43.8% of the insiders who had reached the 2 top categories had been helped to rise by serving close to influential persons. The French-Canadian & Jewish minorities are the only ones represented: the French-Canadian is underrepresented, & has a disproportionate number of outside appointments. Ontario is the only overrepresented region; those underrepresented have the greatest % of outside appointments. In religion, the non-conformist Protestant denominations are dominant whereas Anglicanism is dominant in the econ elite & Roman Catholicism, while much underrepresented is % less than in the econ elite. In soc backgrounds, while only 8.8% of the native Canadians in the group came from elite families, 9.3% came from other Uc families, & 68.7% from Me families; 13.2% rose from below Me, & only 9 of them worked their way up in the service. It seems that the Canadian bur'cy is unrivalled (has a quasi-monopoly of skills & knowledge), is more closed than open, & is based on rationalism. The bur'tic elite is socially homogeneous, & is clearly separated from the econ elite. J. Burnet.

title: Jurgen Habermas and the Dissonance in Western Political Philosophy
abstract: Habermas recognizes a severe tension between two ideals of politics. On the one hand, there is the ideal of a political community that shapes its world through collective action. On the other hand, there is the ideal of the Rechtsstaat or the constitutional state where society is governed by laws instead of men. He believes, however, that this tension can be overcome when both ideals are analyzed & subsequently reconstructed on the basis of discursive ethics. I claim that Habermas impoverishes the idea of the Rechtsstaat. He disregards the meaning & function of the separation between executive & legislative power. He can only make sense of the institution of parliament as a form of free discourse where the force of the best argument prevails. Habermas's synthesis is in fact a reduction of the idea of the Rechtsstaat to the idea of democracy. He makes democracy a radical idea when he states that the only legitimate coercive power (Herrschaft) is rooted in a public discourse free from coercive power. But he does not suspect that coercive power may be problematic in itself, & that it should be limited. Democracy is an answer to the question of how coercive power can be legitimate. A political constitution however, should not only deal with the problem of legitimacy, but also with the question of how far political power should stretch. The tension in Western political thought is caused by certain philosophers who wish to disregard the second problem altogether. 26 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucratic Representation. Civil Servants and the Future
abstract: "Bureaucratic Representation: Civil Servants and the Future" by H. T. Wilson is reviewed.

title: Numeracy or Enumeration? The Uses of Numbers by States and Societies
abstract: The relationship between numeracy & government bureaucracy is presented from the "bottom-up," with theory from sociological & ethnomethodological literature. It is argued that states responded to the rise of numeracy in the population by collecting more detailed records, rather than driving numeracy per se. Fiscal & legal records from late medieval & early modern Tuscany show that rural Tuscans used numeracy in a variety of ways, eg, shopkeepers recording customer debts, landlords & tenants tracking rents, families recording dowries & property transfers, & religious institutions enumerating gifts. Overall, numeracy spread with the development of local markets for land, labor, & commodities, motivated by generalized reciprocity & not necessarily capitalism. Centralized bureaucracies then took advantage of the preexisting level of societal numeracy. 103 References. M. Pflum

title: DETERMINANTS OF SPAN OF CONTROL
abstract: A paper based on the author's unpublished dissertion, 'Formality Versus Flexibility in Complex Organizations: A Comparative Investigation Within a Hospital,' Yale U, 1965. 3 determinants of span of control are explored: on the basis of interview data from 186 supervisors & their employees in a small community hosp: (1) When subordinates' jobs are highly complex, the span of control is decreased. Vice versa, the more complex a supervisor's job, the lower his span of control. (2) Closeness of supervision, upon examination, was found to be unrelated to admin'ors' spans of supervision. (3) Subordinates' & supervisors' job complexity were found to be positively related to control. The more complex the admin'ors' tasks, the fewer are the subordinates they regulate. These findings suggest that technological characteristics of productive processes are key determinants of variations in size of spans of control. Further relationships between job complexity & such factors as degree of coordination required, geographical contiguity of employees, workers' competence, & N of supervisory assistants assigned to the admin'or, should be studied. 5 Tables. Modified HA.

title: Bureaucratic Compliance with Mexico's New Access to Information Law
abstract: We analyze government document custodians' attitudes and behaviors in order to assess the prospects of a new access to information law establishing a citizen's right-to-know in Mexico. The Mexican law is considered one of the best in the hemisphere in terms of broad access and workable enforcement provisions. However, no extra resources were allotted to government agencies for compliance with the law; the country's traditional bureaucratic incentive structures support closure rather than access; and bureaucrats' views on the uses of government information prior to democratization suggest an instrumental approach guided organizational incentives rather than generalized support for either secrecy or access as a principle. We argue that missing or unclear political will at the top is the strongest challenge to Mexico's emerging right to know. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Ethics Creep: Governing Social Science Research in the Name of Ethics
abstract: This article presents an analysis of the Canadian ethics review process by a member of a Research Ethics Board. The author suggests that the new formal system for regulating the ethical conduct of scholarly research is experiencing a form of "ethics creep." This is characterized by a dual process whereby the regulatory system is expanding outward to incorporate a host of new activities & institutions, while at the same time intensifying the regulation of activities deemed to fall within its ambit. These tendencies are demonstrated through an analysis of (1) the scope of research ethics protocols, (2) the concept of "harm" employed by these boards, (3) the use of informed consent provisions, & (4) the presumption that research participants will remain anonymous. To accentuate the nature of this ethics creep, comparisons are made between the ways in which identical knowledge-generation activities are governed within journalism & the academy. The conclusion suggests that one effect of the increasingly formalized research ethics structure is to rupture the relationship between following the rules & acting ethically. Some of the reasons for this "creep" are highlighted along with the risks that it poses for scholarship. 33 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Social Production of Indifference: Exploring the Symbolic Roots of Western Bureaucracy
abstract: Stewart reviews "The Social Production of Indifference:  Exploring the Symbolic Roots of Western Bureaucracy" by Michael Herzfeld.

title: "We Don't Have a Plan. We Should Be Working on a Plan.": Obstacles to Caregiver Transition Planning for Individuals with Fragile X Syndrome
authors: Feinstein, Rebecca T; Pollack, Harold A
abstract: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the most common heritable form of intellectual disability. Adults with FXS vary in their health status and functional capacity and require a range of caregiving activities, including full-time supervision, help with activities of daily living, and coordination of daily activities and services. Through the lens of life course theory, this qualitative study of 39 respondents examines caregiving, transition, and long-term planning for adults with FXS and examines related challenges for social service interventions. In-depth interviews enable caregivers to share their perspectives about many challenges, including the distinctive symptomology of FXS itself, family contextual factors, caregiving in a resource-scarce environment, and ways in which caregivers make choices in a complex bureaucratic system. Although caregivers identify many challenges in formulating and executing long-term plans, we consider several suggestions to improve the provision of services to individuals living with FXS and their families. [web URL: http://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/688502]

title: Waiting for change: youth, caste and politics in India
abstract: This paper examines waiting, caste and politics through reference to the cultural and political practices of educated unemployed young men in India. We show through ethnographic fieldwork in Uttar Pradesh how a shared sense of young male limbo sometimes erodes caste divides. While waiting in poorly provisioned north Indian universities, young men develop novel cultures that bridge caste, class and religion. They also collaborate across class, caste and religious boundaries in protests against the state and university bureaucracies. At the same time, some students have responded to a sense of 'waiting' by developing collusive relationships with local government and university bureaucrats. Waiting emerges not as a passive condition but as a seed-bed for new cultural and political forms. Adapted from the source document.

title: Rational Choice versus Cultural Explanations of the Efficiency of the Prussian Tax System
abstract: A response to criticisms made by Philip S. Gorski (see abstract in SA 44:2) of these authors' rational-choice explanation (see SA 42:5/9409647) of the efficiency of the Prussian tax system & the rise to power of the Prussian monarchy. Issues of disagreement are identified, & it is suggested that Gorski has focused on a very short time period & on a small part of the tax administration. Further, he has minimized the role of secular deviations from bureaucratic recruitment, & he misunderstands how rational-choice models work. It is concluded that there is no empirical support for the alternative argument proposed by Gorski. 24 References. D. M. Smith

title: Hierarchy, Bureaucracy, and Ideology in French Criminal Justice: Some Empirical Observations
abstract: Using observational & interview data from my own empirical study of the investigation & prosecution of crime in France, this article examines critically the extent to which three features generally considered central to inquisitorial procedure -- hierarchy, bureaucracy, & ideology -- exist within the structures & procedures of the French criminal process & the constraining impact they have upon the decision making of the procureur, the judicial officer responsible for supervising the majority of criminal investigations. A broad degree of discretion is found to exist at the local & individual level & the unavailability of resources further increases disparities in practice. Nevertheless, the conventional "ideals" retain a continuing force & relevance for procureurs, who describe their work (both as they understand it to be & as they would wish it to be) in these terms & whose crime control orientation is shielded by redefining it in terms of "representing the public interest.". Adapted from the source document.

title: Setting Up Targeted Research Interviews: A Primer for Students and New Interviewers
abstract: This article analyzes key strategic considerations for setting up targeted research interviews, including human subjects and Institutional Review Board requirements, approaching respondents, the medium of contact, using technology, cultural conceptions of time and commitment, using networks, wading through bureaucracies, and watching for warning signs. By making these considerations explicit and conscious, we can better specify how to gain interviews for our research and how to ethically approach this task. This analysis will be most useful as a pedagogical explanation for students and for scholars newly approaching interviewing. Adapted from the source document.

title: Patterns of 'Mock Bureaucracy' in Mining Disasters: An Analysis of the Westray Coal Mine Explosion
abstract: Examines events leading up to mining disasters that may have been foreseeable & avoidable, discussing how many mining disasters are likely to be the result of "mock bureaucracies"' or situations characterized by overt violation of workplace safety rules. Using the 1992 Westray mine explosion in Pictou County, Nova Scotia, as an illustrative case, traced are the development & institutionalization of a mock bureaucracy in an organization. Implications for further research & understanding of industrial crises are drawn. 2 Tables, 3 Figures, 5 Appendixes, 59 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Feminist Social Service Delivery in India
authors: Kassam, Meenaz; Handy, Femida; Ranade, Shree
abstract: Given the crucial role attributed to women-led NGOs in the social development in India, we examine the organizational structure of such NGOs, the women who lead them, & nature of the social services provided by them. We examine 20 women-led NGOs & find that despite their self-professed feminist ideological leanings, many of them in reality exhibit bureaucratic characteristics -- a finding similar to those found in a study of women-led NGOs in the US (Botch, 1997). We also find that the pragmatic, cultural, & social variables can explain some of theoretical contradictions we find in our data. 3 Tables, 41 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Africa, Asia, and Latin America: Peasant and Bureaucracy in Ba'thist Syria
abstract: Richard T.  Antoun reviews "Peasant and Bureaucracy in Ba'thist Syria:  The Political Economy of Rural Development," by Raymond A.  Hinnebusch.

title: Images of a Culture in Transition: Personal Constructs of Organizational Stability and Change
abstract: Investigates a large government business enterprise to examine the utility of the repertory grid technique in the investigation of organizational culture & to conduct an "audit" of performance culture. The development of a methodology to gauge the rate of uptake of a new culture -- from a public service toward a customer service orientation -- is described. Employing E. Schein's (1990) method, qualitative in-depth interview & quantitative mail questionnaire data from 13 middle managers, ages 28-55, indicated that there was progress in the direction of the new culture desired by management. Three active cultures or groupings were articulated through the language of the participants, which essentially mirrored a culture in transition: those who had adopted, partially adopted, or not adopted the new culture. Findings confirmed that there is gain to be made with the Schein paradigm of culture, & the repertory grid technique is unique in gathering data about the "carriers" of performance culture. 3 Tables, 2 Figures, 1 Appendix, 41 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Max Weber's Sociology of Law; Judge as Mediator
abstract: The substantive underpinnings of Max Weber's `Sociology of Law' and the standing of judges therein are discussed. Foregrounding his conception of the administration of justice, perennial concern with the correlation between personality and the structure of domination, and account of legal rationalization, his discernment of the vital adjudicative role assumed by judges and the bearing of their personal qualifications is elucidated. The focus is placed on Weber's putatively negative assessment of the Common Law. Reading his appraisal of precedent and the charismatic stature of the judge in light of his theory of casuistry and critique of bureaucracy, it is shown that his examination implicitly extols the English administration of justice.

title: Technological Democracy: Bureaucracy and Citizenry in the German Energy Debate
abstract: Kraft reviews "Technological Democracy:  Bureaucracy and Citizenry in the German Energy Debate" by Carol J.  Hager.

title: Knowledge-Based Economy and Social Exclusion: Shadow and Light in the Roman Socio-Economic Model
authors: De Muro, Pasquale; Monni, Salvatore; Tridico, Pasquale
abstract: The article aims to analyse the evolution and modernization of Rome in the last 30 years. To this end, we focus on both structural and institutional change and try to identify the main ruptures, continuities and driving forces of the new Roman model. After the second world war, Rome was generally considered to be a cumbersome capital city with a heavy bureaucratic sector and without any strong 'local' political forces and social movements capable of bringing about economic and political change. Nevertheless, a new and more democratic local governance and subregulation mode emerged during the post-Fordist era, which allowed the production and reproduction of new socioeconomic relations that in turn influenced a new economic model for the city. This new governance has led to some interesting forms of 'democratization' that are difficult to find in other post-Fordist metropolises. However, the Roman model is also characterized -- as in other global metropolises -- by forms of social exclusion, poverty and polarization between the peripheries and central/high-income districts, in a sort of two-speed development. At the same time, the traditional bureaucracy and its connected 'state bourgeoisie', although still relevant, are no longer dominant. New service activities have brought about new agents, new powers and new institutions. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: SPECIAL ADMINISTRATIVE DIVISIONS: SOME INSTITUTIONS OBSOLETE?
abstract: The article is based on a double empirical finding: firstly, special constituencies make the Colombian electoral process in general increasingly difficult to understand for voters and hard to manage for the authorities. Secondly, the results they get do not help indigenous and afrocolombian social movements as they are supposed to do, especially since the political reform of 2003. The paper discusses the reasons for this situation and proposes a debate on it. The author considers that if the mechanisms of positive discrimination are correctly adapted, the indigenous and afrocolombian movements would gain competing in national constituency within the framework of a single party for each one, in which internal differences would be resolved by preferential vote. In this way, if they leave the special constituencies, these minorities could benefit political reform rather than suffer its effects, which is what happens now. This would not only improve their political representations, but also allows them to consolidate as movements towards public opinion. Adapted from the source document.

title: Roesmiddelen en regulering: oude wijn in nieuwe regels?: Inleiding / Intoxicants and regulation: old wine in new rules ?: Introduction
abstract: In contrast with the critical, innovative ideas developed between the 1960s and the 1980s regarding the way we deal with illegal drugs in our societies, the current dominant approaches frame the issue of drugs as a matter of crime, public order, and control. Pleasurable substances have always existed and always will, and so the efforts to cope with them. However, we witness today remarkable developments at local, national and international levels in the fields of drug policies (on cannabis for example), drug trafficking (new routes, new actors) and drug use (new substances, new drug cultures), all of which deserve our attention and push us to think beyond the repressive paradigm. This contribution, which also serves as an introduction for this special issue of ToCC on drugs, aims to present an overview of the main developments taking place, and challenges ahead, within the three above-mentioned fields. There are new markets and trends in the use of legal and illegal pleasurable substances, particularly regarding synthetic drugs (amphetamines, methamphetamines and new psychoactive substances or NPS), tobacco and alcohol. Illegal drugs are supplied from changing countries and through new routes, while retailing increasingly takes place through the so-called cryptomarkets (online). Effective policies are rendered impossible by the fundamental repression paradox: the more intensive and effective the repression, the larger the profits of drug traffickers and the balloon effects (displacement). Despite the harms and negative effects of repressive policies have extensively been documented, a societal debate towards the regulation of illegal drugs is hindered by the use of false dichotomies or presuppositions, by the use of ethical or moral appeals, or by lack of political will. Also the debate in the media is static, superficial and full of cliches. Scientific research on drugs also follows specific agendas and it is focussed on particular aspects of the problem. Changes to end the 'war on drugs', certainly regarding cannabis, are however underway in many places at local and national level (Uruguay, Canada, US, Spain, etc.), this despite UN bureaucracies and international conventions that fiercely resist those changes.

title: Contesting the Bureaucracy: Examining Administrative Appeals
abstract: This article explores citizens' use of administrative hearings to appeal adverse government decisions about their welfare benefits. It draws on interviews with 79 welfare participants and observations of hearings and interviews with administrative law judges in a state in the United States to understand what hearings, and the act of appealing, mean to citizens. I find that beyond individual redress, participants view appealing as an opportunity to expose and repair social injuries and to renegotiate social relationships, social identities and their status as citizens. Their ability to rehabilitate strained social identities and establish their deservingness as citizens is contingent and variable, with hearings sometimes reproducing appellants' powerlessness and other times allowing for a more positive enactment of citizenship and social status. Over time, participants experience an increase in legal consciousness, using the knowledge of the law and bureaucratic practices they glean from hearings to better navigate the welfare bureaucracy. While this transformation of legal consciousness emphasizes individual gains rather than collective or systemic change, it cultivates a culture of complaining, rather than acquiescing, within the welfare bureaucracy. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The End of the Whitehall Model?
abstract: One of the most influential & enduring models of political-bureaucratic relations has been the Whitehall model derived from British practices. Yet the relationship between bureaucrats & politicians in GB, often poorly understood in the past, has changed in recent years to such an extent that the continued existence of the Whitehall model can be doubted. Drawing on published sources & interviews conducted since 1989 with higher (Grade III & above) civil servants & current or former ministers, explored here are how & why the Whitehall model is threatened with extinction. The wider implications of this development for British policy making & for the study of the relations between bureaucrats & politicians are also considered. Adapted from the source document.

title: Power without representation? Socialisme ou Barbarie or the party that no party would be
abstract: This article investigates the role of political parties from a Marxist perspective. More in particular, it looks at the French activist group Socialisme ou Barbarie (founded by Cornelius Castoriadis and Claude Lefort in 1949), which had many characteristics of a political party in statu nascendi yet consciously refused to become one. The group was united around a critique of bureaucracy and, more in general, of all organs claiming to represent the proletariat, such as parties and labour unions. Yet despite its mistrust of the logic of representation, the group's attempts to mobilize the workers inevitably placed it in a role very similar to that of a political party. The difficulties to define the group's role in a different way, and the many disagreements that ensued, eventually led to the group's dissolution. Socialisme ou Barbarie's internal discussions reveal the ambiguous yet inevitable connection between power and representation, and clearly informed Lefort's later ideas on that same topic. Adapted from the source document.

title: POLITICIANS BUREAUCRATS, AND DEVELOPMENT IN INDIA
abstract: India's pol'al development was unique, both in formal preparation & in the qualities of the modernizing elite which was fundamentally alien to Indian society. The separation of alien elite & Indian masses is a historic condition, approaching the quality of a `praetorian society' & setting the context for efforts to create a nat'l development effort. The pol'al system was parliamentary democracy, & by 1957 was representing the effective centers of power in Indian society. Nehru's leadership, the Congress party's policty consensus, & the dominant role of the bur'cy throughout the 1st decade of independence characterized the system. In legislation, response, & recruitment the pol'al system proved flexible, sensitive, & viable. Indian planning continued to have a technical bias because of the relative isolation of the bur'cy both by soc origin & gov'al position. The admin'- ive machinery of the state is relatively weak in comparison to the problems of stimulating development or using high levels of coercion in change, but strong enough to continue to dominate the decision-making process in the central gov. The democratic system of soc change has been more effective in India than the bur'tic system of econ planning. The links between the 2 portions of the pol'al community have been weak & sometimes hostile, limiting development. AA.

title: Street-level bureaucracy and depoliticized North Korean subjectivity in the service provision of Hana Center
abstract: This paper explores how institutional service provision for North Koreans in South Korea contributes to formulating specific kinds of North Korean subjectivity. North Korean matters are still controversial and riddled with various political issues, including the Cold War, ethnic homogeneity, and neoliberal changes. There has been significant critique on over-competition, resource misuse, and inadequate services for this population in South Korea to date. Semi-government resettlement agencies called Hana Centers have attempted to standardize and individualize service provision to North Koreans since 2009 reflecting neoliberal welfare trend in South Korea. In the space where the stated policy and actual practices create gap in-between, the values of practicality and neutrality take precedence in operating the Hana Centers. Bureaucratic practices of Hana Centers on the ground reveal contradictory and divergent operations, featuring street-level bureaucracy and localized governmentality. This paper specifically attends to the depoliticizing and decontextualizing effects that the Hana Centers exert in configuring North Korean subjectivity, with detailed descriptions of bureaucratic operations.

title: THE BUREAUCRACY PROBLEM
abstract: It is pointed out that the federal bur'cy, whose growth & problems were once only the concern of the Right, has now become a major concern of the Left, Center, & almost all points in between. The apparent agreement among polemicists of the Right & Left that there is a bur'cy problem accounts for the fact that nonbur'tic solutions to contemporary problems seem to command support from both groups. Several bur'cy problems are cited: (1) the problem of accountability or control (getting the bur'cy to serve agreed-on nat'l goals); (2) the problem of equity (getting bur'crats to treat like cases alike & on the basis of clear rules, known in advance); (3) the problem of efficiency (maximizing output for a given expenditure); (4) the problem of responsiveness (inducing bur'crats to meet, with alacrity & compassion, those cases which can never be brought under a single nat'l rule & which seem to require that an exception be made or a rule stretched; & (5) the problem of fiscal integrity (properly spending & accounting for public money). It is indicated how each of these problems mobilizes a somewhat diff segment of the public. The more a bur'cy is responsive to its clients, the less it can be accountable to presidential directives. It is stressed that facing the issue means admitting what, in our zeal for new programs, we usually ignore: 'There are inherent limits to what can be accomplished by large hierarchical org's.' Coping with the burley problem is inseparable from rethinking the objectives of the programs in question. E. Weiman.

title: Examining red tape in public and private organizations: A further look at the role of individual perceptions and attributes
abstract: The growing number of studies on red tape over the last several years has led to notable progress in the understanding of red tape. Scott presents an overview of this lineage of research, with particular focus on red tape's subjective/individualistic nature.

title: PROFESSIONALIZATION AND BUREAUCRATIZATION
abstract: Professionalization is a dominant trend among occup's. At the same time the majority of professionals are employed in org's of various types. In order to assess the reciprocal relationship between professional & org'al expectations, a variety of professions are studied in a variety of org'al settings. Professionalization was measured using techniques developed by H. L. Wilensky (see SA 1020/B5278a) as well as several attitude scales. Among the professional att'al attributes touched upon is use of the professional org as a reference, belief in service to the public, belief in self-regulation, sense of calling to the field, & a feeling of autonomy in work. The scales utilize the Likert technique & format. Analyses of structural & att'al aspects of professionalization, & of the org'al settings in which the professions are found, suggest that there is generally an inverse relationship between professionalization & bur'ization, although there is considerable variation within the relationship. The data further suggest that the structural & att'al aspects of professionalization do not necessarily vary together. The org's in which professionals work also differ in their degree of bur'ization. It is suggested that the presence of professionals in an org affects the structure of the org, while at the same time, the org'al structure can affect the professionalization process. AA.

title: MANAGERS AND ENTREPRENEURS: A USEFUL DISTINCTION?
abstract: Study of underdeveloped areas reveals the importance of Schumpeter's concept of 'entrepreneur'. However, in advanced economies bur'tic managers seem to replace entrepreneurs. This essay advances the continued relevance of the distinction; however, it follows Weber rather than Schumpeter. The defining characteristic of entrepreneurship for Schumpeter was innovation, but his discussion was vague. The Weberian concept of formal authority is appealed to instead. The entrepreneur is the source of all formal authority within the org, while the manager's authority is delegated. The manager, however, acquires independent 'functional' authority from his admin'ive competence. Nevertheless, formal authority continues to be the defining factor since it rests on nonrational legitimating foundations: ultimate values, tradition, or charisma. An example is used as a test case in the decision between Schumpeter & Weber: the German entrepreneur, which confirms the Weberian analysis. Another attempt to make the distinction, on the basis of decision-making (entrepreneur makes crucial decisions; manager makes routine decisions) is rejected as not making the distinction sufficiently precise. B. Beck.

title: Feminist Social Service Delivery in India
authors: Kassam, Meenaz; Handy, Femida; Ranade, Shree
abstract: Given the crucial role attributed to women-led NGOs in the social development in India, we examine the organizational structure of such NGOs, the women who lead them, & nature of the social services provided by them. We examine 20 women-led NGOs & find that despite their self-professed feminist ideological leanings, many of them in reality exhibit bureaucratic characteristics -- a finding similar to those found in a study of women-led NGOs in the US (Botch, 1997). We also find that the pragmatic, cultural, & social variables can explain some of theoretical contradictions we find in our data. 3 Tables, 41 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucratic Role Characteristics and Member Affective Response in Organizations
abstract: An examination of the relationships between three bureaucratic role-structure dimensions & affective responses in organizations (including job satisfaction). Contrary to much theory, it is hypothesized that formal structuring of activities has a positive effect on members' satisfaction & perceived climate; consistent with bureaucratic theory, it is hypothesized that both role constraints & rule enforcement have negative effects. Results from a questionnaire sample of 332 members of Ur midwestern work organizations largely support this model. In addition, structural analysis techniques demonstrate no significant group-level effects, suggesting that the influence of bureaucratic structure is mediated largely through individual roles. 3 Tables, 66 References. Modified AA.

title: Children's services in the iron cage of performance management: street-level bureaucracy and the spectre of Svejkism
authors: Wastell, D; White, S; Broadhurst, K; Peckover, S; Pithouse, A
abstract: Recent UK government reforms have introduced a range of measures to regulate practice in child welfare, with professional work increasingly structured into formal processes embedded in information technology. This prompts obvious anxieties about the erosion of professional discretion. Using Lipsky's concept of the street-level bureaucrat, we report on an ethnographical study examining how social workers organise their practice in an atmosphere of performance management. Clear indications of attenuated discretion are revealed, reflecting the shift to a managerial model of control. Of concern is the emergence of a pattern of formally conformant behaviour in which the letter of the organisational law is obeyed but without genuine commitment. Drawing on the anti-hero of Hasek's celebrated satire, we denote this form of passive resistance ' Svejkism '. While showing up the absurdities of excessive managerial power, such behaviours are ultimately dysfunctional for the organisation; an alternative governance paradigm, based on professional values, is briefly outlined.  [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The institutional construction of the Brazilian trade policy: the Foreign Trade Chamber (CAMEX) in the Cardoso government
authors: FERNANDES, Ivan Filipe de Almeida Lopes
abstract: The aim of this paper is to analyze the institutional building process of the Brazilian foreign trade policy during the Cardoso government, focusing on the relationship between institutional change and the political bureaucratic dynamics of the the Executive Branch, evaluating the conditions that make the bureaucratic conflict an important variable in the process of institutional change. Since the foreign trade policy is a broad activity, we have chosen to analyze its coordination framework: the formation and reforms of the Foreign Trade Chamber (CAMEX). At the first part of the study, we developed an analytical framework based on a brief overview of what has been produced about the influence and implications of the involvement of the bureaucracy in the political game, from which we have derived our hypotheses. After, we analyzed the role played by the struggle between the executive agencies involved in the trade policy and what were the Presidency actions about that issue. Finally, we propose that the struggle between the executive agencies was a determining factor of the institutional instability during the Cardoso government and the consolidation of a sub-optimal institutional set, which has difficulty in fulfilling the coordination functions of the Brazilian foreign trade. From the proposition of a new theoretical framework which concatenate different debates about the bureaucratic politics, we derive the central proposition of the research that lies on the expectation of how the interactions between the political and bureaucratic actors within the Executive Branch affect the results of the decision-making processes of institutional change. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucratic Legitimation: Marihuana and the Drug Enforcement Administration
authors: Koski, Patricia R; Eckberg, Douglas Lee
abstract: How organizations use mixtures of "fact" & "value" statements in order to legitimate policy & policy changes is addressed, arguing that the legitimation process does not require intellectual or moral candor or accuracy, but rather consistency. Utilizing the dramatic change in stance toward marijuana policy by agencies of the federal government between 1977 & 1980, the ways in which members of one organization, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), used facts & values to justify a changed stance are examined. The new argument involved two points: (1) moral arguments legitimating federal indifference to marijuana use, & (2) scientific evidence on the adverse health impact of marijuana. Analysis reveals that evidence was treated in the following ways: (A) as "new" & convincing when in fact it was not; (B) evidence indicating the seriousness of marijuana use was emphasized, whereas previously it had not been; (C) evidence was distorted to play up the seriousness of the marijuana problem; & (D) speculation by expert witnesses was employed as evidence. The DEA's statements illustrate the usefulness of paying attention to a fact/value intermix for understanding the process of legitimation. 41 References. Modified HA.

title: BUREAUCRATIC MAN
Risk-Handling on the Shop Floor: Bureaucracy and Craftsmanship
abstract: Two approaches towards safety culture can be distinguished, of which the dominant one focuses on risk handling based on bureaucracy & the other one on craftsmanship. Bureaucratic risk handling pertains to rules & procedures, formal training & education, & enforcement of rule compliance; craftsmanship to discretionary specialization, tacit knowledge & personal responsibility. The purpose of our study was to measure both risk handling strategies with a survey (N = 265) in a Dutch utility company. We show that bureaucratic risk handling can be measured as such, while discretionary specialization, tacit knowledge & personal responsibility can be measured as separate informal risk handling strategies, but can not be brought under the general heading of craftsmanship. Moreover, we demonstrate that while the perceived presence of bureaucratic risk handling decreases unsafe behavior, the perceived presence of the three dimensions of craftsmanship have mixed effects on unsafe behavior. We conclude that we have succeeded in validating the measurement of bureaucratic risk handling & of the three dimensions of craftsmanship and, hence, that we have managed to bring the two strands of safety culture research together. Adapted from the source document.

title: Fragility of the Third World's regimes
abstract: Many third world regimes face difficulties generated by the contemporary world capitalist system and the power position of public bureaucracies.  The regimes' inability to handle serious domestic and international problems are discussed.

title: 'BUREAUCRACY' AND 'RATIONALITY' IN WEBER'S ORGANIZATION THEORY: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY
abstract: 7 of M. Weber's ideal-typical specifications for `rational bur'cy' are reformulated as a system of 3 'bur'tic' & 4 'rational' variables. It is proposed that (a) bur'tic variables are positively associated; (b) rational variables are positively associated; but that (c) rational variables are negatively associated with bur'tic variables. This hypo is supported by a comparative analysis of 150 formal org's in 150 non-industrial societies, using data largely from the Human Relations Area Files. Implications of the findings are explored for: (1) the use of the concept `informal org', & (2) the development of a general org'al model. Such a model is proposed in outline & illustrated from the descriptive industrial sociol'al literature. AA.

title: THE STRUCTURE OF BETRAYAL: TRADE UNION BUREAUCRACY AND PUBLIC SECTOR STRUGGLES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
Centralization or Diffusion? Two Tales of Online Government
abstract: Can the new information & communication technologies (ICTs) such as the Internet change the power relationships within a bureaucracy? The dominant centralization approach argues that the existing power elite manipulates computers to perpetuate & augment its power. Although not a coherent school of thought, other scholars suggest that technology can decentralize bureaucratic structure & diffuse bureaucratic power. The little-known history of the ICT revolution in the Israeli public sector suggests that the same empirical evidence can be woven into two starkly different historical narratives supporting each of these approaches depending on the kinds of questions scholars ask at the onset of their research. 60 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Max Weber and Karl Marx
abstract: It is indicated that in Max Weber's sociol the fate of Western capitalism is equated with that of rationality. Weber correctly saw the connection between bur'cy & capitalism. The technically perfect bur'cy is an outcome of applied rationalism which is hostile to personal liberty. But while Weber rejected rationality as expressed in bur'tic org, he felt that discarding the rational world view would mean the end of the soc system. He saw the salvation in "new prophets" who would become the propagators of a modern rationalism incorporating both personal responsibility & liberty. It was up to K. Marx to solve the problem of the depersonalization of the individual in capitalist society, however, by showing up the soc antagonism underlying impersonal power. He saw elimination of alientation as the way to free the individual. The liberal bourgeois intellectual, it is indicated, with M. Weber sees certain contradictions in capitalist development but cannot go beyond the limits of bourgeois thinking because of his own class position. M. Maxfield.

title: The Consociational State. Hypotheses regarding the Political Structure and the Potential for Democratization of the European Union
abstract: This essay centers attention on the political structure of the European Union (EU) & its potential for democratization. To illuminate the constituent nature & potential for democratization of the EU, a useful theory will be employed that was until now underrepresented in research on European integration, namely consociational theory. Regarding the political structure, it will be argued, the EU is a case of a consociation, albeit not of a democratic consociation. The EU is rather a bureaucratic consociational state with a structural democratic deficit. Whether the democratic deficit of the EU can be ameliorated, & if so, to what extent, will be examined with conceptual tools & hypotheses derived from consociational theory. 1 Table, 72 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Hidden Regulation of Carbon Markets
abstract: This article tracks the creation and maintenance of markets for emission rights and the role that law-creation plays within this process. From a recent example of a market creation - the European Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS) -, insights will be gained about the intrinsic and fundamental connections between market creation and bureaucratization. This process unfolds in a paradoxical way: The free-market hypothesis is, in fact, creating a demand for regulation, administration, and control. Law creation that is informed by the free-market hypothesis (the Law and Economics School in general, the EU Directive as a specific case), separates the 'inside of the market' from the 'outside of the market.' This, firstly, causes a need for extra-administration at the 'outside of the market' in order to resolve the uncertainty that emanates from the self-imposed requirement of leaving 'the market itself' unregulated. And it, secondly, exposes the 'rational actor' to an open and uncertain situation, which then leads to private regulative and administrative attempts at the 'inside of the market.'. Adapted from the source document.

title: Evaluation of China's Bureaucratic Reforms
abstract: Among the various reforms initiated by the post-Mao leadership in China, the most crucial for stability of the political leadership & continuity of the policy line is that of the bureaucracy. In the name of making the state apparatus more efficient for economic development, the central party leaders promoted to leadership positions a new set of cadres who are "revolutionized, better educated, professionally competent, & younger." Evaluated are the results of the reform in three important organs: the Central Committee, the central government ministries, & the provincial Party secretaryship. It is found that although a large number of the bureaucratic technocrats has replaced veteran cadres of the civil war era, the gains are temporary, & the regime's efforts to rationalize & institutionalize personnel management will encounter much more serious obstacles imposed by the structural conditions of the Leninist party-state. 4 Tables. HA.

title: BUREAUCRACY AND THE LOWER CLASS
authors: Sjoberg, Gideon; Brymer, Richard A; Farris, Buford
abstract: The main hypothesis advanced is that bur'tic structures not only encounter major difficulties in coping with the Lc, but also serve to maintain & reinforce patterns that are associated with the `culture of poverty.' These structures are a key medium through which the Mc maintains its advantaged position vis a vis the Lc. The analysis of the effect of the client-centered bur'cy upon the Lc is cast in theoretical terms. However, illustrative materials based on res among Lc Mexican Amer's in San Antonio as well as writings of other scholars provide support for these generalizations. The orientation of the bur'cy towards the Lc as well as the orientation of the Lc toward the bur'tic structure are examined. A discussion of the org'al & pol'al implications of modern bur'tic systems as these bear upon soc stratification is presented in conclusion. AA.

title: Citizenship Lessons from the Past: The Contours of Immigrant Naturalization in the Early 20th Century
abstract: Objectives: What were the determinants and patterns of naturalization in the first two decades of the 20th century? Low levels of citizenship acquisition among contemporary immigrants are frequently contrasted to the assumed rapid naturalization of prior European migrants, but in truth we know little about the earlier period. Historic data are well suited to investigate four explanations for naturalization: individuals' resources and skills; regulatory and bureaucratic barriers to citizenship; relative costs and benefits of citizenship; and the degree of political mobilization directed to immigrants. Methods: I use U.S. Census microfile data to run logistic regression models, and documentary material to examine the contours of immigrant naturalization in the early 20th century. Results: I find that while individual attributes matter, place of residence could be even more important; in 1900, where an immigrant lived influenced naturalization more than birthplace, ability to speak English, or literacy. Residence effects seem linked to a state's relative openness to immigration and local political mobilization. Over time, however, residence effects attenuate as the 1906 Naturalization Act and establishment of a federal naturalization bureaucracy appear to make citizenship patterns more uniform across the country. Conclusions: These findings suggest that historic and contemporary explanations of immigrants' naturalization should focus as much on the context of reception as the presumed quality of immigrants. Tables, Figures, References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Coping with Bureaucracy: Survival Strategies in Irrigated Agriculture
abstract: Although small-scale family farming & centralized bureaucratic management are incompatibile in many ways, the two are often combined in modern irrigation systems. Bureaucrats & farmers cope by means of informal adjustments, which vary according to their differential access to resources, particularly labor. The effects of bureaucratic control & associated informal adjustments are illustrated by reference to three large-scale irrigation systems noteworthy for their high degree of centralization & for their success in achieving high productivity by family farm operators: the Israeli cooperative farming sector, the Gezira scheme in Sudan, & the Mwea scheme in Kenya. 33 References. HA

title: FATALISM IN THAI BUREAUCRATIC DECISION-MAKING
abstract: The Thai admin'or is seen to have a lower sense of selfpotency (perception of the degree to which his competence & actions can affect future events) than his US counterpart. He will typically assign a lower subjective probability to his bein able to influence a given outcome. Lowered self potency is partially seen as arising from the operation of certain suprahuman forces which predispose certain outcomes; this is part of an implicit set of cultural assumptions which the admin'or has learned to use in viewing his larger world. The result is that the perceived probabilities which link choice alternatives to various outcomes become quite unclear & difficult to estimate. The predisposition for outcomes comes from 2 factors which are only partially diff'iated: (a) kam or karma (causative forces arising from the effects of one's past deeds), & (b) something which might be called chance or luck. The interplay of kam & luck, & the uncertainties which attend them, have several effects upon the ways in which admin'ive decisions are implemented. Most pervasive is the tendency to place low reliance on planning in the implementation of decisions once they are made. In lieu of planning, the Thai admin'or comes to rely on a strategy of coping, which utilizes soc manipulation as a means of goal accomplishment. Among the Lc's some admin'ors may engage in a variety of religious or magico-religious observances in order to supplicate & improve their stock of merit or luck. Lastly, the admin'or may ride with the tide of suprehuman forces by divining them & thus take them into account in making his decisions. E. Weiman.

title: The Oral Form in Action Coordination Practices
abstract: Survey data gathered 1996/97 from about 200 employees in local & central services of a branch of France Telecom & observations of six coordination sessions reveal that forms of coordinating action have undergone significant transformations, particularly increased use of the spoken word where once the written word was the norm. It is argued that employee frustration & dissatisfaction with bureaucracy reveals that public service needs to be disassociated from bureaucracy. Whether increased use of the spoken word is indicative of a real transition or marks the beginning of a new organization-centered form of work is considered. 38 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Professional Control through Bureaucratic Routine: A Study in the Selection of Physician Assistant Trainees
