abstract: A field study of Duke U's physician assistant program's admissions interviews shows how the interviews reflect the medical profession's ideology of dominance & authority. Focus is on interviewers' patterns of inquiry, attitudes toward the bureaucratic imperatives of selection, & background assumptions. It is shown that medicine's dominance is as much a matter of trying to get a job done within institutional constraints as it is a matter of self-conscious ideology. The dominance is mundanely institutional rather than conspiratorial. AA.

title: THE COMPENSATION OF EXECUTIVES
abstract: Compensation of business executives has been shown to be primarily a function of the size of the org. Z annual compensation (C) of the highest paid official is=to a constant (k) times annual $ sales (s) taken to a constant exponent (a). The formula on a logarithmic scale is: log C=a log s + k'. David R. Roberts developed the formula & interprets it as a derivative from marginal productivity theory. There is some question that executives' salaries are a function of their marginal contribution to company profits. An alternative sociol'al explanation is that compensation is a function of recruitment (how much incoming personnel have.to be paid), the number of status levels, & the org's 'norm for the. ratio of an executive's salary to the salaries of his immediate subordinates.' This alternative explanation can also be mathematized & seems to be consistent with the data. C. R. Shepherd.

title: THESIS ABOUT BUREAUCRACY AS A PARTICULAR STRATUM IN CONTEMPORARY SOCIETIES
abstract: A short account is given of the development of state officials & employers in a capitalist economy during the past 100 yrs. It is held that 2 categories influenced the evolution of contemporary bur'cy: (a) authority, which in soc life is being affirmed as a sphere of relatively independent decision-making, ie, a sphere of DGDGsoc compulsion,' & (b) a relative emancipation of the members of the decision-making group from their mandates. The focus is on the latter, & examples are given of the emancipation of the state burley from the Re & the monopolistic bur'cy from holders of monopolies. Under state-capitalist conditions, both types fall into a new &, for many contemporary societies, characteristic, soc category-state capitalist bur'cy. For direct producers the econ consequences of these processes are reflected in their constant alienation from the means of production & the products of their labor. This raises the question of the class character of burley. In contrast to the thesis that contemporary bur'cy constitutes the new class of exploiters, the thesis is presented that bur'cy is not an econ-soc group (as SC's are) but a pol'al one, an emanation of the contemporary state. The soc power of the exploiting classes is based on private ownership & the soc power of the contemporary bur'cy on the pol'al functions of its members. Modified HA.

title: Disorganizing China: Counter-Bureaucracy and the Decline of Socialism
abstract: With original research on key variables including social composition of faculty members, authority relations, income distribution, disciplinary actions and life experiences, the book demonstrates that the workplace in Mao's China placed conspicuous stress on political ideology, personal loyalty and coercion.  The communist party-state, "a monolithic power state" (Weber's term) which controls every aspect of political, economic and social life, is by definition incompatible with the rule of law and other basic liberal and democratic values and institutions of the modern world, and hence precludes the possibility of modern bureaucracy based on the dominance of legal, universal and impersonal norms.

title: "Outlawing War", 1919-1930. The Origins of the Definition of the International Political Order
abstract: The many institutional devices designed between the two world wars in order to impose "peace by law" are rejected by most authors as naive expressions of the good intentions of European democracies. To the extent that "the spirit of Geneva" has become a sort of negative myth of international politics, this has impaired research into the conditions in which these sophisticated legal mechanisms came to represent an unprecedented & fundamental model, which still informs our conception of multilateral relations. This article proposes to study how a transnational community of international jurists cultivated & attracted politicians &/or national bureaucracies to this complex machinery in order to insert state interests in this system of objective constraints. Owing to the intensity of the post-war diplomatic negotiations, negotiators managed to establish a set of legal positions relatively autonomous vis-a-vis national authorities. By relying at times on learned arguments, at times on political clout, by acting at the national or international level, they alternated the promotion of an international legal order free from the interference of state sovereignty & a renewed loyalty to their own governments. Thanks to this subtle double game, they imposed their juridical purposes as a central stake of international politics during the interwar period. Adapted from the source document.

title: Social Justice and Men's Interests; The Case of Title IX
authors: Messner, Michael A; Solomon, Nancy M
abstract: Men's superordinate status sets the stage for them to understand their interests as opposed to those of women. But hierarchies among men complicate this. Through an examination of the narratives by critics of Title IX at the U.S. Secretary of Education's 2002 hearings on Title IX, the authors argue that subordinated groups of men within sports (i.e., those in vulnerable "nonrevenue" sports like wrestling, tennis, and gymnastics) tend to articulate their interests as congruent with men in central, privileged sports (football and basketball). But this articulation of men's interests does not take the form of antiwoman backlash. The critics tell stories of individual men who are victimized by the "unintended consequences" of liberal state policies--stories that rest on an essentialist assumption that men are naturally more interested in sports than are women. The critics' language of bureaucratic victimization of individual men--especially as symbolized by the threatened "walk-on"--may find especially fertile ground among young white males, who face a world destabilized by feminism, gay and lesbian liberation, the civil rights movement, and shifts in the economy.

title: COMMENT: ANALYZING THE 2004 HEU STRIKE AND UNION BUREAUCRACY
ANCHORAGE IN ORGANIZATION: A DIALECTICAL THEORY
authors: Grosof, Elliott H; Gross, Llewellyn Z; YERACARIS, CONSTANTINE A; Hobbs, Walter C
abstract: A theory of participant behavior in hospital org's is presented which integrates internal & external cultural influences on such behavior. Emphasis is placed upon the relationship between extra-org'al variables (esp ascribed & achieved statuses) & model types of org'al 'anchorages' in the authority system, the co-worker system & the clientele system. The hypothesis is developed that participants with Ls in society have status deficits which lead to 'authority anchorage' in the org'al system. When org participants are confronted with org authority, the resulting dilemma is resolved in the processes of identification & submission which are at the root of the authority anchorage thesis of org'al stability. Through identification, Ls participants affectively align themselves with representatives of the authority system, creating conditions favorable to mutual respect & approval. The authority system's gain in control is proportionate to the participant's deficit in technical competence. The net effect of the authority anchorage process is the instit'ization of Ls behavior around the authority system at the expense of co-worker & client-concerns: the hospital employs a class of participants who have status deficits, & the process of authority anchorage creates participant stability at the cost (dysfunction) of the primary org'al goal, patient care. Clientele anchorage follows the same dialectic of identification & submission reflected in authority anchorage. The Hs MD seeks fulfillment by personalizing his relationship with the patient. The intermediate status person who floats freely on org'al structure cannot realize himself through either clientele or authority identification. He therefore concentrates on an org'ly based pursuit of status achievement, bereft of the substantive meaning entailed in the cultural ideal which the org expresses. A bur'tic personality type emerges. It is concluded that equilibrium between org'al inducements & participant contributions is relational & constitutive rather than accidental or oppositional. The anchorage thesis aims to approximate a ,reality principle' of large-scale org's without giving priority to either participant needs or org'al demands. It requires continuous empirical scrutiny. Modified HA.

title: The Logical Origins of Social Disembedding
abstract: The formal logic has found out that numeric functions and algorithms have a common root. This means that either the dominant cognitive knowledge (the mathematical representation of the world), or the dominant performative knowledge (the organization of processes according to formal rules) are based on the same logic and on the same culture, which is that of the recursive formalism. Using the recursivity concept, it is possible to understand better the historical and conceptual relationships among phenomena which have marked the transition from the traditional world to the modern word. That allows us -- and this is the goal of this paper -- matching different approaches to the social disembedding problem, typical of modern society. Understanding that calculus (used by both science and capitalism) and algorithms (used by bureaucratic organizations) have worked with a common logic makes possible to overcome the apparent contrast between the recent concept of "disembedding" as a result of "time-space distanciation", and the classic ideas of "alienation", "atomization", etc., tied to the formalization of the "work-discipline". At the same time, studying these concepts with the same analysis grid -- freeing them from different models of interpretation -- allow us to compare them on the bases of their common characteristics and different peculiarities. Adapted from the source document.

title: BEYOND BUREAUCRACY
abstract: It is asserted that the dominant type of org, bur'cy, is hopelessly out of joint with contemporary realities, such that new models of org currently recessive but emerging, will soon overshadow them in modernized societies. These changes can be summarized under the idea of modernization & include such factors as the rate of sci'fic change & technological change, the separation of property from power, & a shift in the value-systems toward democratic -humanitarian-sci'fic values. Bur'cy has been esp vulnerable to these changes on 2 accounts: reciprocity, or the balance between individual needs & org'al goals & adaptation, or how the enterprise manages rapid change springing from the external environment. Due to these problems, new forms of org's must & are replacing more traditional bur'tic structures. They can be seen most vividly in those co's which reflect a sci'fic basis. These new org's are called organio-adaptive & are primarily problem-solving groups of specialists from diverse disciplines who come together for short periods of time, who are on the boundary system of their clients, & who dissolve when the problem is solved. These organic-adaptive systems rely heavily on imagination & fantasy & do not require the surplus repression so necessary to harness the muscle power of the 19th cent, so they allow more freedom & more opportunity for motivation to be based on an intrinsic basis. AA.

title: Becoming Less Illegal: Deservingness Frames and Undocumented Migrant Incorporation
abstract: Over the last two decades, research on unauthorized migration has departed from the equation of migrant illegality with absolute exclusion, emphasizing that formal exclusion typically results in subordinate inclusion. Irregular migrants integrate through informal support networks, the underground economy, and political activities. But they also incorporate into formal institutions, through policy divergence between levels of government, bureaucratic sabotage, or fraud. The incorporation of undocumented migrants involves not so much invisibility as camouflage - presenting the paradox that camouflage improves with integration. As it reaches the formal level of claims and procedures, legalization brings up the issue of the frames through which legal deservingness is asserted. Looking at the moral economy embedded in claims and programs, we examine a series of frame tensions: between universal and particular claims to legal status, between legalization based on vulnerability and that based on civic performance, between economic and cultural deservingness, and between the policy level and individual subjectivity. We show that restrictionist governments face a dilemma when their constructions of "good citizenship" threaten to extend to "deserving" undocumented migrants. Hence, they may simultaneously emphasize deservingness frames while limiting irregular migrants' opportunities to deserve, effectively making deservingness both a civic obligation and a civic privilege.[PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Disciplinary Society: From Weber to Foucault
abstract: Max Weber's analysis of bureaucracy is framed in terms of the legal & rational accounting requirements of political & economic organizations. These, in turn, furnish legal domination with its aura of administrative rationality & adequacy. The formal analytic features of bureaucratic discipline are drawn from Weber's studies of the army, church, U, & political party, as well as from the organization of the discovering social sciences. Michel Foucault's studies of the hospital, prison, & school, in addition to accounts of the factory system by Karl Marx & recent social historians, ground Weberian formal analysis in the history of various social techniques for the administration of corporeal, attitudinal, & behavioral discipline, ie, the disciplinary society. Foucault's studies, however controversial, may be seen to extend Weber's concept of rational-legal discipline through studies of the discursive practices that construct a physiology of power/knowledge that deserves the attention of social scientists. 51 References. HA

title: Writing on the Margins from the Center: Homeless Youth + Politics at the Borders
authors: Tierney, William G; Hallett, Ronald E
abstract: Research with homeless youth requires negotiating with Institutional Review Boards (IRB), school districts, and social service agencies. Youth that are homeless live a life different from the researcher, thus issues of trust and caring need to be considered before asking a vulnerable young person to share his or her story. The authors share insight learned from a qualitative study of the educational barriers of homeless youth that highlight these issues. The overarching finding is that homeless youth are invisible and silenced in a social service system overwhelmed with red tape and bureaucratic procedures. The authors suggest that program developers, researchers, and policymakers give voice to homeless youth by listening to the stories they tell and then enacting policies that build on their recommendations.

title: Bureaucrat, Heal Thyself! Lessons from Three Administrative Reforms
abstract: Discusses three major government reforms in the twentieth-century US that are potential models for South Korea & other developing countries: the New Deal of the 1930s, which created new organizations to carry out added government functions; the Hoover Report of the 1940s, which strengthened central authority; & the National Performance Review of the 1990s, aimed at enhancing the efficiency of government agencies. By disaggregating their principal elements, it is possible to discover patterns applicable elsewhere. The concept of public annoyance as a motivating factor for reform is described, & some lessons gleaned from the three reforms are offered for the US & other countries. 40 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Family Physician: A New Role In Process Of Development
abstract: Family physicians, the most recently recognized specialists in American medicine, are in the enigmatic situation of developing the occupational role which they simultaneously occupy. In 1969 the Council on Medical Education of the American Medical Association (AMA) formally approved family medicine as the 20th specialty. Both prior to and since this date the emergence of this new discipline has been heavily rooted in reforms to correct deficits in contemporary practices of patient care. Family physicians are dedicated to providing continuing, comprehensive, primary care to families. This approach is viewed as a corrective for the fragmented, episodic, highly bureaucratic, and technocratic care many patients now receive. Interwoven with family physicians' reform efforts are their concerns with establishing a firm position of status, influence, and academic respectability within the institutional structure of medicine. These two issues -- reform and family medicine's position within medicine -- have influenced and most likely will continue to influence the process of development of this new role.For a complete reprint of this article contact Haworth Press by telephone (1-800-HAWORTH) or EMail (getinfo@haworthpressinc.com). Copies are available from: Haworth Document Delivery Center, The Haworth Press, Inc., 10 Alice Street, Binghamton, NY 13904-1580. Article copyright The Haworth Press, Inc.

title: The Interpenetration of Communicative Contexts: Examples for Medical Encounters
abstract: Two senses of context, as it involves conversational interaction in a bureaucratic environment, are discussed. This use of the term context includes an institutionalized framing of activities or ways that group-derived prescriptive norms pressure &/or channel people with designated titles, presumed competencies, duties or responsibilities into certain physical spaces at certain times in order to engage in a finite number of specifiable activities. Within this institutionalized context or framing of activities, emergent processes of talk appear that create a more narrow view of context in the sense of locally organized & negotiated interaction. A conversation among three MDs in a U medical center is used to underscore the importance of context at different levels of analysis. The analyst's decision to focus on particular sociolinguistic notions rather than the interrelationship between discourse & broader & narrow senses of social structure will frame different expectations for the reader & different substantive conclusions on the part of the researcher. 10 References. Modified HA

title: Bureaucracy and Growth: A Cross-National Analysis of the Effects of "Weberian" State Structures on Economic Growth
abstract: The role of bureaucratic authority structures in facilitating economic growth has been a sociological concern since Max Weber's classic contributions. Here, based on the evaluations of 126 experts, the characteristics of core state economic agencies & the growth records of a sample of 35 developing countries, 1970-1990, are examined. A "Weberianness Scale" is utilized that offers a simple measure of the degree to which these agencies employ meritocratic recruitment & offer predictable, rewarding long-term careers. Analysis shows that these Weberian characteristics significantly enhance prospects for economic growth, even when controlling for initial levels of gross domestic product per capita & human capital. Results imply that "Weberianness" should be included as a factor in general models of economic growth, & suggest the need for more attention by policymakers to building better bureaucracies & more research by social scientists on variations in how state bureaucracies are organized. 3 Tables, 3 Figures, 3 Appendixes, 60 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Legal Change on Non-Profit and For-Profit Organizations: The Case of the Israeli Long-Term Care Insurance Law
abstract: This article evaluates the impact of legal change on nonprofit & for-profit organizations providing home care services mandated in the Israeli Long-Term Care Insurance Law, through the lens of neo-institutional & resource dependency theories. The findings of the study, which was conducted over a 10-year period, revealed that the distinctions between organizations in the two sectors are blurring due to coercive, mimetic, & normative isomorphism. Considerable dependence on government funding provided for in the law forces these organizations to adopt behavior that conforms to government policies & standards for service provision. Moreover, the growing tendency toward mimetic behavior & the increasing proportion of professional workers in both sectors causes for-profit & nonprofit organizations to adopt similar bureaucratic behavior & organizational structures. 5 Tables, 54 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Reflections on a Half-Century of Organizational Sociology
abstract: For the past half-century, the study of organizations has been an active area within sociology. I provide an overview of the emergence of this specialty during the second half of the twentieth century, its relation to the larger field of organization studies, & the important theoretical advances associated with the adoption of an open system framework during the 1960s. Among the recent trends I describe are changes in our conceptions of organization boundaries, strategies, & controls, & the beginning of a shift from an entity-based to a process-based view of organization. Evidence of success -- the number of sociologists now employed in professional schools -- simultaneously raises concerns about the source of future organizational sociologists. 120 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Predicting and Understanding Organization Structure
abstract: Whether size can predict org structure was tested via data from a British sample of 82 business org's, stratified in terms of 6 industries & number of employees. Data from British labor unions, engineering firms, & the "Aston sample of varied work org's" (res carried out by Derek Pugh, Malcolm Warner, & Lex Donaldson at the Industr Admin Res Unit, U of Aston, Birmingham, England) were also used. Where possible, comparisons were made with the results of a US study (Peter M. Blau & Richard A. Schoenherr, see SA 19:7/71F2317). While org size does allow for predicting fairly reliably the broad outlines of formal org'al structures, a comparison of size-structure regressions across diff industries suggests that other variables must also be taken into account. A theoretically & statistically more satisfying solution emerges when complexity is distinguished from other aspects of structure which more directly constitute the framework of bur'tic control--ie, the degree of formalization & decentralization. It is then found that while size predicts complexity (using technology, location & environmental variables), the degree of complexity, itself, is more directly related to formalization than to size. Size, however, remains the major predictor of decentralization. It is concluded that, in the org's studied, complexity cannot be satisfactorily predicted or fully understood without reference to the econ's of scale, but that it is neither theoretically convincing nor statistically demonstrable that size in itself is the major determinant of formalization. 4 Figures, 9 Tables. Modified HA.

title: Bureaucratic Insurgency: The Vatican and the Crisis of Modernism
authors: Lyng, Stephen G; Kurtz, Lester R
abstract: Mayer N. Zald's & Michael A. Berger's model of "bureaucratic insurgency" (see SA 26:4 78J5014) is assessed in light of data of the "modernist movement" in the Roman Catholic Church. A historical case study of this movement produces evidence that generally supports the model, but that also indicates the need for some important modifications. In particular, it is shown that the Zald & Berger propositions are appropriate only to the later stages of the modernist movement. The earlier stages of the movement's development appear to have been governed by an entirely different dynamic, a process whereby the conflict between organizational authorities & bureaucratic insurgents paradoxically produced resources for both groups. In an effort to organize these findings theoretically, several propositional frameworks are reviewed that deal with the paradoxical, ironic aspects of authority/insurgent interaction. Finally, these different perspectives are synthesized into a single "dialectal" model that can be appended to the Zald & Berger model. 83 References. HA.

title: The Presidency and Policy Studies
abstract: Studies of presidential policy making have generally focused on the bureaucratic structures from which policy emerges. Only Steven Shull's Presidential Policy Making: An Analysis (Brunswick, Ohio: King's Court Communications, 1979) has analyzed presidential policy with regard to the boundaries of the policy process itself. Shull's framework allows for analysis of substance & process, & is used in a review of policy-related research on the presidency. Substantive research issues are basically divided between those concerned with domestic & those concerned with foreign & defense policies. Presidential policy is seen to have been increasingly influenced in recent years by international economic problems at an aggregate level. Policy processes fall within two main theoretical frameworks -- the pluralistic politics model, & the bureaucratic politics model. Organizational analyses of the presidency are also reviewed. D. Dunseath.

title: System Size and Ruling Elites
abstract: A baseline model is developed to show that, when other variables are held constant, G. Mosca's proposition on the relationship between the relative size of ruling elites & the sizes of the systems they govern follows from the definitions of the variables. The model provides a baseline against which empirical trends may be assessed. The implications of this model for the much studied relationship between admin'ive ratios & org'al size are discussed. While the model cannot be applied to this relation on a purely definitional basis, it can be applied in conjunction with R. Michels' prediction of minority rule. If Michels' prediction holds (POLITICAL PARTIES, New York, NY: Free Press, 1962) the observed results from most studies can be deduced from the baseline model. Michels' expectation is sufficient to account for the general nature of the relationship between the relative size of the admin'ive component & org'al size. Some specific models are illustrated to indicate the effects of observing various maximum relative sizes of admin'ive components. Modified HA.

title: Can the Government Regulate Itself?
abstract: A discussion of the extent to which one government agency can modify the behavior of another, noting that "in general, it is easier for a public agency to change the behavior of a private organization than of another public agency." Several government agencies & their activities are cited as examples of existing constraints on achieving badly-needed changes. Affirmative-action employment policies are offered as the clearest example of the weakness of intragovernmental controls. Organizational autonomy exists, as does mutual independence, among government agencies. With regard to the problem of bureaucracy, everyone agrees about the undesirability of "excessive government regulation." However, equally important is the growing problem of the "inefficacy of government regulation caused by the shift of functions from the private to the public sector." J. Shiffer.

title: Pantouflage in France [1880-1980]
abstract: The movement of upper-level bureaucrats into the private sector (pantouflage) has been developing in France for about a century. Secondary data from various sources are synthesized to show how this phenomenon first appeared in the stratum of bureaucrats with technical capabilities, then in the main body of bureaucrats, due to political purges, & finally, among high-level army officers. In each group, reasons for pantouflage differed, depending on economic & administrative conjunctures, as well as the age & social extraction of resigning bureaucrats. At a deeper level, this phenomenon is a sign of the dysfunctionality of the French administration, especially during the Third Republic, but also of the lack of channels to provide special training to upper-level officials in economic sectors who were partly siphoned off from the public sector. The effects of this brain drain, however, were not entirely negative; in the long run, it led to administrative reform & contributed to the indirect democratization of recruitment in business circles. In addition, economic power's domination over administrative power was increased, even when social differentiation of recruitment of these two types of elites was accentuated. Modified HA

title: Efficiency of Bureaucracy assessed by Russians
abstract: Traces Russians' attitude toward the efficiency of the state bureaucracy. States that the majority of respondents, especially those who have dealt with bureaucrats, consider bureaucratic efforts inefficient. Informs that not even positive economic developments can change stereotypical attitudes toward bureaucrats. Explains the origins of the stereotype of the bureaucrat. Examines three ways suggested by respondents to improve the efficiency of bureaucrats. Concludes that respondents consider the president to be most capable of controlling the bureaucracy. Figures. K. Duft

title: Intelligentsia as Mythological Phenomenon. A Sociological and Historical Review
abstract: Looks at intelligentsia as a phenomenon pertaining to the realm of social mythology. Discussing various aspects of myth (its aims, functions, & basic significance), the myth of the intelligentsia is analyzed in these terms. Its emergence in Russia is linked to political development, ie, to the making of the bureaucratic apparatus. Following this, author turns to 18th-century events shaped by a transition from corporate representative monarchy to the absolutist one, to Peter the Great reforms. A review of intelligentsia evaluations as they had taken shape on the brink of 19th & 20th centuries permit the author to point at essential feature of this group as a kind of counter-bureaucracy opposing the existing political regime & attempting to displace it. Disappearance of the intelligentsia & eventual prospects for its re-emergence are considered. 22 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Roots of Officialese
abstract: The underlying reasons for the specialized lang used in government documents & its undesirable effects are discussed. It is suggested that "officialese" can be traced to: (1) its function as a linguistic marker of membership in a privileged group; (2) writers' intellectual laziness; & (3) its ability to obscure meaning. P. Farrell

title: Organizational Characteristics of Agencies and the Distribution of Services to Applicants
authors: Greenley, James R; Kirk, Stuart A
abstract: This paper develops hyp's regarding the impact of select org'al factors on the distribution of service among applicants to health or welfare agencies. It is hyp'ed that agencies with more control over exchange with their environments, ie, more "boundary control," will under conditions of surplus applicants choose to serve smaller & more homogeneous applicant pop's. Also, applicants will tend through referral & rejection processes to flow from agencies with high boundary control to agencies with low boundary control. The extensiveness of agency domains is hyp'ed to be directly related to both size of the applicant pop's & the number of applicants serviced. Finally, the size of "domain discrepancy" is seen as directly related to the proportion of applicants rejected & referred. This framework has important implications for the study of client careers, the soc construction of public & personal identities, & for program planning. Further, res bases on the diagnosed problems of clients may overlook the extent to which findings are shaped by org'al characteristics of the agencies rather than by the problems of the applicants. The necessity to relate other org'al characteristics to referral & rejection patterns is thus stressed. Modified HA.

title: Organizations, internal labor market policies, and gender inequality in workplace supervisory authority
abstract: It is often assumed that bureaucratic labor policies associated with internal labor markets (ILMs) promote the efficient use of workers' skills and foster equality in the workplace by publicizing managers' decisions and increasing the accountability they face.  These assumptions about ILM policies are tested with regard to gender inequality in workplace supervisory authority.

title: The politics of ethnic representation in Philippine bureaucracy
abstract: The good governance argument for diversity in civil service is based on the notion that creating a bureaucracy that represents the diverse communities it serves strengthens government accountability and legitimacy. This paper argues that ethnic representation in national bureaucratic governance in the Philippines primarily constitutes a means for political reallocation of space, as it is embedded in the government's framework of asymmetric political autonomy. Mired in intersecting political and ethnic tensions (i.e. blurred ethnic distinctions/ethnic identity disputes and politico-ethnic conflicts), patrimonial forces could easily exploit the country's bureaucratic representation policies as spaces for patronage and as superficial tokens to mollify interethnic factions of their share of the national polity. Thus, instead of facilitating equitable voice in bureaucratic governance, such policy framework could only hold ordinary indigenous and minority ethnic communities captive in the elite-dominated interethnic struggle for representation.

title: Scripting Dissent: US Abortion Laws, State Power, and the Politics of Scripted Speech
abstract: Abortion laws offer a point of entry for "the state" to intervene in intimate clinical matters. In this article, I explore the various uses of scripts and scripting in state-mandated abortion counseling following the implementation of North Carolina's (2011) Woman's "Right to Know" Act. The law mandates that women receive counseling with specific, state-prescribed information at least 24 hours prior to an abortion. Drawing on interviews with abortion providers in North Carolina, I analyze how the meaning of scripting shifts across different clinical and bureaucratic contexts and show that abortion providers perceived themselves to be scripted by "the state" even though their words were not explicitly chosen by lawmakers. Thus, rather than viewing the law merely as a product of North Carolina legislative activity, I argue that abortion providers also help to create the law, and its social and moral power, by interpreting and enacting it. However, abortion providers also revealed creative strategies for "scripting dissent" from the law--that is, rejecting, challenging, or otherwise subverting the state's ideological message. This demonstrates that the linguistic force of the script stretches beyond its textual meaning to encompass the way it is performed within a particular context and how it is sometimes used for unexpected ends. [abortion, reproduction, biopolitics, the state, law, medicine, United States]RESUMENLas leyes sobre el aborto ofrecen un punto de entrada para la intervención del "Estado" en temas clínicos de la intimidad. En este artículo exploro los varios usos de las guías y escritura de las mismas en el asesoramiento mandado por el Estado para los casos de aborto siguiendo la implementación de la Ley "del Derecho a Saber" de la Mujer (2011) en Carolina del Norte. La ley determina que las mujeres reciban asesoramiento con información especifica, prescrita por el Estado al menos 24 horas antes del aborto. Basada en entrevistas con los que practican abortos en Carolina del Norte, analizo cómo el significado de la escritura de las guías varía a través de los diferentes contextos clínicos y burocráticos y muestro que los que practican abortos se perciben así mismos como instruidos por "el Estado" aunque sus palabras no fueron explícitamente seleccionadas por los legisladores. Por consiguiente, en vez de mirar la ley meramente como un producto de la actividad legislativa de Carolina del Norte, argumento que los que practican abortos también ayudan a crear la ley, y su poder social y moral, al interpretarla y promulgarla. Sin embargo, los que practican abortos también revelaron estrategias creativas para el "disentimiento en la escritura de las guías" de la ley--esto es, rechazando, retando o de otra manera subvirtiendo el mensaje ideológico del Estado. Esto demuestra que la fuerza linguística de las guías se extiende más allá de sus significados textuales para incluir la manera en que son representadas dentro un contexto particular y cómo son algunas veces usadas para fines imprevistos. [aborto, reproducción, biopolítica, el Estado, ley, medicina, Estados Unidos]

title: Recent Soviet Contributions on the Theme of Bureaucracy
abstract: A review of Soviet literature on this topic reveals that the problems engendered by Soviet bureaucracy are more a function of the economic & social conditions of that country than of some pathology of the administration itself. It is suggested that bureaucracy results from the stagnation that sometimes follows social or political crises, & that the worsening of conditions in the USSR since the revolution has simultaneously seen an increase in bureaucracy & a decrease in human values. 11 References. L. Baker

title: Knowledge, Practice, and Political Community: The Making of the "Custom" in Turkey
abstract: This article begins with the observation that the honor crime (the murder of a woman by her family because of actual or deemed sexual acts that are considered an offense to the culturally defined terms of family honor) has received increasing attention in Turkey during the last decade. Although Turkish feminists have long worked to raise awareness of the gendered inequality and violence involved, their efforts until recently were met with stark silence. The increased attention given to honor crimes involves little interest in the patriarchal excesses that affect women across class and ethnic groups in Turkey, tending to focus attention, rather, on an essentialized "Kurdish" or "Eastern" culture as the main dynamic behind honor crimes. Blame for the practice is attributed to the intractable customs of backward peoples, customs that are disconnected from discussions of capitalism, state bureaucracy, armed conflict, or familial practice prevalent in Turkey's public sphere. Drawing on extensive archival research and fieldwork, the author argues that the recent focus on the "custom" is symptomatic of a shift from a developmentalist/assimilationist to a cultural/racial imaginary. By looking at the intricate web of practices, meanings, institutions, and policies that make up the Turkish public sphere, this article sheds light on how the custom came to be recognized in Turkey and how familial modes of conduct influence current modes of governing minorities. Adapted from the source document.

title: RU 486 and abortion practices in Europe): From legalization to access
abstract: RU 486 has been heralded as "the gentle abortion" by its supporters and vilified by opponents as "the pill of death." It has been available for a decade to women in France, Britain, and Sweden, and to women in nine other European Union countries since 1999. We explore the impact of this controversial technology on abortion rates and practices in Europe, looking first at the EU region as a whole, then examining more closely the politics of RU 486 in France and Germany. We find no evidence that access to medical abortion with RU 486 has increased abortion rates in Europe. We do find large national differences in the use of medical versus surgical abortions. These abortion practices are shaped by economic incentives, the organization of medical services, bureaucratic accounting rules, and physicians' choices. We conclude that effective implementation, with governmental support, has a critical impact on access to medical abortion services.

title: Chinese Diaspora Entrepreneurship, Development, and the World Capitalist System
abstract: Diaspora 6:2 1997 Chinese Diaspora Entrepreneurship, Development, and the World Capitalist System Paul Bolt United States Air Force Academy1 The Chinese Diaspora and Mainland China: An Emerging Economic Synergy. Constance Lever-Tracy, David Ip, and Noel Tracy. London: Macmillan Press; New York: St. Martin’s Press, 1996. In the summer of 1997, two issues involving diaspora Chinese captured headlines across the United States. The first was the return of Hong Kong to Chinese control after more than a century of British rule; coverage of this issue focused not only on the future of human rights in Hong Kong, but also on the close economic linkages between Hong Kong and China and on the importance of Hong Kong to China’s economic future. The second was the scandal involving alleged illegal contributions of foreign funds to the Democratic and Republican parties in the United States. Senate hearings in the cases of both parties centered on political contributions funneled through wealthy diaspora Chinese entrepreneurs. Republicans tried especially hard to demonstrate that China had orchestrated an attempt to illegally influence the US political system, using diaspora Chinese as intermediaries. To the consternation of a great many Chinese living in the United States, the proceedings raised questions regarding the loyalty of diaspora Chinese and their connections with China, as well as reviving stereotypes of shadowy and mysterious connections among ethnic Chinese.2 In this climate of increased interest in the Chinese diaspora, Constance Lever-Tracy, David Ip, and Noel Tracy provide a timely analysis of the economic links between mainland China and the Chinese diaspora, as well as of the effects of such links on China’s economy. Focusing on transnational (as opposed to interstate) relations between entrepreneurs, the authors take a multidisciplinary approach to the topic, attempting to overcome the barriers that divide the academic disciplines as traditionally conceived. Nevertheless, the study is not all-encompassing and the work tends to focus on an issue that might be defined as the “sociology of transnational diaspora business,” with an effort to tie the findings to theories of political economy.3 xxxxxxxxxxxx 215 Diaspora 6:2 1997 The three authors address three main themes in this work (16). First, they attempt to demonstrate that Chinese diaspora capitalism has unique attributes that have a profound effect on world capitalism . This unique category of capitalism is defined largely by transnational linkages among diaspora Chinese that are used extensively in business. Second, the authors describe the important role that the Chinese diaspora has played in China’s recent development, as well as the role that economic opportunities in China have had in forwarding the economic interests of diaspora capitalists. Third, the book addresses the question of economic scale, especially as it relates to issues of development and success in the current world capitalist environment. Here, the authors argue that large corporate size is no longer necessary to compete in the global economy, and probably is a liability. The primary conclusion of the work, which ties together all three of the above themes, is that “the linkages established between diaspora capital and entrepreneurship and the booming economies of the towns and villages of the coastal provinces along China’s east coast are the key to China’s economic miracle and the continuing success of the economic reform process in China” (x). The key contribution of Chinese Diaspora is its illustration of the way in which diaspora capitalists have contributed to China’s development. This point is often ignored or downplayed in analyses of China’s economic growth. In terms of investment and export generation, the impact of diaspora capitalists has been tremendous: they have contributed over three-quarters of foreign investment in China. However, as the authors make clear, diaspora entrepreneurs have also had an impact on China’s economic development through their modeling of successful management and marketing techniques . Thus the diaspora has contributed to both the “hardware” and the “software” of China’s economic development. Much more controversial are the authors’ assertions that the success of Chinese diaspora enterprises brings the future of large, bureaucratic multinational corporations (MNCs)4 into question. Certainly the Chinese diaspora has led the way in investing in China, but generalizing from...

title: Mises versus Weber on Bureaucracy and Sociological Method
abstract: Compares & assesses the work of Max Weber & Ludwig von Mises on bureaucracy through a study of their distinctive methodological starting points & their analyses. Weber & Mises were two intellectuals who valued each other's work, & they each studied bureaucracy as a theoretical construct as well as a part of society's structural & cultural organization. The author assesses the scientific utility of Mises's & Weber's views of bureaucracy & argues that Mises's emphasis on human action, rather than Weber's reliance on integrative conceptualization, better describes the origins of bureaucracy & provides a superior conceptual/methodologial & ethical assessment of its dangers. The author concludes that people choose bureaucracy due to fear of cooperation & competition & the uncertainty associated with risk. Those who value freedom & recognize the benefits achieved under the market system can confront bureaucracy. This study gives a better understanding of Weber's & Mises's strengths & weaknesses in sociological theory & of the proper foundation for a social science based on human action. 55 References. L. A. Hoffman

title: A Kafkaesque state: deportation and detention in South Africa
abstract: Deportation practices are commonly described through the lens of a "state of exception", a condition where government assumes extra-judicial and near absolute authority over its subjects. Yet, within the contemporary deportation regime, we find examples of state fragmentation and resistance. Individual officials take decision-making power into their own hands, and deportable populations reassert control over their movement and their lives. Hence, deportation is not a "bare" form of politics, but a rich and contested realm, in which officials and deportees struggle for power and freedom. This article attempts to define and describe the unique character of this realm of politics in South Africa's particularly prolific and harsh deportation system. Drawing on a wide array of survey, interview and ethnographic material, we explore both the inner workings of South Africa's deportation bureaucracy and deportees' narrative and emotive responses to detention conditions. To make sense of this material, the article draws on the unique description of state power and authority in Franz Kafka's classic The Trial. For Kafka, the power of officials in a state of exception stems from an ability to prolong administrative procedures, while individuals seek to retain their capacity to imagine and chart a broader migration story. We show that many anomalies and informal practices in the South African deportation system can be understood as part of this Kafkesque struggle. Adapted from the source document.

title: Three Traditions? Marxism and the USSR
abstract: The tidy-but misleading-classifications of critical-Marxist writing about the USSR are interrogated in a historical narrative that traces Marxist scholarship on the USSR throughout the twentieth century. Review of the dismissal of Trotsky during the 1920's by recent scholarship delineates his contradictory definition of capitalism, the tension between the Bolshevik's & the social democrats, & Urbahn, Zinoviev, & Carter's views of the bureaucratic counter revolution. The claim of a state-capitalist USSR during the 1930's & 1940's is identified in the political classification of political substance, & Cliff's "virtues". The late 1940's refutation of Cliff's analysis traces the development of the "state-capitalist" or "bureaucratic-collectivist" class identified by Haynes, Burnham, & Laurat, Hilferding & Schactman. The picture that critical Marxism portrayed of the USSR in the 1960's that characterizes the orthodox Trotskyist "degenerated workers state" was developed further by Deutscher, Bensaid, Ticktin's, tied to a deformed and degenerated worker's state-ism, & the post Chinese Cultural Revolution revival of the dichotomous state-capitalist/bureaucratic collectivism debate. Neither the "convergence" of the USSR back to Western capitalism seen in the 1920's "state-capitalist" theories, nor the "convergence" of the advanced capitalism's towards USSR-type "statism" of the 1930's & 1940's happened. Rather, capitalism is concluded to have followed a trajectory different from Western Europe, & it was that other trajectory that provided the grid for the Stalinist USSR. References. J. Harwell

title: Patron-Client Relations in Thailand
abstract: This paper examines the nature of patron-client relations in Thailand, both formal & informal, with particular reference to the Thai bur'cy & to its relations with other groups in society. The focus of the discussion is on the role of power & relative status disparities in determining the content of patron-client relations. Various psychol'al, cultural & historical theories about the development of patron-client relations are discussed, & the existence of reciprocal, contractual relations between superiors & subordinates in Thailand posited by many scholars is questioned. It is found that the content of patron-client relations varies considerably with the relative disparity in status between the superior & the subordinate. Most writing of the subject has failed to take this sufficiently into account. Patron-client relations may involve in varying ways & to varying degrees such factors as love & loyalty, psychol'al satisfaction, personal self-interest, rights & obligations, shared benefits, compliance with cultural norms, power & coercion. Modified HA.

title: The State of Bureaucracy: Public Opinion about the Performance of Government Agencies in Israel
abstract: Vigoda-Gadot and Yuval offer an attitudinal-behavioral platform for the measurement of public sector government agency performance, a format that is based on a recent two-year survey of Israeli citizens.

title: Accountable and Countable: Information Management Systems and the Bureaucratization of Social Work
authors: Burton, Judith; van den Broek, Diane
abstract: Summary A key feature of new public management is the tendency to equate quality and accountability with documentation (Tsui and Cheung, 2004). Human service organizations increasingly rely on computer databases to compile and record client information and to demonstrate outcomes for quality assurance and accountability purposes. This has resulted in substantial changes in work practices, processes and relationships for social workers. This paper draws on interview data from social workers in several Australian agencies to examine professional interactions with, and response to, changes in their work after the introduction of new technologies. It particularly focuses on the shift of accountabilities from professional values and identities to organizational and bureaucratic accountabilities. The paper recognizes that while social workers have always been subject to organizational accountabilities, due to the changes in social service delivery and limited practitioner input into the implementation of new technologies, tensions between professional and bureaucratic accountabilities have intensified. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Influence of Social Context on Partnerships in Canadian Health Systems
authors: Scott, Catherine M; Thurston, Wilfreda E
abstract: Partnerships, collaboration, joined-up government; these terms have become common elements of global health & social policy discourse. The terms may be pervasive but there remain significant challenges to collaborative ways of working. We argue that some of these challenges arise from a failure to account explicitly for the influence of social context. Between 1999 & 2001 we conducted a comparative case study of partnerships in Canadian health systems in which we examined specifically the roles of social context & gender. Social structures directly linked to formalized health systems are embedded in social institutions based on patriarchal & bureaucratic practices that do not traditionally support the relational practices required for the development of partnerships. While individuals within such organizations may have the knowledge, skills & commitment to collaborate, in such an environment, tremendous resource expenditures are required to achieve & maintain collaborative advantage. 1 Table, 99 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Nationalism, Bureaucracy and the Developmental State: The South African Case
abstract: This article undertakes a concrete analysis of the workings of the post-apartheid South African state bureaucracy, within the state hospitals and provincial health departments, in an effort to understand the reasons for its poor functioning. The research points to a contradictory set of rationales shaping the workings of the bureaucracy, which may be ascribed to the tensions identified within the nationalist project by Partha Chatterjee. The article discusses six key features of the post-apartheid bureaucracy: class formation, ambivalence towards skill, the importance of 'face', hierarchy, ambivalence towards authority, and budgetary rituals. It argues that these constitute a set of informal rationales shaped by the imperative to undo racism and white domination in the state and in the society more broadly, and that they tend to work against and erode the Weberian rationales for a meritocratic and effective state bureaucracy. There is a tension at the heart of the nationalist project, between the aspiration to construct a 'modern' state and the drive to assert African sovereignty through dismantling white domination. There is little chance of establishing a developmental state (for which the hallmark is effective bureaucracy) in South Africa unless nationalism can be reshaped to define meeting the needs of the people as the central strategy for overcoming the legacy of apartheid. Adapted from the source document.

title: Barrier to Technical Innovation
abstract: The reason why excellent planning & superior leadership at the highest echelons of US gov are not necessarily translated into action at the operational level is seen to lie in the enormous number of admin'ive agencies & their discontinuities. The fact that innovation must be widely accepted if it is to become part of the normal org'al process is noted. Such acceptance depends on individual att's & behavior. These in turn depend not only on personality but role structure, & one way in which they can be modified is by shifting an actor from one role to another. This would mean giving civil service personnel an opportunity to work in the federal service & letting federal personnel serve with state & local systems for a while. This would facilitate the transfer of new ideas from one system to another, & aid the various levels of gov in understanding each other's problems. Any such program must, however, be accompanied by comparable efforts at the city level. Local community control is bound to be ineffective unless greater receptivity to change is inculcated into the personnel who man the bur'cy. A citizen group is limited in its perspective & can, no less than the bur'cy, become stagnant. Thus public agencies must transfer information to their clientele as well as to their superiors. M. Maxfield.

title: Social and Spatial Politics in the Construction of Regent Street
abstract: London's Regent Street, constructed in the 1810s and 1820s, was at the center of the large-scale metropolitan improvements carried out by the Crown in the pre-Victorian era. But while the boulevard and its creative genius, John Nash, have been alternately celebrated and reviled, scholars have paid little attention to the actual building of the street and the fate of those whose property was compulsorily acquired by the Crown. This essay looks at the struggle between the Crown and its bureaucrats and the mostly plebeian residents of the neighborhoods around Swallow Street, Piccadilly, and St. James's Market and examines how these Londoners thought about the relationship between space and status, about the political and social--as well as financial--value of property, and about the nature of London's spaces. The Crown believed in the abstract, exchangeable, and easily valued character of its freehold property. But dispossessed tenants and leaseholders insisted that the valuation of their neighborhoods--carried out by bureaucrats, architects, solicitors, and in some cases, Westminster juries--also take into account the customary use of London's streets, markets and alleys, and the inherent value that everyday use gave these spaces. Although Nash succeeded in building his boulevard, the great and unanticipated cost of the project suggests that inhabitants' promotion of local knowledge and local geographies was not merely subversive but was given credence (and assigned material value) over and against the rational and bureaucratic vision of John Nash and Crown bureaucrats.  [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Child abuse and the bureaucratisation of social work
abstract: After child abuse became a public issue in the early 1970s, the way public inquiries and government departments framed the problem of and produced the solutions to child abuse was legalistic and bureaucratic.  The development of social services in handling cases of child abuse is detailed.

title: The Development and Trials of a Decision-Making Model: An Evaluation
authors: Peters, Michael; Marshall, James; Shaw, Robert
abstract: A description of an evaluation undertaken on contract for the New Zealand State Services Commission of a major project (the Administrative Decision-Making Skills Project) designed to produce a model of administrative decision making & an associated teaching/learning package for use by government officers. A philosophical model of decision making & the associated teaching/learning package in the setting of the New Zealand public service, where a deliberate attempt has been initiated to improve the quality of decision making, especially in relation to moral factors, are evaluated. 1 Figure, 2 Appendixes, 17 References. HA

title: Theories on the Bureaucracy and Bureaucratic Organization
abstract: Bur'cy, due to a series of ocon, sociol'al. pol'al & ideological causes, & at the same time both objective & subjective, is an important & general fact of contemporary society. At the center of the problems posed by the theory of bur'cy is a sociopol'al notion, one which does not exclude the need for a sci'ific analysis of other notions relevant to the general conceptualization of bur'cy, & this concept is that of bureaucratism. The postulates of Marx, Engels, & their followers, constitutes the only basis necessary for a general theory of bur'cy as well as explaining bur'cy & bureaucratism in socialist societies. It is worth noting that the works of Western theoreticians include material of value in the theoretical study of this socio-pol'al phenomenon. (Tr by J. A. Broussard from IPSA).

title: Fascist Era Elites (3). Salazar's ministerial elite, 1933-44
abstract: This article analyses the composition and modes of recruitment of Salazar's ministerial elite during the 'fascist era'. The main characteristics of the Estado Novo's governing elite was that it belonged to a small and exclusive political and bureaucratic class that almost completely dominated the senior ranks of the armed forces, the senior administration, and the universities - within which the legal profession was strongly represented. Salazar's single party, being kept organizationally weak and dependent, was never an important element in either the political decision-making process or in the selection of the ministerial elite. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Nationalization and Denationalization: The Case of Eccentric Religious Groups
abstract: The relationships between three religious groups -- the Jehovah's Witnesses, the Montreal Hassidim, & the Catholic Pentecostalists -- & the nationalist processes of Canada & Quebec are analyzed in an ideal-typical model. The goal is to show how state & church bureaucracies are legitimated & then to focus on the denationalization processes of dissident religious movements, their peripheral status with established institutions of church & state, & their rejection of nationalist ideologies. 52 References. Modified HA.

title: Challenging Beliefs and Bureaucracies in an Urban School System
abstract: Urban school districts face substantial challenges in developing conflict resolution, mediation, & violence prevention programs. Observations of the implementation of different conflict resolution programs over 5 years in a mid-sized urban school district revealed that while programs were visible & supported, implementation was haphazard. As a result of this experience, 5 critical factors are identified for conflict resultion programs: development of a shared understanding of language & definitions; consensus on realistic, desired behavioral outcomes; assessment of underlying beliefs driving the school system; recognition of extreme differences within school culture; & provision for sufficient human & financial resources. The strengths & weaknesses of 4 types of conflict resolution/violence prevention approaches are assessed: school-based student skill development, school-based development of prosocial school cultures & peaceable classrooms, school-based violence prevention/intervention, & school- & community-based violence prevention/intervention. It is recommended that time be allowed for ongoing assessment of programs. 1 Table. M. Pflum

title: Bureaucracy and Constitution
abstract: A speech made in Apr 1992 at a conference of the Society of Government Management in Chicago, IL. To understand the functions & limitation of government bureaucracy, one must first understand the constitutional framework within which it must operate. The founding fathers of the US designed a government structure of checks & balances to prevent the abuse of power & tyranny by the majority. They did not foresee that these checks & balances could make it difficult for the executive & legislative branches to agree, delaying action on pressing issues. Intrinsic problems with US-style presidential systems are reviewed. To a large extent, the US has avoided difficulties encountered by other presidentialist regimes because the civil service bureaucracy is not as strongly entrenched. Contrasts are drawn between the US, the UK, & Latin American bureaucracies. Special attention is given to professionalism & superprofessionalism. To preserve the US presidential system will require a high level of professionalization among the bureaucracy. 22 References. M. Meeks

title: Weber and His Concept of Possible Democracy
abstract: The article is a reconstruction of Max Weber's theory of democracy. First, it specifies his notion of democracy. Later, he reconstructs the bureaucracy-politics conflict, which properly articulates politics & democratic themes in the German sociologist's thought. Subsequently it tackles some ideas Weber maintains about State, parliament, & parties as eminently political institutions, & it emphasizes their relation with democracy. The dissertation finishes analyzing the public servant as a leader -- mass relation as opposed to a parliamentary function. The resume evaluates the extents & restrictions of Weber's reflections to think about democracy today. References.

title: Feeling like a State: Design Guidelines and the Legibility of 'Urban Experience' in Singapore
abstract: This article examines how 'urban experience' is objectified and transformed into something that is legible to the state and its experts. It conceptualizes design guidelines as a political technology where bodies of expert knowledge, emplaced in a planning bureaucracy, shape the way the built environment is produced and experienced. Using Singapore as an example of a centralized planning bureaucracy, I analyze how lighting, public art and advertisement signs are targeted to produce a total environment with normative narratives. This article makes two contributions. First, it unpacks the processes that translate different modes of legibility in an attempt to make 'experience' legible for planners. The political efficacy of guidelines and pre-established bureaucratic boundaries means that planners can only intervene through a series of combinations, mediations and approximations. Thus, legibility proceeds in a way that is akin to 'feeling around'. Second, it foregrounds the 'middle layer of urban governance' that is often ignored in the discipline. Guidelines represent one coordinate in a system of political technologies that is concerned with producing the norm, that substrate of urban production mechanized through a series of repetitions, gradations and classifications. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Modernity and Totalitarianism
abstract: Zygmunt Bauman's (1989) assertion that the Holocaust was engendered by the bureaucratic rationality of the Germans is challenged, arguing that his interpretation of the linkage between modernity & the Holocaust is based on a distorted understanding of totalitarianism. Further, Bauman is charged with identifying modernity in relation to an instrumental rationality. Bauman's spurious understanding of modernity is connected to Max Horkheimer & Theodor Adorno's (1972 translation) text that associates modernity with totalitarianism & Herbert Marcuse's (1960) treatment of the combat between dialectical & positivistic forms of reason in the modern world. Identified are seven essential characteristics of modernity, including universalized rights of citizens & capitalist rationalization. The search for an autonomous civil society is held responsible for the development of modern civilization & its defining characteristic -- the normalization of perpetual change. The conception of the modern city as promulgated by the Bolshevik Revolution is perceived as a response to Western culture. It is concluded that totalitarianism is the product of a form of anticapitalist domination rather than of instrumental rationality. J. W. Parker

title: Citizen Demands and Urban Services: The Distribution of Bureaucratic Response in Chicago and Houston
abstract: Citizen contacts with public authorities are a major form of political participation in US cities. Examined is whether public officials view their control over responsiveness to citizen grievances as a political resource that can be used to reward & punish, or whether responsiveness is accomplished according to routinized procedures institutionalized in a set of bureaucratic decision rules. Responses to citizen complaints in Chicago, Ill (N = 781), & Houston, Tex (N = 497), are compared. Although the contacting process is more political in Chicago than in Houston, service outcomes are structured in a similar fashion in the two cities. Variations in responsiveness can best be understood in terms of the administrative procedures developed by individual bureaucrats to process citizen demands & the level of resources required to resolve the service grievance. 5 Tables, 16 References. Modified HA.

title: Choreographing Justice: Administrative Law Judges and the Management of Welfare Disputes
authors: Lens, Vicki; Augsberger, Astraea; Hughes, Andrea; Wu, Tina
abstract: A significant form of civil justice is administrative hearings, used to resolve individual disputes in the provision of government welfare benefits. Drawing from ethnographic observations, analysis of recorded transcripts of the hearings, and interviews with administrative law judges in the United States, we examine two contrasting approaches to judging, one a 'bureaucratic' approach which replicates the style of decision-making on the front lines, and the other an 'adjudicatory' approach which relies on the norms and conventions of judicial decision making. To understand how each approach manifests in the hearing room, we use the methodology of conversation analysis to compare and contrast the different verbal strategies and techniques that characterize each approach. To understand why a judge may choose one approach over another we explore how judges construct their professional identity and manage the tasks of judging. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: INNOVATION IN BUREAUCRATIC INSTITUTIONS
abstract: In the framework of a review article of S. M. Eisenstadt (ESSAYS ON COMPARATIVE INSTITUTIONS, New York, Wiley, 1965) & on the basis of data from Eisenstadt's work, a classificatory scheme is developed for the purpose of measuring & comparing degrees of innovative tendencies in bur'cies with differing pol'al orientations. Innovation is defined as change in an org which requires the development of performance programs not previously part of the org's repertory. The various purposes of innovation in org's are classified as innovation concerning ends, means, power distribution, & heuristic processes. Degrees of innovation in these 4 categories present in 4 types of bur'tic systems suggested by Eisenstadt are then compared & evaluated. Of the 4 bur'tic systems examined with the aid of the classificatory scheme, those in which the bur'cy's service goals are displaced in favor of aggrandizement of bur'tic power show the highest rate of innovative activity, while those in which the bur'cy is a passive tool of the rulers exhibit the lowest rate. IPSA.

title: Comment Analyzing The 2004 HEU Strike And Union Bureaucracy
abstract: The article is a commentary that both discusses and addresses significant issues for the Canadian working-class movement and the 2004 strike of British Columbia's Hospital Union (HEU). Though sympathetic the author states the study compiled in 2006 suggests the need for militant organization; critiques the defeat of the strike; and elaborates further into contemporary Canadian trade unionism deserving discussion. The article also looks into Chris Hurls article The Structure of Betrayal: Trade Union Bureaucracy and Public Sector Struggles in British Columbia; delving into the critique, as the author correlates themes in both articles, particularly focusing on social relation patterns. Then the article conceptualizes the HEUs Strike; and tries to bring some understanding to into bureaucratic trade unionism. In the concluding paragraphs, the author opines on union social structuring and hierarchy, as well as other viewpoints on Hurls statements. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucracy Transcended? New Patterns of Employment Regulation and Labour Control in the International Automotive Industry
abstract: Contemporary changes in patterns of work and management are alleged to have given rise to the post-modern organisation and the diminishing importance of traditional bureaucracy. This paper is concerned with the changing nature of labour control in new 'multi-enterprise' settings in the international automotive sector. Rather than eliminating bureaucracy, the tools of industrial bureaucracy are becoming more sophisticated. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Clinical Gains for Youth in Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facilities: Results from a State-Wide Performance Information System
authors: Kapp, Steve; Rand, April; Damman, Jeri L
abstract: This article presents findings on clinical gains for youth in psychiatric residential treatment facilities (PRTF) through the use of state-wide performance management information. Data was collected on 1,258 youth admitted to one of seventeen PRTF facilities in a single, mid-western state. Results suggest that youth made positive clinical changes during treatment. Furthermore, results indicate that parent and youth hopefulness and satisfaction were significant predictors of positive clinical changes in problem severity and youth functioning. These findings contribute to current literature on PRTF effectiveness in achieving positive youth outcomes and the role of consumer attitudinal factors in treatment.

title: Nazi Germany and the Karaites in 1938-1944: between racial theory and Realpolitik
abstract: This article explores the policies of Nazi Germany towards the Karaites, a group of Jewish ancestry which emerged during the seventh to the ninth centuries CE, when its followers rejected the mainstream Jewish interpretation of Tanakh. Karaite communities flourished in Persia, Turkey, Egypt, Crimea, and Lithuania. From 1938 to 1944, the Nazi bureaucracy and scholarship examined the question of whether the Karaites were of Jewish origin, practiced Judaism and had to be treated as Jews. Because of its proximity to Judenpolitik and later to the Muslim factor, the subject got drawn into the world of Nazi grand policy and became the instrument of internecine power struggles between various agencies in Berlin. The Muslim factor in this context is construed as German cultivation of a special relationship with the Muslim world with an eye to political dividends in the Middle East and elsewhere. Nazi views of the Karaites' racial origin and religion played a major role in their policy towards the group. However, as the tides of the war turned against the Germans, various Nazi agencies demonstrated growing flexibility either to re-tailor the Karaites' racial credentials or to entirely gloss over them in the name of "national interests," i.e. a euphemism used to disguise Nazi Germany's overtures to the Muslim world. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Recognition of Qualification: An Obstacle Race
abstract: Various studies have progressively shown that many immigrants coming to Italy are highly qualified in terms of professional skills. In the meantime it is more evident the mismatch between qualifications & insertion in the labor market. This article focuses on the issue of non-recognition of foreign educational credentials in Italy, describing, through the survey data, the various difficulties immigrants meet in their attempts: bureaucracy (both in Italy & in their countries of origin), lack of proper information & shortage of money & time to invest in order to collect all necessary documents. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucratic Corruption in Nigeria: A General and Sociological Insight into the Problem
authors: Aluko, M A O; Adesopo, A A
abstract: Corruption is incipient in all human societies & in most human activities. The increasing wave of widespread corruption in Nigerian bureaucracies should therefore be of concern to all. This concern derives from the fact that bureaucracies are expected to be avenues through which socioeconomic policies & developmental efforts could be enhanced & sustained. The paper focused on the problem from sociological & general perspectives. The origin, causes, & manifestations of bureaucratic corruption were identified & discussed. The literature revealed that the problem is largely traceable to breakdown in societal values & constraints rather than to individual dispositions. The paper therefore suggested some categorical imperatives for alleviating the problem. This includes the implementation of radical changes in the value system, making the socioeconomic conditions of the nation more favorable to the working & governing classes, erring bureaucrats should be made to face the law to serve as a deterrence to others, the establishment of an Anti-Corruption Bureau, a reduction in bureaucratic protocols & procedures, &, finally, the establishment of a National Ethics Commission was suggested to reorient the people. The paper concluded that bureaucratic corruption is not desirable, &, as such, must be dealt with squarely & head-on at all fronts. Apart from everything else, it could undermine the basis of order, progress, & development in a country. 24 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: BUREAUCRACY AND ECONOMIC REFORM: THE EXPERIENCE OF CALIFORNIA, 1899-1911
abstract: The civil service in Amer has played a most important role in the accomplishment of reform at various stages in the history of the US. Esp during the Progressive Era, while the glare of newspaper & magazine publicity focused on the activities of pol'al reformers, bureaucrats at all levels of gov exerted a powerful, if quiet & unobtrusive influence in the renovation of an antiquated admin've structure. California during the yrs 1899-1911 provides a good case study of this experience for here, as elsewhere, civil servants had accomplished a whole range of reform measures in the decade before 1911, when the Progressive governor, Hiram Johnson, assumed office & made the claim to initiating much needed change. AA- IPSA.

title: Faith, Politics, and Power: The Politics of Faith-Based Initiatives
abstract: [...] ambiguous legislation allows politicians to benefit from 'faith' without the controversy that would come with greater public funding of religious groups" [95].  Sager focuses on state liaisons who have the job of implementing policies and working with faith-based organizations despite a dearth of funding and staff.  Because of this, they typically rely on network ties.

title: Polity and Economy in Suharto's Indonesia
abstract: Analyzes the political economy of Indonesia's New Order, which has ruled since 1966, & weighs the future prospects of President Suharto's regime. The New Order's political structure is described as a pyramid with Suharto at the top, followed by the army, the civilian bureaucracy, & then everyone else. The civilian bureaucracy is heavily penetrated by the military, & all towns have military command posts to enforce internal security. Indonesia's political economy is characterized by three key traits: extensive state ownership & regulation, state revenue that is largely independent of the domestic economy, & a pattern of private entrepreneurship based on political connections. Suharto's longevity is attributed partly to the political skills & ability to balance repression & responsiveness. His continued success & a constant investment climate are considered likely. 11 References. E. Blackwell

title: Institutionalism or Bureaucracy in American Society
