abstract: In spite of the fundamental division between capitalist & Wc's, US society has become institutionalized or bureaucratized in the course of its evolution. Each of the groups which make up the bur'cy has manifested a tendency toward independence; it is the state bur'cy, much less numerous than the econ cur'cy, which has gone furthest in this direction. In the domain of essential foreign & domestic problems, this bur'tic structure has not imposed its views & methods upon the society. It has on the contrary manifested a tendency toward compromise with soc movements on the econ & soc welfare levels. Experience has demonstrated that the functioning of as complex a soc & econ system as the US one cannot be guaranteed by the defending of the independence of the bureaucrats. (Tr by J. A. Broussard from IPSA).

title: Biofuels in Brazil: debates and impacts
abstract: This article presents an analysis of the two major components of Brazil's biofuels initiatives -- ethanol from sugarcane and biodiesel from a variety of raw material sources. With the crisis unleashed at the end of 2008, huge question marks hang over the timetable and the scope of future investments in the sector. Even prior to the current crisis the biofuels debate was suffering a sharp volte-face with earlier euphoria being replaced by sustained critiques from NGOs, social movements, influential representatives of the techno-bureaucracy, and global agrifood firms. As a result governments are currently reviewing their policies, further exacerbating the uncertainties surrounding biofuels. Brazil is already assuming a protagonist role in the promotion of biofuels and its biofuels programs occupy a central place both in global debates on this issue and in the eventual emergence of global biofuels markets. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Unequal Burdens of Repatriation: A Gendered View of the Transnational Migration of Mongolia's Kazakh Population
abstract: Beginning in 1992, the newly independent government of Kazakhstan has facilitated the in-migration of 944,000 Kazakhs from neighboring countries, with the majority migrating as family units. Using the post-Soviet repatriation of Kazakhs as an example, we illustrate in this article how socially constituted notions about gender and kinship help reinforce institutional and informal power structures that favor men at three different points in the migration process: in making the decision to migrate, in dealing with the bureaucratic aspects of migration, and in facing the consequences of migration. First, patriarchal power dynamics often mean that women have less influence than men on the decision to migrate. Second, the legal framework for repatriation is based on an implicit assumption that Kazakh households correspond to a patriarchal model, and this has financial consequences for women. Third, transnational migration widens the physical separations from natal kin that women already experience due to Kazakh kinship practices that emphasize patrilineal descent, clan-based exogamy, and patrilocal marriage.

title: New Deal, Old Deck: Business and the Origins of Social Security, 1920-1935
abstract: The Social Security Act (now widely considered a monument to antibusiness policy and bureaucratic excess) was shaped by profound sectoral and regional imbalances in the industrial economy, by the regulatory efforts of competitive industries in the 1920s and, as "the state" intervened at various levels, by the asymmetry between the economic and political foci of regulation.

title: Judges between Bureaucracy and the Political Role. The Judiciary's Outlook Redefined
abstract: An examination of the role played by judges, based on A. Panebianco's comments on the political role of bureaucracies in Manuale di scienze della politica ([Manual of Political Science] Bologna: Il Mulino, 1986). An exploration of the meaning of "bureaucracy" & "policy making" in recent literature suggests that judges' policy-making activity is a political process aimed not only at the distribution but also at the acknowledgement of values, interests, & expectations. If bureaucracy refers to government by officials, then this political model can coincide with the administrative one; otherwise, the administrative model is an instrument of the political one. The administrative model is more open than the political one to structural change, but at the same time ensures role stability. Modified HA

title: The Bureaucracy and Ruling Authority
abstract: English translation (C) 2008 M. E. Sharpe, Inc., from the Russian text (C) 2006 the author. "Biurokratiia i vlast'," Sotsiologicheskie issledovaniia, 2006, no. 3, pp. 9-15.

title: Women and Social Work Bureaucracy
authors: York, Reginald O; Henley, H Carl
abstract: The literature on the subject of women & bureaucracy offers two contrasting viewpoints: one suggests that women find a bureaucratic form of organization more agreeable than men; the other suggests the opposite. In a mail questionnaire survey of social workers in NC, Rs were asked whether they believed their organizations had too much or too little of each of 5 features of the bureaucratic model. Analysis of 109 usable responses (approximately 67% from Fs) supports the conclusion that men & women do not differ on the level of their satisfaction with bureaucracy. 3 Tables, 14 References. Modified HA

title: Why Do Public Bureaucracies Follow Legal Rules?
abstract: An attempt to corroborate theoretically the following hypothesis: public bureaucracies are by nature law-abiding; they follow the prescriptions of the legal system in their activities. This hypothesis, elaborated by Max Weber, has been neglected in the past. A Marxist methodology is applied to determine factors underlying norm compliance in public bureaucracies. Focus is limited to the experiences of socialist public bureaucracies, especially Hungarian public administration. The drive toward political efficiency creates a state bureaucracy in which the requirement of regular work output reinforces the formally rational framework of intra- & interorganizational social relations. The content of activities in organizations may, however, be irrational. Formal rationality implies law observance because the internal structure of public bureaucracies enables them to operate only on the assumption that there is some external goal to be attained in accordance with definite regulations. State agencies operate in accordance with laws due to the economic structure within which the organization operates. Internal organizational needs & the socialization of the officials also contribute to law observance in public bureaucracies. Modified AA.

title: Linking Passive and Active Representation by Gender: The Case of Child Support Agencies
authors: Wilkins, Vicky M; Keiser, Lael R
abstract: Does it matter whether political institutions are representative in terms of the characteristics of the people who work there? We explore this question by empirically examining whether passive representation leads to active representation in child support-enforcement bureaucracies for women. Our findings support the hypothesis that passive representation leads to active representation for women in gendered policy areas like child support. Furthermore, the link between passive & active representation only exists when the distributional consequences of the policy directly benefit women as a class. Tables, References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Reinvention of Development Planning in China, 1993-2012
abstract: In studies of China's economic rise and political system, multiyear comprehensive and sectoral plans issued by the national government tend to be played down as futile efforts at reigning in a political economy increasingly driven by market incentives and decentralized decisions. Contrary to this, we provide evidence that China's planning system has been transformed alongside the economic transition, yet remains central to almost all domains of public policy making and the political institutions that have fostered China's high-speed growth and economic stability. The incorporation of experimental programs into macro-plans, a tiered hierarchy of policy oversight, newly introduced mid-course plan evaluations, and systematic top-level policy review have allowed Chinese planners to play a central role in economic policy making without succumbing to the rigidity traps that debased traditional planned economies. By better understanding how the planning cycle influences incentives and resources of successive layers of bureaucracies and jurisdictions, and how it updates itself and adapts to new challenges, it is possible to explain a greater proportion of the Chinese policy-making process, including many of its successes and pathologies. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright holder.]

title: Public Choice in Melanesia: Community, Bureaucracy and the Market in Land Management
abstract: The relationship between & functions of bureaucracy, market, & community are examined in the small island states of the South Pacific. The three categories are related analytically in terms of the idea of "public goods," & were historically introduced via the establishment of colonial states in the previously stateless socities of Melanesia. Examples are drawn from land management practices in the now independent Melanesian states of Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Fiji, & Vanuatu. Land policy making in Melanesia in the 1970s mainly addressed the relationship between bureaucracy & community. In the 1980s, the government has been more concerned with the relationship between bureaucracy & the market, representing a "public choice" approach to administrative theory. 3 Tables, 47 References. Modified HA

title: EXPECTATIONS CONCERNING POWER IN A BUREAUCRATIC ARENA
abstract: Admin've sci has developed a new interest in the enlistment of creative intelligence by org's, as well as in the achievement of commitment & conformity of officials. One such problem is consensus within work groups & program units about power relations. This problem is esp serious when functional rationality is required of them. Difficulties associated with various forms of consensus & dissensus are discussed. Empirical materials are derived from a study of a Gov agency handling res org's. 200 employees of the agency were interviewed. These were organized into program units, each comprising experts in some category of res. In addition, there were general admin've units. Data on actual work contacts were used to derive actual work groups. These work groups corresponded closely to the program units. Each S was asked to name the 5 most powerful officials in the agency. Consensus within the units was measured by the % of all choices by members of officials receiving a majority of the units choices. Consensus was found to correlate highly (Kendall's tau) with (1) high consultation between group supervisor & members, (2) loose org without great contact among members on a routine basis, (3) outside contacts by individual members, (4) joint decision-making in the group about program, (5) joint decision-making in the group on assigning responsibility, (6) freedom & autonomy, (7) satisfaction with efficacy of agency's system of communication, (8) satisfaction with general agency performance, & (9) demands by members for changes in top management methods. In general, consensus was associated with high substantial rationality. B. Beck.

title: Interdependence and Hierarchy in Organizations
abstract: The large size of org's appears to promote structural diff'iation & to stem the expansion of the admin'ive apparatus, so that the indirect effect of size, mediated by diff'iation accompanying it, counteracts its direct effect on admin. These conclusions are based on 6 sets of quantitative data on gov bur's, private firms, U's & Coll's, & hosp's. 2 basic theoretical hyp's can explain the findings. 1st, diff'iation of functions among interdependent subgroupings transforms a work org's employees, who have little in common, into a coherent soc enterprise &, in addition, has instrumental advantages for operations that make manag interested in furthering such diff'iation. 2nd, the initial investments in admin'ive time & effort required for organizing operations reduce the proportion of admin'ive man hours needed as the volume of operations increases. A refinement of the last principle is that a large volume of homogeneous tasks has the opposite effect. In conclusion, the theory is put into deductive form. In doing so, explications & refinements of the theoretical propositions are ignored, & so are definitions & purely tautological statements. 9 theoretical assumptions or axioms are used to deduce 7 theorems or empirical propositions. Modified HA.

title: OPTIMIZING RESEARCH OPPORTUNITIES: A METHODOLOGICAL NOTE ON THE COMPARATIVE STUDY OF BUREAUCRACY
authors: LaPorte, R Jr; Petras, J F
abstract: An examination of 5 public agencies to illustrate the influence of the factors of timing & pol'al environment on data collection. The agencies include the Damodar Valley Corp (India), the Nat'l Office of Agrarian Reform (Peru), the Instil of Agrarian Development & the Agrarian Reform Corp (Chile) & the Agency for Internat'l Development (US). Data collection is related to the operational histories of the agencies examined. Each case reveals diff's re the availability of reports & documents as well as access to agency personnel for interviews. Time periods which coincide with unfavorable or adverse pol'al conditions for agency survival tend to be the most advantageous ones for data collection. An agency whose budget has been severly cut, has suffered a decline in pol'al support, & has an unstable personnel cadre would be in a prime period for analysis. The concept of optimal time periods for admin'ive analysis is useful in maximizing res opportunities & in providing information on the interplay between pol'al & admin'ive variables. IPSA.

title: Innovation in Professional Organizations
authors: Delbecq, Andre L; Pierce, Jon L
abstract: To determine whether innovation correlates of bureaucratic organizations apply to medical organizations, 30 multispecialty fee-for-service medical groups from a midwestern state were studied by interview & questionnaire in 1975. Modal group practical size was 15 MDs. Innovation is seen in 4 phases: informal discussion, formal proposal, adoption, & implementation. Innovation was assessed by asking Rs to rate their organization's innovation phase with respect to 87 identified medical innovations. Structural, attitudinal, & affective response correlates were measured. Results indicated that formal hierarchical decision making & affective responses were significantly related to various stages in the innovation process. Participation by all MDs in strategic decisions was negatively related to each phase in the innovation process. By contrast, organization size, complexity, formalization, & person specialization were not related to innovation activity. It is speculated that minimal bureaucratization may be necessary to move the innovation process in differentiated professional groups. 3 Tables. Modified HA.

title: THE FRENCH BUREAUCRACY AND ITS STUDENTS: TOWARD THE DESANCTIFICATION OF THE STATE
abstract: Despite the importance they have ascribed to it, French pol pol'al sci'ts have not considered the state bur'cy an attractive subject for study. Only recently have a number of studies appeared that aim to deviate from the juridical approach hitherto dominant in the study of public admin. Unfortunately, most of these studies contribute little that is new & are often cast within a juridical framework. This is esp the case in a work like the TRAITE DE SCIENCE ADMINISTRATIVE (Paris, France: Mouton, 1966). Also, most of these studies manifest an unmistakable ideological conservatism. The authors of these studies continue to believe, either implicitly or explicitly, in the futility of the empirical approach to the study of public admin. It is a recent work of some French sociol'ts that appears to point to a new direction. The sociol'ts of org's see admin'ive instit's as dynamic & operating within a set of power relations. They also view instit's as functioning within a specifiable context rather than in a void. IPSA.

title: Worthy widows, welfare cheats: Proper womanhood in expert needs talk about single mothers in the United States, 1900 to 1988
abstract: Brush analyzes expert needs talk in case vignettes published in the US in which experts turn single mothers into "file persons," the basic unit of bureaucratic welfare management.

title: The impact of the Holocaust
abstract: The Holocaust has become a cultural code for the deadly combination of ideology with the technology, modernism, bureaucracy and expertise to implement evil.  Future prevention of genocide depends on careful analysis and on comparisons that are not hastily drawn.

title: The Effect of Competition on Some Dimensions of Organizational Structure
abstract: The effect of the competitiveness of an org's environment on org'al structure is examined for 38 small mfg firms. Competitiveness is hyp'ed to increase the demand for control & coordination within the org. Consistent with this hyp, the extent of competition in the environment is positively associated with the f of reporting, the extent to which decision procedures are specified in advance & weakly associated with a relatively taller org'al structure. Evidence is also presented indicating that the competitiveness of an org's environment interacts with production technology, the number of products, & the extent of product design & production process change in determining org'al structure. Change in product design & production process, & the number of products are associated with decentralization, less formalization, & more dept's only in the less competitive environmental contexts. HA.

title: Governments vs States: decoding dual governance in the developing world
abstract: This article begins by questioning the transferability of Western conceptualisations of the 'state' to the developing world, particularly to those areas in which security concerns are extreme. It proposes that the complicated relationship between security and political liberalisation produces a reform - security dilemma, which in turn may result in dual-governance structures consisting of an autonomous 'state' bureaucracy and a relatively newer, political 'government'. The dynamics of such a duality are explored through a longitudinal comparison of two critical cases: Iran and Turkey. Both cases reveal evidence of the 'state' and 'government' as distinct bodies, emerging over time in response to conflicting pressures for security and liberalisation. While the Iranian case remains entrenched in a static duality with an advantaged 'state', the Turkish case provides optimism that, under certain conditions, an eventual subordination of the state to the political government can take place. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Who Gets the Daddy Bonus?; Organizational Hegemonic Masculinity and the Impact of Fatherhood on Earnings
authors: Hodges, Melissa J; Budig, Michelle J
abstract: Using the 1979-2006 waves of the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, we investigate how the earnings bonus for fatherhood varies by characteristics associated with hegemonic masculinity in the American workplace: heterosexual marital status, professional/managerial status, educational attainment, skill demands of jobs, and race/ethnicity. We find the earnings bonus for fatherhood persists after controlling for an array of differences, including human capital, labor supply, family structure, and wives' employment status. Moreover, consistent with predictions from the theory of hegemonic masculinity within bureaucratic organizations, the fatherhood bonus is significantly larger for men with other markers of workplace hegemonic masculinity. Men who are white, married, in households with a traditional gender division of labor, college graduates, professional/managerial workers and whose jobs emphasize cognitive skills and deemphasize physical strength receive the largest fatherhood earnings bonuses.

title: The gendered bureaucracy: Agency mission, equality of opportunity, and representative bureaucracies
abstract: The implementation of equal opportunity policies across governmental bureaucracies has not uniformaly advanced the interests of men, women and minorities therein. This paper examines this common occurrence of the unequal outcomes associated with equal opportunity policies.

title: Culminations of Complexity: Cultural Dynamics in Norwegian Local Government
abstract: Political discourse in the Norwegian welfare state is characterized by the ambition to establish & secure universal welfare. In comparative terms, it has been quite successful in translating utopian goals to practical politics. The modernization of Norway, more so than most other western countries, has nourished a shared sense of politics as a collective activity & as the privileged tool for the realization of humanistic goals. The article attempts to show how this presumably salient element of Norwegian political culture developed as a part of the extraordinary continuity, characterizing both economic growth & the strengthening of a sense of political community, transcending the divisive effects of class differences. The contemporary version of local political discourse in Norway, while keeping the ambition of universal welfare very much alive, is faced with severe overload problems. Thus, local politicians, responsible as they are -- both ideologically & institutionally -- for providing welfare for the local population, find themselves simultaneously deeply involved in attempts to control swelling budgets & act according to the ideals of rational organizational management. These politicians think & act within an institutional field that, probably more so than most other such fields in modern society, is characterized by deep contradictions. By focusing on the complexity of the ideological & institutional field of local politics, the article demonstrates not only that this particular field absorbs contradictions, but that it transforms political activity & the politicians' sense of self in specific ways. Politicians often experience a sense of personal fragmentation as they attempt to represent their constituencies & 'the weak ones in society', develop policies, represent the state's budget reduction requirements, control the municipal organization, while remaining loyal both to the bureaucracy & their sense of moral self. The concept of complexity helps to illuminate the ways in which the cleavages of early industrial society have 'migrated', as it were, from the realm of political collectivities to the level of the self. 19 References. [Copyright 2002 Sage Publications Ltd.]

title: Power/Knowledge Failure: Epistemic Practices and Ideologies of the Secret Police in Former East Germany
abstract: This paper traces the epistemic practices & ideologies that Stasi (East Germany's former secret police) used to construct the GDR peace & civil rights movements during the 1980s as one of the GDR's key enemies. In particular, the paper addresses the question of how communications in organized social encounters that are hierarchized by a cultivation of secrecy (legitimized by a Manichaean worldview) & corresponding myths about the distribution of knowledge & the proximity to an absolute social good have shaped interpretive processes. The particular epistemic style of Stasi is analyzed as a peculiar conflation of ethics & epistemology that was, ironically, profoundly undialectic, ie, monothetic, & thus unable to react constructively to interpretive failures in response to a fast-changing environment. 18 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Race-Ing the Bootstrap Climb: Black and Latino Bureaucrats in Post-Reform Welfare Offices
abstract: The substantial incorporation of people of color into government and quasi-government employment raises previously unexplored questions about the significance of race, class, and gender in street-level bureaucracies. Relying on interview data collected from black and Latino supervisors and caseworkers implementing welfare reform, I look at whether and how race and other social group memberships are deployed as tools in the delivery of casework services to black and Latino clients. Contrary to our assumptions about the level of impersonality entrenched in public bureaucracies, I find that most caseworkers and supervisors of color conceptualize and operationalize welfare reform in ways that link their goals and experiences as agency employees, members of racial communities, and implementers of social policy. They identify with the circumstances of their clients, but interpret the politics of welfare through not only racialized but also classed and gendered lenses. Consequently, they support and challenge clients of color in a variety of ways. In order to trace the origins of these strategies, I explore how the combination of institutional politics, environmental phenomenon, and black and Latino bureaucrats' personal histories contribute to their understanding of how they should do their jobs. This article suggests that not only inter-racial but also intra-racial politics inform institutional processes within street-level bureaucracies. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Lost Treasure of Arendt's Council System
abstract: Hannah Arendt's On Revolution offers a critique of modern representative democracy combined with a manifesto-like treatise on council systems as they have arisen over the course of revolutions and uprisings. However, Arendt's contribution to democratic theory has been obscured by her commentators who argue that her reflections on democracy are either an aberration in her work or easily reconcilable within a liberal democratic framework. This paper seeks to provide a comprehensive outline of Arendt's writing on the council system and a clarification of her work outside the milieu of the post-cold war return to Arendt. Her analyses bring to light a political system that guarantees civil and political rights while allowing all willing citizens direct participation in government. Framing her discussion within the language of the current renewed interest in constituent power, her council system could be described as a blending together of constituent power and constitutional form. Arendt resists the complete dominance and superiority of either element and argues that the foundation of a free state requires nothing less than the stabilization and persistence of constituent power within an open and fluid institution that would resist either the bureaucratization of politics or its dispersal into a revolutionary flux. Although one may conclude that her institutional suggestions are far from flawless, her political principles allow a conceptualization of democracy in more substantial ways than current liberal political philosophy. Adapted from the source document.

title: Breakfast at Spiro's: Dramaturgy and Dominance
abstract: An approach is presented for analyzing the relationship between cultural & social action in bureaucracy. Symbols & power are shown as the primary variables of sociocultural study, where symbolic forms & techniques are manipulated by asymmetrical groups in the articulation of basic interests. Through their interrelationship, the organizational conditions of production are reproduced or transformed. Social drama is the processual unit through which power relations, symbolic action, & their interaction are played out, & through which social structure is made evident. This perspective is applied to data from an ethnographic study of an advertising agency. 16 References. HA

title: The Paradigm Contingent Career? Women in Regional Newspaper Journalism
abstract: Current commentary on non-manual employment suggests that we are moving into an era of 'contingent careers' where current performance is the only valid criterion for reward and advancement. New-style jobs may be intensive and insecure, it is argued, but they are also less freighted with gender-based assumptions. Newspaper journalism, with its lack of bureaucratic organization, varied tasks, tradition of high employee mobility, and deep-seated belief in meritocracy would seem to fit well within this model. Interviews with women working in the UK regional press indicate, however, that the occupation is less egalitarian that many in the industry believe. Newspaper organisations and status hierarchies continue to be built around 'hard news', despite the commercial importance of other elements of content. Consequently management experience in newsgathering is a key stage in promotion, but this work as currently structured is incompatible with primary domestic responsibility for dependants. Even those without such concerns, or with limited ambitions, find the intensified work rÈgime in today's regional press hard to sustain. Considering why these working practices have remained largely unchallenged, the paper identifies five contributing factors. The epistemological individualism characteristic of women and well as men in journalism, a culture of vocation, the construction of editorial power as charismatic rather than bureaucratic, the commonsense populist style of most regional papers and, not least, journalists' own entrenched belief in the contingent nature of their employment combine to make the profession particularly resistant to acknowledging structural barriers to advancement.

title: Indian Ocean Trade and Sultanic Authority: The nazir of Jedda and the Mamluk Political Economy
abstract: Faced with a mounting economic crisis, the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Barsbay (r.1422-1438) sought new sources of revenue from the commercial economy of the Red Sea port of Jedda, which was emerging in the 15th century as a hub for maritime trade between the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean. This article examines the career of the first nazir, or financial supervisor, of Jedda, a Coptic secretary appointed by Sultan Barsbay. A glimpse at his career sheds light on strategies employed by the Mamluk sultan to align his household bureaucracy with the business of trade at Jedda and the interests of influential merchant networks, as well as the limitations of such strategies. Adapted from the source document.

title: THE SOCIAL ORIGIN OF GERMAN JUDGES: RESEARCH AND DISCUSSIONS
abstract: An overview on res in Germany concerning aspects of the judicial administration is presented. Particular attention is given to studies on the soc origin of judges by W. Richter, J. Feest, K. Zwingmann & R. Dahrendorf. The data collected by these authors indicate that German judges are recruited almost entirely from the upper segment of society & in large part from within the bur'tic structure & the legal professions. The N of judges from the lower as well as the medium to lower strata has increased considerably from 1959-1968, whereas the N who come from the medium to higher soc strata has slightly decreased. The implications which the soc origin of judges have for the exercise of their function in society are explored. Specific res on this subject does not exist. Dahrendorf suggests that the predominantly Uc class origin of judges produces a distorted image of society & a conservative attitude of justice. This has aroused some controversy on the part of German judges in the Deutsche Richterzeitung (German Judges Journal). Zwingmann, it is asserted, in his repudiation of Dahrendorf's thesis, has had little empirical evidence to offer in defense of the judges. He has rejected the implication that the judge in his judgments is bound to the values of his class, & imposes upon society its own normative principles. The polemic on the juridical office is in reality a polemic involving diff conceptions of German society. For Dahrendorf, German society is cut in half & governed by an elite which, regardless of any pluralism, even today maintains a conspicuous degree of homogeneity & a notable SD from the Lc's. For Zwingmann, German society is composed of a plurality of groups among which it becomes ever more difficult to distinguish who is on top & who at the bottom. Dahrendorf has ignored the changes which the role of the judge has undergone over the yrs. German society is no longer composed of opposing classes, only of opposing interests. Modified HA.

title: Welfare Systems Differentiation: The Incoherencies of Liberal and Mediterranean Systems
abstract: The last twenty or so years have seen the end of the steady expansion of welfare states, and a movement towards more mixed systems of financing and provision. Nearly all European governments are now seeking ways to control expenditure and reduce their involvement in the delivery of services. There is growing decentralisation and territorial variation, with differences also emerging in the rationales underlying services like social security, health and personal social services. The picture is further complicated by the move away from hierarchy and bureaucracy towards "soft" governance approaches in the management of services. Such developments are placing the schemes developed by Esping-Andersen and other authors for classifying welfare states under strain, and necessitate a review of the factors and typologies used in undertaking international comparisons. This paper presents two case studies (of a Mediterranean and a liberal regime), in an attempt to highlight critical factors in current ways of classifying welfare systems. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Fluctuating Fortunes of Traditional Rulers in Nigeria
abstract: Using Max Weber's different typologies of authority, the move from traditional authority in the precolonial era to present-day bureaucratic authority in Nigeria is examined. It is suggested that rulers in precolonial Nigeria enjoyed a power similar to that of monarchs in European countries. However, with the advent of colonialism, their power became dependent on British policy. It is argued that since independence, these rulers have steadily lost their authority &, currently, bureaucratic authorities have little intention of expanding the role of traditional rulers. Conclusions note that traditional rulers are further debilitated because they have no control over legitimate force. L. Baker

title: Social transformations & state bureaucracy
abstract: Examines the notion of 'state bureaucracy.' Introduces the history & development of bureaucratic structures over different time periods & around the world. Traces M. Weber's vision of 'state bureaucracy.' States that M. Weber's model of state bureaucracy does not exist in Anglo-Saxon countries where radical administrative reforms occurred. Concludes that even post-industrial society will preserve some bureaucratic elements, e.g., formalized rules, work discipline, impartiality, & so on. K. Duft

title: Politics as Fate
abstract: A review of Esad Cimic's Politika kao sudbina -- Prilog fenomenologiji politickog stradalastva ([Politics as Fate -- A Contribution to the Phenomenology of Political Martyrdom], Beograd: Mladost, 1982 [see listing in IRPS No. 26]). The book is marked by unusually bold references to the phenomenon of socialist bureaucracy in Yugoslavia & offers a sustained discussion of some peculiar features of bureaucratic practice & its standard-bearers as a group. The general theoretical discussion is offered against the background of Cimic's own political persecution, which began with the publication of two articles in a journal he edited, & then led, step-by-step, to his removal from other public & academic posts. S. Karganovic.

title: The Realpolitik of Nuclear Risk: When Political Expediency Trumps Technical Democracy
abstract: In recent years, a growing number of researchers in science and technology studies have begun to examine the relationship between science and politics. Specifically, they focus on citizen participation in highly technical policy problems and explore the possibility of a technical democracy that avoids pitfalls of technocracy. This focus, however, downplays a possibly more serious obstacle to technical democracy than technocracy, namely, realpolitik. Based on ethnographic and textual data on citizen-government interactions in the aftermath of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Disaster, we first show how citizens mobilised radiation detectors and counter-experts to force the Japanese government to admit scientific uncertainty about the permissible dose limit. We then explain why this successful mobilisation nonetheless had only a small impact on evacuation and compensation policies in terms of the pre-disaster structure of Japanese politics: the dominance of commission-based policy-making allowed the bureaucratic government to play realpolitik in the face of scientific uncertainty to expediently pursue its own interest, circumventing both democratic deliberation and technical rigour.

title: Leadership and Bureaucracy: The Folk Theorem and Real Folks
abstract: In the midst of state budget cuts, Director Victor Wirth transformed the Illinois Department on Aging (IDOA) from a demoralized agency drowning in the paperwork of a massive compliance system into a cooperative organization devoted to service quality. I develop & apply a game-theoretic model of IDOA that shows how & why the management strategies pursued by Wirth brought about this transformation. Combining the model with detailed empirical evidence, I identify the key factors that allowed Wirth to lead the agency to a new equilibrium. His detailed knowledge of the strategic structure of IDOA allowed him to choose a new equilibrium. His desire & ability to communicate with every level involved in the implementation of the CCP as well as his considerable autonomy from the governor enabled him to create, articulate, & implement the strategies necessary to change the equilibrium. & finally his reputation in the aging field served as a bond that allowed him to enforce the new agency equilibrium, thereby overcoming problems of renegotiation proofness. This article also provides an empirical illustration of the folk theorem. 2 Tables, 5 Figures, 1 Appendix, 35 References. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright 2005.]

title: Bureaucratic Politics and Power: Developments in the Study of Bureaucracy
abstract: A model of bureaucracy is proposed & applied to the administrative behavior of government in GB. Many writings on bureaucracy share a monolithic conception of it as a homogeneous system, & much attention has been given to power conflicts within bureaucracies, although this approach has limitations. Two frameworks have been developed that seek to explain the influence of bureaucracy on policy: bureaucratic politics & public choice. Insights from these alternative frameworks are applied to administrative behavior in GB, as revealed in the research literature. A theory of bureaucracy based on political & developmental models of organization appears to be a desirable approach. W. H. Stoddard.

title: BUREAUCRATIC COMPETENCE AND SUCCESS IN DEALING WITH PUBLIC BUREAUCRACIES
Age and Rank in the Big Corporation
abstract: To provide some evidence on changes in recent decades in the relationship between rank & age, some data are presented from a study of managers of 7 large Corp's conducted during the Sum of 1966. 429 managerial R's were given a questionnaire. In order to explore relationships among the variables, Pearsonian r's & slelected first-order partials were employed. Age & educ are measured in numbers of yrs, & level of entry into the LF is ordered blue collar, lower white collar, manag trainee & specialist, & coded accordingly. To examine possible changes in the importance of age as a determinant of rank, R's were divided into 2 cohorts. The sample was divided at its Md age of 42 yrs. Thus, all the younger cohorts entered the LF no earlier than the end of WWII. It is found that the r's of present position are quite diff for the 2 cohorts. For the older cohort, the major r's are educ & level of entry. For the younger cohort, the major r is age. It is suggested that the variable which has given rise to the diff patterns of r in these 2 cohorts is the diff rates of econ expansion of the 2 time periods. The data provide no evidence for the decreasing importance of age as a criterion for the allocation of rank within large-scale org's. Rather, there may have been some increase in its importance, although the rate of that increase in the future will probably depend on the extent to which it is possible to maintain an expanding economy. E. Weiman.

title: The bureaucratic making of national culture in North-Western Ghana
abstract: In this article I explore the making of national culture through bureaucratic routines in the Centre for National Culture in Wa, North-Western Ghana. I focus on an aspect of bureaucracy that is usually left aside: the productivity and creativity of bureaucratic routines. State, nation and culture are not fixed entities, but have to be constantly produced through processes of negotiation and meaning-making and through the continual reproduction of their boundaries and the categories that determine what is to be promoted or preserved. Bureaucratic routines and administrative processes are analysed as practices objectifying and nationalising culture and naturalising the boundaries and categories created through the cultural officers' practices. Adapted from the source document.

title: Regional Bureaucracy
abstract: In all industrialized countries today there is a crisis of the State which coincides with the proliferation of regionalism. The problem of local autonomy & of local bureaucracies is caught up in the dialectic of the devolution of power to the local level & the reaching of a certain social equilibrium. This model, for the time being, applies mostly to certain Western countries, eg England, Germany, Belgium, & Holland. It does not, however, apply to the same degree to more traditionally centralized countries such as France & Italy. The paradox is that the countries which have traditionally known the greatest measure of local autonomy are now faced with a well formed & entrenched bureaucracy on the local level. Italy is in the relatively worst position among these countries; she enjoyed a period of local vitality before the advent of fascism, but it was all eradicated by fascist centralization. Today, Italy faces 2 interrelated problems: creation of administrative structures, & creation of an efficient bureaucracy on the local level. The formation of training centers for administrators along the lines of the British Civil Service Coll is urged. S. Karganovic.

title: The Administrative Component in Complex Organization
abstract: This study examines the relationship between org'al size & the proportional size of the admin'ive component. The hyp is that org'al size is directly related to the diff between the relative sizes of the clerical & managerial components--the clerical ratio minus the managerial ratio. The data, drawn from general hosp's, show that the managerial component & org'al size are negatively related, & that org'al size & the relative size of the clerical component are not related. AA.

title: Is a grand bargain between left and right possible?
authors: Lamar, Alexander; Bolick, Clint; Rotherham, Andrew; Feldman, Sandra
abstract: Alexander et al discuss whether it is possible for the political Left and Right to come to some sort of agreement on the issue of school vouchers. Bolick argues that more money poured into education tends only to create more bureaucracy.

title: Post-Industrialization of Japan and the Fluidity of Youth Employment: Looking from the Simultaneity of Bureaucracy and Individualization
abstract: The aim of this paper is to examine the fluidity of youth employment & the tertiary industrialization that is part of international trade & the change in Japan's industrial policy. This process, known as "post-industrialization," occurred in every developed country; however, Japan contained the following unique characteristics: (a) a cruel division, known as "company-centricism," existed between employees inside/outside the companies; (b) the two Oil Crises had comparatively weak consequences in Japan because of the strong cooperation between capital & labor, so that the dominant position of existing large corporations did not collapse, as in the case of the United States & UK; (c) lower-class labor, which inevitably increases during the "postindustrialization" process, was supplied by the nation itself & not by immigrants. At that time, the increase in the fluidity of youth employment was explained by policymakers as a positive contribution to the national economy, although the same phenomenon is viewed as a symptom of economic crisis today. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Welfare State as an Expression of Crisis -- Not as Its Solution
abstract: The welfare state & its crisis are discussed in the context of the similarity of bureaucratic & social science jargon. The main problems of present-day politics are dealt with from a socialist-democratic viewpoint. The welfare state is seen as a product of crisis, not its permanent solution. It has superimposed bureaucratic forms & measures on the existing capitalism, but has saved the private structure of the capitalist economy. Contemporary politics has changed in the direction of an increased apparatus of domination, not democratization of society. The real crisis is the lowering of the existence level of large groups of people dependent on the welfare state. The welfare state is no longer a viable formula for reform. New alternatives are needed. 6 References. F. Rasmussen

title: State, Bureaucracy and Change in India
abstract: A discussion of the nature of the Indian state & bureaucracy. During the 1980s, it was widely believed that Indian bureaucracy constituted a dominant class & that this dominance is the root cause of economic stagnation. However, analysis of government survey data reveals a much more complex reality. A revised theoretical framework of the role of the state & public bureaucracy in India is outlined. 3 Tables, 1 Figure, 61 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Organizational Ideology: Some Functions and Problems
abstract: Bureaucratic ideologies help explain what an organization is doing, what it ought to be doing, & they help mold the will of the individual to the organizational needs. They are also effective in garnering support from the government & developing an autonomy for the agency. NASA & the Peace Corps both have bureaucratic ideologies which were highly successful at the outset & have since lost much of their strength. NASA was formed for the public as a visible demonstration that the US was a major technological & scientific power. It was given autonomy from the Defense Dept to avoid military domination. Private industry was to benefit from government contracts. Political leaders were to gain in prestige & funds for education were to increase. The public mood has changed since the inception of NASA. Sound research reasons must be forthcoming if the program is to continue. NASA's ideology must be changed as national priorities change & public attention focuses on other issues. At its inception the Peace Corps hired generalists who were highly motivated & dedicated. It moved quickly with a high degree of autonomy. Host countries then began to request specialists, forcing changes in the ideology. Several problems of bureaucratic ideologies are discussed: resistance to change; inconsistency & inability to explain the facts of experience; & the subsequent restriction of choice range. An ideology which synthesizes the values & norms of society can facilitate organizational goals. Inappropriate ideologies must be changed to meet societies' expectations or they will find their effectiveness decreased. B. Weisbrod.

title: BUREAUCRATIC AND PROFESSIONAL ORIENTATION PATTERNS IN SOCIAL CASEWORK
abstract: A report on a survey designed to determine orientations of soc workers; it is based on 'The Role of the Social Worker in a Child Protective Agency: A Comparative Analysis,' an unpublished PhD dissertation submitted to Brandeis U, Waltham, Mass: 1964. The R's were 110 professionally trained soc caseworkers & casework supervisors in 2 voluntary, nonsectarian professional casework agencies in Mass, a target agency which is a child protective agency, & a comparative agency which is a fam counseling agency. R's were presented with 6 conflicting conditions involving each of 4 subsystems. Data are presented in 3 tables. 4 patterns of moral evaluative orientations, suggesting 4 types of soc workers, emerge: (1) 'professionals' (37-16 in fam, 21 in protective agency), oriented primarily to professional standards; (2) 'bur'crats' (34-15, 19), oriented primarily to agency policies & procedures; (3) 'conformists' (18-13, 5), committed to both; & (4) 'innovators' (21-5, 16), who evidenced relatively low commitment to both in relation to meeting client needs. It is concluded that soc workers, while somewhat more bur'tic than some of the more independent professional workers, tend to exhibit the same general types or patterns of orientation. I. iangnas.

title: Theoretical Explanatory Model of International Adoption Failure: Attachment and Ecological Systems Perspectives
abstract: International adoption, the transfer of children for parenting purposes from one nation to another, presents an extreme form of what is often known as "stranger" adoption, in contrast to relative adoption (Bartholet, 2005, p. 8). Adoption brings major changes to the lives of children and adoptive parents. Intercountry adoptions are associated with high monetary costs, long waiting periods to adopt, changes of the family environment, and cultural challenges, along with other bureaucratic and socioeconomic factors. This paper explores the issue of international adoption failure through the prism of two theories: attachment theory and ecological systems theory. The author begins with a brief history of international adoption into the United States, followed by a discussion of factors contributing into adoption failure as discussed in other literature. Next, adoption failure is theoretically analyzed using the concepts of attachment and ecological systems theories. Suggestions for adoption practitioners are included.

title: Post-Soviet integration and the interaction of functional bureaucracies
abstract: This paper focuses on post-Soviet regional integration as a special case where integration projects are established by countries that originally comprised a single political entity after its collapse. It shows that in this framework the existing economic ties between countries are likely to affect adversely the interest of functional bureaucracy to support regional integration given that cutting existing connections is often more promising from the point of view of the budget expansion. Hence, the interaction of national and supranational bureaucracies is unlikely to generate impetus for increasing regional cooperation, which, surprisingly, can, however, be supported by adverse economic shocks. The results are validated using the experience of two 'low-level politics' sectors of interaction in the post-Soviet space: electricity and transportation. Adapted from the source document.

title: Identity Politics: DNA Profile and the Genetic-Criminal Identity
authors: Machado, Helena; Silva, Susana; Amorim, Antonio
abstract: DNA is seen by many as the "true" basis of human identity, insofar as it is a biological structure that is, in principle, unique in each individual. This notion of "uniqueness," a fundamental pillar of criminal investigation & forensic genetics, has fostered identity politics by modern states through the classification & storage of information about "criminals." This article explores the alignment of science & state bureaucracy for producing the "genetic-criminal" identity in the context of the Portuguese forensic DNA database for forensic purposes. We discuss the impacts of this sort of identity politics for the management, categorization, & surveillance of individuals classified as criminals. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Legibility of Class
abstract: A comment on Alejandro Portes's essay, "The Resilient Importance of Class: A Nominalist Interpretation" (2000), maintains that the most distinctive elements of his analysis are the exploration of class formation in the new economy & the recognition that class divisions have changed in the context of modern capitalism. His ideas are expanded on by considering class consciousness, an aspect Portes mentioned only briefly. The Marxist notion of class consciousness is reviewed, noting that his immediate followers contrasted class consciousness with self-consciousness, & class action with self-creation. The impact of the evolution of bureaucracy is discussed, along with recent efforts to dismantle the institutional hierarchy to make businesses more responsive to changing markets. It is maintained that bureaucratic changes in the new economy differ from the Weberian pyramid in terms of time. A discussion of the results of the short-term character of new bureaucracies contends that consciousness of where one belongs has become obscured & the existing consciousness of differentiation does not lead to solidarity with others. The implications for social theory are discussed. J. Lindroth

title: The Computerizing of Administration: Continuity and Change
abstract: Computers have not brought about any basic organizational changes within large public & private bureaucracies: they are included within the functional logic of the bureaucratic system. If they have caused a "Taylorization" of office work, as has often been said, this is only because office work has been based on Tayloristic principles for a long time. The computer, however, does have an effect on organization: it automizes functions that were formerly in the hands of the middle management. Dispossessed of their technical role by machines as well as by specialists in data processing, those former high-level staff members have recently been confined to the primary aspect of their role-related authority; which has resulted in their experiencing a cultural crisis. These observations are supported by a case study of an unidentified public welfare agency, described as a typical bureaucracy. 30 References. Modified HA

title: 20th Century Limited: Capital, Labor, and Bureaucracy in the Age of Nationalism
abstract: The growth & evolution of the state & bureaucracy in the twentieth century & their relationship to changes in capital, labor, & class to national struggles are examined. The twentieth century has been dominated by three types of struggles: the class struggle between labor & capital, over the command of labor power; the political struggle between state & community, over control of land; & the struggle over political, human, & social between the masses & capital & the state. These struggles have interacted with one another in a variety of ways, but three general movements have emerged: the labor & social democratic movement in the West, the radical nationalist movements in the South, & the communist movements in the East. Each of these movements led to the establishment of large bureaucracies, which remained stable so long as the national economies kept growing & social demands were kept in check. Since the 1970s, however, national economies & bureaucracies have faltered, & social movements -- eg, gay rights, feminism, & peace movements -- emerged, creating conditons that have allowed the emergence of global capital & the rudiments of the global state. D. Generoli

title: The Theory of Street-Level Bureaucracy: State of the Debate
abstract: The paper summarises the recent debate on the street-level bureaucracy perspective elaborated by Michael Lipsky (1980) and developed in the last decades and on its implementation, especially in the field of social policies and services. It deepens a recent relevant symposium on this topic, edited by Evelyn Brodkin, one of the main experts about the perspective. It also explains the reasons why this perspective can be interesting in the study of welfare policies and services in the Italian context. Adapted from the source document.

title: Mussolini, Charisma and Decision-Making
abstract: Mussolini's authority was established on the basis of a complex system of rivalries that existed between different agencies (political, personal, party, senior administration, traditional and parallel bureaucracies, business, etc.) which brought the competition into a political market. In this market, the Duce and the Fascist Party -- each with their own respective infrastructures -- controlled access to resources and exchange mechanisms that determined the quality of the actors. Mussolini was perfectly aware of this, and he managed it by favouring the most faithful and loyal of groups. At the same time, he had to be vigilant not to dilute his charismatic authority by becoming merely the organisation's leader: such work required the continuous intensification of his myth. All these operations inevitably led to a process of deregulation that upset the decision-making process. Adapted from the source document.

title: THE THAI BUREAUCRACY
abstract: The Thai bur, viewed as a subsystem of Thailand's self-contained pol'al system, variously manifests cultural uniqueness. Insulated from external pressures as a result of the absorption of major societal interests within the gov, the bur's orientation & preoccupations are conspicuously introverted. Pol'al influence, personalities, &prerogative provide the immediate frames of reference of admin'ive officialdom. Career strategies, working doctrines, & standards of conduct in the civil service are flexibly calibrated to the particularistic norms of ranking superiors. Authority relationships structured mainly by impermanent personal clique groupings, are tenuous &unstable. But efforts to institutionalize formal sanctions & channels of accountability founder on a cultural predilection for informal & covert control devices. IPSA.

title: Access to the Child Support Grant: Are the Batho Pele Principles Working?
authors: Charles, M A; Matthias, C R
abstract: This article presents an analysis of some primary data relevant to the Child Support Grant (hereafter referred to as the CSG). Specifically, this article provides an evaluation of the degree to which the Batho Pele principles are being implemented in order to facilitate access to the grant. This article reports the findings of a study in KwaZulu Natal in which the researcher observed the extent to which the Batho Pele principles were applied by clerks when they processed CSG applications. In addition, the researcher obtained data from applicants on their perceptions about treatment by clerks &, more generally, their experiences in applying for the CSG. In order to place the study results in context, the following will be discussed in this article: important features of the CSG; relevant aspects of the Batho Pele principles; the methodology of the study & the results of the study are discussed. 27 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Neopatrimonialism Reconsidered: Critical Review and Elaboration of an Elusive Concept
abstract: The article provides a critical discussion of the literature on 'patrimonialism' and 'neopatrimonialism' in Development Studies in general and African Studies in particular. Based on Max Weber's concept of patrimonialism and legal-rational bureaucracy the authors present their own definition of 'neopatrimonialism'. Three key conceptual questions are addressed. These are related to the operationalisation of the concept in empirical research: (1) how can neopatrimonialism be delimited vis-a-vis the concepts 'clientelism' and 'patronage'?: (2) how can neopatrimonialism be 'measured'?, and (3) how does neopatrimonialism relate to classical typologies of political regimes? Adapted from the source document.

title: From Modernisation to Big Society: Continuity and Change in Social Work in the United Kingdom
abstract: In this paper, I will explore developments in social work in the United Kingdom since the formation of the Conservative/ Liberal Democrat Coalition Government in May 2010. I will argue that the period since then has been characterised by elements both of continuity and change: continuity in that the neoliberal assumptions which underpinned New Labour's approach to social work continue to inform the approach of the Coalition; change, in that there is evidence of a more vigorous anti-statist rhetoric, reflected both in a critique of "bureaucracy" and also in the promotion of the Big Society as an all-embracing ideological framework. Against those who see the Big Society project as providing an opportunity for the emergence of a more progressive social work, I will argue that its primary rationale is to shift responsibility from the welfare state onto individuals and communities. The final part of the paper will explore some of the implications of the Big Society approach for social work and social care, through consideration of the policies of personalisation, localism and "open public services". Adapted from the source document.

title: The Benefits of Being There: Evidence from the Literature on Work
authors: Tope, Daniel; Lindsey Joyce Chamberlain; Crowley, Martha; Hodson, Randy
abstract: This study draws on the sociology of work to extend discussions of informational yield in ethnographic research. The authors examine the existing population of English-language workplace ethnographies and find that relative to interviews, observation and especially participant observation consistently yield more information. Participant observation provides greater informational yield as well as more detailed descriptions of workplace behaviors and group dynamics. Interviews, however, are more likely to provide information on basic organizational characteristics, such as organization size and product market conditions. The authors' findings have important implications for university institutional review boards, which have in recent years made it increasingly difficult for projects based on participant observation to receive human subjects clearance. Our conclusions caution against bureaucratic and legalistic curtailments of embedded field observation. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: "Wild Ghost," "Backer," Or More? A Continuum Of Views About The State In A North China Village
abstract: There have been plenty of studies on the contemporary Chinese state, given its omnipresence and central role in the daily operations of Chinese society. Yet the "state," often reified as an entity, is treated as the antithesis of another mystified entity called "society." Recent ethnographic studies of the Chinese state have provided us with a more nuanced picture. But only a few of them seriously address the issue of what the state really means to ordinary Chinese. Regrettably, in these studies, the state is portrayed as either a terrifying monster and "wild ghost" (Mueggler 1999, 2001), a "backer" and "patron" (Wang and Wu 2011; Zhang 2001), or a bifurcated bureaucracy (Li 2004; Li and O'Brien 1996; O'Brien and Li 2006; Ying 2011; Yu 2010). By detailing the personal histories of six different groups of villagers and their dealings with or avoidance of the state and its local personnel in a North China community, this article shows that the views of ordinary Chinese about the state are far more diverse than previously depicted. As the majority of villagers adopt an indifferent attitude, their varying views can be placed on a continuum that ranges from love and loyalty at one end to fear and hatred at the other. The article also argues that the Chinese state has succeeded to a certain extent in producing its totalizing effects. Adapted from the source document.

title: Domestic Capital, Civil Servants and the State: Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic under Globalisation
abstract: This article studies the impact of neoliberal globalisation on the relative strength of different social actors & on the relations between these actors & the state in Costa Rica & the Dominican Republic. In particular, the article analyses the responses of large domestic capitalists to the new global environment & to the new policies implemented, as well as the effect of these policies on public servants (who have traditionally been an influential political force, at least in Costa Rica). The paper makes two basic claims. First, globalisation has had some common effects on the politico-economic structures of Costa Rica & the Dominican Republic, despite the vastly different historical trajectory of state-society relations in the two countries. In both countries, there has been an increasing concentration & financialisation of capital & a weakening of the state bureaucracy. Second, these changes in the politico-economic structure have imposed new, country-specific constraints for the consolidation of the neoliberal economic model, signalling the need to introduce institutional reforms in the near future. Tables. Adapted from the source document.

title: Return to Bosnia
abstract: The author, who directs Soul of Europe, a mediation project working in the Balkans for the last fifteen years, assesses the changes that have taken place in Bosnia -- 'a broken country'. He contrasts the thoughtful creative work of community-based people's plenums with the crushing uncaring bureaucracy of international agencies, particularly via the EU -- the latest imperial power. It is, he argues, the clarity and practicality of the plenum movement's demands in dealing with corruption and the need for justice that puts it in the political vanguard.

title: THE SOCIAL DYNAMICS OF ELDER CARE: RITUALS OF BUREAUCRACY AND PHYSICAL NEGLECT IN NURSING HOMES
authors: Ulsperger, Jason S; Knottnerus, J David
abstract: This research concerns nursing home rituals involving bureaucracy and physical neglect. It uses 40 ethnographies, biographies, and autobiographies to explore various symbolic themes expressed through everyday interaction in nursing homes. The themes involve bureaucratic concepts such as staff separation, rules, documentation, and efficiency. They also involve ideas of physical neglect, such as medical dereliction, personal negligence, environmental negligence, and bodily harm. Relying on structural ritualization theory, this work argues ritualized symbolic practices of bureaucracy unintentionally manufacture attitudes and acts of mercilessness for workers in both for-profit and nonprofit nursing homes. This aids in the development of rituals facilitating the physical maltreatment of residents. Adapted from the source document.

title: A Study of Role Conceptions in Bureaucracy
abstract: Abstract not available.

title: Elite education and the State in France: durable ties and new challenges
abstract: Employing a Weberian understanding of the centrality of a strong bureaucracy in the modern nation-state, this article examines the relationship between the state and elite education in France. Through a historical analysis and an examination of two current issues facing education -- widening participation and pressures to internationalise -- we illustrate how the legitimacy of the administrative and political establishments, as well as the status granted to elite education tracks, has been largely preserved. Furthermore, dominant social classes have actively played a role in this alliance, thereby limiting the circle of eligible individuals who can aspire to future elite positions.

title: Politicians, Bureaucrats and Farmers: A Zambian Case Study
abstract: Case study evidence from eastern Zambia challenges the thesis that after independence an elite of privileged farmers entrenched itself through domination of the local political arena & a coalition with the civil service. It is argued that such a view may be a reification due to misplaced assumptions about historical continuity & the uniformity of social behavior; a lack of attention to the actual operation of government departments at the lowest levels; & neglect of how people construct ways of life on the basis of different interpretations of the world. 16 References. HA.

title: Defining and classifying technocrat-led and technocratic governments
abstract: Governments led by technocrats remain a nebulous category in political science literature, with little clarity about how they differ from party governments, how many have existed and how we can differentiate between them. This article aims to provide that conceptual and empirical clarity. Having proposed an ideal type definition of 'technocratic government', it sets out three conditions for an operational definition of a 'technocrat' and, on that basis, lists the 24 technocrat-led governments that have existed in 27 European Union (EU) democracies from the end of the Second World War until June 2013. It then classifies these according to their partisan/technocrat composition and remit. This allows for the presentation of a typology of four different types of technocrat-led governments and the definition of 'full technocratic governments' as those which contain a majority of technocrats and - unlike caretaker governments - have the capacity to change the status quo. The article concludes that full technocratic governments remain extremely rare in EU democracies since there have been only six cases - of which three have occurred in the last decade.[PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: In Search of 'Invisible' Actors: Barriers to Access in Refugee Research
abstract: The paper traces the early history of refugee research and shows how, from originally being prime movers in the research, refugees today have largely been reduced to invisibility. In the South, access to refugees held in camps is controlled by local government bureaucracies and by lead agencies, and may be severely restricted or completely denied; in the North, refugees held in detention centres are equally difficult to access and even more disempowered. Examples are given of studies carried out in Sierra Leone, Sudan, Egypt, Kenya, Greece and the Former Soviet Union. The paper also considers barriers to disseminating refugee research, and concludes that now more than ever the duty of the researcher is to speak on behalf of refugees. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Bureaucratic Phenomenon in Rome
abstract: Rome is considered a bureaucratic & tertiary center. Its bureaucratic character has been developing through history, ever since the Papal Rome of the 800's. Rome also divides the north & the south, & in this way, it is to some extent the center for "reconciliation" between them. Sella wanted it to be not only the political & the administrative capital of the country, but also the intellectual one, center of science & culture. The industrial & economic underdevelopment of Rome is therefore a consequence of a political choice; which has set Rome up as a consumer rather than a producer city. Most people work for the Public Administration (21%), the rest are divided in smaller numbers among various industries & services. There is a slight tendency for the bourgeoisie to be in the majority, & most are employees, not laborers. The figures for the change in population from 1951 to 1961 are also given. An analysis of the data regarding Rome & the Lazio reveal that in Rome there is a preponderance of professional, or liberal arts people, which accounts for the bureaucratic characteristic of the Eternal City. The tertiary sector predominates, meaning that most of the work that is done involves administrative & political control, directed not only to Rome but to the rest of Italy as well. In the last 10 years there has been a stagnation of industry, an expansion of services, & an increase of employees. The Italian state is more centralist than it is regionalist, & thus supports the position that Rome holds. Rome has not only the Ministeries, but also the headquarters of many of the most powerful & influential companies, not only on the national, but also on the international level. There is an old & a new bureaucracy; different forms, which practice different controls of power, one control & the other profit. There appears to be a change in the bureaucracy of Rome; a sociological phenomenon that is directly related to the important aspect of control & government. 21 Tables. A. Leon.

title: Reading Bauman for Social Work
abstract: This article draws on the social theories of Zygmunt Bauman to provide some analytical purchase on the state of contemporary social work. It outlines key themes in Bauman's writing and considers features of current social work practice against these. The starting point for Bauman's work is his explication of modernity and in particular the shift he identifies from what he calls 'solid' to 'liquid' modernity. The implications for social work within solid and liquid modern imaginaries are considered. Essentially, modernity, in its dominant guises, conceives of social work as a technical-rational endeavour whereas Bauman would argue that it is an irredeemably moral one. The moral dimension, however, is swept aside by the bureaucracy of solid modernity and by the neoliberal tenets of liquid modernity. This creates a growing dissonance between the original ethical impulse that brings people into social work and the job they are increasingly expected to do. Bauman argues that an ethical stance involves social workers 'being for' those they work with. It cannot come about through recourse to rules and codes but ultimately relies on workers taking personalised and situated moral positions. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: BUREAUCRACY IN THE REHABILITATION INSTITUTION: LOWER LEVEL STAFF AS A TREATMENT RESOURCE
abstract: Larger inmate pop & greater division of labor staff has stimulated bur'ization of mental hosp's & prisons. The top administrator of the rehabilitation institution faces twin problems; greater treatment caseload with relatively less resources: & growth of formalistic impersonality characteristic of bur'cy. These problems impede the individualization & client-staff rapport essential to the rehabilitative process. 2 existing resources for meeting these problems are cited: employee & employee-inmate informal groupings which are a by-product of institutional life; & the skills & experience of staff members at the lowest levels of the formal org where contact with the inmate is maximal. Through communication & persuasion, employee informal structure would be diverted to serve formal org'al ends. 'Custodian' & 'human enthusiast' roles are contrasted to analyze the process of remotivation of existing staff as a means of exploiting these resources. AA.

title: Dealing with Law in Migration Control: The Powers of Street-level Bureaucrats at French Consulates
abstract: This article examines how street-level bureaucrats within migration control use their scope for discretionary powers. On the basis of two ethnographic studies of French consulates in Yaounde and Tunis, we argue that state agents' practices are significantly shaped by organizational constraints such as how decision-making processes are organized and the bureaucratic habitus, including the fear of fraud. Like other street-level bureaucrats, consular agents are able to draw on legal frameworks in a flexible and instrumental manner. Yet, in the field of migration policy, their scope for discretionary decision making is wider and influenced by their belief that they are acting to defend the national interest. This gives a more political dimension to the way such agents deal with law. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Representative Bureaucracy; Understanding the Correlates of the Lagging Progress of Diversity in Policing
abstract: The domination of policing by White males has long been considered a threat to the legitimacy of the profession, as police agencies have struggled with attracting, retaining, and promoting women and minorities within their agencies for decades. Female and minority representation are hardly stable across agencies with some agencies employing no women or people of color, while others are more representative of the communities they serve. Using a national sample of 1,478 police jurisdictions, this study further explores the correlates of diversity of women and racial minorities using a framework informed by representative bureaucracy theory. Findings suggest that the same factors are not predictive of representation of women and racial minorities.

title: From concerned to convinced: reaching decisions about out-of-home care in Norwegian Child Welfare Services
abstract: Placing children in out-of-home care constitutes one of the strongest public interventions in families. This paper explores how Norwegian Child Welfare Service (CWS) workers present their reasons as well as their work processes in the course of deciding to place children in out-of-home care. The analysis is based on interviews with 83 social workers and concerns 109 children recently removed from their homes. Three central elements were identified in the social workers' accounts: (1) a description of worrying conditions in the family; (2) the workers' long-term back-and-forth process, which revolved around experiences from the case, particularly around interactions with the parents; and (3) a triggering factor that made the out-of-home placement take place when it did. These elements underline the need to include both substance (conditions related to the child and his/her family) and procedure (conditions related to the work on the case) to understand what leads CWS to removing children. Both types of conditions put the parents, rather than the children, in the centre of the workers' attention, which may be explained by the position and role of the CWS workers as street-level bureaucrats. The findings emphasize the importance of acknowledging the contradictory position of CWS workers.   [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Predatory Democracy: Family, Bureaucrats and Gangsters
abstract: The implications of the conflict between peoples loyalty to family, bureaucracy, & gangster systems for democratization are considered. Overviews of the family, bureaucracy, & gangster systems that strongly influence social organization in most cultures are provided. Factors that contributed to the historical transition from the family unit to a bureaucratic model as the key force behind social organization are contemplated; in addition, circumstances that permitted the gangster system to infiltrate the familial-bureaucratic model of social organization are highlighted, eg, small private business owners resistance to large-scale industrialization in several European & Asian countries. Differences between the amalgamation of the family, bureaucratic, & gangster systems in European nations & the US are noted; specifically, it is argued that the strength of the US family system resulted in the incorporation of gangsterism & prevented the replacement of democracy with either communism or socialism. Noting the function of these three systems within post-Soviet Polish society, it is demonstrated that Polish society has largely accepted predatory democracy.
