The manifestation of predatory democracy & gangsterism in several cultures in the post-September 11, 2001, world is also noted. J. W. Parker

title: Neopatrimonialism Reconsidered: Critical Review and Elaboration of an Elusive Concept
abstract: The article provides a critical discussion of the literature on 'patrimonialism' and 'neopatrimonialism' in Development Studies in general and African Studies in particular. Based on Max Weber's concept of patrimonialism and legal-rational bureaucracy the authors present their own definition of 'neopatrimonialism'. Three key conceptual questions are addressed. These are related to the operationalisation of the concept in empirical research: (1) how can neopatrimonialism be delimited vis-à-vis the concepts 'clientelism' and 'patronage'?; (2) how can neopatrimonialism be 'measured'?; and (3) how does neopatrimonialism relate to classical typologies of political regimes?

title: Unrepresentative Bureaucracy
abstract: Sociological concern with the social & educational origins of British higher civil servants is interpreted on the basis of various explicit & implicit theses--representative bureaucracy, model employer, educational origins, & social origins. All such approaches rest on 2 unexamined assumptions: preoccupational socialization is vital for the later attitudes of higher civil servants, &, it is possible to modify the social & educational origins of this group. Comparative information & historical data on the British situation show that such modification is unlikely without a radical transformation of values guiding a public bureaucracy. There was a higher % of "Oxbridge" (Oxford & Cambridge U's) graduates in the 1971 administrative higher civil service (66%) than in the 1959 group (60%), & the % in 1971 was almost as high as in 1929 (69%). Research on organizational structures & on the influence of preoccupational & postoccupational experience are essential for a sound discussion of the theses as well as for any future discussions of the responsiveness of public bureaucracies. 1 Table. Modified HA.

title: Navigating Bureaucratic Narratives
authors: Gurung, Barun; Syiem, Darilyn; Gurung, Nawraj
abstract: This article questions some of the implicit assumptions that underlie a managerial approach to gender mainstreaming. It argues that for gender mainstreaming strategies to become effective, they need to be based on an understanding of the structure and cultural practices of institutions, together with analyses of the strategic actions of intermediaries of change within the restricting and constrained environments of bureaucracies. By analyzing gender mainstreaming experiences from Nepal and the northeastern Indian states of Sikkim and Meghalaya, this article argues for a view of institutional change as resulting from multiple "encounters" that ensue between the actions and strategies advanced by change intermediaries to transform the dominant narratives of bureaucracies. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: In Search of Autonomy: Cornelius Castoriadis
abstract: French philosopher Cornelius Castoriadis (born 1922) proposes a social & intellectual plan in which the desire for transformation of the world is built on a fundamental critique of bureaucratic institutions & of the inherited thought patterns that have inspired them. The epistemological bases of this plan are outlined within the context of social imagination, in order to demonstrate how a sociology of self-management, autonomy, & liberty could draw from them the sources of a new paradigm, in which concepts of the imaginary & of social production would replace those of the rational & of social reproduction. Modified HA.

title: Educational Credentials, Elite Dualism, and Elite Stratification in China
abstract: Despite the general consensus on the importance of university degrees in leadership selection, researchers in elite studies have not focused on how education differentiates & stratifies elites. Many important questions remain unanswered, eg, are the returns to education linear in different political institutions? Is the payoff to education allocated among different dimensions of educational attainment? Using a 1994 data set on top Chinese leaders, I show different effects of educational credentials on elite stratification in two major bureaucratic structures in the People's Republic of China. I conclude with a discussion of the nature of the political elite in China & the implications of my study for future research on educational credentialism & elite stratification. 2 Tables, 89 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Immigration control in Ultima Thule: Detention and exclusion, Norwegian style
abstract: The Aliens Holding Centre at Trandum, about 40 minutes north of Norway's capital city of Oslo, is the country's only closed immigration detention centre. Although detainees are held there as a result of having violated the Immigration Act and not the Penal Code, and whilst their detention is meant to facilitate deportation and not as punishment, Trandum's Centre looks and feels exactly like a conventional prison in a variety of ways. The aim of this article is to introduce the Aliens Holding Centre at Trandum as part of a wider Norwegian (and thus European) immigration control regime, as well as detailing information about the centre in itself, drawing to this end on publicly available reports by the Norwegian Parliamentary Ombudsman for Public Administration, the Independent Council in charge of monitoring operations at Trandum's Centre, and the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications, Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: Inside the Welfare Contract: Discretion and Accountability in State Welfare Administration
abstract: A case study of the Job Opportunities & Basic Skills program in Chicago, IL, highlights problems that arise when state agencies have discretion in administering a welfare contract built around work. Observations reveal the role bureaucratic discretion plays in giving specific meaning to the welfare contract. In addition, contextual factors that influence how state welfare agencies respond to their policy obligations at the street level are identified. Illuminated are the risks of welfare reforms that increase state administrative flexibility under conditions of limited resources & minimal accountability for performance. Adapted from the source document.

title: Rural Intelligentsia and Path Dependency in Post-socialist Civic Organising: The Case of Lithuania
authors: Juska, Arunas; Poviliunas, Arunas; Ziliukaite, Ruta; Geguziene, Vilma
abstract: Since the late 1990s the number of rural community development groups in Lithuania has grown exponentially. The article presents the results of one of the first representative surveys of rural NGOs ( N = 326) in Lithuania designed to evaluate their structure and resources. Unlike civic organising during the perestroika period, which was characterised by charismatic personalities and organisational innovations, the most recent surge in rural activism follows a path-dependent trajectory. The movement is lead by representatives of former collective farms, or kolkhoz intelligentsia (white-collar professionals who served in collective farm social infrastructure during Soviet times) engaged in reconstituting volunteer groups based on a modified Soviet institution of the rural 'culture house' or Soviet civic centre (SCC). The prevalence of the SCC-based rural organising model provided opportunities as well as imposed limitations on post-socialist civic activism. Community development groups were relatively successful in the types of activities in which SCCs were effective as well (such as culture, leisure and sports), while their capacity to deliver social services were marginal. Although this survey reported relatively high levels of engagement by the community groups with local and county governments, their influence remains constrained by the paternalistic, client-patron type of power relationships that prevail in rural areas. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Feminist activism within bureaucracy: Process of formulating and implementing regulations governing the protection of women's rights in Taipei
abstract: This study documents and analyses the process of the formulation of the "Regulations Governing the Projection of Women's Rights" in Taipei, Taiwan, China a feminist experiment the author engineered as an activist in the City Government. Scholars and experts from the feminist community involved in working with women bureaucrats adopted both the "outsider tactic" of consciousness-raising and the "insider tactic" of lobbying for support. The creation of the Regulations outside the women's policy agency and without legal mandate or outside pressure demonstrates the vitality and versatility of feminist activism. The author identifies an active and visible feminist community and special bond of sisterhood as the crucial elements that led to the success of the project. [Copyright 2008 Elsevier Ltd.]

title: Administrative Decentralization for Regional and Local Development in Japan
abstract: Administrative decentralization for regional & local development in Japan has, until recently, been initiated mainly by the central government. With the drafting of the Third Plan in 1978, however, the role of local governments in the formulation of national development plans was recognized. Presently, a new regional development policy of "technopolis" is being proposed to make Japanese industries' structure more knowledge-intensive, & to attain regional development objectives. The future of Japan's regional development will depend on how local governments plan & implement original & creative policies for regional & local development. HA

title: PROFESSIONAL/BUREAUCRATIC CONFLICT: THE CASE OF THE MEDICAL PROFESSION IN THE NATIONAL HEALTH SERVICES
abstract: THE RELEVANCE OF THE THEORY OF PROFESSIONAL/BUREAUCRATIC CONFLICT FOR UNDERSTANDING THE POSITION OF THE MEDICAL PROFESSION IN THE HOSPITAL SERVICE IN SCOTLAND IS DISCUSSED. WORK ON PROFESSIONAL/BUREAUCRATIC CONFLICT IN A NUMBER OF SETTINGS IS ANALYZED & AREAS OF PROFESSIONAL/BUREAUCRATIC CONFLICT ARE DERIVED. THE FIELDWORK WAS RESTRICTED TO THE LEVEL OF BOARD OF MANAGEMENT & WAS CONDUCTED IN 3 HOSPITALS: A MAJOR TEACHING HOSPITAL, & A LARGE & A SMALL GENERAL HOSPITAL. THE INTERACTION OF THE MEDICAL PROFESSIONAL & THE ADMINISTRATION IS EXAMINED IN RELATION TO CONFLICTS WHICH AROSE BETWEEN THE 2 GROUPS DURING THE FIELDWORK; THESE ISSUES ARE EXAMINED TO DETERMINE THE REASONS FOR CONFLICT. THE RESULTS OF ANALYSIS SUGGEST THAT THE OCCURRENCE OF PROFESSIONAL/BUREAUCRATIC CONFLICT IS RELATIVELY LIMITED. THIS IS ATTRIBUTED TO THE INFLUENCE WHICH THE PROFESSION HAS BEEN PERMITTED IN THE SERVICE & THE INTERNAL NATURE OF THE PROFESSION, IE DIFFERENCES IN SPECIALTY PERSPECTIVE & INTERSPECIALTY COMPETITION. THE INFORMAL POWER OF THE PROFESSION & ITS INTERNAL DIFFERENCES MAKE THE PROFESSIONAL/BUREAUCRATIC CONFLICT UNSUITABLE FOR UNDERSTANDING THE CHARACTER OF PROFESSIONAL INTERACTION WITH THE ADMINISTRATION. A MORE USEFUL APPROACH FOR UNDERSTANDING PROFESSIONAL/ADMINISTRATIVE INTERACTION WOULD START WITH THE INTERNAL DIVISIONS OF THE PROFESSION & SEE THE VARIOUS SPECIALTY GROUPS ACTING AS INTEREST GROUPS IN RELATION TO THE ADMINISTRATION. AA.

title: Measuring social capital: An exploration in community-research partnership
authors: Chaskin, Robert J; Goerge, Robert M; Skyles, Ada; Guiltinan, Shannon
abstract: Large numbers of social policy initiatives and community organizations are currently engaged in community building efforts that seek, in part, to strengthen informal relationships and the organizational infrastructure of communities and to build the capacity of communities to manage and foster community change. One critical requirement for improving such practice is for communities to have greater access and capacity to use information for planning, advocacy, and assessment. There are, however, a number of challenges to this, especially as it concerns understanding complex, sometimes elusive, dimensions of community circumstances and dynamics--the level of community social capital, for example--that are of central interest to those involved in community-building efforts. The authors describe what was learned through a community-research partnership that attempted to test practical options for community-based organizations (CBOs) to measure aspects of community social capital for their own purposes and within the constraints of budget, time, and skills under which they work. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: A Critical Reflection on Urban Spatial Planning Practices and Outcomes in Post-Apartheid South Africa
abstract: The spatial planning and policy framework and associated implementing tools in South Africa have undergone fundamental changes since the onset of the democratic era in 1994. The effectiveness and influence of urban spatial planning on restructuring South African cities are however increasingly being questioned and there remains a surprising paucity of empirical evidence to evaluate the impact of these plans. Seven key challenges are identified as impacting on the effectiveness of urban spatial planning in the democratic era. The responses to these challenges as reflected by the urban spatial plans of a cross-section of cities indicate moderate levels of progress with improving the horizontal and vertical alignment of spatial planning processes and with the integration of sustainability principles into spatial planning. Some limited improvement was noted with the understanding of the urban space economy and the alignment of infrastructure development and capital investment with spatial planning. However, very little progress is evident with the principle of physical and social economic integration of cities, considering the informal sector in mainstream spatial planning processes, and with the use of appropriate indicators and quantified targets to monitor the implementation and impact of spatial plans. The application of innovative spatial and statistical techniques will not only greatly enhance the understanding of these issues, but will also provide the basis for formulating appropriate and robust indicators and targets to monitor the impact of spatial plans. Adapted from the source document.

title: Becoming Visible: Religion and Gender in Sociology
abstract: The European men canonized as the founders of sociology sought to explain the societal shifts they associated with modernization including urbanization, the development of bureaucracy, and the emergence of the nation state. In this essay, I suggest how developing theoretical and methodological tools have gone hand in hand with social changes and new questions about the place of religion in con temporary society to make religion more visible in the discipline of sociology. Seeing gender has also been problematic in sociology, although in somewhat different ways. I show how asking questions about gender illuminates the unevenness of the secularization process. I outline recent developments in feminist thinking. I show how considering gender and religion together enhances our understanding of both.

title: Welfare Reform, Jobcentre Plus and the Street-Level Bureaucracy: Towards Inconsistent and Discriminatory Welfare for Severely Disadvantaged Groups
abstract: A defining feature of UK welfare reform has been concerted moves towards greater conditionality and sanctioning which has stimulated much academic debate. However, few policy articles have sought to examine how welfare reforms are actually implemented. Lipsky (1980) has shown that the intentions of policy makers may be frustrated by the behaviour of public service workers operating in a 'corrupted world of service'. This article draws upon the findings of the evaluation of the Jobseekers Mandatory Activity to discuss how key welfare reforms are likely to be implemented. It argues that that discretion remains a significant feature of front-line practice with potentially profound implications for severely disadvantaged groups. Adapted from the source document.

title: Interpersonal Dynamics in Network Organizations
abstract: Network organization holds much promise of reaching organizational flexibility. It is often argued that by means of tearing down the walls of bureaucratic authority organizations can promote organization-wide cooperation & integration, essential features of competitive organizations in a changing marketplace. In this paper we look at a simpler version of network organization, ie, matrix organization, to study interpersonal dynamics in an organization. Specifically, we look at social networks & show that the patterns of relationships predicted by the expectations of theory of network organization does not emerge. Contrary to expectations, we find the lack of lateral networks & strong vertical communication with direct supervisors. The paper concludes by proposing a theory of status uncertainty as an explanation for the failure of network organizations to eschew bureaucracy & generate company wide integration & cooperation. The tearing down of bureaucracy creates status uncertainty in organizations, which leads actors to build protective networks recreating hierarchies in the process. The paper suggests that bureaucracy could be altered in many ways to accommodate flexibility. But flexibility cannot be achieved by tearing down bureaucracy. 6 Tables, 53 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: "A Certain Light, But Only a Juridical Light": The Legal Aesthetics of Thomas Bernhard's The Lime Works
abstract: Servais treats Thomas Bernhard's 1970 novel The Lime Works, with its hybridization of literary and legal languages. Servais helps to understand this new language by thawing on Habermas's account of juridification processes and Adorno's aesthetics of reification. The current era, so Servais, is marked by "subjecting even the most intimate areas of people's lives to increasing legal and bureaucratic regulation," which in turn explains "the prevalence, in the heyday of the welfare state, of a specifically legalistic style of literary prose."

title: Underdevelopment, Urban Squatting, and the State Bureaucracy: A Case Study of Tanzania
abstract: The underdevelopment approach to the study of public bureaucracies in the Third World is analyzed, arguing that the approach -- while valid in principle -- is deficient in practice since it often uses global categories that do not easily apply to small areas or particular economic sectors. The empirical study of underdevelopment as it applies to bureaucracy should include variables related to economic scarcity, as well as those dealing with SC. The interrelationship of these groups of variables is shown to have heuristic value in the study of Ur squatting & the Tanzania government/World Bank response to squatting in Dar es Salaam. In a situation of extreme poverty, a SC bias in the bureaucracy in Dar es Salaam was accentuated by scarcity; this situation in some crucial respects was reinforced by the agreement between the Tanzanian government & the World Bank. Ur case study material collected in the early 1970s is presented, updated by data gathered during a visit to Dar es Salaam in the summer of 1980. Modified AA.

title: Reinventing the Pentagon: How the New Public Management Can Bring Institutional Renewal
abstract: 'Reinventing the Pentagon: How the New Public Management Can Bring Institutional Renewal,' by Fred Thompson and L. R. Jones, is reviewed.

title: Social Work and the New Integrative Hospital: Response to Dr. Falck
abstract: In response to Hans S. Falck's commentary on Globerman & Bogo's "Social Work and the New Integrative Hospital" (for both, see abstracts in SOPODA 18:1), it is pointed out that unequal power relations exist in both hierarchical & decentralized organizations. However, social work in health care organizations has not had power, & administrators transforming hierarchical hospital arrangements have overlooked social work. The challenge was to design alternative frameworks to house social work functions rather than to address underlying assumptions of hierarchy. V. Wagener

title: MECHANISTIC AND ORGANIC MODELS OF PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION IN DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
abstract: The analysis by F. W. Riggs & V. A. Thompson of the shortcomings of public administration in developing countries are discussed. Thompson advocates some kind of organic model for these countries as opposed to the varieties of the mechanistic model which developing countries usually try to follow. In fact, the cultures in developing countries do not permit either mechanistic or organic org's to work effectively. Hyp's are advanced on the diff's in org'al loyalty & on the effects of formal & informal org between developing & developed countries. HA.

title: The Decentralized Enterprise as Imaginary Institution
abstract: A 'new decentralization' is the leading idea in current enterprise management concepts & reorganization strategies. The consideration of its ideological content shows that it is deeply rooted not only in capitalistic, but also in bureaucratic 'social imaginary significations' (Castoriadis). Aiming at the definition of new problem & conflict constellations in enterprise management & on the shop floor, the paper discusses empirical findings on forms & consequences of decentralization strategies. It seems that the initiation of 'internal markets' causes distinct changes in the relationship of central management & direct command structures in organizational subunits. But this does not mean 'debureaucratization'. And the further down one moves the hierarchical steps, the lesser one finds antibureaucratic effects of the 'new decentralization'. New forms of work organization (e.g. group work) fall between economizing pressure & managed participation & are thus characterized by new kinds of contradictory action requirements. In a conclusion it is asked why German industrial sociology has problems with the interpretation of these phenomena, & what questions are raised for further research. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Urban 'Failures': Municipal Governance, Planning and Power in Colonial Delhi, 1863-1910
abstract: This article highlights the relationship between the 'failures' of municipal governance and the reproduction of its power in the colonial city. It examines the everyday operations of the Delhi Municipality between 1863 and 1910 and shows how the 'failure' to promote urban renewal actually provided 'opportunities' for the municipality's own longevity. After the Rebellion of 1857, the Delhi Municipality was invested with a wide variety of powers to check sanitary offences and regulate building construction in Delhi. This article discusses how this very growth and centralisation of powers created severe challenges for the functions of the municipality. The growing complexity of its operations, recommendations of experts, costs of ambitious projects and resistance from city dwellers, it is suggested, constantly subverted municipal intentions. Yet, in bringing to light the 'failure' of municipal policies, this article will argue that failure was profoundly productive. Municipal 'failure' was always accompanied by the growth in its bureaucratic capabilities and regulatory powers.

title: Higher Education and Social Security Services in the Netherlands: Institutionalism and New Public Management
abstract: In this paper the aim is to investigate the similarities & differences in the basic assumptions of NPM & post-NPM as concepts for public sector reform; the recognition, application, & consequences of NPM & post-NPM in reforms in public services & theoretical explanations for the relationship between reforms & NPM/post-NPM from neo-institutional theory. The empirical focus is on the public services of higher education & social security in the Netherlands. This country is an interesting case because of its mix of Anglo-Saxon & European-continental models & its position in the forefront of public management reform in the European Union. 2 Tables, 44 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Institutional Regulation and the Challenge of the New Ethics: The Case of Voluntary Action in Italy
abstract: Sociological & policy-making aspects of the institutional regulation of voluntary service in cooperative societies are analyzed. Based on a review of laws in 18 regions of Italy over the last 15 years, it is noted that the increasingly complex local differences in associationism are reflected in problems with the technical & legal terminology describing volunteerism. In general, a distinction is made between organizational & activity type among associations providing interventions in income assistance, education, social, & health services. The passage of a 1991 national law reestablished norms for volunteer work by defining operational links between the individual & the state. Such normalization & rationalization of voluntary service must balance the ideologies of a secular & clerical public ethics in which these various associations operate. 3 Tables, 26 References. J. Sadler

title: The Philanthropic Ogre
abstract: In the twentieth century the state has become a self-reproducing machine, which has only recently been exposed to criticism. The state plays a peculiar role, both patrimonial & modernizing, in Latin American nations, of which Mexico offers an example. The state founded by the PRI party has grown strong while weakening the society in which it operates, creating parallel bureaucracies of politicians & administrators/technocrats. This state's two bureaucracies are run respectively on personal & technical patterns. Mexico has not undergone genuine modernization, due partly to attempts to adopt patterns of modernity from other countries rather than developing them indigenously. W. H. Stoddard.

title: Gendered organizational dynamics: The elephant in the room for Australian allied health workforce policy and planning?
abstract: Australian governments have reported an impending 'crisis' with workforce shortages in the health sector expected to deepen over the next decade. The allied health professions, however, have barely rated a mention despite the fact their retention rates are low and they are expected to play an expanded and more preventive role in the future. This article examines current Australian public policy approaches to the allied health professions in relation to workforce shortages. It identifies the dominance of technocratic representations of the problem, noting that these have become more pervasive and robust with the New Public Management (NPM). Recent Australian sociological discussion suggests that technocratic 'framing' of allied health workforce shortages is limited by its failure to address the role of organizational and institutional dynamics. Such an analysis advances prevailing policy-based problematizations of allied health workforce shortages, but is itself constrained by the lack of acknowledgement of the gendered character of Australian health services organization and the role this may play in allied health workforce shortages.

title: Managing State-Owned Enterprises: Lessons from India
abstract: A comparative-historical approach is employed to determine the success of some state-owned enterprises in India, drawing on a 1991-1993 case study of the poorly performing Steel Authority of India & Maruti Udhyod Limited & their relationship with the Indian Administrative Service, which comprised 100+ interviews with government & company officials & state, private, & print media documents. It is suggested that noncontractual relations between the elitist bureaucratic government service & Maruti Udhyod Limited guaranteed the success of contractual relations by altering disadvantageous economic factors such as trade restrictions. Implications for privatization & economic transition are discussed. 4 Figures, 58 References. J. W. Parker

title: How to be Modern: New Labour's Neoliberal Modernity and the Change for Children programme
abstract: In England the New Labour administration is seeking to embed a 'transformational reform agenda' within children's service. Social workers, among others appear, however, to be wary of the agenda which is now rhetorically rooted in the Every Child Matters: Change for Children programme (CfC). The main social work practice elements of this programme are associated with the introduction of a Children's Index, a multidisciplinary Common Assessment Framework and the role of Lead Professional. In terms of the promotion of this programme, the government has maintained that the focal aim is to create a 'modern' children's workforce. However, the entire 'transformational agenda' can be interpreted as reflecting New Labour's neoliberal modernity. This is particularly apparent in the terms of the ideas associated with 'flexibility' which are so central to the CfC programme. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Organization Structure and Strategies of Control: A Replication of the Aston Study
abstract: A replication of the Aston study of org structure (a conglomerate study of work org's in the English Midlands laying stress on the development of a methodology of org'al characteristics which employed a multivariate approach), employing the original measurements, reports data secured from a sample of 82 British org's. The replication confirms the tight nexus between specialization, standardization of procedures, paper-work, & vertical span expressed by the concept "structuring of activities." In contrast to the Aston study, centralization of decision making is found to be related negatively to structuring in a way that conforms closely to M. Weber's description of the bur'tic mode of admin'ive control. Further examination of the replication results draws attention to problems in carrying forward the Aston program of comparative org'al res, problems both of a theoretical & operational nature. Modified HA.

title: REFORM OF THE PUBLIC SERVICES: PROBLEMS OF TRANSITIONAL BUREAUCRACIES IN COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN STATES
abstract: The major pre-occupation of the nat'l gov's of the independent & associated Commonwealth States of the Caribbean is considered to be the modernization of their island societies. 2 issues are raised in the context of a modernization of public admin: (a) the role of gov in nat'l development with special reference to the new ex-colonial states of the Commonwealth Caribbean; & (b) the problems engendered by the persistence, in the public services of the region, of colonial instit's & values which emasculate the efforts required for the effective management of change & development. It is felt that the public service, the sole admin'ive agency available to the state, is the most important instrument of innovation & change in developing systems. This role ought to be carefully studied by the new pol'al elites before these public services are committed to the challenges of the new order. Transition from colonialism to selfgov in Commonwealth Caribbean States reveals an emphasis on the formal pol'al aspects of state control (eg, progressive reallocation of pol'al power to indigenous pol'al elites). The development of a functionally relevant admin'ive machine would involve a penetrative survey of the civil service system inherited from the passing order. 'Pre-disposing factors' & 'inhibiting factors' are distinguished in the public service system. The former include size, variety of skills & knowledge, COMM link, & influence on pol'al leadership, the latter lack of adequate preparation for self-gov, law & order orientation, & income (as against output) orientation, traditional non-involvement in policy formulation, shifts in bur'tic power, & the heritage of paternalism. Civil service in a self-governing society must be the efficient dedicated public servant charged with managing the changes required for development & for continuous promotion of nat'l well-being, according to policies articulated by the mass of the people through their pol'al representatives. M. Maxfield.

title: Rent Control Legislation and the National Housing Corporation in Tanzania, 1985-1990
abstract: Following a general overview of housing problems in Third World countries, discussed are difficulties faced by the Tanzanian National Housing Corporation (NHC) in its estate management functions that hinged on getting higher rents from its nearly 13,000 housing units, located mainly in urban areas. Rent revision proved difficult given the sociopolitical status of the NHC, as well as its subjection to the country's rent control legislation. Analysis highlights the problems of supplying public housing at realistic rents where the general public & government ideology support low rents. It also exposes the dilemmas faced by governments in dealing with NHCs, especially in African urban areas, where the NHCs can only house a tiny minority of households, at high cost to the public. 2 Tables, 46 References. Modified AA

title: South Africa’s Transition to a Low-Carbon Economy: The Role of Cooperatives
abstract: The South African energy sector has been plagued by incessant power outages in recent years due to decreasing energy generating capacity, increased population and economic growth, political interference with the country’s energy provider, and a lack of maintenance of aging energy infrastructure. Economists are unanimous that incidences of load shedding have resulted in a loss of billions of Rands in revenue. Using a desktop review, this paper examines the potential roles of cooperatives in South Africa’s budding clean energy sector. The paper argues that although cooperatives can potentially contribute to the country’s clean energy transition, challenges such as policy constraints, access to finance, dearth of technical skills as well as poor understanding of the cooperative movements are barriers to cooperatives’ involvement in South Africa’s low-carbon future. The paper a rgues that these barriers must be addressed in order to unlock the contributions of cooperatives to the country’s clean energy transitions.

title: Haussmannization in the tropics: Abject urbanism and infrastructural violence in Nicaragua
abstract: This article considers the underlying dynamics of the elite-oriented urban transformation that Managua, the capital city of Nicaragua, has undergone during the past decade and a half. It begins by drawing a cross-historical comparison between Managua's metropolitan makeover and a paradigmatic case of planned urban change, that of 19th-century Parisian Haussmannization, in order to highlight the systemic and purposeful nature of the former's transformation from a top-down perspective. It then focuses ethnographically on the grassroots consequences of specific instances of infrastructural development that have affected two poor neighbourhoods in the city, providing a bottom-up view on the way that these have constituted the poor communities as 'pacified spaces', to the extent that their inhabitants can be said to have internalized a form of 'abject urbanism' that actively contributes to sustaining the unequal spatial order of the city. When seen from this perspective, the planned urban transformation of Managua emerges as a systemic form of violence mediated by the workings of infrastructure, a process that I suggest can be termed 'infrastructural violence'. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: Sociological Imagination and the Citation Index
abstract: The relatively insignificant presence of sociology in Citation Index journals serves as prelude to the debate about the identity crisis of sociology. With reference to C. Wright Mills' publication "The Sociological Imagination" (1959), the article extensively explains the three major traps sociology has fallen into: theoretical, methodological, & bureaucratic. Yet, it must be concluded that sociology has an important role to play in the next decades: to help define a society, in which diversity & cohesion need to be reconciled. 2 References. A. Michaux

title: Performance Management and Evaluation in Norwegian Local Government: Complementary or Competing Tools of Management?
abstract: This chapter identifies some important factors that can explain the use of performance management, and discusses how performance management and evaluation can complement each other. The chapter draws on the life-cycle approach to performance management, as well as previous empirical studies of performance management in Norwegian local government. Both performance management and evaluation are subject to organizational and partisan politics, possibly to different degrees. Better utilization of complementarities could improve both performance management and evaluation. Performance management and evaluation compete for institutional power and scarce resources, which affects how well these tools are integrated or developed as competing systems. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucracy and Professions: The Case of Hospital Doctors
abstract: Presented is a cross-national study on the problem of conflict or convergence between bureaucracy & the professions, specifically, the medical profession. Studied are various national relationships between the different national welfare systems. After a review of the literature on organizations & professions, the hospital is defined as a complex organization. A comparison of the evolution of the medical systems in Europe & the US serves as an introduction to the analysis of hospital power structure. Conclusions are drawn about the fundamental role of the state in the process of convergence of the medical profession & the hospital bureaucracy. Modified HA.

title: Barrio Women and Popular Politics in Chavez's Venezuela
abstract: Since President Hugo Chavez came to power in Venezuela in 1998, ordinary women from the barrios, or shantytowns, of Caracas have become more engaged in grassroots politics, but most of the community leaders still are men. Chavez's programs are controlled by male-dominated bureaucracies, and many women activists still look to the president himself as the main source of direction. Nevertheless, this article argues, women's increasing local activism has created forms of popular participation that challenge gender roles, collectivize private tasks, and create alternatives to male-centric politics. Women's experiences of shared struggle from previous decades, along with their use of democratic methods of popular control, help prevent the state from appropriating women's labor. But these spaces coexist with more vertical, populist notions of politics characteristic of official sectors of Chavismo. Understanding such gendered dimensions of popular participation is crucial to analyzing urban social movements. Adapted from the source document.

title: Formal and Informal Rules of Doing Business in Poland in the Context of Accession to the European Union: An Analysis of the Institutional Changes
authors: Bukowski, Andrzej; Gadowska, Kaja; Polak, Paulina
abstract: From the perspective of new institutionalism, this article studies the rules of doing business in Poland in the context of the country's accession to the European Union. The article's starting point is the premise that interaction between formal and informal institutions leads to an institutional balance or imbalance and determines the final shape of the economy and its effectiveness. Accordingly, the authors analyze four types of relations occurring between the formal and informal rules of doing business in Poland: (1) the influence of the restrictiveness of regulations on informal relations between the public administration and business; (2) the relation between the low effectiveness of the law in regards to running a business and informal adaptive reactions; (3) the effects of EU law on business strategies; (4) the effects of the global economy on the extent and forms of cooperation between the public administration and business. Analysis of empirical material provides a basis for constructing four institutional models of the rules of doing business in Poland: the 'antagonistic' model, in which the administration and business are striving for mutually exclusive goals; the 'parallel' model, where formal and informal institutions create separate orders; the 'alternative' model, in which formal, new, EU solutions are created; and the 'integrated' model, where actors are encouraged to realize common aims. Adapted from the source document.

title: White Racism, Social Class, and the Backlash Against Affirmative Action
abstract: Among scholars in sociology and history, the backlash against affirmative action has been blamed on White working-class Americans. What has received far less attention is the individual and collective institutional role(s) played by the White middle and upper middle-class in backlash politics. Given that individuals in these social classes have far greater institutional power than White working-class Americans, their beliefs and practices deserve sustained critical attention, and, as the few existing research studies demonstrate, White middle-class and upper middle-class Americans have played an influential role in backlash politics. Part of the reason for this gap in the literature is that these groups are more difficult to access as research subjects. Gaining access to this population may require working through many levels of a bureaucratic organization designed to protect their time and privacy. Moreover, when interviewed, these Americans are more likely than their working-class counterparts to mask racist sentiments through the polite language of "color blindness." Research methods that complement surveys and in-depth interviews are recommended as strategies for probing White middle and upper middle-class Americans' deeply hidden beliefs. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Current World of Citizenship, the State and Public Administration
abstract: Discusses characteristics of contemporary citizenship, its global form, & its relationship with the state & public administration in the worldwide democratization of public life. A reciprocity between citizenship, public administration, & government is established as necessary for a functioning civil society in the 1990s, where expanded commerce & technology have widened public life around the world. The roles & obligations of public administration & citizenship are listed, each guaranteeing & promoting representation & participation. It is contended that governments must accept globalization as inevitable & structure public administration accordingly, providing for citizenship in the global village. 12 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Informality in the Philippine Civil Service
abstract: Philippine political and bureaucratic organisations are usually presented as weak, permeable, distorted and corrupt and, as such, lie some way from a proper condition of formality. There is no question that informal behaviour can and does have a deleterious effect on the civil service and the organisations it staffs. But it is also clear that, within the bureaucracy, there is a deal of positive informal behaviour. It is suggested here that informality is essential to the day-to-day operation of bureaucratic organisations, a vital source of innovation, and the base material from which the formal is shaped. Possible explanations for the emergence of these qualities are also revealed. There are, in particular, overlapping and mutually reinforcing circumstances or conditions - negative informality, divergent representations, divisions in authority, and over-conformity - that appear to excite positive informality , and that may constitute useful elements in developing an explanatory model of informality in Philippine bureaucracy. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Colonial Response to Population Depletion in Early Congo, ca. 1890-1936
abstract: This article demonstrates that even when the desire for quick economic returns was at the zenith, the administration, companies, & missions took initiatives to reduce the destruction of population, "for the sake of agriculture & mines." While the colonial administration yearned to alter household structure, private companies pursued the policy of high childbirths. In contrast to colonial government officials & private companies' administrators, Catholic missionaries endeavored to change local ideologies, which underpinned biological reproduction, & institutions, which in their understanding created sexual imbalance & low fertility. In different but complementary ways, they sought to eradicate diseases & minimize the negative effects of migrations, porterage, & recruitments on the reproductive capacity of local communities. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaulinguistics: A Practicing Linguist in Central Administration
abstract: Paper presented at the Minnesota Regional Conference on Language and Linguistics, 11-12 May 1984. Some personal experiences involving the use of lang in bureaucratic settings are related. Among the items discussed are the pronunciation of etcetera as /ekseter(schwa)/, the use of the suffix -ize, & the use of euphemisms. B. Annesser Murray

title: Contesting a Hybrid Firm at a Traditional University
abstract: This paper presents a challenge to the idea of what some scholars have called the entrepreneurial university. By applying and elaborating on Thomas Gieryn's concept of boundary work, it offers evidence to the effect that developing an entrepreneurial university is not as straightforward as it may seem from a more generalized perspective. Developing such an entity, at least in the confines of traditional, public-funded universities, is complicated by the emergence of a boundary between public and private activities. This study focuses on a potential hybrid research group: an academic group that sought to fuse its research with potential business activity within an ordinary university department. Controversies over four distinct issues arose: 1) the bureaucratic authority of a department chairman, 2) the allocation of teaching loads, 3) the ownership of research tools and materials and 4) the intellectual property rights of the researchers. Ultimately, the controversy was resolved through a formal written contract that established two boundaries: a border between the social roles of university researchers and those of private entrepreneurs, and a physical separation of the work done by academic projects from that of corporate development. As a result, the hybrid research group/firm was 'purified' into a private entity with no direct ties to the university.  [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Bootstrapping reform: Rebuilding firms, the welfare state, and unions
abstract: The ways in which the to and fro of adjustment between firms, public authorities and labor unions is transforming each while creating the elements of a framework that may encompass and stabilize them all are discussed.  The decentralization of decision making in the firms is the clearest instance and efficient cause of the current restructuring.

title: SOCIAL AND PROFESSIONAL PROBLEMS OF FEMALE EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION
abstract: An attempt to probe the professional & soc problems of F employment in public administration (PA). An inquiry was conducted among F personnel employed in PA in Ghent, Belgium, the sample consisting of 33% of the pop (N=219). After a description of the characteristics of the S's, their professional careers, response to the working group, to their job, & to some aspects of working in PA, are discussed. Separate Chpt's deal with union membership & motives that influence the decision to go to work. Some light is thrown on the measures taken by F's with fam charges to cope with domestic duties & what happens to their offspring during working hours. Some attention is devoted to att's to part-time work. A short note on vacation, leisure activities, & contacts with colleagues outside working hours is added. It is concluded that like most working F's the married F clerks in PA work primarily to improve their financial position & the unmarried & widowed work to provide their financial needs. The psychol'al urge that impels married F's to find interests outside their home environment appears less prevalent than 1 would imagine. Modified HA.

title: Religious diversity in the neoliberal welfare state: Secularity and the ethos of egalitarianism in Sweden
authors: Schenk, Susanne; Burchardt, Marian; Wohlrab-Sahr, Monika
abstract: Sociologists interested in religious change and state-church relations have, by and large, ignored how regimes of religious diversity and secularism interact with factors that are seemingly external to religious dynamics such as cultural notions of the welfare state and its neoliberal restructuring. This article fills this lacuna by exploring the social dynamics around secularity and religious diversity as they emerge in contestations around educational reforms in Sweden. The authors show that the language of 'consumer choice' that pervades discourses around public service provision in many late capitalist societies coalesces with human rights driven legal demands for greater religious freedom in justifying religious pluralism in education. These arguments, though, run up against Swedish understandings of egalitarianism as chiefly implemented through unified schools that are widely, but especially in governmental bureaucracies, viewed as a Swedish 'tradition'. Theoretically, the article develops and builds the concept of 'Multiple Secularities'.

title: A pollution incident at a Qiaoxiang village in China: the role of migration in civic organization and political participation
abstract: Through an analysis of a pollution-based incident at Refinery-G in an infamous Qiaoxiang town in Fujian, China, this paper analyses how transnational migrants participate in and influence the public management activities in their hometowns. This paper underscores four factors driving civic and political participation that emerged during the revelation, resistance, negotiation and settlement of this incident: (1) the role of the 'leisured' villager; (2) the role of overseas Chinese in caring for the developmental path of their hometown; (3) the role of independent civic organizations; and (4) the role of the news media in shaping public opinion. Qiaoxiang's civic participation is both more active and more effective. With the development and globalization of modern communication technology and low-cost and convenient communication and transportation systems, it is possible for overseas migrants to influence public management activities in their hometown through civic organization and political participation.

title: A Progressive Authoritarianism? The case of post-2006 Fiji
abstract: Post-development has matured well beyond the romanticism and celebration of the local of its early proponents. The new 'conditions of possibility' that embody the latest contributions to the field are studies in governmentality. This paper explores the heterogeneous postcolonial spaces of post-2006 Fiji by deploying a Foucauldian analysis of Bainimarama's government, particularly focusing on the formation of identities and the attributes of a 'normalised citizenry'. The analysis aims to help explain why the implementation of a liberal rationality, in the form of racial equality for sociopolitical change in the country, calls for citizens to be subjected to various arts of government -- surveillance, physical and psychological violence and, in some cases, incarceration and torture. An understanding of this brutal and puzzling irony is found in Fiji's colonial legacies and the ongoing contestation over what constitutes a 'normalised citizenry' in the country. I propose that Fiji's present contestations and anomalous coalescence of liberal rationalities and non-liberal means are best explained with reference to the paradoxical notion of progressive authoritarian governmentality. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Serbian Public Administration's Attitudes towards Work
abstract: The aim of this paper is to diagnose the Serbian public administration's attitudes towards work, from the point of view of professional values of employees, normative system of evaluation of administrative tasks, as well as the system of values determined in the Serbian Strategy of Public Administration Reform. Attitudes towards work are considered from the organizational culture concept viewpoint. Several research methods were used: content analyses, review of results of relevant domestic & international researches, & comparative functional analysis of some elements of attitudes towards work in the public administrations of Croatia, Bosnia & Herzegovina & Montenegro. The Serbian public administration's attitudes towards work are evaluated in the conclusion. The evaluation is based on the values defined in the Serbian Strategy of Public Administration Reform. The research results have indicated that the Serbian public administration's attitudes towards work are not in accordance with the state's goal to offer quality service to its citizens. These attitudes could be significantly improved through a change of the public administration's organization culture. Recommendations based on evaluation are created in the human resources framework. Adapted from the source document.

title: Accounting for State Intervention: The Social Histories of 'Beneficiaries'
abstract: How does the state imagine the people? In what ways does it come to know the targets of its policies? This paper examines the transformation of the state through a focus on the visions implied in tools and practices of results-based management in state bureaucracies. When scholars have discussed the state's vision or imagination they have often critically examined how the state constructs aggregates of the population as a whole. But an emphasis on or critique of aggregation can only be the beginning of understanding the multiple and sometimes contradictory ways in which people are imagined in governance today. Results-based management has created a new way in which the state imagines people. In some policy arenas citizens have been turned into 'beneficiaries' through the practices of state managers. Beneficiaries differ from citizen in a number of ways: Citizens are thought to benefit from policies with broad goals; beneficiaries are shown to benefit from specific interventions. Citizens are owed service; beneficiaries are selected for intervention if it suits specific funding priorities. Citizens are the origins of politics and the end of policies; beneficiaries are a means to an organization's success. Adapted from the source document.

title: To Think and Practice Justice
authors: Gruppo di studio di Aggiornamenti Sociali
abstract: The insertion of the territorial connection Berlin-Palermo in the list of priorities of Europe infrastructure has led to heated discussions & controversy. According to this article, the project for the building of the bridge over the Straight of Messina would mean economic advantages to the European Union, Italy & its South. The article answers the objections of the staunchest opponents to the project, & also offers a positive take on the realization of the bridge: the shifting of the geopolitical & economic barycenter of the European Community towards South; increased employment in the South, territorial marketing that would highlight the economic potential of the south, less pollution due to navigation. 2 Figures. Adapted from the source document.

title: Sustainable Cities: Safety and Security
abstract: The major cities of highly industrialized societies are the nodes that connect a mass network of critical infrastructure services. Thus the cities themselves comprise the most critical infrastructure of the society. The resilience & robustness of the infrastructure of cities is thus essential to their sustainability. Since most of enterprises providing these services are privately or corporate owned & are highly competitive, their drive for economic efficiency also tends to make cities increasingly vulnerable to three kinds of disasters: technogenic, natural, & intentional. This paper explores the factors that govern the willingness or reluctance of private & corporate owners of critical services to invest in catastrophic risk reduction & the degree of public-private cooperation required to make cities more sustainable. Ultimately some changes in the political relationship between cities & states & the national governments that exercise sovereign authority over them will be required, as cities become the primary structure for the social & economic lives of people everywhere. References. [Copyright 2005 Elsevier Ltd.]

title: 'Techniques' for governance
abstract: Issues relating to governance are among the most critical in terms of sustaining viable political and social arrangements.  In terms of democracies and their bureaucratic organizations, understanding how governing works leads to improved understandings of how to government best.

title: INJUSTICE AND BUREAUCRACY
abstract: Not every power-wielder within a bur'cy craves authority or is unjust, but insofar as the position calls to & molds character, it produces those in whom burns little passion for justice. Whether control over others, or simply success, is a central need of a man's personality, the quest for position & power may blind him to the ends of others. Friendship or love might conquer this unconcern for others, but these qualities have small place in hierarchical relations. To find justice in the fam, where everyone counts, is hard enough; to find it in a bur'cy, where no one counts, is infinitely more difficult. IPSA.

title: The Appointed Burgomaster: Appointments and Careers of Burgomasters in the Netherlands
abstract: Dutch burgomasters (or mayors) are appointed by the Queen through her Ministers for a term of six years. The Minister of Internal Affairs appoints mayors for cities under 50,000 population after a recommendation by the Queen's Commissioner in the Province. For cities with more than 50,000 inhabitants & provincial capitals the appointment is considered by the entire cabinet. Almost without exception the burgomasters appointed are members of the five (presently three), major political parties in the Netherlands. The procedure is similar to a modified 'spoils system', in particular to the appointments of US federal judges. However, it is only by exception that a party profits by having a Minister in the Home Office. By far the most important criterion by which burgomasters are apportioned to the political parties is the communalistic one. This means that a person appointed burgomaster should be of the same political persuasion as the dominant subculture in the community. The criterion of proportionality (each party getting the same share of burgomasters as it has of the votes in national elections) plays only a secondary role. Once appointed, burgomasters tend to make a career in the mayorality only. The larger the number of inhabitants of a municipality, the more influence & SS its burgomaster has, & the higher his income is. Consequently, a burgomaster can make a career by seeking appointment as burgomaster in a larger municipality or by population growth in his own municipality. These two career-patterns are negatively correlated, indicating that they are not cumulative, but rather that population growth may compensate for not getting promoted to a larger community. The findings about the political aspects of mayoral appointments are based on data about all burgomasters in office in 1970. The conclusions about the mayoral careers are based on similar data for 1975. 6 Tables, 1 Figure. AA.

title: Japanese Bureaucrats and Policy Implementation: Lessons for America?
abstract: It is widely agreed that policy implementation in the US involves considerable 'slippage' between policy intent & achievement; by contrast, Japanese public policy is usually implemented effectively & efficiently. It is argued that allowing civil servants to participate more fully in policy formulation, & the development of an elite corps of top civil servants would contribute to better policy making & implementation in the US. 45 References. Modified HA

title: Celebrating Distinctions: Common And Conspicuous Weddings In Rural Namibia
abstract: In many parts of southern Africa, weddings have become expensive, blending local ritual practices with Western middle-class consumption habits. Ethnographic fieldwork in the Fransfontein region of northwest Namibia indicates that the transformations in wedding consumption are linked to social class formation. Until the 1970s, wedding celebrations in Fransfontein were relatively modest affairs. With the establishment of new bureaucracies and the emergence of localized elites at the end of the 1970s, wedding celebrations gradually developed into costly celebrations of class distinction. An important outcome of this is that it has become increasingly more difficult for most people to marry; consequently, marriage rates have substantially declined. Adapted from the source document.

title: Making Organizations Work; Exploring Characteristics of Anti-Oppressive Organizational Structures in Street Youth Shelters
abstract: * Summary: Human service organizations are often viewed by clients                as bureaucratic, formal, oppressive and insensitive environments. Through structured                interviews with 42 service providers and 65 street youth in Toronto, Montreal and                Guatemala, and participant and non-participant observations in all three locations,                this analysis explores tenets of antioppressive organizational structures within the                youth shelter construct.* Findings: Anti-oppressive organizations allow for the emergence                of meaningful and vibrant community settings by embracing grass-root social                development, active participation, a structural analysis of the problem,                consciousness raising and social action. These findings can be interpreted as                lessons from the field - noting what seems to work best for hard-core and                marginalized street youth populations. The current academic discourse concerning                notions of anti-oppression has tended to focus upon pedagogy and/or practice; this                analysis moves the discussion to a new realm involving organizational behavior.                Anti-oppressive organizational structures attempt to build safe and respectful                environments for marginalized populations.* Applications: Such findings can hopefully impact the manner by                which social work administrators and practitioners understand service delivery                within their particular organizational setting and more specifically, how they                conduct meaningful social work within their day-to-day practices.

title: Institutional Analysis and Decentralization: Developing an Analytical Framework for Effective Third World Administrative Reform
abstract: Scholarly studies over several decades have generally concluded that the centralized, hierarchical, bureaucratic administrative model for Third World (TW) countries has failed. Research findings have stimulated efforts to change both policies & programs in these countries, including a reorientation to rural & agricultural development of the World Bank & decentralization of TW governments. It is recommended that institutional analysis be used to explore (& improve) the performance of TW administrative systems. In a proposed eight-variable analytical model, key features of given goods or services & their production processes are the level of analysis, & the individuals responsible for producing those goods or services are the unit of analysis. Also examined are variations of institutional arrangements, explaining how they neutralize or reinforce the incentives & disincentives to produce various goods & services. 73 References. S. Millett

title: Europas ,,Bewegungslandschaft" oder was ist europäische Zivilgesellschaft?
abstract: What is European Civil Society? Against the background of personal observations of the European crisis landscape, this deliberately provocative article argues against an uncritically enthusiastic support for "grassroots-driven" civil society politics -- an attitude that is often encountered, including in the Forschungsiournal Soziale Bewegungen. Even though Europe's multiple crises have increased calls for civil society participation and indeed led to the emergence of multiple movements, these actors -- according to the author - lack adequate and comprehensive answers to Europe's fundamental systemic crisis. Calls for participation and protest are not enough. Civil society actors can at best scrape at the surface of the real problem, which is that the institutional set of the European Community and its actors have ceased to function. European civil society thus heralds European politicisation, but not European politics. The article argues for a return to the emphasis on institutional politics in Europe and for a consistent Europeanization of political processes, bureaucracies and decision-making structures.

title: Research in Societal Organization: Max Weber and Thoughts on a Historical Theory of Bureaucracy
abstract: It is argued that current Swedish social science lacks theories & analyses of the development of societal organization. One such analysis of industrial capitalism is presented, tracing its development & organization from the late nineteenth century to modern times. The analysis is based on Max Weber's science-theoretical & historical usage of the notion of "bureaucracy.". 1 Figure. Adapted from the source document as translated

title: Telework in a European Perspective
abstract: The objectives & activities of the European Foundation for the Improvement of Living & Working Conditions, an autonomous European Union (EU) body instituted in 1975 & based in Dublin, Ireland, are presented, highlighting initiatives in the field of flexible work time & telework. The foundation's cooperation with the European Commission is mentioned, & results of a survey on telework in public administration in EU member countries, conducted for both organizations by Fritz Betz, Johanna Riegler, & Irene Schwarz, of the Center for Social Innovation in Vienna, Austria, are presented. Findings indicate that telework is only marginally practiced, & its introduction is linked primarily to matters of urban planning & traffic congestion reduction. It is frequently motivated by the integration of the disabled into the mainstream workforce. The flexibility of workload & time management & the reduction of commuting cost & time are cited as the principal causes for the introduction of telework into the domain of public administration. Alternating telework with office work is the dominant pattern, & practitioners' positive experiences outnumber negative ones. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Effects of Social and Institutional Change on Data Production. The Case of Welfare State Reforms on the Rise and Decline of Unemployment and Care-Giving in the German Pension Fund Data
abstract: Using longitudinal life-course data of the German pension fund, the paper discusses effects of first-time institutionalization and of institutional filters on data production on the fields of unemployment and care-giving. Concerning (1) first time institutionalization, the data show at certain historical moments an increase/decrease which is due to the new institutional rules and regulations and not to a drastic social change. This period effect is important if different age cohorts are compared at the same age, but different social policy periods are encompassed. (2) Institutional filters also influence the gathered information due to eligibility rules: The change in the unemployment assistance scheme resulted in an increase of the number of the registered unemployed, but the longitudinal data show that the registered unemployed have also been partly exchanged. Adapted from the source document.

title: "WHOSE NEEDS ARE BEING SERVED?" QUANTITATIVE METRICS AND THE RESHAPING OF SOCIAL SERVICES
Cleansing Procedures for Overlaps and Inconsistencies in Administrative Data. The Case of Length of Unemployment in German Labour Market Data
abstract: Surveys often cope with special problems: gaps in retrospection appear or respondents could not provide details. Sometimes these problems can be solved by using additional qualitative information. Another - so far disregarded - possibility is to use process-generated data to expand survey data. The focus of this article is on the potentials and problems of linking administrative and survey data. In particular this is shown by comparison of retrospective survey information on employment cycles and the according process-generated data. Adapted from the source document.

title: Documents and Bureaucracy
abstract: This review surveys anthropological and other social research on bureaucratic documents. The fundamental insight of this literature is that documents are not simply instruments of bureaucratic organizations, but rather are constitutive of bureaucratic rules, ideologies, knowledge, practices, subjectivities, objects, outcomes, even the organizations themselves. It explores the reasons why documents have been late to come under ethnographic scrutiny and the implications for our theoretical understandings of organizations and methods for studying them. The review argues for the great value of the study of paper-mediated documentation to the study of electronic forms, but it also highlights the risk of an exclusive focus on paper, making anthropology marginal to the study of core bureaucratic practices in the manner of earlier anthropology. Adapted from the source document.

title: Questions Connected with the Reform of Public Administration in Slovakia in Regard to the Nationally Mixed Areas
authors: Bacova, Viera; Homisinova, Maria; Cooper, Marc-Philippe
abstract: Explores how public administration reform in the context of overall decentralization has impacted ethnic minorities in independent Slovakia. Models of centralized public & locally controlled administration are contrasted. From the standpoint of ethnic Hungarians, the fragmentation of individual political & administrative units is needed to create smaller territorial structures, interconnecting points between the local unit & the center. Since summer 1991 a guarantee of representation has been sought for the Hungarian minority. Other proposals have been made to treat the Slovak & Hungarian communities as equal partners. The Hungarian position has been to seek autonomy in the areas of culture & education, to increase the authority of local government, to define boundaries of administrative units in relation to minorities, & to guarantee language rights in bilingual areas. 11 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The American New State of Mary Parker Follett
abstract: This research tries to answer one of the major questions that has been discussed in the literature of Public Administration (PA) repeatedly. The question is: Has 21st century American government succeeded in achieving a genuinely democratic administration where efficiency and democratic values are reconciled? The main argument of this research is that it has not been possible in spite of the calls of many public administration theories which have encouraged the adoption of Follett's equation based on the partnership between efficient government and active citizen participation. The research argues that Follett's assertion sounds rather optimistic but it has not been implemented seriously on the ground. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Formulation of Principles in Public Administration
abstract: This article has an aim to make it evident that public administration, such as other social sciences, has stated from its origin the elevated epistemological problems regarding its disciplinary condition. And that its scientific statute, ever since, has lived with the same objections as the kindred disciplines. Certainly arid, the epistemological problem has not been alien to it, so that public administration is not a barren land in that set of topics dealt with inside its pages. Adapted from the source document.

title: THE BUREAUCRACY AS DOMINANT CLASS
abstract: An examination of the theoretical position advanced in Claude Lefort's ELEMENTS OF A CRITIQUE OF THE BUR- EAUCRACY (Geneve-Paris, France: Librairie Droz, 1971), which Is both a work of sociol & of pol'al set. Soctoilly, it is the best example of the Frankfort Sch, a discourse on the society & not an array of soc facts. For most professional pol'al sci'ts, Lefort's position is too critical with respect to org's, & too individualistic to be considered seriously. Lefort focuses on the relations between the burley & the communist parties, which is closer to the center of his analyses than is the question of the state. The 1st part of Lefort's work is made up of texts dealing with instit'al practice & history, while the 2nd part is consecrated to the 'crisis of totalitarianism,' ie, various attempts to maintain Stalinism & processes of destalinization following the Cold War. M. Duke.

title: When Clients Complain: Bureaucratic Responsiveness in Large Federal Agencies
abstract: High error rates in entitlements & slow responses to client complaints by federal agencies are analyzed from a market-power frame of reference, focusing on the relative powerlessness of agency clients in relation to the agencies themselves, which hold monopolies of life-sustaining benefits. Data from a survey of 125 members of the US Congress are presented to provide an estimate of error rates. Three alternative structural solutions to the problem of unresponsiveness are assessed, including increased congressional casework service, ombudsmen services, & the use of federal information centers to aid clients. Necessary quality control procedures to facilitate each solution are described. 2 Tables. Modified HA.

title: Administrative Modernisation and the Logic of Politics
abstract: On the basis of data from a current research project, this article examines the extent to which administrative modernisation in keeping with the New Steering Model (NSM) has changed the relationship between local politics and administration. This field of modernisation has evidenced the least change. No overall improvement in political controllability is in evidence; on the contrary, a loss of local government control is more likely. One key reason for this development is that the promoters of NSM have misconceived the rationale underlying political action. Adapted from the source document.

title: Public Policy and Public Employee Strikes
abstract: Study is made of the impact of public policy, as reflected in state public employee bargaining laws, on public employee strike levels. To explore the impact of policy, data were gathered by states for 3 employee groups--teachers, local government employees (excluding police & firefighters), & state government employees. Four ratio scale measures of strike activity were used as dependent variables, with separate measurements being made for each employee group. These indicators of strike activity were correlated with six independent variables hypothesized to be antecedents of public employee strikes, as well as three indices of legal policy. Statistical analysis indicated some of the hypothesized relationships are either insignificant or significant but in the wrong direction, & there are substantial differences among the three employee groups in terms of which variables are significant. Various explanations exist for why state legal policy had so little impact, eg, only formal state legal policies were measured--policies in practice may be very different, or since the analysis dealt only with one outcome variable (strikes), it provides a necessarily limited view of the role of policy as an intervening variable. For instance, state policy might have a more substantial effect on labor-management cooperation or on the terms of agreements than on strikes. 2 Tables. AA.

title: Elites and Agencies: Forging Labor Policy at China's Central Level
abstract: A synergy between bureaucratic bargaining theory & elite analysis theory is created to evaluate the development of central-level labor policy in post-Mao China. Interviews were conducted throughout the People's Republic of China with members of various labor service companies & employment management agencies in an effort to show how the conditions of workers can be ascertained through studying the central government. A strong tie between bureaucratic agencies & elites is present in China. When elites are in disagreement over economic policy, as they were during the 1980s & much of the 1990s, bureaucratic agencies seem unable to function cooperatively. In the late 1990s, however, two opposing groups of elites managed to achieve a consensus, & this led to cooperative behavior among bureaucratic agencies, who were able to sustain the threatened Reemployment Project, set up to help laid-off state workers find new employment. 74 References. D. Weibel

title: Support for torture over time: Interrogating the American public about coercive tactics
authors: Mayer, Jeremy D; Armor, David J
abstract: In this study, we examine what influences public attitudes toward torture and whether the public's attitude affects or is affected by shifts in presidential policy on torture. We employed ten surveys over five years that looked at approval of torture, as well as two surveys that asked questions about specific methods. We find that public support for torture has risen mildly, but a resilient ambivalence best describes the public's attitude. The public was not affected by the change in government from an administration that strongly supported enhanced interrogation techniques to one that opposed them, and labeled them torture. Public opinion also seemed unaffected by the increased criticism of torture generally. Large majorities oppose most specific methods of interrogation, while at times a majority supports torture in general. We also find support for torture and specific methods is affected most strongly by partisanship and ideology. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Captain Planet and the Planeteers: Kids, environmental crisis, and competing narratives of the new world order
abstract: An environmental cartoon is critiqued as representing and promoting a liberal environmental paradox espousing a simultaneous call for children to both conserve and consume and simplistic solutions to complex corporate and bureaucratic problems.

title: Bureaucracy and Rural Development
abstract: Examines the current problems & potential benefits of refined bureaucratic participation in rural development in Third World nations.
