abstract: In formulating social policy the administrative arm of government relies heavily on number-based significations of knowledge, such as needs indicators & performance measures. Relying on numbers increases administrators' confidence in their decisions & shifts responsibility for error away from the decision-maker & towards the numbers. A close examination of the technology of social quantification reveals instability in many of the definitions & codes that needs analysts & program evaluators adopt when numerically inscribing social entities. To deal with these risks, bureaucracies must establish ways of explicitly assessing the uncertainty, imprecision & social construction that often lies behind the evidence presented as numbers, evidence that can easily be accepted on face value & be turned uncritically into decision-making rationales. References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The army of 'unemployed' young people
abstract: Youth employment has jumped to the forefront of the international development agenda, especially with regards to stabilizing so-called fragile states. Liberia is a case in point. Here post-conflict stability has been cast as deeply connected to the issue of youth idleness. The objective of the article is first to show how the provision of jobs and the idea of youth employment is given paramount importance for the stabilization of fragile post-conflict states like Liberia and the achievement of a 'liberal' peace. In what way precisely does unemployment constitute a problem? Is Liberian youth jobless? What about the place of informality and hustling in the livelihood strategies of youth? I address the issue of unemployment, security and the role of 'informality' in the lives of youth drawing on ethnographic material. I use one of my informants, Adonis, to situate and contextualize the discussion. The intention is to turn upside down the bureaucratic gaze that categorizes youth merely as 'unemployed' and show the way in which Adonis, like thousands of other youngsters, engages in the 'informal' economy.

title: Gender and Style in Bureaucracy
authors: Lahti, Georgia Duerst; Johnson, Cathy Marie
abstract: Using data from a survey of Wisconsin professional and executive civil servants, this article examines the gendered nature of the Weberian bureaucracy by exploring respondents' behavioral styles and their views of the ideal bureaucrat. We find that the preferred bureaucrat is gender neutral with equal value placed on feminine and masculine characteristics. Both women and men cross gender stereotypes in their behavioral styles as well as in their perceptions of good administrators and good colleagues. Women shun negative masculine and feminine traits while endorsing those traits valued most by bureaucrats, especially those important for achieving results.For a complete reprint of this article contact Haworth Press by telephone (1-800-HAWORTH) or EMail (getinfo@haworthpressinc.com) Article copyright The Haworth Press, Inc.

title: Russia in a global system of social coordinates: A sociological analysis and prognosis
abstract: The article is an abridged version of a report that was presented at the Second Congress of Russian Sociologists. The author develops four stages of the social modernization of Russia. The first two stages occurred from 1985 to 1987 and encouraged the socio-economic development and democratization of the country. The third and fourth stages, which began after the collapse of the Soviet Union, were characterized by massive economic modernization. This was a highly ideological process that placed an absolute value on market economics. This economic shock therapy came with a sharp decline in social morale. Survey data show that a majority of those polled believe that the Russian government expresses and defends the interests of only rich citizens. The survey also shows the population's indifference to the bureaucratization of power. The author then enumerates the factors which determine Russia's position in the world, which includes the volume of foreign investing, patent and invention activity, and steady social development, and shows that Russia performs poorly according to all of these factors. The Index of the Development of Human Potential also demonstrates the uneven socio-economic development of the population. K. Cargill

title: Gender, Myth and Fable: The Perils of Mainstreaming in Sector Bureaucracies
abstract: This article examines how gender & development discourses & frameworks were appropriated into development policy & practice through gender mainstreaming efforts in developing country sector bureaucracies. It uses an example of an attempt to mainstream gender equity objectives into a large health sector program in a national bureaucracy heavily reliant on external aid. It argues that these efforts mis-specify the nature & role of bureaucracies. A health sector bureaucracy should be expected to improve health systems, not act as an engine of social & political transformation. This is linked to failure to understand the policy domain & how gender & development advocates can engage with it. Two main questions are explored. How did the project of social transformation become translated into practice in the increasingly professionalized world of gender & development? How were the links between theory, policy, & practice rendered unproblematic by naivety about "policy" & how progressive change comes about? 7 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Motivation to Manage: A Study of Women in Chinese State-Owned Enterprises
authors: Chen, Chao C; Yu, K C; Miner, J B
abstract: Using 1989 & 1992 scale data from 82 women & 121 men in the People's Republic of China, women's motivation to manage is assessed in relation to managerial success in state-owned enterprises. Results indicate that overall managerial motivation of Chinese women is as high as that of men, & overall managerial motivation is positively related to hierarchical job level in both men & women. However, while motives to exercise power predicted job levels for both men & women, motivations to stand out from the group predicted only women's job levels, & motivations regarding competition & routine administrative functions predicted only men's job levels. Results support the applicability of J. B. Miner's (1993) hierarchic role motivation theory in Chinese bureaucratic organizations. Research & practical implications of the study are discussed. 3 Tables, 42 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucracies of mass deception: Institutional review boards and the ethics of ethnographic research
authors: Bosk, Charles L; De Vries, Raymond G
abstract: Ethnographers have long been unhappy with the review of their research proposals by institutional review boards (IRBs). In this article, we offer a sociological view of the problems associated with prospective IRB review of ethnographic research. Compared with researchers in other fields, social scientists have been less willing to accommodate themselves to IRB oversight; we identify the reasons for this reluctance, and in an effort to promote such accommodation, we suggest several steps to reduce the frustration associated with IRB review of ethnographic research. We conclude by encouraging ethnographers to be alert to the ways the procedural and bureaucratic demands of IRBs can displace their efforts to solve the serious ethical dilemmas posed by ethnography. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Public imprisonment by private means
abstract: The US, the UK and Australia are the only countries that have so far moved to delegate operations of imprisonment facilities to private entities.  The development of private prisons in the US, the UK and Australia is discussed.  The role of the government in prison administration in the US, the UK and Australia is addressed.

title: GENDER, LABOUR, AND STATE FORMATION IN SIXTEENTH-CENTURY SWEDEN
abstract: This article examines how the system for organizing resources created by the Swedish state in the sixteenth century was formed by, and intersected with, local societies. By looking at the organization of the local administration and economic production within crown demesnes and estates, this article nuances and broadens the understanding of the early phases of the fiscal-military state. It shows that notions about gender and especially the gender division of labour were important for the organization and further development of the state in its endeavour to mobilize and transform resources. This article argues that gendered divisions of labour and traditional ways of organizing work and administration played a crucial role in the first phases of early modern Swedish state formation; women's work affected the organization of the state and vice versa. By looking at the emergence of the male official and the all-male bureaucracy from a gender perspective, and by emphasizing the household as an organizational form, the present study contributes to the understanding of both state formation and gender relations in the early modern period. Adapted from the source document.

title: Checkpoint Watch: Bureaucracy and Resistance at the Israeli/Palestinian Border
abstract: This article sketches my personal impression of the changes that have occurred over the last decade in the Israeli checkpoints in and around Jerusalem. These changes have manifested both in the physical design of the checkpoints and in their human management. I discuss these changes through focusing on the women's human rights organization 'MachsomWatch'. The role of this organization, I claim here, has changed in ways that parallel the solidification and the bureaucratization of the border. Especially noticeable is the shift in the location of resistance and its characterization, from a direct confrontation model that occurs at the physical space of the border to a focus on legal actions and administrative strategies, performed in distant and at times even virtual locations. Alongside this process, MachsomWatch women -- avid protestors of Israel's occupation of the Palestinian West Bank -- have, despite themselves, become a routine feature of Israel's occupational apparatus. This essay's grounded ethnographic account provides a vivid illustration of the ways in which resistance feeds from and into power. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: America at Risk: Threats to Liberal Self-Government in an Age of Uncertainty
abstract: America at Risk: Threats to Liberal Self-Government in an Age of Uncertainty edited by Robert Faulkner and Susan Shell is reviewed.

title: The Foundation of Merit: Public Service in American Democracy
abstract: Nigro reviews "The Foundation of Merit:  Public Service in American Democracy" by Patricia Wallace Ingraham.

title: War, the state and the formation of the North Korean industrial working class, 1931-60
abstract: This article examines how Koreans became industrial workers in the first and second phases of industrialisation on the peninsula: under Japanese colonial rule, 1931-45 and under the DPRK's post-Korean War heavy industrialisation, 1953-60. While the political regimes of the Japanese colony and postcolonial DPRK were different, industrialisation occurred under similar conditions, characterised principally by war, state capitalism and imperialism. Processes of proletarianisation also reveal similarities in the two periods, including the widespread use of forced mobilisation and immobilisation of workers, and a bureaucratic apparatus supporting close control of labour. The article contributes to the critique of conventional views about the role of 'free wage labour' during the transition to capitalism.

title: White Collar Crime: Re-Examination of a Concept
abstract: Crimes uncovered in the Watergate scandal in the US point to the need to reevaluate the basis & thrust of sociological theories of criminality, & particularly, white-collar crime. Since 1950 there has been an escalation of the stakes of political victories & payoffs as bureaucratic government has become intertwined with giant business. Thus, crime is now being committed by established, favored groups that are already successful. New opportunity structures create revolutions of rising expectations in which socially favored groups seek to more fully exploit & maintain their favored positions. None of the prevailing theories of criminality can explain this phenomenon, including those of Edwin H. Sutherland (eg, White Collar Crime [see SA 9:4/61A0863]) & Robert K. Merton (no reference given), or consensus, deviance, or labeling theories. Max Weber's theory of bureaucracy & legitimacy, though descriptive of his time, also failed to foresee the possibility of bureaucracy as a means of criminal activity. Sociologists have focused on blue-collar crimes & delinquency; perhaps they are afraid to tackle problems closer to home. Modified AA

title: EL PROYECTO CIUDADES RURALES SUSTENTABLES Y EL INVOLUCRAMIENTO DE SUS HABITANTES
abstract: En 2007 el gobierno de Chiapas instauró el proyecto Ciudades Rurales Sustentables (crs) que propuso reacomodar a la localidad de Ostuacán y Santiago El Pinar en centros poblacionales con infraestructura, servicios básicos y vivienda. Los habitantes de esas comunidades aceptaron los recursos que llevó el proyecto, pero éstos no contribuyeron a mejorar su calidad de vida. Esta investigación da cuenta de las diversas formas en que los “beneficiarios” participaron y usaron los recursos del proyecto crs.

title: Patterns in Welfare: A Bureaucracy to Neighborhood Services
abstract: In Mar 1968 a pilot study project was undertaken by the Los Angeles County Dept of Public Soc Services to study the feasibility of creating neighborhood fam day care services in poverty areas of the city. This paper discusses this exp & identifies the program as representing a transitory phase in the shift of services from a centralized bur'cy of welfare into a neighborhood based setting. The need for decentralized welfare services to poor communities is underscored. Despite criticism, there has been a limited & rigid response to changing the functional components of the system of public welfare. In the present program 2 problems were attacked: providing new & community based services, & enhancing the employment opportunities for the poor. Recruitment & selection processes are reviewed. The final group of participants were 21 mothers from Watts & Venice who were known to Soc Services as having received aid. The Neighborhood Fam Day Care Parent Training Program involved a series of brief but intense group-oriented programs: (1) special structured classroom educ'al sessions; (2) experiential learning through site-field activity; & (3) equi-spaced small group evaluative sensitivity sessions. The curriculum focused on child care, HB, health care, & first aid. 6 S's were hired as day care parents, & today neighborhood fam day care homes are located within the neighborhoods of the fam's who use them. However, several concerns remain to be examined: Whether the purpose of such programs is to involuntarily force the recipient into work attainment; whether the training programs lead to jobs which are not in "terminal-employment categories," but rather represent career-line job opportunities; & do the delivery patterns of the new services closely coincide with the life styles & needs of the service users. The project's importance can be judged positively in that it demonstrated that an important stage--the transition of needed services from the large, impersonal, bur'tic system of public soc welfare to an accessible community location--is not only feasible but possible. Modified HA.

title: Exchange between Superiors and Subordinates in Large Organizations
authors: Marcus, Philip M; House, James S
abstract: Soc exchange theory is drawn upon to formulate hyp's about superior-subordinate relations in large, complex org's. The behavior of superiors was divided into 2 modal types: expressive & instrumental, on the basis of a reconceptualization in terms of exchange theory of the HR & Weberian models of supervisory behavior. It was predicted that both modes of behavior increased the subordinates' soc profit & resulted in increased loyalty to the superior, greater compliance with his demands, & reduced conflict between the 2 org'al levels. However, the intermediary exchange processes differ in the 2 categorizations. Expressive behavior de-emphasizes status distinctions & fosters a supportive work environment. It thus reduces the subordinates' costs of interaction on the job. Instrumental behavior maintains status distinctions between the 2 levels, while providing rewards to subordinates. Data from self-admin'ed questionnaires, collected from 180 subordinates & 21 superiors at the 1st, 2nd, & 3rd echelons of a large, midwestern Co, support the hyp's derived from the theoretical model & suggest the usefulness of further res based on soc exchange theory. 2 Tables. Modified HA.

title: When safety culture backfires: Unintended consequences of half-shared governance in a high tech workplace
abstract: This paper applies concepts from the sociology and anthropology of organizations to understand limits to the implementation of a more effective safety culture in the workplace. It highlights unintended consequences of combining bureaucratic control and shared governance and identifies sources of inertia within already existing safety cultures. The data come from focus group interviews with workers in a research and development facility of a multinational corporation in the Western U.S. It is found that safety protocols, rules, and rhetoric, combined with efforts to give workers more responsibility for safety in the workplace, create tendencies toward worker alienation, shame with regard to injuries, complacency, and fear of bureaucratic processes. Therefore it appears that some efforts to create safety culture in the workplace may unintentionally undermine the goal of manufacturing safety. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Revisiting Second Image Reversed: Lessons from Turkey and Thailand
abstract: This article draws attention to some surprising similarities between the recent political trajectories of Turkey and Thailand in order to argue that international norms strongly shape domestic cleavage formations. The timing and the manner of incorporation of particular states into the international system affects not only their political and economic development, but also the way various domestic groups see their mission, their identity, and their opposition. In both Turkey and Thailand, what development has brought is neither the opposition between traditional status groups and the market generated social forces, nor the tradition/religion‐based opposition to modernization and democracy that is typically assumed to mark developing societies. What we find in both cases instead is a modernization‐generated statist/bureaucratic social middle class that justifies its skepticism of democratization on the basis of norms upheld by the international society itself.

title: REFLECTIONS ON PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION AND NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
abstract: 2 levels of reflection are noted: (1) concerning the practical problems involved in the transplantation of modern' or 'Western' instit's into the newly developing nations, & (2) whether current soc sci theories or methodologies offer any promise of helping to solve the deeper problems involved in 'importing' instit's. The ambiguities & mysteries of the concept of development are discussed; is development a process that can be followed without regard to diff cultural environments, geopol'al limitations & temporal dimensions? The instit of major interest is burley, & M. Weber's characterization of this instit as the most rational & efficient means of achieving collective purposes is found to be quite ethnocentric: the question is whether indeed any attempt to find generalizations about org's that transcend cultural specificity can provide much more than common sense wisdom. It is argued that decisions to adopt admin'ive or other instit's are not value-neutral choices. These decisions will often irrevocably decide the life style & destiny of the nation. Thus cultural & value dispositions of a nation are parameters that limit any rational choice of instit'al means. AA.

title: An Asian Perspective on the Global City
abstract: The transformation of several Asian cities into global cities -- centers of control, management, & finance that are network dependent & technologically oriented -- has resulted in a changing socieconomic milieu. Described are ways in which cities in Asia are developing infrastructure to prepare themselves for the roles of global cities, & in which land use patterns, employment structure, & population composition have changed. Implications are drawn for inhabitants' daily lives, including some of the negative consequences. 1 Photograph, 15 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: 'One country, three systems': The recruitment of administrative elites in Portugal, 1999-2009
abstract: What is the position of the Portuguese administrative elites in terms of professional autonomy and politicization recruitment patterns? In Portugal there prevails a pattern of professional autonomy at central government; however, this pattern has certain clientelist traits at the local administrative level. The Portuguese case also reveals a new kind of politicization in public administration agencies - in line with what happens in other Western democracies. Portugal has a hybrid administrative elite recruitment pattern, containing elements of professional autonomy at the central government, elements of political control at the agencies level and even clientelist elements at the state local branches. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: From the Credibility Crisis of Formal Organizations to the Re-Emergence of the Group: An Ecosystemic Approach
abstract: The concept of ecosystem is used here as a paradigm for analyzing the current problems of credibility suffered by large bureaucratic, political, or managerial organizations. The process of social globalization & the crisis of the postmodern era form the context of these problems. Collective uncertainty & pessimism have increased, especially since the balance of power collapsed between East & West at the end of the Cold War & in the present welfare state crisis. In these circumstances, an existential environment emerges in which social bonds are also in crisis. In response to the individual absorption brought about by formal organizations, there is now a trend toward the reemergence of fundamentalisms or social movements of a strong community or group nature. 36 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Patterns of Growth in Welfare Bureaucracies
abstract: A longitudinal study of the growth of 46 state welfare departments is described, taking as a point of departure a closed system model of organizational growth. The various components (central office size & managerial, caseworker, & clerical components) are analyzed in terms of: (1) the relationship between the initial size of a component & its growth rate; (2) a comparison of different components; & (3) the influence of increased work load & environmental complexity on the growth of components. The findings indicate that, for the central office, managerial, & clerical components, initial size & growth rate are negatively related. The casework component accounts for the greatest amount of total organizational growth & is directly affected by increased work load. Finally, the growth of the managerial component is directly influenced by both increased work load & environmental complexity (ie, urbanization). 3 Tables. AA.

title: THE PROFESSIONAL SOCIAL WORKER IN A BUREAUCRACY
abstract: The experiences of neophyte professional soc workers in a large public agency are described. The soc worker is on a low level of authority & power & is admin'ively responsible to an ascending hierarchy. An analysis of the supervisor-worker transactions reveals a bur'tic structure in which the soc worker is manipulated for the preservation of the status quo. He must struggle on behalf of his clients from a position of powerlessness. In being an impassioned advocate for his clients he comes into conflict with agency admin'ors as well as professional colleagues. If he finds no support from colleagues & org's representing the clients he is forced to leave the agency; if he remains & eventually becomes a supervisor, he has to 'play the game,' which includes accepting the meager systemic inputs & the dysfunctional aspects of the bur'tic structure. The bur'tic system stimulates & reinforces defensive rather than coping behavior by keeping the worker off balance. The emotional & physical fatigue caused by large caseloads & the structural restraints of the bur'cy often drive him to avoid meaningful contacts with his clients through compulsive defensive behavior. The importance of informal org's for letting off steam is discussed. Gripe sessions provide emotional support for the worker & deflect his need for a more formally org'ed, systematic approach to his problem as a worker in a bur'cy. It is time for the soc work profession, bur'crats, & Sch's of soc work to face up to facts about the bur'tic nature of soc work agencies. A new vision is needed to reconstruct the working lives of soc workers, & new ways must be found for them to relate to each other & to those they serve. M. Maxfield.

title: Systems Theory and Organization Change: A Case Study
abstract: A case study of a voluntary Jewish Employment & Vocational Service is presented. The agency's development from the 1940's to the 1960's is traced. A theoretical framework of org'al change is used which utilizes Talcott Parsons' AGIL (see SA 0312/D8260). The model specifies 3 developmental stages: self-interest, professionalism, & soc interest. The central question is whether an org retains its unique identity & character as it moves through the developmental stages. It is found that this agency has functioned as an autonomous & integrated system, controlling its development & change on the basis of its functional requirements. Relationships with other agencies also changed from an initial involvement only with other Jewish services to a broader participation in the general health & welfare community. Parsons' model proved useful. Modified HA.

title: Space for pluralism? Examining the Malibya land grab
abstract: Recent years have seen a flood of pseudo-facts and falsely precise data on land deals. This has led some to call for a more careful approach to the study of land deals that moves away from the current hectare-centric focus towards a grounded case-study methodology. Heeding such calls, this contribution draws on fieldwork undertaken in Mali during 2011 to examine a well-known land deal, the Malibya project, which involved a contract for the transfer of control of 100,000 hectares of land within the Office du Niger. Locally and globally, the deal was denounced following the destruction of homes and gardens as a result of a canal development associated with project. In contrast, the Malian government has argued such projects are vital for expanded irrigation infrastructure and thus securing food self-sufficiency for Mali. Somewhere in between are the farmers of the Office du Niger, some of whom argue for the cessation of the project and others of whom argue the expansion of irrigation in the zone could benefit farmers, particularly those without sufficient access to land. This paper explores the differing viewpoints of the actors involved and the role the land-grabbing frame has played in mobilising these different responses.

title: Which penology for decision making in French prisons?
abstract: This article argues that while France's old penology remains well defended due to professional discretion and individualization of professional judgment in high security prisons (maisons centrales), a new penal trend akin to an actuarial justice is observed in detention centres. This trend consists in governing 'at a distance' a mixed population of very different prisoner types. However, a cacophony of voices in the decision-making process, discretion, professional and unions stakes, face-to-face interactions, abilities of inmates to negotiate with staff members as well as disconnections and contradictions between fields of decision making are factors that explain the failure of the new penology in the most secure prisons. These organizational and professional factors are not linked to political conditions such as the welfare state or the new management of poverty as indicated by the authors of the new penology. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Rationalizing Play: A Critical Theory of Digital Gaming
abstract: This article constructs a new framework for the study of games as sites of social rationalization, applying Feenberg's critical theory of technology. We begin by making the case for a consideration of games as systems of social rationality, akin to other modern systems such as capitalist markets and bureaucratic organizations. We then present a conceptualization of play as a process through which the player focuses attention away from the undifferentiated action of everyday life toward a differentiated sphere of playful activity. This approach reveals how the experience of play changes as it becomes rationalized through the technological mediation and widespread standardization that occurs as games become large-scale social practices. We propose a theory of the rationalization of play (ludification), which outlines the key components of socially rationalized games, which we then apply to the specific example of massively multiplayer online games (MMOGs). Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucracy, Size, and Staff Expectations for Client Independence in Halfway Houses
abstract: A sample of 23 halfway houses for alcoholics in Fla was studied to determine the relationship of organizational structure to staff members' normative expectations for residential clients to be independent & self-sufficient in their daily functioning. Data were collected from open-ended interviews with the administrative chief of each house & questionnaires were administered to all available staff & residents. Organizational structure is studied in terms of four dimensions of bureaucracy (complexity, decentralization, impersonality of interpersonal relations, & technical qualifications of staff), & two dimensions of size (number of members & the staff/client ratio). Under certain conditions, various aspects of bureaucracy (eg, greater complexity, decentralization, & impersonality) are positively associated with (greater) staff expectations for client independence. Greater organizational size in terms of numbers of staff & residents is negatively associated with such expectations, while a higher staff/client ratio has a positive impact. Discussion focuses on the complex interrelationship of bureaucracy & size, as these affect staff & client outcomes & on possible directions for future research. 2 Tables. Modified HA.

title: The study of the third sector in Quebec: how to capture the distinctiveness of Quebec?
abstract: This article provides a review of the current uses of the comparative approach in the study the third sector in Quebec and in Canada. Drawing on her own research experience, the author discusses some of the conceptual and methodological challenges that result from using a comparative approach to study these phenomenons. The unique perspective used by Quebec researchers in that specific field of study is illustrated. Finally, the contribution of a greater recourse to comparative analyses between Quebec and Canada, and between Quebec and other Canadian provinces is explored in order to better understand their reciprocal realities and singularities, and in so doing, enrich their mutual understanding. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucratic versus Nonbureaucratic Structure and the Process of Innovation and Change
abstract: The dual needs for innovation & stability represent a dilemma for organizations. A review is presented of current models that relate structural characteristics of organizations to this dilemma, comparing these models to the empirical literature. A modified framework is proposed that explains how organizations achieve the required amount of both innovation & stability in various environmental settings. 6 Tables, 4 Figures. HA.

title: STRATEGY VERSUS TACTICS AS THE OBJECT OF RESEARCH IN PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION
abstract: To be of value to current use by admin'ors, res in the admin'ive process, which involves staggering management problems & the unrelated development of amazing technical equipment, requires a channelling of res capabilities to subjects which will produce results for current operating use. Application of behavioral res to matters of org & process too frequently lacks understanding of admin'ive processes, fails to identify completely the nature of the org's involved, & overlooks the power impact of external & internal pressure groups not a part of the work groups. Admin'ive societies should officially suggest needed new res or postulates needing further examination, & indicate the relative priority in view of existing problems. They should attack problems for which solutions will not have already been out-dated by technological advances - eg, analysis of the effective exercise of leadership in fashioning goals, establishing devices & processes to ensure their accomplishments, & motivating employees to an understanding of the purpose sought & reasons why they are important. IPSA.

title: Conformity in the Face of Ambiguity: A Bureaucratic Dilemma
abstract: Examination of the bureaucratic review process in federal information collection demonstrates a system of individual positions whose job relations are official, but not hierarchical, resulting in multidimensional, multipersonality, & multiorganizational ambiguity. Case studies of the processing of two common document requests illustrate the complexity & variability of the clearance process in the US Office of Management & Budget. While practical ambiguity in decision making may be less than described by the analysis, it remains a core feature of bureaucratic behavior. Formal, hierarchical frameworks or models distort social processes acting within bureaucracies. 1 Figure, 43 References. M. Lemons

title: Public Bureaucracy and Its Clients: Toward a Theoretical Framework
abstract: The distribution of public goods among client groups provides one approach to the study of public bureaucracy. However, a sampling of recent Norwegian empirical research in medical sociology, the sociology of law, & related fields shows the need for a theoretical framework that analyzes the relations between bureaucracies & clients. An outline for such a framework is presented, which stresses organizational aspects within the bureaucracy & delineates the interaction between the public bureaucracy, its clients, & its environment. 4 Figures, 41 References. Modified HA.

title: 'Reflecting the diversity of the French population': birth and development of a fuzzy concept
abstract: While "reflecting the diversity of the French population" is currently an objective to which political parties, television channels, large corporations and higher education establishments subscribe, it was first formulated with respect to the national civil service. In this context, the theme is inseparable from an imported, specifically American model of "representative bureaucracy", the import of which was itself determined by pragmatic considerations related to the peculiar problems faced by two institutions: the Army and the national police service. However, when one extends the objective of "diversity" to all public servants while simultaneously emphasising, in more or less explicit fashion, the 'ethnic' dimension of diversity, one encounters, in France, insuperable sociological and legal difficulties. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Border Scans: Sovereignty, Surveillance and the Customs Service in Ghana
abstract: This article explores the relationship between surveillance techniques & the production of sovereign statehood in an effort to track the day-to-day practices through which state authority is constituted in the context of globalization. This article explicitly probes the processes through which new forms of sovereignty come into being within the life of the state. It takes as its point of departure the operations of Ghana's Customs Service, a body charged with policing the nation's frontiers & collecting the bulk of state revenue. Contrasting the work of a multinational firm contracted by the government of Ghana to carry out Customs duties & the conventional roles of Ghanaian Customs officers, this article examines the ways in which the manifold technologies of neoliberalism (from contractual forms & modes of accountability, to the apparatuses of surveillance) redefine the capacities, authority, & imagination of both state & self, held by state agents. Here we see a sovereignty that is increasingly derived outside of the state even as the play of sovereign power is intensified & deeply diffused within it. 4 Figures, 68 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Modernization and Sex Roles: The Status of Women in the Thai Bureaucracy
authors: Springer, J Fred; Gable, Richard W
abstract: Thai women have traditionally been active in the economy & enjoy a social equality unusual for Asian women. To examine F roles in a modernizing bureaucracy, data were gathered through 414 in-depth interviews with officials of the Rice Production Project, 50% from Bangkok offices & 50% from field locations. F participation in the project was 17.7% -- many times higher than in similar programs in Indonesia, South Korea, & the Philippines. Despite comparable educational credentials, however, F Thai civil servants were found to have lower rank, lower pay, & less supervisory responsibility than Ms, & tended to be clustered in clerical occupations. They were also less likely to be married or have children, suggesting that they needed to make sacrifices in family life to compete with Ms. F Rs, however, expressed greater job satisfaction than did the Ms. 7 Tables. C. Waters.

title: A Businessman Becomes a President -- Marc Ravalomanana in Madagascar
abstract: This article examines the state of affairs in Madagascar five years after Ravalomanana was elected President. Results vary. The area of infrastructure shows some success: the road network has been improved & 382 elementary schools have been built or modernized. However, the development of TIKO (Ravalomanana's business) & the political development of the President are inextricably linked. However, what made him very successful in business (innovative ideas, autonomous decision making) are not commensurate with the role of President. Ravalomanana took office with the resolution to make the poor richer without making the rich poorer. However, in this he has failed. The expected economic stimulus did not materialize & due to economic liberalization, living conditions for a majority of the population have deteriorated. References. E. Sanchez

title: THE PROCURING OF INFORMATION FROM BUREAUCRATIC SOURCES IN RELATION TO THE SOCIAL CHARACTERISTICS OF A RURAL AREA IN THE STATE OF RIO
abstract: Res from the Ru areas of the municipalities of Paraiba do Sul, Cachoeiro do Macacu, Itaborai & Itaguai, carried out during Jul 1962 by the author, is reported. 11 variables were drawn from previous res which reported these variables as characteristic of individuals who highly utilize official sources of agri'al information. It was hyp'ed that utilization of official sources of information was positively associated with informal soc participation, with SES, & with spatial mobility; but that no association existed between utilization of official sources of information & such personal characteristics as age, religion, fam status, & race. Data were gathered via interviews from a sample of 20% of the 3,037 Ru households of the above municipalities (136 head of households from Cachoeiro, 156 from Itaborai, 118 from Itaguai, & 174 from Paraiba). The +r between using official sources of information & informal soc participation was confirmed, as was the +r between using official sources of information & SES. The hyp'ed +r re spatial mobility was also supported. The hyp'ed lack of r between use of official sources of information & personal characteristics was only partially confirmed. Age, religious belief, & fam status were not associated with use of official sources of information. It is indicated that other, not specified personal traits, may be associated with use of official sources. This is in agreement with the findings in previous res from the US, other areas of Brazil, Australia, the Netherlands, & New Zealand. M. Maxfield.

title: Dealing with Bureaucracy: The Effectiveness of Different Persuasive Appeals
abstract: A report on findings from an experiment measuring the effectiveness of different persuasive appeals -- normative, altruistic, reciprocal positive, & reciprocal negative -- when dealing with different types of bureaucratic organizations. Loglinear analysis is used to compare the possible combinations of relations of organization types & persuasive appeals to various measures of effectiveness. The results support the exchange theory view that the client's "bargaining power" is the key factor behind an appeal's effectiveness. Comparison of actual measures of effectiveness with the clients' expectations is used to discuss the existence of "bureaucratic competence." The results reemphasize the claim that the bureaucrat's attitudes & behavior are less universalistic & impersonal than is stipulated by the Weberian model of ideal-type bureaucracy. 4 Tables, Appendix. Modified HA.

title: A LABORATORY EXPERIMENT ON BUREAUCRATIC AUTHORITY
authors: Evan, William M; Jr, Morris Zelditch,
abstract: Forces inherent in both centralization & bur'cy tend to transcend the pol'al diff's of the USSR & the US. The Russians rely on planning to secure greater areas of freedom of action than operating officials have had; Americans are trying to decide whether additional planning would limit their greater operating freedom, & if so how much & is it worth the cost. The Soviet system of planning & control facilitates co-ordination, contrarily to what happens in the US. The Russians have borrowed the econ incentive system, while Americans seem to be dropping it more than is advisable. The Russian educ'al system encourages thoroughness & mental discipline, the US originality & resourcefulness. In the end, both countries attempt to add these factors to produce totals that are somewhere near equal. What is at stake is the key to survival & influence. IPSA.

title: Individualized Service Provision in the New Welfare State Lessons from Special Education in Finland
abstract: Welfare states in the advanced countries are responding to the rise of new, immeasurable risks by relying less on social insurance and more on the provision of customised social services, such as education, which enable citizens to acquire the capacities needed to respond to the risks they face. These services are provided by a novel form of organisation that addresses the classic problems of public administration -- how to limit discretion while increasing the responsiveness of the organisation to changing circumstance -- by authorising front-line workers to search for new solutions, but with the requirement that they explain and justify their decisions to peers. The successful Finnish school system exemplifies this new type of organisation. Adapted from the source document.

title: Urban Regeneration and Transport Investment: A Case Study of Sheffield 1992-96
abstract: Issues relating to the impact of transport investment on economic regeneration at the urban scale were addressed by a major empirical study conducted in Sheffield, England, during the early 1990s. The research methods adopted involved breaking down impacts into five thematic areas (image, property, land use, business location & operations, & labor market) & exploring the different mechanisms whereby effects might have become apparent in each. Findings from each of the themes are briefly summarized, the overall conclusion being that, in current circumstances, the impact of transport investment on regeneration is not particularly strong. In a broader policy context, however, the study also pointed to the improbability of securing regeneration benefits from transport infrastructure, given the lack of coordination & integration between the two policy areas, & the increasingly fragmented nature of urban governance in general. 7 Tables, 41 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Symbiosis, re-use and evolution: administrators, politicians, citizens, and governance in post-colonial India
abstract: Democracy, governance and citizenship in post-colonial states are crucially contingent on how civil servants and political leaders see one another. Civil servants and political leaders are important links in the national chain of governance, joining the modern state and traditional society. A trained, professional, politically neutral bureaucracy, held accountable to local, regional and national leaders, is the core of India's strategy of governance. Based on the management of order, welfare and identity, this design underpins the vast expanses of the Indian political system, reaching out to every corner of the country, constantly extracting and circulating new ideas and resources, and functioning as the veins and arteries of this complex body politic. The evolution of this complex system, the fortuitous result of the symbiosis of administrators and politicians, and the strategic re-use of the colonial and the pre-modern past, accounts for the puzzle of the formal continuity of a colonial institution in India's post-colonial context. The article examines this argument on the basis of narratives, conversations with regional elites (the empirical analysis draws on interviews with 150 of them, drawn from six states) and findings from a cross-section survey of the Indian electorate.

title: A study of the advancement of women in municipal government bureaucracies: Persistence of glass ceilings?
authors: Reid, Margaret; Kerr, Brinck; Miller, William H
abstract: If women's advancement to the highest-level decision-making positions in governmental bureaucracies is to be enhanced, a better understanding of the continued impediments to such progress is essential. This study employs a large, previously underutilized national data set obtained from the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) to answer two questions.

title: Next Practices: Knowledge, Infrastructure, and Public Goods at the Bottom of the Pyramid
abstract: How to move beyond the failures of development? In the bottom of the pyramid (BOP) approach, the state, development, and public goods disappear. Instead, nongovernmental organizations help businesspeople realize poor people's capacity to create infrastructure and business models. I draw on the history of development to show how the BOP is an unintended outgrowth of the critique of development. Drawing on previous formulations of the BOP, I propose that the infrastructures created by poor people's social practices can also be understood as a "commons" for which compensation should be paid or as a public good to be regulated by the state. Adapted from the source document.

title: Navigating Globalization: Immigration Policy in Canada and Australia, 1945-20071
abstract: Scholarship on immigration and globalization has failed to adequately analyze the nation-state's regulatory capacities, insisting instead that contemporary patterns of migration jeopardize national sovereignty and territoriality. While recognized that states possess the legitimate authority to control their territorial and membership boundaries, recent transformations of these capacities remain largely unanalyzed. This article's historical analysis of Australia and Canada's postwar immigration policies demonstrates that the contours of state regulation are intimately connected to the exigencies of state administration and nation building and-in contrast to the expectations of dominant theories-have intensified and expanded within the globalization context. The literature's inattention to the fundamentally political nature of immigration has obscured the critical effects of national policies within both the migratory and globalization process. Australia's and Canada's contemporary policies constitute a unique model of migration control and reflect attempts by both countries to strategically position their societies within the global system and resolve a number of economic, political, cultural, and demographic transitions associated with globalization. Adapted from the source document.

title: Maintaining Climate Change Experiments: Urban Political Ecology and the Everyday Reconfiguration of Urban Infrastructure
abstract: Climate change governance is increasingly being conducted through urban climate change experiments, purposive interventions that seek to reconfigure urban sociotechnical systems to achieve low-carbon and resilient cities. In examining how experiments take effect, we suggest that we need to understand not only how they are made and assembled, but also how they are maintained within specific urban contexts. Drawing on literatures from urban political ecology and the specific debate on urban repair and maintenance, this article examines maintenance in two case studies of climate change experiments in housing in Bangalore (India) and Monterrey (Mexico). We find that maintenance is a crucial process through which not only urban obduracy is preserved, but also the novel and innovative character of the experiment is asserted and reproduced. The process of 'maintaining' experiments is a precarious one, which requires a continuous external input in terms of remaking the experiment materially and discursively. This process causes further reconfigurations beyond the experiment, changing the patterns of responsibility attribution and acceptability that configure the urban fabric. Adapted from the source document.

title: Operational and Organizational Adaptations of Fire Department to Civil Disturbances
abstract: The adaptations made by fire dept's in 6 civil disturbance cities in the 1960's are studied. As Ur disturbances increased in US cities in the middle & late 1960's, fire dept's developed a task force concept to protect men & equipment. They tended to ignore box alarms as being untrustworthy & developed priorities. They made modifications in their fire suppression techniques. They evoked mutual aid pacts. They made changes in their usual decision-making & in effect changed their predominant orientation. Each of these operational adaptations is examined in detail. The org'al adaptations are discussed as they refer to (1) admin, (2) fire prevention, (3) fire suppression, & (4) COMM's. 3 of the cities experienced fluctuation stress, the 3 others experienced peak stress. The possibility of diff'ial consequences of operational adaptations due to diff in type of stress es explored. It is found that some sections of the dept experienced more stress than others, & some sections had to make more changes than others. There was no unitary pan-org'al response. Throughout the org at selected points either new structures or functions emerged or there was no change at all. 4 types of internal adaptation to the stress situation were found: (a) retaining pre-emergency structure & pre-emergency functions in the dept; (b) modification or emergence of a new structure & the continuance of regular functions; (c) modification or change in the functions & continuance of the regular structure; (d) modification or change in both the structure & the functions of a section. 1 Table. M. Maxfield.

title: CAREER ATTAINMENT IN CANADIAN BUREAUCRACIES: UNSCRAMBLING THE EFFECTS OF AGE, SENIORITY, EDUCATION, AND ETHNOLINGUISTIC FACTORS ON SALARY
abstract: 5 hyp's re the influence of age, seniority, expertise (educ), & informal factors on salary attainment of 296 men in bur'tic careers in the Canadian Federal administration (professional, sci'fic, technical & admin'ive employees) were tested. R's ranged from 25 to 45 in age. A multiple regression analysis showed that age, seniority, & educ were positively related to salary, but the relationships were stronger for the Anglophone majority than for the Francophone minority. Older Francophones range behind the Anglophone equivalents. These findings are explained on the basis of career disadvantages of able Francophones who are leaving the Federal administration's because they are discriminated against. The state of French-Canadian educ a generation ago also put Francophones at a disadvantage vs the Anglophones, particularly in sci & engineering. Career discrimination is seen as the primary factor accounting for salary diff'ials. Data support the hyp's that the process of aging, job seniority, & the level of educ, influence the general range of salary in the Canadian admin. These factors bring greater gains for majority men than minority men; thus, while the hypothesis that educ (expertise) is more important for advancement than seniority is supported, its effect is blunted by minority status. Younger majority & minority men were on a par, however. It is hoped that the implementation of some of the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism & Biculturalism plus the recent focus on the 'French fact' in Canada will end career discrimination in the public service. 2 Tables, 1 Figure. Modified HA.

title: Critical Social Work with Older People in Neo-liberal Times: Challenges and Critical Possibilities
abstract: This article argues that the United Kingdom is institutionally ageist, a situation compounded by the current neo-liberal consensus embraced by all main political parties. It explores the concept of ageism, the practise of discrimination against older members of society. Involved is a discussion of critical gerontology, the role played by society in creating the condition of, and how this contributes to, the problematisation of old age. The role of social work with older people is also problematised given the changes associated with the managerialism, resulting in bureaucracy and targets, and the ever increasing need to ration resources. Despite all this, the argument is for a critical practice, one which seeks to genuinely address the needs of older people as well as aiming to create a more just and equal society that refutes ageism. Adapted from the source document.

title: Constraints on Administrator Discretion: The Limited Influence of Mayors on City Budgets
abstract: The effect of the mayor on eight expenditure categories as well as on the property tax level & the general debt was examined for thirty US cities for the period 1951-1968. Mayoral influence on expenditures was relatively small compared to that associated with the city itself, typically accounting for only 5% to 10% of the variance of the dollars spent in the eight categories compared to 80% of the variance associated with the city. Mayors tended to account for more of the variance in the allocation of funds for libraries, parks & recreation, & health services than they did in the allocation of funds for police, fire, & highways. Both the relatively limited impact of the mayor on budget outcomes, & the fact that this impact is less on issues where organized interest groups are involved, are consistent with the conceptualization of organizations as coalitions in which the activities of the nominal leader are constrained. 2 Tables, Appendix. AA.

title: Adaptive Publics: Building Climate Constituencies in Bogotá
abstract: This essay foregrounds the political constituencies assembling around the problem of climate change in cities. Recent experiments in urban climate governance in Bogota, Colombia, are shown to challenge liberal democratic notions of the "public" by linking a redistributive economic agenda to the technical project of adaptation. An analysis of interventions aimed at building social infrastructure throughout the city's hydrological systems reveals how the inclusion of the urban poor is enacted through practices of measurement. While urban politics in Latin America has long revolved around popular demands to be counted, climate change adaptation is the most recent idiom in which claims to recognition-through-enumeration are being articulated. [web URL: http://publicculture.dukejournals.org/content/28/2_79/389.abstract]

title: Not a Soldier, Not a Slacker: Conscientious Objectors and Male Citizenship in the United States during the Second World War
abstract: This essay argues that the 1940 Selective Service Act introduced new tensions between pacifism and male citizenship in the United States. Even as the draft required tens of millions of American men to answer Uncle Sam's call and promoted a new norm of male military obligation, it also specified the acceptable grounds for conscientious objection and created bureaucratic mechanisms for distinguishing between sincere objectors and 'slackers'. Using Selective Service and organisational records, letters, diaries, interviews and the media, I suggest that male citizenship has been defined not only by idealised and gendered duties, but also by the difficulties and exceptions involved in their practical realisation. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: When Intranet Networks Support a Reappropriation of Occupations by the Organisation
abstract: We have carried out an exploratory investigation into networks of professionals in the field of mechanical engineering inside a major French public administration. Adapted from the source document.

title: The hospital and the hospital: Infrastructure, human tissue, labour and the scientific production of relational value
abstract: How does science make a home for itself in a public hospital? This article explores how scientists working in 'resource poor' contexts of global health negotiate relationships with their hosts, in this case the doctors, nurses and patients who already inhabit a provincial-level hospital. Taking its lead from recent works on science, ethics and development, this article seeks to 'provincialize the laboratory' by focussing on the scientific tropics as a space of productive encounter and engagement. A view from the hospital reveals the tenuous process of 'setting up' a place for science, in a world that does not immediately recognize its value. The article examines the material exchanges of infrastructure, bodily tissues and labour that enable one young scientist to establish a scientific life for himself. The success of those transactions, it argues, ultimately derives from their objectification of scientific vulnerability and their enactment of relationships of mutual recognition. As opposed to asking how scientific knowledge is produced in the tropics, the view from the hospital challenges us to focus on the establishment of relationships between scientists and their hosts as a productive endeavour in its own right.

title: The Political Economy of Federal Government Paperwork
authors: Bennett, James T; Johnson, Manuel H
abstract: Despite all the paperwork generated by the federal bureaucracy, little has been done to reduce its burden on individuals & private businesses. Since the late 1880s, a host of agencies, boards, bureaus, committees, commissions, departments, & task forces have undertaken appraisals, analyses, hearings, investigations, & studies that have resulted in directives, executive orders, legislation, recommendations, & reports to control federal paperwork. All to no avail. By almost any method of measurement, the dimensions of the paperwork created by the federal bureaucracy are enormous. In 1972, the federal government reported that 5,566 repetitive-use forms were being employed which generated more than 400 million responses from the private sector & required more than 145 million man-hours to complete. Because of the costs & the potential for abuse of the information collected through the paperwork process, some method must be instituted to reduce bureaucratic appetites for paper. Among such measures are a "tax" on bureau budgets which reduces funds available for such purposes as travel when a bureau increases paperwork, & continued monitoring & public exposure of the volume of paperwork generated on an agency-by-agency basis. It would be helpful, for instance, if every government form were to be required to display, in prominent type, the cost to the taxpayers of printing all copies of that form. Modified AA.

title: Living on the Ground: The "Culture Woman" and the "Missus"
abstract: In "Living on the Ground" I investigate the cultural interactions between White & Indigenous people in a remote Indigenous settlement in Australia's Great Sandy Desert. Drawing on my own experience as a White Irish-Australian woman living in an Indigenous domain, I distinguish between the "Culture Woman" & the "Missus" as the difference between two worlds. The "Culture Woman" was formed in the gynocentric Indigenous environment of a women's Tjilimi (camp), where I lived with 13 women elders as they apprenticed me in their ways, their rituals & every-day customs. This contrasted starkly with the "Missus" -- a conduit constructed by the elders to facilitate their access to resources tightly controlled by a hegemonic White society. The "Missus" is the nexus between Indigenous peoples' cultural needs & the demands of an inflexible White bureaucracy. These paradigms are created in a context of acute cultural clash where two societies are divided by even seemingly innocuous issues such as dirt & "mess." This article is a call to White & Other-than-Indigenous researchers, consultants & community service providers to find ways of working which respect & advance Indigenous cultural self-determination. References. [Copyright 2005 Elsevier Ltd.]

title: When Public Institutions Fail: Coping with Dysfunctional Government in Post-Soviet Russia
abstract: Americans take for granted that public institutions such as schools & courts will function in an effective, predictable way. Contemporary Russia shows what happens when they do not. People's lives are thrown into turmoil, & how they cope can become part of the problem. 6 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: On the Social Structure of Soviet Society
abstract: It is argued that bureaucracy constitutes a distinct social class in Soviet society. According to Vladimir Lenin's definition of social classes, the bureaucratic class differs from the working class, farmers, & intellectuals in four fundamental areas: (1) it does not produce material or moral values; (2) it enjoys exclusive ownership of production means; (3) it reorganizes its own functions so as to misappropriate maximum economic surplus; & (4) a bureaucrat is paid according to his position, rather than according to criteria of performance & competence. It is argued that bureaucracy in the USSR actually impedes efficient economic production & social progress. The resolution of the current situation will require elimination of the favored status of bureaucracy. 12 References. M. Polinsky

title: The 'Goan Impasse': land rights and resistance to SEZs in Goa, India
abstract: Conflicts over land-grabs for industry, infrastructure and urbanization are on the rise in emerging economies. A slew of policy measures undergird such land deals in India but have encountered successful resistance from peasants and citizens groups. In Goa, resistance led to the revocation of the state's special economic zone (SEZ) policy and cancellation of all approved SEZs, many developed by prominent realty firms. As battle over three SEZs continues in the Supreme Court of India, there is hope that commons will be returned to local communities. There is, however, an impasse on the ground that begs resolution if the gains over SEZs are to be secured. The Goan Impasse can be resolved with egalitarian and ecologically appropriate rights to land- and resource-use for all that counter existing inequalities. This requires programmatic social movements reconstituting relationships around and to land and resources from below.

title: Health Department Administration of the Canadian Health Care Program
abstract: Public administration of the Canadian health care program successfully preserved a single-tiered system, ensuring accessiblity & accountability, reducing administrative costs & the need for regulation, & achieving orderly planning & cost control. Although the provincial programs are administered by health departments, failure to link personal to public health services has robbed them of a population perspective, resulting in insufficient emphasis on prevention & on the effectiveness of interventions, which has hampered the development of comprehensive primary care. Four lessons for a national health care program are drawn: (1) keep it public; (2) use a single payer; (3) link personal health services to public health; & (4) provide health departments with policy expertise. Despite its overall success, the Canadian program can no longer be afforded, but many reform proposals challenge the values on which it was built. 7 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Institutional Change and the Delivery of Urban Public Services
abstract: Problems associated with providing efficient & equitable distribution of public services are attributable in part to the inabilities of gov or other public instit's to be responsive to requirements of their clientele. To permit a better understanding of the nature of such instit'al failures, & to suggest avenues of effective reform, the paper views instit'al systems of service provision in a "control systems" framework. In this perspective, the elements of "feedback" are seen as essential to successful system performance over time & changing conditions. The paper identifies the kinds of "error signals" a system needs to generate, & the types of "corrective mechanisms" that it may employ, & then discusses 3 basic modes of instit'al reform--performance evaluation, decentralization, & market competition--for improving the dynamic capability of systems & providing Ur public services. 2 service areas--sanitation & criminal correction--are used for illustrating possible implications of the reform strategies. Modified HA.

title: Rebuilding Communities After Natural Disasters: The 2009 Bushfires in Southeastern Australia
abstract: Through nonrandom purposive sampling, this article examines the ways three Catholic agencies offered bushfire recovery assistance after the 2009 bushfires in the Australian state of Victoria. Participants from Catholic welfare agencies (29), local and state government (8), international recovery agencies (2), and others such as clergy, church, and medical (6) were selected, and senior managers, middle managers, and workers on the ground were interviewed up to 3 times during a 3-year period. The forty-five people were interviewed a total of 74 times. Study results illustrate the importance of adaptability, flexibility, and preplanning as the core of recovery assistance. Linking with local and state government disaster management plans and developing mechanisms to inform other groups as to the services that new agencies could provide were essential for filling gaps in services and establishing cooperative ventures. Recommendations are provided but more research is needed on how other agencies can benefit from the knowledge gained in this study. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Whistleblowing Process: Retaliation and Perceived Effectiveness
authors: Near, Janet P; Jensen, Tamila C
abstract: An examination of 1979 questionnaire data from 72 F Rs who blew the whistle on their employers with regard to alleged sex discrimination. Results indicate that whistleblowers considered the process to be more effective when their cases were determined to have merit & when they felt they had succeeded in changing management's attitudes. Retaliation by employer had little influence on whether the whistleblower considered the process to be effective, & was less likely to occur when the whistleblower's case was determined to have merit. 5 Tables, 2 Figures. HA.

title: The Politics of Force: Conflict Management and State Violence in Northern Ireland / Unfinished Business: State Killings and the Quest for Truth
abstract: "The Politics of Force: Conflict Management and State Violence in Northern Ireland" by Fionnuala Ni Aolain and "Unfinished Business: State Killings and the Quest for Truth" by Bill Rolston are reviewed.

title: Strategies of Discourse and Knowledge Use in the Practice of Bureaucratic Research
abstract: The impact of the politics, strategies, & tactics of bureaucratic practice on research was examined through case study analysis of a large federally funded US educational research project. Political activity was found to often aim at manipulating knowledge through reinterpretation of information or reconfiguration of knowledge elements. Subordinate staff members were particularly prone to this practice in an effort to resist the decisions of research administrators & thereby retain autonomy & control over the research activity. These conflicts took a variety of forms, including disputes over the presentation of findings, the objectification of flows of knowledge, & the noncontestable/objective vs the conditional/problematic status of knowledge, & most often occurred at the writing stage of the research. Implications of conducting research in settings permeated by bureaucratic power struggles are discussed. 26 References. D. Generoli

title: The Nonsense of Neutrality
abstract: Empirical analysis of the operations of political-administrative systems in some Caribbean countries gives evidence that two-party parliamentary systems with neutral bureaucracies are ineffective as means to modernization. Neutral functionaries cannot mobilize mass action for development; politicized bureaucracies are needed. Democracy is essentially a myth, & one whose applicability to the Third World is limited. A one-party state with a politicized bureaucracy is more appropriate, if the dangers of this approach can be avoided. W. H. Stoddard.

title: A MULTI-DIMENSIONAL APPROACH TOWARD A TYPOLOGY OF BUREAUCRACY
abstract: A study that attempts to derive a typology of industr bur'tic profiles. For this purpose altogether 4 dimensions are specified, which may appear universally but in varying intensities in modern bur'tic org's, & which would seem to be essential in defining the profiles of bur'cies: (a) structural control, as embodied in the hierarchy, (b) functional diff'iation of the DofL, (c) interlevel impersonality, & (d) normativity as reflected in rules & regulations. Contextual variables, namely: size of plant, production system, ownership, size & age of enterprise, were assumed to affect the specific configuration of the above variables, & were therefore included in the profiles. Data were collected from a sample of 30 industr plants stratified by size, ownership, & production system. The variables were measured by factual & objective data collected by means of structured checklists. Only the variable of interlevel impersonality' was defined by means of closed questionaire items which formed a Guttman scale. This t was admin'ed to 250 1st level supervisors in these plants. To measure structural control & functional diff'iation, special mathematical formulae were developed. Each plant was scored on each of the bur'tic & contextual variables, thus being characterized finally by a profile of its contextual & structural dimensions. The data were analyzed by means of the Guttman-Lingoes multidimensional scalogram Analysis I (GL-MSA-I), which presents in a visually striking manner the classification of the diff profiles. By this method of analysis, 6 types of industr bur'tic profiles emerged which were named Rudimentary, Emergent, Interpersonal, Balanced, Managerial & Technical Bur'cies. These types indicate that the dimensions of bur'cy do not necessarily differ on a uniform scale of intensity. Diff patterns are found, with more intense bur'ization being possible in some areas, while others may be much less bur'ized in the same plant. However, since it was also found that each contextual variable affects only certain of the structural dimensions-eg the type of production is related to the degree of functionalization, normative & interpersonal relations-only a limited number of structural patterns are likely. AA.

title: Organizational Control: An Evolutionary Perspective
abstract: The literature on organizational control processes has traditionally been based on concepts of cybernetics, power, & authority. Here, an alternative way of considering the control phenomenon is explored by introducing the idea of an evolutionary "controlling" cycle. This idea is derived by modifying the basic organizing cycle (enactment, selection, retention) to a hierarchical form, with two distinct components. The model is applied to understand the basic control modes informing markets, bureaucracies, & clans. Future directions of the bureaucratic mode of organizational control are proposed. 3 Tables, 4 Figures, 66 References. Modified HA

title: An Examination of the Blau -- Scott and Etizioni Typologies: A Critique
abstract: The conclusions reached by R. H. Hall, J. E. Haas & N. J. Johnson (see SA 0624/C9026) in their comparative evaluation of the Blau -- Scott & A. Etzioni typologies (no reference given) fail to reflect their own empirical & statistical findings. In their article indicators of such concepts as complexity, formalization, goal specificity & org'al activities were correlated with the typologies, while the chi-square statistic was used to determine the nature of -- he relationships. No cutting points were introduced to indicate the level of signif, nor were the levels themselves published; only the chi-square value appeared in the tables. Analyzing the df presented in the tables, the reader can determine the level of signif of the X2 values. The results of this simple exercise raise serious doubts about the conclusions which Hall et al drew from their findings. Their approach shows little concern for conceptual definition & operationalization, esp in the issue of conceptual dimensionality. Because of these methodological shortcomings, they overstated their negative evaluation of the typologies. REPLY TO WELDON by Richard H. Hall, J. Eugene Haas & Norman J. Johnson (U of Minnesota, Minneapolis, U of Colorado, Boulder, & Carnegie -- Mellon U, Pittsburgh, Pa), states that the purpose of a typology is to allow us to combine a number of variables into a single construct & thus allow us to deal with extremely complex phenomena in a relatively simple fashion. The argument is that the 2 typologies do not do this, despite Weldon's often correct evaluation of levels of signif & their usage. The purpose was to point out the pitfalls of typologies based on a limited number of variables. E. Weiman.

title: Urban Infrastructure Financing in Reform-era China
authors: Wang, De; Zhang, Li; Zhang, Zhao; Zhao, Simon Xiaobin
abstract: Urban infrastructure has been substantially upgraded in reform-era China. This paper explains, contextually and empirically, how Chinese cities finance their infrastructure. It demonstrates that China has succeeded in addressing urban infrastructure backlogs by opening up new venues for financing, but simultaneously, heavily relying on unconventional sources. The paper also argues that urban infrastructure financing has much to do with the country's transition to a market-oriented economy that fosters the pro-growth role of city governments as well as the redistribution of fiscal power between the levels of the urban hierarchy that produces significant variation of financial capacities among the different administrative ranks of cities. Adapted from the source document.

title: "Inverting the Bureaucratic Pyramid": Reconciling Aboriginality and Bureaucracy in New Zealand
abstract: Based on recent developments within the Maori Affairs Dept in New Zealand, efforts to reconcile the contrasting principles of bureaucracy & Maori aboriginality are examined. Evidence suggests that the establishment of "Tu Tangata" as a framework for Maori policy administration initiated a series of organizational shifts with respect to philosophy (cultural-based community development), structure (indigenization), style (decentralization), & commitment (devolution). However, while these attempts at debureaucratizing the Maori Affairs Dept have had some success, problems of considerable magnitude remain: eg, the imperatives of bureaucratic logic appear to be inconsistent with the aboriginality of Maori nationalism. Despite conciliatory efforts, a compromie between the organizing principles of bureaucracy & Maori aboriginality remains elusive. 89 References. HA

title: ARRESTED DEVELOPMENT? UNHCR, ILO, AND THE REFUGEES' RIGHT TO WORK
Israel: state management of religion or religious management of the state
abstract: In Israel, the Jewish religion, which is unique among world religions in the primacy it accords to filiation rather than belief as a criterion of belonging, operates as a formal criterion of citizenship, but in substance different ways of being Jewish are expressed in different political forces which in turn struggle for control of the state's religious orientation. This political struggle leads the state to favour ultra-Orthodox observance and criteria of belonging, even though that is a minority strand in the country itself and even more so outside. Religious interests and ideologies have found substantial niches in the legal system, in education, in the army and in the West Bank settlements, by exploiting the state's corporatist character, leading to a type of multiculturalism in which the once-secular centre has been seriously eroded. Adapted from the source document.

title: Conflict measures in cooperative exchange models of collective decision-making
authors: Marcel van Assen; Stokman, Frans; Reinier van Oosten
abstract: This study focuses on externalities of exchanges of voting positions in collective decision-making. Exchanges are represented by non-constant two-person cooperative games. It is assumed that the rate of exchange is specified by the Raiffa-Kalai-Smorodinsky solution, and a model is specified to identify the exchanges. Externality effects of these exchanges are assessed with two conflict measures we develop here. The measures assess within-group and between-group conflict, respectively, and are applied to collective decision-making in the European Union regarding support for fishery infrastructure. The application shows that the measures provide indispensable insights into the decision-making setting and that these can be used for strategic intervention in the setting. It also shows that both actors' power and the outcomes in exchange with externalities are very different from those in exchange without externalities as studied by theories of network exchange.

title: Crews, Camps, and Communities: Place and Belonging in Jam Festival Scenes
