Organisational problems in decision-making on sensitive issues are studied. The paper ends with a review of suitable theoretical approaches to explain behaviours of universities, among them Minzberg's (1993) characterisation of 'professional bureaucracies'. Adapted from the source document.

title: Sovereigns and citizens in close encounter: Airport anthropology and customs regimes in neoliberal Ghana
abstract: Through the examination of encounters between Customs officers and travelers at Ghana's international airport, I pose a series of arguments regarding sovereignty and citizenship within a developing state deeply enmeshed in processes of liberalization. Supporting the contention that transnational flows and supranational interventions restructure rather than undermine state power, the Ghanaian case reveals neoliberal conditions to facilitate the expansion of administrative authorities oriented to the cross-border mobility of persons, capital, and commodities. Such bureaucratic realms emerge, in turn, as key arenas for an expression of state sovereignty that is not founded on social alienation and absolute distinctions between rulers and ruled. Because of the multiplicity and ambiguity of regulatory orders at play, sovereignty here hinges on intimacy, emotion, and identification as much as on force and legal sanction. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: "A Sense of Discovery, Mixed with a Sense of Justice": Creating the First Women's Studies Program in Canada
abstract: Drawing on personal experience, considered is the intertwining of personal & institutional transformation. In establishing the first credited multicourse women's studies program at the U of British Columbia, students & faculty challenged not merely an institution's hidebound conservatism. They also confronted resistance to interdisciplinarity, resistance to student activism, maddening bureaucracy, & irrational, often fear-laden responses to the possibility of admitting women to full intellectual & professional equality in the university. 24 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Organization and Impact of Inspector Discretion in a Regulatory Bureaucracy
authors: Lynxwiler, John; Shover, Neal; Clelland, Donald A
abstract: An examination of the organization of inspection & enforcement practices in the federal Office of Surface Mining Reclamation & Enforcement (OSM). The creators of the enabling legislation & the agency top executives went to great lengths to circumvent inspector discretion. Data gathered through personal interviews of OSM inspectors & former inspectors (N = 43) & a questionnaire mailed to the entire inspector corps (N = 126) suggest that such efforts were only partially successful. Not only do field-level personnel employ discretionary practices, but the nature of the regulated industry structures the context of inspector discretion. A relationship between corporate size & the exercise of inspector discretion is demonstrated & patterns of inspector discretion are shown to affect the size of civil fines imposed for regulatory violations. Modified HA.

title: Conducting fieldwork with Tarieng communities in southern Laos: Negotiating discursive spaces between neoliberal dogmas and Lao socialist ideology
abstract: Based on research with ethnic minorities in Laos aimed at understanding how they cope with and negotiate political and economic 'double domination', this article examines the experiences of prolonged fieldwork in a remote Tarieng area in the Annam Range, southern Laos. After briefly reviewing Lao ethnographical policy and practice regarding ethnic minorities, I introduce the Tarieng people. I detail how I initially gained access to these local communities via long-term engagement with a range of development project initiatives. Then, after eight years of conducting such fieldwork in a Tarieng area 'below the radar of the state', I managed to obtain official authorisations to continue research as a graduate student. In this new position, I accessed the field via different negotiations with central, provincial and local official bureaucracies. After detailing this process, back in the field I reveal my strategies to create a discursive space that has allowed me to access dissident Tarieng voices and agency. Finally, I highlight four central elements that have continued to shape my field research: language proficiency, working with research assistants, awareness of political relations and cultural sensitivity, and ethical concerns. These have emerged while the possibilities and constraints of political engagement with the Tarieng people are explored. Adapted from the source document.

title: A Cross-Cultural Material Development Project to Train Turkish Development Personnel in the Southeastern Anatolia Regional Development Project (GAP)
authors: Cushner, Kenneth; Robertson, Linda; Kirca, Suheyla; Cakmak, Melek
abstract: The southeastern region of Turkey has been undergoing extensive water & human development efforts since the 1970s through the Southeastern Anatolia Regional Development Project, known worldwide by its Turkish acronym -- GAP (Guneydogu Anadolu Projesi). This project has its goal the building of 22 dams along the Tigris & Euphrates river valleys that will provide 22% of the nation's hydroelectric power & irrigate 1.7 million hectares (4.2 million acres) of land. The region contains some of Turkey's greatest cultural & social diversity, & is home to significant populations of Turkish nationals of Kurdish & Arabic heritage. Considerable concern exists among the GAP Administration that Turkish development personnel, who, for the most part, are urban-educated in the cities of Ankara or Istanbul & find themselves assigned to work in the southeastern region, lack sensitivity & knowledge about issues related to cross-cultural communication & interaction. An established Memorandum of Understanding between the GAP Administration & Kent State U led to an invitation to provide training in intercultural communication, with the goal of developing training materials designed for use within the region. This article documents the collaborative undertakings that occurred between 2001 & 2002 that included initial training of GAP employees, joint material development based on the culture general assimilator (Cushner & Brislin, 1996), a concurrent training of trainers effort, application of the developed materials by trained GAP employees supported by a grant from the British Embassy, & evaluation of the impact of training by an external agency. 1 Table, 14 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: On the Maturation of Socialism
abstract: The crisis in Poland has placed its participants in a novel historical position. Both the state & workers had learned the lessons of the 1970 & 1976 attempts to regulate prices before the 1980 attempt. The workers had also learned that persons in authority are less important than the structure of authority relations, & that the party structure cannot generate effective reforms by itself. The workers now know that a strike alone will not accomplish lasting results, & that free trade unions are needed. However, workers' organizations have refused to represent their positions as political, a response to the automatic definition of politics in terms of party dictatorship, which means that any political concern must have a place in the hierarchy or go unrecognized. This pattern is similar to that of feudal societies prior to the emergence of civil society. The implicit aim of the Polish crisis is the creation of a socialist civil society, fulfilling the original Marxist understanding of socialism as the resistance of the workers to bureaucratic dictatorship. W. H. Stoddard.

title: Good Boundaries Make Good Neighbors: Boundary Management -- Tearing Down the Walls and Fostering Organizational Change
abstract: This article focuses on the ubiquitous problem of bureaucratic fragmentation experienced by organizations of all kinds. It proposes the strategy & practice of boundary management as a way of addressing the problem while creating organizational change. Based on a classic case of an aging midwestern US steel mill, the purpose of the article is threefold: (1) to define the problem of bureaucratic segmentalism & fragmentation as having to do with the formation of divisive & impenetrable barriers & walls, (2) to suggest the importance of developing & maintaining permeable boundaries designed to open up & integrate the organization, & (3) to develop the concept & practice of boundary management & its usefulness in tearing down the walls & creating organizational change. 31 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Social exclusion, mobility and access
authors: Noel Cass, Elizabeth Shove, John Urry
abstract: Much of the literature on social exclusion ignores its 'spatial' or 'mobility' related aspects. This paper seeks to rectify this by examining the mobile processes and infrastructures of travel and transport that engender and reinforce social exclusion in contemporary societies. To the extent to which this issue is addressed, it is mainly organized around the notion of 'access' to activities, values and goods. This paper examines this discourse in some detail. It is argued that there are many dimensions of such access, that improving access is a complex matter because of the range of human activities that might need to be 'accessed', that in order to know what is to be accessed the changing nature of travel and communications requires examination, and that some dimensions of access are only revealed through changes in the infrastructure that 'uncover' previously hidden social exclusions. Claims about access and socio-spatial exclusion routinely make assumptions about what it is to participate effectively in society. We turn this question around, also asking how mobilities of different forms constitute societal values and sets of relations, participation in which may become important for social inclusion. This paper draws upon an extensive range of library, desk and field research to deal with crucial issues relating to the nature of a fair, just and mobile society.[PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Demographic Characteristics of High School Math and Science Teachers and Girls' Success in STEM
authors: Stearns, Elizabeth; Bottía, Martha Cecilia; Davalos, Eleonora; Mickelson, Roslyn Arlin; Moller, Stephanie; Valentino, Lauren
abstract: Given the prestige and compensation of science and math-related occupations, the underrepresentation of women and people of color in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics majors (STEM) perpetuates entrenched economic and social inequities. Explanations for this underrepresentation have largely focused on individual characteristics, including uneven academic preparation, as well as institutional factors at the college level. In this article, we focus instead on high schools. We highlight the influence of the intersection between race and gender of female math and science teachers on students' decisions to major in STEM fields. Theoretically, this article extends the political science concept of representative bureaucracy to the issue of women's and disadvantaged minorities' underrepresentation in STEM majors. We analyze longitudinal data from public school students in North Carolina to test whether organizational demography of high school math and science faculty has an association with college major choice and graduation. Using hierarchical probit models with an instrumental-variable approach, we find that young white women are more likely to major in STEM fields and to graduate with STEM degrees when they come from high schools with higher proportions of female math and science teachers, irrespective of the race of the teacher. At the same time, these teachers do not depress young white or African American men's chances of majoring in STEM. Results for African American women are less conclusive, highlighting the limitations of their small sample size.

title: Party patronage in contemporary democracies: Results from an expert survey in 22 countries from five regions
authors: Kopecky, PETR; Meyer Sahling, JAN-HINRIK; Panizza, FRANCISCO; Scherlis, GERARDO; Schuster, CHRISTIAN; Spirova, MARIA
abstract: This Research Note presents a new dataset of party patronage in 22 countries from five regions. The data was collected using the same methodology to compare patterns of patronage within countries, across countries and across world regions that are usually studied separately. The Note addresses three research questions that are at the centre of debates on party patronage, which is understood as the power of political parties to make appointments to the public and semi-public sector: the scope of patronage, the underlying motivations and the criteria on the basis of which appointees are selected. The exploration of the dataset shows that party patronage is, to a different degree, widespread across all regions. The data further shows differences between policy areas, types of institutions such as government ministries, agencies and state-owned enterprises, and higher, middle and lower ranks of the bureaucracy. It is demonstrated that the political control of policy making and implementation is the most common motivation for making political appointments. However, in countries with a large scope of patronage, appointments serve the purpose of both political control and rewarding supporters in exchange for votes and services. Finally, the data shows that parties prefer to select appointees who are characterised by political and personal loyalty as well as professional competence.

title: The Avoidance of Punishment: A Legal-Bureaucratic Model of Suspended Sentences in Federal White-Collar Cases Prior to the Federal Sentencing Guidelines
abstract: A legal-bureaucratic framework of sentencing in white-collar crime cases is proposed that goes beyond the legal/extralegal debate by specifying how an interplay between legality & bureaucratic interests intervenes in the relationship between defendant characteristics, case complexity, & sentence outcomes. Analysis of data on 1,503 defendants, 1976-1978, reveals that in decisions to suspend punishment in federal district courts prior to the federal sentencing guidelines, the structural model reveals both direct & indirect effects of pleading guilty & case complexity on the decision to suspend an incarceration sentence. In addition, findings offer modest support for the hypothesis that defendant's location in the stratification system translates into advantage at sentencing via a structural link with case complexity & pleading guilty -- the nexus of the legal-bureaucratic model. 2 Tables, 1 Figure, 1 Appendix, 43 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Policy and Geopolitics: Bounding Europe in EUrope
abstract: This article analyzes geopolitics as a bureaucratic practice conducted by career policy professionals. Empirically, I investigate how the European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP) continuously produces and transforms the geopolitical category of "Europe" inside the European Union's (EU) policymaking bureaucracy -- or EUrope as it is called colloquially. Drawing in part from forty-six interviews with thirty-five policy professionals, the article elucidates how these professionals use the concept of Europe in their daily work on ENP -- not how they understand the concept intellectually but how they actually deploy it in policy discussions. Theoretically, I clarify how practical geopolitics operates through banal assumptions that are activated occasionally but present in an unremarkable way every day, how geopolitical categories are problematized inside policymaking bureaucracies, and how grand geopolitical visions are given specific technical content within everyday policy processes. The EU is an important example of this process because of its sheer global weight as well as the novel transnational character of its institutions. The argument advances two related strands of work in human geography: one on the role of public policy in producing social realities and the other on the capacity of specific individuals to shape geopolitical discourses. Adapted from the source document.

title: BUREAUCRACY AND POLITICS
abstract: Bur'cy is a form of admin'ive org whose application defers to the decisions made in a pol'al system. In principle, bur'cy can only fulfil admin'ive & not pol'al functions; its members must have a technical background & do not serve the gov but the public interest, performing highly specialized & varied functions Nevertheless, it does happen that a bur'cy places itself at the disposal of a particular soc group, eg, when most of its members come from that group. It is also possible that a bur'cy has first & foremost its own interests at heart, ,& transforms itself into a closed & privileged society imbued with a marked esprit de corps. Besides, the pol'al influence of functionaries increases in direct ratio to the importance of the practical application following the decision-making act. The distinction between pol'al activities & technico-admin'ive activities, because of this, becomes therefore purely formalistic. Yet it must be kept, since this distinction alone bridges the exigencies of a democracy & those of techniques. IPSA Tr by C. Akin.

title: Carl Schmitt, Modernity, and the Secret Roads Inward
abstract: Versluis undertakes an inquiry into the intellectual lineage of Carl Schmitt's account of modernity. He emphasizes on the two primary hidden lines shaping the substructure or intellectual infrastructure of Schmitt's works. Furthermore, he traces discussions back to late antiquity and conflicts between an orthodoxy emerging around the Church and the mystical radicalism of Gnostic heresies.

title: Two Dilemmas of Capitalist Political Bureaucracy
abstract: Two age-old dilemmas of capitalist political bureaucracy center on status or power & the internal nature of bureaucracy. Both social science research & PO are influenced by the dilemmas. Social scientists tailor their conceptualization of social reality to that held by the political bureaucracy. The origin of the dilemmas lies in capitalist ideology. Orthodox Marxist thought holds that political bureaucracy is the instrument of the bourgeoisie. Gaetano Mosca & Robert Michels, however, hold that capitalist political bureaucracy serves the bourgeoisie only when it becomes the dominant class after defeating classical elitism. By its hierarchic DofL, hierarchic delegation of authority, professionalism, & diffusion of an ethic of efficiency, the political bureaucracy shapes the capitalist state's society, irrationally promoting a social system of growing economic exploitation & increasing violence. Capitalist political bureaucracies should be analyzed with regard to their external & internal contradictions from a dialectic viewpoint, by analyzing the contextual structure of the two dilemmas; the bureaucracies' power status & scope of action within the social structure should be studied. S. Whittle.

title: Autonomy and democracy in an autocratic organization: The case of the Roman Catholic Church
abstract: The pluralism that exists in the Roman Catholic church in the US raises questions about the possibilities of organizational change within the Church.  Data from surveys and other sources reveal that the laity of the Roman Catholic church in the US are bringing about change in the face of Vatican bureaucracy and its teaching authority.

title: Toward an Anthropology of Bureaucracy
abstract: Studies on forms of domination originally provided entry points for an anthropology of bureaucracy. Many scholars followed Max Weber's theorizing in this area, & beyond Weber, the theory of organizations was used to study bureaucracy. An overview of the state of the anthropology of bureaucracy is presented here, limited to articles in: the US publications Annual Review of Anthropology, American Anthropologist, Current Anthropologist, Cultural Anthropologist, & American Ethnologist; the Latin American Research Review; & the Mexican journals Nueva Anthropologia & Anales de Anthropologia. It is observed that bureaucracy has been little studied by anthropologists, but where it has, its place has been as an intrinsic aspect of complex societies. M. Pflum

title: The depopulation of the Bulgarian villages
abstract: The depopulation process in Bulgaria, especially in rural areas, is intensifying due to deepening unfavourable trends in the dynamics of demographic processes. Depopulation is a typical process in the fourth phase of demographic transition in rural areas of Bulgaria. The death rates exceed birth rates in the rural areas in the mid-1970s. The size of rural population and the number of villages in the country has been decreasing in the last decades. A large part of the villages were affected by depopulation processes during the period 1985-2007. A high depopulation level is observed in border and mountainous regions. The depopulation generates an array of different negative trends in the spatial aspect -- in socio-economic development, technical and social infrastructure, as well as the erasure of many small villages. The regional development plans need to embed measures for infrastructural development in order to attract and retain residents, utilise natural and cultural-historical heritage, and to stimulate economic activities and the development of various types of tourism, etc. Adapted from the source document.

title: ORGANIZATIONAL STRAINS IN THE COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT BLOCKS IN INDIA
abstract: The org'al tensions in CD in India, as reflected in the strains in org'al structure & goals & in the inter-personal relations among CD workers are analyzed on the basis of org theory. It is noted that the underdeveloped state of the sociol of bur'cy in India & the Indian tradition of bur'tic secrecy have led to a scarcity of res into public affairs. The following structural sources of tension in CD in India are discussed: (1) dual system of control over personnel (scalar vs functional, ie, on the district vs the block & local level); (2) supervision of the technical staff by a 'general' admin'or (Block Development Officer, etc); (3) role conflict (many CD officers remain as much dedicated to the maintenance of their admin'ive status as to the performance of their practical roles); (4) conflicting loyalties (loyalty of personnel to their parent dept in the gov rather than to the Dept of CD). Tensions inherent in the conflict between soc system imperatives & bur'tic rationality are: (a) fam & kinship ties as a strain on bur'tic behavior; (b) the influence of the caste system on bur'tic behavior; (c) conflict of the CD personnel between personal status & bur'tic status; (d) the influence of fam background on the attitude held by the people toward formal authority, ie, a CD officer from a formerly royal fam may command more authority than one from a Is fam. It is hyp'ed that the farther away a society is from industr economy, the lower is its bur'cy on the legal rational scale. Moreover, Ru bur'cy tends to be less efficient than Ur bur'cy, even in non-Western, pre-industr societies. This is viewed as due to the wider informational perspective available in the Ur context. M. Maxfield.

title: Neoliberalism, welfare policy, and feminist theories of social justice; Feminist Theory Special Issue: `Feminist Theory and Welfare'
abstract: An overview of the feminist theory literature on welfare policy and politics is presented. This introductory essay places a particular emphasis on the works that fall within the political sociology and normative political philosophy genres. In a lengthy digression, the article offers a tribute to the work of Iris Marion Young. It examines the centrality of her thinking about distribution, cultural marginalization, the welfare state bureaucracy, transnational responsibility and solidarity, and the pitfalls of maternalist discourse for this field. In the conclusion, the article makes brief remarks about each of the contributions to the special issue on Feminist Theory and Welfare.

title: Bureaucrats as "Social Engineers": Federal Welfare Programs in Herbert Hoover's America
abstract: Historians studying twentieth-century US reform often seek to analyze the ideologies of political leaders separately from the institutions that these same leaders created. Such emphasis on ideas, as opposed to actions, has led "revisionist" US historians to argue that the presidencies of Herbert Hoover & Franklin D. Roosevelt were "conceptually continuous." Based on historical studies & government documents & reports, an examination of the major social welfare programs undertaken by the US federal government in the 1920s disputes this claim. Examination of the operations of the federal bureaucracy instead of the rhetoric of politicians demonstrates the existence of decided policy differences between the Hoover & Roosevelt eras. Background is provided for increased understanding of some of the policy implications of the US's contemporary welfare debate -- particularly concerning "rehabilitation" strategies & rationales for action in the social welfare field. Modified HA.

title: State, Bureaucracy and Polity in Modern Thai Politics
abstract: The Thaksin Shinawatra government has recently implemented the most extensive reforms of the Thai bureaucracy since King Chulalongkorn sought to modernize it in the 19th century, an attempt to reform a bureaucracy it sees as unresponsive, inefficient, & unwieldy, as a barrier to democracy. Interestingly, the reforms come at a time when most scholars have declared the death of the "bureaucratic polity," & the victory of democracy & civil society (eg, Prizzia, 1985; Pisan & Guyot, nd [1986?]; Bidhya, 1989; Anek, 1992; Ockey, 1992; Pasuk & Baker 1995, 1996; Yoshinori, 2002). If the bureaucratic polity is indeed dead, why does the Thaksin government conceive of the bureaucracy as such a barrier to democracy? And why does the "bureaucratic polity" continue to haunt scholars of Thai studies, so that it must repeatedly be declared dead? To answer these questions, we begin by briefly outlining the influence of the "bureaucratic polity" model on scholars of Thai politics. I will argue that even in the way it is being abandoned, it continues to affect Thai studies. We then turn to contemporary Thai politics to sketch out the nature of the Thai state, the bureaucracy, the regime, & the polity. Finally, borrowing & adapting an existing model for examining the state, we look at the implications of recent changes in the bureaucracy & the polity for conceptualizing Thai politics. 56 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Pathologies in De-Bureaucratic Public Organizations in Nigeria
abstract: Because of the nouveau and rapidly growing interests in, and acceptance of, de-bureaucratization (popularly called "deregulation" in Nigeria), as a more attractive organization concept than bureaucratization, the central concern of this paper is an identification and objective analysis of bureau-pathologies in de-bureaucratic public organizations in Nigeria, in response to those of bureaucratic organizations which have already been analysed in the literature. The major and prevalent bureau-pathologies identified and analyzed are inconsistency and unpredictability, informality and denials, unlimited or uncircumscribed flexibility, personalization, limitation of de-categorization, laziness, and goal displacement. Their effects can be summarized as the prevalence of worrying degree of arbitrariness which distorts effective operations in Nigerian public organizations. The paper recommends the promotion of a higher level of certainty in Nigerian public organizations, through more effective and strict implementation of the avowed limited or adequate rules available. Adapted from the source document.

title: Western Marxist Interpretation of the Soviet Union: Between Hostility and Neutrality
abstract: Marxism and the Soviet Union: a Survey of Critical Theories and Debates since 1917 focuses on the Western Marxist interpretation of the Soviet Union in a historical context. Van der Linden categorized the various interpretations under four broad theoretical approaches. The theory of state capitalism insisted that the Soviet mode of production was a specific stage of capitalism. On the other hand, the Trotskyist theory of the degenerated workers' state indicates that, even though the working class owned the means of production in the Soviet Union, it was deformed by the ascendancy and hegemony of bureaucracy. Nevertheless, this theory rejects the thesis that the Soviet bureaucracy was a coherent and self-perpetuated ruling class. The theory of the new mode of production with a consolidated ruling class generally characterized the Soviet society as a non-socialist and non-capitalist new mode of production, and bureaucracy formed a ruling class. This new ruling class was sui generis different from the previous ruling classes in the sense that it was not the possessor of the means of production. However, it expropriated the surplus value. The theory of the new mode of production without a consolidated ruling class, on the other hand, asserted that, instead of a new ruling class, the elite, which comprised a coalition of state managers, technical work force and bureaucrats, maintained hegemony over the Soviet working class. Moreover, van der Linden's book also coveres a long list of writers who do not belong to any theoretical approach but had significant repercussions for the development of these approaches to a certain degree. Covering a wide range of views and having a detailed historical analysis of various theoretical approaches, van der Linden's book is a major contribution to the forgotten debate about the Soviet Union. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Financing Suburbia: Prudential Insurance and the Post-World War II Transformation of the American City
abstract: Innovations in financing & the role of the Prudential Insurance Co in driving the suburbanization of the US after WWII are explored, referencing the company's internal magazine. During the 1930s, Prudential initiated a system of regional branch offices empowered to invest in productive investments, eg, federally insured mortgages, but then lobbied to change the laws so that they could develop any type of real estate. They built apartments, stores, offices, & industrial parks, & lent money to suburban homebuilders. Prudential supplied the funding for a number of well-known developments in the 1940s & 1950s, but explicitly rejected putting money into existing neighborhoods or factories. For the period, Prudential was the nation's largest mortgage lender & largest private owner of retail property. M. Pflum

title: SOME ISSUES IN THE STUDY OF BUREAUCRACY AND ALIENATION
authors: Bonjean, Charles M; Grimes, Michael D
abstract: Reflected are alternative choices available to the res'er interested in this relationship: (1) The concern may be with alienation from the org or with general alienation, or both. (2) The orientation may be macro (using 'global' or 'analytical' properties of org's to explain diff's between org's), micro (using the individual as the unit of analysis & focusing on diff's within org's or other meaningful soc units or categories), or both. Where findings are negative, the micro perspective is the most valie; where they are positive, the macro approach is more appropriate. (3) Conceptualization may be structured by techniques of data analysis (probably yielding a 'clean' analysis but less continuity with previous work), or may be guided by conceptualization (probably yielding greater continuity with previous work but less confidence in the instrumentation), or to some extent, both. AA.

title: Neighborhood-Based Foster Care: A Critical Examination of Location-Based Placement Criteria
abstract: Faced with large caseloads and poor outcomes for children, child welfare agencies across the country are developing new strategies for serving vulnerable families. Many of the recent approaches move the locus of services from centralized, distant bureaucracies to local neighborhoods, where families at risk are most likely to reside. Current innovations in part suggest that treatment interventions such as foster care should also be located in children's communities of origin. This article offers a critical examination of the neighborhood approach to foster care placement. Although neighborhood foster care placements have potential benefits for some children, the research reviewed here does not fully support the existence of these benefits for the development and well-being of many children. An evidence-based practice approach that takes into account many factors besides neighborhoods thus is more likely to produce beneficial outcomes for children placed in out-of-home care. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: MOBILIZATION AND BUREAUCRATIZATION IN CUBA
abstract: THE RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN INSTITUTIONALIZATION & MOBILIZATION IS UNCLEAR. DEINSTITUTIONALIZATION IS ONE OF THE CONDITIONS OF MOBILIZATION. THE CONTRAST BETWEEN BUREAUCRACY & MOBILIZATION IS ESPECIALLY EVIDENT IN CUBA. IN 1956 CUBAN REBELS BEGAN THE STRUGGLE AGAINST BATISTA IN A REMOTE PART OF ORIENTE PROVINCE. AFTER THE TAKE-OVER OF HAVANA IN 1958 THE MOVEMENT BEGAN TO DISINTEGRATE. THE COMMUNISTS, WHO HAD NOT TAKEN AN ACTIVE PART IN THE REVOLUTION, WERE THE ONLY ONES WHO HAD KNOWLEDGE & PEOPLE AVAILABLE TO ESTABLISH A GOVERNMENT; THE FIRST CASTRO GOVERNMENT INCLUDED A LARGE NUMBER OF COMMUNISTS. THE IDEOLOGY TENDED TO BE MOSTLY PERSONAL STATEMENTS MADE BY CASTRO IN SPEECHES TO THE PEOPLE. IN THE EARLY YEARS AFTER THE REVOLUTION, A STATE OF ECONOMIC ANARCHY EXISTED, WHICH WAS SOON REPLACED BY A CONTROLLED ECONOMY INVOLVING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A BUREAUCRACY TO REGULATE IT. PROBLEMS IN FAILING TO ACHIEVE ECONOMIC GOALS WERE CONSIDERED INDIVIDUAL, RATHER THAN INSTITUTIONAL SHORTCOMINGS. THE MILITARY WAS DEPLOYED TO MOBILIZE THE PEOPLE, SINCE IT WAS THE ONLY INSTITUTION WHICH COULD COMBINE BUREAUCRACY WITH THE CAPACITY TO MOBILIZE. P. TIERSMA.

title: Individual and Organization
abstract: A psychosociological analysis of the relations between the individual & organization is presented. 5 concepts are explored: the organization, the bureaucratization of the organization, the formal organization--the informal organization, the motivational basis of participation, & the participants. The organization is defined as (1) a system made of rules & norms with a view to reaching a certain goal & (2) people in interaction, & differentiated according to their place in the structure of the functional-hierarchy. One distinguishes "what is already organized" (the structure) from organization (the process of actualizing the structure); the former term, representing the fundamental requirement, designates the organization, the latter refers to the comportamental possible through which the process is made evident. Thus, the motivational system is not suspended in a social vacuum; it is supported by the members' attitudes & behaviors. The effects of bureaucracy upon the "organizational conditioned man," & the circumstances in which he can turn into a "bureaucratic personality," are analyzed. The relation between formal & informal within an organization is discussed. Reviewing several theories which discuss the participation motivation, it is evident that all of them regard motivational conditioning from the viewpoint of the interests of the organization, & not from that of all the participants. The organization adjustment to the participants' motivation, & not their adjustment to the requirements of the organization is suggested. AA.

title: Mad Kings, Proper Houses, and an Asylum in Rural Ireland
abstract: Data collected during fieldwork are drawn on to examine aspects of the local history & cultural life of St. Columba's mental hospital, a formerly large asylum in the west of Ireland. The way local people talk about the hospital as a place & the way the institution mixes its local, colonial, & national histories reveal that native spatial logics have succeeded in at least partially domesticating this bureaucratic structure, even as the asylum & the thinking that motivated it have contributed to historical changes at this periphery. 90 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Assessing Policy Implementation Success: Observations from the Philippines
abstract: Analyzes the establishment & start-up of the One Stop Shop Inter-Agency Tax Credit & Duty Drawback Center in the Philippines, with respect to the adoption of strategic management principles & techniques. The policy change agenda embodied in the center's creation is described, & developments during its first eight months of existence are outlined. The impact of bureaucratic complexity on the ability of center management & Dept of Finance staff to implement the policy reform agenda is explored. 1 Table, 17 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Should I tell the City Council about this? Social Workers between Vocation and Bureaucracy. An Ethnography of a Public Social Welfare Network in Madrid
abstract: Starting from an ethnographic description of how a public social welfare network in the center of Madrid works, paying special attention to the testimony and an analysis of the practice of its social workers, this article seeks to show, empirically, how and in what sense public policies reproduce social marginality and how social workers, located at the institution's frontier, experience very intimately all the contradictions implicit in the system. Adapted from the source document.

title: HOSPITAL PROFESSIONS AND DIVISION OF LABOR
abstract: THE PROGRESSIVE BUREAUCRATIZATION OF THE HOSPITALS HAS LED TO A DOFL AMONG HOSPITAL FUNCTIONS THAT IS THE ORIGIN OF PROFESSIONAL MOVEMENTS AMONG NURSES FOR THE REEVALUATION OF THEIR WORK & AMONG CERTAIN GROUPS OF MD'S. 3 TYPES OF HOSPITAL SERVICES ARE DISTINGUISHED: GENERAL CARE, MASS SPECIALTY CARE, & RESEARCH-ORIENTED CARE. GENERAL MEDICAL SERVICES HAVE BECOME LIMITED TO THE CARE OF DISADVANTAGED SC'S. SPECIALTY MASS CARE HAS BECOME DISCONNECTED FROM RESEARCH. THE NURSING PROFESSION, BEING DEPENDENT UPON MD'S & IN COMPETITION WITH THE NEW MEDICAL AUXILIARIES, WILL HAVE DIFFICULTY IN CONTROLLING ITS OWN DOMAIN. MEDICAL UNITY HAS BEEN ERODED BY SPECIALIZATION & BY THE RECRUITMENT OF MEDICAL AUXILIARIES. SPECIALIZATION IS AS MUCH THE PRODUCT OF HIERARCHIZATION AS OF TECHNICAL RATIONALE. ADMINISTRATIVE POLITICS, THE PRIVILEGED STATUS OF SPECIALTY CARE, & BUREAUCRATIC STANDARDS HAVE INTERVENED IN HOSPITAL AFFAIRS, AT THE EXCLUSION OF CONSIDERATION OF TECHNICAL MATTERS & QUALIFICATIONS. HA TR & MODIFIED BY D. BURKENROAD.

title: The postneoliberal fabulation of power: On statecraft, precarious infrastructures, and public mobilization in Brazil
abstract: In Brazil's hybrid government of social protection and market expansion, there is under way a fabulation of power, which ultimately serves to "de-poor" people seeking care, working infrastructures, and justice while also shoring up state politics as usual. This process became evident through the failure of a collaborative research project that I coordinated on right-to-health litigation. In rethinking that failure as an experiment in public ethnography, I draw on core disagreements with public officials over the interpretation of our findings from a legal database. Analyzing these disagreements provides an entry point into the mechanisms of veridiction and falsification at work in Brazil, whose government sees itself as providing public goods beyond the minimum neoliberal state. Countering state mythology, public ethnography thus illuminates the improvised quality of postneoliberal democratic institutions and opens up new avenues for theorizing power and the political field. [web URL: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/amet.12337/full]

title: Predicting Bureaucratic Control: Evidence from the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments
abstract: Determines whether it is possible to develop a general means of predicting control, or at least of predicting what is termed "intent to control," based on the assumption that legislators' preferences toward agency responsiveness reflect the nature of the policy environment. Application to the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 finds strong empirical evidence that statutory provisions vary predictably, depending on whether legislators possess the requisite technical ability & are likely, or wish, to be held politically accountable. Results indicate that control varies for reasons that fit well with the understanding of how elected officials deal with complexity & their own political situations. Findings also imply that subtle, but measurable, differences in the specific policy environment are crucial for understanding control. 5 Tables, 38 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucracy and Rationality in Weber
abstract: Bureaucracy is discussed in terms of the significance assigned to it by social scientists who are studying the phenomenon of stratification in contemporary society. Questions that M. Weber did not fully deal with are discussed here: (1) technical & scientific rationality as an administrative mode, (2) modern bureaucratic rationality, (3) the historical inevitability of bureaucracy & its breakdown as a result of charismatic modes of power, & (4) the contrast between the modern rational bureaucracy & its traditional, affective predecessor. The position of scholars like C. W. Mills, who maintain that bureaucracy is a power elite inevitable in modern society, whether capitalist or socialist, is correct. The claim put forward by Marxists that communist society will feature no bureaucracy is fallacious. If Weber's position, which emphasizes the dominance of politics, is correct, it will be impossible to get rid of bureaucracy until the apparatus of the state is completely dismantled. S. Karganovic.

title: Mapping women in Tehran's public spaces: a geo-visualization perspective
abstract: Functioning public spaces, as 'public' political, social, and cultural arenas of citizen discourse, affect not only the citizen's quality of life, but are also indispensable infrastructure in democratic societies. This article offers a nuanced understanding of Iranian women's usage, feelings, and preferences in public spaces in present-day Tehran by not simply importing Western theories that sustain distinctions between traditional and modern women, but instead by hearing women's stories. This article raises concerns related to the gender identities, the politics of space, and design of these places. Meidan-e-Tajrish, Sabz-e-Meidan, and Marvi Meidancheh in Tehran accommodate an ethnographic visualization of gendering space. The process by which Iranian women attach symbolic meanings to those public spaces offers insight into the mutual construction of gender identities and space politics. The contrasting urban locations, different design styles, and distinct social activities provide an excellent comparison between the selected public spaces. Findings suggest caution in using gender as an essential category in feminist geography research to better represent the diversity of experiences in public spaces. Binary categorization of modern versus traditional, secular versus religious, public versus private, and male versus female in urban studies should be carefully validated as Iranian women's lived experiences challenge the homogenizing Western theories, particularly the predominant critics of modern public spaces in North America. The research process also highlights the benefits of geo-visualization in understanding the complex interaction between gender identities and the built environment.

title: ADMINISTRATION AND BUREAUCRACY
abstract: The unavoidable growth of bur'cy in underdeveloped countries leads to dysfunctions which may paralyze all chances of progress, or, in any case, only allow it at the cost of a considerable waste of human energy. The problem is analyzed re org'al sociol. The uncontrolled development of a rigid bur'cy, based on a Taylorian mechanistic type of rationality, is esp dangerous for such countries, since it implies a deep cleavage between the leaders & the led. New conceptions & new methods of admin'ive action, based on a more supple & less oppressive rationale, are presently coming into practice. Could they not benefit the administration's of underdeveloped countries, & help find solutions more adapted to the problem of rapid growth? Thus some of the greatest difficulties the Western world has known under the oppressive influence of 19th cent positivism could be by-passed. AA.

title: Pakistani immigrant organisational spaces in Toronto and New York City
authors: Chaudhary, Ali R; Guarnizo, Luis Eduardo
abstract: This study examines how 'contexts of reception' in two migrant cities shape the organisational infrastructure for Pakistani immigrant communities in Toronto and New York City (NYC). Previous research is divided into two epistemic camps, one focusing on locally oriented organisations promoting settlement/incorporation and the other on transnational organisations-thus obscuring the relationships between these organisations. The present study transcends this division by examining how the combined effect of state policies, socioeconomic incorporation, community characteristics and societal attitudes shape the composition and geographical orientation of an immigrant group's collective organisational space-comprised of local and transnationally oriented organisations. Data come from a newly constructed database of Pakistani non-profit organisations based in Toronto and NYC and from qualitative research conducted in both cities. Contrary to our expectations and previous research, we find that state-sponsored multiculturalism in Toronto is not associated with a larger or more transnationally oriented organisational space. Rather, it is the affluence of the Pakistani community in NYC that is associated with the larger and more transnational of the two Pakistani organisational spaces. Findings also reveal tensions between local and transnationally oriented organisations in both cities, reflecting a growing fragmentation between affluent cosmopolitan immigrant elites and the impoverished segments of Toronto and NYC Pakistani communities.

title: Becoming Alienated and Reversing the Process
abstract: Two major factors influencing the occurrence of alienation are blocked social achievement & the uncaring attitude of modern bureaucracies. The difficulty of attaining goals set by the social structure & the tendency of bureaucracies to view people as statistics results in reactions of withdrawal, passivity, renunciation of the system, or participation in changing the social structure. Self needs are distinguished from survival needs & are necessary to the establishment of interpersonal relationships & the development of a reason for living. A capitalistic type of system frustrates the satisfaction of self needs, thus promoting alienation. The social structure pressures individuals to conform to society at the expense of their self needs & goals. The tendency of schools to evaluate all children with the same set of standards is one way society promotes feelings of alienation & inferiority, especially if the child does not meet the school's standards. The alienation of man will cause problems in the operation of social institutions. M. K. Razo.

title: The proposal economy
abstract: Using the case of Cobalt, a former silver mining town in Northern Ontario, Canada, we trace the transition from social funding as a feature of the welfare state to social funding based on application, adjudication and award. We identify a process in the community development arena, whereby local governments, community organizations and community members are increasingly enmeshed in the bureaucratic and socially disengaging processes of proposal-writing. Cobalters regard aspects of this downward deflection of the locus of economic responsibility as fairer, and more transparent, than the previous funding regime. We show how a local moral economy and understanding of citizenship based on an ethic of caring has contributed, in a counterintuitive way, to an interim outcome of more public services. At the same time, the current pursuit of development funds via proposal is undermining the practices of civic engagement which have allowed the town to remain distinct for the past century.

title: The Styles of Management Inventory: A Methodological Analysis of a Training and Research Instrument
abstract: In recent yrs several theoretical ideas have been advanced in the area of problem-solving & decision-making in admin, with a focus on "leadership" styles. Instruments have been designed to operationalize the theory & for purposes of training & res. However, there has been little systematic testing of such instruments. The theoretical underpinnings of one particular instrument, the Styles of Manag Inventory, are examined. Then, a test is made for internal consistency by using multidimensional scaling. This theoretical model of manag was originally conceived by R. Likert, by R. R. Blake & J. S. Mouton, & was operationalized into the instrument studied here by J. Hall, J. B. Harvey & M. Williams (STYLES OF MANAGEMENT INVENTORY, New York, NY: Nat'l Council on Crime & Del'cy, 1964). Briefly, it is designed to reflect the R's general managerial orientation through the R's stated preference for certain behaviors, which represent diff managerial orientations to various manag situations. The results indicate that the Styles of Manag Inventory does not test out well from the point of view of internal consistency & of assumed patterning. Data were obtained from 288 probation admin'ors in the US. 3 Figures, 2 Tables. Modified HA.

title: From mobilization to institutionalization? The case of Norwegian environmentalism
abstract: A widespread view contends that, in due course, political mobilization gives way to institutionalization; that is, vibrant movements turn into rigid hierarchic organizations. In the aftermath of the political radicalization of the 1960s and 1970s, the literature on social movements announced that this 'impasse' belonged to the past: new social movements were taken to be anti-bureaucratic and anti-hierarchical; representing a new historical subject, beyond Marxist determinism, yet retaining a certain leftist-liberalist political imprint. More recently, an almost diametrically opposed contention seems to have gained hegemony: the (new) social movements are becoming institutionalized and are being incorporated, or even co-opted, by the 'establishment'. These general statements stand in glaring contrast to the theoretical progress made within contemporary social movement theory, and accordingly, the purpose of this article is to contribute to a more nuanced approach to the phenomenon of 'institutionalization of social movements', on both a theoretical and an empirical level. Against the backdrop of a short review of literature in the field, a theoretical framework is introduced: institutionalization as an open and multidimensional process, encompassing structural, normative and cognitive elements. Thereafter, this typology is applied in order to study institutionalization as part of a wider context. In one section the Norwegian case is introduced and includes the descriptive empirical analyses: how are Norwegian environmental organizations institutionalized? Thereafter, the context of institutionalization is studied: which strategies are chosen in order to gain influence, and what are the prevalent political ideological orientations? A final section summarizes and discusses the empirical findings in light of the theoretical framework.  [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The ecology of online newspapers: The case of China
abstract: He and Zhu examine the development of online newspapers in China through a "social environment" framework and find several adverse factors in policies, regulations, economic structure, business conventions and telecommunications infrastructure.

title: The mismatch between the map and the terrain-evidence-based social work in Sweden
authors: Bergmark, Anders; Bergmark, Ake; Lundstrom, Tommy
abstract: In this article we will give an account of the introduction of evidence-based practice (EBP) in Swedish social work. The Swedish development may serve as an example of what happens when the process is driven by bureaucracy with a strong public funding/back-up rather than by the academy. This is not to say that the Swedish case is unique, but rather that problems and controversies that are well established on the international arena are in Sweden framed in a very particular context. The most far reaching efforts to implement EBP in Swedish social work have been carried out by central bureaucracy. The introduction of EBP may be depicted as a top-down guideline project, with randomized controlled trials as the gold standard. Shortage of evidence paired with political pressure to implement EBP has to a certain extent also brought about dissolution of the basic concept. The article concludes with an elaborated assessment of how current conceptions of EBP relates to professional and contextual conditions of Swedish social work practice. We also address the issue of how to establish what adequate and valid evidence is by suggesting an approach that deviates from predominant evidence hierarchies and polarized extremes. Adapted from the source document.

title: How to Overcome Challenges for Meaningful Implementation of Inclusive Education in Lesotho
authors: Khoaeane, T J; Naong, M N
abstract: This study explores the extent to which inclusive education is appropriately and adequately implemented in Lesotho schools. The study, which was conducted among 256 randomly selected teachers in the two districts of Lesotho, namely Lithabaneng and St. Bernadette, reveals a depressing picture. A semi-structured questionnaire with multiple Likert rating scales was used to collect data from the respondents. Teachers still find it difficult to deal with learners with various learning disabilities, while schools' lack of suitable infrastructure compounds the problem for teachers. The findings show that 63 percent of the teachers bemoan a lack of proper training in order to deal with these learners with disabilities; no support material; and no sympathy from parents and authorities. This situation does not only impact negatively on the morale of these teachers, but also defeats the intentions of ensuring that inclusive education is executed in a manner consistent with government policies.

title: Contradictions, and a Glimpse of Utopia: Daily Life in a University Women's Studies Program
abstract: Based upon the experiences of the Michigan State U Women's Studies Program, an analysis is made of the contradictions resulting from efforts of women's studies participants (committed to social change, equality, & valuing women) to make headway in a bureaucratic university environment founded on hierarchy, competition, & the devaluation of women. Three principle areas of conflict are identified: (1) there are conflicts between hierarchy & collectivity, (2) individual faculty members often feel caught between the demands of feminism & of academic careers, & (3) within the larger university, there are conflicts as women's studies programs struggle for legitimacy while also seeking institutional & social change. These conflicts are seen as a positive, although frustrating, force shaping the character of women's studies programs. Modified HA

title: Ideal Types in Public Service Television: Paternalists and Bureaucrats, Charismatics and Avant-Gardists
abstract: Over time, the broadcast media develop conventions of self-presentation that are formulated more or less explicitly by academics & media professionals as ideal types. The article discusses four such ideal types of self-presentation in television: paternalists & bureaucrats, charismatics & avant-gardists. It demonstrates how they have been formulated & evaluated by researchers & media professionals. Following Raymond Williams's notion of 'dominant', 'residual' & 'emergent' forms, the article also discusses the historical interactions & contests between them. Examples are drawn from Nordic & British public service broadcasting. A case is made for acknowledging the coexistence of several ideal types, rather than taking at face value notions of some general 'slide' from a paternalist past to a charismatic present. The article draws particular attention to the importance of bureaucratic modes of self-presentation for understanding early public service television, & of avant-gardist modes for understanding more recent developments. 41 References. [Copyright 2002 Sage Publications Ltd.]

title: Bureaucracy and its limits: accountability and rationality in higher education
abstract: Alongside debates concerning managerialism, marketisation and performativity, the question of accountability in higher education has come to the fore in recent commentary. Discussion of the subject has tended to be divided into two distinct camps. On the one hand, there are strong calls for more accountability to the public purse - a desire to witness more productive returns and efficiency on investment in higher education. On the other, there are academics who rail against the oppressive, panoptican-like nature of the audit culture, emphasising the debilitating effects of quality assurance mechanisms on academic life. The paper suggests that one way out of this impasse is to place the current accountability agenda - what Travers refers to as the 'new bureaucracy' - in the context of Max Weber's account of bureaucracy and rationality. Habermas' reconstructed version of Weber's work is identified as a possible means of delineating the reaches and limits of modern bureaucratic accountability. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Restratification, Hybridity and Professional Elites: Questions of Power, Identity and Relational Contingency at the Points of 'Professional-Organisational Intersection'
abstract: This paper re-visits and re-appraises Freidson's restratification thesis. His thesis was proposed in the mid-1980s to counter the idea of de-professionalisation, suggesting professional elites can retain collective interests in a more bureaucratic and marketised workplace. Contemporary research highlights the growth of professional-managerial hybrids, and the blurring of professional and organisational boundaries. Within this context, the restratification thesis offers a relevant sociological lens for understanding the emergence and implications of these hybrid elite roles. Research tends to support the broad descriptive aspect of the thesis, but there remains much debate about its explanatory accuracy. The paper reviews Freidson's thesis and develops three areas of theoretical debate and elaboration related to questions of elite power, culture and identity, and relational contingency, with particular reference to the experiences of the medical profession. The paper re-interprets hybrid elite roles in terms of their points of 'professional-organisational intersection' from which it develops a tentative extension of Freidson's categorisation.

title: State Education Agencies' Acquisition and Use of Research Knowledge for School Improvement
authors: Massell, Diane; Goertz, Margaret E; Barnes, Carol A
abstract: Over the last two decades, state education agencies (SEAs) have been given considerable responsibilities for improving low-performing schools and for adopting research-based practices in doing so. Yet we know little about how and where these organizations search for, select, and use research and other kinds of evidence. We examined these questions as they relate to school improvement designs and strategies in three SEAs using a combination of surveys and interviews conducted in 2010-11. We found that SEA staffs relied most heavily on their colleagues for information but that information often flowed across departments and offices, contrary to the usual image of the SEA as a segmented and siloed bureaucracy. A large number of external organizations were identified in SEA research advice networks and played a catalyzing role in the design or elaboration of research for policy. Although most sources were named by just one person, each SEA also had central internal staff who played an important role in brokering research on school improvement. Identifying and cultivating such influential actors, and connecting individuals who are now isolated or only weakly engaged in these communication networks, could create a more robust exchange of knowledge around school improvement. Adapted from the source document.

title: Documents and Bureaucracy
abstract: This review surveys anthropological and other social research on bureaucratic documents. The fundamental insight of this literature is that documents are not simply instruments of bureaucratic organizations, but rather are constitutive of bureaucratic rules, ideologies, knowledge, practices, subjectivities, objects, outcomes, even the organizations themselves. It explores the reasons why documents have been late to come under ethnographic scrutiny and the implications for our theoretical understandings of organizations and methods for studying them. The review argues for the great value of the study of paper-mediated documentation to the study of electronic forms, but it also highlights the risk of an exclusive focus on paper, making anthropology marginal to the study of core bureaucratic practices in the manner of earlier anthropology. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Social Control in Organizations
authors: Miliham, Spencer; Bullock, Roger; Cherrett, Paul
abstract: Using evidence from the authors' res into many residential org's such as boarding Sch's, penal instit's, hosp's, service training centers, & religious orders, an attempt is made to distinguish & explain the effectiveness of differing processes of soc control in order to explore which kinds of control will be most effective in diff org's. The author's concept of control removes the ambiguities that arise when A. Etzioni's concepts of coercive, remunerative & normative controls are applied to empirical situations (COMPLEX ORGANIZATIONS, Glencoe, Ill: Free Press, 1964). When control processes in a variety of org's are compared, diff's are found in the areas of behavior subject to control & the effects of controls on members' commitment to goals. The 1st reflect the goals of the org while the latter variations are influenced by the presoc'ization experiences of members, the norms of outside society on the acceptability of controls, the legitimacy afforded to controls by informal norms within the org & the dependency of members on the org to meet needs. In a situation where members are dependent on the org, where their needs are met & where their informal norms support the goals of the org, normative & orientation controls will be sufficient. Where inmates are less dependent, where their informal system rejects formal goals, then coercive sanctions, remunerative & instit'al controls & structural controls over office are essential to maintain order. This approach complements Etzioni's contributions not only by acknowledging the importance of forces external to the actor but also by stressing a perspective where individuals interpret, evaluate & give definition & meaning to the actions which they produce & which impinge on them. This concept of soc control is useful in helping us to understand real life interactional contexts such as those found in Sch's & hosp's. It is important to realize that staff & inmate definitions of instit'al values, rewards & sanctions are as vital to the understanding of them as are a priori labels. Modified AA.

title: Inequality, Health Infrastructure, and Spatial Context: Understanding Pathways to Variations in the Causal Determinants of Race-Specific Mortality Rates
authors: James, Wesley L; Porter, Jeremy R
abstract: Previous research examines the ecological relationship between income inequality and mortality, and results are inconclusive. This analysis builds upon these findings by implementing a spatially weighted path analysis to better understand the mediating relationships of economic and social inequality, health infrastructure, and mortality. In the analysis, overall and race-specific mortality rates are combined with local health infrastructure data, income inequality and racial segregation data, and a series of ecological controls to undertake this examination. Ultimately, findings show that income inequality is a stronger determinant of mortality than is segregation, for whites and blacks, regardless of the existing health infrastructure. We also find racial disparities in the direct effect of local health infrastructure on mortality. In contrast to previous literature suggesting no association between income inequality and mortality after accounting for race and model sophistication, we argue that the significance of the relationship persists using race-specific, spatially weighted path models. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Japanese Managerial Behavior and "Excessive Competition"
authors: Abegglen, James C; Rapp, William V
abstract: It is argued that a number of aspects of Japanese corporate behavior, including experience with rapid growth & financial & personnel policies as well as the cost effects of growth, make the maintenance of market share a critical objective of Japanese manag. A major consequence of this concern is the degree of pre-emptive capital investment & pricing that is termed "excessive competition." In this context, the causes & consequences of pricing behavior in Japan are examined, & the pricing, investment, & experience curve is traced. Rapid growth in demand stimulates rapid investment; rapid investment & increased market share translate directly into visible cost advantage; high fixed costs ensure that the additional capacity will be fully utilized; & financial & competitive practices are such that margins in excess of the financial requirements for growth penalize firms in high-growth business. Under these conditions price & rapid investment in capacity become the primary competitive weapons of the Japanese Co. The firms which have most successfully manipulated this investment-demand process have captured market growth & have increased their market share. The meaning of this system for the Western businessman is explored. The Japanese econ system is closely tied to the culture; it cannot be transplanted. Western businesses should seek competitive strategies that are both appropriate to their own culture & successful in countering the Japanese system. The appropriateness of Japan's system may become less clear in the post-industr era when skill-intensive services assume a greater econ role. But for the time being, "excessive competition" will continue to be successful behavioral strategy for Japanese managers of high-growth businesses. 3 Figures. M. Maxfield.

title: Bureaucratic Deformation of Consciousness and the Fight against Bureaucratism
abstract: Bureaucracy is a serious, complex social evil that has been fought throughout Soviet history with varying degrees of success. Currently, the Twenty-Seventh Communist Party Congress is waging a decisive, merciless war on bureaucracy, which is seen as an impediment to accelerated SE development. The bureaucratic personality shows indifference to the consequences of his actions, preference of his own interests over those of the state, deference to the organizational hierarchy not as a factor of rational organization but as an end in itself, & an irrationally conservative attitude toward organizational change. Various management styles aiding the reduction of bureaucracy are reviewed. G. Prostakov

title: Soviet Society and State Apparatus [1936-1938]: Contradictions and Interferences
abstract: The Soviet purges in the 1930s were initially conceived to impose uniform rules of conduct on bureaucrats of the State apparatus who frequently resorted to economically inefficient & politically dangerous methods of management. The bureaucrats, however, made use of their prerogatives to subvert these campaigns, to divert them by finding scapegoats, & by purging advocates of strict political control, plunging the country into virtual civil war. This state of affairs had to be stopped in 1938 not only to save the state apparatus from total breakdown but to temper the growing unruliness of the masses. The purges did not succeed in curbing nonaccountable methods of management, but they did result in a radical renewal of management personnel. The methods proved inseparable from the system & impossible to eradicate without destroying the apparatus. The bureaucracy's interest in maintaining the unity of the apparatus precluded a change in its methods, & the masses were rendered powerless to organize & bring about changes. Modified HA.

title: THE GROWTH OF A BUREAUCRACY
abstract: United Community Funds in the US are criticized for a change of emphasis from providing for the needy to financing leisuretime & health activities; for using pressure tactics to induce contributions; for not eliminating other money-raising drives as was promised; & for adopting a paternal att. The Funds display bureaucratic tendencies in constantly expanding their activities, good times or bad, regardless of need. They have taken on characteristics of a gov body in virtually taxing the people through pressurizing contributions, in exercising control over welfare org's, & in an ambition for expanded operations. They have become paternal in attitude toward both old & young, which is quite at variance with the historical individualism & self-sufficiency of the American people. It is suggested that contributors do not submit to pressure but follow their convictions, giving less if they see fit until the Funds are brought back into serving real need again, & are thus induced to accept their allotted place in community life. AA-IPSA.

title: Is Productivity the New Paradigm for the Salaried University? The Case of the Autonomous University of Metropolitan Xochimilco
abstract: The article analyzes educational reforms within the contexts of salaries & tax policies. During the 1990s, there was a good amount of reform regarding salaries & infrastructure in Mexican institutions of higher learning, including the Autonomous University of Metropolitan Xochimilco. The motive behind these reforms was to ensure a continuing improvement in academic quality, as determined through institutional evaluations & accreditation policies. Academic work itself was reorganized to achieve quantitative & qualitative improvements. The processes of evaluation & accreditation eventually formed the hard nucleus & paradigm of a new rationality. The result of these efforts has been a drastic redrawing of the relationship between nominal salaries & tax incentives based on productivity, with the level of productivity being the ultimate beneficiary. Tables, Graphs, References. R. Young

title: Pyramids, Status and Careers II. - Promotion by Selection
abstract: A continuation of an article by the author, "Pyramids, Status, and Careers I. - Promotion by Seniority," Population, 1971, 26, 3, 463-86. Here, promotion by selection is examined to see whether this kind of promotion lessens the effects of fluctuations & inequalities for people starting their careers at various dates. It is shown that selection does not reduce the results of recruitment "jolts" & career inequalities which result from them. Within the framework of promotion, real or referential seniority must be determined, such as a certain number or proportion of people who have either more seniority or less seniority; from this, calculations related to those of a Md or a quartile are derived. Laisser-faire policy in the manag of personnel leads to marked inequalities in the promotion of workers, depending upon whether they enter an org at a favorable time, before an increase in manpower, for example, or at an unfavorable time. When selection exists, laisser-faire can lead to absurd situations in the first few decades of the Co's existence. 3 Charts, 2 Graphs, 11 Tables & 2 Appendices. J. Weiner.

title: Bureaucracy and Bourgeoisie: Reform and Revolution in the Age of Imperialism
abstract: Neo-Marxist & other perspectives on the SC structure of the Ottoman Empire during the period of its peripheralization are described, focusing on the role of the bureaucracy & bureaucratic reforms. Bureaucracy must be identified with a group capable of social action in order to explain bureaucratic reforms, bringing up political issues, the relationship of the local bourgeoisie & the bureaucracy, & the topic of the bourgeois revolution. A synthesis of three perspectives is attempted. 25 References. A. Waters

title: Socioeconomic System of the Oil Boom and Rural Community Development in Western North Dakota
authors: Fernando, Felix N; Cooley, Dennis R
abstract: An oil boom is a complex social and economic phenomenon. The socioeconomic system presented in this article represents a novel effort to explicate boom impacts and changes, within a systems framework, at the community level to enhance community planning and development efforts. Most boomtown studies focus on longitudinal changes of a boom-bust-recovery cycle or social-disruption-based approaches. This article is an effort to demonstrate that longitudinal changes or social disruptions of a boom manifest through the interactions and interrelationships between social entities and stakeholders acting within the boom conditions and surrounding conditions. The socioeconomic system approach in this article analyzes the boom as a system, which provides a useful lens for many other rural communities currently experiencing unconventional oil and gas development in the United States. The socioeconomic system highlights five main challenges or factors that need to be addressed through community development strategies: develop affordable housing, invest in community infrastructure, expand public services, attract new businesses to the area, and develop better community integration strategies to build trust and unity within the community. This article is qualitative and exploratory in nature. As a result, it explicates the functions, structure, and relationships between system entities to provide a broader understanding of coherence, conflicts, and synergies within a system.

title: Power in the Field. Explaining the Legitimisation of Large-Scale Farming in Romania
abstract: Examining the development of Romanian agriculture, one may wonder how a few large-scale agribusinesses have managed to legitimise their position and to deflect open criticism even as they control a disproportionate share of arable land. Clarification may be provided by Pierre Bourdieu's concept of field, which involves the simultaneous characterisation of sets of objective positions and symbolic struggles over the definition of hierarchical principles. This analytical framework allows us to shed light on the economic field and its relationships with other fields, which each have their own structure and are each influenced by specific struggles. Large-scale agricultural holdings in Romania find support within the political and the scientific fields, each of which provides supports within the bureaucratic field. The coincidence of different fields prevents any questioning of the economic model on which the development of large-scale farming is based.

title: Limits of Empire: The French Colonial State and Local Patrimonialism in North Africa
abstract: The article shows that the concept of patrimonialism is useful for the analysis not only of nation-states, but also of local and imperial power structures. Highlighting the limits of empires, we consider how local conditions shaped the strategies of colonial states in the process of empire building. We argue that the strength of local patrimonial networks before colonization, coupled with the sequencing of colonial conquests, either facilitated or hindered the French colonial and imperial project. Using a comparative-historical approach based on the analysis of two cases, Algeria and Tunisia, we find that the French colonial state employed markedly differing strategies of domination in each case. In Algeria, the French initially attempted and failed to destroy local patrimonial networks and the social practices associated with them through extensive military action. The failed attempt to destroy local practices resulted in over a century of resistance and bloodshed. When military rule became too costly, the French opted instead to rely on decentralized control that used the very structures they originally sought to eradicate. With constant reminders of the misguided colonial strategy in Algeria, the French used a different form of rule in Tunisia. They incorporated the existing Tunisian bureaucracy into their own political project, using it to limit the power of local patrimonial networks and transforming them instead through the development of capitalistic agriculture. The article illustrates the importance of paying close attention to local patrimonial networks in the analysis of colonial and imperial strategies.

title: Repertoires of state-society interaction in a heterogeneous state: the Lula Era experience
authors: ABERS, Rebecca; SERAFIM, Lizandra; TATAGIBA, Luciana
abstract: This article examines the combination of interaction routines of the State with social movements in the designing of public policy during the Lula government in three sectors: rural development, urban policy and public security. The central argument is that in a context characterized by unprecedented permeability of the State, social movements and State actors created a historical pattern of State-society interaction. Under the motto 'participation of civil society', social movements and state actors resorted to a repertoire of diversified interaction, which included institutional participations, protests, occupying posts in the pubic bureaucracy and personal relationships, with varying emphases depending on past patterns of State-society interactions in each sector. Adapted from the source document.

title: Interlocking Patrimonialisms and State Formation in Qing China and Early Modern Europe
abstract: Familial power contributed to binding territories together and systematically severing them in both China and early modern European states. In the early Qing (1644-1911) Empire, Manchu conquerors met the challenges of securing and expanding rule by discovering ways to use laterally related brothers and imperial bondservants to hold Chinese bureaucrats in check, while deploying bureaucracy to restrain princely brothers from partitioning the state. The ensuing interlock of patrimonial practices and bureaucracy, developed in a style similar to ancien regime France, stabilized political power for centuries. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Inc., copyright The American Academy of Political and Social Science.]

title: Bureaucracy, Authoritarianism and the Future of Democracy in Russia ["Round Table" Materials]
abstract: A round-table discussion was held in June 1992 to assess the impact of Russia's long-standing bureaucratic tradition on the chances for present-day reforms to succeed. V. M.
