Mezhuev (Russian Academy Sciences, Leninsky Prospekt 14, Moscow V-71) opened by asking in what direction Russia is headed. The historical uniqueness of Russia's current transition from a socialist to a market economy was emphasized. Yu. A. Zamoshkin noted the paradoxical existence of democratic institutions in a land without democracy. V. M. Makarenko (Rostov State U, Russia) spoke on bureaucracy & government formalism. T. A. Alekseeva discussed the rationalization of bureaucracy. V. K. Kantor analyzed differences between bureaucracy in Russia & the West. A. S. Panarin (Russian Academy Sciences, Leninsky Prospekt 14, Moscow V-71) described old & new myths about bureaucracy. Yu. E. Milovanov (Rostov State U, Russia) analyzed authoritarian aspects of the former USSR. V. M. Bychenkov investigated the relationship between bureaucracy & property. A. P. Ogurtsov distinguished between various types of bureaucracy. M. Meeks

title: Instruments for Development in EU-15
abstract: This article analyzes the role of education investment & infrastructures as instruments for social development within the European Union (EU), using stochastic frontier techniques to estimate the technical efficiency of each of the component economies of the EU over the 1980-1997 period & to investigate whether those instruments influenced the results obtained. The research project uses a database prepared by the authors from investment information extracted from Eurostat's New Cronos database & figures on education spending provided by the OECD. Tables, Graphs, Appendixes. Adapted from the source document.

title: Public Bureaucracies and Policy Implementation
abstract: As agents of policy implementation, public bureaucracies have significant margins for discretionary action in fulfilling their tasks. This raises problems of efficiency & effectiveness. The latter is focused on & attitudinal & structural determinants of agency behavior in policy implementation are analyzed. AA.

title: The Career as a System to Manage Employment Relations: Functions and Structural Features of the Internal Career
abstract: The scope, structural features, & promotion criteria are examined as the three principal issues in research on internal careers (ICs). The reproduction & selection of human resources as an incentive mechanism are discussed as the functions of ICs identified in the literature. The efficiency conditions of ICs as incentive systems & the various organizational configurations of ICs are investigated, & the functions, scopes, & promotions mechanisms are also addressed in the context of the distinction between vertical & horizontal ICs. The role of ICs in the changing structure of a business enterprise is assessed, in particular, the reduced space for vertical careers, the functioning of ICs as devices of professional resource reproduction, & changes in the nature of horizontal careers. 102 References. Z. Dubiel

title: Measuring Alienation in Bureaucrat-Client Relationship
abstract: A concept of alienation comprising the categories of powerlessness, meaninglessness, normlessness, isolation, & self-estrangement is used as a basis for measuring levels of alienation in bureaucrat-client relationships. Measures were completed by 200 bureaucrats & 200 clients in a district of Bihar State, India. A strong component of alienation is found to be present in the mutual relationship of these two groups. 25 References. W. H. Stoddard.

title: When It Comes to Product Innovation, What Is So Bad about Bureaucracy?
abstract: Attempts to illuminate the specific relationship between bureaucracy & innovation, building on an interpretive vs a structural perspective to analyze 134 people's experiences with product innovation in 15 large bureaucracies. Data obtained during interviews revealed 4 patterns of bureaucratic thinking & acting that systematically inhibited effective action in defining, organizing, evaluating, & staffing the innovation effort; these patterns are described & illustrated at some length. Then, drawing on Max Weber's original theory of bureaucracy & other classics of innovation, it is theorized that it is an interpretive system of instrumental rationality, not only a bureaucratic structure, that creates & maintains these patterns. Speculation is offered on how large bureaucracies can become more innovative without losing their efficiency. 3 Tables, 59 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: State of play: The political ontology of sport in Amazonian Peru
abstract: Building on the importance of "play" in traditional sociality, organized team sports such as soccer are instrumental in promoting a new moral and political order among Urarina people of Peruvian Amazonia, one grounded in notions of roles, rules, and the abstract individual. As a vehicle of nationalist sentiment, highly amenable to ritualization and bureaucratization, sport is central to the process by which the state expands its territory and influence. Like warfare, but unifying rather than fragmenting in its effects, sport harnesses the energy and vitality of youth and co-opts them for other ends. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Effects of Bureaucratisation on Teacher Morale in Schools
abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine the effects of bureaucratisation on the teacher morale of elementary schools in central Denizli, Turkey. The sample comprised 436 randomly selected primary school teachers. The data was collected by administering the Elementary Schools Bureaucracy Level Scale developed by E. Gaye Ermec and the Elementary School Teachers Morale Survey. Regression Analysis was used to determine the impact of bureaucracy on teachers' morale. The results showed that bureaucracy has a significant impact on teacher morale. The regression analysis showed that the predictability of bureaucracy level on teacher morale in the sub-dimensions: 'satisfaction with teaching', 'teacher load' and 'community pressure' differ significantly between public and private elementary schools. Adapted from the source document.

title: Children's services in the iron cage of performance management: street-level bureaucracy and the spectre of Svejkism
authors: Wastell, D; White, S; Broadhurst, K; Peckover, S; Pithouse, A
abstract: Recent UK government reforms have introduced a range of measures to regulate practice in child welfare, with professional work increasingly structured into formal processes embedded in information technology. This prompts obvious anxieties about the erosion of professional discretion. Using Lipsky's concept of the street-level bureaucrat, we report on an ethnographical study examining how social workers organise their practice in an atmosphere of performance management. Clear indications of attenuated discretion are revealed, reflecting the shift to a managerial model of control. Of concern is the emergence of a pattern of formally conformant behaviour in which the letter of the organisational law is obeyed but without genuine commitment. Drawing on the anti-hero of Haek's celebrated satire, we denote this form of passive resistance 'vejkism'. While showing up the absurdities of excessive managerial power, such behaviours are ultimately dysfunctional for the organisation; an alternative governance paradigm, based on professional values, is briefly outlined. Adapted from the source document.

title: Ethical procedures, ethics, and bureaucracy in a research experience with indigenous population /Trâmites éticos, ética e burocracia em uma experiência de pesquisa com população indígena
authors: Christine Ranier Gusman; Rodrigues, Douglas Antonio; Wilza Vieira Villela
abstract: Based on an experience that occurred during a doctoral research, this article aims to discuss the bureaucratic procedures of social research in Brazil and some of its practical implications. We raise some questions regarding location and the decision-making power granted (or not) to an indigenous individual or population, as well as reflections on the resolutions approved by the National Committee for Research Ethics, their applicability and the (in)adequacy of forms and models used in social research. The article focuses on ethical issues, analyzing operational flows from and among agencies responsible for regulating research carried out with indigenous populations. It also includes reflections on the trace left by the tutelary condition of indigenous people and how this condition continues to limit research guidelines. By sharing this experience, this article intends to incite debates on the ethical implications of situations in which neutrality is replaced by bonds, as well as to demystify the idea that simplifying overly bureaucratic procedures would be a threat to ethical principles.

title: Reducing Bureaucratic Inflexibility
abstract: It is generally agreed that public welfare organizations are bureaucratic. The literature dealing with bureaucratic phenomena is examined; the relevant variables are identified & hypotheses developed. The hypotheses were tested in eighteen public welfare agencies; the findings challenge the idea that large organizations are necessarily bureaucratic, suggesting that the size of an organization is not directly related to bureaucratic inflexibility, & that large organizations may reduce bureaucratic inflexibility by promoting more professionalization, higher specialization, & reduction of centralization. 4 Tables, 1 Figure. Modified HA.

title: Partynomialism, Bureaucratism, and Economic Reform in the Soviet Power-System
abstract: A theoretical investigation of the connections between economic reforms & party monopoly in the USSR. It is argued that the fluctuations between hard-line authoritarianism & liberalization programs in the political sphere are due to the numerous "system contradictions" in Soviet society, including: the ideology of total equality vs the formal hierarchy of power concentrated in the party; a bureaucracy that does not operate by "rational-legal authority" (Max Weber's formulation); the use of state terror to control the peasants; partly elite polarization between intellectuals & bureaucrats; & disruptions of stratification patterns after the shift to market socialism. It is concluded that the goal of the party is to alleviate these contradictions by making minimal reforms & concessions in order to stabilize party rule. E. Swank

title: When looking for anarchy, look to the state: Fantasies of regulation in forcing disorder within the Australian Indigenous estate
abstract: This article questions the foundational binary 'anarchy-bureaucracy' and the multiple articulations at play in the state's refraction of anarchic qualities onto Indigenous Australians. Launching from the Northern Territory Emergency Response of June 2007, in which the Australian government assumed direct control of 73 Aboriginal communities in the north of Australia, it asks why bureaucracy is considered the antonym of anarchy and not its synonym. In mobilizing accounts of anarchic Aboriginal depravity to authorize an ongoing bureau-professional presence in Indigenous worlds, links to other matters of interest, such as the state's dependence on mining revenues, let alone any account of the affective dimension of policy life, were removed from view. Reconsideration of the anarchy-state binary offers a lens to explore the emotional compulsions that are suppressed in the work of upholding the myth of a rational state and how this suppression further authorizes ongoing (anarchic) interventions into Indigenous worlds. [Reprinted by permission of Sage Publications Ltd., copyright holder.]

title: PROFESSIONALIZATION, BUREAUCRATIZATION AND RATIONALIZATION: THE VIEWS OF MAX WEBER
abstract: SOME OF M. WEBER'S RICH INSIGHTS INTO THE NATURE OF PROFESSIONALIZATION & ITS RELATIONSHIP TO BUREAUCRATIZATION & RATIONALIZATION ARE DISCUSSED. WEBER REGARDED PROFESSIONALIZATION AS AN ASPECT OF THE PROCESS OF RATIONALIZATION. UNLIKE SOME CONTEMPORARY SOCIOLOGISTS, WEBER SAW THAT PROFESSIONALIZATION & BUREAUCRATIZATION ARE NOT ANTITHETICAL. WEBER SAW THAT PROFESSIONALIZATION MUST BE VIEWED FROM THE STRUCTURAL, PROCESSUAL, & POWER PERSPECTIVES. WEBER'S UNDERSTANDING OF THE PROFESSIONS IS ATTRIBUTED TO 2 FACTORS: (1) WEBER SAW PROFESSIONS AS PART OF THE RATIONALIZATION PROCESS, & (2) HIS THINKING WAS NOT DISTORTED BY THE ABERRANT CASE OF THE MD IN PRIVATE PRACTICE AS THE PROTOTYPE OF THE PROFESSIONS. SINCE WEBER IGNORED THIS ABERRANT CASE, HIS IDEAS ARE MORE VALID. WEBER'S THINKING WAS EMBEDDED IN HIS BROADER ORIENTATION TOWARD THE RATIONALIZATION OF THE OCCIDENT. MODIFIED HA.

title: Applying Theory to Practice: Putting Deleuze to Work
abstract: The work of Deleuze and his associates has been widely discussed, and there is a burgeoning literature on the political implications for the education system specifically. Examples in Sweden, the UK and the USA are discussed. Deleuzian writing offers a powerful critique of educational bureaucracies, but the work also highlights problems in connecting work with a definite philosophical agenda to critical and political analyses of empirical processes and situations. Deleuze's philosophical agenda leads to radical but also to highly unconventional thinking and writing and this makes the argument notoriously inaccessible. Some general paradoxes in linking theory to practice emerge through Ranciere's discussion of philosophical autonomy and heteronomy. The work of Bourdieu in particular can also help to explain the difficulties of Deleuzian writing in terms of possible residual effects of a particular social context - the elite French university system of the 1960s and 1970s which fostered a particularly allusive style. Adapted from the source document

title: Breaking from the Past: The Challenge of Documenting Intimate Partner Violence in Southeastern Europe
abstract: Without systematically collected data on violence against women, it is difficult to know how often the violence occurs and what populations are most in need of services. These efforts are especially needed in southeastern Europe, where there have been significant legislative changes in the last ten years but few mechanisms for monitoring progress or enforcement of policies. Efforts to establish systematic data collection are hampered by a lack of infrastructure to support such projects, cultural emphasis on male authority, and long-standing conflicts in the region. Recommendations for further research in the region are included. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Collapsing under the Weight of Success: An NGO in Jakarta
abstract: This paper describes the changes that an NGO in Jakarta underwent as it grew larger, better funded & more closely linked to local government, while also becoming less accountable to & supportive of low-income groups. This NGO grew from being a small microbank working with women in one neighborhood to managing wide ranging "good governance" programs in five city districts, covering more than 100,000 people. Part of the reason for this change was more donor funding available for governance projects. Beginning as a small grassroots project driven by needs & capacities of local women, it became a large, complex, top-down, technically oriented bureaucracy guided by government & large international donors. The early focus on grassroots communications & networking changed to an emphasis on formal office meetings & official ceremonial events. Yet the NGO's new directions are judged by many government officials & donors to be a success. Adapted from the source document.

title: The Context and Process for Performance Evaluations: Necessary Preconditions for the Use of Performance Evaluations as a Measure of Performance--A Critique of Perry
abstract: This article challenges Perry's research using performance evaluations to determine whether the educational background of child welfare workers is predictive of performance. Institutional theory, an understanding of street-level bureaucracies, and evaluations of field education performance measures are offered as necessary frameworks for Perry's findings. Performance evaluations are insufficient absent a discussion of the link between organizational goals, supervisor training, practice protocols, and performance measurement tools. Three questions inform this critique and examples from child welfare practice illustrate the ways performance measures in this study may actually be a measure of organizational stasis and pressure to conform to practice as it has been. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: The Impact of Outside Agencies on Institutional Mental Health Care
abstract: Explores how intertwined bureaucracies shaped mental health care on an inpatient crisis stabilization ward, based on 5,000+ hours spent on the unit under 3 different administrations, operating alternately as a private & public institution. It is argued that the control of outside agencies over the delivery of therapeutic care limits the staff's ability to respond. It is suggested that the tensions between the hospital's supposed humanistic orientation & its strategies of risk management & stance of institutional paranoia create significant difficulties for staff members, whose terms of employment violate their roles as healers. It is concluded that the routines & procedures designed by insurance companies & other agencies have come to take priority over therapeutic activities. 2 Tables, 1 Appendix, 32 References. D. Schwartz

title: Bureaucracy: A Part of Society or Its Counteragent?
abstract: Examines the relationships among society, state, & bureaucracy in Russia. Traces the results of two surveys, one among the population & the other among officials/bureaucrats, conducted in July 2005 & in all regions of the country. States that most Russians consider bureaucracy harmful to the nation's interests, while officials believe their primary purpose is to preserve & increase their influence & power. Concludes that Russian officials have become a privileged segment of society. Tables, Figures. K. Duft

title: Living in a Walking World: Rural Mobility and Social Equity Issues in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Accessibility & mobility are embedded in the development nexus in far-reaching ways. Field studies of mobility among women & men in rural settlements with poor road access illustrate the frustrations & costs of living off-road. They are frequently marginalized & invisible, even to local administrations. State decentralization appears to have had little positive impact in reducing "tarmac bias" & improving rural service delivery. A range of potential interventions, from Intermediate Means of Transport to electronic communications is reviewed, & opportunities for building social capital in off-road areas through nurturing improvements in state-civil society relations are considered. 81 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Tensions in the Troubled Bureaucracy: Reform Initiatives in Public Organizations and Service Delivery Systems
abstract: Examines the outcome of several decades of attempts to reform public service delivery systems & the impediments posed by government bureaucracies. The public sector organization is confronted with dysfunctions of administration, rising public expectations, budgetary deficits, declining resources, & increases in population. Reforms are either inward-looking -- implementing improvements in accountability, efficiency, & effectiveness at the organizational level; or outward-looking -- where organizations are reconceptualized as open systems in dynamic relations with the client-user, the community, or the private sector. Among inward-looking reform measures are government reorganization, the public enterprise system, decentralization, & the integrated area development approach. It is suggested that redesigned inward-looking reforms integrate the outward-looking concept of partnership. 72 References. J. Sadler

title: 'Premium Network Spaces': A Comment
abstract: This paper is a response to some of the arguments developed by Stephen Graham in an article published in IJURR in Mar 2000. In that article, Graham argues that the contemporary conditions of development of infrastructure networks worldwide are particularly favorable to "secessionary tendencies" & lead to the deliberate creation of premium network(ed) spaces, ie, "new or retrofitted transport, telecommunications, power or water infrastructures that are customized precisely to the needs of powerful users & spaces, while bypassing less powerful users & spaces." In this response, I discuss cases in a variety of urban & national contexts that appear to stand in contrast with Graham's narrative. In conclusion, I stress four directions which additional empirical research on these issues should address: incorporating the role of historical time; differentiating between developed & developing countries; expanding the analysis to spaces other than large cities; & integrating the features of sociopolitical regimes. 18 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Technology and Organizational Structure: A Re -- Examination of the Findings of the Aston Group
abstract: Investigators of org'al behavior disagree about the importance of technology in a theory of org'al structure. The Aston group (D.S. Pugh, D.J. Hickson, C.R. Hinings, K.M. MacDonald, C. Turner & R. Lupton, see SA A9585 asserts that its res shows technology to be much less important than other variables, such as size. The purpose here is to investigate the importance of technology, giving special attention to whether it should be considered an independent or dependent variable in org'al theory. This question is examined by reanalyzing the data collected by the Aston group from 46 mfg & service org's. Their res was carried out at the Industr Admin Res Unit of the U of Aston in Birmingham, England. Their statement concerning size, technology & structure is first examined, with an assessment made of the degree to which their interpretations are supported by a more rigorous analysis of the data. The concepts & variables they developed are then reviewed to demonstrate how they can be put together into a theory of org'al structure which makes theoretical & empirical sense. Their data is reanalyzed by means of path analysis. A plausible theory which treats technology as an independent variable is then developed. Finally, a fairly complex model for org'al structure is reconstructed from the Aston group's data. Both these efforts reaffirm the value of treating technology as an independent variable & of using theory -- oriented path analysis. Modified HA.

title: Ethics Creep: Governing Social Science Research in the Name of Ethics
abstract: This article presents an analysis of the Canadian ethics review process by a member of a Research Ethics Board. The author suggests that the new formal system for regulating the ethical conduct of scholarly research is experiencing a form of "ethics creep." This is characterized by a dual process whereby the regulatory system is expanding outward to incorporate a host of new activities & institutions, while at the same time intensifying the regulation of activities deemed to fall within its ambit. These tendencies are demonstrated through an analysis of (1) the scope of research ethics protocols, (2) the concept of "harm" employed by these boards, (3) the use of informed consent provisions, & (4) the presumption that research participants will remain anonymous. To accentuate the nature of this ethics creep, comparisons are made between the ways in which identical knowledge-generation activities are governed within journalism & the academy. The conclusion suggests that one effect of the increasingly formalized research ethics structure is to rupture the relationship between following the rules & acting ethically. Some of the reasons for this "creep" are highlighted along with the risks that it poses for scholarship. 33 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Assessing the influence of regional Environmental Protection Agency offices on state hazardous waste enforcement decisions
abstract: In assessing the influence of regional Environmental Protection Agency EPA offices on the state management of hazardous waste programs, we focused on the extent to which federal administrative decisions affect levels of enforcement activity by state environmental agencies and whether these effects vary over time. Our results indicated that state enforcement actions were affected by state program capacity variables such as primacy and the strength of existing hazardous waste policies as well as one federal-level factor-the distribution of grant monies. The impact of federal oversight decisions was minimal. [Copyright 2007 Elsevier Inc.]

title: The Formal Analysis of Concepts
abstract: An exploration of concept content extraction using a formal logical/mathematical methodology (automatically, exclusively by rule). A fully formal definition of concept content is based on a German government initiative to establish "standards" regarding concepts, in conjunction with efforts to stipulate precisely (& then derivatively through computer programs) data requirements in certain government offices. 1 Figure, 23 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Information Sources and the Coverage of Social Issues in Partisan Publications: A Content Analysis of 25 Years of the "Progressive" and the "National Review"
authors: Tawnya Adkins Covert; Wasburn, Philo C
abstract: An extensive research literature concludes that, in the United States, mainstream media tend to present a remarkably narrow, homogenous and centrist conservative view of political life that tends to support maintenance of the status quo. This is often attributed to heavy media reliance on government officials, leaders of political groups, and large bureaucratic organization as routine, predictable sources of information. In this context, it is important to understand how explicitly partisan publications construct their accounts of public affairs that provide citizens with alternatives to this perspective proffered by the dominant media. A content analysis of 25 years of 2 of America's leading partisan magazines, the conservative "National Review" and the liberal "Progressive", provides data that raise questions about the extent to which information sources do influence the partisanship of media content. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Stress at Work: A Study of Organizational-Professional Conflict and Unmet Expectations
abstract: This study examines how certain conditions of work affect human service workers' job stress. We propose & assess a model of organizational-professional conflict to determine how professional & bureaucratic conditions of work influence service providers' expectations & in turn their job stress. The model was tested using data from a survey of 514 human service providers in Alberta, Canada. The findings suggest that whether service providers' expectations are met is critical in explaining job stress. Professional conditions of work relating to working relationships & client interactions are key to fulfilling service providers' expectations, whereas bureaucratic conditions of work that reflect role conflict & excessive role demands are particularly stressful. An unexpected finding is that bureaucratization of procedures that may limit service workers' control over their work does not contribute significantly to their job stress. 2 Tables, 2 Figures, 72 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Social Networks and the Importance of Political Intermediation on Commerce on Public Roads
abstract: This paper shows the relevance of studying the social networks of commerce on public roads. It focuses particularly on extant networks with the political-institutional system, due the fact that those links are the ones which make possible the use of public space. Through a qualitative analysis of these networks, we will show some of their main features & the centrality of political intermediation. This last element, far from being unique to commerce in the public space, is one of the main features of Mexican politics culture. Graphs, References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Far from Manila: Political Identities on a Philippine Island
abstract: Ethnographic fieldwork among Philippine islanders of the central Visayas is used to document the different ways -- both complementary & supplementary -- in which different persons on the island of Siquijor construct their social identities. Examined is the extent to which such social identities match the embeddedness of the administrative framework that is imposed by the central government in Manila. Confronted with a plurality of identities, whether national, provincial, or local, the islanders tend to refuse to choose & to live amid apparent & culturally acceptable contradictions that only reflect the seemingly permanent effervescence of their social situation. 13 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: A Reply to Michael Lipsky and Frederic Viguier's Comments
abstract: Herrick Chapman and the editorial board of French Politics, Culture & Society were kind enough to do me the honor of organizing this forum on my book The Bureaucrat and the Poor, which brings insights from Michael Lipsky, whose seminal Street-Level Bureaucracy has been highly influential on my own work, and Frederic Viguier, who has deep knowledge of the social and political history of French social welfare. I want, first of all, to warmly thank them for providing this opportunity for debate. While it is beyond the scope of this reply to address all of the many questions raised by my two colleagues, I will use this space to shed light on aspects of the book that may have remained unclear or implicit, and to provide some complementary comments. Adapted from the source document.

title: From "Observation Dude" to "An Observational Study": Gaining Access and Conducting Research Inside a Paramilitary Organization
Unions, Bureaucracy, and Change: Old Dogs Learn New Tricks Very Slowly
abstract: The paradigm of bureaucracy is used to examine the resistance to change that seems to characterize US unions. An institutional commitment to the status quo among union officials who have been unable or unwilling to adapt to changes in the workplace & the market is identified. Several factors that cause unions to resist change are specified: classical bureaucratic constraints, eg, hierarchy; union leadership & political limitations; the combative nature of union ideology; & the culture of insecurity & defensiveness. It is concluded that change will only occur when it is absolutely necessary, & even then will be encumbered by much foot-dragging. In Unions, Bureaucracy, and Change: Comment, Paul H. Rubin (Emory U, Atlanta, Ga) finds Craft's analysis unconvincing, & criticizes him for not incorporating a theory of rational behavior into his analysis & for providing a tenuous theory of the behavior of union officers. A theory of rational behavior that posits workers as principals & unions as agents is outlined. 55 References. W. Howard

title: THE PSYCHOLOGICAL INTERDEPENDENCE OF FAMILY, SCHOOL, AND BUREAUCRACY IN JAPAN
abstract: The Japanese 'examination hell' phenomenon is viewed as a series of rites through which the child passes from fam-centered to peer group-centered values in a 'particularistic' society. It is held that this model has greater explanatory power than the 'minimization of competition' mode proposed by others & that it also helps to explain the phenomenon of student radicalism & centrifugal relationship in Me communities. Modified HA.

title: Some Observations on Developmental Change and Bureaucracy in Developing Countries
abstract: Factors behind developmental change & the resistance to change are defined. The advantages & disadvantages of different types of change are compared. Change is defined as a transformation, a substitution of new ways of life for the prevailing old ones. Concern centers on what is to be changed, where, & how. Because change represents a move from the known to the unknown, there will be resistance to it. Uncertainty, detriment, & conservatism are considered the main factors underlying resistance to change. Change may be either comprehensive or partial. Advantages & disadvantages of each type of change are listed & compared. Change here is discussed on the assumption that the government of the country in question will take the greatest role in implementing change. Comprehensive change is more likely to be chosen in a state which has abundant material & human resources, a stable political structure, medium or better level of health & education standards, & an even-tempered population. Partial change is best suited to states which have poor resources, an unstable political base, low health & education standards, & an impatient & emotional people. Change may occur at different rates. Comprehensive change usually occurs rapidly while partial change occurs gradually. Immediate change is favored in countries where popular demands are urgent & there is a desire for rapid initiation of new programs. Gradual or incremental change is more appropriate to countries with inadequate resources which have relative political stability. Immediate comprehensive change is sought in such countries as the USSR where the government is very centralized. Gradual partial change is seen in countries with decentralized government & economy, ie, Pakistan & Turkey. Bureaucratic agencies involved in change may be either deliberative (eg, the parliament, party leadership, formal organizations, etc) or implementive (including such domestic agencies as public & private industries, such foreign agencies as UN bureaus, & private foreign enterprise). In most countries where change is required today, gradual partial change is probably the most effective means of implementation. Modified HA.

title: Out-of-Home Care Programs in Argentina: Contradictions Between Effective Protection and Long-Term Permanency
abstract: According to UNICEF, in 2011 nearly 14,700 children lacking parental care were attended by public protection measures, such as out-of-home care devices. The aim of this work is to account for the operating conditions of such interventions in Buenos Aires province. Our approach agrees with methodological perspectives guiding current interventions aimed at childhood, which consider children as subject-bearing rights and request all social institutions watch their well-being. The analysis exploits documentary and primary sources of information based on interviews with actors involved in public special protection devices. Our focus is directed towards the analysis of suggested and effective conditions of permanence in special protective measures and, therefore, in exiting from such devices. One of the main conclusions is that bureaucratic requirements aimed to establish an explicit time horizon for public cash transfers face conflicts with more general guidelines that should guide interventions with childhood.

title: Human-Social Development: Positivity and Paradox 1
abstract: This presentation seeks to unravel positivities and paradoxes of human-social development (HSD). The Enlightenment paradox has transformed epistemic ethos into bureaucratized disciplinarities. As a consequence, specialization of knowledge unwittingly breeds anti-intellectualism because both epistemic discourse and discursive formations are subverted by arrogance and ignorance. Our developmental hubris is a an outcome of this negative epiphany. Adapted from the source document.

title: Colonialism, Neopatrimonialism, and Hybrid State Formation in Malaysia and the Philippines
abstract: In Weberian scholarship, conventional wisdom views the corruption of the modern rational-legal bureaucratic state by local patrimonialisms as an endemic feature in non-Western postcolonial state formation. The resultant neopatrimonial state is often blamed for the social, political, and economic ills plaguing these societies. This essay challenges conventional wisdom and argues that neopatrimonialism is a process of hybrid state formation that has its origins in the cultural politics of colonial state building. This is achieved by drawing on a comparative study of British Malaya and the American Philippines, which offers contrastive trajectories of colonialism and state formation in Southeast Asia. Because of the precariousness of state power due to local resistance and class conflicts, colonial state building involved the deepening of patron-client relations for political control and of rational-legal bureaucracy for social development. In the process, local political relations were marked and displaced as traditional patrimonialisms distinguished from the new modern center. Through native elite collaborators and paternal-populist discourses, new patron-client relations were institutionalized to connect the colonial state to the native periphery. However, colonial officials with different political beliefs and ethnographic world views in the center competed over native policy and generated cyclical crises between patron-clientelist excess and bureaucratic entrepreneurship. Instead of the prevailing view that postcolonial states are condemned to their colonial design, and that authoritarian rule favors economic development, my study shows that non-Western state formation is non-linear and follows a cyclical pattern between predation and developmentalism, the excesses of which could be moderated.

title: Bureaucratic Birthdates: Chronometric Old Age as Resource and Liability in U.S. Refugee Resettlement
abstract: This article examines age in refugee resettlement by connecting it to the bureaucratic contexts in which refugees acquire and become categorized by birthdates found in their documents. Frequently used as an objective metric, chronometric age takes on new meaning in migration and determines access to work and welfare. This article traces the trajectory of age documents of refugees in a program for “seniors” (sixty and up) in Chicago, Illinois. Drawing upon anthropology and critical gerontology scholarship, I resituate chronometric age in the dynamic relationship between institutions and definitions of old age in the United States. My purpose is to call attention to the consequences of applying U.S. concepts of age to refugees with limited resources.

title: Management Tenure and Network Time: How Experience Affects Bureaucratic Dynamics
abstract: Meier & O'Toole have developed an empirical model that allows scholars to test for the impact of managers on a system & its outputs. In this article I attempt to add to management theory & analysis by examining the impact of time in the system & management tenure. I use ordinary least squares to replicate & expand upon Meier & O'Toole's results, using school superintendent survey responses along with outcome measures from school districts in Texas. The most interesting results suggest that (1) networking has a much larger impact when one controls for experience with the system; (2) experience with the system has independent effects on outcomes; (3) management tenure interacts with networking, resulting in greater outcomes; & (4) new managers may find alternative (possibly deceitful) ways of affecting outcomes other than working their networks. 6 Tables, 1 Appendix, 23 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Bureaucracy: Museums, Cultural Policies and Labor Flexibility in Guayaquil
abstract: Theoretically & methodologically, this analysis derives from an ethnographic view of the state as the concrete result of actors & institutions that channel ideologies & micro-practices to operate in the social world of ordinary subjects. Specifically, it explores the construction in Guayaquil of the Museum of Anthropology & Contemporary Art of the Central Bank of Ecuador (MAAC). The museum began its public activities in 2001 with the idea of projecting the work of society, independently from the collections or exhibitions also available. The "museum beyond the four walls,' it was called, "alive, engaging in a dialogue with society' through social research; public education in music, cinema, visual anthropology, & arts; & recreational activities -- all appealing to a wide variety of audiences. The official inauguration of the museum in July 2004 celebrated its completion with all the required rituality for the dedication of a classic museum for the city. Photographs. Adapted from the source document.

title: Gender, Vulnerability, and the Experts: Responding to the Maldives Tsunami
abstract: This article examines the initial response by national and international agencies to gender issues during the aftermath of the Maldives tsunami, arguing that it was, in general, inadequate. Some agencies took a gender blind approach, ignoring different impacts on men and women, as well as the effects of complex gender relations on relief and recovery efforts. Other agencies paid greater attention to gender relations in their response but tended to focus exclusively on the universal category of the 'vulnerable woman' requiring special assistance, whilst at the same time ignoring men's vulnerabilities. This article argues that such language entrenched women as victims, excluding them from leadership and decision-making roles and as such served to reinforce and re-inscribe women's trauma. It is suggested that it is partly because of the nature of international bureaucracies and the fact that this disaster drew foreign 'experts' from around the world that the response neglected or over-simplified gender issues. Adapted from the source document.

title: "A Scramble for Freight": The Politics of Collaboration along and across the Railway Tracks of Korea under Japanese Rule
abstract: From the American plains to the subcontinent of India, railroads have helped inscribe power on uncharted lands, opening the way for settlement & serving the empire. This paper explores another use of the railways -- during Japan's territorial colonization of Korea in which railway building & other infrastructural projects played a major part of the modernization of the colony. When Japanese rule of Korea ended along with WWII in 1945, Korea's rail system was second only to Japan's. It did not, however, evolve exactly as its Japanese colonial rulers wished. The Japanese tended to rule through cooperation with local Korean leaders, who neither desired nor were able to build a consolidated rail system. Rather, a disjointed system emerged in which swarms of petty Japanese & Korean freight carriers both on & off the rails, & competition among local transport agents, in a "scramble for freight," began to seriously disrupt any kind of state management of railways or stations. Rather than consolidation, there emerged a politics of collaboration among the many different carriers & local agents. Complete defiance against the colonial state was impossible, but the collective resistance of Korean & Japanese carriers certainly imposed serious limits on Japanese policy implementation. Figures, References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Time and Rulemaking: An Empirical Test of Theory
authors: Kerwin, Cornelius M; Furlong, Scott R
abstract: Factors influencing rule making by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) are investigated, with attention to legal requirements, bureaucratic elements, & political influences that may have impacted the passage of time in the issuance of 150 rules between 1986 & 1989. Data were obtained from EPA files. While the models employed account for a substantial amount of the variation in the time it takes to issue rules, their performance is erratic, & much remains to be explained. Existing theory offers important insights into delay in rule making, but more work is needed to identify & refine variables. 5 Tables, 2 Appendixes, 25 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Overcoming apartheid's legacy: The ascendancy of neoliberalism in South Africa's anti-poverty strategy
abstract: Poverty in South Africa is intertwined with a host of social and economic issues. The burden of poverty is exacerbated by limited access to basic services, poor housing, limited employment opportunities and inadequate infrastructure, which are an outcome of the terrible legacies of apartheid. During its first year in office, the ANC-dominated government officially endorsed a policy of 'growth from redistribution', whereby a strong state and a strong market were expected to serve as vehicles for generating growth and reducing poverty and inequality. By 1996, however, the government had embraced a standard neoliberal strategy as a central piece of its anti-poverty strategy. This article examines the potential contradictions between what appears to be on the surface progressive social policy on the one hand, and on the other, the implementation of aggressive neoliberal strategies of privatisation, liberalisation and deficit reduction to stimulate the economy and create jobs. This heavy reliance on market-led solutions is a high risk strategy, since there exists no example internationally where neoliberal adjustment of the sort championed by President Thabo Mbeki and Finance Minister Trevor Manual has produced a socially progressive outcome, especially in a country like South Africa, which is marked by extreme disparity and poverty.

title: European Union transgovernmental networks: The emergence of a new political space beyond the nation-state?
abstract: Does the European Union (EU) represent a new political order replacing the old nation-states? The assessment of the real character of political orders requires the identification of political key actors and of the specific structure of their interactions. Transgovernmental networks have been considered to be one of the most important features of EU integration. Unfortunately, the network structures, processes and the impact of these informal horizontal inter-organisational relations between nation-states are mostly unknown. The main objective of this article is to measure and explain the selective pattern of informal bilateral relations of high officials of the EU Member States' ministerial bureaucracies on the occasion of an EU Intergovernmental Conference. The quantitative data used rely on standardised interviews with 140 top-level bureaucrats. The statistical estimation of network choices is based on recent developments of exponential random graph models. Adapted from the source document.

title: Re-Enchanting Social Work? The Emerging 'Spirit' of Social Work in an Age of Economic Crisis
abstract: Luc Boltanski and Eve Chiapello's (2005) The New Spirit of Capitalism argues that capitalism has the capacity to absorb critique and become ideologically energised and discursively reinvigorated on account of this capacity. This article argues that their theorisation provides a useful theoretical lens through which to view and comprehend present attempts to re-enchant the profession and discursively infuse it with a new 'spirit', in times of 'austerity' and budget cuts: hence, the emerging emphasis on social work as a 'creative' profession needing to free itself from 'bureaucracy'. Although partly heeding the critique derived from the academic literature illuminating the constraints imposed on social work by an ever-expanding digital e-workload, this move is deeply ideological and needs to be warily regarded. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: КОРРУПЦИЯ: ИНСТРУМЕНТАЛЬНАЯ КОНЦЕПТУАЛИЗАЦИЯ
abstract: Статья посвящена инструментальной концептуализации корруп- ции, включая классификацию ее форм и определение институционального механиз- ма. Анализируются традиционные подходы к коррупции; акцентированы проблем- ные вопросы нормативно-ценностного подхода. Обоснована несостоятельность утверждений о позитивных функциях коррупции в качестве средства преодоления бюрократических барьеров. Представлена авторская трактовка понятия “политиче- ская коррупция” и описана иерархия форм политической и экономической корруп- ции, вершина которой – коррупционный “захват государства”. Определен институ- циональный механизм коррупции в сфере публичной власти, как злоупотребление, противоправное использование должностным лицом ресурсов власти не для реа- лизации функций государства и целей общественного развития, а для получения не- правомерного преимущества, извлечения личной и (или) групповой выгоды, имею- щей как материальное, так и нематериальное выражение.

title: The Stalinist Bureaucracy as a Social "Estate": Considerations from Rakovsky and Trotsky
abstract: The development of the concept of the "bureaucratic state" is traced in the writings of Marxist theorists, Leon Trotsky & Christian G. Rakovsky. Trotsky first warned that bureaucratization threatened Bolshevism in 1923, & in 1927 called it a "distinct social stratum." Rakovsky refined the concept into a general model describing the "divergence between a revolutionary class & its agents in power." Trotsky coined the term "bureaucratic caste" to differentiate it from a SC. Trotsky appears to have equated "caste" with "estate." Here, the bureaucratic "estate" is compared with the clerical "fourth estate" of the Middle Ages: both were hierarchical, denied private property, concentrated power & privilege at the apex of the hierarchy, & focused on ideology as their unifying force. In sum, the USSR & East European states are described as "bureaucratic states of Wc origin," but which do not represent the power of the proletariat. 12 References. J. Woodward.

title: The Impact of Mobile Phone Coverage Expansion on Market Participation: Panel Data Evidence from Uganda
abstract: An increased information flow due to mobile phone network expansions is expected to reduce marketing costs of agricultural commodities. We investigate this using panel data of 856 Ugandan households in 94 communities, where the number of communities covered by mobile phone networks increased from 41 to 87 between surveys in 2003 and 2005, respectively. After the expansion of coverage, we find increased sales of banana in remote communities but not of maize. The mobile phone coverage expansion seems to induce the market participation of farmers in remote areas who produce perishable crops. [Copyright Elsevier Ltd.]

title: INDUSTRIAL TRIAL ADMINISTRATION IN COMMUNIST EAST EUROPE
abstract: Industrial org throughout the Communist world reveals certain common features & faces certain common difficulties. The results of a Radio Free Europe study of East Europe are utilized to analyze some of these & a study of the Czechoslovak coal mining industry is used as an illustrative case. Communist control in these industrial fields overlies original org's in the Western mode. Its chief characteristics are centralized bur'tic control for pol'al orthodoxy & weeding out of unreliable managers; one-man leadership combined with a 3-part hierarchy-manag, union & party. The manager is in a difficult position since great pressure for output is placed on him, & he is suspect & ideologically unsavory in Communist soc structure. One-man leadership makes him responsible for results, but the collective controls of union & party render him vulnerable. Various informal & illicit practices have arisen which afford the manager greater security. However this evasion of danger is viewed officially as a threat & an anti-soc act & severely punished. Many of the characteristics of Communist industrial org seem inefficient & contrary to canons of admin'ive set, but when the pol'al goals of Communist society are taken into account these features are more understandable & appropriate. B. Beck.

title: Public Policy, Bureaucracy and the Institutionalization: The Case of the Bank of Brazil
authors: Prates, Antonio Augusto Pereira; Rocha, Daniele Fernandes
abstract: Discusses the relationships between state, bureaucracy, & society through a case study of a large bureaucratic institution -- the Bank of Brazil. An attempt is made to show the effects of bureaucratic structural change on the crystallization of the character ^& identity that make the institution a self-interested political actor in the state bureaucratic apparatus. Analytical dimensions from the sociology of organizations' theoretical tradition, especially the institutional paradigm, are emphasized. 2 Tables, 42 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: STATE, BUREAUCRACY, AND DEMOCRACY IN MARXIST THEORY
abstract: Certain texts of K. Marx & esp of F. Engels invite the establishment of a clear distinction between pol'al power & econ power. In this very subtle version of Marxist sociol, the state no longer appears to be a simple excrescence of the dominant class & its genesis is attributed to a dialectic larger than that which presided over the formation of the classes & their antagonism. Issuing from the society, the state becomes an independent power by its own logic. The state is more than the simple machine by which one class oppresses another: all of society, therefore all of the classes, are alienated. But, after having believed, with the liberals, in the progressive disappearance of the state, Marx discovered that the bur'tic state did not cease to progress & to extend its prerogatives. The state has developed its own dynamics of expansion. The general interest transforms itself into the private property of the bur'cy & into power which oppresses the citizens. This signified for Marx an alienation equivalent to econ alienation. He then attempted to explain this evolution & the mounting offensive of the burley, but he completely misunderstood the real nature of modern bur'cy, taking it for a simple, passing epiphenomenon. Modified IPSA Tr by M. Duke.

title: 'BUREAUCRATIC' ELEMENTS IN ORGANIZATIONS: SOME RESEARCH FINDINGS
abstract: An analysis based on 25 examples of bureaucratic production org's (BPO) in 19 diff societies, using data collected from Human Relations Area Files. A production org is defined as any soc group oriented to the combination or transformation of raw materials into material goods & such an org is called bureaucratic, if it has 3 or more levels of authority. Concern here is with 4 frequently cited attributes: a specialized division of labor, segmental participation of members, 'compensatory' rewards, &, emphasis on performance. Initial examination revealed not every BPO possesses all 4 or even any of these characteristics. If the pattern suggested by our data is generally valid, it has some far-reaching implications. It suggests that, for segregated participation to be institutionalized in any BPO performance emphasis, specialized division of labor, & compensatory rewards must also be institutionalized. It similarly suggests an order in which diff characteristics must be introduced in the course, of org'al development under conditions where they cannot be introduced simultaneously, as is often the case in underdeveloped areas. This pattern is in effect a scale, with the response pattern in accord with criteria for Guttman scaling. At this res stage this fact is merely noted. Our findings further suggest the usefulness of a new approach to Weber's construct of 'rational bur'cy'. Certain biases in selection of our cases were noted. Furthermore, some societies are represented more than once. In addition, it is apparent that our 'sample' is not very representative on a cross-cultural basis. Moreover, the fact that the pattern was discovered accidentally, ex post facto, indicates that it might well have occurred by chance. Thus there is no claim of definitive general validity for our results. H. H. Smythe.

title: Dignity and indignation: How people experiencing homelessness view services and providers
abstract: This article examines how people experiencing homelessness view their interactions with service providers. Drawing on a database of more than 500 transcribed interviews with people experiencing homelessness we find that descriptions of interactions with staff and providers were predominantly expressed in sharply negative terms, with experiences of objectification and infantilization being commonplace. In response to these experiences, nearly all were angry, and many simply opted out of the social service system in order to maintain a sense of dignity and self-respect. We argue that these responses should not simply be analyzed as an individual psychological or cognitive response, but rather as a result of the power relations and social inequities in the provider-client relationship. This suggests that the perpetuation of homelessness is not internal to the homeless individual as many claim, but rather may be embedded in the service industry itself, which subjects both clients and providers to bureaucratic forms of authority and experiences of disrespect. These negative descriptions are juxtaposed with positive comments, which offer potential solutions from homeless individuals themselves. We conclude that qualitative research, in contrast to a reliance on statistics and best practice assessments, is an important tool in developing socially just policies and programs serving those in need. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Is Weber's Type of Bureaucracy an Objective, True Type? Remarks on a Thesis by Renate Mayntz
abstract: A critical evaluation of Renate Mayntz's thesis that Max Weber's type of bureaucracy must be viewed as an 'objective, true type' shows that the thesis is not valid. Weber's understanding of bureaucracy was based on the Prussian-German type of administration at the turn of the century, referring extensively to the studies of Gustav Schmoller (1894, 1898) that dealt with Prussian bureaucracy & urban administration. Weber's concept of bureaucracy is therefore not an objective, true type; it is based on a nineteenth-century sociology of domination, in which the bureaucrat holds power over his client. Weber's notion of a 'rational bureaucracy' based on the thesis that the perfection of domination is rational, is considered a more valid & objective type applicable to various bureaucratic systems, rather than that of nineteenth-century Prussia alone. Modified HA.

title: Human Aspects of the National Information Infrastructure
abstract: Describes the impact of the national information infrastructure (NII) on US communities & culture. Increasing isolation of individuals, changing conceptions of privacy, & a breakdown in face-to-face relationships are among the social consequences of the NII. The massive federal investment in the NII requires a proportional effort to understand its human aspects & consequences. 2 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Miller's Silence on Bureaucracy
abstract: In a critique of David Miller's On Nationality (1995), it is argued that a state cannot be identified with the will of a nation or any other collection of citizens. Instead, a state is defined as a bureaucratic apparatus of rule, which in liberal democracies may encompass a unique source of legitimation, leadership, & policy separate from nationalist ties. However, as is argued by Alisdair MacIntyre (1985), & noted by Miller himself, a state may also erode nationalist ties through its predominant form of organization: bureaucratic hierarchies. It does so by abstracting individuals from social identities, destroying communal ties, & undermining cooperative practices hostile to its own power. Though these facts are recognized by Miller, he does not discuss how modern state bureaucracies fit into his communitarian vision of nationality. It is claimed that Miller's theory of nationalities will not cohere until he has dealt with the problem of bureaucracy in a way that fits into his extant claims concerning political community. 12 References. D. M. Smith

title: Clerical child sex abuse: The response of the Roman Catholic Church
abstract: The response of the Roman Catholic Church (RCC) to the clergy child sex abuse crisis is examined in the context of six cases in an Irish archdiocese. The RCC was not proactive in engaging with complainants and did not accept organizational responsibility for its personnel. Its statements on the crisis were abstract and sometimes transcendent in tone and its attempts to account for its inaction used apologia rather than apology. The Church's reliance on apologia is similar to that found in secular bureaucracies that believe themselves to be 'client-independent.' It is argued the Church needs to implement a 'client complaint' procedure similar to that found in 'client-dependent' commercial enterprises and that it must also reconnect with its own core values. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Mozambique: The Rise of a Micro Dual State
authors: Meneses, Maria Paula; de Sousa Santos, Boaventura
abstract: The decade from 1990 to 2000 was a period of sustained political activity in Africa, leading towards democratisation. Under this scope, Mozambique is widely seen as one paradigmatic success story. Yet, the country's multiparty democratic system remains challenged by a strong authoritarianism that hampers open deliberation in political public discourse. This paper discusses some reasons for this democratic hold-up in Mozambique's political and social transition within the broad and ongoing democratisation process in Sub-Saharan Africa. With an emphasis on the analysis of the political situation in the northern town of Angoche, this article argues that the persistence of central government authoritarianism is a reminder of a political liberalisation without democratising the political systems. Indeed, local municipal officials are now elected and receive revenue transfers, but remain limited by other measures.2 The central state successfully resists attempts to devolve broader decision-making authority to municipalities. Far from the ideal Weberian type of state bureaucracy, public administration is highly politicised in the sense that the building up of the administrative capacities of the state are seen as a way of consolidating the political leverage of the ruling party Frelimo. The paper defends, however, that indeed, a detailed analysis of the public political actions at local level, between distinct political structures, shows that successive authoritarian regimes have not totally erased the freedom of speech and thought, even if they have relegated opposition to ever more marginal spaces. Adapted from the source document.

title: Gender, Work and Transitions in the Local State
abstract: The paper describes the current employment patterns of men & women in local government in Scotland, Wales, & England, & examines the gender relations of work during a period of restructuring that is challenging the professionalized welfare bureaucracy & replacing it with a managerialized state informed by market principles. Men are declining as a percentage of employees, alongside decreasing numbers of full-time jobs & increasing part-time & temporary contracts, suggesting some decrease in the relative desirability of public service employment. Nevertheless the challenges to traditional conceptions of paternalistic, bureaucratic welfare have facilitated women's increasing access to professional & managerial grades, but men have continued to dominate most positions of power & authority. The continuing gender divisions of labor, & women's perceptions of a sharper axis of gender conflict surrounding the period of reorganization into single tier authorities in Scotland & Wales, suggest that it is not simply a matter of time until a rational, functional state eradicates remaining inequalities between the sexes. Neither however can a radical feminist perspective, which treats the state as bound to reproduce women's subordination, account for the degree of progressive change. Instead it is argued that there is genuine indeterminacy in the restructuring process, which, given women's representation & participation, seems likely to disrupt further the legacy of patriarchal relations informing the trajectory of state bureaucracies. 5 Tables, 53 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Writing Upwards: How the Weak Wrote to the Powerful
abstract: "Writing Upwards" describes a genre of letter-writing between two very unequal correspondents. Humble subjects wrote individually to monarchs and other rulers, workers wrote to factory bosses, impoverished refugees wrote to relief committees, parishioners wrote to their clergy and also to God. Often, but not always, they wrote in pursuit of some personal advantage. They trusted in the power of a personal approach to by-pass bureaucratic procedures which seemed insensitive and obstructive. In order to ingratiate themselves, they borrowed or at least crudely imitated the language of their superiors. My paper draws on published research from Italy and elsewhere to identify the principal modes of "writing upwards," whether deferential, demanding or downright abusive. In the case of the letters of Australian Aboriginal people to their administrators, new elements emerge: an appeal to shared Christian values, and the notion of a contractual obligation yet to be fulfilled. [web URL: http://jsh.oxfordjournals.org/content/49/2/317.abstract]

title: Bureaucracy and Development in Syria: The Case of Agriculture
abstract: The Syrian bureaucracy is examined through a case study of its role in agricultural development. Discussion centers on: (1) the degree of technocratic rationality imparted to agrarian policy; (2) the effectiveness of the bureaucracy in carrying out its agricultural policy; (3) the beneficial role of the bureaucracy for the agrarian economy & the peasantry; & (4) the political consequences of the bureaucracy's role in agriculture. It is shown that, while senior public officials play a role in shaping agrarian policy, this role is in turn shaped by Ba'thist ideology & a political structure that vests control over high policy in the presidency & the ruling party rather than in the ministerial bureaucracy. Implications for agricultural planning, administrative leadership, & patronage politics are discussed, & it is concluded that the bureaucracy has implemented development programs that have greatly benefited agriculture. 17 References. Modified HA

title: Burundi: Seven Years of Refugee Return
abstract: Before UNHCR started its facilitated return programme in spring 2002 Burundi ranked second (after Afghanistan) in UNHCR's global 'country of origin' statistics, despite its small size. With the return of half a million refugees and the majority of the country's 375,000 internally displaced persons since then, the war-ravaged country of some eight million people has had to reintegrate about 10% of its population. Refugee return has taken place mostly to rural areas in border provinces, in a context of widespread poverty, lack of basic infrastructure and scarcity of land. To gain better information on the situation of returned refugees, UNHCR set up a country-wide returnee monitoring scheme. This, and a number of assessments organised with partners, generated the following conclusions. Adapted from the source document.

title: Ideology and Organizations in Agricultural Development: The Case of Malaysia
abstract: Examined is the hypothesis that the growing public enterprise involvement in the Malaysian agricultural sector represents a definite policy choice & ideological commitment to public enterprise over either private firms or egalitarian institutions. However, the rapid growth of such public enterprises brings with it a three-fold impact. Ideologically, it reflects a trend toward greater centralization of decision-making. Administratively, it creates problems of interbureaucratic conflict & duplication & projects a real need for ongoing evaluation. In terms of human resource development, maximum attention should be given to the role of bureaucracies in creating new farmer leadership material & greater farmer involvement. This role has been completely neglected in the past. 1 Figure. Modified HA.

title: The Inter-American Commission of Women and Women's Suffrage, 1920-1945
abstract: In studies of the international dimensions of women's suffrage, the role of international organisations has been overlooked. This article examines the suffrage activities of the Pan-American Union (PAU), and in particular those of the Inter-American Commission of Women (IACW), between 1920 and 1945. Attentive to historical context, the examination suggests that international organisations can be both bearers of state interests and platforms for social movement interests. The article also argues that while not independent bureaucracies, the PAU and IACW nevertheless had some importance for suffrage that cannot be attributed either to their state members or to the suffragist movements. Adapted from the source document.

title: EXPANSION AND TENDENCY OF PUBLIC BUREAUCRACY
abstract: The growth of admin'ive bur'cy in contemporary society is discussed & some observations as to the methodological difficulties involved in analyzing this phenomenon are offered. Predictions & early studies made by H. Spencer, K. Marx, G. Mosca, & M. Weber are reviewed. Recently, L. Neunderfer in DIE ANGESTELLTEN, NEUER VERSUCH EINER STANDORT- BESTIMMUNG (White-Collar Employees, A New Attempt at Determining Their Position, Stuttgart, Germany:1961) is cited in his thesis that intellectuality has been greatly bur'ized, but that bur'cy in its part has been impaired by the intellectual ferment. Res which demonstrates methods of measuring the bur'tic phenomenon with particular reference to the US is discussed (eg, C. N. Parkinson, PARKINSON'S LAW OR THE PURSUIT OF PROGRESS, 1957, M. Abramovitz & V. Eliasberg, THE GROWTH OF PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT, Princeton, NJ: 1957). Bur'ization in Europe as studied by E. Sturm is considered. 2 developments are found indisputable: (a) The increase in the tasks of the state, beginning at mid-cent & up to the present, as initiated by the parliaments; (b) The sacrificing of the principle of efficiency in personnel policy for the cause of assumptions motivated by party interests. These developments are observed in various European countries: France, Switzerland, Austria, the UK, Germany, & also in Italy. The scope & extent of bur'ization in Italy are analyzed through statistics on the N of persons in the employment of state & local gov's from 1923-1964. The distribution of leading state functionaries by province within Italy as well as those concerned with activities directed towards foreign countries is examined. A heavy concentration of bur'ization in the South is noted, which showed a considerable increase (35.76% for the peninsular South, & 20.55% for the Italian islands) between 1954 & 1961. The consequences of this phenomenon are considered & it is concluded that the situation must be considered in an historic context & in connection with efforts at ED. A loss in operative efficiency is seen as inevitable for the bur'cy of countries which are on the road to ED without sufficient planning. Sociol'al res is suggested to study the pol'al measures which have to be taken to avoid distortion of civil service recruitment to absurd dimensions. M. Maxfield.

title: The Social Psychology of Making and Responding to Hospital Complaints: An Account Model of Complaint Processes
abstract: Draws on a study of 399 formal complaints by patients against UK hospitals to analyze the interaction between complainant & hospital as a social episode in which the hospital is called to account for violation of the complainant's normative expectations. The noninstrumental & uncrystallized character of many complaints is emphasized. Letters of complaint & replies from the hospital provide insights into the social psychology of complaining, the goals of complainants, & the elements of successful apologies. Factors correlating with complainants' satisfaction confirm the importance of a socially appropriate response to complaints. Implications are discussed both in relation to hospital complaints & in the context of the literature on disputes in general. 7 Tables, 33 References. Adapted from the source document.

title: Managerial and mobilizing internationalism in the British docks and seafaring sector
abstract: This article considers two types of internationalization process among British docks and seafaring unions, distinguishing between 'mobilizing' and 'managerial' internationalism with reference to two case studies. The article argues that an internationalism which seeks to mobilize membership in an oppositional way is dependent on the framing, by union leadership, of particular material grievances as necessitating an international, rather than national, response. Managerial internationalism, by contrast, sees a more classically bureaucratic division of labour, in which officials administer more general political and regulatory priorities that are derived from membership concerns. The underlying material determinant of these types is argued to be the degree of labour market security possessed by unions involved. Where workers experience a strong challenge to their employment through international labour competition a mobilizing internationalism is more likely to emerge. But these material conditions also engender spatial and temporal limits within which mobilizing internationalism is constrained. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Means to an End: An Assessment of the Status-blind Approach to Protecting Undocumented Worker Rights
abstract: This article applies the tenets of bureaucratic incorporation theory to an investigation of bureaucratic decision making in labor standards enforcement agencies (LSEAs), as they relate to undocumented workers. Drawing on 25 semistructured interviews with high-level officials in San Jose and Houston, I find that bureaucrats in both cities routinely evade the issue of immigration status during the claims-making process, and directly challenge employers' attempts to use the undocumented status of their workers to deflect liability. Respondents offer three institutionalized narratives for this approach: (1) to deter employer demand for undocumented labor, (2) the conviction that the protection of undocumented workers is essential to the agency's ability to regulate industry standards for all workers, and (3) to clearly demarcate the agency's jurisdictional boundaries to preserve institutional autonomy and scarce resources. Within this context, enforcing the rights of undocumented workers becomes simply an institutional means to an end.

title: State Practices and Exercising Citizenship: Encounters between People and Bureaucracy in Bolivia
abstract: This text analyses the state practices that limit and expand the experience of citizenship, and the strategies used by people in order to exercise their rights. The work is based on an ethnographic study that looks at the encounters between Bolivian population and state bureaucracy. The study looks at those organs of the State responsible for the registration of identity of individuals (identity cards), as well as the assignation of legal status to associations (legal entity). The study explores the meanings given to citizenship in the space that divides de jure equality from de facto equality, which are experienced through day-to-day encounters with state bureaucracy. Adapted from the source document.

title: Fishing for Development? Tuna Resource Access and Industrial Change in Papua New Guinea
abstract: Papua New Guinea (PNG) is an island state with sovereign rights over valuable tuna resources. Historically, PNG captured value from tuna only by charging licensing fees to foreign fishing fleets, which relegated PNG as a source of raw material for the global tuna industry. To capture more value from tuna -- including much-needed jobs and infrastructure -- the PNG government now offers firms that invest in domestic tuna processing plants strategic, long-term fishing licences. This strategy of "obligating embeddedness" enables PNG to reorder the international division of labour in the canned tuna sector, but socio-economic outcomes are shaped by competition within the global tuna industry, the core business strategies of foreign firms and domestic conditions in PNG. Ultimately, a state's right to control the terms of access to tuna is not synonymous with its ability to shape the local-level consequences that emerge as firms comply. These findings reveal the peculiar nature of state sovereignty over pelagic marine resources and the complications of exploiting them to achieve domestic economic and social objectives. Adapted from the source document.

title: Natural Resources and Bureaucratic Predators
abstract: Bureaucrats responsible for natural resource management systematically advocate programs that are financially irrational or environmentally costly, & increase the command sector of the economy at the expense of voluntary exchange, as exemplified in timber production & range land management. The logic underlying this bureaucratic behavior is presented. Since it is bureaucratically profitable to provide programs that yield concentrated benefits to politically important, supportive clientele groups, such programs continue to be advocated even if they are socially costly. However, bureaus grow along with their programs, & budgets for managing socially costly programs are financed out of the treasury, which is a common pool resource funded by the taxpayers. Society as a whole increasingly loses productive resources to socially costly programs, & is forced to bear the cost of more & more decisions in which it has no voice. Advocated is a "predatory" bureau, whose budget is an increasing function of the number of socially costly bureaucratic programs that it can demonstrate to exist. Those who might argue that this device is "just another bureau" should understand that the predatory bureau would harness the bureaucrats' own incentive structure to counter common bureaucratic pathologies. Modified AA.

title: Intellectuals: Public and Proletarian
abstract: A review essay on a book by Russell Jacoby, The Last Intellectuals: American Culture in the Age of Academe (New York: Basic Books, 1987 [see listing in IRPS No. 50]). Jacoby describes the demise of the public intellectual & the rise of the academic bureaucrat. The Last Intellectuals dwells on the borderland between philosophy, sociology, & politics that Georg Simmel called cultural history; as a cultural historian, Jacoby belongs to the line of thought initiated after WWI by Karl Mannheim & Jose Ortega y Gasset, who independently discovered the generation as a central concept in sociological enquiry. Jacoby describes three generations: the generation of 1900, the high-water mark of the public intellectual; the generation of 1920, which carried through the transition from the public to the academic intellectual; & the generation born in the 1940s, most of whom made the move to academia. Jacoby's work occupies an important position in the debate about the meaning of modernity; his essential contribution to contemporary thought is to have demonstrated the exhaustion of the progressive democratic myth of open discussion in a genuine public situation. F. S. J. Ledgister

title: Constructing Isomorphism in an Interorganizational Network
authors: Glazier, Jack D; Hall, Peter M
abstract: P. DiMaggio & W. Powell's (1983) isomorphic model recognizes the potential for social construction in a social system.
